Volume 1

Foundations

Data structures, algorithms, operating systems, the Node.js runtime and networking. The layer underneath every framework.

Part 7 — Computer Science Fundamentals: Data Structures

7.1 Why a backend engineer must care about data structures

A data structure is a way of arranging data in memory so that certain operations are cheap. That is the whole idea. An array makes "give me item number 4,096" cheap. A hash map makes "give me the record for key order:8813" cheap. A heap makes "give me the most urgent job" cheap. Every structure buys some cheap operations by making other operations expensive, and a senior engineer's job is to know which operations the system will actually perform millions of times, and to pick accordingly.

You may think you rarely choose data structures. You do it all day; you just do it through libraries and databases:

  • Request handling. Every HTTP request arrives as a byte array (Buffer). Headers are parsed into a hash map. The JSON body becomes a tree of JavaScript objects. The router walks a trie (Fastify) or a list of regular expressions (Express) to find your controller.
  • Caching. An in-memory cache is a hash map plus an eviction policy (LRU, LFU). Redis is a hash map of hash maps, lists, sets, sorted sets and streams that you talk to over TCP.
  • Queues. BullMQ, RabbitMQ and Kafka are queues with different guarantees. A Kafka partition is an append-only array on disk. A RabbitMQ queue is a linked list in memory that spills to disk under pressure.
  • Indexes. A PostgreSQL B-tree index is a balanced tree of 8 KB pages. A GIN index is an inverted index: a map from a token to a sorted array of row pointers. A hash index is a hash map on disk.
  • Rate limiting. A token bucket is a counter plus a timestamp in a hash map keyed by client id. A sliding-window log is a sorted set of timestamps.
  • Feeds and rankings. Merging the 50 most recent posts from 300 followed accounts is a k-way merge with a heap. De-duplicating "already seen" items is a set, or at billions of items, a Bloom filter.

The reason this matters more for backend engineers than for almost anyone else is the multiplier. A frontend function that takes 30 ms runs once, for one user, on their machine. A backend function that takes 30 ms runs for every request, on your machine, and in Node.js it runs on the single thread that every other in-flight request is waiting for. At 500 requests per second, 30 ms of CPU per request means 15 CPU-seconds of work per wall-clock second. You would need 15 cores to keep up, and a Node.js process has one.

7.1.1 How the wrong structure becomes an incident

Imagine an e-commerce notifications service. Marketing triggers a campaign to 80,000 customers. The code de-duplicates the recipient list like this:

const unique: string[] = [];
for (const email of recipients) {
  if (!unique.includes(email)) unique.push(email); // O(n) scan for every item
}

Array.prototype.includes scans the array from the start. For 80,000 recipients the loop performs roughly 80,000 x 40,000 = 3.2 billion string comparisons. On a fast core that is 3 to 6 seconds during which the event loop does nothing else: no health checks answered, no other requests served. Kubernetes marks the pod unready, traffic shifts to the remaining pods, each receives more campaign traffic, and each freezes in turn. The fix is a Set, which does the same job in about 8 milliseconds. The bug was invisible at 500 recipients in staging.

That is the pattern to remember: data-structure mistakes are silent until n gets large, and n gets large in production, at night.

7.1.2 Big-O in one table

Big-O notation describes how the cost of an operation grows with the number of items, n. We ignore constant factors and care about the shape of the curve. Read the table as "roughly how many steps for n = 1,000 versus n = 1,000,000":

Growth Name n = 1,000 n = 1,000,000 Typical backend example
O(1) constant 1 1 hash map lookup, array index, heap peek
O(log n) logarithmic 10 20 binary search, B-tree index lookup, heap push and pop
O(n) linear 1,000 1,000,000 array scan, includes, indexOf, linked-list search
O(n log n) linearithmic 10,000 20,000,000 sorting, building a heap by repeated pushes
O(n^2) quadratic 1,000,000 10^12 nested loops, includes inside a loop, splice inside a loop

Three words you will meet throughout this Part:

  • Amortized means "averaged over many operations". An array push is usually O(1), but occasionally the array must grow and copy everything, which is O(n). Averaged over all pushes it is still O(1).
  • Contiguous means "stored side by side in memory". CPUs love contiguous data because they fetch memory in 64-byte cache lines and prefetch the next lines. Scattered data (linked lists, objects pointing at objects) defeats that and costs a cache miss of roughly 100 ns per hop.
  • In-memory means the data lives in the process heap and dies with the process. Everything in this Part is in-memory. Each concept ends by telling you what replaces it when data must survive a restart or be shared between pods: Redis, PostgreSQL or Kafka.

A note on V8. Node.js runs on Google's V8 engine, and V8 makes many decisions on your behalf: how arrays are stored, when an object silently turns into a hash table, when a string is really a tree of string pieces. Those decisions change the constants hidden inside your Big-O, and at scale the constants are the difference between 2 ms and 200 ms. We point them out where they matter.

7.2 Arrays

Concept

An array is a contiguous block of memory holding items in order, addressed by an integer index starting at 0. Because the items sit side by side and each slot has the same size, the address of item i is start + i * slotSize, which is one multiplication and one addition. That is why reading arr[i] costs the same whether the array has 10 items or 10 million.

In JavaScript, Array is the everyday array, and it hides a lot: it can grow, it can hold mixed types, and V8 changes its internal representation depending on what you put in it. Typed arrays (Uint8Array, Float64Array, Buffer) are the "real" fixed-size arrays of raw numbers.

Why does it exist?

Without arrays there is no "a list of things" in memory. Every request body, every result set from PostgreSQL, every batch of messages from Kafka arrives as an array. The alternative, a chain of individually allocated objects (a linked list, Section 7.4), costs a pointer per item and a cache miss per hop. Arrays exist because the CPU is fastest when data is packed and sequential, and because index arithmetic is the cheapest lookup there is.

Mental model

Imagine a street of identical houses, numbered from 0. To find house 4,096 you do not knock on 4,095 doors; you compute the position and walk straight there. Adding a house at the end of the street is easy if there is empty land; if not, the city buys a bigger plot and moves every house (the resize). Inserting a house in the middle means shifting every house after it by one lot, which is the expensive operation arrays are bad at.

How it works

  1. Allocation. V8 allocates a JSArray object with a length and a pointer to a backing store (a FixedArray or FixedDoubleArray). The backing store has a capacity that is usually larger than length.
  2. Growth. When you push past capacity, V8 allocates a new backing store of size old + old/2 + 16, copies the elements, and frees the old one. Copying is O(n), but it happens rarely, so push is O(1) amortized.
  3. Elements kinds. V8 tracks what kind of elements the array holds so it can pick the fastest storage. Small integers (Smis) are stored unboxed. Doubles are stored unboxed in a FixedDoubleArray. Anything else (strings, objects) is stored as tagged pointers. The kind only ever gets more general, never more specific.
  4. Packed vs holey. [1, 2, 3] is packed. new Array(1000) or arr[50] = x on a 10-element array creates holes. Holey arrays make every read check for a hole and, if found, walk the prototype chain, which is slower and defeats some optimizations.
  5. Dictionary mode. If an array becomes very sparse (arr[1_000_000] = 1 on an empty array), V8 gives up on contiguous storage and turns the elements into a hash table. Index access is then a hash lookup, not pointer arithmetic.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> PACKED_SMI: literal of small integers
    PACKED_SMI --> PACKED_DOUBLE: push a fractional number
    PACKED_DOUBLE --> PACKED_ELEMENTS: push a string or object
    PACKED_SMI --> HOLEY_SMI: write past length leaving gaps
    HOLEY_SMI --> HOLEY_DOUBLE: push a fractional number
    HOLEY_DOUBLE --> HOLEY_ELEMENTS: push a string or object
    PACKED_ELEMENTS --> HOLEY_ELEMENTS: delete an element
    HOLEY_ELEMENTS --> DICTIONARY: very sparse index write

Time complexity

Operation Best Average Worst Notes
Read arr[i] O(1) O(1) O(1) O(1) hash lookup in dictionary mode, but with a much larger constant
Write arr[i] = x (in bounds) O(1) O(1) O(1) may trigger an elements-kind transition once
push O(1) O(1) amortized O(n) worst case is the resize copy
pop O(1) O(1) O(1)
shift / unshift O(n) O(n) O(n) V8 sometimes "left-trims" the backing store to make shift cheap; never rely on it
splice insert or delete in the middle O(n) O(n) O(n) shifts everything after the index
indexOf / includes / find O(1) O(n) O(n) best case is a hit at index 0
Binary search on a sorted array O(1) O(log n) O(log n) you must keep it sorted
sort O(n) O(n log n) O(n log n) TimSort, stable; best case is already-sorted input
slice(a, b) / spread O(k) O(k) O(k) k = number of copied elements
concat O(n + m) O(n + m) O(n + m) allocates a new array every time

Memory implications (V8, Node.js)

  • Node.js does not enable V8 pointer compression, so each element in a PACKED_ELEMENTS array is an 8-byte tagged pointer. One million objects in an array cost 8 MB for the pointers plus the objects themselves (a small object with 5 properties is roughly 60 to 80 bytes), so about 90 MB total.
  • PACKED_SMI_ELEMENTS stores each integer in the 8-byte slot directly with no heap object. PACKED_DOUBLE_ELEMENTS stores raw 64-bit doubles. Mixing one string into a million-integer array converts every slot to a tagged pointer and boxes every double into a HeapNumber, which can more than double the memory.
  • Typed arrays (Float64Array, Uint32Array, Buffer) store raw bytes in an ArrayBuffer that lives outside the V8-managed JavaScript heap (it counts toward process.memoryUsage().arrayBuffers). They cannot hold holes or mixed types, and they are the right tool for counters, bitmaps and binary protocols.
  • Backing stores over-allocate by roughly 50 percent, so a 1-million-element array may hold capacity for 1.5 million. arr.length = 0 keeps the backing store; assigning a fresh [] releases it.
  • The maximum array length is 2^32 - 1. Long before that, a 100-million-element array of objects will exhaust the default old-space heap limit (about 2 GB to 4 GB depending on Node.js version and machine memory).

Practical example

Bulk operations are where arrays meet the database. PostgreSQL limits a single statement to 65,535 bind parameters, and a very large INSERT also holds a transaction open longer, so you chunk. Here is a generic chunker and a fixed-size ring buffer, the one array structure every backend engineer should be able to write from memory: it keeps the last N values in a fixed amount of memory by overwriting the oldest slot.

// utils/chunk.ts
export function chunk<T>(items: readonly T[], size: number): T[][] {
  if (size <= 0) throw new RangeError('chunk size must be positive');
  const out: T[][] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i += size) {
    out.push(items.slice(i, i + size)); // slice is O(size); total O(n)
  }
  return out;
}

// metrics/ring-buffer.ts
export class RingBuffer {
  private readonly buf: Float64Array; // contiguous unboxed doubles, off the JS heap
  private head = 0;                   // index of the next write
  private filled = 0;                 // number of slots holding real data

  constructor(private readonly capacity: number) {
    if (!Number.isInteger(capacity) || capacity <= 0) {
      throw new RangeError('capacity must be a positive integer');
    }
    this.buf = new Float64Array(capacity); // 8 bytes per slot, allocated once
  }

  push(value: number): void {
    this.buf[this.head] = value;                 // O(1): overwrite the oldest slot
    this.head = (this.head + 1) % this.capacity; // wrap around
    if (this.filled < this.capacity) this.filled++;
  }

  percentile(p: number): number {
    if (this.filled === 0) return 0;
    // Typed-array sort is numeric, so 10 sorts after 9 (unlike Array.prototype.sort).
    const sorted = this.buf.slice(0, this.filled).sort();
    const idx = Math.min(sorted.length - 1, Math.floor((p / 100) * sorted.length));
    return sorted[idx];
  }

  get size(): number {
    return this.filled;
  }
}

A 10,000-slot ring buffer is 80 KB, allocated once, forever. Compare that with latencies.push(ms) on a plain array in a long-running process, which is a memory leak with a delay.

NestJS example

A latency interceptor that records every request's duration into the ring buffer, and an internal endpoint that exposes p50, p95 and p99. The store is a default-scoped provider, which in NestJS means a single instance per application, shared across all requests in the process.

// metrics/latency.store.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { RingBuffer } from './ring-buffer';

@Injectable()
export class LatencyStore {
  private readonly window = new RingBuffer(10_000); // last 10k requests, 80 KB fixed

  record(ms: number): void {
    this.window.push(ms);
  }

  snapshot() {
    return {
      samples: this.window.size,
      p50: this.window.percentile(50),
      p95: this.window.percentile(95),
      p99: this.window.percentile(99),
    };
  }
}

// metrics/latency.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, finalize } from 'rxjs';
import { LatencyStore } from './latency.store';

@Injectable()
export class LatencyInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(private readonly store: LatencyStore) {}

  intercept(_ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const started = process.hrtime.bigint();
    return next.handle().pipe(
      finalize(() => {
        const elapsedMs = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - started) / 1_000_000;
        this.store.record(elapsedMs); // runs on success and on error
      }),
    );
  }
}

// metrics/metrics.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { LatencyStore } from './latency.store';

@Controller('internal/metrics')
export class MetricsController {
  constructor(private readonly store: LatencyStore) {}

  @Get('latency')
  latency() {
    return this.store.snapshot(); // per-pod numbers; cluster-wide aggregation is Prometheus' job
  }
}

Register the interceptor globally with APP_INTERCEPTOR in a module's providers, and remember this is a per-process view. Aggregating across 12 pods is what Prometheus histograms are for (see the Observability part).

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL has first-class array columns. They are a good fit for small, unordered tag lists that are always read together with the row, and a bad fit for anything you need to join, count or enforce foreign keys on.

CREATE TABLE products (
  id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name        text    NOT NULL,
  tags        text[]  NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  price_cents integer NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents >= 0)
);

-- GIN indexes each array element, so "contains" and "overlaps" use the index.
CREATE INDEX products_tags_gin ON products USING gin (tags);

-- products carrying ALL of these tags
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE tags @> ARRAY['dental', 'consumable'];

-- products carrying ANY of these tags
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE tags && ARRAY['gloves', 'masks'];

-- pass a JS array as ONE bind parameter instead of building "IN ($1,$2,...)"
SELECT id, name, price_cents FROM products WHERE id = ANY($1::bigint[]);
Bitmap Heap Scan on products  (cost=24.31..1893.02 rows=612 width=41) (actual time=0.412..3.870 rows=588 loops=1)
  Recheck Cond: (tags @> '{dental,consumable}'::text[])
  Heap Blocks: exact=402
  Buffers: shared hit=419
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on products_tags_gin  (cost=0.00..24.16 rows=612 width=0) (actual time=0.301..0.301 rows=588 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (tags @> '{dental,consumable}'::text[])
        Buffers: shared hit=17
Planning Time: 0.190 ms
Execution Time: 3.951 ms

The = ANY($1) form matters in Node.js: it keeps one prepared statement regardless of how many ids you pass, so the planner cache stays warm and you never hit the parameter limit.

TypeORM example

// products/product.entity.ts
import { Column, Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn } from 'typeorm';

@Entity({ name: 'products' })
export class Product {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('increment', { type: 'bigint' })
  id!: string; // bigint comes back as a string from the pg driver

  @Column({ type: 'text' })
  name!: string;

  @Column({ type: 'text', array: true, default: '{}' })
  tags!: string[];
}

// products/product.repository.ts
import { ArrayContains, In, Repository } from 'typeorm';

export class ProductQueries {
  constructor(private readonly repo: Repository<Product>) {}

  withAllTags(tags: string[]) {
    return this.repo.findBy({ tags: ArrayContains(tags) }); // tags @> $1
  }

  byIds(ids: string[]) {
    return this.repo.findBy({ id: In(ids) }); // id IN ($1, $2, ...) -- chunk large lists
  }
}

TypeORM's @Index decorator cannot express USING gin, so create that index in a migration with queryRunner.query('CREATE INDEX ... USING gin (tags)').

Sequelize example

import { DataTypes, Model, Op, Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export class Product extends Model {
  declare id: number;
  declare name: string;
  declare tags: string[];
}

export function initProduct(sequelize: Sequelize) {
  Product.init(
    {
      id: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, autoIncrement: true, primaryKey: true },
      name: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false },
      tags: { type: DataTypes.ARRAY(DataTypes.TEXT), allowNull: false, defaultValue: [] },
    },
    { sequelize, tableName: 'products', timestamps: false },
  );
}

// tags @> ARRAY['dental','consumable']
await Product.findAll({ where: { tags: { [Op.contains]: ['dental', 'consumable'] } } });
// tags && ARRAY['gloves','masks']
await Product.findAll({ where: { tags: { [Op.overlap]: ['gloves', 'masks'] } } });

DataTypes.ARRAY is PostgreSQL-only in Sequelize; MySQL users get an error at model definition time.

Production scenario

A product-listing endpoint serves 1,500 RPS with 48 products per page. The PostgreSQL driver returns each page as an array of 48 row objects (roughly 12 KB of JavaScript objects); mapping it to DTOs is 48 iterations, well under 0.1 ms. That is the healthy case: small arrays on the request path are essentially free.

The unhealthy case is a large array on the request path. The same service personalizes results by hiding products the user has blocked. The block list for a power user has 50,000 entries, and the code does page.filter(p => !blocked.includes(p.id)). That is 48 x 50,000 = 2.4 million comparisons, about 3 to 5 ms of CPU per request. At 1,500 RPS that is 4.5 to 7.5 CPU-seconds per second: the process is saturated by a single feature. Converting blocked to a Set once per request (50,000 inserts, about 3 ms) is not the fix either; caching the Set per user in Redis-backed memory, or asking PostgreSQL to exclude blocked ids in the query (AND id <> ALL($2) with an index), is.

Bulk writes are the other place arrays matter. An inventory sync receives 100,000 stock updates every 15 minutes. Chunking into 1,000-row INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE statements (8 columns, so 8,000 parameters each) keeps every statement under the 65,535-parameter limit and each transaction under 50 ms, so the sync finishes in about 6 seconds without blocking anyone.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call engineer is paged: orders-worker is in CrashLoopBackOff. The last log line before each crash is:

FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory

The nightly reconciliation job runs orderRepository.find({ where: { status: 'delivered' } }) and then loops over the result. It has run for two years. Tonight the orders table crossed 2.4 million delivered rows. Each row becomes a JavaScript object of about 220 bytes, the array itself is 19 MB of pointers, and the driver's intermediate row buffers roughly double the peak. The process needs about 1.1 GB and the container's --max-old-space-size is 768 MB. Every restart repeats the same query and dies at the same point; the job never completes and the pod never becomes healthy.

The fix is to never hold the whole result in one array: keyset pagination in chunks of 5,000 rows (WHERE id > $lastId ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000), or a streaming cursor (pg-query-stream) processed with backpressure. Peak memory drops to under 20 MB regardless of table size. The lesson: an array whose size is controlled by the database, not by your code, is an incident waiting for a growth curve.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Default sort is lexicographic. [10, 9, 1].sort() returns [1, 10, 9]. Sorting prices or ids without a comparator silently corrupts order. Always pass (a, b) => a - b.
  • sort and splice mutate in place. Sorting a cached array reorders it for every other caller. Copy first ([...arr].sort(...)) or use toSorted() on Node.js 20+.
  • Spread argument limit. Math.max(...latencies) with a few hundred thousand elements throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded because every element becomes a function argument. Use a loop or reduce.
  • delete arr[i] leaves a hole; it does not shrink the array. Use splice or filter.
  • new Array(n) is holey; Array.from({ length: n }, fn) or new Array(n).fill(0) makes it packed.
  • Mixed types de-optimize. One null pushed into an array of Smis converts the whole array to tagged pointers permanently.
  • Huge JSON.parse blocks the loop. Parsing a 50 MB request body array takes hundreds of milliseconds on the main thread. Limit body size at the gateway and in bodyParser.
  • Arrays are shared by reference. Returning an internal array from a service lets callers mutate your state. Return copies or readonly types.
  • indexOf uses strict equality. Searching for objects by value never matches; searching for NaN never matches (includes handles NaN).
  • shift() in a loop is O(n^2). Draining a queue with while (arr.length) arr.shift() copies the array each time. Use an index pointer or a real queue (Section 7.6).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The first question is never "array or not". It is "who controls n?" If n is bounded by the code (a page of 48, a batch of 1,000), an array is always fine and anything cleverer is over-engineering. If n is controlled by the database, the user or the upstream system, the senior engineer either bounds it (pagination, LIMIT, body size limits) or refuses to hold it in one array (streaming).

The second question is "which operation runs in the hot loop?" Index reads and appends are what arrays are for. Membership tests belong to a Set. Removing from the front belongs to a queue. Keeping things sorted while inserting belongs to a heap or a B-tree. When a senior sees includes, indexOf, shift or splice inside a loop, they read the surrounding code for n before approving the pull request.

The third question is "does this data need to be a JavaScript object at all?" Counters, bitmaps, latency samples and binary payloads belong in typed arrays and Buffers: fixed memory, no GC pressure, no boxing.

Explaining it to a product manager: "The feature works, but its cost grows with the square of the user's block list. A user with 50,000 blocks will make the page 100 times slower than a user with 5,000. We need one day to move the filtering into the database query."

Common mistakes

  • Treating Array as a queue with shift(). Works in tests, degrades quadratically in production.
  • find inside map to join two arrays (orders.map(o => users.find(u => u.id === o.userId))). Build a Map from users first; it turns O(n x m) into O(n + m).
  • Loading unbounded result sets into arrays because "the table is small". Tables grow.
  • Concatenating in a loop (result = result.concat(chunk)) which reallocates every iteration. Use push(...chunk) for small chunks or collect and flatten once.
  • Storing ids as strings in one array and numbers in another, then wondering why includes never matches after a bigint column returns "42".
  • Using array columns in PostgreSQL as a substitute for a join table, then needing a foreign key, a count per tag or an update across all rows.

Interview questions

  1. Why is push O(1) amortized and not O(1)? Expected: the backing store is over-allocated; occasional resizes copy all elements (O(n)) but happen geometrically less often, so the average per push is constant. Follow-up: what growth factor does V8 use, and why not double? (Roughly 1.5x plus 16; smaller factor wastes less memory and reuses freed blocks better.)
  2. What is a holey array and why does it matter? Expected: an array with gaps; V8 must check for holes and consult the prototype chain on reads, which disables the fastest access paths. Follow-up: how does new Array(1000) differ from Array.from({ length: 1000 })?
  3. You need to check whether each of 20,000 candidate products is in a 5,000-item "already seen" list. What do you do and what is the complexity? Expected: build a Set from the seen list (O(m)), then test each candidate (O(1) each), O(n + m) total versus O(n x m) with includes. Why it matters: this exact bug shows up in feed and recommendation code constantly.
  4. When would you choose a typed array over a normal array? Expected: fixed-size numeric data, counters, bitmaps, binary protocols; benefits are no boxing, no GC pressure, off-heap storage, numeric sort. Follow-up: what happens to process.memoryUsage() fields?
  5. A worker crashes with "JavaScript heap out of memory" while processing a table. Diagnose. Expected: unbounded find() into an array; fix with keyset pagination or streaming with backpressure; discuss why offset pagination is also wrong at that size.
  6. Why does PostgreSQL's = ANY($1::bigint[]) beat a generated IN (...) list from Node.js? Expected: single bind parameter, stable prepared statement, avoids the 65,535 parameter limit, and the plan is cached.
  7. What does [10, 9, 1].sort() return and why? Expected: [1, 10, 9]; default comparison converts to strings. Follow-up: is Array.prototype.sort stable in V8? (Yes, since V8 7.0 / Node.js 11.)

Practical exercise

Build a SlidingWindowStats provider in NestJS that records per-route latency using a ring buffer per route.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Memory is bounded: each route keeps at most 5,000 samples in a Float64Array, and a Map<string, RingBuffer> holds at most 200 routes (evict the least recently written route when full).
  • GET /internal/metrics/latency?route=/orders returns { samples, p50, p95, p99 } in under 2 ms for a full buffer (hint: sort a copy, never the live buffer).
  • A load test with autocannon -c 100 -d 30 http://localhost:3000/orders shows no growth in process.memoryUsage().arrayBuffers after the first 10 seconds.
  • Unit tests prove [10, 9, 1]-style ordering bugs cannot happen: percentile of samples [10, 9, 1, 100] at p50 is 9 or 10, never 100.

7.3 Strings

Concept

A string is an ordered sequence of characters. In JavaScript a string is a sequence of 16-bit code units (UTF-16), it is immutable (you can never change a character in place; every "modification" creates a new string), and V8 stores it in one of several internal shapes that you cannot see but will feel in memory and CPU. On the wire (HTTP, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka) text is almost always UTF-8 bytes, and Node.js converts between the two worlds every time you read a request body or write a response. Those conversions, and the difference between "characters" and "bytes", are where backend string bugs live.

Why does it exist?

Backends are text machines. Request bodies, JSON, SQL statements, cache keys, log lines, tokens, e-mail addresses, product names, error messages: all strings. The design choices behind JavaScript strings exist for good reasons: immutability lets V8 share strings freely between objects, cache their hash for use as map keys, and hand them across threads without copying. UTF-16 was chosen in 1995 when 16 bits looked like enough for every character; it was not, which is why emoji and many scripts need two code units and why '😀'.length is 2. Buffer exists because the network and the file system speak bytes, and you need a mutable, fixed-size, off-heap byte array to talk to them efficiently.

Mental model

Imagine a laminated card versus a whiteboard. A JavaScript string is a laminated card: you can read it, copy it, and hand out copies, but to change one letter you print a whole new card. A Buffer is a whiteboard of fixed size: you can write bytes in place, wipe a region, and hand a pointer to someone else who sees the same board. Concatenating strings in a loop is printing a new, slightly longer card each time; V8 cheats by stapling cards together (a "rope") and only printing the final card when someone needs to read it end to end.

How it works

  1. Code units, not characters. str.length counts UTF-16 code units. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (emoji, many CJK ideographs, mathematical symbols) are stored as a surrogate pair of two code units. '😀'.length === 2, [...'😀'].length === 1, '😀'.codePointAt(0) === 0x1F600. str.slice(0, 1) on that string returns a lone surrogate, which is invalid text.
  2. One byte or two. V8 stores a string whose characters are all below 256 as a SeqOneByteString (1 byte per character, Latin-1). If a single character is above 255, the whole string becomes a SeqTwoByteString (2 bytes per character). Adding one emoji to a 10 MB ASCII string doubles its memory.
  3. Ropes. a + b where the result is at least 13 characters does not copy; V8 creates a ConsString node with two pointers. Repeated += builds a tree. The first operation that needs contiguous characters (indexing, regex, comparison, writing to a socket) flattens the tree into a sequential string in one O(n) pass.
  4. Slices. str.substring(i, j) of a string 13 characters or longer creates a SlicedString that points at the parent with an offset, O(1). The parent stays alive as long as the slice does.
  5. Internalized strings and cached hashes. String literals and property names are interned in a table so equal strings share one object and compare by pointer. Every string caches its hash after the first computation, which is why using strings as Map keys is cheap.
  6. UTF-8 conversion. Buffer.from(str, 'utf8') and buf.toString('utf8') walk every character. ASCII is 1 byte, é is 2, ₹ is 3, 😀 is 4. Buffer.byteLength(str) tells you the encoded size without allocating; str.length does not.
  7. Limits. buffer.constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH is about 536 million characters on 64-bit Node.js. JSON.stringify of a response bigger than that throws RangeError: Invalid string length, and you will run out of heap well before you get there.
flowchart TB
    root["ConsString len 41"] --> left["ConsString len 29"]
    root --> right["SeqOneByteString total=129900"]
    left --> ll["SeqOneByteString order:8813:"]
    left --> lr["SeqOneByteString status=paid,"]

Time complexity

Operation Best Average Worst Notes
length O(1) O(1) O(1) code units, not bytes or characters
str[i] / charCodeAt(i) O(1) O(1) O(n) worst case flattens a rope first
a + b O(1) O(1) O(n + m) rope for length >= 13, copy for short strings
substring / slice O(1) O(1) O(k) O(1) creates a sliced view that retains the parent
=== comparison O(1) O(n) O(n) O(1) when pointers match or lengths differ
indexOf / includes O(1) O(n) O(n x m) V8 uses Boyer-Moore-Horspool for longer needles
split / replace / toLowerCase O(n) O(n) O(n) each allocates new strings
Regex test / match O(n) O(n) O(2^n) catastrophic backtracking with nested quantifiers
Buffer.from(str) / toString() O(n) O(n) O(n) full encode or decode pass
Buffer.byteLength(str) O(n) O(n) O(n) no allocation
JSON.stringify / JSON.parse O(n) O(n) O(n) n = total size; single-threaded, blocks the loop

Memory implications (V8, Node.js)

  • A sequential one-byte string costs about 16 bytes of header plus 1 byte per character; two-byte costs 16 plus 2 per character. A ConsString node is 32 bytes, so a rope built from 100,000 tiny appends carries 3.2 MB of nodes until it is flattened.
  • A SlicedString retains its parent. Extracting a 40-character token from a 10 MB request body and caching the token keeps the 10 MB alive. Force a copy with Buffer.from(token, 'utf8').toString('utf8') before storing long-lived substrings of large strings.
  • Buffer memory lives outside the V8 heap (visible in process.memoryUsage().arrayBuffers and external). Buffers under 4 KiB are carved from a shared 8 KiB pool; larger ones get their own allocation. Buffer.allocUnsafe skips zero-filling and may expose old memory, so never send it to a client without fully overwriting it.
  • buf.subarray() shares memory with the parent; Buffer.concat(chunks, totalLength) copies exactly once and is the right way to assemble a body from chunks.

Practical example

Three everyday tasks: build a cache key, measure a string in bytes for a size limit, and truncate text without cutting an emoji in half.

// common/text.ts
export const cacheKey = (...parts: (string | number)[]) => parts.join(':'); // 'order:8813:items'

/** Validate by BYTES because Redis, headers and index entries have byte limits. */
export function assertMaxBytes(value: string, maxBytes: number, field: string): void {
  const bytes = Buffer.byteLength(value, 'utf8');
  if (bytes > maxBytes) {
    throw new RangeError(`${field} is ${bytes} bytes; limit is ${maxBytes}`);
  }
}

/** Truncate by code points so a surrogate pair is never split. */
export function truncateSafe(value: string, maxCodePoints: number): string {
  let out = '';
  let count = 0;
  for (const ch of value) {          // iterates code points, not code units
    if (count === maxCodePoints) break;
    out += ch;
    count++;
  }
  return out;
}

/** Normalize user-entered identifiers so 'é' (1 code point) and 'e' + combining accent match. */
export const normalizeIdentifier = (s: string) => s.normalize('NFC').trim().toLowerCase();

for...of over a string yields code points, so truncateSafe('héllo😀!', 6) returns 'héllo😀' intact, where slice(0, 6) would return 'héllo\uD83D', a broken half of the emoji.

NestJS example

A CSV export that never materializes the whole file as one string. An async generator yields rows as PostgreSQL streams them, Readable.from turns that into a Node.js stream with backpressure, and StreamableFile (a real @nestjs/common class) pipes it to the client.

// exports/orders-export.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Header, Query, StreamableFile } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Readable } from 'node:stream';
import { OrdersExportService } from './orders-export.service';

@Controller('exports')
export class OrdersExportController {
  constructor(private readonly exportService: OrdersExportService) {}

  @Get('orders.csv')
  @Header('Content-Type', 'text/csv; charset=utf-8')
  @Header('Content-Disposition', 'attachment; filename="orders.csv"')
  exportOrders(@Query('merchantId') merchantId: string): StreamableFile {
    const stream = Readable.from(this.exportService.rows(merchantId)); // backpressure-aware
    return new StreamableFile(stream);
  }
}

// exports/orders-export.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersExportService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async *rows(merchantId: string): AsyncGenerator<string> {
    yield 'order_id,status,total_cents,created_at\n';
    let lastId = '0';
    for (;;) {
      // Keyset pagination: bounded memory no matter how many orders exist.
      const page: { id: string; status: string; total_cents: number; created_at: Date }[] =
        await this.dataSource.query(
          `SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at FROM orders
           WHERE merchant_id = $1 AND id > $2 ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000`,
          [merchantId, lastId],
        );
      if (page.length === 0) return;
      for (const r of page) {
        yield `${r.id},${csvEscape(r.status)},${r.total_cents},${r.created_at.toISOString()}\n`;
      }
      lastId = page[page.length - 1].id;
    }
  }
}

function csvEscape(v: string): string {
  return /[",\n]/.test(v) ? `"${v.replace(/"/g, '""')}"` : v;
}

Peak memory is one page of 5,000 rows plus whatever the socket has not drained yet, whether the merchant has 300 orders or 30 million.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL stores text as UTF-8 bytes and counts characters for varchar(n). It has three details every backend engineer eventually hits: length() versus octet_length(), the B-tree index entry limit, and the null byte.

CREATE TABLE users (
  id            bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email         varchar(320) NOT NULL,          -- max valid e-mail length; counts characters
  display_name  text NOT NULL,
  bio           text,
  avatar_bytes  bytea                            -- raw bytes, no encoding validation
);

-- Case-insensitive uniqueness without a citext extension: index the expression.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_lower_uq ON users (lower(email));

SELECT length('naïve😀') AS chars, octet_length('naïve😀') AS bytes;  -- 6 | 11

-- Prefix search that can use a B-tree needs text_pattern_ops under non-C collations.
CREATE INDEX products_name_prefix ON products (name text_pattern_ops);
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE 'Gutta%';

-- Values that will never fit a B-tree entry (limit is 2704 bytes) must be hashed for uniqueness.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX documents_body_sha_uq ON documents (sha256(convert_to(body, 'UTF8')));
Index Scan using users_email_lower_uq on users  (cost=0.43..8.45 rows=1 width=57) (actual time=0.031..0.032 rows=1 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (lower((email)::text) = 'praveen@example.com'::text)
  Buffers: shared hit=4
Planning Time: 0.121 ms
Execution Time: 0.052 ms

The query must use the same expression (WHERE lower(email) = $1) or the planner ignores the index. Values larger than about 2 KB are moved to TOAST storage (compressed, out-of-line), which is transparent but means reading a wide bio column costs extra page reads; select only the columns you need.

TypeORM example

// users/user.entity.ts
import { Column, Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn } from 'typeorm';

const nfcLower = {
  to: (v: string) => v.normalize('NFC').trim().toLowerCase(), // on write
  from: (v: string) => v,                                       // on read
};

@Entity({ name: 'users' })
export class User {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('increment', { type: 'bigint' })
  id!: string;

  @Column({ type: 'varchar', length: 320, transformer: nfcLower })
  email!: string;

  @Column({ type: 'text' })
  displayName!: string;

  @Column({ type: 'bytea', nullable: true })
  avatarBytes?: Buffer; // pg driver maps bytea to Buffer
}

// find by normalized email so the expression index is used
const user = await repo
  .createQueryBuilder('u')
  .where('lower(u.email) = :email', { email: input.normalize('NFC').trim().toLowerCase() })
  .getOne();

The unique expression index itself goes in a migration (queryRunner.query(...)), because @Index cannot express lower(email).

Sequelize example

import { DataTypes, Model, Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export class User extends Model {
  declare id: number;
  declare email: string;
  declare displayName: string;
}

export function initUser(sequelize: Sequelize) {
  User.init(
    {
      id: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, autoIncrement: true, primaryKey: true },
      email: {
        type: DataTypes.STRING(320),
        allowNull: false,
        set(value: string) {
          this.setDataValue('email', value.normalize('NFC').trim().toLowerCase());
        },
        validate: { isEmail: true, len: [3, 320] },
      },
      displayName: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false, field: 'display_name' },
    },
    { sequelize, tableName: 'users', timestamps: false },
  );
}

const found = await User.findOne({
  where: sequelize.where(sequelize.fn('lower', sequelize.col('email')), email.toLowerCase()),
});

DataTypes.CITEXT is also available for PostgreSQL if the citext extension is installed, which removes the need for the expression index.

Production scenario

A catalog service exposes GET /products/all for a partner integration. The response is 2,400 products, about 6 MB of JSON. Per request the process performs JSON.stringify (6 MB string, one-byte because the catalog is ASCII), then Node.js encodes it to UTF-8 into socket buffers (another 6 MB), so roughly 12 MB of transient memory and about 25 ms of CPU. At 5 requests per second that is 60 MB per second of garbage and 12.5 percent of a core. At 40 requests per second, when the partner launches a polling loop, the endpoint alone eats a full core and every other endpoint's p99 climbs from 12 ms to 180 ms. The fix is a cache (serialize once per catalog change, keep the Buffer, send it with Content-Length), plus ETag handling so most polls return 304 Not Modified with zero serialization.

Logging is the other silent string cost. A service writing 10,000 structured log lines per second at 15 microseconds each spends 150 ms of every second serializing logs, which is 15 percent of its capacity. That is why pino (schema-based fast serialization, off-thread transport) beats console.log(JSON.stringify(...)), and why senior engineers sample debug logs in production.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call engineer is paged: reports-api p99 is 30 seconds and two of four pods are OOMKilled. A merchant with 3.1 million orders clicked "Export all orders". The handler ran rows.map(toCsvLine).join('\n'). The array of 3.1 million row objects took 700 MB; map produced 3.1 million small strings; join produced a 410 MB one-byte string; res.send converted it to a 410 MB UTF-8 Buffer. The pod's 1 GB limit was crossed during join. The pod died, the load balancer retried the request on the next pod, which also died, and the merchant's browser retried on timeout, which started a third attempt. Three pods went down in four minutes for one click.

The fix was the streaming export above (bounded at one 5,000-row page in memory), a hard cap of one concurrent export per merchant enforced with a Redis SET NX EX lock, and a Content-Disposition with a job id so retries reattach to the running export instead of starting another.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Byte limits versus character limits. HTTP headers are capped by bytes (Node.js defaults to 16 KB total via --max-http-header-size), Redis keys and PostgreSQL index entries are bytes, varchar(n) is characters, str.length is code units. Validate at the right unit.
  • Splitting surrogate pairs. slice, substring and split('') cut inside emoji. Node.js encodes a lone surrogate as U+FFFD, so the customer sees a question-mark diamond in their name.
  • Unicode normalization. 'é' can be one code point or two. Two users can register visually identical usernames that bypass a unique constraint unless you normalize('NFC') before writing.
  • Null bytes. PostgreSQL text rejects ␀ with invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0x00. JSON allows it. Strip or reject at validation.
  • Catastrophic regex backtracking (ReDoS). /^(\w+\s?)+$/ on a 40-character non-matching string can take seconds. Never run user-controlled regexes; prefer linear-time checks; hoist compiled regexes out of hot functions.
  • Sliced-string retention. Substrings of large bodies stored in caches keep the whole body alive. Copy before caching.
  • Chunk boundaries. A multi-byte character can be split across two TCP chunks. Decoding each chunk with toString() corrupts it; use string_decoder.StringDecoder or concatenate buffers first.
  • Timing attacks. Comparing secrets with === returns early on the first mismatch. Compare tokens with crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length Buffers.
  • Log injection. A user-supplied string containing \n can forge log lines. Structured JSON logging escapes it; string-concatenated logs do not.
  • Locale case mapping. 'I'.toLowerCase() is 'i', but toLocaleLowerCase('tr') gives a dotless ı. Use plain toLowerCase for identifiers and normalize before comparing.
  • Base64 inflation. Encoding a 3 MB image in a JSON body makes it 4 MB and forces a full parse into a string before you can even validate its size. Use multipart uploads or presigned URLs.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The first instinct is to refuse to build a large string when a stream will do. Response bodies, exports, log files and bulk payloads are streamed with backpressure; the memory of a request handler should be independent of the size of the data it moves. When the whole payload really is needed at once (a cached catalog), it is serialized once and stored as a Buffer, never re-serialized per request.

The second instinct is to name the unit. When a spec says "limit names to 100", the senior asks: 100 bytes, code units, code points or grapheme clusters? Then they enforce it at the edge in the unit that matches the storage constraint (bytes for Redis and index entries, characters for varchar).

The third is to treat serialization as CPU you pay per request. They profile with node --cpu-prof and are rarely surprised to find JSON.stringify and logging near the top. They fix that with caching, sampling and ETags before they reach for more pods.

To a product manager: "Exporting three million rows in one click is fine, but the export must stream to the browser instead of being assembled in memory first. Same feature, no outage, one day of work."

Common mistakes

  • Using str.length for Content-Length or a byte-limit check. Off by a factor of up to four for non-ASCII text.
  • Building large responses with += or join when a stream was available.
  • Storing substrings of large bodies (tokens, ids parsed from a webhook payload) in long-lived caches.
  • Truncating with slice and shipping broken emoji to customers.
  • Forgetting normalization on identifiers, then debugging "duplicate" users that look identical.
  • Compiling a regex inside a request handler (new RegExp(pattern) per call) instead of once at module load.
  • Comparing API keys with ===.
  • Choosing char(n) in PostgreSQL, which pads with spaces and makes equality comparisons surprising.

Interview questions

  1. Why is '😀'.length 2, and where does that break in a backend? Expected: UTF-16 surrogate pairs; breaks in truncation, varchar limits, Content-Length, cursor offsets. Follow-up: how do you iterate by code point? (for...of, Array.from, codePointAt.)
  2. How does V8 make s += x in a loop not O(n^2)? Expected: ConsString ropes with O(1) concatenation, flattened lazily on first character access. Follow-up: what is the memory cost of a deep rope, and what forces a flatten?
  3. A 40-byte token extracted from a 10 MB payload is cached for an hour. What is the memory impact? Expected: SlicedString retains the parent; the 10 MB stays alive; fix by copying via Buffer round-trip.
  4. Design an endpoint that exports millions of rows as CSV. Expected: keyset pagination or cursor stream, async generator, Readable.from, StreamableFile, concurrency cap per user, resumable job id. Why it matters: it tests memory discipline, backpressure and idempotent retries together.
  5. What is the difference between length(col) and octet_length(col) in PostgreSQL, and when does the B-tree entry limit bite? Expected: characters versus bytes; index rows above 2704 bytes fail; hash the value for uniqueness.
  6. What is ReDoS and how do you defend against it on a Node.js service? Expected: exponential backtracking in the single-threaded loop; avoid nested quantifiers, limit input length, use linear-time validators, never accept user regexes.
  7. Why does JSON.stringify of a large object hurt more in Node.js than in a Java service? Expected: it runs on the single event loop thread, so every concurrent request waits; mitigations are caching serialized Buffers, streaming JSON, worker threads for offline reports.

Practical exercise

Implement TextLimitsPipe, a NestJS PipeTransform used on a CreateProductDto, and a streaming GET /products/export.csv.

Acceptance criteria:

  • name is rejected if it exceeds 120 code points or 480 bytes; error messages state both measured values.
  • name is normalized to NFC and trimmed before validation, and a test proves that 'é' and 'é' produce the same stored value.
  • description containing ␀ is rejected with a 400, not a PostgreSQL 500.
  • The export endpoint keeps process.memoryUsage().heapUsed under 150 MB while exporting a seeded table of 2 million rows (verify with a test that samples memory every second).
  • A unit test proves truncateSafe('ab😀cd', 3) returns 'ab😀' and never a lone surrogate.

7.4 Linked Lists

Concept

A linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node (a singly linked list), or pointers to both the next and the previous node (a doubly linked list). Nodes are allocated one at a time anywhere in memory; nothing is contiguous. You keep a pointer to the first node (the head) and usually the last one (the tail).

The defining property is the opposite of the array's: reaching the i-th node costs O(n) because you must follow i pointers, but once you hold a node, inserting after it or unlinking it costs O(1) and never moves any other node.

Why does it exist?

Arrays are bad at two things: inserting or removing in the middle (everything after the slot shifts), and giving you a stable handle to an element (indexes change as the array changes). Linked lists fix both. That is why they sit inside almost every structure that needs "remove this exact item quickly, regardless of where it is": LRU caches (Section 7.17), in-flight request registries, connection-pool idle lists, OS schedulers, Node.js stream buffers (Readable keeps its pending chunks in a linked BufferList), and Redis lists (a quicklist, which is a doubly linked list of packed nodes).

Without linked lists you would implement an LRU cache by finding an element in an array (O(n)) and splicing it out (O(n)) on every cache hit. At 50,000 cache hits per second that is not a cache; it is a CPU heater.

Mental model

Imagine a scavenger hunt. Each clue tells you where the next clue is hidden. To read clue 500 you must visit the first 499. But to insert a new clue between clue 3 and clue 4 you only rewrite clue 3, and nobody else in the hunt notices. In a doubly linked version each clue also says where the previous clue was, so you can walk backwards and you can remove any clue you are standing on by telling its neighbours about each other.

How it works

  1. Node. An object { value, prev, next }. In V8 a small object with three fields costs roughly 24 bytes of header plus 8 bytes per field, so about 48 bytes per node, versus 8 bytes per slot in a packed array.
  2. Insert at tail. Create a node, set node.prev = tail, tail.next = node, tail = node. Four pointer writes, O(1).
  3. Unlink a node you hold. node.prev.next = node.next; node.next.prev = node.prev. Two pointer writes, O(1), regardless of list length. In a singly linked list you cannot do this without first finding the previous node, O(n).
  4. Traverse. Follow next from the head. Each hop is a dependent memory load: the CPU cannot fetch node 2 until it has read node 1's pointer. Cache misses to main memory cost roughly 100 ns, so a 1-million-node traversal can take 50 to 100 ms, while a packed array of 1 million integers scans in about 1 ms.
  5. Sentinels. Production implementations use two dummy nodes (head and tail sentinels) so that "insert at front" and "remove the last real node" need no special cases for an empty list. Fewer branches, fewer bugs.
  6. Garbage collection. V8's mark-and-sweep collector handles cycles (prev and next pointing at each other) without trouble. What it cannot handle is your stale references: a node you "removed" but still hold in a closure keeps its neighbours reachable through its pointers. Null out prev and next when unlinking.
flowchart LR
    H["head sentinel"] -->|"next"| A["req 7f1a age 12ms"]
    A -->|"next"| B["req 9c02 age 8ms"]
    B -->|"next"| C["req b7e4 age 1ms"]
    C -->|"next"| T["tail sentinel"]
    C -->|"prev"| B
    B -->|"prev"| A
    A -->|"prev"| H

Time complexity

Operation Best Average Worst Notes
Access by index O(1) O(n) O(n) best is index 0 or the tail
Search by value O(1) O(n) O(n)
Insert at head or tail O(1) O(1) O(1) tail requires a tail pointer
Insert after a node you hold O(1) O(1) O(1)
Delete a node you hold (doubly) O(1) O(1) O(1)
Delete a node you hold (singly) O(1) O(n) O(n) must find the previous node
Delete head O(1) O(1) O(1)
Delete tail (doubly) O(1) O(1) O(1) O(n) for singly linked
Length O(1) O(1) O(1) if you maintain a counter

Memory implications (V8, Node.js)

  • About 48 bytes per node plus the value. A list of 1 million small integers costs roughly 48 MB versus 8 MB for a packed array.
  • Nodes are allocated individually and often survive long enough to be promoted to old space, which makes them more expensive for the garbage collector than a single array backing store.
  • Keep node objects monomorphic: always create them with the same property order (value, prev, next) so every node shares one hidden class and V8 inlines the field offsets.
  • Data locality is poor. For n below roughly 10,000, an array with splice is often faster than a linked list in practice because copying a few kilobytes contiguously is cheaper than chasing pointers.

Practical example

A production-grade doubly linked list with sentinels and O(1) unlink. This is the same class that the LRU cache in Section 7.17 will reuse.

// common/doubly-linked-list.ts
export class ListNode<T> {
  prev: ListNode<T> | null = null;
  next: ListNode<T> | null = null;
  constructor(public value: T) {}
}

export class DoublyLinkedList<T> implements Iterable<T> {
  private readonly head = new ListNode<T>(undefined as T); // sentinel, never exposed
  private readonly tail = new ListNode<T>(undefined as T); // sentinel, never exposed
  private count = 0;

  constructor() {
    this.head.next = this.tail;
    this.tail.prev = this.head;
  }

  get size(): number {
    return this.count;
  }

  pushBack(value: T): ListNode<T> {
    const node = new ListNode(value);
    this.insertBetween(node, this.tail.prev!, this.tail);
    return node; // caller keeps this handle for O(1) removal
  }

  pushFront(value: T): ListNode<T> {
    const node = new ListNode(value);
    this.insertBetween(node, this.head, this.head.next!);
    return node;
  }

  moveToFront(node: ListNode<T>): void {
    this.unlink(node);
    this.insertBetween(node, this.head, this.head.next!);
  }

  remove(node: ListNode<T>): T {
    this.unlink(node);
    return node.value;
  }

  peekFront(): T | undefined {
    return this.count === 0 ? undefined : this.head.next!.value;
  }

  popBack(): T | undefined {
    if (this.count === 0) return undefined;
    return this.remove(this.tail.prev!);
  }

  *[Symbol.iterator](): Iterator<T> {
    for (let n = this.head.next; n !== this.tail; n = n!.next) yield n!.value;
  }

  private insertBetween(node: ListNode<T>, before: ListNode<T>, after: ListNode<T>): void {
    node.prev = before;
    node.next = after;
    before.next = node;
    after.prev = node;
    this.count++;
  }

  private unlink(node: ListNode<T>): void {
    if (node.prev === null || node.next === null) throw new Error('node is not linked');
    node.prev.next = node.next;
    node.next.prev = node.prev;
    node.prev = node.next = null; // drop references so a stale handle retains nothing
    this.count--;
  }
}

NestJS example

An in-flight request registry. Every request is added to the list when it starts and unlinked when it finishes. Requests finish in arbitrary order, so the O(1) unlink by node handle is exactly what we need. The registry powers two things: a health indicator that reports the age of the oldest in-flight request (a stuck request shows up as a growing number), and graceful shutdown that waits for the list to drain before the process exits.

// runtime/inflight.registry.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnApplicationShutdown } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DoublyLinkedList, ListNode } from '../common/doubly-linked-list';

interface InFlight { id: string; route: string; startedAt: number }

@Injectable()
export class InFlightRegistry implements OnApplicationShutdown {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(InFlightRegistry.name);
  private readonly list = new DoublyLinkedList<InFlight>();

  start(id: string, route: string): ListNode<InFlight> {
    return this.list.pushBack({ id, route, startedAt: Date.now() }); // newest at the back
  }

  finish(node: ListNode<InFlight>): void {
    this.list.remove(node); // O(1) no matter how many requests are in flight
  }

  oldestAgeMs(): number {
    const oldest = this.list.peekFront(); // oldest is always at the front
    return oldest ? Date.now() - oldest.startedAt : 0;
  }

  get count(): number {
    return this.list.size;
  }

  async onApplicationShutdown(signal?: string): Promise<void> {
    const deadline = Date.now() + 25_000; // stay under Kubernetes' 30s terminationGracePeriod
    while (this.list.size > 0 && Date.now() < deadline) {
      this.logger.log(`${signal}: waiting for ${this.list.size} in-flight requests`);
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 250));
    }
  }
}

// runtime/inflight.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, finalize } from 'rxjs';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { InFlightRegistry } from './inflight.registry';

@Injectable()
export class InFlightInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(private readonly registry: InFlightRegistry) {}

  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<{ method: string; url: string }>();
    const node = this.registry.start(randomUUID(), `${req.method} ${req.url}`);
    return next.handle().pipe(finalize(() => this.registry.finish(node)));
  }
}

Enable shutdown hooks with app.enableShutdownHooks() in main.ts so onApplicationShutdown runs on SIGTERM. A @nestjs/terminus health indicator can then report oldestAgeMs() and fail readiness when it exceeds, say, 30 seconds.

PostgreSQL example

Two linked lists live inside PostgreSQL whether you want them or not, and one you should never build yourself.

HOT chains. Every UPDATE in PostgreSQL writes a new row version; the old version's t_ctid header field points to the new one, forming a chain inside the page. A row updated 200 times between vacuums has a 200-link chain, and each read of that row walks it. This is the mechanism behind "hot row" slowdowns on counters and inventory quantities, and why autovacuum tuning matters (see the Database Internals part).

The self-referencing "next_id" table, a linked list modeled in SQL, is an anti-pattern for ordered items. It looks natural for playlists, checklist steps or pipeline stages, but every read needs a recursive query and every reorder needs two or three row updates that race under concurrency.

-- Anti-pattern: a linked list of checklist steps
CREATE TABLE steps (
  id           bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  checklist_id bigint NOT NULL,
  title        text   NOT NULL,
  next_id      bigint REFERENCES steps(id)
);

-- Reading in order requires walking the chain one hop per iteration.
WITH RECURSIVE ordered AS (
  SELECT s.*, 1 AS position FROM steps s
  WHERE s.checklist_id = 42 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM steps p WHERE p.next_id = s.id)
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.*, o.position + 1 FROM steps s JOIN ordered o ON s.id = o.next_id
)
SELECT id, title FROM ordered ORDER BY position;

-- Better: an explicit position that can be indexed and read in one range scan.
CREATE TABLE steps_v2 (
  id           bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  checklist_id bigint  NOT NULL,
  title        text    NOT NULL,
  position     numeric NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (checklist_id, position)
);
SELECT id, title FROM steps_v2 WHERE checklist_id = 42 ORDER BY position;
Index Scan using steps_v2_checklist_id_position_key on steps_v2  (cost=0.29..8.60 rows=18 width=45) (actual time=0.019..0.027 rows=18 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (checklist_id = 42)
  Buffers: shared hit=3
Planning Time: 0.098 ms
Execution Time: 0.041 ms

Using numeric for position lets you insert between 3 and 4 as 3.5 without renumbering (fractional indexing); renumber lazily when gaps get too small.

TypeORM example

TypeORM can model both shapes. The self-referencing relation is shown only so you recognize it; the position column is what you should ship.

import { Column, Entity, Index, ManyToOne, PrimaryColumn } from 'typeorm';

@Entity({ name: 'steps_v2' })
@Index(['checklistId', 'position'], { unique: true })
export class Step {
  @PrimaryColumn({ type: 'bigint' })
  id!: string;

  @Column({ name: 'checklist_id', type: 'bigint' })
  checklistId!: string;

  @Column({ type: 'text' })
  title!: string;

  @Column({ type: 'numeric', precision: 20, scale: 10 })
  position!: string; // numeric arrives as a string from pg; compare with a decimal library
}

// ordered read: one index range scan, no recursion
const steps = await repo.find({ where: { checklistId }, order: { position: 'ASC' } });

// insert between two neighbours without touching any other row
const between = (a: string, b: string) => ((Number(a) + Number(b)) / 2).toString();
await repo.insert({ id, checklistId, title, position: between(prev.position, next.position) });

Sequelize example

import { DataTypes, Model, Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export class Step extends Model {
  declare id: number;
  declare checklistId: number;
  declare title: string;
  declare position: string;
}

export function initStep(sequelize: Sequelize) {
  Step.init(
    {
      id: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, primaryKey: true },
      checklistId: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, allowNull: false, field: 'checklist_id' },
      title: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false },
      position: { type: DataTypes.DECIMAL(20, 10), allowNull: false },
    },
    {
      sequelize,
      tableName: 'steps_v2',
      timestamps: false,
      indexes: [{ unique: true, fields: ['checklist_id', 'position'] }],
    },
  );
}

const ordered = await Step.findAll({ where: { checklistId }, order: [['position', 'ASC']] });

Production scenario

Redis lists are the linked list you will meet most often. BullMQ keeps each queue's waiting jobs in a Redis list and moves them to an active list with an atomic Lua script. LPUSH and RPOP are O(1), so a queue with 4 million pending jobs accepts and hands out jobs at 30,000 operations per second on one Redis core. The trap is any command that walks the list. LRANGE queue 0 -1 on those 4 million entries is O(n), takes about 500 ms, and because Redis executes commands on a single thread, every other client in the company stalls for that half second. LINDEX and LINSERT in the middle are O(n) for the same reason. Senior engineers treat Redis lists as deques: touch the ends, never the middle, and paginate with LRANGE 0 99 if a dashboard really must peek.

Node.js streams are the other everyday linked list. A Readable stores chunks it has read but not yet delivered in a BufferList. When a consumer stops reading (a slow client, a paused pipe), that list grows until highWaterMark (16 KB for byte streams) makes push() return false. Producers that ignore that return value are building an unbounded linked list of chunks, which is the memory leak behind many "the upload service slowly grows to 4 GB" incidents.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call engineer is paged: GET /checklists/:id for a subset of customers is timing out after 30 seconds and PostgreSQL CPU is pinned. The checklist steps use the next_id linked-list model. Two support agents reordered the same checklist simultaneously. Each transaction read the chain, computed new pointers, and wrote them; the second write did not conflict at the row level (different rows), so both committed. The resulting chain contained a cycle: step 7 points to step 9, step 9 points to step 7. The recursive CTE that reads the checklist never terminates; it grows a result set until statement_timeout (30 s) kills it, on every request for that checklist, from every pod, while customer retries pile more of them on.

Mitigation at 02:30: add CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path to the CTE (PostgreSQL 14+) so the query stops instead of looping. Fix by morning: migrate to the position column, where the worst concurrent outcome is two rows with a swapped order, never an unreadable checklist. The lesson: a linked list is only safe when one owner mutates it under a lock. A database table with concurrent writers is the opposite of that.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Lost head or tail pointer. Overwriting head without relinking orphans the whole list; the garbage collector reclaims it silently and the data is gone.
  • Removing a node twice. Without the "is it linked" check, the second unlink corrupts neighbours. Null the pointers on unlink and throw on re-removal.
  • Iterating while mutating. Removing the current node during a for...of is fine if you saved next before unlinking; otherwise the loop jumps to null.
  • Recursion over long lists. Recursive traversal of 100,000 nodes overflows the default Node.js stack (about 10,000 frames). Traverse iteratively.
  • Cycles. In memory they hang loops; in SQL they hang recursive queries. Detect with a visited Set or PostgreSQL's CYCLE clause.
  • Polymorphic nodes. Creating nodes with different property orders or sometimes adding extra fields turns the hot loop megamorphic and 5 to 10 times slower.
  • Redis list commands in the middle. LRANGE 0 -1, LINDEX, LINSERT, LREM on big lists block the Redis server.
  • Stream buffer growth. Ignoring push() and write() return values lets internal chunk lists grow without bound.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The question is "will I hold a reference to the element I need to remove?" If yes, and removals are frequent, a doubly linked list is the right tool (LRU cache, in-flight registry, timer wheels, idle-connection lists). If removal is by value or by index, the list gives nothing over an array and costs six times the memory; a Map or an array wins.

Second, "how big is n, really?" Under 10,000 elements the senior often keeps an array; the constant factors of pointer chasing beat the Big-O of splice. They only reach for a linked list when both n and the removal rate are large, and then they prefer a tested library (lru-cache, denque) over a hand-written one, unless the structure is the product.

Third, "where does this list live?" An in-memory list is per-process and dies on restart. A shared, durable list is a Redis list or a database table, with ordering enforced by a position column and a unique index, never by pointers between rows.

To a product manager: "Reordering steps by linking each step to the next is how it works on paper, but two people editing at once can tie a knot the system cannot read. Storing a sort position per step is one day of work and cannot knot."

Common mistakes

  • Modeling order in the database with next_id pointers.
  • Implementing a queue with a linked list and then calling find on it by id on every message; the O(1) benefit vanishes.
  • Recursive toArray() or print() helpers that overflow the stack in production.
  • Keeping "removed" nodes in a closure (a log line, a promise) and wondering why heap snapshots show a chain of old requests.
  • Using LRANGE 0 -1 on a Redis job queue "just to count"; use LLEN.
  • Assuming linked lists are faster than arrays because a textbook said insertion is O(1).

Interview questions

  1. When is a doubly linked list strictly better than an array? Expected: when you hold node handles and need O(1) unlink or move regardless of position, and n is large; canonical example is an LRU cache. Follow-up: why not an array plus indexOf? (O(n) per hit.)
  2. Why can a singly linked list not remove a node in O(1) given only that node? Expected: no pointer to the predecessor; the trick of copying the next node's value into it fails for the tail and breaks external handles.
  3. How would you order items in a PostgreSQL table, and why not with a next_id column? Expected: position with a unique index and fractional insertion; next_id needs recursive reads and races under concurrent reorders (cycles).
  4. What is a HOT chain and how does it relate to linked lists? Expected: row versions chained inside a page by t_ctid; long chains from frequent updates slow reads until vacuum.
  5. Explain why LRANGE key 0 -1 on a large Redis list is a production hazard. Expected: O(n) on a single-threaded server; stalls all clients; use LLEN, paginate, or keep lists small.
  6. How does a Node.js Readable stream buffer data, and how does that become a memory leak? Expected: a linked BufferList of chunks bounded by highWaterMark only if producers honour push() return values.
  7. Given a list of 100,000 nodes, why might your recursive traversal crash and how do you fix it? Expected: default stack depth about 10,000 frames; iterate with a loop or an explicit stack.

Practical exercise

Implement IdleConnectionList, the idle list of a tiny connection pool, on top of DoublyLinkedList.

Acceptance criteria:

  • acquire() returns the most recently released connection (front of the list) in O(1); release(conn) pushes to the front in O(1).
  • A reaper running every 5 seconds via @Interval(5000) from @nestjs/schedule closes connections idle for more than 30 seconds by walking from the back (oldest) and stopping at the first fresh one, so the reaper cost is proportional to the number of stale connections, not the pool size.
  • The list stores node handles in a Map<Connection, ListNode> so a connection that errors while idle can be unlinked in O(1).
  • Unit tests cover: release then acquire returns the same connection; the reaper closes exactly the stale ones; unlinking a node twice throws; iteration order is newest to oldest.
  • A benchmark with 100,000 release/acquire pairs finishes in under 50 ms and shows no growth in heapUsed between two forced GCs (node --expose-gc).

7.5 Stack

Concept

A stack is a collection where you add and remove from the same end: last in, first out (LIFO). The operations are push (add on top), pop (remove the top) and peek (look at the top). In JavaScript an array used only with push and pop is a stack, and it is the fastest stack you can have because both operations touch the end of a contiguous backing store.

Why does it exist?

Stacks exist because nesting is everywhere: function calls inside function calls, transactions with savepoints inside transactions, JSON objects inside objects, interceptors wrapping interceptors. Whenever you must "finish the most recent thing before returning to the thing that started it", you need LIFO order. The call stack that runs your NestJS controller is a stack; when it overflows you get RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, which is one of the few errors that can crash a request without any of your try/catch blocks having a say.

Mental model

Imagine a stack of plates in a restaurant kitchen. Clean plates go on top; the next cook takes from the top. Nobody pulls a plate from the middle. If you keep adding plates without anyone taking them, the stack hits the ceiling; that ceiling is the call-stack limit.

How it works

  1. Array-backed. push writes at index length and increments length; pop reads at length - 1 and decrements. Both are O(1) amortized, with the same 1.5x growth rule as any array.
  2. The call stack. Each function call pushes a frame (arguments, locals, return address) onto a fixed-size native stack, about 1 MB by default in Node.js, which is roughly 10,000 to 12,000 frames of typical size. Recursion deeper than that throws. --stack-size can raise it, but the correct fix is almost always an explicit stack in the heap.
  3. Recursion to iteration. Any recursive algorithm can be rewritten with an explicit stack: push the initial work item, loop while the stack is non-empty, pop an item, do the work, push its children. The heap has gigabytes; the native stack has one megabyte.
  4. Nested savepoints. PostgreSQL savepoints inside a transaction are a stack: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT a discards every savepoint created after a and returns to that state, exactly like popping until you reach a marker.
  5. Middleware unwinding. NestJS interceptors run their "before" logic in registration order and their "after" logic in reverse order, because each one wraps the next.handle() observable of the next. That reverse unwinding is a stack.

Time complexity

Operation Best Average Worst Notes
push O(1) O(1) amortized O(n) worst case is backing-store growth
pop O(1) O(1) O(1)
peek O(1) O(1) O(1) arr[arr.length - 1] or arr.at(-1)
Search O(1) O(n) O(n) stacks are not for searching
Size O(1) O(1) O(1)

Memory implications (V8, Node.js)

  • Array-backed stacks over-allocate by 50 percent; after a burst, pop does not shrink the backing store. For a stack that is occasionally huge and normally tiny, recreate it after the burst.
  • Each recursion frame costs roughly 50 to 150 bytes of native stack, and the limit is per thread; worker threads get their own (smaller by default) stacks.
  • An explicit stack of work items in the heap costs 8 bytes per pointer plus the item; a 1-million-item explicit stack is fine, a 1-million-deep recursion is not.

Practical example

Computing the price of a product bundle that can contain other bundles. The recursive version is natural and dangerous; the iterative version uses an explicit stack and a visited set so a cyclic bundle definition cannot take the process down.

// pricing/bundle-pricer.ts
export interface Bundle {
  id: string;
  priceCents: number;         // own price for simple products
  components: { id: string; quantity: number }[]; // empty for simple products
}

export class CyclicBundleError extends Error {
  constructor(public readonly path: string[]) {
    super(`bundle cycle detected: ${path.join(' -> ')}`);
  }
}

export function totalPriceCents(root: Bundle, lookup: (id: string) => Bundle): number {
  const stack: { bundle: Bundle; multiplier: number; path: string[] }[] = [
    { bundle: root, multiplier: 1, path: [root.id] },
  ];
  let total = 0;
  let steps = 0;

  while (stack.length > 0) {
    const { bundle, multiplier, path } = stack.pop()!; // LIFO: depth-first
    if (++steps > 10_000) throw new Error(`bundle ${root.id} is too large to price`);
    if (bundle.components.length === 0) {
      total += bundle.priceCents * multiplier;
      continue;
    }
    for (const c of bundle.components) {
      if (path.includes(c.id)) throw new CyclicBundleError([...path, c.id]); // path is short
      stack.push({ bundle: lookup(c.id), multiplier: multiplier * c.quantity, path: [...path, c.id] });
    }
  }
  return total;
}

The steps guard is the equivalent of a timeout: a senior engineer bounds every loop whose size is controlled by data.

NestJS example

Nested savepoints with TypeORM's QueryRunner. When a transaction is already open, TypeORM's PostgreSQL driver turns startTransaction() into SAVEPOINT typeorm_N, commitTransaction() into RELEASE SAVEPOINT, and rollbackTransaction() into ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT. The service below places an order and tries to apply a promotion inside a savepoint; if the promotion fails, only that part is undone and the order still commits.

// orders/place-order.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';
import { PromotionService } from '../promotions/promotion.service';

@Injectable()
export class PlaceOrderService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(PlaceOrderService.name);

  constructor(
    private readonly dataSource: DataSource,
    private readonly promotions: PromotionService,
  ) {}

  async place(userId: string, items: { productId: string; qty: number }[], promoCode?: string) {
    const runner = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner();
    await runner.connect();
    await runner.startTransaction();                        // BEGIN (depth 1)
    try {
      const order = await runner.manager.save(Order, { userId, items, status: 'pending' });

      if (promoCode) {
        await runner.startTransaction();                    // SAVEPOINT typeorm_2 (depth 2)
        try {
          await this.promotions.apply(runner.manager, order.id, promoCode);
          await runner.commitTransaction();                 // RELEASE SAVEPOINT typeorm_2
        } catch (err) {
          await runner.rollbackTransaction();               // ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT typeorm_2
          this.logger.warn(`promo ${promoCode} rejected for order ${order.id}: ${String(err)}`);
        }
      }

      await runner.commitTransaction();                     // COMMIT (depth 1)
      return order;
    } catch (err) {
      await runner.rollbackTransaction();                   // ROLLBACK everything
      throw err;
    } finally {
      await runner.release();                               // return the connection to the pool
    }
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, user_id, status) VALUES (8813, 42, 'pending');

SAVEPOINT promo;                                   -- push
UPDATE orders SET discount_cents = 500 WHERE id = 8813;
INSERT INTO promo_redemptions (code, order_id) VALUES ('WELCOME', 8813);
-- unique violation: this user already redeemed WELCOME
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT promo;                       -- pop back to the marker; the order row survives
RELEASE SAVEPOINT promo;

COMMIT;

Without the savepoint, the unique violation would abort the whole transaction (current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block) and the order would be lost too. Each savepoint costs a little: PostgreSQL assigns a sub-transaction id, and more than 64 open sub-transactions per session spill to disk and slow down every visibility check on the server, so do not create a savepoint per row in a bulk loop.

TypeORM example

The QueryRunner pattern above is the explicit form. The nested manager.transaction form is shorter but hides the savepoint, which is why many teams prefer the explicit one for anything that must be reasoned about in an incident.

Sequelize example

await sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  const order = await Order.create({ userId, status: 'pending' }, { transaction: t });

  try {
    // A nested transaction with a parent becomes SAVEPOINT in PostgreSQL.
    await sequelize.transaction({ transaction: t }, async (sp) => {
      await PromoRedemption.create({ code, orderId: order.id }, { transaction: sp });
      await order.update({ discountCents: 500 }, { transaction: sp });
    });
  } catch (err) {
    logger.warn(`promo rejected for ${order.id}: ${String(err)}`); // outer transaction continues
  }
  return order;
});

Production scenario
