A catalog with 40,000 products and 1,200 bundles serves 800 RPS of price lookups. Bundles nest at most four levels deep, so the explicit stack never holds more than a few dozen items and pricing costs under 20 microseconds. The stack matters not for speed but for safety: when a merchant misconfigures a bundle to contain itself, the request returns a 422 with the cycle path in 30 microseconds instead of taking down the pod.

The call stack shows up as a limit in another place: deeply nested JSON. A body with 20,000 nested arrays is accepted by JSON.parse in modern V8, but class-transformer and validators that recurse per level are not always so careful. Cap nesting depth at the edge (a 1 MB body limit rarely allows more than a few thousand levels anyway) and keep recursion out of request-path code you do not control.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call engineer is paged: catalog-api returns HTTP 500 for GET /products/b-4471 and the error rate graph shows one product responsible for 100 percent of failures. The log line: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded at priceOf (bundle-pricer.ts:18). A merchant created bundle b-4471 containing bundle b-4470, which a colleague had, five minutes earlier, edited to contain b-4471. The recursive pricer followed the cycle until the native stack ran out. The exception filter logged it and returned 500, but the product page, the cart and the search index refresh all called the same function, so a single bad row broke three user journeys. The fix was the iterative pricer with cycle detection plus a database-level guard: a trigger that rejects a bundle_components insert if a recursive CTE from the child reaches the parent. Two layers, because "the application validates it" is not a constraint.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Stack overflow is not catchable where you think. The RangeError unwinds many frames before any handler runs; state modified in those frames may be half-applied.
  • Popping an empty stack returns undefined in JavaScript, silently. Check length or wrap in a class that throws.
  • Deep recursion inside async code hides its depth across await boundaries and then overflows in a microtask, with a stack trace that does not name the loop.
  • Savepoint explosion. A savepoint per row in a 100,000-row import creates 100,000 sub-transactions; beyond 64 per session PostgreSQL performance degrades sharply.
  • Forgetting RELEASE. Unreleased savepoints accumulate until COMMIT; harmless in small numbers, a leak in loops.
  • LIFO unwinding order surprises. An interceptor registered first runs its "after" logic last; a cleanup that assumes otherwise runs too early.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Recursion is allowed in tests, scripts and tree code with a proven small depth. On a request path, over data whose shape is controlled by users or merchants, the senior converts it to an explicit stack with a visited set and a step budget, because the alternative is a crash triggered by a single bad row. They also know that "the data cannot have cycles" is only true when a constraint, trigger or serializable check makes it true.

Common mistakes

  • Recursive tree walks over user data without a depth or cycle guard.
  • Using shift/unshift as the stack operations (front of the array, O(n)) instead of push/pop.
  • Wrapping every statement of a bulk job in a savepoint "for safety".
  • Catching the stack-overflow error and retrying, which overflows again.

Interview questions

  1. Why does Node.js throw "Maximum call stack size exceeded" at around 10,000 frames, and how do you process a tree deeper than that? Expected: about 1 MB native stack per thread; use an explicit heap-allocated stack. Follow-up: is --stack-size a fix? (Rarely; it moves the cliff and can segfault.)
  2. How are savepoints a stack, and what does ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT do to savepoints created after it? Expected: discards them; state returns to the marker. Follow-up: why avoid a savepoint per row?
  3. In NestJS, in what order do three global interceptors run before and after the handler? Expected: before in registration order, after in reverse; explain with next.handle() wrapping.
  4. Design cycle-safe pricing for nested bundles. Expected: iterative DFS with path tracking, a step budget, and a database guard against cyclic inserts.

Practical exercise

Implement an iterative CategoryTreeService.flatten(rootId) that returns categories with their depth, using an explicit stack, over a self-referencing categories(id, parent_id) table. Acceptance criteria: processes a seeded tree of 200,000 nodes and depth 50,000 without a stack overflow; detects an injected cycle and throws a typed error naming the cycle; the service loads children in batches with WHERE parent_id = ANY($1) (one query per level, not one per node); a test asserts at most depth + 1 queries for a chain-shaped tree.

7.6 Queue

Concept

A queue is first in, first out (FIFO): you add at the back (enqueue) and remove from the front (dequeue). It is the data structure of waiting. Every job system, message broker, request buffer and event loop is a queue with extra guarantees layered on top.

Why does it exist?

Queues decouple the rate at which work arrives from the rate at which it is done. A checkout endpoint that must send an e-mail, update inventory, notify the warehouse and refresh analytics would take 900 ms and fail if any of those was down. With a queue it writes the order, enqueues "order placed", and returns in 40 ms; workers do the rest at their own pace and retry on failure. Without queues you either couple every latency and failure together, or you lose work during a burst.

Mental model

Imagine the line at a pharmacy counter. People join at the back and are served from the front in order. The line absorbs a bus-load of customers arriving at once; the pharmacist's pace does not change. If the line grows past the door, that is your signal to add a pharmacist (scale consumers) or tell people to come back later (backpressure).

How it works

  1. Ring buffer. A fixed array with head and tail indexes that wrap around. Enqueue writes at tail and advances it; dequeue reads at head and advances it. Both O(1) with no shifting. When full, allocate a bigger array and copy the elements in order.
  2. Why not Array.prototype.shift? shift removes index 0 and moves every remaining element down. Draining 100,000 items costs about 5 billion element moves.
  3. Boundedness. A queue that can grow forever is a memory leak with a business justification. Production queues are bounded and define what happens when full: block the producer, drop the oldest, drop the newest, or reject with an error.
  4. Durability. An in-memory queue dies with the process. Durable queues live in Redis (BullMQ), RabbitMQ (acknowledgements, persistence) or Kafka (append-only partitioned log with consumer offsets).
  5. The event loop's queues. Node.js itself runs on queues: process.nextTick callbacks first, then promise microtasks, then timers, then I/O callbacks. A recursive nextTick or an endless chain of resolved promises starves I/O; the queue that never empties blocks everything behind it.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> waiting: add job
    waiting --> active: worker picks up
    active --> completed: success
    active --> failed: error and no attempts left
    active --> delayed: error with backoff
    delayed --> waiting: backoff elapsed
    completed --> [*]
    failed --> [*]

Time complexity

Operation Best Average Worst Notes
enqueue (ring buffer) O(1) O(1) amortized O(n) worst case is growth
dequeue (ring buffer) O(1) O(1) O(1)
dequeue via Array.shift O(1) O(n) O(n) best case is a 1-element array
peek O(1) O(1) O(1)
size O(1) O(1) O(1)
Search O(n) O(n) O(n) queues are not for searching

Memory implications (V8, Node.js)

  • A ring buffer of capacity c costs 8c bytes of pointers plus the items, allocated once.
  • Growable queues double capacity; after a burst of 1 million items the backing store stays at 1 million slots. Shrink explicitly or recreate.
  • An unbounded in-process queue receiving 3,000 events per second of 1 KB each grows by 3 MB per second when the consumer stalls; a 1 GB container has about five minutes.

Practical example

A growable ring-buffer queue. The deque in Section 7.7 extends it.

// common/ring-queue.ts
export class RingQueue<T> {
  protected buf: (T | undefined)[];
  protected head = 0;   // index of the front element
  protected count = 0;

  constructor(initialCapacity = 16) {
    this.buf = new Array(initialCapacity);
  }

  get size(): number {
    return this.count;
  }

  enqueue(item: T): void {
    if (this.count === this.buf.length) this.grow();
    this.buf[(this.head + this.count) % this.buf.length] = item; // write at the tail
    this.count++;
  }

  dequeue(): T | undefined {
    if (this.count === 0) return undefined;
    const item = this.buf[this.head];
    this.buf[this.head] = undefined;                // release the reference for GC
    this.head = (this.head + 1) % this.buf.length;  // advance, wrapping around
    this.count--;
    return item;
  }

  peek(): T | undefined {
    return this.count === 0 ? undefined : this.buf[this.head];
  }

  protected grow(): void {
    const next = new Array<T | undefined>(this.buf.length * 2);
    for (let i = 0; i < this.count; i++) {
      next[i] = this.buf[(this.head + i) % this.buf.length]; // copy in logical order
    }
    this.buf = next;
    this.head = 0;
  }
}

NestJS example

A durable queue with @nestjs/bullmq: the producer enqueues from the order service with an idempotent job id, and a worker processes with retries and exponential backoff.

// notifications/notifications.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { BullModule } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { NotificationsProcessor } from './notifications.processor';
import { NotificationsProducer } from './notifications.producer';

@Module({
  imports: [
    BullModule.forRoot({ connection: { host: process.env.REDIS_HOST, port: Number(process.env.REDIS_PORT) } }),
    BullModule.registerQueue({ name: 'notifications' }),
  ],
  providers: [NotificationsProcessor, NotificationsProducer],
  exports: [NotificationsProducer],
})
export class NotificationsModule {}

// notifications/notifications.producer.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectQueue } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Queue } from 'bullmq';

@Injectable()
export class NotificationsProducer {
  constructor(@InjectQueue('notifications') private readonly queue: Queue) {}

  async orderPlaced(orderId: string, userId: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.queue.add(
      'order-placed',
      { orderId, userId },
      {
        jobId: `order-placed:${orderId}`,               // duplicate enqueues collapse into one job
        attempts: 5,
        backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 2_000 }, // 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, 32s
        removeOnComplete: 1_000,                        // keep the last 1k for inspection
        removeOnFail: 10_000,
      },
    );
  }
}

// notifications/notifications.processor.ts
import { Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { OnWorkerEvent, Processor, WorkerHost } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Job } from 'bullmq';

@Processor('notifications', { concurrency: 10 })
export class NotificationsProcessor extends WorkerHost {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(NotificationsProcessor.name);

  async process(job: Job<{ orderId: string; userId: string }>): Promise<void> {
    // Must be idempotent: the same job can run twice after a worker crash.
    await this.sendOrderPlacedEmail(job.data.orderId, job.data.userId);
  }

  @OnWorkerEvent('failed')
  onFailed(job: Job, err: Error) {
    this.logger.error(`job ${job.id} attempt ${job.attemptsMade} failed: ${err.message}`);
  }

  private async sendOrderPlacedEmail(orderId: string, userId: string) { /* provider call with timeout */ }
}

PostgreSQL example

When you already run PostgreSQL and need a modest, transactional queue, a jobs table with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is the standard pattern. Workers lock and claim one row each without blocking one another.

CREATE TABLE jobs (
  id         bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  kind       text        NOT NULL,
  payload    jsonb       NOT NULL,
  status     text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued',   -- queued | active | done | failed
  run_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  attempts   int         NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  locked_by  text
);
-- Partial index: only rows a worker could pick are indexed, so the index stays tiny.
CREATE INDEX jobs_ready_idx ON jobs (run_at, id) WHERE status = 'queued';

-- Claim one job atomically.
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'active', locked_by = $1, attempts = attempts + 1
WHERE id = (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
  WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_at <= now()
  ORDER BY run_at, id
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT 1
)
RETURNING id, kind, payload;
Update on jobs  (cost=0.57..8.61 rows=1 width=98) (actual time=0.091..0.094 rows=1 loops=1)
  InitPlan 1 (returns $1)
    ->  Limit  (cost=0.42..0.56 rows=1 width=22) (actual time=0.047..0.048 rows=1 loops=1)
          ->  LockRows  (cost=0.42..1418.32 rows=9812 width=22) (actual time=0.046..0.046 rows=1 loops=1)
                ->  Index Scan using jobs_ready_idx on jobs jobs_1  (cost=0.42..1320.20 rows=9812 width=22) (actual time=0.028..0.028 rows=1 loops=1)
                      Index Cond: (run_at <= now())
  ->  Index Scan using jobs_pkey on jobs  (cost=0.15..8.05 rows=1 width=98) (actual time=0.019..0.020 rows=1 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (id = $1)
Execution Time: 0.152 ms

This works well up to a few hundred jobs per second. Every claim is an UPDATE, which creates a dead tuple, so the table needs aggressive autovacuum settings; and thousands of workers polling creates lock traffic. Beyond that scale you move to Redis or Kafka.

TypeORM example

const job = await dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  const candidate = await manager
    .createQueryBuilder(JobEntity, 'j')
    .setLock('pessimistic_write')
    .setOnLocked('skip_locked')          // FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
    .where('j.status = :s AND j.run_at <= now()', { s: 'queued' })
    .orderBy('j.run_at', 'ASC').addOrderBy('j.id', 'ASC')
    .limit(1)
    .getOne();
  if (!candidate) return null;
  await manager.update(JobEntity, candidate.id, { status: 'active', lockedBy: workerId });
  return candidate;
});

Sequelize example

const job = await sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  const candidate = await JobModel.findOne({
    where: { status: 'queued', runAt: { [Op.lte]: new Date() } },
    order: [['runAt', 'ASC'], ['id', 'ASC']],
    lock: t.LOCK.UPDATE,
    skipLocked: true,                    // FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
    transaction: t,
  });
  if (!candidate) return null;
  await candidate.update({ status: 'active', lockedBy: workerId }, { transaction: t });
  return candidate;
});

Production scenario

An order platform emits 3,000 events per second at peak. BullMQ on a single Redis instance handles this comfortably: each add is one round trip (about 0.3 ms from the same availability zone), and 20 worker pods with concurrency 10 give 200 in-flight jobs. The metrics that matter are queue depth (waiting count) and oldest job age. Depth alone lies: 50,000 waiting jobs with workers draining 4,000 per second is a 12-second backlog, which may be fine; 500 waiting jobs that are 40 minutes old means the workers are dead. Alert on age.

The moment a queue is in the path, the senior mantra applies to every consumer: Can it duplicate? Yes, after a worker crash the same job runs again, so every job handler is idempotent. Can it become slow? Yes, so every job has a timeout and a bounded attempt count. Can it partially succeed? Yes, so multi-step jobs record progress or are split into separate jobs.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call engineer is paged: three api pods were OOMKilled within ten minutes. An analytics interceptor pushed one event per request onto an in-process events: AnalyticsEvent[] array, and a setInterval flushed it to a warehouse HTTP endpoint every second. At 01:58 the warehouse started answering in 20 seconds instead of 200 ms. The flush awaited the slow response; meanwhile 2,800 requests per second kept pushing 1.2 KB events. In four minutes the array held 670,000 events and 800 MB. The pod died, its events were lost, and the replacement pod started the same climb.

The fix had three parts: a bounded RingQueue of 10,000 events that drops the oldest and increments a analytics_events_dropped_total counter when full; a flush with a 2-second timeout so one slow call cannot stall the drain; and an alert on the drop counter. The queue lost some analytics events for twenty minutes, which the business accepted, instead of losing the checkout API.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Unbounded growth when producers outpace consumers; always bound and define the overflow policy.
  • Duplicate delivery after consumer crash, visibility timeout or network partition; make handlers idempotent with a job id or idempotency key.
  • Poison messages that fail every time and block the head of a strictly ordered queue; use a dead-letter queue after N attempts.
  • Consumer lag and rebalancing in Kafka: adding a consumer pauses the group briefly; a consumer that takes too long is kicked and its partition reassigned, often causing duplicates.
  • Out-of-order processing when concurrency is greater than 1; events for the same order must be keyed to one partition or serialized by a lock.
  • Priority inversion: a burst of cheap jobs starves urgent ones; use separate queues or a priority queue (Section 7.13).
  • Redis down means enqueues fail; decide whether the request fails (safer for payments) or the work is written to an outbox table first (the transactional outbox pattern).
  • Lost in-memory work on deploys; drain queues in onApplicationShutdown and keep jobs small.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A queue is the first tool the senior reaches for when a request does more than one thing, and the tool they refuse to run in-process for anything that must not be lost. They start with the simplest durable option that already exists in the stack (a PostgreSQL jobs table under 100 jobs per second, BullMQ on Redis up to tens of thousands per second) and only move to Kafka when they need replay, multiple independent consumer groups, or ordering across a firehose. They ask: what is the overflow policy, who owns idempotency, how do we see the age of the oldest message, and what happens on deploy.

To a product manager: "The order is saved instantly; the e-mail and the warehouse notification are queued and will happen within seconds even if the e-mail provider is having a bad day. If it is down for an hour, the e-mails go out an hour late; the orders are never lost."

Common mistakes

  • Array.shift() as the dequeue operation on a hot path.
  • In-memory queues for work that must survive a restart.
  • Non-idempotent job handlers with attempts: 5; the customer gets five e-mails.
  • No timeout inside the job, so a hung provider call holds a worker slot forever.
  • Alerting on queue depth instead of oldest-job age.
  • One giant job that does 10,000 things and cannot resume.

Interview questions

  1. Why is Array.prototype.shift the wrong dequeue for a hot queue, and what do you use? Expected: O(n) shift of all elements; use a ring buffer with head/tail indexes or a linked list.
  2. Design the overflow policy for an in-process event buffer. Expected: bounded size, drop-oldest or reject, metric on drops, flush timeout. Follow-up: when is dropping unacceptable? (Payments, audit logs: use an outbox.)
  3. How does FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED make PostgreSQL a queue, and what are its limits? Expected: workers claim rows without blocking; limits are dead-tuple bloat, polling load, a few hundred jobs per second.
  4. A job ran twice and the customer got two refunds. Why, and how do you prevent it? Expected: at-least-once delivery; idempotency key on the refund; store the result keyed by job id.
  5. When do you pick Kafka over BullMQ? Expected: replay, multiple consumer groups, partition ordering, very high throughput; cost is operating a distributed log.
  6. What is head-of-line blocking in a queue and how do you avoid it? Expected: a poison or slow message delays everything behind it; dead-letter after N attempts, separate queues per priority or tenant.

Practical exercise

Build BoundedEventBuffer on RingQueue plus a BullMQ-backed EmailQueue. Acceptance criteria: the buffer has capacity 10,000, drops the oldest on overflow and exposes dropped as a Prometheus counter; a flush that exceeds 2 seconds is abandoned via AbortController and the events are retried at the next tick; the e-mail job is idempotent using jobId = order-placed:<orderId>, proven by a test that enqueues twice and observes one send; a chaos test that pauses the worker for 60 seconds must show oldest job age climbing while waiting stays bounded by the number of test orders.

7.7 Deque

Concept

A deque (double-ended queue, pronounced "deck") supports O(1) insertion and removal at both ends: pushFront, pushBack, popFront, popBack. A queue is a deque you only use one way; a stack is a deque you only use at one end. Redis lists are deques (LPUSH, RPUSH, LPOP, RPOP), and the in-memory job list that BullMQ drains is used as one.

Why does it exist?

Several backend problems need both ends. A sliding time window keeps timestamps in order, adds new ones at the back and expires old ones from the front. A "retry this job first" feature pushes a job to the front of a queue (BullMQ's lifo: true option does exactly that with RPUSH instead of LPUSH). A "last 100 errors" buffer appends at the back and trims from the front. Work-stealing schedulers let the owning thread pop from one end while other threads steal from the opposite end to reduce contention. A queue or stack alone cannot do any of these in O(1).

Mental model

Imagine a train platform with doors at both ends of the carriage. Passengers may board or alight at either door, but nobody climbs through the windows in the middle. That is the whole contract: both ends are cheap, the middle is not your business.

How it works

The ring buffer from Section 7.6 already stores elements in a circular array with a head index. Adding to the front is one subtraction with wraparound: head = (head - 1 + capacity) % capacity, then write at head. Removing from the back is reading at (head + count - 1) % capacity and decrementing count. Nothing shifts. A doubly linked list gives the same O(1) at both ends with worse locality; the ring buffer wins in JavaScript unless you also need O(1) removal from the middle by node handle.

Time complexity

Operation Best Average Worst Notes
pushFront / pushBack O(1) O(1) amortized O(n) worst case is growth
popFront / popBack O(1) O(1) O(1)
peekFront / peekBack O(1) O(1) O(1)
Index access O(1) O(1) O(1) ring buffer only; O(n) for linked list
Insert or remove in the middle O(n) O(n) O(n) not what deques are for

Memory implications

Identical to the ring queue: one contiguous backing array, 8 bytes per slot plus items, no per-element allocation. The denque npm package is the standard production implementation and is what several Redis clients use for their pending-command queues.

Practical example

The deque itself, extending RingQueue, and a monotonic deque that answers "what is the maximum latency in the last N samples?" in O(1) amortized per sample. The trick: keep the deque sorted in decreasing order by evicting smaller values from the back when a bigger one arrives; the front is always the current maximum.

// common/deque.ts
import { RingQueue } from './ring-queue';

export class Deque<T> extends RingQueue<T> {
  pushBack(item: T): void {
    this.enqueue(item);
  }

  pushFront(item: T): void {
    if (this.count === this.buf.length) this.grow();
    this.head = (this.head - 1 + this.buf.length) % this.buf.length; // step back with wraparound
    this.buf[this.head] = item;
    this.count++;
  }

  popFront(): T | undefined {
    return this.dequeue();
  }

  popBack(): T | undefined {
    if (this.count === 0) return undefined;
    const idx = (this.head + this.count - 1) % this.buf.length;
    const item = this.buf[idx];
    this.buf[idx] = undefined;
    this.count--;
    return item;
  }

  peekBack(): T | undefined {
    return this.count === 0 ? undefined : this.buf[(this.head + this.count - 1) % this.buf.length];
  }
}

// metrics/sliding-max.ts  -- max of the last `windowSize` samples, O(1) amortized per push
export class SlidingMax {
  private readonly dq = new Deque<{ seq: number; value: number }>();
  private seq = 0;

  constructor(private readonly windowSize: number) {}

  push(value: number): void {
    const seq = this.seq++;
    // Drop smaller values from the back: they can never be the max while `value` is in the window.
    while (this.dq.size > 0 && this.dq.peekBack()!.value <= value) this.dq.popBack();
    this.dq.pushBack({ seq, value });
    // Expire the front if it has left the window.
    if (this.dq.peekFront()!.seq <= seq - this.windowSize) this.dq.popFront();
  }

  max(): number {
    return this.dq.size === 0 ? 0 : this.dq.peekFront()!.value;
  }
}

NestJS example

A sliding-window-log rate limiter guard with one deque of timestamps per client. New requests push at the back; timestamps older than the window pop from the front. Each client's memory is bounded by the limit itself, because we stop pushing once the deque is full. This is a per-pod limiter; for a cluster-wide one you move the same logic into a Redis sorted set (see the API Design part) or use @nestjs/throttler with a Redis storage.

// rate-limit/sliding-window.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, HttpException, HttpStatus, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Deque } from '../common/deque';

@Injectable()
export class SlidingWindowGuard implements CanActivate {
  private readonly windows = new Map<string, Deque<number>>();
  private readonly limit = 100;          // requests
  private readonly windowMs = 60_000;    // per minute

  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<{ ip: string; headers: Record<string, string> }>();
    const key = req.headers['x-api-key'] ?? req.ip;
    const now = Date.now();

    let dq = this.windows.get(key);
    if (!dq) {
      dq = new Deque<number>(this.limit);
      this.windows.set(key, dq);
    }
    while (dq.size > 0 && dq.peek()! <= now - this.windowMs) dq.popFront(); // expire old hits

    if (dq.size >= this.limit) {
      const retryAfterSec = Math.ceil((dq.peek()! + this.windowMs - now) / 1000);
      throw new HttpException({ message: 'Too many requests', retryAfterSec }, HttpStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS);
    }
    dq.pushBack(now);
    return true;
  }
}

The windows map must be swept periodically (drop keys whose deque is empty), otherwise one-off clients leak entries; that sweep is the hash-map hygiene covered in Section 7.8.

Production scenario

The natural home of the deque at scale is Redis. LPUSH a job and BRPOP from the other side gives you a durable FIFO shared by every pod; RPUSH a job to jump the line. A "recent activity" feed per user is LPUSH user:42:feed <event> followed by LTRIM user:42:feed 0 99, which keeps exactly the last 100 items in O(1) per write and reads them with LRANGE 0 99 in about 0.3 ms. At 20,000 feed writes per second a single Redis node stays under 30 percent CPU, because every one of those commands touches only the ends of a list.

Failure scenario

A rate limiter used a plain array with shift() to expire old timestamps and unshift() for a "priority client" feature. At 200 RPS per client it was invisible. A partner integration then sent 4,000 RPS from a single API key; each request shifted an array of 4,000 entries, and the guard alone consumed 40 percent of the event loop while rejecting requests it was supposed to reject cheaply. The rate limiter became the thing that needed rate limiting. Replacing the array with a deque cut the guard's cost to under 1 microsecond per request.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Wraparound arithmetic errors (negative modulo in JavaScript) when stepping the head backwards; always add capacity before taking the modulus.
  • Growth while wrapped must copy in logical order, not physical order, or the queue reorders silently.
  • Per-key deques leak when keys are unbounded (IP addresses); sweep or use an LRU map of deques.
  • Clock skew between pods makes per-pod sliding windows disagree; cluster-wide limits belong in Redis.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Deques are the workhorse for anything "bounded and recent": recent errors, recent latencies, recent timestamps, recent feed items. The senior picks the ring-buffer deque for locality, bounds it explicitly, and moves it to a Redis list the moment it must be shared across pods. They never touch the middle.

Common mistakes

  • Using unshift for front insertion on large arrays.
  • Implementing a deque with a linked list when a ring buffer would be 5 times faster and use a sixth of the memory.
  • Forgetting LTRIM after LPUSH, so Redis feed lists grow forever.

Interview questions

  1. How do you get O(1) pushFront in an array-backed structure? Expected: circular buffer with a head index that steps backwards with wraparound.
  2. Explain the monotonic deque and one backend use. Expected: keep candidates in decreasing order, evict dominated ones from the back; sliding-window max latency, or max in-flight count over the last N seconds.
  3. How would you keep a per-user "last 100 events" list in Redis, and what is its complexity? Expected: LPUSH plus LTRIM 0 99, O(1) amortized per write.
  4. A per-client rate limiter works at 100 RPS and collapses at 5,000 RPS from one client. Diagnose. Expected: shift/unshift on arrays; replace with a deque; then discuss moving to Redis for multi-pod correctness.

Practical exercise

Implement RecentErrorsService that keeps the last 200 unhandled exceptions per pod in a Deque, captured by a global exception filter, and exposes them at GET /internal/errors. Acceptance criteria: memory is bounded regardless of error rate (prove with a test that raises 100,000 errors and checks size === 200); entries include timestamp, route and a truncated stack (max 2 KB per entry, truncated by bytes); the endpoint returns newest first without copying the whole deque more than once; and a SlidingMax over the last 1,000 request latencies is exposed on the same endpoint, verified against a brute-force Math.max in tests.

7.8 Hash Map

Concept

A hash map (hash table, dictionary) stores key-value pairs and finds a value by its key in O(1) on average. It does this by running the key through a hash function that produces a number, using that number to pick a bucket in an array, and storing the pair there. Two keys that land in the same bucket are a collision, handled by chaining entries or probing for a free slot.

In JavaScript you have three hash maps: Map (any key type, insertion order, size in O(1)), the plain object (string and symbol keys, fast when its shape is fixed, surprising when used as a dictionary), and WeakMap (object keys held weakly, for metadata that must not keep its key alive). Redis is a hash map you reach over the network; a PostgreSQL hash join is a hash map built for one query.

Why does it exist?

Almost every "find X by its id" in a backend is a hash lookup: sessions by token, users by id, feature flags by name, routes by path, in-flight requests by idempotency key, DI providers by token, HTTP headers by name. Without hashing you scan, and scanning at 10,000 lookups per second over 100,000 entries is a billion comparisons per second. The hash map turns lookup cost from "proportional to the data" into "proportional to the key".

Mental model

Imagine a coat check with 1,000 numbered hooks. The attendant does not search for your coat; she computes a hook number from your ticket (say, the last three digits) and walks straight to it. If two tickets map to the same hook, both coats hang there and she checks the tags on that hook only (chaining). When coats outnumber hooks so much that every hook holds a pile, she opens a bigger room and re-hangs everything by the new numbering (resizing). The load factor is coats per hook.

How it works

  1. Hashing the key. V8 computes a 32-bit hash for a string once and caches it in the string's header, so repeated lookups with the same key skip the hashing. Small integers hash by value. Objects used as keys get a random identity hash on first use, which is why Map keyed by objects compares by identity, never by content.
  2. Choosing the bucket. index = hash & (bucketCount - 1) with a power-of-two bucket count. The bits are cheap; the quality of the hash decides how evenly keys spread.
  3. Collisions. V8's Map and Set use an ordered hash table: entries live in a flat data array in insertion order, each bucket points at the newest entry that hashed into it, and each entry stores a chain pointer to the previous entry in the same bucket. Lookup walks the chain comparing keys. Average chain length is the load factor.
  4. Load factor and resizing. V8 keeps roughly two entries per bucket. When the entry array fills, it allocates a table of double the capacity and reinserts every live entry, an O(n) pause. Deleted entries leave holes that are compacted during the next resize, so a Map with heavy churn is periodically rebuilt.
  5. Insertion order. Because entries sit in a flat array in insertion order, iteration is ordered and cheap. This is also why a Map alone can implement an LRU cache: delete and re-insert moves a key to the end.
  6. Plain objects and hidden classes. V8 does not store { id, name, price } as a hash table. It assigns the object a hidden class (V8 calls it a Map, confusingly) describing where each property lives, and property access compiles to a fixed offset read. Objects created with the same properties in the same order share the class, and call sites that always see one class become monomorphic inline caches, about 1 nanosecond per access.
  7. Dictionary mode. If you delete a property, add properties in varying orders, or add more than about 128 out-of-object properties dynamically, V8 abandons the hidden class and converts the object into a real hash table ("slow properties"). Access is then 5 to 10 times slower and inline caches go megamorphic. An object used as a dictionary with thousands of computed keys is always in this mode; use Map instead.
  8. Hash flooding. An attacker who can predict the hash function sends thousands of keys that collide, degrading every lookup to O(n). V8 randomizes its hash seed per process, and body parsers cap the number of parameters (qs defaults to 1,000) for the same reason.
flowchart LR
    subgraph Buckets
        B0["bucket 0"]
        B3["bucket 3"]
        B5["bucket 5"]
        B7["bucket 7"]
    end
    K1["key order:8813"] -->|"hash and 7 = 3"| B3
    K2["key user:42"] -->|"hash and 7 = 5"| B5
    K3["key cart:77"] -->|"hash and 7 = 3"| B3
    B3 --> E3["entry cart:77"]
    E3 -->|"chain"| E1["entry order:8813"]
    B5 --> E2["entry user:42"]

Time complexity

Operation Best Average Worst Notes
get / has O(1) O(1) O(n) worst case is every key in one bucket
set O(1) O(1) amortized O(n) worst case is the resize
delete O(1) O(1) O(n) leaves a hole compacted at next resize
size (Map) O(1) O(1) O(1) Object.keys(obj).length is O(n)
Iteration O(n) O(n) O(n) insertion order for Map
Resize O(n) O(n) O(n) happens at powers of two

Memory implications (V8, Node.js)

  • A Map entry costs three slots (key, value, chain) of 8 bytes plus its share of the bucket array and over-allocation, roughly 40 to 60 bytes per entry on top of the key and value objects. A Map<string, number> with 1 million 12-character keys is about 90 MB.
  • A plain object with a fixed shape stores property values inline or in a small properties array with no per-property hashing overhead; that is why DTOs and rows should be objects and dictionaries should be Maps.
  • Resizing a 4-million-entry Map allocates a new table of about 100 MB and reinserts everything in one synchronous step, a pause of 50 to 150 ms on the event loop. Pre-size by inserting into a Map you keep, or shard into several maps if the pause matters.
  • A Map never shrinks its bucket array unless a resize happens; a map that once held 5 million keys and now holds 50 still owns the large table.
  • WeakMap entries disappear when the key object becomes unreachable, which makes it the correct structure for per-request metadata keyed by the request object.

Practical example

Single-flight request coalescing. When 400 concurrent requests miss the cache for the same product, only the first should query PostgreSQL; the other 399 should await the same promise. A Map<string, Promise<T>> of in-flight lookups does this in-process.

// common/single-flight.ts
export class SingleFlight<T> {
  private readonly inFlight = new Map<string, Promise<T>>();

  async run(key: string, loader: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    const existing = this.inFlight.get(key);      // O(1): someone is already loading this key
    if (existing) return existing;

    const p = loader().finally(() => this.inFlight.delete(key)); // release the slot on settle
    this.inFlight.set(key, p);
    return p;
  }

  get pending(): number {
    return this.inFlight.size;
  }
}

The finally is the important line: without it, a rejected promise stays in the map and every later caller receives the same stale rejection forever.

NestJS example

A product read service that combines single-flight with @nestjs/cache-manager. Cache hits skip everything; cache misses are coalesced per key; the loader talks to PostgreSQL once.

// products/product-read.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CACHE_MANAGER } from '@nestjs/cache-manager';
import { Cache } from 'cache-manager';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Product } from './product.entity';
import { SingleFlight } from '../common/single-flight';

@Injectable()
export class ProductReadService {
  private readonly flight = new SingleFlight<Product>();

  constructor(
    @Inject(CACHE_MANAGER) private readonly cache: Cache,
    @InjectRepository(Product) private readonly repo: Repository<Product>,
  ) {}

  async byId(id: string): Promise<Product> {
    const key = `product:${id}`;
    const cached = await this.cache.get<Product>(key);
    if (cached) return cached;

    return this.flight.run(key, async () => {
      const product = await this.repo.findOne({ where: { id } });
      if (!product) throw new NotFoundException(`product ${id} not found`);
      await this.cache.set(key, product, 60_000); // ttl in ms for cache-manager v5
      return product;
    });
  }
}

Register with CacheModule.register({ ttl: 60_000, max: 10_000 }) in the module; max bounds the in-memory store, which is the LRU cache of Section 7.17. Note that coalescing is per pod; twelve pods still send up to twelve queries for one hot key, which is why hot keys also get a Redis lock or a short "negative cache" entry.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL uses hash tables in three places you will see: hash indexes, hash joins and hash aggregates.

-- Equality-only lookups on long random tokens: a hash index is smaller than a B-tree
-- because it stores a 4-byte hash per entry instead of the whole 64-character key.
CREATE INDEX sessions_token_hash ON sessions USING hash (token);
SELECT user_id, expires_at FROM sessions WHERE token = $1;

-- A hash join builds an in-memory hash table from the smaller input, then probes it.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT o.id, u.email
FROM orders o JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE o.created_at >= now() - interval '1 day';
Hash Join  (cost=3462.00..18211.44 rows=48210 width=40) (actual time=21.3..96.8 rows=47955 loops=1)
  Hash Cond: (o.user_id = u.id)
  Buffers: shared hit=6104
  ->  Index Scan using orders_created_at_idx on orders o  (cost=0.56..13640.90 rows=48210 width=16) (actual time=0.04..41.2 rows=47955 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (created_at >= (now() - '1 day'::interval))
  ->  Hash  (cost=2211.00..2211.00 rows=100080 width=32) (actual time=20.9..20.9 rows=100080 loops=1)
        Buckets: 131072  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 7281kB
        ->  Seq Scan on users u  (cost=0.00..2211.00 rows=100080 width=32) (actual time=0.01..9.8 rows=100080 loops=1)
Planning Time: 0.41 ms
Execution Time: 99.1 ms

Buckets: 131072 Batches: 1 tells you the whole hash table fit in work_mem. When you see Batches: 8, PostgreSQL ran out of memory and split the join into batches spilled to temp files; raising work_mem for that session, or shrinking the build side with a better filter, fixes it. Hash indexes are equality-only (no ranges, no sorting, no uniqueness constraint) and have been crash-safe only since PostgreSQL 10; B-tree remains the default for good reasons (see Part 19 — Indexes).

TypeORM example

The most common hash-map win in ORM code is turning an N+1 pattern into one query plus an O(1) in-memory join.

// orders/order-enricher.ts
import { In, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';
import { User } from '../users/user.entity';

export class OrderEnricher {
  constructor(private readonly users: Repository<User>) {}

  async attachUsers(orders: Order[]): Promise<(Order & { user?: User })[]> {
    const ids = [...new Set(orders.map((o) => o.userId))];        // unique ids only
    const rows = await this.users.findBy({ id: In(ids) });        // ONE query, not orders.length
    const byId = new Map(rows.map((u) => [u.id, u]));             // O(n) build
    return orders.map((o) => ({ ...o, user: byId.get(o.userId) })); // O(1) per order
  }
}

Sequelize example

const ids = [...new Set(orders.map((o) => o.userId))];
const users = await User.findAll({ where: { id: { [Op.in]: ids } }, raw: true });
const byId = new Map<number, typeof users[number]>(users.map((u) => [u.id, u]));
const enriched = orders.map((o) => ({ ...o.get({ plain: true }), user: byId.get(o.userId) }));

Both examples are the DataLoader pattern by hand: batch the ids, one round trip, hash join in memory.

Production scenario

At 2,000 RPS an API gateway keeps a Map<string, ApiKeyRecord> of 40,000 API keys in memory, refreshed from PostgreSQL every 30 seconds. A lookup costs about 50 nanoseconds; the map costs about 8 MB. Redis is not consulted per request at all. That is the healthy shape: a bounded, read-mostly map whose size is controlled by you.

The unhealthy shape is a map whose keys come from the outside world. A per-IP rate limiter keyed by client address accepts 300,000 distinct IPs per day from a mobile fleet behind carrier NAT. Without expiry, the map grows by about 30 MB per day and the pod is restarted "for no reason" every ten days. Bound it (an LRU with a maximum of 100,000 keys), expire it (a sweep every minute), or move it to Redis with EXPIRE, where memory is shared and eviction is a configuration line.

Redis itself is the hash map at scale. A Redis hash (HSET user:42 name "Ana" plan "pro") with fewer than 128 fields is stored as a compact listpack; above that it becomes a real hash table. HGET is O(1) and about 0.2 ms from the same zone. HGETALL on a 2-million-field hash is O(n) and blocks the server; use HSCAN.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call engineer is paged: auth-api p99 is 1.8 seconds and rising, GC logs show 400 ms major collections every few seconds, and memory has climbed from 300 MB to 3.1 GB over six days. A heap snapshot shows one Map with 9.4 million entries: sessionsByToken. A "small optimization" three weeks earlier cached every validated session in memory to skip Redis. Sessions expired in Redis after 24 hours; the map never expired anything. Each entry held the token (a 64-character string, about 80 bytes), the session object (about 200 bytes) and map overhead, roughly 340 bytes, times 9.4 million entries.

The immediate fix was a rolling restart. The real fix was replacing the Map with an LRU of 50,000 entries and a 60-second TTL, which kept the Redis hit rate benefit for hot sessions while capping memory at 17 MB. The lesson: a map keyed by external data without an eviction policy is a memory leak with a delay measured in days.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Key equality is SameValueZero. map.get(1) and map.get('1') are different keys; NaN matches NaN; two equal-looking objects are different keys unless they are the same reference. Serialize composite keys to a canonical string (${merchantId}:${sku}).
  • Plain objects coerce keys to strings. obj[1] and obj['1'] collide; obj[{}] becomes obj['[object Object]'].
  • Prototype pollution. body['__proto__'] or body['constructor']['prototype'] written into a plain object via a naive deep merge changes every object in the process. Use Map, Object.create(null), or validate keys.
  • Integer-like keys iterate first in ascending order on plain objects, regardless of insertion order; Map preserves insertion order.
  • JSON.stringify(new Map()) is {}. Convert with Object.fromEntries(map) or serialize entries explicitly.
  • Hash flooding via query strings, JSON keys or headers; cap counts at the edge.
  • Resize pauses on very large maps block the event loop; shard or pre-warm.
  • Map shared across requests is mutable global state; one handler's clear() empties everyone's cache.
  • Stale entries when the source changes; a map without a refresh or TTL is a cache that lies.
  • Redis as the map at scale: a hot key (one product id read 50,000 times per second) pins one Redis shard; replicate hot keys into process memory with a short TTL.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The first question is "what controls the number of keys?" If the code does (a fixed set of routes, feature flags, API keys refreshed from the database), a Map is free and there is nothing to discuss. If users, IPs or upstream data do, the senior insists on a bound (LRU, TTL, sweep) before the first deploy, because they have seen the six-day memory graph.

The second is "objects for records, Map for dictionaries." DTOs, rows and config objects keep a fixed shape and stay fast. Anything indexed by a computed key goes in a Map; anything keyed by an object goes in a WeakMap.

The third is "per pod or shared?" An in-process map is a per-pod cache, never a source of truth. If two pods must agree (rate limits, sessions, idempotency), the map lives in Redis, and the in-process map is at most a short-TTL front for it.

To a product manager: "Caching sessions in memory made login 2 ms faster and took the service down every six days. Capping the cache keeps the speed and removes the outage; it is a two-line change and a test."

Common mistakes

  • Using a plain object as a dictionary with thousands of dynamic keys (dictionary mode, prototype keys, O(n) Object.keys).
  • Unbounded Map keyed by user or client data.
  • Forgetting finally cleanup in single-flight maps, so a rejection is served forever.
  • JSON.stringify on a Map and shipping {} to the client.
  • Rebuilding a Map from a large array inside every request instead of once per refresh.
  • Trusting a per-pod map for cluster-wide decisions such as rate limits or idempotency.

Interview questions

  1. How does V8's Map handle collisions and why does it preserve insertion order? Expected: ordered hash table with a flat entry array and per-bucket chains; order comes from the entry array. Follow-up: what happens on delete? (A hole, compacted at the next rehash.)
  2. When does a plain object fall into dictionary mode and why does it matter? Expected: delete, too many dynamic properties, inconsistent shapes; access becomes a hash lookup and inline caches go megamorphic.
  3. Design an in-memory cache of validated sessions. Expected: bounded LRU with TTL, per-pod, Redis remains the source of truth; discuss the memory per entry and the eviction policy. Why it matters: it is the most common self-inflicted memory leak.
  4. What is hash flooding and how do Node.js and PostgreSQL defend against it? Expected: adversarial collisions; randomized hash seeds, parameter-count limits; PostgreSQL uses batches and work_mem bounds for hash joins.
  5. Explain Buckets: 131072 Batches: 8 in an EXPLAIN plan. Expected: the hash join did not fit in work_mem and spilled; fix by filtering the build side or raising work_mem.
  6. When would you choose a hash index over a B-tree in PostgreSQL? Expected: equality-only lookups on long keys where size matters; never when you need ranges, ordering or a unique constraint.
  7. Why does map.get(userId) fail when userId came from a bigint column? Expected: pg returns bigint as a string; 1 and '1' are different keys.

Practical exercise

Implement BoundedTtlMap<K, V> and use it for API-key validation in a NestJS guard. Acceptance criteria: entries expire after a configurable TTL and the map never exceeds a configured capacity (evict the oldest on overflow, using Map insertion order); a sweep removes expired entries every 30 seconds with @Interval and is O(expired), not O(size); a load test with 500,000 distinct keys shows heap growth bounded by capacity; prototype-pollution keys (__proto__, constructor, prototype) are rejected by a validation pipe with a test; and pending single-flight promises are cleaned on both resolve and reject, proven by a test that fails the loader once and succeeds on the next call.

7.9 Set

Concept

A set stores unique values and answers "is X in here?" in O(1) on average. JavaScript's Set is the same ordered hash table as Map without the value slot. Sets also give you the classic operations: union, intersection and difference, which Node.js 22 exposes directly (a.union(b), a.intersection(b), a.difference(b), a.isSubsetOf(b)).

Why does it exist?

Membership questions are everywhere: is this user in the beta group, is this product id already in the response, has this message id been processed, is this role allowed, has this node been visited. Answering with array.includes costs O(n) per question and turns loops quadratic. The set is the structure that makes "have I seen this before?" free.

Mental model

Imagine a guest list at a door. The bouncer does not read the list top to bottom for every guest; the list is sorted into alphabet tabs (the hash) and each name appears once. Adding a name that is already there changes nothing.

How it works

Identical to the hash map: hash the value, pick a bucket, walk the chain to check for an equal value, insert if absent. Equality is SameValueZero, so objects are members by identity and '42' is not 42. Insertion order is preserved and the entry array is compacted on resize.

Time complexity

Operation Best Average Worst Notes
add / has / delete O(1) O(1) O(n) worst case is adversarial collisions
size O(1) O(1) O(1)
Union / intersection / difference O(n + m) O(n + m) O(n + m) iterate the smaller set and probe the other
Iteration O(n) O(n) O(n) insertion order
Build from array O(n) O(n) O(n) new Set(array) de-duplicates as it goes

Memory implications

Two slots per entry (value and chain) plus the bucket share, roughly 30 to 40 bytes per entry on top of the value. A Set of 1 million 36-character UUID strings is about 110 MB, because each UUID string costs about 56 bytes on its own. When membership sets reach tens of millions of items you move to Redis sets (about 60 to 90 bytes per member server-side), or, when a small false-positive rate is acceptable, to a Bloom filter at about 10 bits per member (Section 7.16).

Practical example

The de-duplication from Section 7.1, done right, plus the role check every API needs.

// notifications/recipients.ts
export function uniqueRecipients(emails: readonly string[]): string[] {
  const seen = new Set<string>();
  const out: string[] = [];
  for (const raw of emails) {
    const email = raw.trim().toLowerCase();  // canonical form, or duplicates slip through
    if (seen.has(email)) continue;           // O(1)
    seen.add(email);
    out.push(email);
  }
  return out;                                 // 80,000 recipients in about 8 ms
}

// auth/roles.ts
export function hasAnyRole(userRoles: readonly string[], required: ReadonlySet<string>): boolean {
  for (const r of userRoles) if (required.has(r)) return true; // O(user roles), not O(u x r)
  return false;
}

NestJS example

A RolesGuard that reads required roles from metadata into a Set once per handler and checks the user's roles against it, and a consumer-side de-duplication service that uses a Redis set operation for cluster-wide "have we processed this message?".

// auth/roles.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, Injectable, SetMetadata } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';

export const ROLES_KEY = 'roles';
export const Roles = (...roles: string[]) => SetMetadata(ROLES_KEY, roles);

@Injectable()
export class RolesGuard implements CanActivate {
  private readonly cache = new WeakMap<object, ReadonlySet<string>>(); // per handler, GC-safe

  constructor(private readonly reflector: Reflector) {}

  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const handler = ctx.getHandler();
    let required = this.cache.get(handler);
    if (!required) {
      required = new Set(this.reflector.getAllAndOverride<string[]>(ROLES_KEY, [handler, ctx.getClass()]) ?? []);
      this.cache.set(handler, required);
    }
    if (required.size === 0) return true;
    const user = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<{ user?: { roles: string[] } }>().user;
    return !!user && user.roles.some((r) => required!.has(r));
  }
}

// messaging/processed-messages.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

@Injectable()
export class ProcessedMessagesService {
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  /** Returns true the first time a message id is seen in the last 24h, false afterwards. */
  async claim(messageId: string): Promise<boolean> {
    // SET NX EX is an atomic "add to a set with expiry" that all pods share.
    const result = await this.redis.set(`msg:seen:${messageId}`, '1', 'EX', 86_400, 'NX');
    return result === 'OK';
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

The database is the set that matters. A unique index is a set with the membership check enforced under concurrency, which no application-level Set can do across pods.

-- "Add to set if absent" that is safe with 50 concurrent workers.
INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id, processed_at)
VALUES ($1, now())
ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING event_id;   -- returns a row only for the first insert

-- Set operations in SQL
SELECT product_id FROM wishlist_items WHERE user_id = 42
INTERSECT
SELECT product_id FROM products WHERE in_stock;

-- DISTINCT is a set build; the planner picks HashAggregate when it fits in work_mem
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM orders WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '7 days';
HashAggregate  (cost=9021.17..9203.51 rows=18234 width=8) (actual time=48.9..52.3 rows=17902 loops=1)
  Group Key: user_id
  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 1809kB
  Buffers: shared hit=3882
  ->  Index Scan using orders_created_at_idx on orders  (cost=0.56..8206.55 rows=325848 width=8) (actual time=0.03..29.1 rows=325112 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (created_at >= (now() - '7 days'::interval))
Execution Time: 53.4 ms

TypeORM example

// "add to set" with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; affected rows tells you whether it was new
const result = await dataSource
  .createQueryBuilder()
  .insert()
  .into(ProcessedEvent)
  .values({ eventId, processedAt: new Date() })
  .orIgnore()                 // ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
  .execute();
const isFirstTime = result.identifiers.length > 0;

Sequelize example

const [row, created] = await ProcessedEvent.findOrCreate({
  where: { eventId },
  defaults: { processedAt: new Date() },
  transaction: t,
});
// Or for bulk: ProcessedEvent.bulkCreate(rows, { ignoreDuplicates: true })

findOrCreate in Sequelize uses a transaction and catches the unique violation internally, so it needs the unique index to exist; without it, two concurrent calls both create.

Production scenario

A campaign service sends 80,000 e-mails in under a second of CPU thanks to Set de-duplication. The same service must also answer "has this user already received this campaign?" across 12 pods and 30 days of history for 50 million users. An in-process Set cannot do that (it is per pod and would cost 5 GB). A Redis set SADD campaign:2024-09:sent 8813 works to about 50 million members at roughly 4 GB of Redis memory; SISMEMBER is O(1) at 0.2 ms. Beyond that, or when memory is the constraint, a Bloom filter answers the same question in 60 MB with a 1 percent false-positive rate, and a false positive here only means one user misses one marketing e-mail, which the business happily accepts.

Failure scenario

A webhook receiver de-duplicated payment events with an in-memory Set<string> of event ids. It worked for a year on one pod. The team scaled to three pods; the load balancer sent Stripe's retry of the same event to a different pod, whose set had never seen it, and 214 customers were charged twice in one afternoon. The fix was the ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING insert above, inside the same transaction as the charge, so "seen" and "charged" commit or roll back together. A per-pod set is not a set; it is a guess.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Canonical form. 'Ana@Example.com' and 'ana@example.com' are different members unless you normalize first.
  • Objects by identity. new Set([{ id: 1 }, { id: 1 }]) has two members. Use ids or canonical strings.
  • Per-pod sets cannot enforce uniqueness across a cluster; only a unique index or a Redis atomic operation can.
  • Unbounded growth of "seen" sets; expire (Redis EXPIRE) or move to a time-partitioned table.
  • Set difference on huge sets is O(n + m) and allocates a third set; stream from the database with EXCEPT instead.
  • Set methods on Node.js below 22 do not exist; polyfill or spread into a new set.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

An in-process Set is for de-duplicating within one request or one batch. Uniqueness that must hold across time, pods or retries is a database unique constraint or a Redis atomic operation, and the senior never ships the in-memory version for money-moving code, no matter how well it worked on one pod. When the set is large and approximate answers are acceptable, they reach for a Bloom filter; when they only need the count of unique items, they reach for Redis HyperLogLog, which counts 100 million distinct ids in 12 KB with 0.8 percent error.

Common mistakes

  • array.includes in a loop instead of a Set.
  • Building a Set from the same array on every request instead of once per refresh.
  • Trusting an application-level uniqueness check without a unique index ("we check before insert").
  • Using Set for objects and expecting value equality.

Interview questions

  1. You need to de-duplicate 80,000 e-mails. Compare includes and Set with numbers. Expected: O(n^2), billions of comparisons, seconds; O(n), milliseconds.
  2. How do you guarantee an event is processed exactly once across many pods? Expected: you cannot in general; you get effectively-once with a unique index (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) or Redis SET NX plus idempotent handlers.
  3. When would you replace a Redis set with a Bloom filter or a HyperLogLog? Expected: membership at huge scale with tolerable false positives; distinct counting without storing members.
  4. Why does findOrCreate still need a unique index? Expected: without the constraint two concurrent calls both insert; the constraint is the only atomic membership check.

Practical exercise

Build an idempotent webhook receiver. Acceptance criteria: the same event id delivered 50 times concurrently (use Promise.all in a test against a real PostgreSQL) results in exactly one charges row and 49 responses of 200 OK with { duplicate: true }; the uniqueness is enforced by a unique index, verified by a test that deletes the index and shows the duplicate; a Set-based per-request de-duplication handles batched deliveries of up to 1,000 events in one request in under 5 ms; and the receiver expires processed_events rows older than 30 days with a partition drop, not a DELETE.

7.10 Tree

Concept

A tree is a set of nodes connected parent-to-child with exactly one path between any two nodes. One node is the root; nodes without children are leaves; the number of edges from the root to a node is its depth; the longest such path is the tree's height. A tree with at most two children per node is a binary tree; a general tree can have any number.

Backends are full of trees you did not build on purpose: product categories, comment threads, organization charts, folder hierarchies, the JSON body of every request, the NestJS module graph at bootstrap, the EXPLAIN plan PostgreSQL prints (each indented line is a child node), and the abstract syntax tree TypeScript compiles.

Why does it exist?

Hierarchy is a fact of the domain, and flat structures cannot express "is inside" or "belongs under". Trees also give algorithms a way to cut a problem in half repeatedly, which is where every O(log n) in this Part comes from. Without a tree, "all products under Dental > Consumables" is a scan over every product with string matching; with a tree it is a walk from one node down.

Mental model

Imagine a company org chart. Everyone has one manager except the CEO (the root). To list everyone under the VP of Engineering you start at her box and walk down; you never look at Sales. To find someone's chain of command you walk up. The chart is a tree because nobody has two managers; the moment they do, it is a graph (Section 7.15) and the questions get harder.

How it works

  1. In memory. A node is { value, children: Node[] } (or parent pointers too). Building a tree from flat database rows is a two-pass O(n) job: first put every node in a Map by id, then attach each node to its parent via the map.
  2. Traversal. Depth-first (pre-order: visit then children; post-order: children then visit) uses a stack, explicit or the call stack. Breadth-first visits level by level using a queue. Post-order is what you need to compute subtree totals (stock under a category); pre-order is what you need to print a hierarchy.
  3. In the database. Four storage patterns exist, each cheap at different questions:
    • Adjacency list: a parent_id column. Reads need a recursive CTE.
    • Materialized path: each row stores its full path (root.dental.consumables). PostgreSQL's ltree extension indexes it with GiST for "descendants of" and "ancestors of" in one index scan.
    • Nested sets: each row stores a left and right number; descendants are a range query; every insert renumbers half the table.
    • Closure table: a separate table of every (ancestor, descendant, depth) pair; fast reads, O(depth) rows per insert.
  4. Depth bounds. Every traversal on user-controlled trees needs a depth limit and a cycle check; a parent_id column has no constraint that stops row 7 from being its own great-grandparent.
