Time complexity

Operation Best Average Worst Notes
peek (min or max) O(1) O(1) O(1)
push O(1) O(log n) O(log n) best case stops after one comparison
pop O(log n) O(log n) O(log n)
Build from n items (heapify) O(n) O(n) O(n) versus O(n log n) for n pushes
Search for arbitrary item O(n) O(n) O(n) heaps are not for searching
Remove arbitrary item O(n) O(n) O(n) O(log n) if you keep an index map
Top-k of n O(n log k) O(n log k) O(n log k)
k-way merge of N items O(N log k) O(N log k) O(N log k)

Memory implications (V8, Node.js)

  • One array of 8-byte pointers plus the items: a heap of 1 million job records costs 8 MB for the structure and whatever the records cost. No per-node objects, no pointer chasing.
  • Keep the items monomorphic (same shape) and the comparator simple; a heap's cost is dominated by comparisons, and a megamorphic comparator that touches nested objects is 10 times slower than one comparing two numbers.
  • Node.js stores each pending setTimeout in a list per duration and keeps those lists in a priority queue keyed by expiry; a million timers with distinct durations cost roughly 200 bytes each for the Timeout objects, which is why "one timer per job" scheduling is a memory problem before it is a CPU problem.

Practical example

A generic binary heap, a top-k helper, and a k-way merge that builds a social timeline from per-user post lists.

// common/binary-heap.ts
export class BinaryHeap<T> {
  private readonly a: T[] = [];

  /** `less(x, y)` returns true when x should come out before y. */
  constructor(private readonly less: (x: T, y: T) => boolean) {}

  static from<T>(items: readonly T[], less: (x: T, y: T) => boolean): BinaryHeap<T> {
    const h = new BinaryHeap<T>(less);
    h.a.push(...items);
    for (let i = (h.a.length >> 1) - 1; i >= 0; i--) h.siftDown(i); // heapify: O(n)
    return h;
  }

  get size(): number { return this.a.length; }
  peek(): T | undefined { return this.a[0]; }

  push(item: T): void {
    this.a.push(item);
    this.siftUp(this.a.length - 1);
  }

  pop(): T | undefined {
    const a = this.a;
    if (a.length === 0) return undefined;
    const top = a[0];
    const last = a.pop()!;
    if (a.length > 0) { a[0] = last; this.siftDown(0); }
    return top;
  }

  private siftUp(i: number): void {
    const a = this.a;
    while (i > 0) {
      const p = (i - 1) >> 1;
      if (!this.less(a[i], a[p])) break;
      [a[i], a[p]] = [a[p], a[i]];
      i = p;
    }
  }

  private siftDown(i: number): void {
    const a = this.a, n = a.length;
    for (;;) {
      const l = 2 * i + 1, r = l + 1;
      let m = i;
      if (l < n && this.less(a[l], a[m])) m = l;
      if (r < n && this.less(a[r], a[m])) m = r;
      if (m === i) return;
      [a[i], a[m]] = [a[m], a[i]];
      i = m;
    }
  }
}

// common/top-k.ts -- the k largest by score, O(n log k), O(k) memory
export function topK<T>(items: Iterable<T>, k: number, score: (t: T) => number): T[] {
  const h = new BinaryHeap<T>((x, y) => score(x) < score(y)); // min-heap keeps the k largest
  for (const it of items) {
    h.push(it);
    if (h.size > k) h.pop();                                   // drop the smallest of the k+1
  }
  const out: T[] = [];
  while (h.size) out.push(h.pop()!);
  return out.reverse();                                        // largest first
}

NestJS example

A timeline service that merges the latest posts of every followed account into one feed. Each followed account's recent posts come from Redis (a list per author, newest first), and a heap does the k-way merge so we stop after 50 posts instead of sorting everything.

// feed/timeline.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { BinaryHeap } from '../common/binary-heap';

interface Post { id: string; authorId: string; createdAt: number }
interface Cursor { list: Post[]; idx: number }

@Injectable()
export class TimelineService {
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async build(followedIds: string[], limit = 50): Promise<Post[]> {
    const pipeline = this.redis.pipeline();
    for (const id of followedIds) pipeline.lrange(`author:${id}:posts`, 0, limit - 1); // newest first
    const replies = await pipeline.exec();                                          // one round trip

    // Heap keyed by the newest unread post of each author: k = followed accounts, not total posts.
    const heap = new BinaryHeap<Cursor>((x, y) => x.list[x.idx].createdAt > y.list[y.idx].createdAt);
    for (const reply of replies ?? []) {
      const raw = reply[1] as string[];
      if (raw.length) heap.push({ list: raw.map((s) => JSON.parse(s) as Post), idx: 0 });
    }

    const out: Post[] = [];
    while (out.length < limit && heap.size) {
      const cur = heap.pop()!;                       // author with the newest pending post
      out.push(cur.list[cur.idx]);
      if (++cur.idx < cur.list.length) heap.push(cur); // advance that author and re-insert
    }
    return out;                                       // O(limit x log followed)
  }
}

For a user following 300 accounts, the heap holds at most 300 cursors and the loop does 50 pops and pushes: about 50 x 9 comparisons, a few microseconds. The pipeline round trip (about 1 ms) dominates.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL uses a heap internally whenever you write ORDER BY ... LIMIT k. The plan says so.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total_cents FROM orders
WHERE merchant_id = 42
ORDER BY total_cents DESC
LIMIT 10;
Limit  (cost=4211.53..4211.55 rows=10 width=16) (actual time=9.812..9.815 rows=10 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=1123
  ->  Sort  (cost=4211.53..4302.11 rows=36232 width=16) (actual time=9.810..9.811 rows=10 loops=1)
        Sort Key: total_cents DESC
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 25kB
        ->  Index Scan using orders_merchant_idx on orders  (cost=0.56..3428.66 rows=36232 width=16) (actual time=0.031..6.402 rows=36104 loops=1)
              Index Cond: (merchant_id = 42)
Execution Time: 9.845 ms

top-N heapsort Memory: 25kB is the tell: 36,104 rows flowed through a 10-element heap and only 25 KB of memory was used. Remove the LIMIT and the same query reports Sort Method: quicksort Memory: 2,812kB or, above work_mem, external merge Disk: 4,120kB. If the query runs thousands of times per second, an index on (merchant_id, total_cents DESC) removes the sort entirely and turns it into an index scan that stops after 10 rows.

TypeORM example

The database is the heap; the ORM only needs to express ORDER BY and LIMIT, and the entity needs the index that makes it cheap.

@Entity({ name: 'orders' })
@Index('orders_merchant_total_idx', ['merchantId', 'totalCents'])
export class Order { /* columns as in Section 1.11 */ }

const biggest = await repo.find({
  where: { merchantId },
  order: { totalCents: 'DESC' },
  take: 10,                       // ORDER BY total_cents DESC LIMIT 10
});

Sequelize example

const biggest = await Order.findAll({
  where: { merchantId },
  order: [['totalCents', 'DESC']],
  limit: 10,
});

Production scenario

A retry scheduler for outbound webhooks holds 300,000 pending deliveries with nextAttemptAt timestamps and receives 2,000 new or rescheduled entries per second. With a binary heap, each insert costs about 18 comparisons (log2 of 300,000), so the scheduler spends about 2 ms of CPU per second on ordering and the rest on I/O. A @Interval(100) loop pops every entry whose time has come and hands it to a worker pool.

The same problem at cluster scale is a Redis sorted set: ZADD webhooks:due <timestampMs> <deliveryId> and ZRANGEBYSCORE webhooks:due -inf <now> LIMIT 0 100 followed by ZREM, or ZPOPMIN in newer Redis. Each operation is O(log n) on a skip list, about 0.3 ms round trip, and the set survives pod restarts. BullMQ's delayed jobs are exactly this: a delayed sorted set scored by the time the job becomes runnable.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call engineer is paged: webhook deliveries are 40 minutes late and the webhooks-scheduler pod shows 100 percent CPU. The scheduler kept pending deliveries in an array and, after every insert, called pending.sort((a, b) => a.nextAttemptAt - b.nextAttemptAt) to keep the earliest first. With 4,000 pending entries in staging that was invisible. A partner's endpoint went down at 01:30, retries with backoff piled up to 300,000 pending entries, and each of the 2,000 inserts per second now sorted 300,000 items: about 5.4 million comparisons, roughly 30 ms, per insert. The scheduler needed 60 seconds of CPU per wall-clock second. Deliveries to healthy partners were stuck behind the sorting.

The fix was the BinaryHeap above (18 comparisons per insert instead of 5.4 million) and, the following week, moving the schedule into a Redis sorted set so a scheduler restart no longer lost the in-memory queue. The lesson: "keep it sorted" with sort() after each insert is O(n log n) per operation, and n is decided by the slowest partner you have.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Ties. Two items with equal keys pop in unspecified order. If FIFO among equals matters (fairness), add a monotonically increasing sequence number to the key.
  • Mutable keys. Changing an item's priority after insertion silently breaks the heap property. Either remove and re-insert, or use lazy deletion: keep a version number and skip stale entries on pop.
  • Comparator errors. A comparator that returns inconsistent results (NaN timestamps, comparing strings as numbers) produces a heap that "works" but returns wrong items.
  • Iteration is not sorted. Walking the array gives heap order, not sorted order; if a dashboard needs a sorted list, pop into a new array or sort a copy.
  • Unbounded growth. A heap is a queue with an order; the overflow policy from Section 7.6 still applies.
  • In-memory loss on crash. Anything that must survive a restart lives in a Redis sorted set or a database table with an index on the key.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Whenever the senior sees sort() inside a loop, sort() followed by slice(0, k), or setTimeout per scheduled job, they ask whether a heap is the right shape. Their default answers: top-k of a stream is a heap of size k; merging sorted sources is a k-way heap merge; scheduling is a heap in one process or a sorted set in Redis; and "the k most recent/largest rows" is ORDER BY ... LIMIT with a supporting index, so the database's own heap does the work close to the data.

Common mistakes

  • Sorting the whole array to get the top 10.
  • One setTimeout per delayed job (memory and no durability) instead of one timer and a heap.
  • Mutating priorities in place.
  • Building a heap by n pushes (O(n log n)) when heapify (O(n)) was available for the initial batch.

Interview questions

  1. Why can a heap be stored without pointers, and what are the child indexes of node i? Expected: completeness guarantees no gaps; 2i+1 and 2i+2; parent (i-1)/2.
  2. Find the 10 largest of 50 million records streaming from a file with 100 MB of memory. Expected: min-heap of size 10, O(n log 10), O(1) memory beyond the heap. Follow-up: what if records arrive from 20 sorted files? (k-way merge.)
  3. What does Sort Method: top-N heapsort mean in an EXPLAIN plan, and how do you remove the sort entirely? Expected: a bounded heap for ORDER BY ... LIMIT; add an index matching the order so the scan stops early.
  4. How would you schedule 5 million delayed jobs across 12 pods? Expected: Redis sorted set keyed by due time, workers poll ZRANGEBYSCORE with a lock or atomic pop; not in-process heaps.
  5. A heap-based scheduler must cancel jobs. How? Expected: lazy deletion with a tombstone set or version counter; or an index map for O(log n) removal.

Practical exercise

Implement WebhookScheduler with BinaryHeap. Acceptance criteria: 300,000 pending deliveries with 2,000 inserts per second keep the scheduler under 5 percent CPU (measure with process.cpuUsage() in a test); cancelling a delivery is O(1) via a tombstone Set and popped tombstones are skipped; deliveries with equal nextAttemptAt are dispatched in insertion order (test with 1,000 equal timestamps); and a second implementation backed by a Redis sorted set passes the same test suite so the two can be swapped by configuration.

7.13 Priority Queue

Concept

A priority queue is an abstract type: insert items with a priority, and always remove the item with the highest priority (or the earliest deadline, or the lowest cost). The heap from Section 7.12 is its usual implementation, but not the only one: Redis sorted sets use a skip list, PostgreSQL uses a B-tree index on the priority column, and for a handful of fixed priority levels a bucket per level (an array of queues) is O(1) and simpler than any of them.

A FIFO queue says "the oldest first". A priority queue says "the most important first", and the definition of important is a function you write.

Why does it exist?

Real work is not equally urgent. A food-delivery dispatcher must assign the order promised in 8 minutes before the one promised in 40. A payments retry queue must retry a 3,000-dollar capture before a 3-dollar one when the gateway recovers. A notification system must send the password reset before the marketing push. Plain FIFO processes a burst of cheap, unimportant work before the critical item that arrived a second later; the priority queue reorders the world so the critical item goes first.

Mental model

Imagine an emergency room. Patients are seen by severity, not by arrival time. Two design problems appear immediately, and they are the same problems you will have in production: someone with a sprained ankle may wait forever if ambulances keep arriving (starvation), so the system slowly raises the priority of anyone who has waited too long (aging); and a patient's condition can change while they wait, so the board must support re-prioritizing (decrease-key).

How it works

  1. Key. Combine the priority with a sequence number: (priority, seq). Equal priorities then dequeue in FIFO order, which keeps the system fair and deterministic.
  2. Storage. A binary heap for one process; a Redis sorted set (ZADD queue <score> <id>) when pods must share; a database table with an index on (priority, run_at) when it must be transactional; separate queues per level when there are only a few levels (BullMQ supports a priority job option, 1 being the highest, implemented with a separate sorted structure in Redis).
  3. Re-prioritizing. Heaps do not support changing a key in place. Use lazy deletion: give each item a version, store (key, version, item), and when popping, skip any entry whose version is not the item's current version. Redis ZADD simply overwrites the score.
  4. Aging. Compute the effective priority as basePriority - waitedMinutes * factor so old low-priority items eventually win, or reserve a share of capacity for each priority class (weighted fair scheduling), which is easier to reason about.
  5. Starvation and inversion. Any priority scheme can starve the lowest class and can let a low-priority item hold a resource a high-priority item needs. Bound the wait time with aging, and bound the resources a single item can hold with timeouts.

Time complexity by implementation

Implementation Insert Pop highest Change priority Shared across pods Durable
Binary heap (in process) O(log n) O(log n) O(log n) lazy no no
Bucket per priority level (L levels) O(1) O(L) O(1) no no
Redis sorted set (skip list) O(log n) O(log n) O(log n) yes yes with AOF or RDB
PostgreSQL table with index on (priority, run_at) O(log n) O(log n) plus lock O(log n) yes yes, transactional
Kafka topic O(1) append O(1) in order not supported yes yes

Kafka has no priorities; the idiom is separate topics per class with more consumers on the urgent one.

Practical example

A stable priority queue with lazy re-prioritization on top of BinaryHeap.

// common/priority-queue.ts
import { BinaryHeap } from './binary-heap';

interface Entry<T> { priority: number; seq: number; version: number; id: string; item: T }

export class PriorityQueue<T> {
  private readonly heap = new BinaryHeap<Entry<T>>(
    (x, y) => x.priority < y.priority || (x.priority === y.priority && x.seq < y.seq), // lower number = more urgent
  );
  private readonly versions = new Map<string, number>(); // current version per id; absent = removed
  private seq = 0;

  push(id: string, priority: number, item: T): void {
    const version = (this.versions.get(id) ?? 0) + 1;    // invalidates any older heap entry for this id
    this.versions.set(id, version);
    this.heap.push({ priority, seq: this.seq++, version, id, item });
  }

  reprioritize(id: string, priority: number, item: T): void {
    this.push(id, priority, item);                        // lazy: old entry becomes a tombstone
  }

  remove(id: string): void {
    this.versions.delete(id);
  }

  pop(): { id: string; item: T } | undefined {
    for (;;) {
      const e = this.heap.pop();
      if (!e) return undefined;
      if (this.versions.get(e.id) !== e.version) continue; // stale or removed: skip
      this.versions.delete(e.id);
      return { id: e.id, item: e.item };
    }
  }

  get size(): number { return this.versions.size; }       // live items, not heap entries
}

The heap can hold stale entries; they cost memory until popped. If items are re-prioritized far more often than popped, compact periodically by rebuilding from the live entries.

NestJS example

A delivery dispatcher. Orders enter the queue with a priority derived from the promised delivery time; a dispatch loop assigns the most urgent order to the nearest free rider. Cancellations remove; delays re-prioritize. This is the per-pod version; the production note below shows the Redis form.

// dispatch/dispatch.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Interval } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { OnEvent } from '@nestjs/event-emitter';
import { PriorityQueue } from '../common/priority-queue';
import { RiderPoolService } from './rider-pool.service';

interface PendingOrder { orderId: string; promisedAt: number; pickupLat: number; pickupLng: number }

@Injectable()
export class DispatchService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(DispatchService.name);
  private readonly queue = new PriorityQueue<PendingOrder>();

  constructor(private readonly riders: RiderPoolService) {}

  @OnEvent('order.ready_for_dispatch')
  onReady(order: PendingOrder): void {
    this.queue.push(order.orderId, order.promisedAt, order); // earlier promise = more urgent
  }

  @OnEvent('order.cancelled')
  onCancelled(payload: { orderId: string }): void {
    this.queue.remove(payload.orderId);                     // O(1); heap entry becomes a tombstone
  }

  @OnEvent('order.delayed')
  onDelayed(order: PendingOrder): void {
    this.queue.reprioritize(order.orderId, order.promisedAt, order);
  }

  @Interval(500)
  async dispatchTick(): Promise<void> {
    let assigned = 0;
    while (assigned < 20) {                                  // bound work per tick to keep the loop responsive
      const next = this.queue.pop();
      if (!next) return;
      const rider = await this.riders.nearestFree(next.item.pickupLat, next.item.pickupLng);
      if (!rider) {                                          // nobody free: put it back and stop this tick
        this.queue.push(next.id, next.item.promisedAt, next.item);
        return;
      }
      await this.riders.assign(rider.id, next.id);           // idempotent on (rider, order)
      assigned++;
    }
    this.logger.debug(`dispatched ${assigned}, pending ${this.queue.size}`);
  }
}

The cluster-wide version replaces PriorityQueue with a Redis sorted set per city: ZADD dispatch:city:42 <promisedAt> <orderId> on ready, ZREM on cancel, ZADD again on delay, and ZPOPMIN dispatch:city:42 20 in the tick, so twelve pods share one queue and a pod restart loses nothing.

PostgreSQL example

A transactional priority queue is the jobs table from Section 7.6 with a priority column and an index that matches the ORDER BY exactly.

ALTER TABLE jobs ADD COLUMN priority smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 100;   -- lower = more urgent

CREATE INDEX jobs_ready_priority_idx ON jobs (priority, run_at, id) WHERE status = 'queued';

UPDATE jobs SET status = 'active', locked_by = $1
WHERE id = (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
  WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_at <= now()
  ORDER BY priority, run_at, id
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT 1
)
RETURNING id, kind, payload, priority;

-- Aging: nothing waits more than ~30 minutes regardless of priority.
-- Computed priorities cannot use the index; run this variant from a separate low-frequency worker.
SELECT id FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'queued'
ORDER BY priority - (extract(epoch FROM now() - created_at) / 60)::int, id
LIMIT 50;
Limit  (cost=0.42..0.61 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=0.038..0.039 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  LockRows  (cost=0.42..1523.10 rows=8110 width=14) (actual time=0.037..0.037 rows=1 loops=1)
        ->  Index Scan using jobs_ready_priority_idx on jobs  (cost=0.42..1442.00 rows=8110 width=14) (actual time=0.021..0.021 rows=1 loops=1)
              Index Cond: (run_at <= now())

Because the index order is (priority, run_at, id), the scan starts at the most urgent, oldest job and stops after the first unlocked row: O(log n) per claim.

TypeORM example

const next = await manager
  .createQueryBuilder(JobEntity, 'j')
  .setLock('pessimistic_write')
  .setOnLocked('skip_locked')
  .where('j.status = :s AND j.run_at <= now()', { s: 'queued' })
  .orderBy('j.priority', 'ASC').addOrderBy('j.run_at', 'ASC').addOrderBy('j.id', 'ASC')
  .limit(1)
  .getOne();

Sequelize example

const next = await JobModel.findOne({
  where: { status: 'queued', runAt: { [Op.lte]: new Date() } },
  order: [['priority', 'ASC'], ['runAt', 'ASC'], ['id', 'ASC']],
  lock: t.LOCK.UPDATE,
  skipLocked: true,
  transaction: t,
});

Production scenario

A food-delivery platform dispatches 5,000 orders per minute per city at peak. Orders stay in the dispatch queue for 30 to 90 seconds, so the queue holds about 5,000 entries; each ZADD or ZPOPMIN is 13 comparisons on the skip list and about 0.3 ms over the network. The dispatch tick runs every 500 ms on every pod; each pod pops a batch of 20, which keeps the per-tick latency under 20 ms and avoids one pod hogging all riders. Delayed orders are re-scored, cancellations removed, and the on-call dashboard graphs the age of the oldest entry, exactly as with FIFO queues: the age, not the count, is the alarm.

Decision table: which priority queue

Situation Choose Why
One process, thousands of items, loss on restart acceptable BinaryHeap / PriorityQueue fastest, simplest
Three to five fixed classes (critical, high, normal, low) one queue per class, weighted polling O(1), no starvation with reserved capacity
Shared by many pods, sub-millisecond, durable enough Redis sorted set or BullMQ priority O(log n), atomic pops
Must commit with business data PostgreSQL table with (priority, run_at) index and SKIP LOCKED transactional; hundreds per second
Firehose with replay and ordering per key Kafka topics per class no priorities inside a topic

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call engineer is paged by a merchant, not by a monitor: invoices have not been e-mailed for nine hours. The notifications worker used one BullMQ queue with priorities: push notifications at priority 1, transactional e-mails at 5, invoices at 10. A flash-sale campaign generated 40 million push notifications starting at 17:00; the worker pool never got below priority 1 because new priority-1 jobs kept arriving faster than they were processed. Nothing was wrong technically; the priority queue did exactly what it was told, and starved everything else. Nobody had alerted on the age of the oldest job per priority class.

The fix was structural: separate queues per class, with the worker pool split so that even during a campaign 20 percent of capacity processes the normal queue and 10 percent the low queue (weighted fair scheduling), plus an "oldest job age per queue" alert. Aging would also have worked, but reserved capacity is easier to explain to the merchant.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Starvation of low priorities; fix with aging or reserved capacity.
  • Priority inversion when a low-priority job holds a lock a high-priority one needs; bound lock hold times.
  • Ties without a sequence number produce nondeterministic order and make incidents hard to reproduce.
  • Stale heap entries after many re-prioritizations consume memory; compact.
  • Priority as a user input: a client that can set its own priority sets it to 1. Derive priority server-side from business rules.
  • Skew between pods when each pod has its own in-memory queue; global ordering needs a shared queue.
  • Redis eviction under allkeys-lru can evict a sorted set holding jobs; queue data belongs in an instance configured with noeviction.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Priorities are a business policy encoded in a data structure, so the senior asks the product owner the awkward questions first: what happens to the lowest class during a burst, how long may it wait, and who decides the priority. Then they pick the implementation from the decision table, add a sequence number for fairness, and alert on the age of the oldest item per class. They prefer a few queues with reserved capacity over one clever queue with an aging formula, because the former is explainable at 02:14.

Common mistakes

  • One shared queue with priorities and no protection for the lowest class.
  • Letting the caller choose the priority.
  • Re-sorting arrays on each insert (Section 7.12's incident).
  • Alerting on total queue depth, which hides a starving class behind a healthy one.

Interview questions

  1. How do you change an item's priority in a heap-based queue? Expected: lazy deletion with versions, or an index map with sift-up/down; Redis ZADD overwrites.
  2. Design dispatch for a delivery platform across 12 pods. Expected: Redis sorted set per city keyed by promised time, batch ZPOPMIN, idempotent assignment, age-based alerting.
  3. What is starvation and how do you prevent it without an aging formula? Expected: reserved capacity per class or weighted round-robin across class queues.
  4. Why is ORDER BY priority, run_at LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED O(log n), and when does it stop being enough? Expected: index order matches; dead tuples, polling load and lock traffic at high rates push you to Redis.

Practical exercise

Build NotificationDispatcher with three BullMQ queues (critical, normal, low) and a worker allocation of 70/20/10 percent, plus an in-process PriorityQueue for batching within each worker. Acceptance criteria: a test that enqueues 100,000 critical and 100 low jobs shows every low job completed within 60 seconds; per-queue "oldest job age" is exported as a Prometheus gauge and a test asserts the gauge is set; re-prioritizing a pending job via reprioritize is reflected in pop order (test with 1,000 random re-prioritizations against a brute-force sorted array); and no client-supplied field can set priority (a validation test sends priority: 1 in the payload and observes it ignored).

7.14 Trie

Concept

A trie (pronounced "try", from retrieval) is a tree where each edge carries one character and each path from the root spells a prefix. Every key that shares a prefix shares the nodes for that prefix. A node is marked terminal when the path to it spells a complete key. Searching for a key, or for "everything that starts with glo", walks one edge per character, so the cost depends on the length of the query, not on how many keys are stored.

A radix tree (also called a Patricia trie or compressed trie) merges chains of single-child nodes into one edge labelled with a whole substring, which cuts memory by five to ten times. HTTP routers such as find-my-way (the router behind Fastify, and therefore behind NestJS with the Fastify adapter) are radix trees over URL paths; Redis Streams and RediSearch are built on a radix tree called rax; IP routing tables are tries over address bits.

Why does it exist?

Hash maps cannot answer prefix questions: "all keys starting with X" requires scanning every key. Sorted arrays and B-trees can (binary search to the first match, then walk), and a PostgreSQL index does exactly that; but in memory, at thousands of requests per second, a trie with precomputed top results per node answers "top 10 completions for glo" in a few hundred nanoseconds with no comparison of whole strings at all. Autocomplete for product search, command palettes, typeahead for customer names, longest-prefix matching for routes and phone-number normalization are trie problems.

Mental model

Imagine the tabs on a paper dictionary. The first tab takes you to G, the next to GL, then GLO. At each tab you can see every word below it without reading the rest of the dictionary. A trie is a dictionary with a tab for every prefix, and, in the version we build here, each tab also has a sticky note listing the ten most popular words under it, so you never need to flip through.

How it works

  1. Insert. Normalize the key (lowercase, NFC, trim). Starting at the root, for each character follow the child edge, creating it if absent. Mark the final node terminal. O(L) for a key of length L.
  2. Search. Follow the edges for each character; if any is missing, the key is absent. Terminal check at the end. O(L).
  3. Prefix query. Follow the edges for the prefix; every terminal node in the subtree below is a completion. Collecting them is O(size of subtree), which for the prefix a in a 100,000-term index is tens of thousands of nodes: too slow for a request path.
  4. Top-k per node. Store, at every node, the k best completions (by popularity) among all keys below it. Inserting a key with score s updates the top-k list of each node along its path: O(L x k). Querying becomes O(L) plus returning k items. This trades memory for guaranteed latency.
  5. Deletion. Unmark the terminal flag; optionally prune childless, non-terminal nodes upward. Top-k lists need a rebuild or a lazy filter for removed keys.
  6. Radix compression. Chains of single-child nodes (g-a-u-z-e) become one edge gauze; lookups compare substrings instead of characters, and node count drops dramatically for natural-language keys.
flowchart TB
    root(("root")) --> g["g"]
    g --> gl["l"]
    gl --> glo["o"]
    glo --> glov["v"]
    glov --> glove["e  terminal: glove"]
    glove --> gloves["s  terminal: gloves"]
    gl --> glu["u"]
    glu --> glue["e  terminal: glue"]
    g --> ga["a"]
    ga --> gau["u"]
    gau --> gauz["z"]
    gauz --> gauze["e  terminal: gauze"]

Time complexity (L = key or prefix length, k = results, N = keys, S = subtree size)

Operation Best Average Worst Notes
Insert O(L) O(L) O(L x k) with per-node top-k maintenance
Exact search O(1) O(L) O(L) best case is a missing first character
Prefix exists O(1) O(L) O(L)
Collect all completions O(L) O(L + S) O(L + N) unbounded; never on a request path
Top-k completions with per-node cache O(L) O(L + k) O(L + k)
Delete O(L) O(L) O(L x k) plus top-k repair
Sorted array with binary search (alternative) O(log N) O(log N + k) O(log N + S) k results after the first match

Memory implications (V8, Node.js)

  • A node with a Map of children costs about 40 bytes for the node object plus roughly 100 bytes for a small Map, plus the top-k array (10 slots, 80 bytes, with suggestion objects shared across nodes). Budget about 250 bytes per node.
  • Node count is what matters. 120,000 product names of about 30 characters is 3.6 million characters, but shared prefixes typically cut that to 1 to 1.5 million nodes: about 300 MB, too much for a pod. Index words (tokens) instead of whole names and cap depth at 12 to 16 characters, and the same catalog becomes about 350,000 nodes, or 80 MB. Radix compression brings it under 20 MB.
  • Children as a plain object with computed keys fall into dictionary mode (Section 7.8); use Map, or for a known small alphabet, an array indexed by character code.
  • Build the trie off the request path and swap the reference atomically; a half-built trie must never be visible to requests.

Practical example

An autocomplete trie with per-node top-k, indexing each word of a product name so gloves matches "Nitrile Examination Gloves".

// search/autocomplete-trie.ts
export interface Suggestion { term: string; score: number }

class TrieNode {
  readonly children = new Map<string, TrieNode>();
  terminal = false;
  readonly top: Suggestion[] = [];              // best k under this node, sorted by score desc
}

export const normalizeTerm = (s: string) => s.normalize('NFC').toLowerCase().trim();

export class AutocompleteTrie {
  private readonly root = new TrieNode();
  private nodeCount = 1;

  constructor(private readonly k = 10, private readonly maxDepth = 16) {}

  get size(): number { return this.nodeCount; }

  /** Index `term` under each of its words so mid-name words are reachable. */
  insert(term: string, score: number): void {
    const key = normalizeTerm(term);
    const suggestion: Suggestion = { term, score };
    for (const word of new Set(key.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean))) {
      let node = this.root;
      let depth = 0;
      for (const ch of word) {                    // code points, so emoji do not split
        if (depth++ >= this.maxDepth) break;
        let next = node.children.get(ch);
        if (!next) { next = new TrieNode(); node.children.set(ch, next); this.nodeCount++; }
        node = next;
        this.offerTop(node, suggestion);          // O(k) insertion into a tiny sorted array
      }
      node.terminal = true;
    }
  }

  /** O(prefix length): returns the cached top-k, never walks the subtree. */
  suggest(prefix: string): readonly Suggestion[] {
    let node = this.root;
    for (const ch of normalizeTerm(prefix)) {
      const next = node.children.get(ch);
      if (!next) return [];
      node = next;
    }
    return node.top;
  }

  private offerTop(node: TrieNode, s: Suggestion): void {
    const top = node.top;
    const dup = top.findIndex((x) => x.term === s.term);
    if (dup >= 0) top.splice(dup, 1);             // same product reached via another word
    let i = top.length;
    while (i > 0 && top[i - 1].score < s.score) i--;
    if (i < this.k) {
      top.splice(i, 0, s);
      if (top.length > this.k) top.pop();
    }
  }
}

NestJS example

The trie is built at startup from PostgreSQL, rebuilt every 10 minutes off the request path, and swapped atomically. The DTO enforces a minimum prefix length so the root node's top-k is never a substitute for search.

// search/suggest-query.dto.ts
import { IsString, MaxLength, MinLength } from 'class-validator';

export class SuggestQueryDto {
  @IsString()
  @MinLength(2)
  @MaxLength(40)
  q!: string;
}

// search/suggest.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { AutocompleteTrie, Suggestion } from './autocomplete-trie';

@Injectable()
export class SuggestService implements OnModuleInit {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(SuggestService.name);
  private trie = new AutocompleteTrie(10);
  private builtAt = 0;

  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> {
    await this.rebuild();                       // readiness should wait for this
  }

  @Cron('0 */10 * * * *')
  async rebuild(): Promise<void> {
    const started = Date.now();
    const rows: { name: string; popularity: number }[] = await this.dataSource.query(
      `SELECT name, popularity FROM products WHERE is_active ORDER BY popularity DESC LIMIT 200000`,
    );
    const fresh = new AutocompleteTrie(10);
    for (const r of rows) fresh.insert(r.name, r.popularity);
    this.trie = fresh;                          // atomic reference swap; old trie is garbage collected
    this.builtAt = Date.now();
    this.logger.log(`rebuilt trie: ${rows.length} products, ${fresh.size} nodes, ${Date.now() - started} ms`);
  }

  suggest(prefix: string): readonly Suggestion[] {
    return this.trie.suggest(prefix);          // ~1 microsecond
  }

  get ageMs(): number { return Date.now() - this.builtAt; }
}

// search/suggest.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Query, ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import { SuggestQueryDto } from './suggest-query.dto';
import { SuggestService } from './suggest.service';

@Controller('search')
export class SuggestController {
  constructor(private readonly suggest: SuggestService) {}

  @Get('suggest')
  get(@Query(new ValidationPipe({ transform: true, whitelist: true })) query: SuggestQueryDto) {
    return { suggestions: this.suggest.suggest(query.q) };
  }
}

Twelve pods each rebuild from the same query every 10 minutes; stagger the cron with a random delay or an advisory lock so they do not all hit PostgreSQL in the same second after a deploy.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL answers prefix queries with a B-tree, which is a sorted structure and therefore trie-like for prefixes, as long as the index uses byte-wise ordering. Infix and fuzzy queries need pg_trgm. SP-GiST's text operator class is literally a radix tree on disk.

-- Prefix search under a non-C collation needs text_pattern_ops (or COLLATE "C").
CREATE INDEX products_name_lower_prefix ON products (lower(name) text_pattern_ops);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, name FROM products
WHERE lower(name) LIKE 'glo%'
ORDER BY popularity DESC LIMIT 10;
Limit  (cost=812.14..812.16 rows=10 width=41) (actual time=1.402..1.404 rows=10 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=634
  ->  Sort  (cost=812.14..813.71 rows=628 width=41) (actual time=1.401..1.402 rows=10 loops=1)
        Sort Key: popularity DESC
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 26kB
        ->  Index Scan using products_name_lower_prefix on products  (cost=0.42..798.57 rows=628 width=41) (actual time=0.038..1.211 rows=611 loops=1)
              Index Cond: ((lower(name) ~>=~ 'glo'::text) AND (lower(name) ~<~ 'glp'::text))
              Filter: (lower(name) ~~ 'glo%'::text)
Execution Time: 1.431 ms

The planner rewrote LIKE 'glo%' as the range >= 'glo' AND < 'glp', which is how a sorted structure does prefixes. Then the heap from Section 7.12 picked the top 10.

-- Infix and typo-tolerant search: trigram GIN index.
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX products_name_trgm ON products USING gin (lower(name) gin_trgm_ops);
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE lower(name) LIKE '%glov%';                 -- index-assisted infix
SELECT id, name, similarity(name, 'glvoes') AS s FROM products
WHERE name % 'glvoes' ORDER BY s DESC LIMIT 5;                                  -- fuzzy

-- A radix tree on disk: SP-GiST with the starts-with operator.
CREATE INDEX products_name_spgist ON products USING spgist (name);
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name ^@ 'Glo';

TypeORM example

Always escape % and _ in user input before it reaches LIKE, or a query for % becomes a full scan.

import { Raw, Repository } from 'typeorm';

const escapeLike = (s: string) => s.replace(/[\\%_]/g, '\\$&');

export class ProductSearch {
  constructor(private readonly repo: Repository<Product>) {}

  byPrefix(prefix: string, limit = 10) {
    const p = escapeLike(prefix.normalize('NFC').toLowerCase());
    return this.repo.find({
      where: { name: Raw((alias) => `lower(${alias}) LIKE :p ESCAPE '\\'`, { p: `${p}%` }) },
      order: { popularity: 'DESC' },
      take: limit,
    });
  }
}

Sequelize example

const p = escapeLike(prefix.normalize('NFC').toLowerCase());
const rows = await Product.findAll({
  where: sequelize.where(sequelize.fn('lower', sequelize.col('name')), { [Op.like]: `${p}%` }),
  order: [['popularity', 'DESC']],
  limit: 10,
});

Op.startsWith exists in Sequelize and builds LIKE 'value%', but it does not escape wildcards inside the value; escape first.

Production scenario

A storefront's search box fires a suggestion request on every keystroke: 3,000 RPS at peak, prefixes of 2 to 12 characters. With the in-memory trie each request costs about 1 microsecond of CPU and returns in under 1 ms end to end; the whole feature uses less than 1 percent of a pod. The same feature backed by the PostgreSQL prefix query costs about 1.5 ms of database time per request plus a pooled connection, which at 3,000 RPS is 4.5 database-seconds per second: a third of a large instance for typeahead. The trie is per pod (80 MB times 12 pods) and 10 minutes stale, which for suggestions is fine.

Beyond a few million terms, or when suggestions must be personalized and fresh, the structure moves out of the pod: Redis ZRANGEBYLEX over a sorted set of lowercase terms gives lexical prefix ranges in O(log n); RediSearch's FT.SUGADD/FT.SUGGET is a server-side trie with scores; Elasticsearch's completion suggester is a finite-state transducer, a trie relative, built for tens of millions of terms.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call engineer is paged: search-api CPU is at 100 percent on all pods and p99 for every endpoint, not just suggestions, is above 2 seconds. A change two days earlier replaced the per-node top-k with "collect all completions under the prefix, then sort by popularity" because the top-k lists were "hard to keep in sync with deletions". At normal traffic, prefixes were 3 or more characters and subtrees were small. Tonight a marketing e-mail linked to the search page with a pre-filled query of a. Each request now walked a subtree of about 38,000 nodes, built an array of 9,000 suggestions and sorted it: about 12 ms of CPU. At 3,000 RPS the pods needed 36 cores.

The fix restored per-node top-k (deletions handled by a lazy isActive check at query time and a full rebuild every 10 minutes) and added @MinLength(2) at the edge. The lesson: any operation whose cost is proportional to the size of a subtree is unbounded from the request's point of view; cache the answer at the node or bound the walk.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Normalization. Glove, glove and glové must be normalized consistently at insert and query time or prefixes silently miss.
  • Wildcards in LIKE. Unescaped % or _ from users turn a prefix scan into a full scan.
  • Empty or one-character prefixes return the root's subtree; reject them.
  • Memory growth with whole-name keys; index tokens and cap depth.
  • Deletions and score changes invalidate cached top-k lists; rebuild periodically or filter lazily.
  • Rebuild storms when every pod rebuilds at once after a deploy; stagger or gate with a lock.
  • Half-built structures visible to requests if you mutate in place; build fresh and swap.
  • Very long keys (a 10 KB "name") create 10,000 nodes; cap key length at validation.
  • Locale-dependent lowercasing (Turkish I) makes the same product unreachable from one locale; use plain toLowerCase for indexing.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior sees autocomplete as a read-heavy, staleness-tolerant, latency-critical feature and designs for the request path first: O(prefix length) with precomputed results, a minimum prefix length, an atomic swap on rebuild, and a memory budget stated in megabytes per pod. They keep PostgreSQL for the durable search (with text_pattern_ops and pg_trgm) and treat the trie as a derived index that can be rebuilt from scratch at any time. When the term count or freshness requirement outgrows a pod, they move to Redis or a search engine rather than making the in-process trie cleverer.

To a product manager: "Suggestions will be at most ten minutes behind catalog changes and will need two characters before they appear. In exchange, they respond in under a millisecond and cost almost nothing at peak."

Common mistakes

  • Walking the subtree per request instead of caching top-k per node.
  • Building the trie inside the request handler or on first request without readiness gating.
  • Using a plain object as the children map.
  • Forgetting to escape LIKE wildcards.
  • Indexing whole names with no depth limit and running out of memory at the first big catalog import.

Interview questions

  1. Why is a trie better than a hash map for autocomplete, and when is it worse? Expected: O(L) prefix queries versus O(N) scans; worse in memory for large key sets and useless for exact-match-only workloads.
  2. How do you make "top 10 completions" O(prefix length)? Expected: cache top-k per node, maintained on insert in O(L x k).
  3. How does PostgreSQL execute LIKE 'glo%' with an index, and why did your index not get used? Expected: rewritten as a range on a byte-ordered index; requires text_pattern_ops or C collation; expression must match.
  4. What is a radix tree and where have you used one without knowing? Expected: compressed trie; Fastify's router, Redis rax, IP routing.
  5. A prefix of one character takes 12 ms. Why, and what are two fixes? Expected: subtree walk; per-node top-k and a minimum prefix length.

Practical exercise

Build SuggestModule end to end. Acceptance criteria: the trie for a seeded catalog of 150,000 products indexes tokens with a depth cap of 16 and uses under 120 MB (assert with process.memoryUsage().heapUsed deltas around the build); GET /search/suggest?q=gl returns in under 2 ms at p99 under autocannon -c 50; a one-character query returns 400; a query containing % never reaches PostgreSQL unescaped (assert the SQL via a query logger); the rebuild is triggered by a cron and by a product.changed event, and a concurrent test confirms requests during a rebuild always see either the old or the new trie, never an empty one.

7.15 Graph

Concept

A graph is a set of vertices (nodes) connected by edges. Edges may be directed (A follows B does not mean B follows A) or undirected (A and B are friends), weighted (the road from A to B takes 7 minutes) or unweighted. A graph with no directed cycles is a DAG (directed acyclic graph), the shape of every dependency system. A tree is a graph with exactly one path between any two nodes; the moment a node can be reached two ways, you have left Section 7.10 and entered this one.

Backends are full of graphs: the NestJS dependency-injection container resolves a graph of providers and modules at bootstrap and throws on a cycle; a distributed trace is a graph of service calls; the order status machine (pending -> paid -> shipped -> delivered, with cancelled reachable from several states) is a directed graph; followers, friends, "customers also bought", fraud rings of accounts sharing a device, delivery routes over a road network, and workflow steps with dependencies are all graphs.

Why does it exist?

Hierarchies and lists cannot express "many-to-many with structure". A user can follow 500 accounts and be followed by 5,000; a build step can depend on three others; a city block connects to four neighbours. The questions people ask of such data (shortest path, reachability, ordering that respects dependencies, communities, influence) have no answer without the graph abstraction and its algorithms: breadth-first search, depth-first search, topological sort, Dijkstra, union-find.

Mental model

Imagine a metro map. Stations are vertices, lines between them are edges. "How do I get from A to B with the fewest stops?" is breadth-first search. "With the least travel time?" is Dijkstra, because edges have weights. "Can I reach B from A at all?" is reachability. "Which stations form one connected system?" is connected components. Nobody stores the map as a giant table of every station pair; each station lists its neighbours. That list-per-station is the adjacency list.

How it works

  1. Adjacency list. A map from each vertex to its neighbours: Map<string, Set<string>> (or an array of neighbour ids). Memory is O(V + E). Iterating a vertex's neighbours costs O(degree). This is the representation for almost every real graph, because real graphs are sparse: a social graph with 10 million users and an average of 200 follows has 2 billion edges, not 100 trillion.
  2. Adjacency matrix. A V x V table where cell (i, j) holds the edge weight or a boolean. Edge lookup is O(1) and the representation is dense and cache-friendly, but memory is O(V^2): a 100,000-vertex matrix is 10 billion cells. Use it only for small, dense graphs (state machines with 12 states, a distance table between 50 warehouses).
  3. Breadth-first search (BFS). Start at a vertex, visit all neighbours, then their neighbours, using a queue and a visited set. Finds shortest paths by hop count and "everything within 2 hops" (friends of friends). O(V + E).
  4. Depth-first search (DFS). Follow one path as deep as possible before backtracking, using a stack. Detects cycles: while exploring, a vertex that is "in progress" and reached again means a cycle. O(V + E).
  5. Topological sort (Kahn's algorithm). Count incoming edges per vertex; repeatedly take a vertex with zero incoming edges, emit it, and decrement its neighbours. If vertices remain with non-zero counts, there is a cycle. This is how dependency resolution, build systems and workflow engines decide order and how they reject circular definitions.
  6. Dijkstra. Shortest path with non-negative weights: a priority queue (Section 7.13) of vertices by tentative distance; pop the closest, relax its edges. O((V + E) log V).
  7. Union-find. Merge sets of vertices as edges arrive; ask "are A and B in the same group?" in near O(1). The tool for connected components on streams of edges, such as accounts linked by shared payment instruments.
flowchart LR
    gw["api-gateway"] --> orders["orders-svc"]
    gw --> catalog["catalog-svc"]
    orders --> payments["payments-svc"]
    orders --> inventory["inventory-svc"]
    orders --> notify["notifications-svc"]
    payments --> notify
    catalog --> inventory
    inventory --> pg[("PostgreSQL")]
    payments --> pg
adjacency list of the same graph (directed):
  api-gateway       -> [orders-svc, catalog-svc]
  orders-svc        -> [payments-svc, inventory-svc, notifications-svc]
  catalog-svc       -> [inventory-svc]
  payments-svc      -> [notifications-svc, PostgreSQL]
  inventory-svc     -> [PostgreSQL]
  notifications-svc -> []
  PostgreSQL        -> []
reverse index ("who depends on me") is a second adjacency list.

Time complexity (V vertices, E edges, d = degree of a vertex)

Operation Adjacency list Adjacency matrix Notes
Add vertex O(1) O(V^2) resize
Add or remove edge O(1) O(1) list with Set neighbours
Has edge (u, v) O(1) with Set, O(d) with array O(1)
Iterate neighbours of u O(d) O(V) matrix scans a whole row
BFS / DFS O(V + E) O(V^2)
Topological sort O(V + E) O(V^2)
Dijkstra with binary heap O((V + E) log V) O(V^2) matrix version without a heap is O(V^2)
Memory O(V + E) O(V^2)

Memory implications (V8, Node.js)

  • Map<string, Set<string>> costs about 150 bytes per vertex (map entry plus an empty Set) and about 40 bytes per edge, plus the id strings. A service graph of 100 vertices is nothing; a follow graph of 10 million vertices and 2 billion edges is about 100 GB and does not belong in a process.
  • For static, large graphs in memory (road networks for a routing worker), use the compressed sparse row layout: two typed arrays, offsets: Uint32Array(V + 1) and neighbours: Uint32Array(E), 4 bytes per edge, contiguous, and immune to GC pressure.
  • Recursive DFS overflows the stack on long paths (Section 7.5); use an explicit stack for graphs whose size users control.

Practical example

A small graph library with BFS shortest path, Kahn's topological sort with cycle detection, and Dijkstra using the BinaryHeap from Section 7.12.

// common/graph.ts
import { BinaryHeap } from './binary-heap';

export class DirectedGraph {
  private readonly out = new Map<string, Map<string, number>>(); // vertex -> (neighbour -> weight)

  addVertex(v: string): void {
    if (!this.out.has(v)) this.out.set(v, new Map());
  }

  addEdge(from: string, to: string, weight = 1): void {
    this.addVertex(from);
    this.addVertex(to);
    this.out.get(from)!.set(to, weight);
  }

  neighbours(v: string): ReadonlyMap<string, number> {
    return this.out.get(v) ?? new Map();
  }

  /** Fewest hops from `start` to `goal`, or null. O(V + E). */
  shortestHops(start: string, goal: string, maxDepth = 6): string[] | null {
    const prev = new Map<string, string | null>([[start, null]]);
    const queue: [string, number][] = [[start, 0]];
    for (let i = 0; i < queue.length; i++) {              // index pointer: no shift()
      const [v, depth] = queue[i];
      if (v === goal) return this.pathTo(prev, goal);
      if (depth >= maxDepth) continue;                    // bound the search radius
      for (const n of this.neighbours(v).keys()) {
        if (!prev.has(n)) { prev.set(n, v); queue.push([n, depth + 1]); }
      }
    }
    return null;
  }

  /** Kahn's algorithm. Throws with the offending vertices if a cycle exists. O(V + E). */
  topologicalOrder(): string[] {
    const indegree = new Map<string, number>();
    for (const v of this.out.keys()) indegree.set(v, 0);
    for (const edges of this.out.values()) for (const n of edges.keys()) indegree.set(n, indegree.get(n)! + 1);

    const ready: string[] = [...indegree].filter(([, d]) => d === 0).map(([v]) => v);
    const order: string[] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < ready.length; i++) {
      const v = ready[i];
      order.push(v);
      for (const n of this.neighbours(v).keys()) {
        const d = indegree.get(n)! - 1;
        indegree.set(n, d);
        if (d === 0) ready.push(n);
      }
    }
    if (order.length !== this.out.size) {
      const stuck = [...indegree].filter(([, d]) => d > 0).map(([v]) => v);
      throw new Error(`cycle detected among: ${stuck.join(', ')}`);
    }
    return order;
  }

  /** Cheapest path by weight. O((V + E) log V). */
  dijkstra(start: string, goal: string): { cost: number; path: string[] } | null {
    const dist = new Map<string, number>([[start, 0]]);
    const prev = new Map<string, string | null>([[start, null]]);
    const heap = new BinaryHeap<[number, string]>((a, b) => a[0] < b[0]);
    heap.push([0, start]);
    while (heap.size) {
      const [d, v] = heap.pop()!;
      if (d > (dist.get(v) ?? Infinity)) continue;        // stale heap entry
      if (v === goal) return { cost: d, path: this.pathTo(prev, goal) };
      for (const [n, w] of this.neighbours(v)) {
        const nd = d + w;
        if (nd < (dist.get(n) ?? Infinity)) { dist.set(n, nd); prev.set(n, v); heap.push([nd, n]); }
      }
    }
    return null;
  }

  private pathTo(prev: Map<string, string | null>, goal: string): string[] {
    const path: string[] = [];
    for (let v: string | null = goal; v !== null; v = prev.get(v) ?? null) path.push(v);
    return path.reverse();
  }
}

NestJS example

A fulfilment workflow defined as a DAG of steps. The service validates the graph at startup (fail fast on cycles, exactly as NestJS does for its own providers) and runs steps level by level, in parallel where dependencies allow.

// fulfilment/fulfilment-workflow.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DirectedGraph } from '../common/graph';

type StepFn = (orderId: string) => Promise<void>;

interface StepDef { name: string; dependsOn: string[]; run: StepFn }

@Injectable()
export class FulfilmentWorkflowService implements OnModuleInit {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(FulfilmentWorkflowService.name);
  private readonly graph = new DirectedGraph();
  private readonly steps = new Map<string, StepDef>();
  private levels: string[][] = [];

  constructor() {
    this.define({ name: 'reserveInventory', dependsOn: [], run: async () => { /* ... */ } });
    this.define({ name: 'chargePayment', dependsOn: ['reserveInventory'], run: async () => { /* ... */ } });
    this.define({ name: 'createShipment', dependsOn: ['chargePayment'], run: async () => { /* ... */ } });
    this.define({ name: 'sendConfirmation', dependsOn: ['chargePayment'], run: async () => { /* ... */ } });
    this.define({ name: 'notifyWarehouse', dependsOn: ['createShipment'], run: async () => { /* ... */ } });
  }

  onModuleInit(): void {
    const order = this.graph.topologicalOrder();          // throws on a cycle: the app refuses to start
    // Group into levels: a step's level is 1 + max level of its dependencies.
    const level = new Map<string, number>();
    for (const name of order) {
      const deps = this.steps.get(name)!.dependsOn;
      level.set(name, deps.length ? Math.max(...deps.map((d) => level.get(d)!)) + 1 : 0);
    }
    this.levels = [];
    for (const [name, l] of level) (this.levels[l] ??= []).push(name);
    this.logger.log(`workflow levels: ${JSON.stringify(this.levels)}`);
  }

  async run(orderId: string): Promise<void> {
    for (const names of this.levels) {
      // Steps in one level are independent: run them concurrently, all idempotent by orderId.
      await Promise.all(names.map((n) => this.steps.get(n)!.run(orderId)));
    }
  }

  private define(step: StepDef): void {
    this.steps.set(step.name, step);
    this.graph.addVertex(step.name);
    for (const dep of step.dependsOn) this.graph.addEdge(dep, step.name);
  }
}

NestJS itself does the same at bootstrap: modules and providers form a graph, and a cycle produces the familiar "A circular dependency between modules" error, solved by breaking the edge or with forwardRef().

PostgreSQL example

Most production graphs live in PostgreSQL as an edges table with indexes in both directions. Two-hop queries are joins; deeper traversal is a bounded recursive CTE; anything beyond that is a job for a graph database or precomputation.

CREATE TABLE follows (
  follower_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  followee_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id)                 -- "who do I follow" in one index
);
CREATE INDEX follows_followee_idx ON follows (followee_id, follower_id); -- "who follows me"

-- Friends of friends, excluding people already followed and self, most common first.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT f2.followee_id AS suggested, count(*) AS mutuals
FROM follows f1
JOIN follows f2 ON f2.follower_id = f1.followee_id
WHERE f1.follower_id = 42
  AND f2.followee_id <> 42
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM follows f3 WHERE f3.follower_id = 42 AND f3.followee_id = f2.followee_id)
GROUP BY f2.followee_id
ORDER BY mutuals DESC
LIMIT 20;
Limit  (cost=2931.10..2931.15 rows=20 width=16) (actual time=18.24..18.26 rows=20 loops=1)
  ->  Sort  (cost=2931.10..2958.47 rows=10948 width=16) (actual time=18.23..18.24 rows=20 loops=1)
        Sort Key: (count(*)) DESC
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 26kB
        ->  HashAggregate  (cost=2529.37..2639.85 rows=10948 width=16) (actual time=14.91..16.88 rows=11302 loops=1)
              Group Key: f2.followee_id
              ->  Nested Loop Anti Join  (cost=0.99..2461.62 rows=13550 width=8) (actual time=0.06..11.02 rows=13791 loops=1)
                    ->  Nested Loop  (cost=0.57..1811.20 rows=14120 width=8) (actual time=0.04..6.31 rows=14210 loops=1)
                          ->  Index Only Scan using follows_pkey on follows f1  (actual time=0.02..0.09 rows=312 loops=1)
                                Index Cond: (follower_id = 42)
                          ->  Index Only Scan using follows_pkey on follows f2  (actual time=0.01..0.02 rows=46 loops=312)
                                Index Cond: (follower_id = f1.followee_id)

Execution Time: 18.41 ms

A user following 312 accounts with 46 follows each produced 14,210 candidate rows in 18 ms. The same query for a user following 5,000 accounts that each follow 5,000 produces 25 million rows; that is the supernode problem, and no index fixes it.

-- Bounded reachability with cycle protection (PostgreSQL 14+): who can I reach within 3 hops?
WITH RECURSIVE reach AS (
  SELECT followee_id AS id, 1 AS depth FROM follows WHERE follower_id = 42
  UNION ALL
  SELECT f.followee_id, r.depth + 1 FROM follows f JOIN reach r ON f.follower_id = r.id
  WHERE r.depth < 3
) CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT DISTINCT id FROM reach WHERE NOT is_cycle;

TypeORM example

@Entity({ name: 'users' })
export class User {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('increment', { type: 'bigint' }) id!: string;

  @ManyToMany(() => User, (u) => u.followers)
  @JoinTable({
    name: 'follows',
    joinColumn: { name: 'follower_id' },
    inverseJoinColumn: { name: 'followee_id' },

  following!: User[];

  @ManyToMany(() => User, (u) => u.following)

}

// Never load `following` relations for traversal; query the edge table directly.
const suggestions = await dataSource.query(

   JOIN follows f2 ON f2.follower_id = f1.followee_id

Production scenario

Service graph. OpenTelemetry traces from 80 services produce an edge list of about 300 call relationships, rebuilt every minute. A DFS from payments-svc over the reverse graph answers "which user-facing endpoints break if payments is down" in microseconds; the graph fits in one Map. That is the sweet spot for in-process graphs: small, derived, rebuilt often.

Social graph. 20 million users and 1.5 billion follow edges live in the follows table (about 90 GB with indexes), partitioned by follower_id. Feeds are computed by fan-out on write for ordinary users (each post is pushed to followers' Redis lists, Section 7.7) and by fan-out on read for accounts with more than 100,000 followers, precisely because the degree of a supernode makes push cost unbounded. This decision is a data-structure decision about degree, and it is covered again in the System Design part.

Routing. A delivery-routing worker loads a city's road network (600,000 vertices, 1.4 million edges) into compressed sparse row arrays (about 12 MB) and runs Dijkstra with a binary heap in about 40 ms per query, restricted to a bounding box so most queries touch a few thousand vertices.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call engineer is paged: PostgreSQL CPU is at 100 percent, connection pool wait time is 4 seconds, and the slow-query log is full of the friends-of-friends query for user_id = 771204. That user is a brand account following 48,000 people, most of whom are other brands following tens of thousands. The two-hop join produced 900 million intermediate rows, spilled HashAggregate batches to disk, and held a connection for 190 seconds. The mobile app retried on timeout every 30 seconds, and the user was on a train tapping the "suggestions" tab repeatedly. Four concurrent copies of the query saturated the primary.

The fix in the first ten minutes: statement_timeout = 5s for that query's role. The fix that week: degree caps in the query (LIMIT 500 on the first hop, sampled), a precomputed suggestions table refreshed nightly for accounts above 5,000 follows, and a per-user single-flight lock in Redis so retries wait instead of piling up. The lesson: traversal cost is the product of degrees along the path; bound the degrees or precompute.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Supernodes (celebrities, brand accounts, the "all" tag) make any neighbour-based query explode; cap, sample or precompute.
  • Cycles hang naive traversals; use visited sets in code and CYCLE or depth bounds in SQL.
  • Direction mistakes. "Follows" is directed; treating it as undirected doubles the graph and breaks semantics.
  • Missing reverse index makes "who follows me" a sequential scan.
  • Self-loops and duplicate edges need a primary key on (from, to) and a check constraint from <> to.
  • Unbounded depth in recursive CTEs; always set a depth stop.
  • Recursion in DFS over user data overflows the stack.
  • Consistency: removing a vertex must remove its edges (foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE), or the graph accumulates dangling references.
  • Stale in-process graphs after the source changes; rebuild on a schedule and expose the build age.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior keeps the graph in PostgreSQL as an edges table with both indexes until multi-hop traversals dominate the workload, because a relational edge table gives them transactions, constraints, backups and one operational surface. They bound every traversal by depth and degree, precompute for supernodes, and treat any in-process graph as a small, derived, rebuildable index. They reach for a graph database (Neo4j, or the Apache AGE extension inside PostgreSQL) only when queries of four or more hops are the product, and they know that decision adds a system to operate. For dependency graphs (workflows, module wiring, build steps) they validate acyclicity at definition time, not at run time.

To a product manager: "Suggestions for normal users are instant. For accounts following tens of thousands of people, we compute suggestions overnight instead of live; the feature looks identical, and it stops one user from taking the database down."

Common mistakes

  • Loading user.following relations through the ORM to traverse; use the edge table.
  • Forgetting the reverse index.
  • Unbounded recursive CTEs over data that can contain cycles.
  • Modelling a DAG of steps as a list and discovering the ordering bug in production.
  • Choosing an adjacency matrix for a sparse graph "for O(1) edge checks" and running out of memory at 50,000 vertices.

Interview questions

  1. Adjacency list versus matrix: when does each win? Expected: list for sparse graphs (almost all real ones), O(V + E) memory; matrix for small dense graphs and O(1) edge checks.
  2. How does NestJS detect circular dependencies, in data-structure terms? Expected: the providers and modules form a directed graph; resolution is a topological order; a cycle leaves unresolved vertices; forwardRef defers one edge.
  3. Design "people you may know" for 20 million users. Expected: two-hop join with degree caps for normal users, precomputation for supernodes, indexes in both directions, single-flight for retries.
  4. Explain Kahn's algorithm and what it returns when there is a cycle. Expected: in-degree counting with a queue of zero-in-degree vertices; leftover vertices with positive in-degree identify the cycle.
  5. Why would you run Dijkstra with a binary heap, and what breaks it? Expected: O((V + E) log V); negative edge weights break it (use Bellman-Ford).
  6. When is a graph database justified? Expected: when deep, variable-length traversals are the core workload; otherwise the operational cost outweighs the query convenience.

Practical exercise

Build SuggestionsModule over a follows table seeded with 1 million users following a power-law distribution (most users 50 to 300 follows, 100 users above 20,000). Acceptance criteria: GET /users/:id/suggestions answers in under 50 ms at p99 for ordinary users; for users above 5,000 follows it serves a precomputed table refreshed by a nightly job and the response includes computedAt; the live query has statement_timeout of 5 seconds and returns 503 with Retry-After on timeout instead of 500; a workflow DAG test defines a cycle and asserts the application fails to start with an error naming the cycle; and Dijkstra over a 10,000-vertex generated grid returns paths equal to a brute-force BFS on unit weights.

7.16 Bloom Filter

Concept

A Bloom filter is a set that can be wrong in exactly one direction. Ask it "is X in the set?" and it answers either "definitely not" or "probably yes". It never says "no" for something you added (no false negatives), but it sometimes says "yes" for something you never added (false positives), at a rate you choose when you size it. In exchange it uses about 10 bits per item at a 1 percent false-positive rate, compared with 60 to 100 bytes per item for a Set of strings: fifty to eighty times smaller.

You cannot list the members, you cannot count them exactly, and the basic version cannot delete. What you get is a membership test for tens of millions of items in a few megabytes, which is exactly what several backend problems need.

Why does it exist?

Two problems drove its adoption. First, cache penetration: a request for a key that does not exist misses the cache, misses the database, and misses again on the next request, because there is nothing to cache. Bots probing random product ids, or a scraper enumerating /users/{n}, turn your database into the cache. A Bloom filter of all existing ids answers "definitely not" in 100 nanoseconds without touching Redis or PostgreSQL. Second, "have we already shown or processed this?" at scales where a real set is too large: which of 50 million users have seen a notification, which of 2 billion URLs a crawler has visited, which keys are not in an SSTable so the storage engine can skip reading it (RocksDB, Cassandra, LevelDB all do this).

Mental model

Imagine a hotel guest book that only records checkmarks, not names. Every guest, on arrival, puts a checkmark in seven boxes chosen by a fixed rule from their name. Later you ask "has Ana ever stayed here?" You compute Ana's seven boxes. If any box is empty, Ana was definitely never here. If all seven are checked, Ana probably stayed, but the checks might have come from other guests whose boxes overlap. The more guests, the more overlap, the more "probably" answers are wrong; a bigger book with more boxes keeps the overlap rare.

How it works

  1. Bit array. Allocate m bits, all zero (a Uint8Array of m / 8 bytes).
  2. k hash functions. Each maps an item to a position in [0, m). In practice you compute two independent 32-bit hashes h1 and h2 and derive the k positions as (h1 + i * h2) mod m for i in 0..k-1 (double hashing), which is as good as k real hash functions and much cheaper.
  3. Add. Compute the k positions and set those bits to 1.
  4. Query. Compute the k positions; if any bit is 0, answer "no"; if all are 1, answer "probably".
  5. The math. With n items inserted, the false-positive probability is approximately (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k. For a target rate p, the optimal size is m = -n ln(p) / (ln 2)^2 bits and the optimal number of hashes is k = (m / n) ln 2. For n = 10 million and p = 1 percent: m is about 95.9 million bits (12 MB), k = 7. Rules of thumb: 9.6 bits per item for 1 percent, 14.4 for 0.1 percent, 29.2 for 0.01 percent.
  6. Capacity. The rate is a promise only up to the n you sized for. Insert twice as many items and the rate rises steeply (from 1 percent to about 6 percent for the numbers above). Size for the maximum, or use a scalable Bloom filter that adds a new, larger filter when the current one fills.
  7. Deletion. Clearing a bit could remove another item's evidence, so plain filters cannot delete. A counting Bloom filter keeps a small counter per position instead of a bit (4 to 8 times the memory); a cuckoo filter supports deletion at similar memory to a Bloom filter. Or you rebuild periodically from the source of truth, which is usually the simplest.
  8. Sharing. Because the filter is just bits, it can be serialized and shipped to every pod, stored in Redis as a string with SETBIT/GETBIT, or kept server-side in Redis with the RedisBloom module (BF.RESERVE, BF.ADD, BF.EXISTS, BF.MEXISTS). The hash implementation and seed must be identical everywhere that reads the same bits; version the filter format.
flowchart LR
    subgraph Bits
        b0["0"] --- b1["0"] --- b2["0"] --- b3["1"] --- b4["0"] --- b5["0"] --- b6["0"] --- b7["0"]
        b8["0"] --- b9["1"] --- b10["0"] --- b11["0"] --- b12["0"] --- b13["0"] --- b14["1"] --- b15["0"]
