Time complexity (k hash functions, m bits)

Operation Best Average Worst Notes
add O(k) O(k) O(k) k is 7 for 1 percent; a few hundred nanoseconds
mightContain O(1) O(k) O(k) best case: the first probed bit is 0
Union of two same-size filters O(m / 64) O(m / 64) O(m / 64) bitwise OR; lets pods merge their filters
Serialize / deserialize O(m / 8) O(m / 8) O(m / 8) 12 MB for 10 million items at 1 percent
Delete not supported counting or cuckoo variants, or rebuild
Exact count / enumerate not supported keep the source of truth elsewhere

Memory implications (V8, Node.js)

  • The bit array is a Uint8Array, allocated once, off the V8-managed heap (arrayBuffers in process.memoryUsage()): no GC pressure, no per-item objects.
  • 10 million product ids: about 12 MB as a Bloom filter at 1 percent, about 1.1 GB as a Set<string> of UUIDs, about 900 MB as a Redis SET.
  • Building a filter of 10 million ids takes 3 to 6 seconds of CPU (hashing dominates); do it before the pod reports ready, and consider shipping a prebuilt filter from an object store instead of rebuilding on every pod.

Decision table: membership at scale

Need Structure Memory for 10M items Wrong answers
Exact membership in one process, small Set about 1 GB (UUID strings) none
Exact membership shared across pods Redis SET or a unique index about 900 MB in Redis none
Membership with tolerable false positives, huge Bloom filter 12 MB at 1 percent false "yes" only
Membership with deletes, huge cuckoo filter or counting Bloom 15 to 50 MB false "yes" only
Count of distinct items only HyperLogLog (PFADD, PFCOUNT) 12 KB about 0.8 percent count error

Practical example

A Bloom filter with double hashing over FNV-1a, sized from capacity and target rate, with export and import so pods can share it.

// common/bloom-filter.ts
function fnv1a32(str: string, seed: number): number {
  let h = (0x811c9dc5 ^ seed) >>> 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < str.length; i++) {
    h ^= str.charCodeAt(i);
    h = Math.imul(h, 0x01000193) >>> 0;   // FNV prime, kept in 32 bits
  }
  h ^= h >>> 16; h = Math.imul(h, 0x85ebca6b) >>> 0;  // final avalanche mixing
  h ^= h >>> 13; h = Math.imul(h, 0xc2b2ae35) >>> 0;
  return (h ^ (h >>> 16)) >>> 0;
}

export class BloomFilter {
  static readonly FORMAT_VERSION = 1;              // bump when the hash or layout changes
  private readonly bits: Uint8Array;

  private constructor(readonly m: number, readonly k: number, bits?: Uint8Array) {
    this.bits = bits ?? new Uint8Array(Math.ceil(m / 8));
  }

  /** Size for `capacity` items at `falsePositiveRate` (e.g. 0.01). */
  static forCapacity(capacity: number, falsePositiveRate: number): BloomFilter {
    const m = Math.ceil((-capacity * Math.log(falsePositiveRate)) / (Math.LN2 * Math.LN2));
    const k = Math.max(1, Math.round((m / capacity) * Math.LN2));
    return new BloomFilter(m, k);
  }

  add(item: string): void {
    const h1 = fnv1a32(item, 0x9747b28c), h2 = fnv1a32(item, 0x5bd1e995) | 1; // h2 odd: better spread
    for (let i = 0; i < this.k; i++) {
      const pos = (h1 + i * h2) % this.m;
      this.bits[pos >>> 3] |= 1 << (pos & 7);
    }
  }

  mightContain(item: string): boolean {
    const h1 = fnv1a32(item, 0x9747b28c), h2 = fnv1a32(item, 0x5bd1e995) | 1;
    for (let i = 0; i < this.k; i++) {
      const pos = (h1 + i * h2) % this.m;
      if ((this.bits[pos >>> 3] & (1 << (pos & 7))) === 0) return false; // definitely not
    }
    return true;                                                            // probably
  }

  /** Header (version, m, k) + bits, for Redis, S3 or a file. */
  export(): Buffer {
    const header = Buffer.alloc(12);
    header.writeUInt32BE(BloomFilter.FORMAT_VERSION, 0);
    header.writeUInt32BE(this.m, 4);
    header.writeUInt32BE(this.k, 8);
    return Buffer.concat([header, Buffer.from(this.bits.buffer, this.bits.byteOffset, this.bits.byteLength)]);
  }

  static import(buf: Buffer): BloomFilter {
    if (buf.readUInt32BE(0) !== BloomFilter.FORMAT_VERSION) throw new Error('bloom filter format mismatch');
    const m = buf.readUInt32BE(4), k = buf.readUInt32BE(8);
    return new BloomFilter(m, k, new Uint8Array(buf.subarray(12)));
  }
}

FNV-1a with mixing is adequate for ids and short keys; for adversarial input or very long keys, prefer a proper 64-bit hash (an xxHash or MurmurHash3 binding) and split it into h1 and h2.

NestJS example

Cache-penetration protection for product lookups, plus a cluster-wide "seen this notification" check with RedisBloom. The filter is rebuilt every 10 minutes from PostgreSQL; ids created after the last build are allowed through by an id watermark so a stale filter cannot produce false "not found" answers.

// products/product-existence.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { BloomFilter } from '../common/bloom-filter';

@Injectable()
export class ProductExistenceService implements OnModuleInit {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(ProductExistenceService.name);
  private filter = BloomFilter.forCapacity(1, 0.01);
  private watermark = 0n;      // highest product id included in the filter

  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> {
    await this.rebuild();
  }

  @Cron('30 */10 * * * *')
  async rebuild(): Promise<void> {
    const [{ count, max }] = await this.dataSource.query(`SELECT count(*)::int AS count, max(id)::text AS max FROM products`);
    const fresh = BloomFilter.forCapacity(Math.max(count * 1.5, 1_000_000), 0.01); // headroom for growth
    const rows: { id: string }[] = await this.dataSource.query(`SELECT id::text FROM products`);
    for (const r of rows) fresh.add(r.id);
    this.filter = fresh;                          // atomic swap
    this.watermark = BigInt(max ?? '0');
    this.logger.log(`rebuilt product filter: ${rows.length} ids, ${(fresh.m / 8 / 1024 / 1024).toFixed(1)} MB`);
  }

  /** Called by insert hooks on this pod; other pods rely on the watermark until their next rebuild. */
  addLocal(id: string): void {
    this.filter.add(id);
  }

  /** false means "definitely does not exist": safe to answer 404 without any I/O. */
  mightExist(id: string): boolean {
    if (!/^\d{1,18}$/.test(id)) return false;    // malformed ids are rejected before hashing
    if (BigInt(id) > this.watermark) return true; // created after the last build: let it through
    return this.filter.mightContain(id);
  }
}

// products/product-read.service.ts (excerpt)
async byId(id: string): Promise<Product> {
  if (!this.existence.mightExist(id)) throw new NotFoundException(`product ${id} not found`); // ~200 ns
  // ... Redis cache, single-flight, PostgreSQL as in Section 1.8
}

// notifications/seen.service.ts -- shared across pods with the RedisBloom module
@Injectable()
export class SeenNotificationsService {
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async markSeen(userId: string, notificationId: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.redis.call('BF.ADD', 'notif:seen', `${userId}:${notificationId}`);
  }

  async probablySeen(userId: string, notificationId: string): Promise<boolean> {
    return (await this.redis.call('BF.EXISTS', 'notif:seen', `${userId}:${notificationId}`)) === 1;
  }
}

Create the Redis filter once with BF.RESERVE notif:seen 0.01 100000000 (1 percent, 100 million capacity, about 120 MB); RedisBloom filters can also be created as scalable so they grow instead of degrading.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL ships a bloom index type: a signature per row across several columns, useful when queries filter by equality on arbitrary subsets of columns and one B-tree per combination would be too many. It is lossy, so the plan always shows a recheck.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS bloom;

-- One small index instead of a B-tree per column combination.
CREATE INDEX orders_bloom_idx ON orders
USING bloom (merchant_id, status, channel, country, payment_method)
WITH (length = 80, col1 = 4, col2 = 2, col3 = 2, col4 = 2, col5 = 2);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'refunded' AND channel = 'app' AND country = 'IN';
Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (cost=13210.00..14392.10 rows=402 width=8) (actual time=88.4..91.2 rows=388 loops=1)
  Recheck Cond: ((status = 'refunded') AND (channel = 'app') AND (country = 'IN'))
  Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 1417
  Heap Blocks: exact=1620
  Buffers: shared hit=9832
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on orders_bloom_idx  (cost=0.00..13209.90 rows=1805 width=0) (actual time=86.9..86.9 rows=1805 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((status = 'refunded') AND (channel = 'app') AND (country = 'IN'))
Execution Time: 91.6 ms

Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 1417 are the false positives: the index said "probably" for 1,805 rows and the heap check kept 388. The index scan itself reads every signature (it is not a tree), so this is a win over a sequential scan only when the table is wide and the index is much smaller than the table. PostgreSQL 14 also added a BRIN bloom operator class (int8_bloom_ops) for the same idea inside block-range indexes.

TypeORM example

Keep the filter warm as rows are created, so the watermark rarely has to do the work.

// products/product.subscriber.ts
import { EntitySubscriberInterface, EventSubscriber, InsertEvent } from 'typeorm';
import { Product } from './product.entity';
import { ProductExistenceService } from './product-existence.service';

@EventSubscriber()
export class ProductSubscriber implements EntitySubscriberInterface<Product> {
  constructor(private readonly existence: ProductExistenceService) {}

  listenTo() { return Product; }

  afterInsert(event: InsertEvent<Product>): void {
    this.existence.addLocal(event.entity.id);   // this pod only; other pods rely on the watermark until rebuild
  }
}

Register the subscriber as a provider and in the TypeOrmModule.forRoot({ subscribers: [...] }) options; TypeORM subscribers are constructed by the DI container when listed as providers in NestJS.

Sequelize example

Product.addHook('afterCreate', (product: Product) => {
  existenceService.addLocal(String(product.id));
});

Hooks run in the process that performed the insert; cross-pod freshness still comes from the watermark or a pub/sub message.

Production scenario

A catalog API with 9 million products receives 800 RPS of lookups, of which a scraper contributes 300 RPS of random, non-existent ids. Without the filter each of those 300 misses the Redis cache and runs a primary-key lookup in PostgreSQL: 300 useless queries per second, about 15 percent of the database's capacity, and Redis holds nothing for them. With a 1 percent filter, 297 of those 300 are answered with a 404 in 200 nanoseconds and 3 fall through as false positives. The filter costs 11 MB per pod and 4 seconds of CPU at startup.

The second use is notification de-duplication across a 50-million-user base: 200 campaigns a month means 10 billion (user, campaign) pairs a year. A Redis SET per campaign is 50 million members at about 90 bytes each: 4.5 GB per campaign. A RedisBloom filter per campaign is 60 MB at 1 percent, and a false positive means one user does not receive one marketing push, which the business signs off on in writing.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call engineer is paged by support: newly published products return 404 on three of twelve pods. Those pods had lost their Redis pub/sub connection during a Redis failover at 23:40 and missed the product.created messages that other pods used to add ids to their filters; the nightly rebuild was at 04:00. The filter itself was not wrong: it had never been told about the new ids. A Bloom filter has no false negatives for what was added to it; staleness is a false negative from the system's point of view.

The immediate mitigation was a rolling restart of the three pods. The durable fix was the watermark: any id greater than the highest id at the last build bypasses the filter. Time-ordered ids (bigint sequences, ULIDs) make this a one-line check. The other lesson: a probabilistic structure must be wrong only in the safe direction. Here the safe direction is "let a real product through to the database"; the filter must never be allowed to say "no" for something that might exist.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Under-sizing. Insert past capacity and the false-positive rate climbs; size with headroom and monitor the insert count.
  • Staleness produces false negatives for items added after the build; use watermarks, events with a fallback, or short rebuild intervals.
  • Hash mismatch across pods when sharing bits: same hash, seed, m and k, enforced with a version header.
  • No deletion. Deleted products stay "probably present" until a rebuild, which costs one database miss per hit; harmless if the rebuild is frequent.
  • Adversarial keys. With a weak hash an attacker can craft ids that are false positives, defeating the protection; use a strong hash for untrusted input.
  • Startup time. Building from 10 million rows delays readiness; ship a prebuilt filter from object storage and rebuild in the background.
  • Wrong direction. Never use "probably yes" to grant something (access, a discount) or "definitely no" to skip a safety check that must not be skipped.
  • Redis eviction. A filter stored in Redis under allkeys-lru can be evicted like any key; keep it in a noeviction instance or rebuildable from the source.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior asks two questions before using any probabilistic structure: what does a wrong answer cost, and in which direction can it be wrong? A false positive in cache-penetration protection costs one database lookup; a false positive in notification de-duplication costs one missed message; both are acceptable and documented. A false negative would cost a 404 for a real product, which is unacceptable, so the design guarantees the filter can never produce one. They size for growth, version the format, rebuild from the source of truth on a schedule, and keep the source of truth exact (PostgreSQL, a unique index). They reach for RedisBloom when pods must share, and for HyperLogLog when the question is "how many", not "which".

To a product manager: "We can stop bots from hammering the database for products that do not exist, using about 11 MB of memory. About one in a hundred of those bogus requests will still reach the database; real products are never affected."

Common mistakes

  • Using a Bloom filter where an exact answer is required.
  • Sizing for today's row count with no headroom.
  • Forgetting that a filter built at 04:00 knows nothing about rows created at 09:00.
  • Storing the filter in Redis with SETBIT and issuing k round trips per check instead of one BF.EXISTS or a pipelined BITFIELD.
  • Hashing untrusted input with a trivial hash and calling the result "protection".

Interview questions

  1. What can a Bloom filter never do, and what does it do well? Expected: no false negatives (for added items), no deletion, no enumeration; tiny memory for membership with tunable false positives.
  2. Size a filter for 20 million ids at 0.1 percent. Expected: about 14.4 bits per item, 288 million bits, 36 MB, k of about 10.
  3. Explain cache penetration and two defences. Expected: misses for non-existent keys bypass caches; Bloom filter of existing keys, and negative caching of 404s with a short TTL.
  4. New rows return 404 after you added a Bloom filter. Why, and how do you fix it without disabling the filter? Expected: staleness; watermark on time-ordered ids, or event-driven adds with a periodic rebuild.
  5. When would you pick a cuckoo filter, a counting Bloom filter or HyperLogLog instead? Expected: deletion, deletion with simpler semantics at more memory, distinct counting.
  6. Where do Bloom filters appear inside databases? Expected: LSM engines skip SSTables, PostgreSQL bloom index and BRIN bloom opclass, Cassandra and RocksDB.

Practical exercise

Build ExistenceFilterModule for a seeded products table of 5 million rows. Acceptance criteria: a load test with 90 percent random non-existent ids shows PostgreSQL query rate under 2 percent of request rate (measure with pg_stat_statements before and after); the measured false-positive rate over 1 million random probes is between 0.5 and 1.5 percent; a product inserted after the last rebuild is retrievable immediately on every pod (integration test with two application instances and the watermark); the filter is exported to Redis after each rebuild and a fresh pod imports it in under 500 ms instead of rebuilding; and a test proves mightExist returns false for malformed ids without hashing them.

7.17 LRU Cache

Concept

An LRU (least recently used) cache is a bounded key-value store that, when full, evicts the entry that has gone longest without being read or written. It is the structure behind almost every in-process cache you will use (lru-cache, the memory store of @nestjs/cache-manager, HTTP client caches) and the policy behind Redis's allkeys-lru and, in spirit, PostgreSQL's buffer cache. It combines two structures from this Part: a hash map for O(1) lookup by key and a doubly linked list ordered by recency for O(1) "move to front" and "drop the back".

Why does it exist?

Memory is finite and access patterns are skewed: a small fraction of products, users and sessions receive most of the reads, and what was hot a minute ago is likely hot now (temporal locality). A cache without eviction is the six-day memory leak from Section 7.8. A cache that evicts randomly throws away hot entries. LRU keeps the recent working set with a policy that is cheap (O(1) per operation), needs no statistics, and is right often enough that it became the default everywhere.

Mental model

Imagine a desk with room for ten documents. Every time you use one, you put it on top of the pile. When an eleventh document arrives, the one at the bottom, untouched the longest, goes back to the archive. You never search the pile for the oldest; it is always at the bottom, because using a document moves it to the top. The hash map is the index card that tells you where in the pile a document currently is, so you never rummage.

How it works

  1. Two structures, one entry. Each cache entry is a node in a doubly linked list holding the key and value. A Map maps the key to that node. The list's front is the most recently used entry; its back is the least.
  2. get(key). Look up the node in the map (O(1)). If absent, miss. If present, unlink it and relink it at the front (O(1), four pointer writes), then return the value.
  3. set(key, value). If the key exists, update the value and move the node to the front. Otherwise create a node at the front and add it to the map. If the size now exceeds capacity, unlink the back node and delete its key from the map.
  4. TTL. Store an expiresAt per entry and treat an expired entry as a miss on read (lazy expiry); optionally sweep periodically. TTL bounds staleness; capacity bounds memory; you usually want both.
  5. The Map-only shortcut. Because a JavaScript Map iterates in insertion order, delete followed by set moves a key to the end, and map.keys().next().value is the oldest. That gives an O(1) LRU in fifteen lines with no list at all; the explicit list version is clearer, supports eviction callbacks cleanly, and is what libraries do.
  6. Weaknesses and cousins. LRU is not scan-resistant: one pass over a million cold keys evicts the entire hot set. LFU (least frequently used) resists scans but adapts slowly. 2Q, ARC and W-TinyLFU (used by Caffeine on the JVM) combine recency and frequency. Redis approximates LRU by sampling a few keys (maxmemory-samples, default 5) rather than maintaining a list, and offers LFU with a logarithmic counter and decay. PostgreSQL uses a clock sweep: each buffer has a usage count (max 5) incremented on access; a clock hand walks the buffers decrementing counts and evicts the first buffer it finds at zero, and large sequential scans get a private 256 KB ring so they cannot flush the working set.
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Before get of key B"
        h1["head most recent"] --> c1["C"] --> a1["A"] --> b1["B"] --> t1["tail least recent"]
    end
    subgraph "After get of key B"
        h2["head most recent"] --> b2["B"] --> c2["C"] --> a2["A"] --> t2["tail least recent"]
    end
    m["Map get B returns node in O(1)"] -.-> b1
    b1 -->|"unlink and relink at head"| b2
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Set D when capacity is 3"
        h["head"] --> d["D new"] --> b["B"] --> c["C"]
        c -.->|"popBack then Map delete A"| a["A evicted"]
    end

Time complexity

Operation Best Average Worst Notes
get O(1) O(1) O(n) worst case is a pathological hash collision in the map
set (new or existing) O(1) O(1) O(n) includes eviction; worst case is a map resize
delete O(1) O(1) O(1) node handle from the map
Evict least recent O(1) O(1) O(1) it is always the tail
Iterate by recency O(n) O(n) O(n)
Sweep expired entries O(n) O(n) O(n) run off the request path

Memory implications (V8, Node.js)

  • Per entry: a map entry (about 50 bytes), a list node (about 56 bytes), the key string and the value. Budget about 150 bytes of overhead per entry plus the payload. Ten thousand product records of 2 KB each is about 21.5 MB per pod.
  • Capacity is in entries; if values vary wildly in size (a 20 KB product with 200 images next to a 300-byte one), either count bytes (Buffer.byteLength(JSON.stringify(v)) at set time, which costs CPU) or cap the value size at insertion.
  • Values are shared by reference. A caller that mutates a cached object mutates it for everyone. Freeze cached objects (Object.freeze) in development, or clone on read for mutable use.
  • Churn creates garbage: at 20,000 sets per second the old nodes and values are short-lived young-generation objects, which V8 handles well; long-lived entries promoted to old space cost more on major GCs. Keep capacity modest and let TTL do the rest.

Decision table: eviction policy

Policy Keeps Weakness Where you meet it
LRU recently used scans flush the hot set lru-cache, cache-manager memory store, Redis allkeys-lru (approximate)
LFU frequently used slow to adapt; needs decay Redis allkeys-lfu
FIFO newest ignores popularity simple ring buffers
TTL only everything until expiry unbounded memory TypeORM query cache, naive Map with timestamps
Clock sweep with usage counts recently and repeatedly used approximate LRU PostgreSQL shared_buffers
2Q / ARC / W-TinyLFU recency plus frequency, scan-resistant complexity Caffeine, some database buffer pools

Practical example

A production-grade LRU with TTL, eviction callback and hit statistics on top of the DoublyLinkedList from Section 7.4, followed by the fifteen-line Map-only version.

// common/lru-cache.ts
import { DoublyLinkedList, ListNode } from './doubly-linked-list';

interface Entry<K, V> { key: K; value: V; expiresAt: number }

export class LruCache<K, V> {
  private readonly map = new Map<K, ListNode<Entry<K, V>>>();
  private readonly list = new DoublyLinkedList<Entry<K, V>>();
  hits = 0;
  misses = 0;
  evictions = 0;

  constructor(
    private readonly capacity: number,
    private readonly defaultTtlMs = 0,                        // 0 = no expiry
    private readonly onEvict?: (key: K, value: V) => void,
  ) {
    if (!Number.isInteger(capacity) || capacity <= 0) throw new RangeError('capacity must be a positive integer');
  }

  get(key: K): V | undefined {
    const node = this.map.get(key);
    if (!node) { this.misses++; return undefined; }
    if (node.value.expiresAt !== 0 && node.value.expiresAt <= Date.now()) {
      this.drop(node);                                          // lazy expiry
      this.misses++;
      return undefined;
    }
    this.list.moveToFront(node);                                // O(1): now the most recently used
    this.hits++;
    return node.value.value;
  }

  set(key: K, value: V, ttlMs = this.defaultTtlMs): void {
    const expiresAt = ttlMs > 0 ? Date.now() + ttlMs : 0;
    const existing = this.map.get(key);
    if (existing) {
      existing.value.value = value;
      existing.value.expiresAt = expiresAt;
      this.list.moveToFront(existing);
      return;
    }
    this.map.set(key, this.list.pushFront({ key, value, expiresAt }));
    if (this.map.size > this.capacity) {
      const victim = this.list.popBack()!;                      // least recently used is always the tail
      this.map.delete(victim.key);
      this.evictions++;
      this.onEvict?.(victim.key, victim.value);
    }
  }

  delete(key: K): boolean {
    const node = this.map.get(key);
    if (!node) return false;
    this.drop(node);
    return true;
  }

  get size(): number { return this.map.size; }
  get hitRate(): number { const t = this.hits + this.misses; return t === 0 ? 0 : this.hits / t; }

  private drop(node: ListNode<Entry<K, V>>): void {
    this.list.remove(node);
    this.map.delete(node.value.key);
  }
}

// common/tiny-lru.ts -- the Map insertion-order trick, also O(1)
export class TinyLru<K, V> {
  private readonly map = new Map<K, V>();
  constructor(private readonly capacity: number) {}

  get(key: K): V | undefined {
    const value = this.map.get(key);
    if (value === undefined) return undefined;
    this.map.delete(key);
    this.map.set(key, value);                                   // re-insert: now the newest entry
    return value;
  }

  set(key: K, value: V): void {
    if (this.map.has(key)) this.map.delete(key);
    this.map.set(key, value);
    if (this.map.size > this.capacity) this.map.delete(this.map.keys().next().value as K); // oldest first
  }
}

NestJS example

Two ways to get an LRU in NestJS. The framework way: @nestjs/cache-manager with max and ttl, whose memory store is an LRU. The explicit way: a provider around LruCache that exposes metrics and, crucially, a bypass flag so bulk jobs cannot flush the hot set (the failure scenario below).

// app.module.ts (framework way)
import { CacheModule } from '@nestjs/cache-manager';

@Module({
  imports: [CacheModule.register({ isGlobal: true, ttl: 60_000, max: 10_000 })], // ms in cache-manager v5
})
export class AppModule {}

// products/products.controller.ts
import { CacheInterceptor, CacheKey, CacheTTL } from '@nestjs/cache-manager';

@Controller('products')
@UseInterceptors(CacheInterceptor)                 // caches GET responses by URL, per pod
export class ProductsController {
  @Get('menu')
  @CacheKey('products:menu')
  @CacheTTL(30_000)
  menu() { /* ... */ }
}

// products/product-cache.service.ts (explicit way)
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { LruCache } from '../common/lru-cache';
import { Product } from './product.entity';

@Injectable()
export class ProductCacheService {
  private readonly cache = new LruCache<string, Product>(10_000, 60_000);

  async getOrLoad(id: string, load: (id: string) => Promise<Product>, opts: { bypass?: boolean } = {}): Promise<Product> {
    if (opts.bypass) return load(id);              // bulk exports and backfills must not touch the hot set
    const hit = this.cache.get(id);
    if (hit) return hit;
    const product = await load(id);                // wrap in SingleFlight (Section 1.8) for hot misses
    this.cache.set(id, Object.freeze(product));    // callers cannot mutate a shared cached object
    return product;
  }

  invalidate(id: string): void {
    this.cache.delete(id);                          // called from a product.updated event on every pod
  }

  stats() {
    return { size: this.cache.size, hitRate: this.cache.hitRate, evictions: this.cache.evictions };
  }
}

Expose stats() on an internal metrics endpoint or as Prometheus gauges. A cache without a hit-rate graph is a cache you cannot reason about during an incident.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL's shared_buffers is the LRU-like cache you already run. You can see what it holds, how hot each buffer is, and how often queries hit it.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_buffercache;

-- Which relations occupy the buffer cache, and how "hot" their buffers are (usagecount 0..5).
SELECT c.relname, count(*) AS buffers, round(avg(b.usagecount), 2) AS avg_usage
FROM pg_buffercache b
JOIN pg_class c ON b.relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode(c.oid)
WHERE b.reldatabase = (SELECT oid FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database())
GROUP BY c.relname ORDER BY buffers DESC LIMIT 5;

-- Overall buffer hit ratio; below ~99% on an OLTP database deserves attention.
SELECT round(100.0 * blks_hit / nullif(blks_hit + blks_read, 0), 2) AS cache_hit_pct
FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = current_database();
       relname        | buffers | avg_usage
----------------------+---------+-----------
 orders               |  312440 |      3.87
 orders_pkey          |   88120 |      4.62
 products             |   41200 |      4.91
 order_items          |   38810 |      2.10
 users_email_lower_uq |    9024 |      4.98

 cache_hit_pct
---------------
         99.31

In EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output, shared hit=1489 means those pages came from this cache; read=212 means they came from the operating system or disk. A nightly report that scans a 400 GB table does not flush the cache, because PostgreSQL routes large sequential scans through a small ring of buffers: the scan-resistance that plain LRU lacks and that you must add yourself in application caches.

Redis as the shared LRU. With maxmemory 4gb and maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru, Redis evicts approximately least-recently-used keys by sampling maxmemory-samples (5 by default; 10 is closer to true LRU at slightly more CPU). Each key header carries a 24-bit clock for this purpose. Use volatile-lru when the same instance holds data that must not be evicted (only keys with a TTL are candidates), allkeys-lfu for skewed, stable popularity, and noeviction with alerting for anything that is a queue or a lock store, where losing a key is a bug rather than a cache miss.

TypeORM example

TypeORM has a query result cache. It is TTL-based, not LRU, so bound it by putting it in Redis with an eviction policy rather than in the database table option.

// data-source.ts
export const AppDataSource = new DataSource({
  type: 'postgres',
  // ...
  cache: { type: 'ioredis', options: { host: process.env.REDIS_HOST, port: 6379 }, duration: 30_000 },
});

// cached query: key + TTL; invalidate with dataSource.queryResultCache?.remove(['products:menu'])
const menu = await productRepo.find({
  where: { isActive: true },
  order: { position: 'ASC' },
  cache: { id: 'products:menu', milliseconds: 30_000 },
});

Sequelize example

Sequelize has no built-in result cache; wrap repository methods with ProductCacheService above, and invalidate from afterUpdate and afterDestroy hooks by publishing the id to every pod.

Production scenario

A catalog read path at 6,000 RPS uses three layers. Per pod, a 10,000-entry LRU with a 60-second TTL (about 20 MB) serves 92 percent of reads in about 2 microseconds. Redis (allkeys-lru, 4 GB, 96 percent hit rate on what reaches it) serves most of the rest in about 0.3 ms. PostgreSQL sees roughly 200 queries per second instead of 6,000, and its own buffer cache answers 99.3 percent of those from memory in 1 to 3 ms. Invalidation flows the other way: a product update publishes product.updated on Redis pub/sub; every pod deletes its local entry and the Redis key, so the staleness window is the propagation delay (milliseconds) rather than the TTL, and the TTL remains as the safety net for missed messages.

The per-pod layer costs 20 MB times 12 pods and one subtle behaviour: each pod warms independently, so a fresh deploy briefly shifts load to Redis and PostgreSQL. Rolling deploys of a few pods at a time keep that spike small; a full restart of all pods at once during peak is a self-inflicted stampede.

Failure scenario

At 07:40 the on-call engineer is paged: checkout p99 has climbed from 90 ms to 3 seconds since 06:00, PostgreSQL CPU is at 95 percent, and the per-pod cache hit rate has dropped from 92 percent to 5 percent. Nothing was deployed. The nightly partner-feed export, moved from 02:00 to 06:00 the previous day to fit a new SLA, walks all 2 million products through the same ProductReadService.byId used by the storefront. The export runs at 800 products per second per pod, so every 12 seconds it cycles a full 10,000-entry LRU: the storefront's hot set is evicted continuously, every customer read misses, and the database absorbs the difference. The LRU worked exactly as designed; the design lacked scan resistance.

The fix took twenty minutes: the export passes bypass: true (the flag in the service above) and reads through a keyset-paginated query instead of byId. The follow-up was an alert on cache hit rate below 70 percent for five minutes, which would have paged at 06:05 instead of 07:40. This is the same problem PostgreSQL solves with buffer rings for sequential scans and that 2Q and W-TinyLFU solve inside the cache itself.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Scan pollution from bulk jobs; add a bypass or a separate cache.
  • Stampede on expiry: a hot key expiring on twelve pods at once produces twelve concurrent database loads; use single-flight per pod, jittered TTLs, or stale-while-revalidate (serve the stale value while one loader refreshes).
  • Negative caching: cache "not found" for a short TTL so repeated misses for missing keys do not reach the database (complements the Bloom filter in Section 7.16).
  • Mutable shared values: a handler that does product.price = discounted on a cached object changes the price for every subsequent reader. Freeze or clone.
  • Key collisions across tenants or versions: include tenant id and a schema version in the key (v3:tenant:42:product:8813).
  • Invalidation gaps: a pod that missed the pub/sub message serves stale data until TTL; keep TTLs short enough that this is acceptable and monitor pub/sub disconnects.
  • Size skew: capacity in entries with unbounded value sizes is not a memory bound.
  • Caching errors and partial results: never cache an exception or a half-loaded aggregate.
  • Clock jumps affect TTL math; use Date.now() consistently and tolerate small skew.
  • Redis eviction of non-cache data: a queue, a lock or a Bloom filter placed on an allkeys-lru instance will be evicted under pressure.
  • Hot key on Redis: one product id read 50,000 times per second lands on one shard; the per-pod LRU exists precisely to absorb that.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats every cache as a promise about staleness and memory, and writes both numbers down: "at most 60 seconds stale, at most 20 MB per pod, at most 10,000 entries". They put a hit-rate graph next to the latency graph, because a cache that quietly stops hitting is the most common explanation for "the database got slow and nothing changed". They separate traffic classes (interactive reads versus bulk scans) so one cannot evict the other. They know that a per-pod cache is a cache, Redis is a cache, and PostgreSQL's buffer pool is a cache, and that invalidation must reach all three. And they resist caching until they have measured: a 20 MB cache with a 92 percent hit rate is a great trade; a cache with a 30 percent hit rate is memory and complexity for nothing.

To a product manager: "Product pages read from memory for up to a minute after an edit. The export job was accidentally flushing that memory every twelve seconds, so every customer read went to the database. We separated the two paths; the export is unchanged and the site is fast again."

Common mistakes

  • Unbounded Map "caches" (Section 7.8).
  • LRU with no TTL (stale forever for keys that stay hot) or TTL with no capacity (memory unbounded).
  • Letting bulk jobs share the interactive cache.
  • No hit-rate metric.
  • Caching by reference and mutating.
  • Using allkeys-lru on a Redis instance that also stores queues or locks.
  • Full-fleet restarts at peak, turning cold caches into a database stampede.

Interview questions

  1. Implement an LRU cache with O(1) get and set. Expected: hash map plus doubly linked list, move-to-front on access, evict tail; or the Map insertion-order trick. Follow-up: how do you add TTL without a sweep? (Lazy expiry on read, plus an optional periodic sweep.)
  2. What is scan resistance, and how do PostgreSQL and Redis deal with it? Expected: LRU evicts the hot set during a scan; PostgreSQL uses a buffer ring for large sequential scans and usage counts; Redis LFU or application-level bypass.
  3. How does Redis implement LRU, and why is it approximate? Expected: sampling maxmemory-samples keys with a per-key 24-bit clock; avoids a global list.
  4. Your database load doubled but nothing was deployed. Where do you look first? Expected: cache hit rate; find the traffic class or job that changed access patterns.
  5. Design cache invalidation for product edits across 12 pods and Redis. Expected: event on update, delete locally and in Redis, short TTL as the safety net, versioned keys for schema changes.
  6. Why cache a 404? Expected: negative caching stops repeated misses; short TTL to limit staleness after creation; combine with a Bloom filter.

Practical exercise

Build ProductCacheModule with LruCache, single-flight loading, negative caching and pub/sub invalidation. Acceptance criteria: 100 concurrent misses for one key produce exactly one database query (assert with a query counter); a product update is invisible on both pods of a two-instance integration test within 200 ms; a simulated export of 1 million ids with bypass: true leaves the hit rate for concurrent interactive reads above 85 percent (compare with the same run without bypass, which must drop below 20 percent, proving the mechanism); memory per pod stays under 40 MB with max = 10,000 and values up to 4 KB (reject larger values at set); and GET /internal/cache/stats reports size, hit rate, evictions and the age of the oldest entry.

7.18 Choosing the right structure

Sixteen structures is a lot to hold in your head during a design review. This section compresses them into three tables you can use at the whiteboard: what each structure is for and what replaces it when a single process is no longer enough; the complexity numbers side by side; and the production symptoms that point back at a data-structure mistake.

7.18.1 Structure, use, anti-use, and what replaces it at scale

"At scale" here means one or more of: the data must survive a restart, must be shared between pods, or no longer fits in one process. The right-hand column names the durable, shared version of the same idea.

Structure Typical backend use When NOT to use it What replaces it at scale
Array result pages, batches, ring buffers of samples, bulk-insert chunks as a queue (shift), for membership tests (includes), when the database controls its size keyset-paginated queries, streams, Kafka partitions (an append-only array on disk)
String / Buffer keys, JSON, SQL text, log lines, response bodies building large bodies with += or join; storing substrings of large payloads streamed responses, cached serialized Buffers, object storage for blobs
Linked list LRU recency order, in-flight registries, stream chunk buffers, idle-connection lists indexed access, search by value, small n (arrays win), ordering rows in SQL by next_id Redis lists, position columns with a unique index
Stack recursion made iterative, savepoints, undo, DFS, interceptor unwinding anything FIFO; deep recursion over user-controlled data PostgreSQL savepoints, explicit stacks in the heap
Queue decoupling producers from consumers, batching, job systems in-process for work that must not be lost; unbounded buffers BullMQ on Redis, RabbitMQ, Kafka, PostgreSQL SKIP LOCKED tables
Deque sliding windows, recent-N buffers, rate-limit logs, front-of-line retries touching the middle; per-key deques with unbounded keys Redis lists with LTRIM, sorted sets for sliding windows
Hash map lookup by id, sessions, feature flags, routing, in-memory joins, single-flight keys controlled by outsiders without a bound; plain objects as dictionaries; cluster-wide truth Redis hashes and keys, PostgreSQL hash and B-tree indexes
Set de-duplication, membership, roles, visited sets uniqueness across pods or time; objects by value unique indexes with ON CONFLICT, Redis sets, SET NX, HyperLogLog for counts
Tree categories, org charts, threads, JSON, plan trees, module graphs loading whole user-sized trees; N+1 per node; nested sets on write-heavy data ltree with GiST, recursive CTEs with depth limits, closure tables
BST / ordered map range queries, next-slot lookups, ordered iteration in memory hand-written unbalanced trees; sorted input; shared ordered data PostgreSQL B-tree indexes, Redis sorted sets, sorted arrays with binary search
Heap top-k, k-way merge, timers, schedulers searching or iterating in order; durable schedules ORDER BY ... LIMIT with an index, Redis sorted sets, BullMQ delayed jobs
Priority queue dispatch by deadline, retry by importance, SLA ordering one shared queue with no protection for low priorities; client-chosen priority per-class queues with reserved capacity, Redis ZPOPMIN, jobs tables with (priority, run_at)
Trie autocomplete, routing tables, longest-prefix match exact-match-only workloads; whole-name keys with no depth cap; subtree walks per request text_pattern_ops and pg_trgm indexes, RediSearch suggestions, Elasticsearch completion
Graph dependencies, workflows, social and service graphs, routing ORM relation loading for traversal; unbounded depth; supernodes without caps edge tables with both indexes, bounded recursive CTEs, precomputed neighbourhoods, graph databases
Bloom filter cache-penetration guard, "seen it" at huge scale, skipping storage segments exact answers, deletes, granting access on "probably" RedisBloom, PostgreSQL bloom index, HyperLogLog for counting

7.18.3 From production symptom to data structure

Most data-structure incidents announce themselves with one of a handful of graphs. Learn to read them backwards.

Symptom on the dashboard Likely structural cause First thing to check
CPU grows with data size while RPS is flat O(n) scan inside a loop (includes, find, indexOf, shift, sort per insert) profile with --cpu-prof; look for array methods in hot frames

False 404s for new rows stale Bloom filter or stale per-pod snapshot watermark on new ids; rebuild interval; pub/sub health
Low-priority work never completes starvation in a single priority queue per-class oldest-job age; reserved capacity or aging

Requests hang forever cycle in a linked structure or graph walked without a visited set CYCLE clause, visited sets, step budgets
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded recursion over user-controlled depth or a data cycle explicit stack, cycle guard, depth limit
RangeError: Invalid string length or OOM during export building a huge string or array instead of streaming stream with backpressure; keyset pagination

7.18.4 A decision path for the whiteboard

What is the dominant operation?
  |
  +-- "give me item i" or "append"           -> Array (bounded) / typed array
  +-- "is X present?" / "value for key X"    -> Hash map / Set
  |       +-- across pods or time?           -> unique index / Redis SET / SET NX
  |       +-- huge and approximate is fine?  -> Bloom filter (HyperLogLog for counts)
  +-- "oldest first"                         -> Queue (ring buffer) -> BullMQ / Kafka / SKIP LOCKED
  +-- "most recent first"                    -> Stack / Deque
  +-- "most urgent first"                    -> Heap / Priority queue -> Redis ZSET / (priority, run_at) index
  +-- "everything between A and B" / "next"  -> Sorted array / B-tree index / Redis ZSET
  +-- "everything starting with P"           -> Trie / text_pattern_ops index / RediSearch
  +-- "what is under / above this node"      -> Tree: ltree, recursive CTE, closure table
  +-- "how are these things connected"       -> Graph: edges table + both indexes, bounded traversal
  +-- "remember recent answers, bounded"     -> LRU cache -> Redis allkeys-lru
  +-- "unlink this exact item fast"          -> Doubly linked list (usually inside an LRU)

Then ask, for the chosen structure:
  Who controls n?           (code, user, database, upstream)
  Where does it live?       (request, process, Redis, PostgreSQL, Kafka)
  What bounds it?           (capacity, TTL, LIMIT, depth, degree, body size)
  Can it be wrong?          (stale, approximate, per-pod)  In which direction is wrong safe?
  How do I see it?          (size, age of oldest, hit rate, evictions, drops)

Senior Checklist — Part 7

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can state the best, average and worst-case cost of every operation I put on a request path, and I know who controls n
  • I can explain V8 elements kinds, hidden classes and dictionary mode, and I keep records as objects and dictionaries as Maps
  • I measure strings in the right unit (bytes, code units, code points) and I stream anything whose size the user or the database controls
  • I can implement a ring-buffer queue, a deque, a binary heap, a trie with per-node top-k, a Bloom filter and an LRU cache from memory, with tests
  • I never use shift, unshift, includes, indexOf, splice or sort inside a hot loop without checking n
  • I bound every in-process collection keyed by external data with a capacity, a TTL or a sweep, and I export its size and hit rate as metrics
  • I can read top-N heapsort, Hash Join ... Batches, HashAggregate, Bitmap Heap Scan ... Recheck and Index Scan ... Buffers in EXPLAIN output and name the data structure behind each
  • I know why PostgreSQL indexes are B-trees and can find an index's height with bt_metap
  • I can pick the right durable replacement (unique index, SKIP LOCKED table, Redis list, set, sorted set, RedisBloom, BullMQ, Kafka) and explain what changes when I do
  • I recognise scan pollution, cache stampedes, starvation, supernodes, N+1 recursion and stale probabilistic filters from their dashboard symptoms
  • I design probabilistic structures so they can only be wrong in the safe direction, and I write down what a wrong answer costs
  • I refuse per-pod Sets and Maps as cluster-wide truth for anything involving money, uniqueness or rate limits

Part 7 — Key Takeaways

  • Data-structure mistakes are silent until n gets large, and n gets large in production, at night; always ask who controls n.
  • In Node.js every O(n) on the request path is paid by every concurrent request on one thread; a 30 ms scan at 500 RPS is fifteen cores you do not have.
  • Arrays are for bounded, indexed, appended data; membership belongs to a Set, ordering to a heap or a B-tree, and "remove from the front" to a real queue.
  • Strings are UTF-16 code units in memory and UTF-8 bytes on the wire; measure in the unit the constraint uses, and stream anything large.
  • A linked list earns its 48 bytes per node only when you hold node handles and need O(1) unlink; inside an LRU, yes; as a list you search, no.
  • Every queue needs an overflow policy, an idempotent consumer and an alert on the age of its oldest item; every priority queue also needs protection for its lowest class.
  • Use objects for records with a fixed shape and Map for dictionaries; bound every map keyed by outside data or it becomes a memory leak with a delay measured in days.
  • Uniqueness across pods and time is a unique index or a Redis atomic operation, never an in-process Set.
  • Databases use B-trees because page-sized nodes give height 3 or 4 for hundreds of millions of keys; in memory, a sorted array plus binary search usually beats a hand-written tree.
  • Top-k is a heap of size k, merging sorted sources is a k-way heap merge, and ORDER BY ... LIMIT is PostgreSQL doing exactly that; give it an index so it can stop early.
  • Prefix questions belong to tries and sorted indexes; cache the answer at the node and never walk a subtree per request.
  • Graph traversal cost is the product of degrees along the path; bound depth, cap degree, precompute for supernodes, and validate DAGs for cycles at definition time.
  • A Bloom filter is fifty times smaller than a set and wrong only in one direction; design so that direction is the safe one, and remember that staleness is the false negative you actually get.
  • An LRU cache is a hash map plus a linked list, and a cache is a promise about staleness and memory: write both numbers down, graph the hit rate, and keep bulk scans out of it.
  • The simplest structure that meets the requirement wins, and the durable version (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka) wins the moment data must survive a restart or be shared between pods.

Part 8 — Algorithms for Backend Engineers

Most backend engineers meet algorithms twice: once in an interview, and then again at 02:00 when an endpoint that "worked fine in staging" takes 40 seconds in production. This part is about the second meeting.

You will rarely implement a red-black tree in a NestJS service. But every day you make algorithmic decisions without naming them: you call array.includes inside a map, you write a query that the planner turns into a nested loop, you build a 1-million-element array in a request handler, you sort in the application because "the DB was slow". Each of these is an algorithm choice with a cost curve, and a senior engineer sees the curve before the incident does.

The algorithms in this part are chosen because they show up in real backend systems: in the PostgreSQL query planner, in Redis eviction, in Node's Array.prototype.sort, in rate limiters, job schedulers, dependency graphs, delivery routing and fuzzy search. For each one we explain the mechanism, then show exactly where you will meet it in a NestJS + PostgreSQL + Redis stack.

8.1 Big O — what it measures and what it hides

Concept

Big O notation describes how the cost of an operation grows as the input grows. "Cost" is usually time (number of steps) or space (memory). O(n) means "the work grows in proportion to the input size". O(1) means "the work does not depend on the input size". O(n²) means "double the input, quadruple the work".

Big O is not a stopwatch. It says nothing about how long one step takes. It only tells you the shape of the growth curve. That is its power and its trap.

Why does it exist?

Without a growth model, you can only learn about performance by running the code at every input size, which nobody does. Big O lets you reason about an endpoint at 10,000 users when you have only tested it with 50. It answers the question every senior engineer asks in review: "What happens to this when the table is 100 times bigger?"

What breaks without it: code that is fast on the developer's laptop with 20 seed rows becomes an outage at 2 million rows, and nobody can explain why because "we didn't change anything". The data changed. The algorithm's growth curve did the rest.

Mental model

Imagine a warehouse picker fulfilling an order. If every product has a fixed shelf address printed on the pick list, the picker walks straight there: the time per item is constant, O(1), no matter how big the warehouse is. If the pick list only says "a blue kettle", the picker walks every aisle until they find it: O(n) in the number of shelves. If for every item on the list they have to walk every aisle, and the list has n items in a warehouse of n shelves, that is O(n²).

Now the trap: a picker with a perfect shelf address (O(1)) who has to drive to a different warehouse across the city for every item is much slower than a picker who checks ten shelves by hand (O(n), n=10) in the room they are already standing in. Big O told you the first picker had the better algorithm. Reality told you the second picker finished first. The difference is the constant: the drive.

How it works

Big O is derived by counting the steps an operation performs as a function of input size n, then simplifying:

  1. Count the operations in terms of n. A loop over n orders is n steps; a nested loop over n orders and m products is n * m.
  2. Drop constants. 3n + 20 becomes O(n). A loop that does five things per item is still O(n).
  3. Keep only the dominant term. n² + n log n + n becomes O(n²), because for large n the square dwarfs everything else.
  4. Say which case you mean. Worst case is the default. Average case matters for hash tables (O(1) average, O(n) worst when everything collides). Amortized cost matters for dynamic arrays (push is O(1) amortized because the occasional resize copies everything, but rarely).

Here is that reasoning applied to an order-total handler:

// orders/pricing.service.ts
export class PricingService {
  // n = number of lines in the order, p = number of products in the catalog
  computeTotal(lines: OrderLine[], catalog: Product[]): number {
    let total = 0;
    for (const line of lines) {                                   // n iterations
      const product = catalog.find((p) => p.id === line.productId); // O(p) each
      if (!product) throw new ProductNotFoundError(line.productId);
      total += product.priceCents * line.quantity;                 // O(1)
    }
    return total;                                                  // total: O(n * p)
  }

  // Same result, O(n + p): build the index once, then every lookup is O(1)
  computeTotalIndexed(lines: OrderLine[], catalog: Product[]): number {
    const byId = new Map(catalog.map((p) => [p.id, p]));          // O(p)
    let total = 0;
    for (const line of lines) {                                   // O(n)
      const product = byId.get(line.productId);                   // O(1) average
      if (!product) throw new ProductNotFoundError(line.productId);
      total += product.priceCents * line.quantity;
    }
    return total;
  }
}

With 50 lines and a 20,000-product catalog, the first version does about one million comparisons per order; the second does about 20,050 operations. Same output, fifty times less work, and the difference grows as the catalog grows.

Now the part Big O hides. Every "step" above is assumed to cost the same. In a real backend the steps are wildly different:

Operation Typical latency Relative to L1 cache hit
L1 cache reference ~1 ns 1x
Main memory reference ~100 ns 100x
Compare two integers in a JS loop ~1–5 ns ~3x
Map.get on a small map ~20–50 ns ~30x
SSD random read (4 KB) ~20–100 µs ~50,000x
Redis GET, same availability zone ~0.2–1 ms ~500,000x
PostgreSQL indexed query, same AZ ~1–5 ms ~2,000,000x
HTTP call to another service, same region ~2–20 ms ~10,000,000x
Cross-region HTTP call ~80–150 ms ~100,000,000x

This is why "an O(1) Redis call is slower than an O(n) scan over a 10-element array" is not a joke but an engineering fact. Scanning 10 elements in memory costs about 20–50 nanoseconds. One Redis round trip costs about 300,000 nanoseconds. The array scan is roughly ten thousand times faster, even though its Big O is worse.

Big O hides four things you must add back by hand:

  • Constants. O(1) with a 1 ms constant loses to O(n) with a 2 ns constant until n is around 500,000.
  • Cache locality. A contiguous array of numbers is read sequentially and the CPU prefetches it; a linked list or an array of heap-allocated objects chases pointers and misses cache. Two O(n) loops can differ by 10x for this reason alone.
  • I/O versus CPU. A Node request handler that does 20 CPU operations and 3 database queries is dominated by the queries. The CPU part could be O(n²) and you would not notice until n is in the thousands. The I/O part could be O(1) per item and it will kill you at n = 200.
  • The runtime. V8 JIT-compiles hot loops, but it also deoptimizes when object shapes change, and garbage collection pauses happen when you allocate heavily. A "linear" loop that allocates a new object per iteration can stall for tens of milliseconds in a major GC.
flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|"~50 ms network"| G["API Gateway"]
    G -->|"~0.5 ms"| N["NestJS handler"]
    N -->|"~0.3 ms round trip"| R["Redis GET"]
    N -->|"~2 ms indexed query"| P["PostgreSQL"]
    N -->|"~0.02 ms"| J["JS loop over 1000 items"]

The diagram is the whole lesson: inside one request, the in-process loop over a thousand items is the cheapest box on the page. The network hops are where the time goes.

Practical example

A checkout service must apply tax rules per order line. A developer stores tax rules in Redis, keyed by tax:{countryCode}:{categoryId}, and looks up the rule for every line:

// O(n) Redis round trips: each is "O(1)" and each costs ~0.3 ms
async applyTax(order: Order): Promise<number> {
  let tax = 0;
  for (const line of order.lines) {
    const raw = await this.redis.get(`tax:${order.country}:${line.categoryId}`);
    const rule = raw ? (JSON.parse(raw) as TaxRule) : DEFAULT_RULE;
    tax += Math.round(line.totalCents * rule.rate);
  }
  return tax;
}

For a 40-line B2B order that is 40 sequential round trips: roughly 12 ms of pure waiting, on every checkout. The fix is not a better data structure; it is fewer network hops. Fetch all rules for the country once with a single MGET (or cache the whole country's rule set in process memory for 60 seconds), then do the per-line work in a local Map. The per-line lookup is still O(1), but the constant dropped from 300 µs to 30 ns.

NestJS example

A small in-process cache in a provider keeps the hot path off the network. This is a normal pattern for reference data that changes rarely (tax rules, feature flags, currency rates):

// tax/tax-rules.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRedis } from '@nestjs-modules/ioredis';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

interface TaxRule { rate: number; }

@Injectable()
export class TaxRulesService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(TaxRulesService.name);
  // country -> (categoryId -> rule), refreshed at most every 60 s
  private cache = new Map<string, { loadedAt: number; rules: Map<string, TaxRule> }>();
  private readonly ttlMs = 60_000;

  constructor(@InjectRedis() private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async rulesFor(country: string): Promise<Map<string, TaxRule>> {
    const hit = this.cache.get(country);
    if (hit && Date.now() - hit.loadedAt < this.ttlMs) return hit.rules; // ~30 ns

    // One round trip for the whole country instead of one per order line
    const raw = await this.redis.hgetall(`tax:${country}`);           // ~0.3 ms
    const rules = new Map<string, TaxRule>();
    for (const [categoryId, json] of Object.entries(raw)) {
      rules.set(categoryId, JSON.parse(json) as TaxRule);
    }
    this.cache.set(country, { loadedAt: Date.now(), rules });
    this.logger.debug(`tax rules for ${country} refreshed: ${rules.size} entries`);
    return rules;
  }
}

The ioredis injection decorator comes from the community @nestjs-modules/ioredis package; if you wire Redis yourself, inject the client through a custom provider token instead. The important part is the shape: one I/O operation per country per minute, then pure memory.

PostgreSQL example

The PostgreSQL planner is a Big O calculator with constants filled in. It estimates the cost of each plan using tunable unit costs, then picks the cheapest:

SHOW seq_page_cost;    -- 1.0   cost to read one 8 KB page sequentially
SHOW random_page_cost; -- 4.0   cost to read one page randomly (set ~1.1 on SSD)
SHOW cpu_tuple_cost;   -- 0.01  cost to process one row
SHOW cpu_index_tuple_cost; -- 0.005

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4821;
Index Scan using orders_customer_id_idx on orders  (cost=0.43..37.12 rows=9 width=112)
  Index Cond: (customer_id = 4821)

The cost=0.43..37.12 is the planner's estimate in abstract units: 0.43 to return the first row, 48.12 to return all of them. Compare it with the same query on a tiny table:

Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..1.06 rows=1 width=112)
  Filter: (customer_id = 4821)

The planner chose the O(n) sequential scan over the O(log n) index scan, because with five rows on one page the "worse" algorithm has a smaller constant. That is Big O with the constants put back, computed for you on every query. When random_page_cost is left at the HDD default of 4.0 on an SSD box, the planner overestimates index cost and picks sequential scans too often. Tuning that one constant changes plans across the whole database.

Production scenario

An order-history endpoint serves 400 requests per second at p50 of 18 ms. A profile of one request shows: 0.4 ms in the NestJS pipeline (guards, pipes, serialization), 2.1 ms in one PostgreSQL query returning 50 rows, 0.6 ms in two Redis calls, 0.1 ms in application code that maps and sorts the 50 rows, and the remainder waiting on the network to the client. The application code is O(n log n) because of the sort, and it is the smallest number on the page.

A product manager asks for "order history with the product name on each line". A developer adds a productRepository.findOne inside the map. Same O(n) shape as before, but each step now carries a 2 ms constant. The endpoint goes from 18 ms to 120 ms and the database connection pool saturates at 400 RPS. Nothing about the Big O of the code changed. The constant did.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call gets paged: checkout p99 has crossed 8 seconds and the Redis connection pool is exhausted. The last deploy added "per-line loyalty multiplier lookup". The multiplier lives in Redis. It is a single GET, "O(1), can't be the problem", the author says in the incident channel.

The problem is a B2B customer with an order of 2,300 lines. 2,300 sequential GETs at 0.4 ms is 0.9 seconds of waiting per checkout attempt; the customer's client retries on a 5-second timeout, so three concurrent attempts hold three connections each for a second, while every other request queues behind them. The fix that ships at 02:50 is a single MGET of all keys for the order, which takes 1.2 ms. The post-mortem action item: "any per-item I/O inside a loop requires a comment explaining why batching is impossible".

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Small n hides everything. With n = 20, an O(n²) loop finishes in microseconds. It will show up when the data grows, not in code review by measurement, only by reasoning.
  • Large constants hide in "O(1)". Any await inside a loop is a network round trip per iteration. The Big O is honest; the wall clock is not.
  • Amortized costs bunch up. A Map or array that resizes copies everything at the resize. In a hot path that builds and discards large structures, those copies become GC pressure.
  • Average versus worst case. A hash map degrades to O(n) when many keys collide. Attackers used to exploit this (hash-flooding); V8 randomizes hash seeds, but a home-made hash function in your code might not.
  • Cache locality reverses rankings. Iterating an array of 1,000 numbers beats iterating a Set of 1,000 numbers, even though both are O(n), because the array is one contiguous block.
  • The planner's constants are wrong. Stale statistics or default random_page_cost on SSDs lead PostgreSQL to pick the wrong algorithm for your data.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior engineer uses Big O as a first filter and constants as the second. The questions, in order:

  1. What is n here, and how big can it get? Not today: in two years, or for the biggest customer.
  2. Is the cost per step nanoseconds (memory), microseconds (disk), or milliseconds (network)? A single network hop inside a loop is a red flag regardless of Big O.
  3. Where does the endpoint spend its time now? Measure before optimizing. A 10x improvement in a part that is 1% of the latency is invisible.
  4. Is the growth curve acceptable for the worst realistic input, or only for the average one?

What they refuse to do: optimize an in-memory loop from O(n log n) to O(n) in a handler that spends 95% of its time waiting on the database. What they insist on: no I/O inside loops without a written justification.

Explained to a product manager: "The feature is fine for a normal order. For your biggest customer, the same feature makes 2,000 trips to a server instead of one. We need to make it one trip before we ship it."

Common mistakes

  • Treating O(1) as "fast" and O(n) as "slow" without asking what one step costs.
  • Optimizing CPU-bound code in an I/O-bound endpoint.
  • Believing the developer laptop with 20 rows. Complexity problems are invisible at small n by definition.
  • Assuming Array.prototype.includes, indexOf and find are cheap. They are O(n) scans, and inside another loop they are O(n²).
  • Ignoring memory allocation. An algorithm with a good time complexity that allocates a new object per iteration can be slower than a "worse" algorithm that allocates nothing, because of GC.

Interview questions

  1. "Why can an O(1) operation be slower than an O(n) one?" Expected: Big O drops constants; an O(1) network call costs about a million times more than an O(1) memory read, so for small n the memory scan wins. Why it matters: shows the candidate reasons about real latency, not notation. Follow-up: at what n does the ranking flip for a 0.3 ms Redis call versus a 3 ns comparison? (Around 100,000.)
  2. "What does the PostgreSQL planner's cost number represent, and why might it choose a sequential scan when an index exists?" Expected: an abstract estimate built from page and tuple costs; on small tables or low-selectivity predicates the sequential scan has a lower total cost. Follow-up: what setting would you tune on SSD storage?
  3. "Explain amortized complexity with a backend example." Expected: dynamic array push is O(1) amortized because resizes are rare; a Redis hash that rehashes incrementally spreads the cost. Follow-up: when does amortized cost bite you? (Latency-sensitive paths where one request pays for the resize.)
  4. "A handler is O(n) in the number of order lines and still takes 3 seconds for 2,000 lines. What do you look for?" Expected: an await per iteration, so the constant is a network round trip. Fix by batching (MGET, WHERE id = ANY($1)).
  5. "How does cache locality affect two algorithms with the same Big O?" Expected: contiguous memory is prefetched by the CPU; pointer chasing misses cache; can be a 5–10x difference.
  6. "Worst case, average case, amortized: give one backend example of each mattering." Expected: hash collisions (worst), hash lookup (average), array growth or Redis rehash (amortized).

Practical exercise

Take an existing endpoint in your codebase that loops over a collection. Instrument it with performance.now() at three points: before the loop, after the loop, and around any await inside it. Run it with 10, 100 and 1,000 items. Produce a small table of wall time versus n.

Acceptance criteria:

  • You can state the Big O of the loop body and of the whole handler.
  • You can say what fraction of the time is I/O versus CPU at each n.
  • If there is an await inside the loop, you have rewritten it as a single batched call and measured the difference.

8.2 Time complexity

Concept

Time complexity is Big O applied to running time: how many elementary steps an algorithm performs as a function of input size. The common classes, from cheapest to most expensive, are constant O(1), logarithmic O(log n), linear O(n), linearithmic O(n log n), quadratic O(n²), cubic O(n³) and exponential O(2ⁿ).

Knowing the class tells you which inputs are safe. Backend inputs have predictable shapes: request payloads (tens to thousands of items), query results (tens to millions of rows), and tables (millions to billions of rows). Matching the class to the input shape is the whole skill.

Why does it exist?

Because "it works" is not a property of code; it is a property of code at a particular input size. Time complexity lets you predict the input size at which "works" turns into "times out". The load balancer's 30-second timeout, the Kubernetes liveness probe and the customer's patience are all fixed numbers. Your algorithm's cost is a curve. Where the curve crosses the fixed number is where the incident starts.

Mental model

Imagine a queue at a passport office. O(1) is a self-service kiosk: every person takes the same time regardless of how many are in the building. O(log n) is a receptionist who splits the queue in half at each question ("surname A–M or N–Z?"): even a million people are sorted into the right room after twenty questions. O(n) is one clerk handling each person in turn. O(n log n) is sorting everyone by appointment time before serving them. O(n²) is every person having to shake hands with every other person before anyone is served. At ten people it is a friendly morning. At a thousand people, nobody leaves the building today.

How it works

The classes become concrete when you attach numbers to them. Assume a JavaScript loop body performs roughly 100 million simple operations per second (V8 can do more for tight numeric loops, less for object-heavy ones; 10⁸ is a safe planning figure).

Class n = 1,000 n = 1,000,000 n = 1,000,000,000 What it means in a backend
O(1) 1 op, ~10 ns 1 op 1 op Hash lookup, array index, Redis GET, primary-key fetch (plus the constant)
O(log n) ~10 ops ~20 ops ~30 ops B-tree index descent, binary search, heap push/pop
O(n) 1k ops, ~10 µs 1M ops, ~10 ms 1B ops, ~10 s Sequential scan, one pass over a result set, Array.map
O(n log n) 10k ops, ~100 µs 20M ops, ~200 ms 30B ops, ~5 min Sorting, merge join with unsorted inputs, building an index
O(n²) 1M ops, ~10 ms 10¹² ops, ~3 hours 10¹⁸ ops, ~300 years Nested loops, includes inside map, nested-loop join without index
O(2ⁿ) 10³⁰¹ ops never never Brute-force subset search; only survivable for n under ~25

Three things to read off this table:

  1. O(n) at a billion rows takes seconds even in a tight loop, and you cannot hold a billion rows in Node memory anyway. Anything linear over a whole table belongs in the database or in a batch job, never in a request handler.
  2. O(n²) is fine at a thousand and fatal at a million. The transition happens around n = 10,000–50,000, which is exactly the size where "a large customer's export" lives.
  3. O(log n) barely moves. Thirty steps for a billion rows is why a B-tree index makes a billion-row table feel like a thousand-row table.

The rules for combining complexities in code:

  • Sequential blocks add: an O(n) loop followed by an O(n log n) sort is O(n log n).
  • Nested blocks multiply: an O(m) search inside an O(n) loop is O(n * m).
  • Independent variables stay separate: O(n + m) is not O(n). If n is order lines and m is catalog size, say both.
  • Recursion multiplies depth by work per level: a balanced tree traversal is O(n); a naive recursive Fibonacci is O(2ⁿ) because each call spawns two.

Practical example

A warehouse service receives a shipment manifest of n SKUs and must find which ones are already in stock (an m-row inventory list returned from the database). Two implementations:

// O(n * m): with n = 5,000 SKUs and m = 200,000 inventory rows this is 10^9 comparisons
function findKnownSkusSlow(manifest: string[], inventory: InventoryRow[]): string[] {
  return manifest.filter((sku) => inventory.some((row) => row.sku === sku));
}

// O(n + m): build the set once, then each check is O(1)
function findKnownSkus(manifest: string[], inventory: InventoryRow[]): string[] {
  const known = new Set(inventory.map((row) => row.sku)); // O(m)
  return manifest.filter((sku) => known.has(sku));        // O(n)
}

The first version takes roughly ten seconds. The second takes about two milliseconds. The developer who wrote the first one tested it with a manifest of 12 rows.

The senior fix goes one step further: do not load 200,000 rows into Node at all. Send the manifest to the database and let the index do the work:

SELECT sku FROM inventory WHERE sku = ANY($1::text[]);
-- $1 = the 5,000-element manifest; index on inventory(sku) makes this O(n log m)

NestJS example

Complexity mistakes hide in places that do not look like algorithms. This validation pipe checks that every product in a bulk-update request exists, and is quietly O(n) in database round trips:

// products/pipes/products-exist.pipe.ts
import { Injectable, PipeTransform, BadRequestException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { In, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Product } from '../product.entity';
import { BulkUpdateDto } from '../dto/bulk-update.dto';

@Injectable()
export class ProductsExistPipe implements PipeTransform<BulkUpdateDto> {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Product) private readonly products: Repository<Product>) {}

  async transform(dto: BulkUpdateDto): Promise<BulkUpdateDto> {
    const ids = [...new Set(dto.items.map((i) => i.productId))]; // dedupe, O(n)

    // One query, O(n log m) inside PostgreSQL, instead of n queries of ~2 ms each
    const found = await this.products.find({ select: { id: true }, where: { id: In(ids) } });
    const foundIds = new Set(found.map((p) => p.id));           // O(n)

    const missing = ids.filter((id) => !foundIds.has(id));      // O(n)
    if (missing.length > 0) {
      throw new BadRequestException(`Unknown product ids: ${missing.slice(0, 10).join(', ')}`);
    }
    return dto;
  }
}

Cap the size of dto.items with @ArrayMaxSize(1000) from class-validator on the DTO. A complexity analysis that assumes unbounded n is a denial-of-service analysis.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL chooses between join algorithms with different time complexities, and EXPLAIN shows you which one it picked:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT o.id, c.email
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.created_at > now() - interval '1 day';
Hash Join  (cost=2891.00..14210.55 rows=48120 width=40) (actual time=9.812..61.334 rows=47955 loops=1)
  Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)
  Buffers: shared hit=3120
  ->  Index Scan using orders_created_at_idx on orders o  (cost=0.43..9860.10 rows=48120 width=16) (actual time=0.031..31.902 rows=47955 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (created_at > (now() - '1 day'::interval))
  ->  Hash  (cost=1650.00..1650.00 rows=99280 width=32) (actual time=9.701..9.702 rows=99280 loops=1)
        Buckets: 131072  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 7237kB
        ->  Seq Scan on customers c  (cost=0.00..1650.00 rows=99280 width=32) (actual time=0.008..4.120 rows=99280 loops=1)
Planning Time: 0.301 ms
Execution Time: 63.870 ms

The three join strategies and their complexity, with n outer rows and m inner rows:

Join Complexity When the planner picks it
Nested Loop O(n * m) without index; O(n log m) with an index on the inner side Small outer set, indexed inner side
Hash Join O(n + m) plus memory for the hash table Medium or large sets, equality condition, hash fits in work_mem
Merge Join O(n + m) if both sides are already sorted, else plus sort cost Both inputs sorted (often by an index), range or equality conditions

When you see Nested Loop with loops=48000 and a Seq Scan on the inner side, you are looking at O(n * m) inside the database. The usual cure is an index on the inner join column, which turns each inner probe into O(log m).

Production scenario

A reporting endpoint aggregates daily revenue per merchant. At launch there are 300 merchants and 20,000 orders per day; the handler loads all orders, then for each merchant filters the orders array. That is O(merchants * orders) = 6 million comparisons, about 60 ms. Acceptable.

Eighteen months later there are 4,000 merchants and 900,000 orders per day. The same code does 3.6 billion comparisons: roughly 40 seconds, well past the 30-second gateway timeout. The dashboard shows a 504 every morning. The fix is a GROUP BY merchant_id in SQL with an index on (created_at, merchant_id): about 400 ms for the day's rows, and a materialized daily rollup brings it to 5 ms.

Failure scenario

At 09:03 on a Monday, the operations team reports the fulfilment dashboard "spinning". The on-call engineer sees the pod CPU pinned at 100% and the event loop lag metric at 9 seconds. The Node process is not waiting on anything; it is computing. A CPU profile via --cpu-prof shows 98% of time in Array.prototype.indexOf called from mergeShipments. Over the weekend a new integration started sending manifests with 80,000 lines instead of 800. The indexOf inside a loop that was O(n²) at 800 (640,000 operations, invisible) is now 6.4 billion operations. Because Node is single-threaded, every other request on that pod waits behind it: an O(n²) in one endpoint became an outage for all of them.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Two variables, one name. Calling both the manifest size and the inventory size "n" hides that O(n * m) can be far worse than O(n²) when m is a whole table.
  • Hidden linear operations. array.includes, array.indexOf, array.find, Object.keys(obj).length, spreading into a new array ([...arr, item]) inside a loop, string.concat in a loop building a large string: all linear per call.
  • Sorting by accident. Calling .sort() inside a loop to get "the latest" item turns O(n) into O(n² log n).
  • Event loop monopoly. A CPU-bound O(n²) in one request blocks every request on the process. Node has no preemption.
  • Complexity in the database. A missing index on a join column is an O(n * m) nested loop that you never wrote in TypeScript.
  • Regex backtracking. A catastrophic regex like (a+)+$ is O(2ⁿ) on adversarial input (ReDoS). Validation regexes on user input need bounded patterns.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior question is not "what is the complexity?" but "what is the complexity in terms of the thing that grows?" Order lines grow with customer size. Orders grow with time. Tables grow forever. Any algorithm that is linear or worse in "rows in a table" must live in the database, behind an index, or in an offline job with a bounded window.

The second question: "where is the ceiling?" Every input needs a cap enforced at the boundary (DTO array size, pagination limit, upload size), because an algorithm that is safe at the cap is safe everywhere.

What a senior refuses to do: ship a handler whose cost grows with a whole table, no matter how small the table is today.

Common mistakes

  • Loading a table into Node to filter it in JavaScript. The database has the index; use it.
  • Nested find, filter, includes on two lists that both come from the database.
  • Believing O(n log n) is "basically linear". At a billion rows it is 30x more work; sorting a billion rows is a different engineering problem from scanning them.
  • Forgetting that O(n) over the request payload becomes O(n * RPS) per second on the server. A 10 ms loop at 500 RPS is 5 CPU-seconds per second: five cores, just for that loop.
  • Ignoring exponential regexes in validation.

Interview questions

  1. "At what n does O(n²) become a production problem in Node, and why is that number what it is?" Expected: around 10⁴–10⁵ items, because 10⁸–10¹⁰ operations is 1–100 seconds on one core, and Node is single-threaded so it blocks the whole process. Follow-up: how would you find it in production? (Event loop lag metric, CPU profile.)
  2. "Compare hash join, merge join and nested loop join in terms of complexity and when the planner picks each." See the table above. Follow-up: what does loops=48000 under a nested loop tell you?
  3. "A bulk endpoint is O(n) in database round trips. Rewrite it so it is O(1) round trips and explain the new complexity inside PostgreSQL." Expected: WHERE id = ANY($1) or IN, O(n log m) with an index.
