  4. "Why does a linear scan over a whole table never belong in a request handler even though O(n) is 'fine'?" Expected: n is unbounded and grows with time; latency and memory grow with it; the request path has a fixed timeout.
  5. "Give a case where O(n log n) in the app is the right choice over doing it in the DB." Expected: small n already in memory, or sorting by a computed value the DB cannot index, or offloading CPU from a saturated primary.

Practical exercise

Write a script that generates 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 fake order lines and runs both findKnownSkusSlow and findKnownSkus against an inventory list of the same size. Record the timings in a table. Then implement the SQL version against a local PostgreSQL with an index on sku and add its timing.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The quadratic version shows roughly 100x growth per 10x input; the linear version roughly 10x.
  • You can explain why the SQL version's cost is O(n log m) and where the constant comes from (network + planning + index descents).
  • You add an @ArrayMaxSize cap to the DTO and justify the number.

8.3 Space complexity

Concept

Space complexity is how much memory an algorithm needs as a function of input size. O(1) space means a fixed number of variables regardless of input. O(n) space means memory proportional to the input: building a Set of all SKUs, materializing a query result as an array, buffering a file into memory.

In a backend, space complexity has a multiplier that interview problems do not: concurrency. A handler that uses 50 MB per request is not a 50 MB problem. At 40 concurrent requests it is a 2 GB problem, and the pod limit is 512 MB.

Why does it exist?

Memory is the resource that fails suddenly. CPU saturation makes things slow; memory exhaustion makes things die. In Node the death is a FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit crash; in Kubernetes it is OOMKilled and a restart loop. Before death there is a long illness: as the heap fills, V8 runs garbage collection more often and each major GC pauses the event loop for tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Space complexity is how you predict both the illness and the death.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant kitchen with one counter. A cook who prepares one plate at a time and sends it out uses a fixed amount of counter space no matter how many orders come in: O(1). A cook who insists on plating every dish for a 300-person banquet before sending any of them out needs 300 plates of counter space: O(n). Now imagine forty cooks sharing that one counter, each plating a banquet. That is a Node process with forty concurrent export requests, each building the full result in memory.

How it works

Node's memory, in the terms that matter for space complexity:

  1. The V8 heap holds JavaScript objects, arrays, strings and closures. It is split into a small "new space" for short-lived objects (collected very frequently by a fast scavenger) and an "old space" for objects that survived a few collections (collected by a slower mark-sweep-compact).
  2. The heap limit is finite. Older Node versions defaulted to roughly 1.5 GB of old space on 64-bit; current versions size it from available system memory, often 2–4 GB. Check it with node -e "console.log(v8.getHeapStatistics().heap_size_limit / 1048576)" and set it with --max-old-space-size=<MB>. In a container, the limit must be below the container's memory limit or the kernel kills the process before V8 can.
  3. Buffers and external memory (file contents, Buffer from network sockets, pg driver row buffers) live outside the V8 heap but inside the process's RSS and inside the container's limit.
  4. GC cost scales with live heap. A major GC has to walk everything alive. A process holding 1.5 GB of live objects pauses for hundreds of milliseconds per major GC, and during that pause no request makes progress.

Rough object sizes in V8 (64-bit with pointer compression, which is the default):

Value Approximate heap cost
Small integer in a packed array 4 bytes
Double in a packed double array 8 bytes
Short string (ASCII, ~10 chars) ~24–32 bytes
Empty object {} ~28–56 bytes
Object with 5 small properties ~60–100 bytes
Array of 1,000,000 small integers ~4 MB
Array of 1,000,000 objects with 5 fields ~80–150 MB
Array of 1,000,000 rows from pg with 10 columns incl. strings and dates ~250–500 MB

The last row is the one that matters. "Load all rows, then process" for a million-row table costs a quarter to half a gigabyte, plus the temporary copies made by map, filter and JSON.stringify (which creates a string as large as the output, so serializing 300 MB of objects can peak at 600 MB or more).

flowchart TB
    A["Request: export 1M orders"] --> B{"Materialize or stream?"}
    B -->|"repository.find all rows"| C["Heap grows by ~400 MB per request"]
    C --> D["Major GC pauses of 200 to 800 ms block every other request"]
    D --> E["3 concurrent exports exceed pod limit: OOMKilled"]
    B -->|"stream rows in batches of 1000"| F["Heap stays under ~5 MB per request"]
    F --> G["Client receives first bytes in ~20 ms"]

Practical example

An admin endpoint exports all orders for a merchant as CSV. The first implementation:

// O(n) space in the number of orders, for the whole duration of the request
async exportOrders(merchantId: string): Promise<string> {
  const orders = await this.orders.find({ where: { merchantId } }); // 1M rows -> ~400 MB heap
  const lines = orders.map((o) => `${o.id},${o.total},${o.createdAt.toISOString()}`); // another ~100 MB
  return lines.join('\n');                                            // another ~60 MB string
}

The peak heap for one request is around 560 MB. Two admins exporting at once and the pod is dead. The O(1)-space version streams rows from PostgreSQL in batches and writes each batch to the HTTP response as it arrives; memory stays flat at a few megabytes regardless of n.

NestJS example

Streaming a large result through NestJS with TypeORM's query-builder stream and a PassThrough:

// orders/orders-export.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Param, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Response } from 'express';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Transform } from 'node:stream';
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';

@Controller('merchants/:merchantId/orders')
export class OrdersExportController {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  @Get('export.csv')
  async exportCsv(@Param('merchantId') merchantId: string, @Res() res: Response): Promise<void> {
    res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/csv');
    res.setHeader('Content-Disposition', `attachment; filename="orders-${merchantId}.csv"`);
    res.write('id,total_cents,created_at\n');

    // Node stream over a PostgreSQL cursor: rows arrive in batches, memory stays flat
    const rowStream = await this.dataSource
      .createQueryBuilder()
      .select(['o.id AS id', 'o.total_cents AS total_cents', 'o.created_at AS created_at'])
      .from('orders', 'o')
      .where('o.merchant_id = :merchantId', { merchantId })
      .orderBy('o.created_at', 'ASC')
      .stream();

    const toCsv = new Transform({
      objectMode: true,
      transform(row: { id: string; total_cents: number; created_at: Date }, _enc, cb) {
        cb(null, `${row.id},${row.total_cents},${row.created_at.toISOString()}\n`);
      },
    });

    // pipeline handles backpressure: if the client reads slowly, PostgreSQL is paused too
    await pipeline(rowStream, toCsv, res);
  }
}

Backpressure is the key property. If the client downloads at 1 MB/s, pipeline stops pulling rows from the cursor until the response buffer drains. Without it, a fast database and a slow client fill your heap with unsent rows.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL applies the same discipline on its side. Each backend process gets work_mem (default 4 MB) per sort or hash operation; if the operation needs more, it spills to disk rather than growing without bound:

SET work_mem = '4MB';
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT customer_id, sum(total_cents) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;
HashAggregate  (cost=145210.00..146410.00 rows=98000 width=40) (actual time=812.4..1450.9 rows=98211 loops=1)
  Group Key: customer_id
  Batches: 5  Memory Usage: 4145kB  Disk Usage: 20480kB
  ->  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..120210.00 rows=5000000 width=12) (actual time=0.02..410.3 rows=5000000 loops=1)

Batches: 5 ... Disk Usage: 20480kB tells you the hash table did not fit in 4 MB and was processed in five passes with temporary files. Raising work_mem for that session to 64 MB turns it into Batches: 1 and roughly halves the time. But work_mem is per operation per connection: 200 connections each running a query with three hash operations at 64 MB can theoretically ask for 38 GB. That is space complexity at the database tier, multiplied by concurrency, exactly like the Node heap.

For consuming a large result without loading it into the client, PostgreSQL offers server-side cursors, which is what the TypeORM .stream() above uses underneath:

BEGIN;
DECLARE orders_cur CURSOR FOR SELECT id, total_cents FROM orders WHERE merchant_id = $1;
FETCH FORWARD 1000 FROM orders_cur;   -- repeat until empty
CLOSE orders_cur;
COMMIT;

TypeORM example

Beyond .stream(), the simpler pattern for batch jobs is keyset batching, which is O(batch) in memory and does not hold a transaction open for the whole run:

// jobs/reindex-products.job.ts
async reindexAll(): Promise<void> {
  const batchSize = 1000;
  let lastId = '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000';
  for (;;) {
    // Keyset pagination: O(log n) to find the start, O(batch) rows in memory
    const batch = await this.products
      .createQueryBuilder('p')
      .where('p.id > :lastId', { lastId })
      .orderBy('p.id', 'ASC')
      .take(batchSize)
      .getMany();
    if (batch.length === 0) break;
    await this.searchIndex.upsertMany(batch);
    lastId = batch[batch.length - 1].id;   // the batch is garbage-collectable after this
  }
}

Sequelize example

Sequelize has no built-in row streaming. Use the same keyset loop with Op.gt, or drop to the underlying pg client with pg-query-stream for true streaming:

import { Op } from 'sequelize';

async function forEachProduct(handle: (rows: Product[]) => Promise<void>): Promise<void> {
  let lastId = '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000';
  for (;;) {
    const rows = await Product.findAll({
      where: { id: { [Op.gt]: lastId } },
      order: [['id', 'ASC']],
      limit: 1000,
      raw: true,          // plain objects, roughly half the memory of model instances
    });
    if (rows.length === 0) break;
    await handle(rows);
    lastId = rows[rows.length - 1].id;
  }
}

raw: true matters for space: a Sequelize model instance carries change-tracking metadata and is noticeably heavier than a plain object.

Production scenario

An analytics pod runs with a Kubernetes memory limit of 512 MiB and --max-old-space-size=384. Its baseline heap is 90 MB. A "download report" endpoint materializes results; a typical report is 20,000 rows (~8 MB), fine. One enterprise tenant has 1.4 million rows. Their single request pushes the heap to 700 MB. V8 hits the 384 MB limit first and the process dies with FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory; Kubernetes restarts it; the tenant's browser retries; the pod dies again. Twenty other tenants see their dashboards fail every 40 seconds because of one tenant's report. The fix is streaming plus a hard cap: reports over 100,000 rows are generated asynchronously by a worker and delivered as a signed S3 link.

Failure scenario

At 11:20 the on-call sees p99 latency climbing across every endpoint on the orders service, with no errors. CPU is moderate. The GC metrics (exposed via prom-client's default collectors) show major GC pauses of 600–900 ms happening every few seconds. Heap used is at 1.3 GB and climbing slowly. A heap snapshot shows 900 MB of Order entities held in a Map on a singleton service: someone added an "in-memory cache of recent orders" without a size bound. The cache is O(n) in orders since restart. Memory does not fail suddenly here; it makes every request slow first, because each GC has to walk the ever-larger live set. The fix: an LRU with a maximum of 10,000 entries (see the cache eviction section later in this part).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Concurrency multiplies space. Per-request memory times concurrent requests must fit under the container limit, with headroom for GC.
  • Temporary copies. map, filter, spread, JSON.stringify and Buffer.concat all create full copies. Peak memory is often 2–3x the size of the data.
  • Unbounded caches. Any Map on a singleton provider that only ever grows is a memory leak with a business justification.
  • JSON.parse of large payloads. Parsing a 50 MB request body creates the string (50 MB), then the object graph (often 100–200 MB), synchronously, on the event loop.
  • External memory is invisible to the heap limit. Buffers and native driver memory push RSS past the container limit while heapUsed looks fine.
  • Slow consumers without backpressure. Reading from PostgreSQL faster than the client accepts data buffers the difference in your process.
  • Closures capturing large scopes. A callback stored for later (event listener, promise chain) keeps everything it references alive.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior rule: request handlers use O(1) memory in the size of the data. Bounded page sizes, streamed exports, batched jobs. The only things allowed to be O(n) in memory are explicitly sized caches and in-flight batches with a fixed batch size.

The questions before approving code that materializes a collection: What is the maximum size? Is that maximum enforced or assumed? How many of these can run concurrently? What is the container limit, and is --max-old-space-size set below it so V8 fails gracefully instead of the kernel killing the process mid-write?

To a product manager: "Downloading all 1.4 million rows in one click will crash the server for every other customer. We will generate the file in the background and email a link in about a minute."

Common mistakes

  • repository.find() with no take on a table that grows.
  • Building the full response, then res.json(), for anything larger than a page.
  • Adding an unbounded in-memory cache "for performance".
  • Setting --max-old-space-size equal to or above the container memory limit, so the kernel OOM-kills the process without a stack trace.
  • Loading a whole file upload into a Buffer before validating its size.
  • Using LIMIT/OFFSET batching for full-table jobs; each page re-scans from the start, so the job is O(n²/batch) in rows read.

Interview questions

  1. "A request handler loads a million rows and the pod gets OOMKilled. Walk me through why, with numbers, and the fix." Expected: ~300–500 MB per request for a million rows with copies, times concurrency, exceeds the limit; fix with streaming or async job plus caps. Follow-up: what does --max-old-space-size do and how should it relate to the container limit? (Below it, with ~25% headroom.)
  2. "Why does a growing heap make every endpoint slower before anything crashes?" Expected: major GC pauses scale with live heap and block the event loop.
  3. "Explain backpressure and why pipeline matters when streaming from PostgreSQL to an HTTP client." Expected: slow consumer would otherwise buffer unbounded rows in memory.
  4. "What is work_mem and why is it dangerous to set it high globally?" Expected: per operation, per connection; multiplied across concurrency.
  5. "Compare LIMIT/OFFSET and keyset batching for a full-table job in terms of both time and space." Expected: keyset is O(log n) per batch start; offset is O(offset) per batch, so quadratic overall; both are O(batch) in memory.
  6. "Where does Node memory live outside the V8 heap and why does it matter for containers?" Expected: Buffers, native driver allocations, count toward RSS and the cgroup limit but not toward heap_size_limit.

Practical exercise

Build an export endpoint two ways: materialized (find() then res.json()) and streamed (.stream() with pipeline). Seed a table with 500,000 rows. Run each version while watching process.memoryUsage().heapUsed sampled every 100 ms, and Node's --trace-gc output.

Acceptance criteria:

  • You have a chart or table of heap usage over time for both versions.
  • The streamed version stays under 30 MB of additional heap regardless of row count.
  • You can point to the GC pauses in the materialized run and explain their duration.
  • The endpoint enforces a maximum row count or a time window, and you can explain the number.

8.4 Searching: linear, binary and hash

Concept

Searching is finding the item you want inside a collection. There are only three fundamental strategies, and every search you will ever run in a backend is one of them, possibly in disguise:

  • Linear search looks at every item until it finds a match. O(n). Works on anything, needs no preparation.
  • Binary search works on a sorted collection: look at the middle, decide which half the target is in, repeat. O(log n). Needs sorted data.
  • Hash search computes a number from the key, uses it to jump straight to the bucket where the item lives. O(1) on average. Needs a hash table built in advance, and only supports exact-match lookups.

PostgreSQL uses the same three: a sequential scan is linear search, a B-tree index scan is (a disk-shaped) binary search, and hash joins and hash indexes are hash search.

Why does it exist?

Because a linear scan of a large collection is too slow to do per request. A 10-million-row orders table is about 1.5 GB on disk; scanning it takes seconds even from cache. The other two strategies exist to trade preparation (sorting, building a hash table, maintaining an index) for fast lookups. The whole discipline of database indexing is the question "which searches will we run often enough to pay for preparing them?"

Mental model

Imagine finding a name in a phone book. Linear search: start at page one and read every name. Binary search: open in the middle, see "M", you want "Patel", so ignore the first half; open the middle of the rest, repeat; you find any name in a million-name book in about twenty page flips. Hash search: a magic index card that says "Patel is on page 4,218" because someone precomputed a card for every name. The card is fastest, but it only works for the exact name; it cannot answer "everyone between Patel and Peterson". The sorted book can.

How it works

Linear search is a loop. In JavaScript: array.find, array.includes, array.indexOf, array.some. Cost is proportional to the position of the match (or the whole length if there is no match). Fine for tens of items; a problem inside other loops.

Binary search on a sorted array of n items:

  1. Set lo = 0, hi = n - 1.
  2. Compute mid = lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1) (avoids overflow and floating point).
  3. If array[mid] equals the target, done. If it is less than the target, set lo = mid + 1; otherwise hi = mid - 1.
  4. Repeat while lo <= hi. Each step halves the range: log2(n) steps. A million items: 20 steps. A billion: 30.

Hash search in JavaScript is Map and Set. V8 hashes the key (for strings, a cached hash of the characters; for objects, an identity hash), locates a bucket, and compares. Insert, lookup and delete are O(1) on average, with occasional rehashing when the table grows.

How this maps to PostgreSQL:

Your search PostgreSQL plan node Complexity When it is chosen
Linear Seq Scan O(n pages) No usable index, or the predicate matches a large fraction of rows, or the table is tiny
Binary Index Scan (B-tree) O(log n) descent + O(k) matches, each a random heap read Selective predicate on an indexed column
Binary, no heap visit Index Only Scan O(log n) + O(k) All requested columns are in the index and the visibility map says the pages are all-visible
Binary, many matches Bitmap Index Scan then Bitmap Heap Scan O(log n) + O(k) sorted by page Medium selectivity (roughly 1–20% of rows); reads heap pages in physical order
Hash Hash Join / Hash node O(n + m) Equality join between two sets; hash table built in work_mem
Hash Index Scan on a hash index O(1) average Equality only; rarely worth it over a B-tree 
flowchart TB
    Q["SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4821"] --> P{"Planner estimate"}
    P -->|"no usable index or predicate matches most rows"| S["Seq Scan: read every page in order"]
    P -->|"btree index and predicate is selective"| I["Index Scan: descend 3 to 4 pages then fetch matching heap pages"]
    P -->|"btree index and thousands of matches"| B["Bitmap Index Scan then Bitmap Heap Scan: collect page ids then read them in physical order"]

The planner's decision is driven by selectivity: what fraction of the table the predicate matches. Below roughly 1% of rows an index scan wins clearly; above roughly 20% the sequential scan usually wins, because reading the whole table sequentially is cheaper than thousands of random reads; in between, the bitmap scan is the compromise.

Practical example

A support tool looks up orders by external reference (the payment provider's transaction id). Without an index:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE external_ref = 'ch_3P8xk2LzQ4';
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..248901.00 rows=1 width=24) (actual time=1892.114..2410.552 rows=1 loops=1)
  Filter: (external_ref = 'ch_3P8xk2LzQ4'::text)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 9999999
  Buffers: shared hit=12000 read=111500
Execution Time: 2410.601 ms

Linear search over ten million rows: 2.4 seconds, 123,500 pages touched. With CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_external_ref_idx ON orders (external_ref);:

Index Scan using orders_external_ref_idx on orders  (cost=0.56..8.58 rows=1 width=24) (actual time=0.041..0.043 rows=1 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (external_ref = 'ch_3P8xk2LzQ4'::text)
  Buffers: shared hit=5
Execution Time: 0.071 ms

Five pages instead of 123,500. Thirty-four thousand times faster. That is the difference between O(n) and O(log n) at n = 10⁷, with the disk constant included.

NestJS example

Application-level searching is where hash lookups belong. Here a fulfilment service matches incoming carrier scan events (thousands per batch) to shipments loaded from the database, using a Map instead of repeated find:

// shipments/scan-matcher.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { In, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Shipment } from './shipment.entity';

interface ScanEvent { trackingNumber: string; status: string; at: Date; }

@Injectable()
export class ScanMatcherService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Shipment) private readonly shipments: Repository<Shipment>) {}

  async match(events: ScanEvent[]): Promise<Array<{ shipment: Shipment; event: ScanEvent }>> {
    const trackingNumbers = [...new Set(events.map((e) => e.trackingNumber))];

    // Binary search inside PostgreSQL: index on shipments(tracking_number), one round trip
    const found = await this.shipments.find({ where: { trackingNumber: In(trackingNumbers) } });

    // Hash search in memory: O(1) per event instead of O(shipments) with array.find
    const byTracking = new Map(found.map((s) => [s.trackingNumber, s]));

    const matched: Array<{ shipment: Shipment; event: ScanEvent }> = [];
    for (const event of events) {
      const shipment = byTracking.get(event.trackingNumber);
      if (shipment) matched.push({ shipment, event });
    }
    return matched;
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Choosing the index type is choosing the search algorithm. B-tree is the default and supports equality, ranges, prefix LIKE 'abc%' (with the right operator class or C collation) and ordering. Hash indexes support equality only and are slightly smaller and faster for that single case; since PostgreSQL 10 they are crash-safe, but B-tree is almost always the right choice because it also serves ORDER BY and range queries.

-- B-tree: equality, range, ordering, prefix
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_created_idx ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);

-- Serves all of these with an index scan:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4821;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4821 AND created_at > now() - interval '30 days';
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4821 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Hash: equality only; consider for very long keys looked up only by equality
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY sessions_token_hash_idx ON sessions USING hash (token);
SELECT user_id FROM sessions WHERE token = $1;

Check whether a query actually uses the index with EXPLAIN, and check whether an index is ever used with pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan. Unused indexes cost write throughput: every INSERT and UPDATE on an indexed column updates the index, an O(log n) write per index per row.

TypeORM example

Declare the index in the entity so it is part of the migration, and use findOne for point lookups so the query has a LIMIT 1:

// shipments/shipment.entity.ts
import { Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, Column, Index, CreateDateColumn } from 'typeorm';

@Entity('shipments')
@Index(['carrierCode', 'createdAt'])
export class Shipment {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid')
  id!: string;

  @Index({ unique: true })             // B-tree, unique: equality lookups are O(log n)
  @Column({ name: 'tracking_number', type: 'text' })
  trackingNumber!: string;

  @Column({ name: 'carrier_code', type: 'text' })
  carrierCode!: string;

  @CreateDateColumn({ name: 'created_at', type: 'timestamptz' })
  createdAt!: Date;
}

// Point lookup: index scan + LIMIT 1
const shipment = await this.shipments.findOne({ where: { trackingNumber } });

Sequelize example

import { DataTypes, Model, Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export class Shipment extends Model {
  declare id: string;
  declare trackingNumber: string;
}

export function initShipment(sequelize: Sequelize): void {
  Shipment.init(
    {
      id: { type: DataTypes.UUID, defaultValue: DataTypes.UUIDV4, primaryKey: true },
      trackingNumber: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false, field: 'tracking_number' },
      carrierCode: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false, field: 'carrier_code' },
    },
    {
      sequelize,
      tableName: 'shipments',
      underscored: true,
      indexes: [
        { unique: true, fields: ['tracking_number'] },
        { fields: ['carrier_code', 'created_at'] },
      ],
    },
  );
}

// Equality lookup through the unique index
const shipment = await Shipment.findOne({ where: { trackingNumber } });

Production scenario

A marketplace has 40 million product_listings rows. The search-by-seller page runs WHERE seller_id = $1 ORDER BY updated_at DESC LIMIT 50. With an index on (seller_id) only, the plan is an index scan on seller_id followed by a sort of every listing the seller has (a large seller has 300,000 listings: ~150 ms). With an index on (seller_id, updated_at DESC), the plan walks the index in order and stops after 50 rows: ~0.4 ms. Same search strategy (binary search into a B-tree), but the second index also answers the order, which is the topic of the next section.

Failure scenario

At 17:40 a "find order by phone number" support feature starts timing out. The orders table has a B-tree index on customer_phone. The query is WHERE customer_phone LIKE '%' || $1 || '%', added last week so agents could search by the last four digits. A leading wildcard cannot use a B-tree (the tree is sorted by the beginning of the string, and the search does not know the beginning), so the planner falls back to a sequential scan: linear search over 60 million rows, 9 seconds, on the primary, forty times a minute. The fix is a trigram index (pg_trgm, covered in the search worked example later in this part) or storing the last four digits in a separate indexed column.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Index exists but is not used. Function on the column (lower(email)), type mismatch (text column compared with varchar parameter is fine, but bigint compared with text is not), leading wildcard, or the planner deciding the predicate is not selective enough.
  • Stale statistics. After a bulk load, the planner may think the table is small and choose a sequential scan. Run ANALYZE.
  • Hash lookups on mutable keys. Using an object as a Map key uses identity, not content; two equal-looking objects are different keys.
  • Hash collisions and adversarial keys. V8 randomizes string hashes per process, so hash flooding through JSON keys is mitigated; a custom hash function in your code might not be.
  • Unsorted data given to binary search. Returns wrong answers silently; there is no error. Always know who guarantees the order.
  • Index bloat. Heavily updated indexes accumulate dead entries; the O(log n) descent touches more pages than it should until REINDEX CONCURRENTLY.
  • Index-only scan that is not. If the visibility map is not up to date (recent writes, no vacuum), the "index only" scan still fetches heap pages: check Heap Fetches in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior sees every WHERE clause as a search algorithm request and asks: which index will satisfy it, and is that index worth its write cost? They do not add an index per query; they design a small set of composite indexes that serve the important access paths, and they verify with EXPLAIN on production-sized data.

In application code, the rule is: two collections that must be matched get a Map built from the smaller one, never nested find. And the more important rule: if both collections came from the database, the matching probably belongs in the database as a join.

To a product manager: "Searching by the end of a phone number is like finding a word in a dictionary by its last letters: the dictionary is sorted by the first letters, so we would have to read the whole thing. We need a different kind of index for that search, which takes a day to add."

Common mistakes

  • Filtering in JavaScript what should be filtered in SQL, so the database does a full scan and ships millions of rows over the wire.
  • Nested find over two database result sets.
  • Assuming any index makes any query fast. Column order in composite indexes, wildcards and functions all matter.
  • Adding an index for every query without measuring the write overhead; a table with 15 indexes writes 15 B-tree entries per insert.
  • Using LIKE '%term%' on an indexed column and being surprised.

Interview questions

  1. "Explain how PostgreSQL chooses between a sequential scan, an index scan and a bitmap scan." Expected: cost model driven by selectivity and page cost constants; bitmap scan for medium selectivity to read heap pages in physical order. Follow-up: why can a sequential scan be faster than an index scan for a predicate matching 30% of rows?
  2. "Why can't a B-tree index serve LIKE '%abc'?" Expected: the tree is ordered by string prefix; a suffix search has no starting point. Follow-up: what index type can? (Trigram GIN.)
  3. "When would you choose a hash index over a B-tree in PostgreSQL?" Expected: almost never; equality-only lookups on long keys where the smaller index matters; B-tree also supports ranges and ordering.
  4. "You have two arrays of 50,000 items each from two systems and need the intersection. Complexity of the naive approach and yours?" Expected: O(n * m) = 2.5 billion versus O(n + m) with a Set.
  5. "What does Heap Fetches in an index-only scan mean and how do you reduce it?" Expected: visibility map not set for those pages; VACUUM marks pages all-visible.
  6. "What is the write cost of an index and how do you decide an index is not worth it?" Expected: O(log n) per row per index on writes, plus space and vacuum work; check pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan for unused indexes.

Practical exercise

Create a 5-million-row orders table with a random external_ref. Run the point lookup three ways: no index, B-tree index, hash index. Capture EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for each. Then write a LIKE 'ch_3P%' prefix query and a LIKE '%LzQ4' suffix query and explain which one uses the B-tree and why.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Timings and buffer counts for all three point lookups in a table.
  • A one-paragraph explanation of the plan chosen for each LIKE query.
  • The B-tree index is created with CONCURRENTLY and you can explain what would happen to writers without it.

8.5 Sorting

Concept

Sorting arranges items in order by a key. Every "latest orders", "top sellers", "cheapest first" and every paginated list depends on a sort somewhere: in the database, in the application, or (best of all) in an index that was sorted when it was built.

Comparison sorts (merge sort, quicksort, heapsort, TimSort) cannot do better than O(n log n) in general; that is a proven lower bound. Non-comparison sorts (counting sort, radix sort) can be O(n) for integer keys with a bounded range, which is why databases and Node internally sometimes use them for small integers, but you will rarely write one.

Why does it exist?

Sorting turns a pile into a structure. Sorted data enables binary search, merge joins, deduplication with a single pass, range queries, and "top N" without examining everything. The cost is O(n log n) once; the benefit is O(log n) lookups forever after, which is exactly the deal a B-tree index offers.

Without controlled sorting: pagination returns duplicate or missing rows between pages, "top 10" endpoints sort a million rows to return ten, and application servers burn CPU sorting what the database could have handed over in order.

Mental model

Imagine a mail room. Sorting letters by postcode once (O(n log n)) lets every carrier grab their bundle instantly (O(log n) to find the bundle, O(k) to take it). Re-sorting the whole room every time a carrier arrives is what happens when a query sorts a table on every request. Keeping the shelves sorted as letters arrive (O(log n) per letter) is what an index does.

Stability is this: two letters to the same postcode stay in the order they arrived. An unstable sort may swap them. If you then say "the first letter on the shelf is the oldest", an unstable sort makes that claim false.

How it works

The comparison sorts you will actually encounter:

Algorithm Time Space Stable Where you meet it
Quicksort O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst O(log n) No PostgreSQL in-memory sorts (Sort Method: quicksort)
Merge sort O(n log n) O(n) Yes PostgreSQL external sorts (external merge), k-way merge of feeds
Heapsort O(n log n) O(1) No PostgreSQL top-N heapsort for ORDER BY ... LIMIT
TimSort O(n log n), O(n) on nearly-sorted input O(n) Yes V8's Array.prototype.sort since Node 11
Insertion sort O(n²), O(n) on sorted input O(1) Yes Inside TimSort for small runs; maintaining a tiny sorted list

Stability means equal keys keep their input order. Node's Array.prototype.sort is stable (guaranteed by the ECMAScript spec since 2019; V8 implements TimSort). PostgreSQL's ORDER BY has no such guarantee: rows with equal sort keys come back in whatever order the plan produced them, which can change between executions. This is why every paginated ORDER BY needs a unique tiebreaker column, typically the primary key.

Sorting in the database happens in one of three ways:

  1. Index order. If an index exists whose column order matches the ORDER BY (including direction), the planner walks the index and no sort node appears. Cost: O(log n + k) for k returned rows. This is the goal for every hot paginated query.
  2. In-memory sort. The sort node collects rows and sorts them in work_mem with quicksort. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Sort Method: quicksort Memory: 2048kB. With a LIMIT, PostgreSQL uses top-N heapsort, keeping only the best N rows in a heap: O(n log N) time and O(N) memory.
  3. External sort. If the rows do not fit in work_mem, the sort spills to temporary files and does a merge sort across them. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Sort Method: external merge Disk: 45632kB. This is typically 5–20x slower than in-memory and adds disk I/O on the database server.

PostgreSQL 13 added Incremental Sort: if an index provides order on a prefix of the ORDER BY columns (say customer_id), it sorts only within each group for the remaining columns, in small batches.

Sorting in Node uses TimSort. Practical facts: sorting a million numbers takes roughly 100–200 ms; sorting a million objects by a string property with a plain comparator takes 500 ms–1 s; using localeCompare in the comparator multiplies that by 5–10x because each comparison goes through ICU. For locale-aware sorting of large arrays, create one Intl.Collator and reuse collator.compare, or precompute sort keys once (O(n)) and sort those.

flowchart TB
    A["Need rows in order"] --> B{"Is there a LIMIT or a page?"}
    B -->|"yes"| C{"Index matches ORDER BY columns and direction?"}
    C -->|"yes"| D["Index walk: no Sort node, O of log n plus k"]
    C -->|"no"| E["Add composite index, or accept top-N heapsort"]
    B -->|"no, whole result needed"| F{"Result size?"}
    F -->|"under a few thousand rows already in memory"| G["Sort in Node with TimSort"]
    F -->|"large"| H["Sort in PostgreSQL, check work_mem for external merge"]

Practical example

The order-history page: GET /customers/:id/orders?page=.... Version one sorts in the application:

// Loads every order for the customer, sorts in Node, slices a page: O(n log n) per request
const all = await this.orders.find({ where: { customerId } });
all.sort((a, b) => b.createdAt.getTime() - a.createdAt.getTime());
return all.slice(offset, offset + 50);

For a customer with 30,000 orders this transfers 30,000 rows (~10 MB) and sorts them for every page view. Version two asks the database for the page in index order with a tiebreaker:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_created_id_idx
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC);

SELECT id, total_cents, status, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = $1
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 50;
Limit  (cost=0.56..24.31 rows=50 width=48) (actual time=0.029..0.088 rows=50 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using orders_customer_created_id_idx on orders  (cost=0.56..14260.10 rows=30012 width=48) (actual time=0.028..0.081 rows=50 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (customer_id = 4821)
Execution Time: 0.112 ms

No Sort node. The index is already in the requested order, so PostgreSQL reads 50 entries and stops. 0.1 ms instead of 80 ms plus 10 MB of transfer.

NestJS example

Sort parameters from clients are a classic source of both injection bugs and unindexed sorts. Whitelist them, and always append the tiebreaker:

// orders/dto/list-orders.dto.ts
import { IsIn, IsInt, IsOptional, Max, Min } from 'class-validator';
import { Type } from 'class-transformer';

export const ORDER_SORT_FIELDS = ['createdAt', 'totalCents'] as const;
export type OrderSortField = (typeof ORDER_SORT_FIELDS)[number];

export class ListOrdersDto {
  @IsOptional() @IsIn(ORDER_SORT_FIELDS)
  sortBy: OrderSortField = 'createdAt';

  @IsOptional() @IsIn(['ASC', 'DESC'])
  direction: 'ASC' | 'DESC' = 'DESC';

  @IsOptional() @Type(() => Number) @IsInt() @Min(1) @Max(100)
  limit = 50;
}
// orders/orders.service.ts
async list(customerId: string, dto: ListOrdersDto): Promise<Order[]> {
  // Only whitelisted, indexed columns reach orderBy; the id tiebreaker makes pagination deterministic
  return this.orders
    .createQueryBuilder('o')
    .where('o.customer_id = :customerId', { customerId })
    .orderBy(`o.${dto.sortBy}`, dto.direction)
    .addOrderBy('o.id', dto.direction)
    .take(dto.limit)
    .getMany();
}

Each whitelisted sortBy must have a matching composite index (customer_id, <field>, id); otherwise a large customer triggers a top-N heapsort over all their rows on every page.

PostgreSQL example

Seeing an external sort and fixing it:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM order_events WHERE order_id = ANY($1) ORDER BY occurred_at;
Sort  (cost=98120.44..99370.44 rows=500000 width=96) (actual time=1210.3..1398.8 rows=498877 loops=1)
  Sort Key: occurred_at
  Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 51240kB
  Buffers: shared hit=21044, temp read=6405 written=6410
  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on order_events  (cost=1893.2..40120.9 rows=500000 width=96) ...
Execution Time: 1452.7 ms

Half a million rows, 51 MB of temp files. Options, in the order a senior would consider them:

  1. Do you need all 500,000 rows sorted? Usually the caller wants a page or a per-order timeline; add LIMIT and get top-N heapsort, or query per order with an index on (order_id, occurred_at).
  2. If the full sorted set is required (a batch export), raise work_mem for that session only: SET LOCAL work_mem = '128MB'; inside the transaction. Never globally.
  3. Add an index that provides the order so the sort disappears.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY order_events_order_occurred_idx ON order_events (order_id, occurred_at);
-- Per-order timeline: index walk, no Sort node, sub-millisecond
SELECT * FROM order_events WHERE order_id = $1 ORDER BY occurred_at;

TypeORM example

Index declaration with direction, and a query that lets the index provide the order:

@Entity('orders')
@Index('orders_customer_created_id_idx', ['customerId', 'createdAt', 'id'])
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id!: string;
  @Column({ name: 'customer_id', type: 'uuid' }) customerId!: string;
  @CreateDateColumn({ name: 'created_at', type: 'timestamptz' }) createdAt!: Date;
  @Column({ name: 'total_cents', type: 'bigint' }) totalCents!: string;
}

// Backward index walk: PostgreSQL can scan an ascending index in reverse for DESC, DESC
const page = await this.orders.find({
  where: { customerId },
  order: { createdAt: 'DESC', id: 'DESC' },
  take: 50,
});

TypeORM's decorator does not express per-column direction; a mixed-direction index (created_at DESC, id ASC) needs a migration with raw SQL. For same-direction sorts, PostgreSQL walks the ascending index backward at no extra cost.

Sequelize example

const page = await Order.findAll({
  where: { customerId },
  order: [['createdAt', 'DESC'], ['id', 'DESC']],   // tiebreaker for deterministic pages
  limit: 50,
  raw: true,
});

And when the data is already in memory and small, sort in Node with a reusable collator:

const collator = new Intl.Collator('en', { sensitivity: 'base' });
// Stable TimSort: products with equal names keep their existing order (e.g. by relevance)
products.sort((a, b) => collator.compare(a.name, b.name));

Production scenario

A "top 10 products by revenue this week" widget is called 200 times per second from the home page. The query is SELECT product_id, sum(total_cents) FROM order_lines WHERE created_at > $1 GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 10. The aggregate touches 4 million rows; the sort over ~50,000 product groups with LIMIT 10 is a top-N heapsort (cheap, O(n log 10)); the expensive part is the aggregate. At 200 RPS the primary is at 80% CPU on this query alone. The fix is not a better sort: it is a materialized rollup refreshed every minute, so the request reads 10 pre-sorted rows from a 50,000-row table with an index on (week, revenue DESC). Sorting once per minute instead of 200 times per second.

Failure scenario

At 08:05 a customer reports "the same order shows on page 2 and page 3". The endpoint sorts by created_at DESC with no tiebreaker. A bulk import created 400 orders with identical timestamps (second precision, from a CSV). PostgreSQL returns those 400 in plan-dependent order, and between page 2 and page 3 an autovacuum changed the physical layout, so the order of equal keys changed. Some orders appeared twice, some never. The fix is ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC and the matching index; the deeper fix is keyset pagination (next section), which does not depend on stable offsets at all.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Ties without a tiebreaker. Nondeterministic order across executions; broken pagination.
  • Sorting a LIMIT query without a supporting index. Top-N heapsort still scans all matching rows; fine at 10,000, slow at 10 million.
  • work_mem spills. External merge sorts on the primary compete for disk I/O with everything else.
  • ORDER BY on a computed expression (ORDER BY lower(name), ORDER BY total_cents * fx_rate). No plain index helps; use an expression index or sort in the application for small sets.
  • Collation cost. Sorting text under a non-C collation is 2–5x slower than C collation; localeCompare in Node without a cached collator is far worse.
  • Sorting inside a loop. O(n² log n); the classic "find the latest per group" mistake. Group first, then sort once, or use DISTINCT ON in SQL.
  • Comparator bugs. A comparator that returns true/false instead of negative/zero/positive, or one that is inconsistent (a < b and b < a both true), produces garbage order with no error.
  • Sorting mutable keys. If the key changes during the sort (e.g. Date.now() in the comparator), the result is undefined.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior's hierarchy: index order first, database sort with LIMIT second, application sort only for small in-memory sets or keys the database cannot index. They treat a Sort node in a hot query's plan as a bug to be explained. They always add the tiebreaker. They know that sorting a million rows is a batch job, not a request.

They also know when to not push sorting into the database: a saturated primary with spare application CPU, or a sort key that depends on per-request context (the user's location, a personalization score). In those cases they bound the input size first, then sort in Node.

To a product manager: "Sorting by 'relevance to this user' cannot be pre-sorted by the database because it is different for every user. We can do it for the first 1,000 candidates instantly, but not for all 4 million products."

Common mistakes

  • Sorting in the application and paginating with slice, transferring the whole set on every page.
  • Omitting the tiebreaker column.
  • ORDER BY on a column with no supporting composite index for the common WHERE.
  • Raising work_mem globally to fix one report.
  • localeCompare in a comparator over large arrays without a cached Intl.Collator.
  • Calling .sort() on an array you did not intend to mutate (it sorts in place; use toSorted() on Node 20+ or copy first).

Interview questions

  1. "Why does a paginated ORDER BY created_at need a tiebreaker, and what happens without one?" Expected: PostgreSQL does not guarantee stable order for equal keys; pages can repeat or skip rows. Follow-up: what index makes ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC free?
  2. "What is top-N heapsort and when does the planner use it?" Expected: ORDER BY ... LIMIT N keeps a heap of the best N, O(n log N) time, O(N) memory.
  3. "Explain what Sort Method: external merge Disk: 51240kB tells you and three ways to respond." Expected: spill beyond work_mem; add index, add LIMIT, SET LOCAL work_mem.
  4. "Is Array.prototype.sort stable in Node? Why does it matter?" Expected: yes, TimSort since V8 7.0; multi-key sorting by sorting twice relies on it.
  5. "When would you sort in the application instead of the database?" Expected: small bounded set, per-request computed key, offloading a saturated primary.
  6. "A comparator uses localeCompare and sorting 200,000 rows takes 3 seconds. What do you change?" Expected: cache an Intl.Collator, or precompute sort keys; or push the sort to the database with an appropriate collation.

Practical exercise

Take a paginated list endpoint in your project. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on its query for the customer with the most rows. If you see a Sort node, add the composite index that removes it and re-measure. Add the tiebreaker if it is missing. Then in Node, benchmark sorting 200,000 product names with a naive localeCompare comparator versus a cached Intl.Collator.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Before and after plans, with the Sort node gone and execution time recorded.
  • The endpoint's sort fields are whitelisted in a DTO and every whitelisted field has a supporting index.
  • Node benchmark shows the collator version at least 3x faster, and you can explain why.

8.6 Binary search

Concept

Binary search finds a value in a sorted collection by repeatedly halving the search range. Look at the middle element; if it is what you want, stop; if it is smaller than the target, the target must be in the right half; otherwise, the left half. Each step discards half the remaining candidates, so a million elements take at most 20 steps and a billion take 30.

The exact-match version is the one from textbooks. The versions you actually use in backends are the boundary versions: "the last version whose effectiveFrom is at or before this timestamp", "the first sample at or after this time", "where does the next page start". These are called lower bound and upper bound searches, and they are the same algorithm with a different stopping rule.

Why does it exist?

Because sorted data is everywhere in a backend and scanning it linearly is wasteful. Config versions are sorted by effective date. Price history is sorted by time. Metrics samples are sorted by timestamp. Every B-tree index is sorted by key. Binary search is how you exploit that order: O(log n) instead of O(n), with no extra data structure and no extra memory.

Without it, a lookup into a sorted array of 100,000 price points is 100,000 comparisons per call. With it, 17.

Mental model

Imagine guessing a number between 1 and 1,000 where the only feedback is "higher" or "lower". Guessing 1, 2, 3 in turn takes up to 1,000 guesses. Guessing 500, then 250 or 750, and so on takes at most 10. The B-tree index in PostgreSQL is the same game played on disk pages: each page tells you which child page holds the range you want, and after three or four pages you are at the leaf.

How it works

The lower-bound form, which finds the first index whose value is >= target (returns n if none):

// Returns the index of the first element for which `isAtOrAfter(element)` is true.
// The predicate must be monotonic: false, false, ..., false, true, true, ..., true.
export function lowerBound<T>(items: readonly T[], isAtOrAfter: (item: T) => boolean): number {
  let lo = 0;
  let hi = items.length;              // half-open range [lo, hi)
  while (lo < hi) {
    const mid = lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1); // no overflow, no floating point
    if (isAtOrAfter(items[mid])) hi = mid;   // answer is at mid or to the left
    else lo = mid + 1;                       // answer is strictly to the right
  }
  return lo;
}

// "Latest item at or before t": one past the first item that is after t, minus one.
export function latestAtOrBefore<T>(items: readonly T[], at: (item: T) => number, t: number): T | undefined {
  const firstAfter = lowerBound(items, (item) => at(item) > t);
  return firstAfter === 0 ? undefined : items[firstAfter - 1];
}

The predicate form is worth learning because it generalizes: any question of the shape "find the boundary where a monotonic condition flips" is a binary search. That includes "the largest batch size that still finishes under 100 ms" and "the earliest deploy after which the error rate exceeded 1%".

flowchart TB
    S["Sorted versions by effectiveFrom: 10 entries. Target t = 2024-05-20"] --> A["lo 0 hi 10 mid 5: v5 effective 2024-04-15 is not after t so lo becomes 6"]
    A --> B["lo 6 hi 10 mid 8: v8 effective 2024-09-01 is after t so hi becomes 8"]
    B --> C["lo 6 hi 8 mid 7: v7 effective 2024-07-10 is after t so hi becomes 7"]
    C --> D["lo 6 hi 7 mid 6: v6 effective 2024-06-01 is after t so hi becomes 6"]
    D --> E["lo equals hi equals 6: first after t is index 6, answer is v5"]

Three backend uses:

  1. Versioned config lookup. Pricing rules, tax rates, feature flag schedules and commission tiers all have an effective_from. "Which version applied at the time this order was placed?" is latestAtOrBefore. Keep versions sorted in memory (they change rarely, there are hundreds, not millions) and answer in O(log n) with no I/O.
  2. Time-series lookup. "What was the exchange rate at 14:32:07?", "what was the inventory level when this order was created?" Samples are sorted by time; the answer is the latest sample at or before the instant.
  3. Cursor pagination boundaries. Keyset pagination says "give me 50 rows after (created_at, id) = (X, Y)". Inside PostgreSQL, the B-tree descent to (X, Y) is a binary search over the index pages, and then a sequential walk of 50 leaf entries. That is why keyset pagination is O(log n + 50) regardless of how deep the page is, while OFFSET 1000000 is O(1,000,050).

Practical example

A commission engine applies the merchant's commission tier that was in effect when an order was placed, not the current one (the finance team reprocesses old orders during disputes). The tiers table has about 30 versions per merchant. Loading them once per merchant into a sorted array and binary searching per order is O(log 30) = 5 comparisons, versus a database round trip per order during a 2-million-order reprocessing job.

NestJS example

// commissions/commission-tiers.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { CommissionTier } from './commission-tier.entity';
import { latestAtOrBefore } from '../common/binary-search';

@Injectable()
export class CommissionTiersService {
  // merchantId -> tiers sorted ascending by effectiveFrom (ms since epoch)
  private readonly cache = new Map<string, CommissionTier[]>();

  constructor(@InjectRepository(CommissionTier) private readonly tiers: Repository<CommissionTier>) {}

  async tierAt(merchantId: string, placedAt: Date): Promise<CommissionTier> {
    let versions = this.cache.get(merchantId);
    if (!versions) {
      // One query per merchant per process lifetime; the DB sorts using the index
      versions = await this.tiers.find({ where: { merchantId }, order: { effectiveFrom: 'ASC' } });
      this.cache.set(merchantId, versions);
    }
    const tier = latestAtOrBefore(versions, (v) => v.effectiveFrom.getTime(), placedAt.getTime());
    if (!tier) {
      throw new Error(`No commission tier for merchant ${merchantId} at ${placedAt.toISOString()}`);
    }
    return tier;
  }

  invalidate(merchantId: string): void {
    this.cache.delete(merchantId); // call from the tier-updated event handler
  }
}

The cache is bounded by the number of merchants times ~30 rows; for 50,000 merchants that is about 1.5 million small objects, roughly 150 MB, which is worth a bounded LRU rather than a plain Map in a long-lived process (see the cache eviction worked example later in this part).

PostgreSQL example

The same lookup in SQL, with the index that makes the B-tree do the binary search:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY commission_tiers_merchant_effective_idx
  ON commission_tiers (merchant_id, effective_from DESC);

-- "Latest version at or before placed_at": descend to the boundary, read one row
SELECT rate_bps
FROM commission_tiers
WHERE merchant_id = $1 AND effective_from <= $2
ORDER BY effective_from DESC
LIMIT 1;
Limit  (cost=0.42..3.44 rows=1 width=4) (actual time=0.019..0.020 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using commission_tiers_merchant_effective_idx on commission_tiers
        (cost=0.42..48.10 rows=16 width=4) (actual time=0.018..0.018 rows=1 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((merchant_id = $1) AND (effective_from <= $2))

Keyset pagination is the other everyday binary search. The row-value comparison lets PostgreSQL seek directly to the boundary in a composite index:

-- Page after the cursor (created_at = $1, id = $2), newest first
SELECT id, total_cents, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = $3
  AND (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 50;

With the index (customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC), this is an index descent (O(log n)) plus 50 sequential leaf reads, whether it is page 2 or page 20,000. Compare OFFSET 1000000, which reads and discards a million index entries first.

TypeORM example

async pageAfter(customerId: string, cursor?: { createdAt: Date; id: string }): Promise<Order[]> {
  const qb = this.orders
    .createQueryBuilder('o')
    .where('o.customer_id = :customerId', { customerId })
    .orderBy('o.created_at', 'DESC')
    .addOrderBy('o.id', 'DESC')
    .take(50);

  if (cursor) {
    // Row-value comparison: PostgreSQL seeks straight to the boundary in the composite index
    qb.andWhere('(o.created_at, o.id) < (:createdAt, :id)', cursor);
  }
  return qb.getMany();
}

Sequelize example

Sequelize has no row-value operator, so express the same boundary with Op.or:

import { Op } from 'sequelize';

const where: Record<string, unknown> = { customerId };
if (cursor) {
  where[Op.or as unknown as string] = [
    { createdAt: { [Op.lt]: cursor.createdAt } },
    { createdAt: cursor.createdAt, id: { [Op.lt]: cursor.id } },
  ];
}
const page = await Order.findAll({
  where,
  order: [['createdAt', 'DESC'], ['id', 'DESC']],
  limit: 50,
  raw: true,
});

The planner handles the OR form well when the composite index exists, but check the plan; on some versions it produces a BitmapOr rather than a single seek.

Production scenario

A metrics service stores 1-second samples per host in memory for the last hour (3,600 samples per series, 20,000 series). A dashboard asks "value at time t" for 500 series per refresh, 10 refreshes per second. Linear scan: 500 × 3,600 × 10 = 18 million comparisons per second, about 20% of a core. Binary search: 500 × 12 × 10 = 60,000. The difference does not show up as an incident; it shows up as a smaller instance type.

Failure scenario

At 03:30 a settlement job starts charging merchants the wrong commission. The tiers array was sorted by effective_from in the database with ORDER BY effective_from on a timestamptz column, and binary-searched in Node by comparing Date values. A new tier was inserted with effective_from of '2025-03-30 02:30' in a local-time session during the DST transition, which stored a UTC instant earlier than the previous tier's. The array was no longer sorted at that point, the binary search's invariant broke, and for some placedAt values it returned the tier one position off. Nobody saw an error; the wrong rate was applied to 14,000 orders. The fix: store and compare in UTC only, and assert sortedness when loading the array (an O(n) check that is cheap for hundreds of entries).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Unsorted or partially sorted input. Binary search returns a wrong answer, not an error. Validate the invariant at load time.
  • Off-by-one at the boundaries. Use the half-open [lo, hi) form consistently; test with an empty array, one element, target before first, target after last, target equal to an element.
  • Duplicates. Lower bound returns the first of the equal run; upper bound returns one past the last. Decide which you need.
  • Precision mismatch. Millisecond timestamps in Node versus microsecond timestamptz in PostgreSQL; a version effective at 12:00:00.000500 is "after" the Node value 12:00:00.000.
  • Cursor tampering. A client can forge a keyset cursor. Sign or encrypt cursors, or accept that they are just a (timestamp, id) pair with no security value.
  • Cursor on a mutable sort key. If updated_at is the cursor column and rows are updated between pages, rows move across the boundary. Use immutable keys (created_at, id) for cursors.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior asks: "Is this data sorted, who guarantees it, and are we exploiting it?" A lookup into a sorted in-memory structure with find is a review comment. A paginated endpoint using OFFSET on a large table is a design change request, because the O(offset) cost is a latency cliff waiting for a deep page.

They also see binary search as a debugging tool: bisecting deploys to find which one introduced a regression (git bisect is binary search over commits), bisecting a batch to find the one poison record, bisecting a time range to find when a metric changed.

To a product manager: "Jumping to page 5,000 in the admin list would make the database read and throw away 250,000 rows every time. Infinite scroll with a 'next' cursor is instant at any depth. We can support 'jump to date' too, which is the same trick."

Common mistakes

  • OFFSET-based pagination on tables that grow.
  • Linear scanning sorted arrays because binary search "seems risky".
  • Writing the exact-match version and then hacking it for boundary queries; write lowerBound once and derive.
  • Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2) in languages with fixed-width integers (overflow); in JavaScript it is fine numerically but the shift form is a good habit.
  • Forgetting the equal-key tiebreaker in a keyset cursor, so two rows with the same timestamp cannot both be on the boundary.

Interview questions

  1. "Implement 'latest config version effective at time t' and state its complexity." Expected: lower bound on effectiveFrom > t, minus one; O(log n). Follow-up: what happens if the array is not sorted, and how do you defend?
  2. "Why is keyset pagination O(log n) while OFFSET is O(offset)? Relate it to the index structure." Expected: B-tree descent is a binary search over pages; offset must walk entries.
  3. "What is the difference between lower bound and upper bound, and give a backend case for each." Expected: first >= versus first >; "samples since t" versus "samples up to and including t".
  4. "Give an example of binary searching on a predicate that is not a lookup." Expected: largest batch size under a latency budget; git bisect.
  5. "How would you paginate by updated_at, given rows change between pages?" Expected: you generally should not; use an immutable key, or snapshot the id list.

Practical exercise

Implement lowerBound, upperBound and latestAtOrBefore with unit tests covering empty input, single element, target below/above all, duplicates and exact hits. Then convert one OFFSET-paginated endpoint to keyset pagination with a (created_at, id) cursor and compare EXPLAIN ANALYZE for page 1 and page 10,000.

Acceptance criteria:

  • All boundary tests pass; a property test with random sorted arrays agrees with a linear scan.
  • Page 10,000 with keyset has the same execution time as page 1 (within noise); the OFFSET version shows the difference.
  • The endpoint rejects malformed cursors with a 400.

8.7 Two pointers

Concept

The two-pointer technique walks through one or two sorted sequences with two indices that only ever move forward. Because neither pointer goes back, the total work is the sum of the lengths: O(n + m). It is how you merge two sorted lists, remove duplicates from a sorted list in one pass, find pairs with a given property, and, most usefully in a backend, reconcile two sorted ledgers.

Why does it exist?

Matching two collections naively is O(n * m). Building a hash map from one is O(n + m) but costs O(n) memory and only supports equality. When both inputs are sorted by the same key, two pointers gets O(n + m) time with O(1) extra memory, preserves order in the output, and handles "what is in A but not in B" just as naturally as "what is in both". PostgreSQL's merge join is this exact algorithm.

Mental model

Imagine two clerks each holding a sorted stack of invoices, comparing the top invoice of each stack. If the numbers match, they staple the two together and both take the next one. If one clerk's number is smaller, that invoice has no partner: it goes into the "unmatched" pile and only that clerk advances. Nobody ever looks back into a stack. When both stacks are empty, every invoice has been classified, and each was looked at exactly once.

How it works

Merge two sorted sequences into one sorted sequence:

  1. Start pointers i = 0 on A and j = 0 on B.
  2. Compare A[i] and B[j]. Emit the smaller one and advance its pointer.
  3. When one sequence is exhausted, emit the rest of the other.

Reconcile two sorted sequences by key:

  1. Same setup. Compare keys.
  2. Equal keys: a match; compare the payloads (amounts, statuses) and record a discrepancy if they differ; advance both.
  3. A key smaller: A[i] has no counterpart in B; record "missing in B"; advance i.
  4. B key smaller: record "missing in A"; advance j.
  5. Drain whichever remains as "missing in the other".

Dedup a sorted array in place: a write pointer w and a read pointer r; copy A[r] to A[w] only when it differs from A[w - 1].

Merging k sorted feeds (a social timeline from k followed accounts) generalizes two pointers with a min-heap of the current head of each feed: O(N log k) for N total items. The heap is in the Dijkstra section of this part.

Practical example

Daily payment reconciliation. The internal ledger has 1.2 million captured payments for the day; the payment gateway's settlement file has 1.2 million rows. Both are sorted by the gateway's transaction id. The job must produce three lists: amount mismatches, payments we recorded that the gateway did not settle, and settlements we have no record of. Two pointers does this in one pass of about 2.4 million comparisons, well under a second, with memory for only the discrepancies.

NestJS example

// reconciliation/reconciliation.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';

export interface LedgerRow { txnId: string; amountCents: number; }
export interface SettlementRow { txnId: string; amountCents: number; }

export interface ReconciliationReport {
  matched: number;
  amountMismatch: Array<{ txnId: string; ledger: number; settled: number }>;
  missingInSettlement: string[];
  missingInLedger: string[];
}

@Injectable()
export class ReconciliationService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(ReconciliationService.name);

  // Both inputs MUST be sorted ascending by txnId using the same comparison (plain UTF-16 order).
  reconcile(ledger: readonly LedgerRow[], settlement: readonly SettlementRow[]): ReconciliationReport {
    const report: ReconciliationReport = { matched: 0, amountMismatch: [], missingInSettlement: [], missingInLedger: [] };
    let i = 0;
    let j = 0;
    while (i < ledger.length && j < settlement.length) {
      const a = ledger[i];
      const b = settlement[j];
      if (a.txnId === b.txnId) {
        if (a.amountCents !== b.amountCents) {
          report.amountMismatch.push({ txnId: a.txnId, ledger: a.amountCents, settled: b.amountCents });
        } else {
          report.matched += 1;
        }
        i += 1; j += 1;
      } else if (a.txnId < b.txnId) {
        report.missingInSettlement.push(a.txnId); i += 1;   // ledger has it, gateway does not
      } else {
        report.missingInLedger.push(b.txnId); j += 1;       // gateway has it, we do not
      }
    }
    for (; i < ledger.length; i += 1) report.missingInSettlement.push(ledger[i].txnId);
    for (; j < settlement.length; j += 1) report.missingInLedger.push(settlement[j].txnId);
    this.logger.log(`reconciled: ${report.matched} ok, ${report.amountMismatch.length} mismatches`);
    return report;
  }
}

The comment about the comparison is not decoration. If the ledger was sorted by PostgreSQL under a locale collation and the settlement file was sorted by the gateway using byte order, 'a-1' < 'a1' may be true in one and false in the other, and the pointers will desynchronize silently. Sort both sides yourself in Node, or sort in PostgreSQL with COLLATE "C", and assert sortedness before the walk.

PostgreSQL example

If both sides are in the database, the reconciliation is a FULL OUTER JOIN, and when both inputs are sorted (by an index or an explicit sort) the planner uses a Merge Join, which is two pointers:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT
  coalesce(l.txn_id, s.txn_id) AS txn_id,
  l.amount_cents AS ledger_cents,
  s.amount_cents AS settled_cents,
  CASE
    WHEN l.txn_id IS NULL THEN 'missing_in_ledger'
    WHEN s.txn_id IS NULL THEN 'missing_in_settlement'
    WHEN l.amount_cents <> s.amount_cents THEN 'amount_mismatch'
    ELSE 'ok'
  END AS outcome
FROM ledger_payments l
FULL OUTER JOIN settlement_rows s ON s.txn_id = l.txn_id
WHERE l.settled_on = '2025-06-01' OR s.settled_on = '2025-06-01';
Merge Full Join  (cost=0.85..98210.30 rows=1200000 width=52) (actual time=0.040..1610.221 rows=1200418 loops=1)
  Merge Cond: (l.txn_id = s.txn_id)
  ->  Index Scan using ledger_payments_txn_id_idx on ledger_payments l  (actual time=0.018..520.114 rows=1200103 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using settlement_rows_txn_id_idx on settlement_rows s  (actual time=0.015..498.902 rows=1200315 loops=1)
Execution Time: 1702.556 ms

Two index scans, each in key order, walked in lockstep. No hash table, no work_mem spill, O(n + m). If one side lacked an index, you would see a Sort node above it: PostgreSQL sorts that side first, then merges.

Production scenario

A social feed service merges posts from followed accounts. Each account's posts are already sorted by created_at DESC in a per-account Redis list. For a user following 300 accounts, the service fetches the first 20 posts from each (300 pipelined LRANGE calls, one round trip, ~2 ms) and does a k-way merge with a heap of size 300 to produce the top 50: O(50 log 300) ≈ 400 comparisons. The alternative (concatenate 6,000 posts and sort) is O(6000 log 6000) ≈ 75,000 comparisons, still cheap, but at 3,000 followed accounts and 2,000 RPS the heap version is the one that keeps the CPU flat.

Failure scenario

At 06:10 the reconciliation job reports 340,000 "missing in settlement" and 340,000 "missing in ledger", a wall of false positives. The gateway changed its export to sort transaction ids case-insensitively. The ledger side was still byte-sorted. From the first uppercase id onward, the two pointers walked past each other: every ledger row looked "smaller" than the settlement head, and vice versa, so both were dumped into the unmatched piles. The job "succeeded". Finance opened 340,000 disputes before someone noticed. The fix: sort both inputs in the job itself with the same comparator, and fail fast if either input is not sorted under that comparator.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Different sort orders on the two sides. Collation, case, locale, numeric-versus-lexical ('10' < '9'). The most common two-pointer bug in practice.
  • Duplicates on one side. Two ledger rows with the same txnId (a retry that was recorded twice) will match one settlement row and leave the other as "missing". Decide whether duplicates are an error before the walk, or group them first.
  • Null or missing keys. Sort them to one end explicitly and handle them before the walk.
  • Streaming inputs. Both sides can be streams (a file and a cursor); two pointers works on iterators, which keeps memory O(1).
  • Off-by-one in the drain loops. Forgetting to drain the remainder of one side after the other runs out silently loses rows.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

When two sorted inputs must be compared, the senior reaches for two pointers or a merge join, not for a hash map, because the output is ordered and memory is constant. When the inputs are not sorted and both come from the database, the senior lets PostgreSQL sort and merge them. When one side is a file from an external party, the senior never trusts its order and sorts it locally, because the cost of O(n log n) is far below the cost of a silent desynchronization.

To a product manager: "Reconciliation is like two people walking down two sorted lists at the same time. It is fast, but it only works if both lists are sorted the same way. When the bank changes how they sort, we have to re-sort their file ourselves first."

Common mistakes

  • Assuming external files are sorted because they were last month.
  • Comparing keys with localeCompare on one side and < on the other.
  • Building a hash map when a sorted merge would keep memory flat and output ordered.
  • Not handling duplicate keys.
  • Concatenating and sorting k sorted feeds instead of merging.

Interview questions

  1. "Reconcile two sorted lists of a million payments each. Complexity, memory, and what can go wrong?" Expected: O(n + m), O(discrepancies) memory; failure when sort orders differ or keys duplicate.
  2. "How does PostgreSQL's merge join relate to the two-pointer technique, and when does the planner choose it?" Expected: same algorithm; chosen when both inputs are sorted or cheaply sortable, typically via indexes.
  3. "Merge 300 sorted feeds into a top-50 timeline. Which approach and why?" Expected: k-way merge with a heap, O(50 log 300).
  4. "Dedupe a sorted array in place in one pass." Expected: read/write pointers.
  5. "You receive a 'sorted' CSV from a partner. Do you trust it?" Expected: no; sort it yourself or verify in O(n).

Practical exercise

Implement reconcile over two async iterators (a CSV stream and a PostgreSQL cursor) so memory stays constant. Feed it a 500,000-row settlement file with 200 deliberate mismatches, 50 missing rows on each side and 10 duplicate ids.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The report identifies every planted discrepancy and nothing else.
  • Memory stays flat regardless of file size (verify with process.memoryUsage()).
  • The job aborts with a clear error when an input is not sorted under the job's comparator.

8.8 Sliding window

Concept

A sliding window is a fixed-size range that moves over a sequence, one step at a time, while you maintain some summary of what is inside it: a count, a sum, a maximum, an average. The trick is that as the window slides, you update the summary incrementally (add the element entering, remove the element leaving) instead of recomputing it from scratch. That turns O(n * w) for a window of size w into O(n).

In backends the "sequence" is usually time: requests in the last minute, latency samples in the last 60 seconds, orders in the last hour. Three families of problems use it: rate limiting, moving averages for metrics, and anomaly detection.

Why does it exist?

Because "how many requests did this client make in the last 60 seconds?" is asked on every request, and counting all of them each time is O(requests). Because "average latency over the last minute" is computed every second by every service, and re-summing 60,000 samples each second is a waste. And because fixed windows have edge problems: a limit of 100 per minute with fixed minute buckets allows 200 requests in the two seconds spanning a minute boundary. Sliding windows fix that.

Mental model

Imagine a doorman who allows at most 100 entries per rolling hour. A fixed-window doorman resets his count at the top of each hour, so 100 people at 09:59 and 100 more at 10:01 both get in: 200 in two minutes. A sliding-window doorman keeps a list of entry times and, for each new arrival, crosses out every entry older than an hour, then checks whether fewer than 100 remain. He never recounts from the beginning; he only removes the old and adds the new.

How it works

Sliding window log. Keep the timestamps of every event in the window. On each new event: remove timestamps older than now - windowSize, then count. Exact, but memory is O(events in window) per key. For 100 per minute that is at most 100 timestamps per client; for 10,000 per minute it is 10,000.

Sliding window counter. Keep only two counters: the current fixed window and the previous one. Estimate the rolling count as previousCount * (fraction of the previous window still inside the sliding window) + currentCount. O(1) memory per key, an approximation that assumes events were evenly spread in the previous window. This is what large edge networks use; the error is small in practice and always conservative enough for abuse prevention.

Moving average with a running sum. Keep a ring buffer of the last w values and a running sum. On each new value: sum += value - buffer[oldestIndex], overwrite the slot, advance the index. Average is sum / w. O(1) per update.

Sliding maximum / minimum (for "p100 latency in the last minute" or "peak queue depth") uses a monotonic deque: O(1) amortized per update.

Anomaly detection. Maintain a moving average and a moving standard deviation (or an exponentially weighted moving average, EWMA, which needs no buffer at all: ewma = alpha * value + (1 - alpha) * ewma). Flag a sample when it is more than k standard deviations from the moving mean. This is how a simple "error rate is 4x its normal level" alert works.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as RateLimitGuard
    participant R as Redis
    C->>G: POST /orders
    G->>R: EVAL sliding_log.lua key now window limit
    R->>R: ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key 0 now minus window
    R->>R: ZCARD key then ZADD if under limit
    R-->>G: count 97 allowed
    G-->>C: 201 Created
    C->>G: POST /orders
    G->>R: EVAL sliding_log.lua key now window limit
    R-->>G: count 100 rejected
    G-->>C: 429 Too Many Requests

The full rate-limiter implementations (token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window in Redis Lua, and wiring into @nestjs/throttler) are in the worked example later in this part. Here is the in-process algorithmic core of the two sliding variants:

// rate-limit/sliding-window.ts

// Exact: keeps every timestamp in the window. Memory O(limit) per key.
export class SlidingWindowLog {
  private readonly hits = new Map<string, number[]>();
  constructor(private readonly limit: number, private readonly windowMs: number) {}

  allow(key: string, now = Date.now()): boolean {
    const list = this.hits.get(key) ?? [];
    const cutoff = now - this.windowMs;
    let drop = 0;
    while (drop < list.length && list[drop] <= cutoff) drop += 1; // timestamps are appended in order
    if (drop > 0) list.splice(0, drop);
    if (list.length >= this.limit) { this.hits.set(key, list); return false; }
    list.push(now);
    this.hits.set(key, list);
    return true;
  }
}

// Approximate: two counters per key. Memory O(1) per key.
export class SlidingWindowCounter {
  private readonly buckets = new Map<string, { windowStart: number; current: number; previous: number }>();
  constructor(private readonly limit: number, private readonly windowMs: number) {}

  allow(key: string, now = Date.now()): boolean {
    const windowStart = now - (now % this.windowMs);
    let b = this.buckets.get(key);
    if (!b || b.windowStart !== windowStart) {
      const previous = b && b.windowStart === windowStart - this.windowMs ? b.current : 0;
      b = { windowStart, current: 0, previous };
    }
    const elapsedFraction = (now - windowStart) / this.windowMs;
    const estimate = b.previous * (1 - elapsedFraction) + b.current;
    if (estimate >= this.limit) { this.buckets.set(key, b); return false; }
    b.current += 1;
    this.buckets.set(key, b);
    return true;
  }
}

Practical example

A checkout API allows 20 order submissions per minute per customer to stop scripted bulk-buying during flash sales. A fixed-minute counter lets a script submit 20 at 11:59:59 and 20 more at 12:00:00. The sliding window counter estimates the rolling count and refuses the second burst. Memory per customer is two integers and a window start, so 2 million active customers fit in a few hundred megabytes of Redis.

NestJS example

Moving averages belong in observability code. This interceptor keeps a 60-second moving average and a running standard deviation of latency per route, and flags anomalies to a logger (in a real system you would export to Prometheus and alert there; the point here is the algorithm on the hot path):

// observability/latency-window.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, Logger, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, tap } from 'rxjs';
