class RingWindow {
  private readonly values: number[];
  private readonly squares: number[];
  private index = 0;
  private filled = 0;
  private sum = 0;
  private sumSquares = 0;
  constructor(size: number) { this.values = new Array(size).fill(0); this.squares = new Array(size).fill(0); }

  push(v: number): void {                       // O(1): subtract the leaving value, add the entering one
    this.sum += v - this.values[this.index];
    this.sumSquares += v * v - this.squares[this.index];
    this.values[this.index] = v; this.squares[this.index] = v * v;
    this.index = (this.index + 1) % this.values.length;
    this.filled = Math.min(this.filled + 1, this.values.length);
  }
  get mean(): number { return this.filled ? this.sum / this.filled : 0; }
  get stddev(): number {
    if (this.filled < 2) return 0;
    const m = this.mean;
    return Math.sqrt(Math.max(0, this.sumSquares / this.filled - m * m));
  }
}

@Injectable()
export class LatencyWindowInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(LatencyWindowInterceptor.name);
  private readonly windows = new Map<string, RingWindow>();

  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const route = `${ctx.getClass().name}.${ctx.getHandler().name}`;
    const started = performance.now();
    return next.handle().pipe(tap(() => {
      const ms = performance.now() - started;
      const w = this.windows.get(route) ?? new RingWindow(1000);
      const isAnomaly = w.stddev > 0 && ms > w.mean + 4 * w.stddev; // compare before pushing
      w.push(ms);
      this.windows.set(route, w);
      if (isAnomaly) this.logger.warn(`${route} latency ${ms.toFixed(1)}ms vs mean ${w.mean.toFixed(1)}ms`);
    }));
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Sliding windows over stored data are what SQL window functions are for. A 7-day moving average of daily revenue and a z-score anomaly flag:

WITH daily AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at)::date AS day, sum(total_cents) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '90 days'
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
  day,
  revenue,
  avg(revenue)    OVER w AS moving_avg_7d,
  stddev(revenue) OVER w AS moving_sd_7d,
  (revenue - avg(revenue) OVER w) / nullif(stddev(revenue) OVER w, 0) AS z_score
FROM daily
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
ORDER BY day;

ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is the sliding window; PostgreSQL computes each row's aggregate incrementally where it can. For a rate-limit-style question over stored events ("clients with more than 1,000 requests in any 60-second window today"), a RANGE BETWEEN interval '60 seconds' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW window over request_log ORDER BY ts does the same thing without a self-join.

Production scenario

An API gateway enforces 1,000 requests per minute per API key across 12 gateway pods. In-process windows would give each pod its own count, so the real limit becomes 12,000. The counters live in Redis instead: a sliding window counter needs two INCR-able keys per API key (rl:{key}:{windowStart}), each with a 2-minute TTL, and one Lua script to read both and increment atomically. At 40,000 RPS that is 40,000 Redis script calls per second, about 0.3 ms each on the gateway's critical path, and roughly 4 MB of Redis memory for 20,000 active keys. The sliding log variant would store up to 1,000 timestamps per key (a 16 MB sorted set footprint per 1,000 keys at that limit) and cost O(log n) per ZADD: fine at 100 per minute, wasteful at 1,000, unreasonable at 100,000.

Failure scenario

At 12:00:00 sharp on Black Friday, the checkout service sees a spike of 2x its rate limit for one second and the database connection pool saturates. The rate limiter was a fixed-window counter keyed by minute. Every client that had been throttled at 11:59 retried at exactly 12:00:00 when the window reset, and every one of them had a fresh allowance of 100. Two minutes' worth of allowance landed in one second. Switching to a sliding window counter spread the same allowance over the boundary and the spike disappeared; adding jitter to the client's Retry-After handling removed the synchronization entirely.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Fixed-window boundary burst. Up to 2x the limit at the boundary. Sliding windows exist for this.
  • Clock skew across pods. Sliding windows keyed by wall-clock time on different machines disagree. Use Redis server time (TIME inside the Lua script) or a single time source.
  • Memory growth of window logs. O(limit) per key per window; with many keys and high limits, prefer the counter.
  • Approximation error of the counter. It assumes uniform distribution in the previous window; a burst at the end of the previous window is under-counted for part of the next. Acceptable for abuse control, not for billing.
  • Cold start of moving averages. The first w samples are not a full window; anomaly detection must wait until the window is filled or use a warm-up rule.
  • Anomaly detection on bimodal data. Cache hits and misses produce two latency clusters; the "mean" sits between them and everything looks anomalous. Track them separately.
  • Stale keys. Every per-key window in Redis needs a TTL, or the key space grows forever.
  • Hot keys. One API key at 100,000 RPM concentrates all its Redis traffic on one shard; consider local pre-limiting per pod.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior first asks what the window is for. Abuse prevention tolerates approximation, so a sliding counter in Redis wins on memory and speed. Billing or contractual quotas need exactness and an audit trail, which is a different system (an events table, not a rate limiter). Metrics windows need to be cheap on the hot path, so O(1) ring buffers or EWMA, never re-summing arrays.

They also ask where the window lives. Per-process windows are fast but multiply the limit by the pod count; centralized windows are correct but add a network hop to every request. The usual answer is both: a generous local limit as a circuit breaker, and the real limit in Redis.

To a product manager: "A limit of 100 per minute with a hard reset at each minute lets a bot do 200 in two seconds around the boundary. A rolling window fixes that, and it costs us a few bytes per user."

Common mistakes

  • Fixed windows for rate limiting and then wondering about boundary bursts.
  • Recomputing averages by summing an array on every request.
  • Per-pod rate limits in a horizontally scaled service.
  • Storing window state in Redis without a TTL.
  • Using the mean of latency for alerting (use percentiles from a histogram) while using the sliding window for something it is good at: rates and counts.
  • Sliding log with ZADD for very high limits, where memory and O(log n) per call matter.

Interview questions

  1. "Compare fixed window, sliding log and sliding counter rate limiters on accuracy, memory and cost per request." Expected: fixed is O(1) but allows 2x bursts; log is exact but O(limit) memory; counter is O(1) and approximately accurate. Follow-up: which would you use for a 10,000 RPM limit and why?
  2. "How do you compute a moving average in O(1) per sample?" Expected: ring buffer plus running sum; or EWMA with no buffer.
  3. "Why does a distributed rate limiter need a single time source?" Expected: clock skew moves windows differently on each node; use Redis TIME in the script.
  4. "Design anomaly detection for error rate with a sliding window. What false positives do you expect?" Expected: moving mean and stddev or EWMA with k-sigma; cold start, bimodal data, low-traffic noise.
  5. "Write the SQL for 'API keys that exceeded 1,000 requests in any 60-second window' over a request log." Expected: window function with RANGE ... PRECEDING.

Practical exercise

Implement both SlidingWindowLog and SlidingWindowCounter, then write a simulation that sends bursts at window boundaries and reports how many requests each variant admitted over each 60-second rolling period. Then implement the moving-average ring buffer and feed it synthetic latency data with an injected spike.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The log variant never admits more than limit in any rolling window; the counter variant's overshoot is measured and reported.
  • The ring buffer's mean matches a brute-force recomputation to within floating-point error at every step.
  • The anomaly detector flags the injected spike and no more than one false positive per 10,000 samples on the synthetic data.

8.9 Recursion

Concept

Recursion is a function calling itself on a smaller piece of the problem until it reaches a piece small enough to answer directly (the base case). Trees are the natural home of recursion: "the total product count of a category is its own products plus the totals of its child categories" is a recursive definition, and the code that computes it looks exactly like the sentence.

In a backend, recursion appears in three places: walking hierarchies (categories, org charts, comment threads, folder structures), processing nested data (JSON, permission trees, nested DTOs), and in the database as recursive common table expressions (WITH RECURSIVE). It also appears in a fourth place nobody intends: as a stack overflow at 03:00.

Why does it exist?

Because hierarchical data has unbounded depth and recursion expresses "do this at every level" without knowing how many levels there are. Without recursion (or its iterative twin, an explicit stack), you would write loops with hard-coded depth limits, which break the day someone creates a category five levels deep.

The cost is that every recursive call adds a frame to the call stack, and the call stack in Node is small.

Mental model

Imagine a manager asked "how many people report to you, including indirectly?" She asks each direct report the same question, waits for their answers, adds them up, adds her direct reports, and replies. Each person in the chain is a stack frame: they are waiting, holding partial state, until the people below them answer. If the org chart is 12 levels deep, 12 people are waiting at once. If the org chart accidentally contains a loop (an intern listed as the CEO's manager), the question never comes back, and eventually everyone in the building is standing around waiting. That is a stack overflow.

How it works

  1. The call stack. Each function call pushes a frame holding its arguments, local variables and return address. When the function returns, the frame is popped. Recursion of depth d has d frames alive at once.
  2. Node's stack limit. V8's default stack is about 984 KB on 64-bit builds. A simple recursive function uses roughly 80–150 bytes per frame, so you get about 8,000–12,000 nested calls before RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. Functions with more locals or arguments use bigger frames and overflow sooner. The --stack-size flag can raise the number V8 checks against, but it does not enlarge the actual thread stack the OS gave you, so setting it too high crashes the process with a segmentation fault instead of a catchable error. Treat the limit as fixed.
  3. Depth is the risk, not count. A balanced category tree with a million nodes has depth about 20; recursion is safe. A comment thread where each reply is nested under the previous one is a linked list; at 15,000 replies it overflows.
  4. Recursion to iteration. Any recursion can be rewritten with an explicit stack (an array you push to and pop from). The heap has gigabytes; the call stack has a megabyte. The rewrite is mechanical: what the recursive call would have received becomes what you push.
  5. Async recursion. An async function that awaits and then calls itself does not overflow the call stack (each await unwinds the synchronous stack), but return this.drain() inside an async function chains promises, and each pending outer promise holds its frame's closure alive. A worker loop written as async recursion leaks memory proportional to iterations. Write worker loops as while loops.
  6. Recursive CTEs. PostgreSQL evaluates WITH RECURSIVE iteratively: it runs the base query, then repeatedly runs the recursive part against the rows produced by the previous step, until a step produces no rows. There is no call stack; the "depth" is the number of iterations, and the working set is the rows of the current step. Unbounded depth in a cyclic graph means an infinite loop that fills a temp file, so you add a depth or path guard.

Building a tree from flat rows, recursively and iteratively:

// catalog/category-tree.ts
export interface CategoryRow { id: string; parentId: string | null; name: string; productCount: number; }
export interface CategoryNode extends CategoryRow { children: CategoryNode[]; subtreeProductCount: number; }

// O(n): index every row, then attach each node to its parent. No recursion needed to BUILD the tree.
export function buildTree(rows: CategoryRow[]): CategoryNode[] {
  const nodes = new Map<string, CategoryNode>();
  for (const r of rows) nodes.set(r.id, { ...r, children: [], subtreeProductCount: r.productCount });
  const roots: CategoryNode[] = [];
  for (const node of nodes.values()) {
    const parent = node.parentId ? nodes.get(node.parentId) : undefined;
    if (parent) parent.children.push(node); else roots.push(node);
  }
  return roots;
}

// Recursive post-order: children first, then the node. Fine for depth under ~1,000.
export function rollUpRecursive(node: CategoryNode): number {
  let total = node.productCount;
  for (const child of node.children) total += rollUpRecursive(child);
  node.subtreeProductCount = total;
  return total;
}

// Iterative post-order with an explicit stack: safe at any depth.
export function rollUpIterative(root: CategoryNode): void {
  const order: CategoryNode[] = [];
  const stack: CategoryNode[] = [root];
  while (stack.length > 0) {                 // pre-order traversal collecting nodes
    const n = stack.pop()!;
    order.push(n);
    for (const c of n.children) stack.push(c);
  }
  for (let i = order.length - 1; i >= 0; i -= 1) {   // reverse pre-order = children before parents
    const n = order[i];
    n.subtreeProductCount = n.productCount + n.children.reduce((s, c) => s + c.subtreeProductCount, 0);
  }
}

Practical example

An e-commerce catalog has 40,000 categories up to 8 levels deep. The storefront's left navigation needs the subtree under "Electronics" with product counts rolled up. Three ways to get it:

Approach Where the work happens Cost Best for
Load all 40,000 rows, buildTree, roll up Node, O(n), ~30 ms, ~10 MB Once per deploy or per cache TTL Whole-catalog navigation, cached
Recursive CTE from the subtree root PostgreSQL, O(subtree) with an index on parent_id ~2–10 ms for a few hundred rows Ad hoc subtree queries
Materialized path or closure table Precomputed on write; read is a single indexed range scan O(subtree) read, O(depth) extra write cost Read-heavy hierarchies with frequent subtree queries

NestJS example

A service that returns a bounded subtree using a recursive CTE, with a depth cap and a cycle guard, then builds the tree in memory:

// catalog/categories.service.ts
import { Injectable, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { buildTree, rollUpIterative, CategoryNode, CategoryRow } from './category-tree';

@Injectable()
export class CategoriesService {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly db: DataSource) {}

  async subtree(rootId: string, maxDepth = 6): Promise<CategoryNode> {
    // PostgreSQL walks the hierarchy one level per iteration; the path array stops cycles
    const rows: CategoryRow[] = await this.db.query(
      `WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
         SELECT c.id, c.parent_id AS "parentId", c.name, c.product_count AS "productCount",
                0 AS depth, ARRAY[c.id] AS path
         FROM categories c WHERE c.id = $1
         UNION ALL
         SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, c.name, c.product_count, s.depth + 1, s.path || c.id
         FROM categories c
         JOIN sub s ON c.parent_id = s.id
         WHERE s.depth < $2 AND NOT c.id = ANY(s.path)
       )
       SELECT id, "parentId", name, "productCount" FROM sub`,
      [rootId, maxDepth],
    );
    if (rows.length === 0) throw new NotFoundException(`Category ${rootId} not found`);
    const roots = buildTree(rows);
    rollUpIterative(roots[0]);
    return roots[0];
  }
}

Note the two guards: s.depth < $2 bounds the work, and NOT c.id = ANY(s.path) refuses to follow a cycle. Without them, a corrupted parent_id pointing back into the subtree makes the CTE loop forever.

PostgreSQL example

The plan for the recursive CTE, with the index that makes each iteration cheap:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY categories_parent_id_idx ON categories (parent_id);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, 0 AS depth, ARRAY[id] AS path FROM categories WHERE id = 'cat_electronics'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, s.depth + 1, s.path || c.id
  FROM categories c JOIN sub s ON c.parent_id = s.id
  WHERE s.depth < 6 AND NOT c.id = ANY(s.path)
)
SELECT count(*) FROM sub;
Aggregate  (actual time=3.912..3.913 rows=1 loops=1)
  CTE sub
    ->  Recursive Union  (actual time=0.021..3.640 rows=412 loops=1)
          ->  Index Scan using categories_pkey on categories  (actual time=0.018..0.019 rows=1 loops=1)
                Index Cond: (id = 'cat_electronics'::text)
          ->  Nested Loop  (actual time=0.015..0.480 rows=59 loops=7)
                ->  WorkTable Scan on sub s  (actual time=0.001..0.008 rows=59 loops=7)
                      Filter: (depth < 6)
                ->  Index Scan using categories_parent_id_idx on categories c  (actual time=0.004..0.006 rows=1 loops=412)
                      Index Cond: (parent_id = s.id)
                      Filter: (NOT (id = ANY (s.path)))
Execution Time: 3.960 ms

loops=7 on the recursive part: seven iterations for a six-level subtree (the base plus six). Each iteration does one indexed lookup per row of the previous level. PostgreSQL 14 added built-in helpers: CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path for cycle detection and SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY id SET ordercol (or BREADTH FIRST) for ordered output.

TypeORM example

TypeORM ships tree entities that maintain a materialized path or closure table for you:

// catalog/category.entity.ts
import { Entity, PrimaryColumn, Column, Tree, TreeChildren, TreeParent } from 'typeorm';

@Entity('categories')
@Tree('materialized-path')          // stores an mpath column like "root.electronics.phones."
export class Category {
  @PrimaryColumn('text') id!: string;
  @Column('text') name!: string;
  @Column({ name: 'product_count', type: 'int', default: 0 }) productCount!: number;
  @TreeChildren() children!: Category[];
  @TreeParent() parent!: Category | null;
}

// catalog/categories.service.ts
const repo = this.dataSource.getTreeRepository(Category);
const root = await repo.findOneByOrFail({ id: 'cat_electronics' });
const tree = await repo.findDescendantsTree(root, { depth: 6 });   // one query: WHERE mpath LIKE 'root.electronics.%'
const ancestors = await repo.findAncestors(root);                   // breadcrumbs

The materialized-path read is a prefix LIKE on an indexed column: no recursion at all. The cost moves to writes: moving a subtree rewrites the mpath of every descendant.

Sequelize example

Sequelize has no tree support; run the recursive CTE directly:

import { QueryTypes } from 'sequelize';

const rows = await sequelize.query<CategoryRow>(
  `WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
     SELECT id, parent_id AS "parentId", name, product_count AS "productCount", 0 AS depth, ARRAY[id] AS path
     FROM categories WHERE id = :rootId
     UNION ALL
     SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, c.name, c.product_count, s.depth + 1, s.path || c.id
     FROM categories c JOIN sub s ON c.parent_id = s.id
     WHERE s.depth < :maxDepth AND NOT c.id = ANY(s.path)
   )
   SELECT id, "parentId", name, "productCount" FROM sub`,
  { replacements: { rootId, maxDepth: 6 }, type: QueryTypes.SELECT },
);

Production scenario

A B2B ordering platform has customer organizations with nested cost centers (up to 10 levels). An approval workflow must find "the nearest ancestor cost center with an approver". With an index on parent_id, the recursive CTE walking upward does at most 10 iterations, each a primary-key lookup: about 0.5 ms. The same walk done from Node with one query per level costs 10 round trips, 10–20 ms, and holds a connection for the duration. The rule that falls out: recursion over rows should happen in one query, not in one query per level.

Failure scenario

At 21:40 every product page starts returning 500. The error is RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded from computeBreadcrumbs. The function walks parent_id upward recursively until it finds null. An admin used a bulk-edit tool to "move Electronics under Phones", which is a child of Electronics. The tree now has a cycle: Electronics -> Phones -> Electronics. The recursive walk never reaches null and overflows after about 11,000 frames, on every request that touches either category. The fix in the moment: a depth cap of 32 in the walk, returning an error instead of crashing. The fix that prevents recurrence: a cycle check before any parent_id update (the DFS section below), enforced in the database, not only in the admin UI.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Deep chains. Comment threads, linked-list-shaped data, or corrupted trees exceed the stack. Depth caps and iterative traversal.
  • Cycles. Any recursion over user-editable parent pointers must assume a cycle is possible.
  • Deeply nested JSON. JSON.parse handles depth well, but JSON.stringify and validation libraries that recurse (nested @ValidateNested() DTOs) can overflow or burn CPU on adversarial payloads. Cap request body size and nesting depth at the edge.
  • Recursive CTE without a stop condition on cyclic data: runs until the temp space is exhausted.
  • Async recursion as a loop. Memory grows with iterations because each pending promise retains its frame.
  • Unbounded fan-out. A recursive "load children" that issues one query per node is O(nodes) round trips: the N+1 problem in tree form.
  • Stack overflow is thrown, not a crash, so it can be caught; but state mutated on the way down is left half-updated. Design recursive updates to be idempotent or wrap them in a transaction.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior asks two questions of every recursive function: "What bounds the depth?" and "Who guarantees there is no cycle?" If the answer to either is "the data is always fine", the function gets a depth cap and a visited set before it ships.

They choose the storage model by the read/write ratio: adjacency list with recursive CTEs for write-heavy or rarely-read hierarchies; materialized path or closure table for read-heavy ones where subtree queries are hot. They keep hierarchy traversal inside one SQL statement rather than one query per level.

To a product manager: "Categories can be nested as deep as you like, but we enforce that a category cannot be moved inside its own descendants, because that creates a loop that no page can render."

Common mistakes

  • Recursive traversal without a depth limit over data that users can edit.
  • One database query per level (or per node) inside a recursive function.
  • Raising --stack-size instead of converting to iteration.
  • Using recursion to build a tree from flat rows when a two-pass Map does it in O(n).
  • Async worker loops written as recursion.
  • Trusting parent_id integrity without a database-level cycle check.

Interview questions

  1. "How deep can recursion go in Node, and what happens when you exceed it? How do you make a tree traversal safe at any depth?" Expected: roughly 10,000 frames with the default ~1 MB stack; RangeError; explicit-stack iteration. Follow-up: why not raise --stack-size? (Can exceed the OS thread stack and segfault.)
  2. "Explain how PostgreSQL executes WITH RECURSIVE and why it does not overflow." Expected: iterative evaluation, working table per step, no stack; needs a stop condition on cyclic data.
  3. "Compare adjacency list plus recursive CTE, materialized path and closure table for a category tree." Expected: write cost versus read cost; subtree move cost; index usage.
  4. "An admin can move a category under any other. What do you enforce and where?" Expected: cycle check in a transaction with a lock, ideally also in the database.
  5. "Why is async function loop() { await work(); return loop(); } a memory leak?" Expected: promise chain retains frames; use while.

Practical exercise

Seed a categories table with 50,000 rows, depth 8, and one deliberately introduced cycle. Implement the subtree service with the recursive CTE (with guards) and the iterative roll-up. Then write a recursive version with no guards and observe what happens when it touches the cycle.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The guarded version returns the subtree in under 20 ms and skips the cycle.
  • The unguarded version fails with a clear error you can explain (CTE side and Node side).
  • You add a CHECK-style safeguard (a trigger or application-level check with a lock) that rejects the cycle-creating update.

8.10 Breadth-first search (BFS)

Concept

Breadth-first search explores a graph level by level: first everything one step from the start, then everything two steps away, and so on. It uses a queue (first in, first out) and a visited set. In an unweighted graph, the first time BFS reaches a node is via a shortest path (fewest hops), which is why BFS is the answer to "how many hops between these two users" and "which categories are at depth 2".

Why does it exist?

Because many backend questions are about distance in hops: degrees of separation, "friends of friends", "which pages are two clicks from the homepage", "level-order rendering of a menu". DFS would find a path but not the shortest; Dijkstra would work but is overkill when every edge costs the same. BFS is the simplest algorithm that gives the shortest hop count, and its level-by-level shape maps naturally onto batched database queries: one query per level.

Mental model

Imagine dropping a stone in a pond. The ripple reaches everything at distance 1 first, then distance 2, then 3. Each ring is a BFS level. If you want to know how far the far bank is, you count rings. If the pond is huge and you only care about things within three rings, you stop after three: that is a depth cap, and it is what keeps "friends of friends of friends" from touching the whole social graph.

How it works

  1. Put the start node in a queue and in the visited set.
  2. Pop the front of the queue. For each neighbor not yet visited: mark it visited, record its distance (parent's distance plus one) and optionally its parent, and push it to the back of the queue.
  3. Repeat until the queue is empty or the target is found.
  4. Complexity O(V + E): every node enters the queue once, every edge is examined once. Memory O(V) for the visited set and, at worst, one whole level in the queue.

In a backend, the neighbors usually live in a database or Redis, and the important optimization is to expand a whole level with one query, not one query per node:

flowchart TB
    L0["Level 0: Electronics"] --> L1a["Level 1: Phones"]
    L0 --> L1b["Level 1: Laptops"]
    L0 --> L1c["Level 1: Audio"]
    L1a --> L2a["Level 2: Android"]
    L1a --> L2b["Level 2: iPhone"]
    L1b --> L2c["Level 2: Gaming"]
    L1b --> L2d["Level 2: Ultrabook"]
    L1c --> L2e["Level 2: Headphones"]

One query fetches all of level 1 (WHERE parent_id = 'Electronics'), one query fetches all of level 2 (WHERE parent_id = ANY(level1Ids)), and so on. A tree of depth 6 costs 6 round trips regardless of node count.

Three uses:

  • Shortest hops in a social graph. "Is B within 3 hops of A?" BFS from A with a depth cap. For "shortest path between A and B" on a large graph, bidirectional BFS (expand from both ends and stop when the frontiers meet) reduces the explored set from b^d to roughly 2 * b^(d/2), which for branching factor 300 and depth 4 is 8 billion versus 180,000.
  • Crawling. The URL frontier is a queue; the visited set is a SET in Redis (or a Bloom filter at web scale); BFS order gives broad coverage before depth; per-domain politeness is a rate limiter on dequeue. Depth caps and URL count caps stop a crawl of a calendar site from running until the year 9999.
  • Level-order category trees. Menus rendered level by level, breadcrumbs, "show categories up to depth 2 for the mega-menu".

Practical example

A "people you may know" feature suggests friends of friends who are not already friends. That is BFS to depth 2 from the user, excluding depth-1 nodes and the user, ranked by how many depth-1 nodes connect to each candidate (mutual friend count). For a user with 300 friends who each have 300 friends, level 2 has up to 90,000 candidates; in practice, heavy overlap reduces that to a few thousand. Two batched queries, a Map for counting, one sort of a few thousand items: about 15 ms.

NestJS example

// social/social-graph.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class SocialGraphService {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly db: DataSource) {}

  // Fewest hops from `from` to `to`, or null if not within maxDepth. One query per level.
  async degreesOfSeparation(from: string, to: string, maxDepth = 4, maxFrontier = 50_000): Promise<number | null> {
    if (from === to) return 0;
    const visited = new Set<string>([from]);
    let frontier: string[] = [from];

    for (let depth = 1; depth <= maxDepth; depth += 1) {
      // Expand the whole level with a single indexed query: friendships(user_id, friend_id)
      const rows: Array<{ friend_id: string }> = await this.db.query(
        `SELECT DISTINCT friend_id FROM friendships WHERE user_id = ANY($1::text[])`,
        [frontier],
      );
      const next: string[] = [];
      for (const { friend_id } of rows) {
        if (friend_id === to) return depth;
        if (!visited.has(friend_id)) { visited.add(friend_id); next.push(friend_id); }
      }
      if (next.length === 0) return null;                // graph exhausted
      if (next.length > maxFrontier) return null;        // fan-out guard: refuse to explode
      frontier = next;
    }
    return null;
  }
}

The maxFrontier guard is what makes this safe in production. One celebrity account with 5 million followers turns level 2 into millions of ids and the ANY($1) array into a 100 MB parameter.

PostgreSQL example

Level-order traversal inside PostgreSQL uses the recursive CTE, which is naturally breadth-first (each iteration is one level), and PostgreSQL 14's SEARCH BREADTH FIRST makes the ordering explicit:

WITH RECURSIVE reach AS (
  SELECT friend_id AS user_id, 1 AS depth FROM friendships WHERE user_id = $1
  UNION
  SELECT f.friend_id, r.depth + 1
  FROM friendships f JOIN reach r ON f.user_id = r.user_id
  WHERE r.depth < 3
)
SELECT user_id, min(depth) AS hops FROM reach WHERE user_id <> $1 GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY hops, user_id;

UNION (not UNION ALL) removes duplicate rows between iterations, which acts as a partial visited set; the min(depth) picks the shortest. For the category tree:

WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, name, 0 AS depth FROM categories WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, c.name, t.depth + 1 FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id
  WHERE t.depth < 2
) SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY name SET ord
SELECT id, name, depth FROM tree ORDER BY ord;   -- level by level, alphabetical within a level

Index on friendships(user_id) and categories(parent_id) is what makes each iteration an index scan rather than a table scan.

Production scenario

A crawler for a price-comparison service must refresh 2 million product pages across 400 retailer domains. The frontier is a BullMQ queue; the visited set is a Redis SET of URL hashes (2 million 16-byte hashes: ~100 MB); per-domain politeness limits each domain to 2 requests per second via a token bucket. BFS order ensures every retailer's top-level category pages are fetched before any retailer's deep pages, so the "most-visited products" are refreshed in the first hour even if the whole crawl takes a day.

Failure scenario

At 14:22 the social service's memory triples and the pod is OOMKilled. The "mutual friends" endpoint was called for a user who follows a handful of celebrity accounts. Level 1 was 40 accounts; level 2 was 12 million ids (each celebrity's followers). The code built the level-2 array, the ANY($1) parameter and a Set, about 1.5 GB in total, then died. There was a depth cap but no frontier cap. The fix: cap the frontier, and for accounts over a follower threshold, exclude them from expansion (a "supernode" rule that every large social graph has).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Supernodes. One high-degree node makes a level explode. Frontier caps and supernode exclusion.
  • Missing visited set. In a graph with cycles, BFS without visited never terminates.
  • Directed versus undirected. Friendships are usually stored both ways; follows are directed. BFS on the wrong direction gives wrong answers silently.
  • Stale visited sets in crawlers. Content changes; a visited set with no expiry never re-crawls. Use a "last crawled at" instead of a boolean.
  • Queue persistence. A crawler frontier in process memory is lost on restart. Redis or a durable queue.
  • Huge ANY($1) parameters. Tens of thousands of ids per query is fine; millions is not. Batch the frontier.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior asks what bounds the search: depth, frontier size, wall-clock budget. They want all three. They expand levels with batched queries and never one query per node. For hop-distance queries on a large graph that are hot (a friend-recommendation feed), they precompute offline and serve from a table, because BFS per request at scale is a CPU and I/O budget the request path cannot afford.

To a product manager: "Suggesting friends-of-friends is instant for most users. For users who follow celebrities, 'friends of friends' is millions of people, so we skip the celebrity links and use their other connections instead."

Common mistakes

  • One query per node.
  • No frontier cap; no supernode handling.
  • Forgetting the visited set, or using an array for it (includes is O(n)).
  • Using DFS when the shortest hop count is required.
  • Putting the crawler frontier in process memory.

Interview questions

  1. "Compute degrees of separation between two users on a table of friendships. Complexity and production guards?" Expected: BFS with one query per level, O(V + E) in reached nodes; depth cap, frontier cap, supernode exclusion. Follow-up: how does bidirectional BFS help?
  2. "Why is a recursive CTE naturally breadth-first?" Expected: each iteration computes the next level from the previous one.
  3. "Design a polite crawler's frontier and visited set." Expected: durable queue, hashed URL set with recrawl timestamps, per-domain rate limiting, depth and count caps.
  4. "When does BFS give the shortest path and when does it not?" Expected: unweighted graphs only; weighted needs Dijkstra.
  5. "How would you serve 'people you may know' at 2,000 RPS?" Expected: precompute offline (batch BFS), store top-N per user, serve from a table or Redis.

Practical exercise

Build a friendships table with 1 million users and about 100 million edges (average degree 100 with a few supernodes of degree 1 million). Implement degreesOfSeparation with per-level batching and guards. Measure the time and frontier sizes for a normal user pair and for a pair connected via a supernode.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Normal pairs at distance 3 resolve in under 100 ms.
  • Supernode pairs are refused or degraded predictably instead of exhausting memory.
  • Each level is exactly one query (verify with query logging).

8.11 Depth-first search (DFS)

Concept

Depth-first search explores a graph by going as deep as it can along one path before backing up and trying the next. It uses a stack (the call stack when written recursively, or an explicit array) and a visited set. Where BFS answers "how far", DFS answers "is there a path", "does this graph contain a cycle", "in what order must these things be processed" and "which nodes belong together".

In backends, DFS is the workhorse for cycle detection in anything that can form a graph: dependency graphs, role hierarchies, category parents, workflow step definitions, module imports.

Why does it exist?

Because graphs with cycles break every algorithm that assumes they end: recursive traversals overflow, topological orders do not exist, permission resolution loops forever. Somebody has to check before the cycle is written, and DFS with three colors is the standard check. It also finds cycles in O(V + E), which means you can afford to run it on every edge insert.

Mental model

Imagine exploring a cave system with a ball of string. You go down each tunnel as far as it goes, tying the string as you walk. If you ever walk into a chamber where your own string is already lying on the floor and you have not yet left that chamber on the way back (you are still inside it, on your current path), you have found a loop. Chambers you fully explored and left are safe to re-enter; they cannot be part of a loop that includes your current position. That distinction (still on the path versus already finished) is the three-color trick.

How it works

Three colors per node: white (unvisited), gray (on the current path, not finished), black (finished; all descendants explored).

  1. Start at a node; mark it gray; push it.
  2. For each neighbor: if white, recurse into it; if gray, you have found a back edge, which means a cycle; if black, ignore (already fully explored).
  3. When all neighbors are done, mark the node black and pop it.
  4. Repeat from every white node, so disconnected parts of the graph are covered.
  5. Complexity O(V + E). Memory O(V) for colors plus the stack depth.

The order in which nodes turn black (post-order) reversed is a topological order, which is why DFS and topological sorting are the same section in most textbooks; the topological sort section later in this part builds on this.

flowchart LR
    Admin["Admin"] --> Manager["Manager"]
    Manager --> Support["Support"]
    Support --> Viewer["Viewer"]
    Support -.->|"proposed edge: would create a cycle"| Manager

Adding "Support inherits Manager" while "Manager inherits Support" already holds creates a cycle. DFS from Manager finds Support gray on the path when it reaches the proposed edge.

Practical example

A role-based access system lets admins declare that one role inherits another (Manager inherits Support, which inherits Viewer). Effective permissions are the union of a role's own permissions and those of all ancestors, computed by a walk up the inheritance graph. If a cycle sneaks in, the walk never terminates. Every edge insert must therefore run a cycle check: "starting from the proposed parent, can I reach the proposed child?" If yes, the edge closes a loop and is rejected.

NestJS example

// authz/role-hierarchy.service.ts
import { ConflictException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class RoleHierarchyService {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly db: DataSource) {}

  // Adds "child inherits parent". Serialized with an advisory lock so two concurrent
  // inserts cannot each pass the check and together form a cycle.
  async addInheritance(childRoleId: string, parentRoleId: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.db.transaction(async (tx) => {
      await tx.query(`SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('role_inheritance'))`);

      const edges: Array<{ child_role_id: string; parent_role_id: string }> =
        await tx.query(`SELECT child_role_id, parent_role_id FROM role_inheritance`); // small graph: hundreds of rows

      const parents = new Map<string, string[]>();
      for (const e of edges) parents.set(e.child_role_id, [...(parents.get(e.child_role_id) ?? []), e.parent_role_id]);

      if (this.reaches(parents, parentRoleId, childRoleId)) {
        throw new ConflictException(`Role ${childRoleId} cannot inherit ${parentRoleId}: it would create a cycle`);
      }
      await tx.query(
        `INSERT INTO role_inheritance (child_role_id, parent_role_id) VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`,
        [childRoleId, parentRoleId],
      );
    });
  }

  // Iterative DFS: is `target` reachable from `start` by following parent edges?
  private reaches(parents: Map<string, string[]>, start: string, target: string): boolean {
    const visited = new Set<string>();
    const stack = [start];
    while (stack.length > 0) {
      const node = stack.pop()!;
      if (node === target) return true;
      if (visited.has(node)) continue;
      visited.add(node);
      for (const p of parents.get(node) ?? []) if (!visited.has(p)) stack.push(p);
    }
    return false;
  }
}

Reachability is enough here because we are checking one proposed edge: "would child -> parent close a loop?" is exactly "is child already reachable from parent?". The full three-color DFS is for validating an entire existing graph, which the topological sort section shows.

PostgreSQL example

The same check inside the database, with a recursive CTE, so that it holds even for writers that bypass the service:

-- Does parent_role reach child_role already? If any row comes back, the insert would create a cycle.
WITH RECURSIVE up AS (
  SELECT parent_role_id AS role_id, ARRAY[child_role_id, parent_role_id] AS path
  FROM role_inheritance WHERE child_role_id = $2          -- start from the proposed parent
  UNION ALL
  SELECT ri.parent_role_id, up.path || ri.parent_role_id
  FROM role_inheritance ri JOIN up ON ri.child_role_id = up.role_id
  WHERE NOT ri.parent_role_id = ANY(up.path)              -- guard against existing cycles
)
SELECT 1 FROM up WHERE role_id = $1 LIMIT 1;              -- $1 = proposed child

Wrap it in a trigger BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE ON role_inheritance that raises an exception when a row is returned, and take pg_advisory_xact_lock in the trigger too, so concurrent inserts are serialized. Indexes on role_inheritance(child_role_id) and (parent_role_id) keep each iteration an index scan.

TypeORM example

Moving a category under a new parent is the same check on the category tree; here with a QueryRunner and pessimistic locking on the rows involved:

async moveCategory(categoryId: string, newParentId: string): Promise<void> {
  const runner = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner();
  await runner.connect();
  await runner.startTransaction();
  try {
    await runner.query(`SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('categories_tree'))`);
    const rows: Array<{ id: string }> = await runner.query(
      `WITH RECURSIVE anc AS (
         SELECT id, parent_id, ARRAY[id] AS path FROM categories WHERE id = $1
         UNION ALL
         SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, anc.path || c.id FROM categories c JOIN anc ON c.id = anc.parent_id
         WHERE NOT c.id = ANY(anc.path)
       ) SELECT id FROM anc WHERE id = $2 LIMIT 1`,
      [newParentId, categoryId],
    );
    if (rows.length > 0) throw new ConflictException('Cannot move a category under its own descendant');
    await runner.manager.update(Category, { id: categoryId }, { parent: { id: newParentId } });
    await runner.commitTransaction();
  } catch (err) {
    await runner.rollbackTransaction();
    throw err;
  } finally {
    await runner.release();
  }
}

Production scenario

A workflow engine lets operations staff define order-processing pipelines as steps with "runs after" relationships. Pipelines have 10–60 steps. Every save runs a three-color DFS over the pipeline's steps (microseconds) and rejects cycles with a message naming the loop (fraud_check -> manual_review -> fraud_check). Because the check is O(V + E) on a tiny graph, it runs synchronously in the save request; nobody has to wait for a background validator.

Failure scenario

At 10:05 the authorization service's CPU pins at 100% on every pod and every API call that checks permissions times out. Two admins in different regions, three seconds apart, added Auditor inherits Finance and Finance inherits Auditor. Each request ran the reachability check, saw no cycle (the other edge was not committed yet), and inserted. The effective-permission resolver, a recursive walk with no visited set, now loops forever on any role touching either. The outage lasts 40 minutes while someone finds and deletes the offending edge by hand. The post-mortem yields three changes: an advisory lock around check-and-insert, a visited set in the resolver, and the database-level trigger so no future code path can skip the check.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Check-then-insert race. Two concurrent inserts each pass the check. Serialize with an advisory lock or SERIALIZABLE isolation.
  • Existing cycles. A cycle already in the data makes the reachability CTE loop; the path guard is mandatory.
  • Recursion depth. Long inheritance chains (rare) or deep category trees; the iterative version avoids stack limits.
  • Self-loops. child = parent; check explicitly.
  • Directed versus undirected. Cycle detection in undirected graphs is different (a parent-child edge looks like a cycle if you follow it both ways); use union-find or track the parent.
  • Graph too large to load. For graphs of millions of edges, do the DFS in the database (CTE) or in a graph store; loading the whole edge set per check is O(E) per request.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Any table with a self-reference (parent_id, inherits_from, depends_on) is a graph, and the senior asks "what stops it becoming cyclic?" on the day the table is created. They put the check as close to the data as possible (trigger or constraint-like CTE), serialize writers, and make every reader defensive with visited sets and depth caps even though the writer check exists, because data gets imported, migrated and hand-edited.

To a product manager: "A role cannot inherit from a role that already inherits from it, in any number of steps. We check that instantly on save and reject it with a message showing the loop."

Common mistakes

  • Reachability check without a lock.
  • Readers without visited sets, trusting that writers prevented cycles.
  • Using BFS or DFS interchangeably without noting that only DFS with colors detects cycles in directed graphs simply.
  • Loading a huge edge set into memory per check.
  • Cycle checks only in the UI.

Interview questions

  1. "Detect a cycle in a directed graph. Explain the three-color method and its complexity." Expected: white/gray/black; gray neighbor means back edge; O(V + E). Follow-up: how does it differ for undirected graphs?
  2. "An admin adds a role-inheritance edge. What do you check, and how do you make it safe under concurrency?" Expected: reachability from proposed parent to proposed child; advisory lock or serializable transaction.
  3. "Why is DFS post-order related to topological sorting?" Expected: reversed finish order respects all edges.
  4. "How do you do cycle detection inside PostgreSQL?" Expected: recursive CTE with a path array guard, or CYCLE clause in PG14+, in a trigger.
  5. "A permission resolver hangs. Walk me through the diagnosis." Expected: suspect a cycle; CPU profile shows the resolver; add visited set; find the edge with the CTE.

Practical exercise

Implement RoleHierarchyService.addInheritance with the advisory lock and a Jest test that fires two conflicting inserts concurrently (two transactions in parallel). Then add the PostgreSQL trigger and prove that a raw SQL insert bypassing the service is rejected too.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The concurrent test always ends with exactly one edge committed and one ConflictException.
  • A direct INSERT that would create a cycle fails with the trigger's error.
  • The effective-permission resolver has a visited set and a test with a hand-crafted cycle that proves it terminates.

8.12 Graph algorithms

Concept

A graph is a set of nodes connected by edges. Edges can be directed (A follows B) or undirected (A and B are friends), weighted (this road takes 4 minutes) or unweighted. That is the entire definition, and it covers more of your backend than you might expect: social connections, "customers who bought X also bought Y", role inheritance, module imports, job dependencies, delivery networks, payment flows between accounts, and fraud rings of accounts sharing a device.

The four operations you will actually run on backend graphs are: traversal (BFS and DFS, covered in the previous sections), connected components (which nodes belong to the same cluster), cycle detection (is this dependency graph valid), and shortest path (fewest hops or lowest cost).

Why does it exist?

Because relational tables store relationships as rows, and some questions cannot be answered by a fixed number of joins. "Everyone within 3 hops" is three joins; "everyone connected at all" is an unbounded number of joins. Graph algorithms are the tools for questions where the number of steps is not known in advance. Without them you either write recursive CTEs by hand for every question, or you load the data into memory and improvise, usually with O(n²) results.

Mental model

Imagine a city map. Intersections are nodes, streets are edges, and the minutes it takes to drive each street are weights. "Which neighborhoods are cut off by the flood?" is connected components. "Can I drive in a loop without repeating a street?" is cycle detection. "Fastest route from the depot to the customer" is shortest path. "Everything within a ten-minute walk" is BFS with a cap. The same map answers all four; only the question changes.

How it works

Representation. Three choices, and the database is usually the source of truth for all of them:

Representation Structure Memory Best for
Edge list edges(from_id, to_id, weight) table or array of tuples O(E) Storage in PostgreSQL; input to union-find
Adjacency list Map<nodeId, Array<{ to, weight }>> O(V + E) Traversal (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra); sparse graphs, which is nearly all real graphs
Adjacency matrix weight[i][j] two-dimensional array O(V²) Tiny dense graphs (a few hundred nodes); Floyd-Warshall

In PostgreSQL the graph is an edge table with indexes on both from_id and to_id. Traversal uses recursive CTEs (see the recursion and BFS sections). For heavy traversal workloads a dedicated graph database exists, but most product graphs (millions of nodes, tens of millions of edges) are served well from PostgreSQL plus in-memory algorithms in a worker.

Connected components. Two approaches:

  1. Flood fill: BFS or DFS from every unvisited node; each search marks one component. O(V + E).
  2. Union-find (disjoint set union): process edges one at a time, merging the sets of the two endpoints. With path compression and union by size, each operation is effectively O(1) (technically inverse Ackermann). It works on an edge stream and never needs the adjacency list, which makes it the right tool for large graphs read from a database cursor.
// graph/union-find.ts
export class UnionFind {
  private readonly parent = new Map<string, string>();
  private readonly size = new Map<string, number>();

  find(x: string): string {                       // returns the representative of x's set
    let root = x;
    while (this.parent.get(root) !== undefined && this.parent.get(root) !== root) root = this.parent.get(root)!;
    if (this.parent.get(root) === undefined) { this.parent.set(root, root); this.size.set(root, 1); }
    let cur = x;                                   // path compression: point every node on the path at the root
    while (cur !== root) { const next = this.parent.get(cur)!; this.parent.set(cur, root); cur = next; }
    return root;
  }

  union(a: string, b: string): boolean {           // returns false if a and b were already connected
    let ra = this.find(a);
    let rb = this.find(b);
    if (ra === rb) return false;
    if (this.size.get(ra)! < this.size.get(rb)!) [ra, rb] = [rb, ra];   // union by size: attach smaller under larger
    this.parent.set(rb, ra);
    this.size.set(ra, this.size.get(ra)! + this.size.get(rb)!);
    return true;
  }

  componentSize(x: string): number { return this.size.get(this.find(x))!; }
}

Cycle detection. Directed graphs: DFS with three colors (previous section). Undirected graphs: union-find; if an edge connects two nodes already in the same set, it closes a cycle.

Shortest path. A decision table, because picking the wrong one is the most common graph mistake:

Graph Algorithm Complexity Backend use
Unweighted BFS O(V + E) Degrees of separation, level-order
Non-negative weights Dijkstra O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap ETA, cheapest route, lowest-latency path
Negative weights, no negative cycles Bellman-Ford O(V * E) Currency arbitrage detection, cost graphs with credits
All pairs, small V Floyd-Warshall O(V³) Precomputing a distance matrix for a few hundred zones
Non-negative weights with a good heuristic A* Often far less than Dijkstra in practice Road routing with straight-line distance as the heuristic

Practical example

A fraud team wants "rings": groups of accounts linked by shared attributes (device fingerprint, card hash, shipping address). Model it as a graph where each account is connected to every attribute value it has used; accounts in the same connected component share a chain of attributes. The nightly job streams 12 million account_attribute rows from PostgreSQL through union-find, then writes each account's component id and size back. Accounts in components larger than 50 get flagged for review. Wall time: about 40 seconds for 5 million accounts, in a worker, with memory around 1.5 GB for the two maps.

flowchart LR
    A1["acct 101"] --- D1["device f3a9"]
    A2["acct 102"] --- D1
    A2 --- C1["card hash 88b2"]
    A3["acct 103"] --- C1
    A4["acct 250"] --- D2["device 71cc"]
    A5["acct 251"] --- D2

Accounts 101, 102 and 103 form one component through the shared device and card; 250 and 251 form another.

NestJS example

A worker that computes components with union-find over a streamed edge set and persists the result:

// fraud/fraud-cluster.job.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { UnionFind } from '../graph/union-find';

@Injectable()
export class FraudClusterJob {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(FraudClusterJob.name);
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly db: DataSource) {}

  async run(): Promise<void> {
    const uf = new UnionFind();
    let lastId = 0;
    for (;;) {                                                  // keyset batches keep memory per batch bounded
      const rows: Array<{ id: number; account_id: string; attr_key: string }> = await this.db.query(
        `SELECT id, account_id, attribute_type || ':' || attribute_value AS attr_key
         FROM account_attributes WHERE id > $1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 50000`, [lastId]);
      if (rows.length === 0) break;
      for (const r of rows) uf.union(r.account_id, r.attr_key);  // effectively O(1) per edge
      lastId = rows[rows.length - 1].id;
    }

    const accounts: Array<{ id: string }> = await this.db.query(`SELECT id FROM accounts`);
    const values = accounts.map((a) => [a.id, uf.find(a.id), uf.componentSize(a.id)] as const);
    await this.db.transaction(async (tx) => {
      await tx.query(`CREATE TEMP TABLE cluster_tmp (account_id text, cluster_id text, cluster_size int) ON COMMIT DROP`);
      for (let i = 0; i < values.length; i += 5000) {          // batched multi-row inserts
        const chunk = values.slice(i, i + 5000);
        const params = chunk.flat();
        const placeholders = chunk.map((_, k) => `($${k * 3 + 1}, $${k * 3 + 2}, $${k * 3 + 3})`).join(',');
        await tx.query(`INSERT INTO cluster_tmp VALUES ${placeholders}`, params);
      }
      await tx.query(`UPDATE accounts a SET cluster_id = t.cluster_id, cluster_size = t.cluster_size
                      FROM cluster_tmp t WHERE t.account_id = a.id`);
    });
    this.logger.log(`clustered ${accounts.length} accounts`);
  }
}

Component size in the union-find counts attribute nodes too; subtract them or track account counts separately if the threshold must count accounts only.

PostgreSQL example

One-hop neighborhood queries stay in SQL and need the right indexes; the full component computation lives in the worker:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY account_attributes_attr_idx ON account_attributes (attribute_type, attribute_value);
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY account_attributes_account_idx ON account_attributes (account_id);

-- Accounts sharing any attribute with account $1 (one hop)
SELECT DISTINCT b.account_id
FROM account_attributes a
JOIN account_attributes b
  ON b.attribute_type = a.attribute_type AND b.attribute_value = a.attribute_value
WHERE a.account_id = $1 AND b.account_id <> $1;
HashAggregate  (actual time=0.402..0.410 rows=7 loops=1)
  ->  Nested Loop  (actual time=0.031..0.371 rows=9 loops=1)
        ->  Index Scan using account_attributes_account_idx on account_attributes a  (rows=4 loops=1)
        ->  Index Scan using account_attributes_attr_idx on account_attributes b  (rows=2 loops=4)

Two hops is another join; beyond that, the recursive CTE with a depth cap. Full components over millions of nodes via recursive CTE are possible but slow and memory-hungry; that is the job's work.

Production scenario

A marketplace recommendation feature ("customers also bought") is a bipartite graph of 20 million orders and 2 million products. The nightly job builds product-product co-purchase edges with a GROUP BY in PostgreSQL (O(orders * items²) bounded by small basket sizes), keeps the top 20 neighbors per product by count, and writes a 40-million-row product_neighbors table. The request path is a single indexed lookup: O(log n), ~1 ms. The graph algorithm ran once, offline; the API never sees a graph.

Failure scenario

At 23:50 the fraud clustering job is killed by Kubernetes for exceeding its 2 GB memory limit. A marketing campaign gave every new user the same default "shipping address" placeholder, so 800,000 accounts all link to one attribute node. That is not a memory problem for union-find, but the follow-on step that materialized the members of each component into an array to write "related accounts" per account built an 800,000-element array 800,000 times. The job was rewritten to store only the component id per account and let the reviewers query members on demand, and attribute values with more than 1,000 accounts were excluded as non-discriminative (the graph equivalent of a stop word).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Hub nodes. One attribute or one user connecting everything collapses components into one giant blob. Exclude high-degree nodes.
  • Direction mistakes. Treating a directed "follows" edge as undirected changes every answer.
  • Graph size versus memory. Adjacency lists for 100 million edges need several gigabytes in Node; use union-find over a stream, or process in the database, or shard by component.
  • Stale graphs. In-memory graphs loaded at startup drift from the database; schedule refreshes and version them.
  • Negative weights. Dijkstra silently gives wrong answers; Bellman-Ford or a modeling fix.
  • Disconnected targets. Shortest-path code must handle "no path" without infinite loops or Infinity leaking into responses.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior separates the request path from the graph computation. The request path does O(log n) lookups into precomputed results; the graph algorithm runs in a worker on a schedule or on events. They store the graph in PostgreSQL as an edge table with both indexes, and reach for a graph database only when traversal queries dominate the workload and recursive CTEs have measurably run out of steam.

They also model carefully: is the edge directed, is it weighted, can weights be negative, can the graph have cycles, what is the maximum degree? Those five answers pick the algorithm.

To a product manager: "Finding all the accounts connected to a fraud ring is a nightly job that takes a minute. Showing the ring for one account is instant because we store the answer."

Common mistakes

  • Running graph traversal in the request path over a live table.
  • Loading whole graphs into memory without knowing the edge count.
  • Recursive CTEs for full-graph computation.
  • Ignoring hub nodes.
  • Choosing Dijkstra for unweighted graphs (BFS is simpler and faster) or BFS for weighted ones (wrong answers).

Interview questions

  1. "Find groups of accounts linked by shared devices or cards, across 5 million accounts. Approach, complexity, memory?" Expected: union-find over a streamed edge list, near-linear time, O(V) memory; exclude hub attributes. Follow-up: how do you serve the results at request time?
  2. "When do you use union-find versus BFS for components?" Expected: union-find for edge streams and incremental updates; BFS when you already have adjacency and need the members immediately.
  3. "Pick the shortest-path algorithm for: a social graph, a delivery network, a currency-exchange graph." Expected: BFS, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford (negative cycles mean arbitrage).
  4. "How would you store a graph in PostgreSQL and what indexes does it need?" Expected: edge table with indexes on both endpoint columns; composite for weighted lookups.
  5. "What is a hub node problem and how do you handle it?" Expected: degree explosion; cap, exclude, or treat specially.

Practical exercise

Generate 2 million accounts and 6 million attribute links with a few planted rings and one hub attribute. Implement the clustering job with union-find, exclude hub attributes above a degree threshold, and write component ids back.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Planted rings are recovered exactly; the hub attribute does not merge unrelated accounts.
  • Peak memory of the worker stays under 1 GB (measure it).
  • A one-hop neighborhood query for any account runs under 5 ms with the indexes shown.

8.13 Dijkstra's algorithm

Concept

Dijkstra's algorithm finds the lowest-cost path from one start node to every other node in a graph whose edge weights are non-negative. It repeatedly takes the closest not-yet-finalized node, finalizes its distance, and relaxes its neighbors (updates their tentative distances if going through the current node is cheaper). A priority queue keeps "closest node" cheap to find.

For a backend engineer the canonical uses are ETA and dispatch: how long from this restaurant to this customer, which of these 40 drivers can reach the pickup soonest, what is the cheapest sequence of shipping legs.

Why does it exist?

BFS finds the fewest hops, but real edges have different costs: a highway segment and an alley are both one hop. Trying every path is exponential. Dijkstra exploits a simple fact: if all weights are non-negative, the nearest unfinalized node cannot get any closer via nodes that are farther away, so its distance is final. That single observation turns an exponential search into O((V + E) log V).

Mental model

Imagine water flooding out from the depot along the roads at one meter per minute. The moment the water first reaches an intersection is the fastest time to get there, because water tries every road at once. Dijkstra simulates that flood: the priority queue holds "when will the water reach this intersection, based on what we know so far", and you always process the intersection the water reaches next.

How it works

  1. Set dist[start] = 0 and every other distance to infinity. Put (0, start) in a min-heap.
  2. Pop the smallest (d, node). If d is greater than dist[node], this entry is stale (the node was reached more cheaply after this entry was pushed); skip it.
  3. For each edge node -> next with weight w: if dist[node] + w < dist[next], set dist[next] to the new value, record prev[next] = node, and push (dist[next], next).
  4. Repeat until the heap is empty, or stop early when the target is popped (its distance is final at that moment).
  5. Rebuild the path by following prev from the target back to the start.

The "push duplicates, skip stale" trick (lazy deletion) is what lets you use a plain binary heap without a decrease-key operation. Complexity O((V + E) log V); memory O(V + E) for the graph and O(E) in the heap in the worst case.

// graph/min-heap.ts
export class MinHeap<T> {
  private readonly items: T[] = [];
  constructor(private readonly priority: (item: T) => number) {}

  get size(): number { return this.items.length; }

  push(item: T): void {                          // O(log n): append, then sift up
    this.items.push(item);
    let i = this.items.length - 1;
    while (i > 0) {
      const parent = (i - 1) >> 1;
      if (this.priority(this.items[parent]) <= this.priority(this.items[i])) break;
      [this.items[parent], this.items[i]] = [this.items[i], this.items[parent]];
      i = parent;
    }
  }

  pop(): T | undefined {                         // O(log n): take root, move last to root, sift down
    if (this.items.length === 0) return undefined;
    const top = this.items[0];
    const last = this.items.pop()!;
    if (this.items.length > 0) {
      this.items[0] = last;
      let i = 0;
      for (;;) {
        const l = 2 * i + 1, r = l + 1;
        let smallest = i;
        if (l < this.items.length && this.priority(this.items[l]) < this.priority(this.items[smallest])) smallest = l;
        if (r < this.items.length && this.priority(this.items[r]) < this.priority(this.items[smallest])) smallest = r;
        if (smallest === i) break;
        [this.items[i], this.items[smallest]] = [this.items[smallest], this.items[i]];
        i = smallest;
      }
    }
    return top;
  }
}
// graph/dijkstra.ts
import { MinHeap } from './min-heap';

export interface Edge { to: string; weight: number; }
export type Graph = Map<string, Edge[]>;

export interface PathResult { seconds: number; path: string[]; }

export function dijkstra(graph: Graph, start: string, target: string): PathResult | null {
  const dist = new Map<string, number>([[start, 0]]);
  const prev = new Map<string, string>();
  const heap = new MinHeap<{ node: string; d: number }>((e) => e.d);
  heap.push({ node: start, d: 0 });

  while (heap.size > 0) {
    const { node, d } = heap.pop()!;
    if (d > (dist.get(node) ?? Infinity)) continue;      // stale entry: a cheaper one was processed already
    if (node === target) break;                          // target finalized: early exit
    for (const { to, weight } of graph.get(node) ?? []) {
      if (weight < 0) throw new Error(`negative edge ${node} -> ${to}`);   // Dijkstra's precondition
      const nd = d + weight;
      if (nd < (dist.get(to) ?? Infinity)) {
        dist.set(to, nd);
        prev.set(to, node);
        heap.push({ node: to, d: nd });
      }
    }
  }
  if (!dist.has(target)) return null;                    // unreachable
  const path: string[] = [];
  for (let cur: string | undefined = target; cur !== undefined; cur = prev.get(cur)) path.push(cur);
  return { seconds: dist.get(target)!, path: path.reverse() };
}
flowchart LR
    W["Warehouse"] -->|"4 min"| A["Hub A"]
    W -->|"9 min"| B["Hub B"]
    A -->|"3 min"| B
    A -->|"8 min"| C["Customer"]
    B -->|"2 min"| C

From the warehouse: pop W (0). Relax A to 4, B to 9. Pop A (4): relax B to 7 (via A, cheaper than 9), C to 12. Pop B (7): relax C to 9. Pop C (9): target finalized. Path W -> A -> B -> C, 9 minutes, not the "direct" W -> A -> C at 12.

Practical example

A food-delivery dispatcher must pick, among 40 available riders, the one who can reach a restaurant soonest. Running Dijkstra 40 times (once per rider) is wasteful. Reverse the graph and run Dijkstra once from the restaurant: it yields the travel time from every zone to the restaurant, so ranking the 40 riders is 40 map lookups. On a city graph of 8,000 zones and 30,000 edges, one run takes about 5 ms in Node.

For real road-level routing (millions of nodes), production systems call a routing engine (OSRM, Valhalla, a maps API) that precomputes contraction hierarchies and answers in microseconds; Dijkstra over a zone graph is for your own coarse ETAs, dispatch ranking and surge zones, where you control the graph and the latency budget.

NestJS example

// eta/eta.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron, CronExpression } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { dijkstra, Graph, PathResult } from '../graph/dijkstra';

@Injectable()
export class EtaService implements OnModuleInit {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(EtaService.name);
  private graph: Graph = new Map();          // replaced atomically on refresh; requests keep their reference
  private reversed: Graph = new Map();

  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly db: DataSource) {}

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> { await this.reload(); }

  @Cron(CronExpression.EVERY_5_MINUTES)     // travel times change with traffic; reload the whole graph
  async reload(): Promise<void> {
    const rows: Array<{ from_zone: string; to_zone: string; travel_seconds: number }> =
      await this.db.query(`SELECT from_zone, to_zone, travel_seconds FROM zone_edges WHERE travel_seconds >= 0`);
    const g: Graph = new Map();
    const r: Graph = new Map();
    for (const e of rows) {
      (g.get(e.from_zone) ?? g.set(e.from_zone, []).get(e.from_zone)!).push({ to: e.to_zone, weight: e.travel_seconds });
      (r.get(e.to_zone) ?? r.set(e.to_zone, []).get(e.to_zone)!).push({ to: e.from_zone, weight: e.travel_seconds });
    }
    this.graph = g; this.reversed = r;
    this.logger.log(`zone graph reloaded: ${g.size} zones, ${rows.length} edges`);
  }

  estimate(fromZone: string, toZone: string): PathResult | null {
    return dijkstra(this.graph, fromZone, toZone);          // ~5 ms on 8k zones
  }

  // Travel time from EVERY zone to `toZone` in one run (reversed graph), for ranking candidate riders
  rankRiders(riderZones: Array<{ riderId: string; zone: string }>, toZone: string): Array<{ riderId: string; seconds: number }> {
    const times = new Map<string, number>();
    for (const rider of riderZones) {
      if (!times.has(rider.zone)) {
        const res = dijkstra(this.reversed, toZone, rider.zone);
        times.set(rider.zone, res ? res.seconds : Infinity);
      }
    }
    return riderZones
      .map((r) => ({ riderId: r.riderId, seconds: times.get(r.zone)! }))
      .filter((r) => Number.isFinite(r.seconds))
      .sort((a, b) => a.seconds - b.seconds);
  }
}

rankRiders as written runs Dijkstra once per distinct rider zone with early exit; a variant that runs once without a target and returns the full dist map is the pure single-source version, and is better when riders span many zones.

PostgreSQL example

The graph lives in an edge table. Recursive CTEs can enumerate paths but they explode combinatorially on real graphs, so shortest path in SQL is either a small bounded problem or a job for the pgRouting extension, which provides pgr_dijkstra over an edge table:

CREATE TABLE zone_edges (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  from_zone text NOT NULL,
  to_zone   text NOT NULL,
  travel_seconds int NOT NULL CHECK (travel_seconds >= 0),   -- Dijkstra precondition enforced at the source
  updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX zone_edges_from_idx ON zone_edges (from_zone);
CREATE INDEX zone_edges_to_idx   ON zone_edges (to_zone);

-- With pgRouting installed (CREATE EXTENSION pgrouting), integer node ids are required:
-- SELECT * FROM pgr_dijkstra('SELECT id, source, target, cost FROM zone_edges_int', 1, 42);

The CHECK (travel_seconds >= 0) is the important line: it makes the algorithm's precondition a database invariant rather than a comment.

Production scenario

A ride-hailing service estimates pickup times for 500 requests per second. Each request ranks about 30 nearby drivers. With a reversed single-source Dijkstra per request on a 6,000-zone graph (3 ms), that is 1.5 CPU-seconds per second: two cores. Caching the single-source result per pickup zone in Redis for 30 seconds (drivers move, but zone-to-zone times change slowly) cuts it to a few runs per second per zone. The graph reload every five minutes replaces the Map reference atomically; in-flight requests finish on the old graph, which is fine for ETAs.

Failure scenario

At 18:30 in a monsoon, ETAs go wrong in one direction only: rides into the flooded district show 3 minutes, rides out show 50. A traffic feed updated zone_edges with the same travel_seconds for both directions, but a bug in the feed adapter wrote the outbound rows with negative values (a sign error in "delay minus baseline"). The CHECK constraint did not exist yet, the service's reload query did not filter, and Dijkstra with negative edges finalized nodes too early. The constraint, the WHERE travel_seconds >= 0 filter and the throw in the algorithm were all added the next day; three layers, because a wrong ETA costs money on every ride.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Negative weights. Wrong results, no error. Enforce non-negativity at the source.
  • Unreachable target. Return null, never Infinity in an API response.
  • Graph reload during requests. Swap references atomically; never mutate the live graph.
  • Heap growth. Lazy deletion can push O(E) entries; fine for tens of thousands of edges, watch it for millions.
  • Float weights. Use integers (seconds, meters, cents) to avoid comparison surprises.
  • Same-node start and target. Distance 0, path [start].
  • Per-request graph construction. Building the adjacency list per request is O(E) every time; build once, reuse.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior asks "how big is the graph and how often does it change?" before choosing where Dijkstra runs. Thousands of nodes changing every few minutes: in-process, reload on a schedule. Millions of nodes: a routing engine. They look for single-source reuse (rank many targets from one run), cache by source, and bound the search (early exit, a maximum distance cutoff) so a pathological query cannot walk the whole graph.

To a product manager: "We estimate ride times on a simplified map of a few thousand zones, refreshed every five minutes from traffic data. For turn-by-turn directions we use a routing provider; for 'which driver is closest' our own map is faster and cheaper."

Common mistakes

  • Running Dijkstra once per candidate instead of once from the target on the reversed graph.
  • Allowing negative weights through the data pipeline.
  • Rebuilding the graph on every request.
  • Using an array sorted on every insert as the priority queue (O(n) per operation) instead of a heap.
  • Skipping the stale-entry check with lazy deletion, which corrupts distances.

Interview questions

  1. "Implement Dijkstra with a binary heap and explain the stale-entry trick." Expected: lazy deletion; skip popped entries whose distance exceeds the recorded best. Follow-up: complexity, and why not a Fibonacci heap in practice?
  2. "Why does Dijkstra fail with negative edges, and what would you use instead?" Expected: early finalization assumption breaks; Bellman-Ford, or fix the model.
  3. "Rank 40 drivers by travel time to a pickup point efficiently." Expected: one run from the pickup on the reversed graph.
  4. "How would you serve ETAs at 500 RPS on a 6,000-node graph?" Expected: in-memory graph with scheduled reload, single-source cache per pickup zone, early exit.
  5. "When would you not use your own Dijkstra for routing?" Expected: road-level graphs with millions of nodes; use a routing engine with contraction hierarchies.

Practical exercise

Build a 5,000-zone graph with 20,000 random edges in PostgreSQL. Implement MinHeap, dijkstra and EtaService. Benchmark 1,000 random estimate calls and 100 rankRiders calls with 40 riders each. Then inject a negative edge and show that all three guards (constraint, filter, throw) catch it.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Median estimate under 10 ms; rankRiders under 15 ms.
  • A property test compares dijkstra against a brute-force Bellman-Ford on small random graphs and finds no mismatch.
  • The negative-edge insert fails at the constraint; if the constraint is dropped, the reload filters it; if both are bypassed, the algorithm throws.

8.14 Topological sorting

Concept

A topological order of a directed graph is a sequence of its nodes in which every edge points forward: if A must happen before B, A appears before B. It exists only if the graph has no cycles (a directed acyclic graph, DAG). Topological sorting is how you turn "these things depend on those things" into "do them in this order".

Backend systems are full of DAGs: job pipelines ("load orders after extracting customers"), database migrations ("add the column before the index"), module initialization ("the database module before the modules that use it"), build pipelines ("test after build, deploy after test"), package dependency trees.

Why does it exist?

Because dependencies are declared locally ("B needs A") and execution needs a global order. Without topological sorting you hard-code orders that break when someone adds a dependency, or you run things in declaration order and hope. Its second gift is cycle detection: if the sort cannot place every node, the dependencies are contradictory, and you find out before running anything.

Mental model

Imagine getting dressed. Socks before shoes, shirt before jacket, but socks and shirt in either order. There is no single correct order, only correct orders, and there are many. Topological sort produces one. If someone declares "shoes before socks" and "socks before shoes", no order exists, and the sort tells you so instead of leaving you standing in the hallway.

How it works

Kahn's algorithm (the one to use in backends, because it is iterative, detects cycles, and makes tie-breaking explicit):

  1. Compute the in-degree (number of incoming edges) of every node.
  2. Put every node with in-degree 0 into a ready set. If you want a deterministic or prioritized order, make the ready set a min-heap keyed by priority.
  3. Take a node from the ready set, append it to the output, and decrement the in-degree of each of its successors. Any successor that reaches 0 becomes ready.
  4. Repeat until the ready set is empty.
  5. If the output has fewer nodes than the graph, the remaining nodes are on or downstream of a cycle. Report them.

Complexity O(V + E), or O((V + E) log V) with a heap.

DFS-based sort: run DFS, record nodes in post-order (when they turn black), reverse the list. Detects cycles via gray nodes. Same complexity; less natural for "run everything that is ready now in parallel".

// scheduling/topological-sort.ts
import { MinHeap } from '../graph/min-heap';

export interface Task { id: string; dependsOn: string[]; priority: number; } // lower priority number runs first

export interface TopoResult { order: string[]; cyclic: string[]; }

export function topologicalOrder(tasks: Task[]): TopoResult {
  const byId = new Map(tasks.map((t) => [t.id, t]));
