  const inDegree = new Map<string, number>(tasks.map((t) => [t.id, 0]));
  const successors = new Map<string, string[]>(tasks.map((t) => [t.id, []]));

  for (const t of tasks) {
    for (const dep of t.dependsOn) {
      if (!byId.has(dep)) throw new Error(`task ${t.id} depends on unknown task ${dep}`);
      successors.get(dep)!.push(t.id);
      inDegree.set(t.id, inDegree.get(t.id)! + 1);
    }
  }

  const ready = new MinHeap<Task>((t) => t.priority);        // among ready tasks, highest priority first
  for (const t of tasks) if (inDegree.get(t.id) === 0) ready.push(t);

  const order: string[] = [];
  while (ready.size > 0) {
    const t = ready.pop()!;
    order.push(t.id);
    for (const s of successors.get(t.id)!) {
      const d = inDegree.get(s)! - 1;
      inDegree.set(s, d);
      if (d === 0) ready.push(byId.get(s)!);
    }
  }
  const cyclic = tasks.filter((t) => inDegree.get(t.id)! > 0).map((t) => t.id);
  return { order, cyclic };
}

Where you meet it:

  • Job DAGs. A nightly pipeline: extract_customers, extract_orders (independent), build_customer_orders (needs both), revenue_report and churn_report (need the join). Kahn's ready set at each step is exactly the set of jobs that can run in parallel right now. The job scheduler worked example later in this part builds on this.
  • Database migrations. TypeORM runs migrations in timestamp order; the timestamp is an implicit topological order that assumes nobody creates a dependency backward in time. Two branches merged out of order can violate it: branch A's migration (timestamp 10:00) adds a column, branch B's migration (timestamp 09:30, written earlier but merged later) creates an index on that column. On a fresh database B runs first and fails. The only reliable defense is CI running all migrations from an empty database on every merge.
  • NestJS module initialization. Nest builds a graph from imports, resolves providers in dependency order, and calls lifecycle hooks (onModuleInit, onApplicationBootstrap) module by module, ordering modules by their distance from the root so that dependencies initialize before dependents. A circular import between modules breaks the graph; Nest reports something like Nest cannot create the AuthModule instance. The module at index [0] of the AuthModule "imports" array is undefined. Potential causes: A circular dependency between modules. Use forwardRef() to avoid it. forwardRef() tells Nest to resolve the reference lazily, which is the framework's way of admitting the graph has a cycle and asking you to promise it will work out.
  • Build pipelines. GitHub Actions needs: declares a DAG; the runner topologically sorts it and executes independent jobs concurrently.
flowchart LR
    Config["ConfigModule"] --> Db["DatabaseModule"]
    Config --> Cache["CacheModule"]
    Db --> Users["UsersModule"]
    Db --> Orders["OrdersModule"]
    Cache --> Orders
    Users --> Auth["AuthModule"]
    Auth --> Orders
    Orders --> App["AppModule"]

One valid initialization order: Config, Db, Cache, Users, Auth, Orders, App. Config and nothing else is ready first; then Db and Cache are both ready (either order); and so on.

Practical example

An ETL pipeline definition, stored as rows in a pipeline_steps table with a depends_on array column, is loaded and sorted before execution. The planner rejects the definition if cyclic is non-empty and returns the offending step ids to the person who edited it. Execution then walks the order, dispatching every step whose dependencies have completed. The order also serves as the display order in the operations UI, so humans see the pipeline in a sensible sequence.

NestJS example

A planner service and a GitHub Actions pipeline showing the same DAG in two forms:

// pipelines/pipeline-planner.service.ts
import { BadRequestException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { PipelineStep } from './pipeline-step.entity';
import { topologicalOrder } from '../scheduling/topological-sort';

@Injectable()
export class PipelinePlannerService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(PipelineStep) private readonly steps: Repository<PipelineStep>) {}

  async plan(pipelineId: string): Promise<string[]> {
    const steps = await this.steps.find({ where: { pipelineId } });
    const { order, cyclic } = topologicalOrder(
      steps.map((s) => ({ id: s.id, dependsOn: s.dependsOn, priority: s.priority })),
    );
    if (cyclic.length > 0) {
      throw new BadRequestException(`Pipeline ${pipelineId} has a dependency cycle involving: ${cyclic.join(', ')}`);
    }
    return order;
  }
}
# .github/workflows/ci.yml: a DAG the runner topologically sorts
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci && npm run build
  unit-tests:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm test
  migration-check:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test }
        ports: ['5432:5432']
    steps:
      - run: npm run typeorm migration:run   # from an empty database: catches out-of-order migrations
  deploy-staging:
    needs: [unit-tests, migration-check]      # runs only when both parents succeed
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh staging

unit-tests and migration-check are both ready after build and run in parallel; deploy-staging waits for both. That is Kahn's algorithm executed by the CI runner.

PostgreSQL example

Migration ordering as the database sees it: TypeORM records applied migrations and applies pending ones in ascending timestamp order.

SELECT id, "timestamp", name FROM migrations ORDER BY "timestamp";
 id |   timestamp   |                  name
----+---------------+-----------------------------------------
 41 | 1717400000000 | AddFulfilmentStatusToOrders1717400000000
 42 | 1717398000000 | IndexOrdersFulfilmentStatus1717398000000   <- applied AFTER 41 on this DB

Here migration 42 has an earlier timestamp than 41 but was applied later, because it was merged later and this database had already run 41. On a fresh database, 42 runs first and fails with column "fulfilment_status" does not exist. The dependency edge (41 before 42) exists in reality but not in the timestamps. Fix the timestamp in the branch before merging, and keep the fresh-database migration job in CI.

Production scenario

A data platform runs 340 nightly jobs with 900 dependency edges. The scheduler computes the topological order once per run (well under a millisecond), then keeps the in-degree map live: when a job completes, it decrements its successors and enqueues those that reach zero, with a priority heap so revenue-critical reports go first when workers are scarce. Independent branches run on 20 workers in parallel; the critical path (the longest chain of dependent jobs) is what determines when the last report lands, and it is the number the platform team optimizes.

Failure scenario

At 01:00 the nightly pipeline starts and nothing runs. No errors, no logs, 20 idle workers. An engineer had added refresh_dimensions as a dependency of extract_customers, and refresh_dimensions already depended (through two other jobs) on extract_customers. The DAG became cyclic; every job had in-degree greater than zero after the sort; the scheduler's ready set was empty from the start. The planner's cyclic check had been removed months earlier "because it never triggered". It was restored, wired to fail the deploy of a pipeline definition, and the scheduler now alerts if the ready set is empty while unfinished jobs remain.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Cycles. No order exists; detect and name the nodes.
  • Unknown dependencies. A task depends on an id that does not exist; fail early.
  • Non-determinism. Multiple valid orders; without a tie-break rule, two runs differ, which confuses debugging. Use priority then id.
  • Dynamic graphs. Dependencies added while the pipeline runs; version the definition per run.
  • Partial failure. A failed job should block its successors but not unrelated branches; track state per node, not globally.
  • Migration timestamps as a proxy for order. Breaks on out-of-order merges; only a fresh-database run catches it.
  • forwardRef everywhere. A NestJS module graph with many forward references is a design smell: the modules are one module in denial.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats any "depends on" field as a DAG and validates it at write time, not run time. They ask what the critical path is, because parallelism cannot shorten it. They keep tie-breaking explicit so runs are reproducible. For migrations they trust CI, not timestamps. For NestJS they treat a circular module dependency as a signal to move shared providers into a lower module rather than reaching for forwardRef.

To a product manager: "The pipeline is a set of steps that depend on each other. We compute the order automatically and run independent steps at the same time. The total time is set by the longest chain, which right now is extract -> join -> revenue report; making any other step faster won't shorten the night."

Common mistakes

  • Running jobs in declaration order.
  • Dropping the cycle check.
  • Not distinguishing "blocked by a failed dependency" from "not yet ready".
  • Relying on migration timestamps without a fresh-database CI check.
  • Using DFS post-order when the scheduler needs a live ready set.

Interview questions

  1. "Implement Kahn's algorithm and explain how it detects cycles." Expected: in-degree map, ready queue, leftovers with in-degree above zero are cyclic. Follow-up: how would you add priorities?
  2. "How does NestJS decide the order in which modules initialize, and what does forwardRef do?" Expected: dependency graph from imports; lifecycle hooks ordered by module distance; forwardRef defers resolution to tolerate a cycle.
  3. "Why can migrations that pass on every developer machine fail in production or CI?" Expected: timestamp order versus real dependency order after out-of-order merges; fresh-database runs expose it.
  4. "What is the critical path of a DAG and why does it matter for a scheduler?" Expected: longest dependency chain; bounds total time regardless of workers.
  5. "How do you handle a job failure in a DAG scheduler?" Expected: mark successors blocked, let independent branches continue, support retry and resume from the failed node.

Practical exercise

Model a 12-step pipeline as rows with depends_on arrays, including two independent branches and a shared final step. Implement topologicalOrder with priorities, a planner endpoint that rejects cycles with the offending ids, and a simulation that runs steps with 3 fake workers and records the wall time. Then add a cycle and a bad dependency and confirm the responses.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The order respects every edge (verify with an assertion over all edges).
  • The same input produces the same order on every run.
  • The simulation's wall time equals the critical path length when workers are not the bottleneck.
  • Cyclic and unknown-dependency definitions return 400 with specific ids.

8.15 Greedy algorithms

Concept

A greedy algorithm builds a solution one step at a time, always taking the choice that looks best right now, and never going back to reconsider. Sort the options by some score, walk the list, take what fits. That is the whole strategy.

Greedy is fast (usually one sort plus one pass: O(n log n)) and simple to explain, and for a specific set of problems it is provably optimal: interval scheduling, minimum spanning trees, Huffman coding, Dijkstra itself, coin change with well-behaved denominations, fractional knapsack. For everything else it is a heuristic: often good, sometimes badly wrong, and you must know which case you are in.

Why does it exist?

Because most allocation and scheduling problems in a backend do not need the optimal answer; they need a good answer in milliseconds. Batching deliveries, assigning drivers to shifts, splitting a payment across invoices, choosing which warehouse ships which line: the exact optimum is often NP-hard, and a greedy pass gets within a few percent at O(n log n). The skill is recognizing the small set of problems where greedy is exactly right, the larger set where it is good enough, and the dangerous set where it is wrong and a product rule or dynamic programming is required.

Mental model

Imagine filling a shopping bag at a market with a fixed budget, always buying the cheapest item you have not bought yet. You will get the maximum number of items: greedy is optimal for that goal. Now suppose the goal is the maximum weight of groceries for the budget. Buying by "weight per rupee" gets you close, but the last item might not fit and a different combination might have packed the bag better. Greedy was a good heuristic, not an optimum. Now suppose you must pay exactly 6 with coins of 1, 3 and 4. Greedy takes 4, then 1, then 1: three coins. The optimum is 3 and 3: two coins. Greedy was wrong, and it gave no hint that it was.

How it works

Greedy is correct when the problem has two properties: the greedy-choice property (a locally best choice is part of some globally optimal solution) and optimal substructure (after making that choice, what remains is a smaller instance of the same problem). Proving these is the textbook's job; the engineer's job is to remember which everyday problems have them.

Problems where greedy is optimal:

Problem Greedy rule Backend shape
Interval scheduling (max non-overlapping intervals) Sort by end time, take each interval that starts after the last taken ends Choose the maximum number of non-conflicting bookings for one resource (one meeting room, one delivery van)
Interval partitioning (min resources to cover all intervals) Sort by start; assign each to a free resource, else open a new one; min-heap of end times Minimum number of drivers to cover all shifts; minimum meeting rooms
Coin change with canonical denominations Take the largest denomination that fits Splitting a gift-card balance into fixed denominations; making change in a POS
Fractional knapsack Sort by value per unit, take in order Filling a truck by value density when partial loads are allowed
Minimum spanning tree (Kruskal) Sort edges by weight, add if it connects two components (union-find) Cheapest network linking warehouses
Shortest path, non-negative weights (Dijkstra) Always finalize the nearest node ETA

Problems where greedy is a heuristic (good, not optimal):

  • Delivery batching and routing. Nearest-neighbor routing is typically 20–25% longer than optimal; 2-opt improvement passes recover most of that.
  • Bin packing (fit items into the fewest boxes). First-fit-decreasing (sort items by size descending, place each in the first box with room) uses at most about 11/9 of the optimal number of boxes plus one. Optimal bin packing is NP-hard.
  • Load balancing across workers by "assign to the least loaded" is within a factor of 4/3 of optimal.

Problems where greedy is wrong:

  • 0/1 knapsack. Taking items by value density can miss the optimal set entirely.
  • Coin change with non-canonical denominations (the 1, 3, 4 example).
  • Shortest path with negative edges.
  • Weighted interval scheduling (intervals with different values): earliest-end greedy ignores value; needs dynamic programming.

Two implementations you will reuse. Interval partitioning for shift coverage:

// scheduling/shift-coverage.ts
import { MinHeap } from '../graph/min-heap';

export interface Shift { id: string; startsAt: number; endsAt: number; } // epoch ms

// Minimum number of drivers needed so every shift has a driver; returns assignments. O(n log n).
export function assignDrivers(shifts: Shift[]): Map<string, number> {
  const sorted = [...shifts].sort((a, b) => a.startsAt - b.startsAt);
  const freeAt = new MinHeap<{ driver: number; freeAt: number }>((d) => d.freeAt); // driver who frees up soonest
  const assignment = new Map<string, number>();
  let driverCount = 0;

  for (const shift of sorted) {
    let driver: number;
    const soonest = freeAt.size > 0 ? freeAt.pop()! : undefined;
    if (soonest && soonest.freeAt <= shift.startsAt) {
      driver = soonest.driver;                     // reuse: they are free before this shift starts
    } else {
      if (soonest) freeAt.push(soonest);           // not free yet: put them back
      driver = driverCount;                         // open a new driver
      driverCount += 1;
    }
    assignment.set(shift.id, driver);
    freeAt.push({ driver, freeAt: shift.endsAt });
  }
  return assignment;                                // driverCount === max overlap at any instant
}

Delivery batching by proximity and time window, a greedy heuristic with explicit caps:

// dispatch/delivery-batcher.ts
export interface Order { id: string; geohash6: string; readyAt: number; dueAt: number; }
export interface Batch { orders: Order[]; dueAt: number; }

// Groups orders sharing a coarse geohash whose windows overlap, greedily by earliest due time. O(n log n).
export function batchOrders(orders: Order[], maxPerBatch = 4, maxSpanMs = 15 * 60_000): Batch[] {
  const byCell = new Map<string, Order[]>();
  for (const o of orders) (byCell.get(o.geohash6) ?? byCell.set(o.geohash6, []).get(o.geohash6)!).push(o);

  const batches: Batch[] = [];
  for (const cell of byCell.values()) {
    cell.sort((a, b) => a.dueAt - b.dueAt);          // most urgent first
    let current: Order[] = [];
    for (const o of cell) {
      const fits = current.length < maxPerBatch && (current.length === 0 || o.dueAt - current[0].readyAt <= maxSpanMs);
      if (!fits) { batches.push({ orders: current, dueAt: current[0].dueAt }); current = []; }
      current.push(o);
    }
    if (current.length > 0) batches.push({ orders: current, dueAt: current[0].dueAt });
  }
  return batches;
}

Neither function is optimal for total rider distance; both are predictable, explainable and fast, which is what a dispatcher running every 30 seconds needs.

Practical example

A restaurant-delivery platform batches orders every 30 seconds per city zone. Optimal batching (minimizing total distance under time windows) is a vehicle-routing problem that a solver takes seconds to minutes on. The greedy batcher above runs in under 5 ms for 2,000 pending orders and produces batches about 8% longer in distance than the solver's, measured offline. Product accepted the 8% for the 30-second cadence and the ability to explain any batch to a rider ("these three orders are in the same area and due within 15 minutes").

NestJS example

Exposing the coverage calculation behind a validated DTO, with the greedy result and its guarantee stated in the response:

// scheduling/shift-planning.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Post } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ArrayMaxSize, IsArray, IsInt, IsString, Min, ValidateNested } from 'class-validator';
import { Type } from 'class-transformer';
import { assignDrivers } from './shift-coverage';

class ShiftDto {
  @IsString() id!: string;
  @IsInt() @Min(0) startsAt!: number;
  @IsInt() @Min(0) endsAt!: number;
}

class PlanShiftsDto {
  @IsArray() @ArrayMaxSize(5000) @ValidateNested({ each: true }) @Type(() => ShiftDto)
  shifts!: ShiftDto[];
}

@Controller('shift-plans')
export class ShiftPlanningController {
  @Post()
  plan(@Body() dto: PlanShiftsDto): { driversNeeded: number; assignments: Record<string, number> } {
    const invalid = dto.shifts.filter((s) => s.endsAt <= s.startsAt);
    if (invalid.length > 0) throw new Error(`shifts with non-positive duration: ${invalid.map((s) => s.id).join(', ')}`);
    const assignment = assignDrivers(dto.shifts);
    const driversNeeded = new Set(assignment.values()).size;   // equals the maximum concurrent shifts: optimal
    return { driversNeeded, assignments: Object.fromEntries(assignment) };
  }
}

(Replace the thrown Error with a proper BadRequestException in real code; the point is the ArrayMaxSize cap on n and the optimality note.)

PostgreSQL example

Greedy scheduling decisions must be enforced at write time, not just computed at plan time. PostgreSQL's exclusion constraints stop two shifts for the same driver from overlapping, regardless of which service wrote them:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

CREATE TABLE driver_shifts (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  driver_id uuid NOT NULL,
  during tstzrange NOT NULL,
  EXCLUDE USING gist (driver_id WITH =, during WITH &&)   -- no overlapping ranges per driver
);

-- Interval scheduling in SQL: candidate shifts sorted by end time for the greedy pass
SELECT id, lower(during) AS starts_at, upper(during) AS ends_at
FROM open_shifts
WHERE during && tstzrange($1, $2)
ORDER BY upper(during);

An insert that overlaps fails with conflicting key value violates exclusion constraint, which is the database telling you that a greedy assignment made elsewhere was stale.

Coin-change-style allocation also has a natural SQL form when the business rule is greedy by definition. Applying a payment to the oldest open invoices first (FIFO) is greedy, and it is correct because accounting says so:

-- Allocate $1 cents to open invoices, oldest first
WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT id, balance_cents,
         sum(balance_cents) OVER (ORDER BY issued_at, id) AS running_total
  FROM invoices WHERE customer_id = $2 AND balance_cents > 0
)
SELECT id,
       least(balance_cents, greatest(0, $1 - (running_total - balance_cents))) AS applied_cents
FROM ordered
WHERE running_total - balance_cents < $1;

TypeORM example

Allocating a payment greedily inside a transaction with row locks, so two concurrent payments cannot both apply to the same invoice balance:

async allocatePayment(customerId: string, amountCents: number): Promise<void> {
  await this.dataSource.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const invoices = await tx
      .createQueryBuilder(Invoice, 'i')
      .setLock('pessimistic_write')                       // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
      .where('i.customer_id = :customerId AND i.balance_cents > 0', { customerId })
      .orderBy('i.issued_at', 'ASC').addOrderBy('i.id', 'ASC')   // greedy rule: oldest first
      .getMany();

    let remaining = amountCents;
    for (const inv of invoices) {
      if (remaining === 0) break;
      const applied = Math.min(remaining, inv.balanceCents);
      await tx.update(Invoice, { id: inv.id }, { balanceCents: inv.balanceCents - applied });
      await tx.insert(PaymentAllocation, { invoiceId: inv.id, amountCents: applied });
      remaining -= applied;
    }
    if (remaining > 0) await tx.insert(CustomerCredit, { customerId, amountCents: remaining });
  });
}

Sequelize example

await sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  const invoices = await Invoice.findAll({
    where: { customerId, balanceCents: { [Op.gt]: 0 } },
    order: [['issuedAt', 'ASC'], ['id', 'ASC']],
    lock: t.LOCK.UPDATE,
    transaction: t,
  });
  let remaining = amountCents;
  for (const inv of invoices) {
    if (remaining === 0) break;
    const applied = Math.min(remaining, inv.balanceCents);
    await inv.decrement('balanceCents', { by: applied, transaction: t });
    await PaymentAllocation.create({ invoiceId: inv.id, amountCents: applied }, { transaction: t });
    remaining -= applied;
  }
});

Production scenario

A logistics platform assigns 12,000 daily shifts to a pool of drivers in 40 cities. Interval partitioning per city runs in about 20 ms total and yields the minimum driver count per city (provably, because it equals the maximum overlap). The planners then apply constraints greedy cannot see (driver preferences, maximum hours per week, licenses), which turns the problem into one for a constraint solver that runs for 3 minutes overnight. The greedy result is the lower bound the planners use to sanity-check the solver: if the solver needs 15% more drivers than greedy, something in the constraints is too tight.

Failure scenario

At 16:45 the finance team notices customers are being under-refunded. A "split refund across original payment methods" feature used greedy allocation by largest-balance-first across gift cards with fixed denominations, and a rounding rule that dropped remainders under a cent. For a refund of 6.00 across cards of 4.00 and 3.00 denominations, greedy took 4.00 and then could not place the remaining 2.00 on a 3.00 card without a partial, which the gift-card provider disallowed, so it silently refunded 4.00. The 1, 3, 4 coin problem, in production, with money. The fix used a small dynamic program over the denominations (next section) and an explicit "cannot split exactly" error path that routes the remainder to store credit.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Non-canonical denominations. Greedy coin change fails; verify the denomination set or use DP.
  • Ties. Two intervals with the same end time; deterministic tie-breaking (by id) keeps the plan reproducible.
  • Stale inputs. Greedy decisions based on a snapshot conflict with concurrent writes; enforce with constraints and locks.
  • Caps. Every greedy batcher needs maximum batch size, maximum span, maximum distance; without caps the "best local choice" builds one giant batch.
  • Unbounded input. O(n log n) is fine until n is unbounded; cap the DTO.
  • Metric mismatch. Greedy by "nearest" optimizes distance; the business wants "on time". Choose the sort key to match the goal.
  • Fairness. Greedy "assign to the best driver" starves everyone else; add rotation or fairness constraints.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior asks three questions: Is greedy provably optimal here (interval problems, canonical coins, MST, Dijkstra)? If not, how far from optimal is it, measured offline against a solver on real data? And what caps and constraints stop the greedy choice from doing something absurd on unusual input?

They prefer greedy when the answer is needed in milliseconds, must be explainable to a human, and "within a few percent" is acceptable. They refuse greedy for money-splitting and any problem with exact-fit requirements unless the denominations are canonical, because the failure is silent.

To a product manager: "Batching by 'closest orders first' gets us 92% of the perfect answer instantly, and every rider can see why they got their batch. The perfect answer takes minutes to compute and is impossible to explain."

Common mistakes

  • Assuming greedy is optimal because it "makes sense".
  • Greedy allocation of money without checking exact-fit feasibility.
  • Sorting by the wrong key (distance when the goal is lateness).
  • No caps on batch size or span.
  • Computing an assignment greedily and writing it without locks or constraints.

Interview questions

  1. "Minimum number of drivers to cover a set of shifts. Algorithm, complexity, and why it is optimal." Expected: sort by start, heap of end times, O(n log n); the count equals the maximum overlap, which any solution needs. Follow-up: how would you add a maximum-hours-per-driver rule?
  2. "Give a backend case where greedy is provably wrong and how you would detect it." Expected: non-canonical denominations in refund splitting; verify with DP or an exact-fit check.
  3. "Nearest-neighbor delivery routing: how bad is it and how do you improve cheaply?" Expected: around 25% worse; 2-opt passes.
  4. "When is greedy the right choice over an optimal solver in production?" Expected: latency budget, explainability, "good enough" measured offline.
  5. "How do you enforce a greedy schedule against concurrent writers?" Expected: exclusion constraints, row locks, idempotent assignment writes.

Practical exercise

Implement assignDrivers and batchOrders, then write a brute-force checker for assignDrivers on small random inputs proving the count equals the maximum overlap. Implement greedy coin change and test it with denominations [1, 5, 10, 25] and [1, 3, 4] against a brute-force optimum.

Acceptance criteria:

  • assignDrivers matches brute force on 1,000 random cases.
  • The greedy coin test fails for [1, 3, 4] with amount 6 and the test documents it as expected behavior.
  • batchOrders respects all caps on adversarial input (2,000 orders in one cell).

8.16 Dynamic programming

Concept

Dynamic programming (DP) solves a problem by breaking it into overlapping subproblems, solving each subproblem once, and remembering the answer. Two mechanics: memoization (top-down: write the recursive solution, cache results by input) and tabulation (bottom-up: fill a table from the smallest subproblems upward). Both turn exponential brute force into polynomial time when the problem has optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems.

DP appears in a backend less often than searching or sorting, but where it appears the alternative is either an exponential brute force that times out or a greedy shortcut that gives wrong answers. Cart promotion optimization, shipping box selection, fuzzy text matching, diffing, and certain scheduling and pricing problems are DP-shaped.

Why does it exist?

Because "try every combination" is exponential and greedy is sometimes wrong. With 20 applicable coupons, "try every subset" is a million combinations; with 30 it is a billion; the request times out. DP notices that the best result for the first k coupons within budget b does not depend on how you got there, only on k and b, so there are only k * b distinct subproblems to solve, not 2^k paths.

Mental model

Imagine climbing a staircase where you can take one or two steps at a time and want to count the ways to reach the top. Brute force explores every sequence of steps: exponential. But the number of ways to reach step 10 is just (ways to reach step 9) + (ways to reach step 8), and those two numbers do not care how you reached them. Write each step's count on the step itself as you go, and you climb once. That note on each step is the DP table. Every DP problem is "what is the smallest set of facts about the past that the future needs", and those facts become the table's dimensions.

How it works

  1. Define the state: what parameters identify a subproblem? (Item index and remaining capacity; position in string A and position in string B.)
  2. Define the recurrence: how does the answer for a state depend on smaller states?
  3. Define the base cases.
  4. Choose memoization (natural for sparse state spaces, recursion-shaped problems) or tabulation (iterative, cache-friendly, no stack risk, easy to optimize memory by keeping only the last row).
  5. Complexity is the number of states times the work per state.
flowchart TB
    A["Optimization over combinations"] --> B{"Is greedy provably optimal?"}
    B -->|"yes: intervals, canonical coins, MST"| C["Greedy: O n log n"]
    B -->|"no"| D{"State space small? items x capacity under ~10 million"}
    D -->|"yes"| E["Dynamic programming: exact answer"]
    D -->|"no"| F{"Is near-optimal acceptable?"}
    F -->|"yes"| G["Greedy heuristic with caps, or local search"]
    F -->|"no"| H["Constraint solver offline, or reduce the problem"]

0/1 knapsack for cart promotions: each eligible promotion has a "weight" (the marketing cost it consumes from a per-order budget, or the loyalty points it burns) and a "value" (discount to the customer); choose the subset with maximum value within the budget, each promotion at most once.

// promotions/knapsack.ts
export interface Candidate { id: string; cost: number; value: number; } // cost and value in integer cents

// Maximum total value with total cost <= budget, each candidate used at most once.
// Time O(n * budget), memory O(budget) using a single row. Returns chosen ids.
export function bestSubset(candidates: Candidate[], budget: number): { value: number; chosen: string[] } {
  const n = candidates.length;
  const best = new Array<number>(budget + 1).fill(0);           // best[b] = max value using cost <= b
  const take = candidates.map(() => new Uint8Array(budget + 1));  // take[i][b] = did we take item i at budget b

  for (let i = 0; i < n; i += 1) {
    const { cost, value } = candidates[i];
    for (let b = budget; b >= cost; b -= 1) {                    // descending so each item is used at most once
      const withItem = best[b - cost] + value;
      if (withItem > best[b]) { best[b] = withItem; take[i][b] = 1; }
    }
  }

  const chosen: string[] = [];                                    // walk back through the decisions
  let b = budget;
  for (let i = n - 1; i >= 0; i -= 1) {
    if (take[i][b] === 1) { chosen.push(candidates[i].id); b -= candidates[i].cost; }
  }
  return { value: best[budget], chosen: chosen.reverse() };
}

With 25 promotions and a budget expressed in whole rupees up to 2,000, that is 50,000 cell updates: microseconds. Note the integer arithmetic: money in cents, never floats, and a budget with a bounded, discretized range, because the table has budget + 1 columns.

Shipping box selection. True 3D bin packing is NP-hard; production systems use a volume-and-dimension heuristic. The DP-shaped piece is "can this subset of items reach a total volume within a box's capacity" (subset sum), and, more usefully, "the smallest box in which the items fit" by trying boxes from smallest to largest with a fast feasibility check. For splitting a shipment into the fewest boxes, first-fit-decreasing (greedy) is the standard, and DP over subsets is only feasible for very small item counts (2^n states, so n up to about 20).

Edit distance (Levenshtein) counts the minimum insertions, deletions and substitutions to turn one string into another. O(n * m) time, O(min(n, m)) memory with two rows. It is the re-ranking step of fuzzy product search:

// search/levenshtein.ts
export function levenshtein(a: string, b: string, maxDistance = Infinity): number {
  if (a.length < b.length) [a, b] = [b, a];                        // keep the shorter string as columns
  let prev = Array.from({ length: b.length + 1 }, (_, j) => j);   // distance from "" to b[0..j]
  let curr = new Array<number>(b.length + 1);

  for (let i = 1; i <= a.length; i += 1) {
    curr[0] = i;
    let rowMin = i;
    for (let j = 1; j <= b.length; j += 1) {
      const cost = a.charCodeAt(i - 1) === b.charCodeAt(j - 1) ? 0 : 1;
      curr[j] = Math.min(prev[j] + 1, curr[j - 1] + 1, prev[j - 1] + cost);  // delete, insert, substitute
      if (curr[j] < rowMin) rowMin = curr[j];
    }
    if (rowMin > maxDistance) return maxDistance + 1;              // early exit: cannot get back under the bound
    [prev, curr] = [curr, prev];
  }
  return prev[b.length];
}

The maxDistance early exit matters: for typo tolerance you only care whether the distance is at most 2, and most candidates blow past that in the first few rows.

Why DP appears rarely but matters. Most backend work is I/O-bound and the "algorithm" is a query plan. DP shows up in the CPU-bound corners: pricing and promotion engines, packing and allocation, text similarity, diffing (version comparison of documents), and some scheduling. It appears in interviews far more than in code, but the shape recognition matters daily: when a PR says "we try all combinations of coupons", a senior sees 2^n and asks what n can be.

Practical example

A checkout applies at most one promotion per "exclusivity group" (one shipping promo, one product promo, one payment-method promo) and each promotion has a marketing cost charged to a campaign budget. The naive implementation enumerated all subsets of applicable promotions (typically 8–12, occasionally 25 during festivals) and ran fine until a festival day produced 28 applicable promotions for some carts: 268 million subsets, and the checkout timed out. The knapsack with a group constraint (one item per group, which is the "multiple-choice knapsack" variant with one extra loop) ran in under a millisecond.

NestJS example

// promotions/promotion-optimizer.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { bestSubset, Candidate } from './knapsack';

export interface ApplicablePromotion { id: string; discountCents: number; marketingCostCents: number; }

@Injectable()
export class PromotionOptimizerService {
  private static readonly MAX_CANDIDATES = 60;      // n * budget bounded: 60 * 20000 = 1.2M cells, ~2 ms
  private static readonly BUDGET_UNIT_CENTS = 100;  // discretize the budget to whole currency units

  choose(applicable: ApplicablePromotion[], campaignBudgetCents: number): { discountCents: number; promotionIds: string[] } {
    if (applicable.length > PromotionOptimizerService.MAX_CANDIDATES) {
      // Keep the table bounded: pre-trim by discount, then solve exactly over the survivors
      applicable = [...applicable].sort((a, b) => b.discountCents - a.discountCents)
        .slice(0, PromotionOptimizerService.MAX_CANDIDATES);
    }
    const unit = PromotionOptimizerService.BUDGET_UNIT_CENTS;
    const candidates: Candidate[] = applicable.map((p) => ({
      id: p.id,
      cost: Math.ceil(p.marketingCostCents / unit),    // round cost UP so the budget is never exceeded
      value: p.discountCents,
    }));
    const budget = Math.floor(campaignBudgetCents / unit);
    const result = bestSubset(candidates, budget);
    return { discountCents: result.value, promotionIds: result.chosen };
  }
}

The two constants are the engineering: they bound the state space so the worst case is known (~2 ms), and the rounding direction guarantees the budget constraint holds after discretization.

PostgreSQL example

Fuzzy product search is a two-stage pipeline: the database shortlists candidates with a trigram index (covered in the search worked example later in this part), and edit distance re-ranks the shortlist. PostgreSQL's fuzzystrmatch extension provides levenshtein in SQL, so for small shortlists the whole thing can stay in the database:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS fuzzystrmatch;
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY products_name_trgm_idx ON products USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);

-- Stage 1: trigram similarity shortlist via the GIN index (fast, approximate)
-- Stage 2: exact edit distance on the shortlist (DP, O(n*m) per row, only ~100 rows)
SELECT id, name, levenshtein_less_equal(lower(name), lower($1), 3) AS distance
FROM products
WHERE name % $1                                  -- pg_trgm similarity operator, uses the GIN index
ORDER BY distance, similarity(name, $1) DESC
LIMIT 10;

levenshtein_less_equal(a, b, k) is the bounded version with the same early exit as the TypeScript above. Never run levenshtein over the whole table in the WHERE clause: that is O(rows * n * m) with no index, seconds on a million products.

Production scenario

A product search endpoint handles 300 RPS. Stage 1 (trigram shortlist of up to 200 candidates) costs about 3 ms; stage 2 (Levenshtein re-rank of 200 names of about 40 characters, in Node) costs 200 × 40 × 40 = 320,000 cell updates, about 1 ms. Doing stage 2 for all 2 million products would be 3.2 billion updates per query: the difference between 4 ms and 30 seconds is not the DP, it is bounding what the DP runs over.

Failure scenario

At 19:10 on the first evening of a festival sale, checkout p99 climbs from 400 ms to 25 seconds and the service's event loop lag alarm fires. The promotion engine's "find the best combination" was a recursive subset enumeration with a memo keyed by the set of chosen ids, which is not a smaller state space at all: 2^n keys. At n = 26 it was 67 million map entries and 4 GB of heap before the pod was OOMKilled. The memoization was decorative. The rewrite keyed the state by (index, remainingBudget), which is what DP means: a state space that is polynomial because it forgets the path.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Wrong state definition. Memoizing on something that grows exponentially (the chosen set) gives no speedup and eats memory.
  • Unbounded table dimensions. Budget in cents up to 10 million makes a 10-million-column row per item; discretize.
  • Floating point. Use integers; DP over floats accumulates rounding and makes "equal" comparisons unreliable.
  • Reconstruction memory. Keeping take[i][b] for path reconstruction is O(n * budget) bytes; use Uint8Array and bound n.
  • Recursion depth in memoized versions. Top-down DP over strings of 20,000 characters overflows the stack; use tabulation.
  • NP-hard core problems. Bin packing, general vehicle routing and multi-dimensional knapsack are exponential in the worst case; DP is only feasible for small instances, otherwise heuristics or a solver.
  • Adversarial input sizes. A user-controlled n (number of coupons, length of search string) needs a cap before it reaches the DP.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior recognizes the shapes: "best subset under a constraint" (knapsack), "similarity between two sequences" (edit distance), "count or optimize over paths with a small memory of the past" (staircase, scheduling). They then bound the state space explicitly, in constants with comments, so the worst case is a known number of milliseconds. They keep DP out of the request path unless states * work is under a few million, and they push string similarity into the database's indexed operators with the DP only as a re-rank.

To a product manager: "Finding the best combination of coupons by trying every combination gets slower every time we add a coupon type, and at 30 types it takes longer than the customer will wait. We can compute the exact best answer in a millisecond with a different method, as long as the campaign budget is counted in whole rupees."

Common mistakes

  • Brute-force subset enumeration with a comment saying "n is small".
  • Memoization keyed by the wrong thing.
  • Running Levenshtein against every row instead of a shortlist.
  • DP over money as floats.
  • Not bounding n or the capacity dimension.

Interview questions

  1. "Choose the best set of non-stackable promotions within a marketing budget. Approach and complexity?" Expected: 0/1 knapsack, O(n * budget) with a discretized budget; mention the one-per-group variant. Follow-up: how do you bound the worst case?
  2. "Why does memoizing a subset-enumeration on the chosen set not help?" Expected: the number of distinct keys is still 2^n; the state must be smaller than the path.
  3. "Fuzzy product search over 2 million names: where does edit distance run and on how many rows?" Expected: trigram index shortlist in PostgreSQL; edit distance only on the shortlist.
  4. "Memoization versus tabulation: pick one for edit distance on 10,000-character strings and say why." Expected: tabulation (no recursion depth), two-row memory.
  5. "When is DP the wrong tool even though the problem is an optimization?" Expected: state space too large (NP-hard cores), near-optimal acceptable, or greedy provably optimal.

Practical exercise

Implement bestSubset and levenshtein, plus a brute-force knapsack for n up to 15 as a test oracle. Build the promotion optimizer with its bounds and measure worst-case time at the caps. Then build the two-stage fuzzy search against a 500,000-row products table with pg_trgm and measure p50/p99 for 20 typo queries.

Acceptance criteria:

  • bestSubset matches brute force on 1,000 random cases with n <= 15.
  • The optimizer's worst case at MAX_CANDIDATES and the largest budget completes under 5 ms.
  • Fuzzy search p99 under 15 ms, with EXPLAIN showing the GIN index and the shortlist size logged per query.

8.17 Worked example: rate limiter

Concept

A rate limiter decides, for each incoming request, whether the caller has exceeded an allowed rate, and rejects it (usually with HTTP 429) if so. It is the single most common place where a backend engineer implements an algorithm from scratch rather than calling a library, and it combines three things from this part: a sliding window or bucket algorithm, an O(1) per-request cost budget, and a data structure that must live in Redis because the service runs on many pods.

There are three algorithm families: token bucket (allows bursts up to a capacity, refills at a steady rate), leaky bucket (smooths output to a steady rate, queues or drops the excess) and window counters (fixed, sliding log, sliding counter, covered in the sliding window section). NestJS ships @nestjs/throttler, which implements a window counter and lets you plug in Redis storage.

Why does it exist?

Because a backend has finite capacity and callers do not coordinate. Without limits, one misbehaving integration, one retry storm, or one scraper takes the capacity that every other customer paid for. Rate limiting also protects downstream systems (the database connection pool, a partner API with its own limits) and turns a would-be outage into a polite 429 for one caller.

Mental model

Imagine a bucket with a small hole at the bottom and a tap dripping into it at a steady rate. Each request takes a cup of water out of the bucket. If the bucket is empty, the request waits or leaves. The tap's rate is the sustained limit; the bucket's size is the burst you tolerate. A caller who has been quiet for a while has a full bucket and can make a burst of requests; a caller hammering continuously gets exactly the drip rate. That is a token bucket. A leaky bucket is the same picture viewed from the hole: water (requests) pours in at any rate, but leaves through the hole at a fixed rate, and if the bucket overflows the excess is lost.

How it works

Token bucket. State per key: tokens (a number, possibly fractional) and lastRefillAt. On each request with cost c:

  1. elapsed = now - lastRefillAt; tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * refillPerMs).
  2. If tokens >= c: tokens -= c, allow. Else reject, and report retryAfter = (c - tokens) / refillPerMs.
  3. Store tokens and now.

O(1) per request, two numbers per key. Bursts up to capacity, sustained rate refillPerMs. This is what you want for public APIs: a client that batches 50 calls once a minute should be allowed to, as long as its average stays under the limit.

Leaky bucket as a meter is mathematically the token bucket with a different view (the "generic cell rate algorithm", GCRA, used in telecom). Leaky bucket as a queue is different: requests are enqueued and a worker drains the queue at a fixed rate. Use it when you must shape outbound traffic to a strict rate (calling a partner API that allows exactly 10 requests per second) rather than police inbound traffic.

Sliding window counter (from the sliding window section): two integers per key, O(1), approximate. Sliding window log: a sorted set of timestamps per key, exact, O(log n) per request, O(limit) memory per key.

Algorithm Allows bursts Exact Memory per key Cost per request Use for
Fixed window 2x at boundary No 1 counter O(1) Cheap abuse protection where boundary bursts are acceptable
Sliding window counter Smooth Approximate 2 counters O(1) General API limits at scale
Sliding window log Smooth Yes O(limit) timestamps O(log limit) Low limits that must be exact (login attempts, OTP sends)
Token bucket Yes, up to capacity Yes 2 numbers O(1) Public APIs, per-customer quotas with burst allowance
Leaky bucket (queue) No, shapes to a rate Yes Queue O(1) enqueue Outbound calls to rate-limited partners 
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Full
    Full --> Draining: request consumes a token
    Draining --> Full: refill reaches capacity
    Draining --> Empty: tokens reach zero
    Empty --> Draining: refill adds a token
    Empty --> Empty: request rejected with 429

The multi-pod problem: any in-process limiter multiplies the effective limit by the number of pods and resets on deploy. The state must live in Redis, and the read-modify-write must be atomic, which is what Lua scripts are for. A script runs to completion on the Redis server with no other command interleaved, so "read tokens, compute, write tokens" cannot race with another pod doing the same for the same key.

Token bucket as a Redis Lua script, registered with ioredis's defineCommand:

// rate-limit/redis-token-bucket.ts
import Redis from 'ioredis';

const TOKEN_BUCKET_LUA = `
-- KEYS[1] = bucket key. ARGV: capacity, refill_per_ms, cost
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local refill   = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local cost     = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local t = redis.call('TIME')                                  -- Redis server clock: one time source for all pods
local now = t[1] * 1000 + math.floor(t[2] / 1000)
local data = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(data[1])
local ts = tonumber(data[2])
if tokens == nil then tokens = capacity; ts = now end
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + math.max(0, now - ts) * refill)
local allowed = 0
local retry_ms = 0
if tokens >= cost then
  tokens = tokens - cost
  allowed = 1
else
  retry_ms = math.ceil((cost - tokens) / refill)
end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(capacity / refill) + 1000)  -- idle keys disappear once full again
return { allowed, math.floor(tokens), retry_ms }
`;

export interface BucketDecision { allowed: boolean; remaining: number; retryAfterMs: number; }

export class RedisTokenBucket {
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis, private readonly capacity: number, private readonly refillPerSecond: number) {
    // ioredis caches the script SHA and falls back to EVAL if Redis lost it (restart, SCRIPT FLUSH)
    redis.defineCommand('takeTokens', { numberOfKeys: 1, lua: TOKEN_BUCKET_LUA });
  }

  async take(key: string, cost = 1): Promise<BucketDecision> {
    const client = this.redis as Redis & { takeTokens: (k: string, ...args: (string | number)[]) => Promise<number[]> };
    const [allowed, remaining, retryAfterMs] = await client.takeTokens(
      `rl:tb:{${key}}`, this.capacity, this.refillPerSecond / 1000, cost);   // hash tag keeps the key on one cluster slot
    return { allowed: allowed === 1, remaining, retryAfterMs };
  }
}

Sliding window log as a script, for exact low limits:

// rate-limit/redis-sliding-log.ts
export const SLIDING_LOG_LUA = `
-- KEYS[1] = window key. ARGV: window_ms, limit, member (unique per request)
local t = redis.call('TIME')
local now = t[1] * 1000 + math.floor(t[2] / 1000)
local window = tonumber(ARGV[1])
redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], 0, now - window)     -- drop timestamps that slid out
local count = redis.call('ZCARD', KEYS[1])
if count < tonumber(ARGV[2]) then
  redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], now, ARGV[3])
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], window)
  return { 1, count + 1 }
end
return { 0, count }
`;

Use a unique member (request id or now plus a random suffix), because a sorted set cannot hold two identical members; two requests in the same millisecond with member now would count as one.

Practical example

A payments API exposes POST /charges to merchants. The limit is 100 requests per second sustained with a burst of 300 per merchant, keyed by API key. A merchant's nightly batch sends 300 charges in one second, then 100 per second: all accepted. A misconfigured merchant client retrying in a tight loop at 2,000 per second gets 300 through, then 100 per second, with a Retry-After header telling it when to try again. The database behind the API sees at most the sum of every merchant's sustained rate, which is what it was sized for.

NestJS example

@nestjs/throttler provides the guard, decorators and a pluggable storage. Its built-in behavior is a window counter: the first hit for a key starts a window of ttl milliseconds, limit hits are allowed inside it, and an optional blockDuration can extend the rejection. The community package @nest-lab/throttler-storage-redis provides the Redis-backed storage so all pods share state.

// app.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { APP_GUARD } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ThrottlerModule, ThrottlerGuard } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { ThrottlerStorageRedisService } from '@nest-lab/throttler-storage-redis';
import { ConfigModule, ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

@Module({
  imports: [
    ConfigModule.forRoot(),
    ThrottlerModule.forRootAsync({
      imports: [ConfigModule],
      inject: [ConfigService],
      useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
        throttlers: [
          { name: 'default', ttl: 60_000, limit: 600 },      // 600 per minute per tracker
          { name: 'burst', ttl: 1_000, limit: 30 },          // and at most 30 in any one second
        ],
        storage: new ThrottlerStorageRedisService(new Redis(config.getOrThrow<string>('REDIS_URL'))),
      }),
    }),
  ],
  providers: [{ provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: ThrottlerGuard }],   // global: every route unless @SkipThrottle
})
export class AppModule {}

By default the guard tracks by client IP. Behind a load balancer every request has the balancer's IP, so override the tracker to use the API key (and enable trust proxy if you fall back to IP):

// rate-limit/api-key-throttler.guard.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ThrottlerGuard } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { Request } from 'express';

@Injectable()
export class ApiKeyThrottlerGuard extends ThrottlerGuard {
  protected async getTracker(req: Request): Promise<string> {
    const apiKey = req.header('x-api-key');
    return apiKey ? `key:${apiKey}` : `ip:${req.ip}`;   // per-merchant limits; anonymous traffic by IP
  }
}

Per-route overrides with the real decorators:

// auth/auth.controller.ts
import { Controller, Post, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Throttle, SkipThrottle } from '@nestjs/throttler';

@Controller()
export class AuthController {
  @Post('auth/login')
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 5, ttl: 60_000 }, burst: { limit: 2, ttl: 1_000 } })  // brute-force protection
  login(): string { return 'ok'; }

  @Get('health')
  @SkipThrottle()                                       // Kubernetes probes must never be throttled
  health(): string { return 'ok'; }
}

The guard sets X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset headers on allowed responses and Retry-After on 429s, and throws ThrottlerException (HTTP 429), which your global exception filter can shape into your API's error format. For endpoints that need token-bucket burst semantics rather than a window, write a small guard around RedisTokenBucket that throws HttpException with status 429 and sets Retry-After from retryAfterMs.

PostgreSQL example

Per-second limits do not belong in PostgreSQL: a hot row per API key with an UPDATE per request is 1–5 ms and a lock queue. But hard quotas (monthly call allowances that bill when exceeded) do, because they need durability and an audit trail:

CREATE TABLE api_quotas (
  api_key_id uuid NOT NULL,
  period date NOT NULL,                 -- first day of the month
  used bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  allowance bigint NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (api_key_id, period)
);

-- Atomic consume: returns a row only if the quota had room. No SELECT-then-UPDATE race.
UPDATE api_quotas
SET used = used + $3
WHERE api_key_id = $1 AND period = $2 AND used + $3 <= allowance
RETURNING used, allowance;

Batch the writes: consume 100 units at a time from PostgreSQL into a Redis token bucket, and let Redis serve the per-request decisions. The database row is touched once per 100 requests instead of once per request.

Production scenario

An API gateway layer of 12 pods handles 40,000 RPS across 25,000 active API keys. Each request runs one Lua script call (about 0.3 ms round trip on the same availability zone, about 15 microseconds of Redis CPU). Redis handles roughly 100,000 such scripts per second per core, so one primary is at 40% for rate limiting alone; the team pins rate limiting to its own Redis instance so cache traffic cannot starve it. Memory: 25,000 keys times two hash fields is under 5 MB. p99 added latency: 0.8 ms. When the limits are also enforced by a local token bucket per pod at 5x the global rate as a circuit breaker, a Redis slowdown degrades to "slightly generous limits" rather than "every request waits on Redis".

Failure scenario

At 13:20 Redis fails over. For 8 seconds every rate-limit script call throws ECONNREFUSED. The guard's error handling was catch (e) { throw new ServiceUnavailableException() }: fail closed. 40,000 RPS of legitimate traffic received 503 for 8 seconds, and every client retried at once when Redis returned, creating a 3x spike that the token buckets, now empty of state, let through as a fresh burst. Two lessons became policy: rate limiting fails open (log, count a metric, allow the request) because its job is protection, not correctness, and the local per-pod bucket stays in place so "open" still has a ceiling.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Redis unavailable. Decide fail-open or fail-closed per endpoint: open for general APIs, closed for login and OTP.
  • Clock skew. Use Redis TIME inside the script; never pass pod clocks.
  • Cluster slots. A script touching one key is fine; keys must use hash tags {...} if a script touches several.
  • Hot keys. One key at 100,000 RPS concentrates on one Redis shard; add a per-pod local pre-limiter.
  • Identical members in the log. Use unique members in the sorted set.
  • Cost greater than capacity. A request that costs 500 tokens in a 300-token bucket can never succeed; validate at configuration time.
  • Retry storms. Clients that retry on 429 without honoring Retry-After amplify load; add jitter guidance to API docs and consider a blockDuration.
  • Health checks throttled. A throttled readiness probe takes the pod out of rotation; always @SkipThrottle().
  • Key cardinality. Keying by full URL including query strings creates unbounded keys; key by principal and route pattern.
  • Deploys reset in-memory state. Another reason state lives in Redis.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior decides four things before writing any code: the key (who is limited), the shape (burst allowed or not), the failure mode (open or closed) and the placement (edge, gateway, service). They put coarse limits at the edge (CDN or gateway, by IP), business limits at the service (by API key or user, token bucket) and strict exact limits on the few endpoints where a single extra request matters (login, OTP, password reset: sliding log). They budget the Redis call as part of the request's latency and isolate the rate-limit Redis from the cache Redis.

To a product manager: "Each merchant gets a bucket of 300 requests that refills at 100 per second. A quiet merchant can burst; a noisy one is slowed to the sustained rate and told exactly when to retry. If our limiter itself has a problem, we let traffic through rather than blocking everyone."

Common mistakes

  • In-memory rate limits on a multi-pod service.
  • Read-modify-write in application code instead of an atomic script.
  • Keying by IP behind a load balancer.
  • Failing closed on Redis errors for non-sensitive endpoints.
  • Fixed windows for limits that matter.
  • No Retry-After header, so clients guess.
  • Storing state in PostgreSQL for per-second limits.

Interview questions

  1. "Design a rate limiter for a multi-pod API with per-customer burst allowance." Expected: token bucket in Redis via Lua, keyed by principal, TIME from Redis, fail-open, local circuit breaker. Follow-up: how do you make it survive a Redis failover?
  2. "Compare token bucket and sliding window counter." Expected: burst allowance versus smooth; both O(1) and two numbers per key; exactness differences.
  3. "Why must the check-and-decrement be atomic, and how do you achieve it in Redis?" Expected: two pods racing past the limit; Lua script or MULTI with WATCH.
  4. "How does @nestjs/throttler track callers, and what do you change behind a load balancer?" Expected: IP by default; override getTracker; trust proxy.
  5. "Should a rate limiter fail open or closed?" Expected: depends on the endpoint; protection endpoints open, security endpoints closed.
  6. "A merchant at 100,000 RPS makes one Redis shard hot. What do you do?" Expected: per-pod local pre-limit, key sharding with aggregation, or dedicated infrastructure for that tenant.

Practical exercise

Implement RedisTokenBucket and a guard around it, wire @nestjs/throttler with Redis storage and the API-key tracker, and load-test with 3 app instances behind a local proxy at 2,000 RPS for one API key with a 500 RPS limit.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Across all instances, admitted requests over any 10-second window are within 2% of the limit, with the configured burst visible at the start.
  • Stopping Redis mid-test causes zero 5xx responses (fail-open) and a metric increment; restarting it resumes limiting within one second.
  • 429 responses carry a correct Retry-After.

8.18 Worked example: job scheduler with priorities and dependencies

Concept

A job scheduler runs units of work in an order that respects two things: dependencies (B needs A's output) and priorities (when several jobs are ready, the important one goes first). It is topological sorting with a priority heap as the ready set, made durable and distributed: the graph lives in PostgreSQL, the ready jobs go into a queue (BullMQ on Redis), workers pull from the queue, and completion events feed the next round of readiness.

Why does it exist?

Because "run these scripts in this order with cron at 01:00, 01:30, 02:00" breaks the first night one script runs long, and because a queue without dependency tracking either runs jobs too early or serializes everything. The scheduler makes the DAG explicit, runs independent branches in parallel, blocks successors of failures instead of running them on missing data, and lets you re-run from the failed node.

Mental model

Imagine a kitchen where each dish has prerequisites (the sauce before the pasta is plated) and a priority (the table that has waited longest). The expediter keeps a board of dishes whose prerequisites are done, hands the highest-priority ready dish to the next free cook, and when a dish comes back done, checks which other dishes just became ready. Cooks never decide order; the board does.

How it works

  1. Definition. A pipeline run creates rows in run_jobs with depends_on arrays, priorities and state pending. The planner validates the DAG (Kahn's algorithm; reject cycles) before creating the run.
  2. Readiness. A job is ready when every job in depends_on is succeeded. A scheduler tick finds ready jobs, claims them with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so several scheduler instances do not double-dispatch, marks them queued and adds them to BullMQ with the job's priority.
  3. Execution. Workers process queue jobs, write results, and mark succeeded or failed.
  4. Propagation. On success, trigger a scheduler tick (or run one every few seconds). On failure, mark every transitive successor blocked; other branches continue.
  5. Complexity. Per run, each job is dispatched once and each edge is examined a constant number of times: O(V + E) database work spread across ticks. The ready query is an index scan on (run_id, state).
flowchart LR
    P["Planner validates DAG"] --> S["Scheduler tick: claim ready jobs FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED"]
    S --> Q["BullMQ queue with priority"]
    Q --> W1["Worker"]
    Q --> W2["Worker"]
    W1 -->|"completed"| S
    W2 -->|"failed"| B["Mark successors blocked"]

Practical example

A nightly analytics pipeline: extract_customers and extract_orders (no dependencies, priority 1), build_customer_orders (needs both), revenue_report (priority 1, needs the join) and churn_model (priority 5, needs the join). With 4 workers, the two extracts run in parallel; the join runs when both finish; then revenue_report is dispatched before churn_model because its priority number is lower, so the finance dashboard is fresh first.

NestJS example

// scheduling/run-scheduler.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectQueue } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Queue } from 'bullmq';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

interface ReadyJob { id: string; run_id: string; name: string; priority: number; payload: Record<string, unknown>; }

@Injectable()
export class RunSchedulerService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(RunSchedulerService.name);
  constructor(
    @InjectQueue('pipeline') private readonly queue: Queue,
    @InjectDataSource() private readonly db: DataSource,
  ) {}

  // One tick: claim ready jobs atomically, enqueue by priority. Safe to run from several instances.
  async tick(runId: string): Promise<number> {
    const claimed: ReadyJob[] = await this.db.transaction(async (tx) => {
      const ready: ReadyJob[] = await tx.query(
        `SELECT j.id, j.run_id, j.name, j.priority, j.payload
         FROM run_jobs j
         WHERE j.run_id = $1 AND j.state = 'pending'
           AND NOT EXISTS (
             SELECT 1 FROM run_jobs d
             WHERE d.run_id = j.run_id AND d.id = ANY(j.depends_on) AND d.state <> 'succeeded')
         ORDER BY j.priority, j.id
         FOR UPDATE OF j SKIP LOCKED
         LIMIT 50`, [runId]);
      if (ready.length > 0) {
        await tx.query(`UPDATE run_jobs SET state = 'queued', queued_at = now() WHERE id = ANY($1::uuid[])`,
          [ready.map((r) => r.id)]);
      }
      return ready;
    });

    for (const job of claimed) {
      await this.queue.add(job.name, { runJobId: job.id, payload: job.payload }, {
        jobId: job.id,                          // idempotent: re-adding the same id is a no-op
        priority: job.priority,                 // BullMQ: lower number is processed first
        attempts: 3,
        backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 5_000 },
        removeOnComplete: 1000,
      });
    }
    if (claimed.length > 0) this.logger.log(`run ${runId}: dispatched ${claimed.length} jobs`);
    return claimed.length;
  }

  async onJobFailed(runJobId: string): Promise<void> {
    // Block every transitive successor in one statement: recursive CTE over depends_on
    await this.db.query(
      `WITH RECURSIVE down AS (
         SELECT id FROM run_jobs WHERE $1 = ANY(depends_on)
         UNION
         SELECT j.id FROM run_jobs j JOIN down ON down.id = ANY(j.depends_on)
       )
       UPDATE run_jobs SET state = 'blocked' WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM down) AND state = 'pending'`, [runJobId]);
  }
}
// scheduling/pipeline.processor.ts
import { Processor, WorkerHost, OnWorkerEvent } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Job } from 'bullmq';
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

@Processor('pipeline', { concurrency: 4 })
@Injectable()
export class PipelineProcessor extends WorkerHost {
  constructor(
    private readonly steps: StepRegistry,
    private readonly scheduler: RunSchedulerService,
    private readonly jobs: RunJobsRepository,
  ) { super(); }

  async process(job: Job<{ runJobId: string; payload: Record<string, unknown> }>): Promise<void> {
    await this.jobs.markRunning(job.data.runJobId);
    await this.steps.run(job.name, job.data.payload);         // the actual work, idempotent per runJobId
    await this.jobs.markSucceeded(job.data.runJobId);
  }

  @OnWorkerEvent('completed')
  async onCompleted(job: Job<{ runJobId: string }>): Promise<void> {
    const runId = await this.jobs.runIdOf(job.data.runJobId);
    await this.scheduler.tick(runId);                         // successors may be ready now
  }

  @OnWorkerEvent('failed')
  async onFailed(job: Job<{ runJobId: string }>): Promise<void> {
    if (job.attemptsMade >= (job.opts.attempts ?? 1)) {
      await this.jobs.markFailed(job.data.runJobId);
      await this.scheduler.onJobFailed(job.data.runJobId);
    }
  }
}

StepRegistry and RunJobsRepository are ordinary providers (a map from step name to handler, and a repository over run_jobs). BullMQ also offers FlowProducer for parent-child job trees, which @nestjs/bullmq exposes via BullModule.registerFlowProducer; it is a good fit when the dependency shape is a tree. For a general DAG with shared dependencies, the database-driven readiness above is simpler to reason about.

PostgreSQL example

The schema and the index that keep the ready query cheap:

CREATE TABLE run_jobs (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  run_id uuid NOT NULL,
  name text NOT NULL,
  priority int NOT NULL DEFAULT 10,
  depends_on uuid[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  state text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'
    CHECK (state IN ('pending', 'queued', 'running', 'succeeded', 'failed', 'blocked')),
  payload jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  queued_at timestamptz, started_at timestamptz, finished_at timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX run_jobs_run_state_idx ON run_jobs (run_id, state);
CREATE INDEX run_jobs_depends_on_idx ON run_jobs USING gin (depends_on);   -- for the successor lookups

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is the line that makes multiple scheduler instances safe: each claims a disjoint set of ready rows without waiting on the others.

Production scenario

A platform runs 400 pipelines per day with a median of 30 jobs each and 16 workers. Scheduler ticks are event-driven (on every completion) plus a 10-second sweep for safety. Each tick is a 1–3 ms query. Worker utilization sits at 70%, and the nightly critical path is 42 minutes, dominated by one 25-minute join step, which is the only step worth optimizing.

Failure scenario

At 02:15 the pipeline stalls with 12 jobs stuck in queued. Redis had been restarted with a persistence gap; the BullMQ jobs were lost but the PostgreSQL rows still said queued. Nothing re-dispatched them because the ready query only looks at pending. The fix: the sweep tick re-enqueues jobs queued for more than 5 minutes (idempotent thanks to jobId), and a metric counts them.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Lost queue entries. Re-enqueue stale queued rows; jobId makes it safe.
  • Double execution. A worker crash after doing the work but before marking succeeded leads to a retry; steps must be idempotent per runJobId.
  • Priority starvation. Low-priority jobs may wait forever under constant high-priority load; add aging.
  • Cycle sneaks past the planner. The scheduler must alert when unfinished jobs remain with an empty ready set.
  • Fan-out explosion. One job with 10,000 successors makes the propagation query heavy; batch it.
  • Blocked versus failed semantics. Re-running a failed job should unblock successors automatically.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior keeps the graph in the database (durable, queryable, auditable) and uses the queue only as the dispatch mechanism. They make every step idempotent, every dispatch idempotent, and every tick safe to run concurrently. They measure the critical path and worker utilization separately, because adding workers does not shorten the critical path.

Common mistakes

  • Encoding the DAG in cron times.
  • Dispatching from a SELECT without SKIP LOCKED.
  • Non-idempotent steps with retries enabled.
  • Running successors of a failed job.
  • Assuming the queue is durable.

Interview questions

  1. "Design a scheduler for a DAG of jobs with priorities across many workers." Expected: DB-held graph, ready query, SKIP LOCKED, priority queue, event-driven propagation, blocked successors.
  2. "How do you make dispatch safe with three scheduler replicas?" Expected: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED plus idempotent jobId.
  3. "A job finished but its successors never ran. Where do you look?" Expected: state rows, tick trigger, lost queue entries, sweep.
  4. "How would BullMQ flows differ from this design?" Expected: parent-child trees; not general DAGs with shared dependencies.

Practical exercise

Build the schema, planner, scheduler and processor. Run a 12-job DAG with 3 workers, kill Redis mid-run, and confirm the sweep recovers. Then fail one job deliberately and verify that only its successors are blocked.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Every job runs exactly once per run (assert with a counter table).
  • The run completes after the Redis restart without manual intervention.
  • Blocked jobs are exactly the transitive successors of the failed job.

8.19 Worked example: cache eviction (LRU and LFU)

Concept

A cache with a size limit must choose what to throw away when it is full. LRU (least recently used) evicts the entry that has gone longest without being accessed. LFU (least frequently used) evicts the entry accessed the fewest times. Both can be implemented with O(1) operations, both are what Redis does when maxmemory is reached (approximately), and both are what you need the moment you add an in-process Map cache to a NestJS provider, because an unbounded Map is a memory leak.

Why does it exist?

Memory is finite and access patterns are skewed: a small fraction of keys gets most of the reads. Eviction keeps the hot fraction in memory and lets the rest fall out. Without it, the cache grows until the process dies (in Node) or Redis refuses writes (OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory' under noeviction).

Mental model

Imagine a desk with room for ten documents. LRU: whenever you use a document, you put it on top of the pile; when you need space, you take the one at the bottom, which nobody has touched for the longest time. LFU: each document has a tally of how often you used it; you discard the one with the smallest tally. LRU adapts quickly to new work (yesterday's hot document sinks fast). LFU resists being fooled by a one-time scan through many documents (a single touch does not displace something you use hourly), but it also clings to formerly-hot documents unless the tallies decay.

How it works

LRU in O(1). Classic: a hash map for lookup plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency; on access, unlink the node and move it to the head; on eviction, remove the tail. In JavaScript, Map preserves insertion order and supports O(1) delete and re-insert, which gives you LRU with no linked list:

// cache/lru-cache.ts
export class LruCache<K, V> {
  private readonly map = new Map<K, V>();
  constructor(private readonly capacity: number) { if (capacity <= 0) throw new Error('capacity must be positive'); }

  get(key: K): V | undefined {
    const value = this.map.get(key);
    if (value === undefined) return undefined;
    this.map.delete(key);          // O(1): move to the most-recent end by re-inserting
    this.map.set(key, value);
    return value;
  }

  set(key: K, value: V): void {
    if (this.map.has(key)) this.map.delete(key);
    this.map.set(key, value);
    if (this.map.size > this.capacity) {
      const oldest = this.map.keys().next().value as K;   // first key in insertion order = least recently used
      this.map.delete(oldest);
    }
  }

  get size(): number { return this.map.size; }
}
flowchart LR
    H["Most recently used"] --> K1["user:42"]
    K1 --> K2["product:7"]
    K2 --> K3["cart:99"]
    K3 --> T["Least recently used: evicted next"]

LFU in O(1). Keep, per key, its frequency; keep, per frequency, an ordered set of keys (a Map<number, Set<K>>, insertion-ordered so ties break by recency); track the minimum frequency. On access, move the key from bucket f to bucket f + 1; on eviction, remove the first key from the minimum bucket. Production LFUs also decay counts over time so old popularity fades.

Redis. maxmemory sets the ceiling; maxmemory-policy picks the algorithm:

Policy Evicts from Algorithm
noeviction nothing; writes fail Default; right for Redis used as a database or queue
allkeys-lru any key Approximate LRU
allkeys-lfu any key Approximate LFU with decay
volatile-lru / volatile-lfu only keys with a TTL Same, restricted
volatile-ttl keys with a TTL, shortest TTL first
allkeys-random / volatile-random Cheap, rarely right

Redis does not keep a global linked list. Each key carries a 24-bit clock (LRU) or an 8-bit logarithmic counter plus a 16-bit decay timestamp (LFU). On eviction it samples maxmemory-samples keys (default 5) and evicts the best candidate among them. At 10 samples the result is close to exact LRU at a fraction of the cost. LFU tuning: lfu-log-factor (default 10; how many hits it takes to saturate the counter) and lfu-decay-time (default 1 minute per halving). OBJECT FREQ key shows a key's counter; INFO stats exposes evicted_keys, keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses.

PostgreSQL's shared_buffers uses a related approximation: a clock-sweep over buffer pages with a small usage counter per page, which is LFU-flavored LRU; the pg_buffercache extension lets you inspect it.

Practical example

A product service caches product detail JSON in process for 30 seconds to survive a Redis blip. Bounded by an LruCache of 20,000 entries at about 3 KB each, the cache costs 60 MB and holds the hot catalog; the long tail falls out. The same service uses a Redis instance with maxmemory 8gb and allkeys-lru for the shared cache, and a separate Redis with noeviction for BullMQ queues, because evicting a queue entry is data loss.

NestJS example

@nestjs/cache-manager wraps cache-manager, whose in-memory store accepts a max and evicts LRU:

// products/products.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CacheModule } from '@nestjs/cache-manager';

@Module({
  imports: [CacheModule.register({ ttl: 30_000, max: 20_000 })],   // bounded in-process LRU, 30 s TTL
})
export class ProductsModule {}
// products/products.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CACHE_MANAGER } from '@nestjs/cache-manager';
import { Cache } from 'cache-manager';

@Injectable()
export class ProductsService {
  constructor(@Inject(CACHE_MANAGER) private readonly cache: Cache, private readonly repo: ProductsRepository) {}

  async detail(id: string): Promise<ProductDetail> {
    const key = `product:${id}`;
    const hit = await this.cache.get<ProductDetail>(key);
    if (hit) return hit;
    const fresh = await this.repo.loadDetail(id);          // ~3 ms
    await this.cache.set(key, fresh);                       // LRU keeps the newest 20,000 keys
    return fresh;
  }
}

For the shared layer, use the Redis store package for cache-manager with the Redis instance configured for allkeys-lru.

PostgreSQL example

Eviction policy also decides what is cacheable. A query that runs 400 times per second for 50,000 distinct keys with a Zipf-like distribution gets a 95% hit rate from an LRU holding 10% of the keys; you can measure the distribution before committing memory:

-- How concentrated are reads? Share of requests covered by the top 10% of products (from an access log table)
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT product_id, count(*) AS hits,
         row_number() OVER (ORDER BY count(*) DESC) AS rn,
         count(*) OVER () AS total_keys
  FROM product_views WHERE viewed_at > now() - interval '1 day'
  GROUP BY product_id
)
SELECT sum(hits) FILTER (WHERE rn <= total_keys / 10)::numeric / sum(hits) AS top_decile_share FROM ranked;

A top_decile_share of 0.9 says LRU with 10% of keys will hit about 90% of the time; a flat distribution says caching will not help much at any size.

Production scenario

A Redis cache at 16 GB with allkeys-lru serves 120,000 reads per second at a 97% hit rate. A nightly reindex job reads every product once (2 million keys) through the same Redis, evicting the hot set; the morning hit rate drops to 60% and database load doubles for 20 minutes. Switching to allkeys-lfu keeps the hot keys (their counters are high; the scan's keys are touched once) and the morning dip disappears. Alternatively, the job bypasses the cache.

Failure scenario

At 09:40 writes to Redis start failing with OOM command not allowed. The policy was volatile-lru, chosen so session keys (no TTL) would never be evicted. A refactor removed the TTL from cached product keys "to reduce misses".
