With no TTL-bearing keys left, volatile-lru had nothing it was allowed to evict, memory reached maxmemory, and every SET failed; the application's cache-set path did not catch the error, so product pages returned 500. Fix: allkeys-lru on the cache instance, sessions moved to their own instance with noeviction, and cache writes wrapped so a cache failure is a miss, not an error.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Unbounded Map caches. A leak with a business justification; always bound.
  • volatile-* with no TTL keys. Writes fail.
  • Mixed workloads in one Redis. Queue or session data evicted by cache pressure; separate instances.
  • Scan pollution under LRU. One-time sweeps evict the hot set; LFU or bypass.
  • LFU inertia. Formerly hot keys linger; tune lfu-decay-time.
  • Big values. One 50 MB value evicts thousands of small ones; cap value sizes.
  • Eviction cost. Deleting a huge key (a set with millions of members) blocks Redis; lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes.
  • Thundering herd on eviction. A hot key evicted causes a stampede of rebuilds; single-flight or stale-while-revalidate.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior sizes caches from measured key distributions, not guesses, separates Redis instances by eviction policy (cache: allkeys-lru or -lfu; queues and sessions: noeviction), bounds every in-process cache, and watches evicted_keys and hit rate as first-class metrics. They treat a cache error as a miss.

Common mistakes

  • volatile-lru on a cache with unexpiring keys.
  • One Redis for cache and queues.
  • No max on CacheModule.register.
  • Ignoring evicted_keys until the hit rate collapses.
  • Treating cache-set failures as request failures.

Interview questions

  1. "Implement an O(1) LRU in JavaScript." Expected: Map insertion order with delete-and-reinsert on access.
  2. "How does Redis implement LRU, and why is it approximate?" Expected: per-key clock, sampled eviction, maxmemory-samples.
  3. "When would you pick LFU over LRU?" Expected: scan-heavy workloads polluting the hot set; stable hot sets.
  4. "What happens under volatile-lru when no keys have TTLs?" Expected: writes fail with OOM.
  5. "How do you size a cache?" Expected: measure key access distribution; hit rate versus memory curve.

Practical exercise

Implement LruCache and an O(1) LFU with tests. Run a Redis at maxmemory 64mb with allkeys-lru, replay a Zipf-distributed access log of 500,000 keys, record the hit rate, then simulate a full scan and compare LRU versus LFU recovery.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Both caches pass property tests against a brute-force reference.
  • Measured hit rates before and after the scan are reported for both policies.
  • The application treats Redis SET failures as misses (verify by filling Redis under noeviction).

8.20 Worked example: database indexing, or why a B-tree lookup is O(log n) and what that costs in disk reads

Concept

A B-tree index is a balanced tree of fixed-size pages, sorted by key, with a very high fan-out: each page holds hundreds of keys and pointers to child pages. Finding a key means descending from the root, choosing one child per level, until you reach a leaf that points to the table row. Because each page holds hundreds of children, the tree is extremely shallow: a billion rows fit in a tree four levels deep. That is the concrete meaning of O(log n) for a database index, and it is why a primary-key lookup on a billion-row table takes about the same time as one on a thousand-row table.

Why does it exist?

Because the alternative is reading the table. A billion rows at 100 bytes each is 100 GB; a sequential scan at 1 GB/s from fast storage takes about two minutes. A B-tree descent touches four or five 8 KB pages: under a millisecond. Every WHERE id = $1, every foreign-key join, every ORDER BY ... LIMIT on an indexed column, every keyset-paginated page depends on this structure.

Mental model

Imagine a library with a billion books, sorted by title on the shelves. The catalog's top card says "A–F: floor 1, G–M: floor 2..."; each floor's card says which aisle; each aisle's card says which shelf; the shelf card says which position. Four cards, each narrowing the search by a factor of hundreds, and you are holding the book. The cards for the floors and aisles are used so often that the librarian keeps them on the desk (cache); only the shelf card and the walk to the shelf require leaving the desk (disk reads).

How it works

PostgreSQL's B-tree, in the numbers that matter:

  1. Pages. Every index page is 8 KB. A leaf entry for a bigint key is the 8-byte key plus an 8-byte header plus a 6-byte tuple id (the row's physical address), aligned to 16 bytes, plus a 4-byte line pointer: about 20 bytes. Leaves are filled to about 90% by default (fillfactor), giving roughly 350–400 entries per leaf page. Internal pages hold one key and one child pointer per child: about the same count.
  2. Height. With fan-out 400: 400 rows fit in one leaf; 160,000 rows in two levels; 64 million in three; 25 billion in four. So a billion-row table with a bigint primary key has a B-tree of height 4: one root, two internal levels, one leaf level. That is log₄₀₀(10⁹) ≈ 3.5, rounded up.
  3. Reads per lookup. Four index pages plus one heap page for the row: five page reads. The root and the first internal level together are a few thousand pages (the top three levels of a billion-row index are about 7,000 pages, 56 MB), which live permanently in shared_buffers or the OS cache on any busy system. The leaf page and the heap page are the ones that may actually hit disk. Realistic cost of a point lookup on a cold billion-row table: two random reads, about 100–200 µs on NVMe, plus CPU: well under a millisecond. Warm: about 20–50 µs.
  4. Size. A billion-row bigint index needs about 2.8 million leaf pages: roughly 22 GB. That is the price of O(log n), paid in storage and in write amplification (every insert updates every index on the table).
  5. Range scans. Leaves are linked in key order, so after the descent, WHERE id BETWEEN a AND b or ORDER BY id LIMIT 50 walks siblings sequentially: O(log n + k).
flowchart TB
    Root["Root page: always cached"] --> I1a["Internal level 1: cached"]
    Root --> I1b["Internal level 1: cached"]
    I1a --> I2a["Internal level 2: usually cached"]
    I1b --> I2b["Internal level 2: usually cached"]
    I2a --> L1["Leaf page: key plus tuple id, maybe a disk read"]
    I2b --> L2["Leaf page"]
    L1 --> Heap["Heap page: the row itself, maybe a disk read"]

Seeing the height directly, with the pageinspect extension:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pageinspect;
SELECT level AS root_level, root, fastroot FROM bt_metap('orders_pkey');
-- level 3 means four levels (0 = leaves): root at level 3, two internal levels, leaves
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('orders_pkey')) AS index_size,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('orders')) AS table_size;

And the buffer accounting of one lookup:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 734_112_908;
Index Scan using orders_pkey on orders  (cost=0.57..8.59 rows=1 width=142) (actual time=0.188..0.190 rows=1 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (id = 734112908)
  Buffers: shared hit=4 read=1
Planning Time: 0.061 ms
Execution Time: 0.211 ms

shared hit=4 read=1: four pages found in cache (root, two internal, leaf), one page read from disk (the heap row), 0.2 ms total on a table with 900 million rows.

Practical example

The choices that follow from the mechanics:

  • Composite column order. An index on (customer_id, created_at) is sorted by customer first, so WHERE customer_id = $1 AND created_at > $2 descends once and walks a range. The same index cannot efficiently answer WHERE created_at > $2 alone; that predicate is spread across every customer's section.
  • Covering indexes. CREATE INDEX ... ON orders (customer_id, created_at) INCLUDE (status, total_cents) lets SELECT status, total_cents ... be an index-only scan: the heap page read disappears, if the visibility map says the page is all-visible.
  • Partial indexes. CREATE INDEX ... ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending' indexes only the small hot subset; a 1% subset makes the index 100x smaller and its writes 100x rarer.
  • What B-trees cannot do. Leading-wildcard LIKE, arbitrary functions on the column without an expression index, and full-text search. Those are the next worked example.

NestJS example

Index declarations belong with the entity so migrations and code agree:

// orders/order.entity.ts
import { Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, Column, Index, CreateDateColumn } from 'typeorm';

@Entity('orders')
@Index('orders_customer_created_idx', ['customerId', 'createdAt'])                       // composite for the customer timeline
@Index('orders_pending_created_idx', ['createdAt'], { where: `"status" = 'pending'` })   // partial: the hot 1%
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('increment', { type: 'bigint' }) id!: string;
  @Column({ name: 'customer_id', type: 'bigint' }) customerId!: string;
  @Column({ type: 'text' }) status!: string;
  @Column({ name: 'total_cents', type: 'bigint' }) totalCents!: string;
  @CreateDateColumn({ name: 'created_at', type: 'timestamptz' }) createdAt!: Date;
}

A repository method whose plan you have verified, with the exact-count trap avoided:

// orders/orders.repository.ts
async pendingSince(since: Date, limit = 500): Promise<Order[]> {
  // Uses orders_pending_created_idx: descent + range walk, O(log n + limit)
  return this.repo.createQueryBuilder('o')
    .where(`o.status = 'pending' AND o.created_at >= :since`, { since })
    .orderBy('o.created_at', 'ASC')
    .limit(limit)
    .getMany();
}

Never pair this with getManyAndCount() on a large table without thinking: count(*) over a billion rows is a full scan of the index or table, minutes, and no B-tree makes it O(log n). Use an estimate from pg_class.reltuples or a maintained counter for large totals.

Sequelize example

Order.init({ /* columns */ }, {
  sequelize, tableName: 'orders', underscored: true,
  indexes: [
    { name: 'orders_customer_created_idx', fields: ['customer_id', 'created_at'] },
    { name: 'orders_pending_created_idx', fields: ['created_at'], where: { status: 'pending' } },
  ],
});

Production scenario

An events table grows by 40 million rows a day and is queried by (tenant_id, occurred_at). At 3 billion rows the composite index is 90 GB, height 4, and point-in-range queries still run in 1–2 ms because the top levels are cached. The write side is the cost: each insert adds an entry to the primary key index and the composite index, about 25 µs of CPU and later write I/O per row, plus WAL. Partitioning by month keeps each partition's indexes smaller (height 3) and makes dropping old data a DROP TABLE rather than a billion-row DELETE; see the partitioning material in the database parts of this handbook.

Failure scenario

At 10:15 the orders API's p99 jumps from 4 ms to 900 ms after a "small" deploy. The deploy added ORDER BY updated_at DESC to the customer orders list. The composite index is (customer_id, created_at); updated_at is not in it. For a customer with 400,000 orders, PostgreSQL now walks the whole customer section of the index, fetches 400,000 heap rows, and sorts them (external merge, 50 MB of temp files) to return 50. The plan went from Index Scan with a Limit to Sort over Index Scan. The fix was a new composite (customer_id, updated_at DESC, id DESC) built CONCURRENTLY; the process fix was requiring EXPLAIN output on production-sized data in the PR for any query change.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Bloat. Frequent updates leave dead entries; the tree grows and descents touch more pages. Monitor with pgstattuple, fix with REINDEX CONCURRENTLY.
  • Sequential keys and the rightmost leaf. Monotonic keys (bigserial, time) concentrate inserts on one leaf page, which is fine for B-trees (PostgreSQL handles it well) but makes that page a hot spot for lock contention at very high insert rates.
  • UUID v4 keys. Random keys spread inserts across the whole index: more page splits, worse cache locality, larger WAL. UUIDv7 (time-ordered) avoids most of it.
  • Index too wide. Indexing text columns of hundreds of bytes lowers fan-out from 400 to 20 and adds levels.
  • Too many indexes. Fifteen indexes means fifteen B-tree inserts per row.
  • Statistics stale. The planner chooses a sequential scan because it thinks the table is small; ANALYZE.
  • Index build on a busy table. Plain CREATE INDEX locks writes; always CONCURRENTLY in production, and handle the invalid-index case if it fails.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior thinks in page reads. They know the tree height for the big tables, know which levels are cached, and read Buffers: shared hit/read as the true cost. They design indexes from access paths, not from columns, and count the write amplification of each one. They know the O(log n) promise applies to descents and bounded range walks, never to counts, aggregates or unbounded ranges.

To a product manager: "Looking up any order among a billion takes four steps, and three of those are in memory. What is slow is counting orders or sorting a customer's whole history; those touch everything, and we design around them."

Common mistakes

  • Sorting by an unindexed column on a large filtered set.
  • count(*) for pagination totals on big tables.
  • Wide text columns as leading index keys.
  • One index per query instead of a designed set.
  • Building indexes without CONCURRENTLY.

Interview questions

  1. "How many disk reads does a primary-key lookup on a billion-row table cost, and why?" Expected: height 4 tree, top levels cached, one leaf and one heap page from disk: about two random reads. Follow-up: what changes with an index-only scan?
  2. "Why can't the index on (customer_id, created_at) serve ORDER BY updated_at?" Expected: sort order is by leading columns; a different column requires a walk and a sort.
  3. "What does Buffers: shared hit=4 read=1 tell you?" Expected: four cached pages, one disk read; the tree descent plus the heap fetch.
  4. "Compare bigserial, UUID v4 and UUID v7 as primary keys from the B-tree's point of view." Expected: locality, page splits, WAL volume.
  5. "Is count(*) O(log n) with an index?" Expected: no; it visits every matching entry.

Practical exercise

Create a 100-million-row table with a bigint primary key and a composite index. Use bt_metap to read the tree height, pg_relation_size for sizes, and EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for a cold and a warm point lookup, a range walk with LIMIT, and a count(*).

Acceptance criteria:

  • You can state the tree height and estimate reads per lookup before measuring, and the buffer counts agree.
  • The cold lookup shows read buffers, the warm lookup shows only hit.
  • You explain in one paragraph why the count(*) cost is what it is.

8.21 Worked example: search, from prefix tries to trigrams and pg_trgm

Concept

"Search" in a product backend usually means three different problems: prefix search (autocomplete: "iph" finds "iPhone 15"), substring or fuzzy search ("ipone" or "phone 15" finds "iPhone 15") and full-text search (ranked matching on words and stems across long text). Each has a data structure that makes it fast: a trie or sorted index for prefixes, n-gram (trigram) indexes for substrings and typos, inverted indexes (tsvector) for full text. PostgreSQL provides all three; an in-process trie serves the hottest autocomplete cases.

Why does it exist?

Because LIKE '%term%' over a million product names is a sequential scan with a string comparison per row: 200–500 ms per keystroke, and autocomplete fires on every keystroke. Prefix structures turn that into O(length of the prefix) or O(log n); trigram indexes turn substring and typo-tolerant search into an index lookup on the pieces of the query.

Mental model

Imagine a dictionary. Finding words starting with "pho" is opening at "pho" and reading forward: the dictionary's alphabetical order is the index. Finding words containing "hon" is impossible that way; you would need a second book listing, for every three-letter chunk, all the words that contain it: "hon: honey, phone, iPhone, Honda". That second book is the trigram index. To find "ipone" (a typo), you look up its chunks ("ipo", "pon", "one") and rank words by how many chunks they share: "iPhone" shares "one" and, after lowercasing and padding, more than anything else.

How it works

Trie (prefix tree). Each node is a character; a path from the root spells a prefix; nodes mark word ends and can carry a payload (popularity). Lookup is O(L) for a prefix of length L, independent of the vocabulary size. In JavaScript each node is an object with a Map of children, about 100 bytes per node, so 200,000 terms with an average of 15 characters and heavy prefix sharing is roughly 1.5 million nodes, 150 MB. That is fine for a bounded vocabulary (cities, categories, brand names, top search terms) loaded once per process; it is not fine for a 10-million-product catalog. For ranked completions, precompute each node's top-k terms at build time so a lookup is O(L + k) with no traversal.

// search/trie.ts
interface TrieNode { children: Map<string, TrieNode>; topK: Array<{ term: string; score: number }>; }

export class PrefixTrie {
  private readonly root: TrieNode = { children: new Map(), topK: [] };
  constructor(private readonly k = 8) {}

  // O(L) per insert, plus O(L * k) to maintain each prefix's top-k list
  insert(term: string, score: number): void {
    let node = this.root;
    for (const ch of term.toLowerCase()) {
      let next = node.children.get(ch);
      if (!next) { next = { children: new Map(), topK: [] }; node.children.set(ch, next); }
      node = next;
      node.topK.push({ term, score });
      node.topK.sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score);      // k is tiny, so this is effectively O(k)
      if (node.topK.length > this.k) node.topK.length = this.k;
    }
  }

  // O(L): walk the prefix, return the precomputed completions
  complete(prefix: string): string[] {
    let node = this.root;
    for (const ch of prefix.toLowerCase()) {
      const next = node.children.get(ch);
      if (!next) return [];
      node = next;
    }
    return node.topK.map((e) => e.term);
  }
}

Prefix search in PostgreSQL. A B-tree can serve LIKE 'pho%' if the index uses byte-order comparison: either the column has COLLATE "C" or the index uses text_pattern_ops. Then the query is a range scan from 'pho' to 'php', O(log n + k), and the same index provides ORDER BY name.

Trigram (n-gram) search in PostgreSQL. pg_trgm breaks strings into overlapping three-character chunks (with padding, so "phone" becomes " p", " ph", "pho", "hon", "one", "ne "). A GIN index maps each trigram to the rows containing it. LIKE '%hon%', ILIKE, regular expressions and the similarity operators (%, <->, word_similarity) all become: split the query into trigrams, look each up, intersect or score the row sets, then recheck the candidates against the real condition. Cost is proportional to the posting lists of the query's trigrams, not to the table. The GIN index is typically 2–3x the size of the indexed text and slows inserts noticeably; fastupdate batches insertions in a pending list.

Full-text search. to_tsvector tokenizes, stems and removes stop words; a GIN index on the tsvector makes @@ to_tsquery(...) fast; ts_rank orders results. It is the right tool for descriptions and documents, not for SKUs or names with typos.

Need Structure Where Cost per query Notes
Autocomplete over a bounded vocabulary Trie with top-k In process O(L + k), no I/O Rebuild on a schedule; ~100 bytes per node
Prefix on a large table B-tree with text_pattern_ops or COLLATE "C" PostgreSQL O(log n + k) Also serves ORDER BY
Substring, ILIKE, typos GIN trigram index (pg_trgm) PostgreSQL Proportional to posting lists 2–3x text size; slower writes
Words, stems, ranking over long text GIN on tsvector PostgreSQL Proportional to posting lists Language-aware
Faceting, relevance tuning, multi-field at very high volume Inverted index engine (OpenSearch and similar) External ms A second system to operate and keep in sync
Lexicographic autocomplete of short keys Sorted set with ZRANGEBYLEX Redis O(log n + k) Good for very hot, tiny payloads

Practical example

A storefront search box: as the user types, the first request hits the in-process trie of the 100,000 most-searched terms (O(L), microseconds); if it returns fewer than 5 results, a second request runs a trigram query against 2 million product names (5–20 ms). Submitting the search runs the trigram query plus a Levenshtein re-rank of the top 100 (the DP from the dynamic programming section), then falls through to full-text search on descriptions when names produce nothing.

NestJS example

// search/search.service.ts
import { Injectable, OnModuleInit, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron, CronExpression } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { PrefixTrie } from './trie';

@Injectable()
export class SearchService implements OnModuleInit {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(SearchService.name);
  private trie = new PrefixTrie(8);

  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly db: DataSource) {}

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> { await this.rebuildTrie(); }

  @Cron(CronExpression.EVERY_10_MINUTES)
  async rebuildTrie(): Promise<void> {
    const rows: Array<{ term: string; score: number }> = await this.db.query(
      `SELECT term, hits AS score FROM popular_search_terms ORDER BY hits DESC LIMIT 100000`);
    const fresh = new PrefixTrie(8);
    for (const r of rows) fresh.insert(r.term, r.score);
    this.trie = fresh;                                                 // atomic swap; ~150 ms to build
    this.logger.log(`autocomplete trie rebuilt with ${rows.length} terms`);
  }

  suggest(prefix: string): string[] {
    return prefix.length >= 2 ? this.trie.complete(prefix.slice(0, 40)) : [];   // bound L
  }

  async fuzzyProducts(q: string, limit = 20): Promise<Array<{ id: string; name: string; sim: number }>> {
    // Trigram shortlist via GIN, ranked by similarity; the % operator uses pg_trgm.similarity_threshold
    return this.db.query(
      `SELECT id, name, similarity(name, $1) AS sim
       FROM products
       WHERE name % $1
       ORDER BY name <-> $1
       LIMIT $2`, [q.slice(0, 100), limit]);
  }
}

The two slice calls are the algorithmic safety: L bounded at 40 for the trie, 100 characters for the trigram query, because both costs scale with query length.

PostgreSQL example

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;

-- Prefix: byte-order B-tree
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY products_name_prefix_idx ON products (name text_pattern_ops);
-- Substring and fuzzy: trigram GIN
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY products_name_trgm_idx ON products USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);

SET pg_trgm.similarity_threshold = 0.35;   -- default 0.3; higher is stricter and faster

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name ILIKE '%ipone 15%' ORDER BY name <-> 'ipone 15' LIMIT 20;
Limit  (actual time=6.812..6.901 rows=20 loops=1)
  ->  Sort  (actual time=6.810..6.880 rows=20 loops=1)
        Sort Key: ((name <-> 'ipone 15'::text))
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 27kB
        ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on products  (actual time=3.120..6.402 rows=312 loops=1)
              Recheck Cond: (name ~~* '%ipone 15%'::text)
              Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 1488
              Heap Blocks: exact=1706
              Buffers: shared hit=1912
              ->  Bitmap Index Scan on products_name_trgm_idx  (actual time=2.880..2.881 rows=1800 loops=1)
                    Index Cond: (name ~~* '%ipone 15%'::text)
Execution Time: 6.953 ms

Read it as the algorithm: the index found 1,800 candidates from the query's trigrams, the recheck kept 312 that truly match, a top-N heapsort ranked them, 7 ms total over 2 million rows. Rows Removed by Index Recheck is the trigram index being approximate on purpose. For prefix queries, confirm the B-tree is used:

EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE 'iPhone 1%' ORDER BY name LIMIT 10;
-- Index Scan using products_name_prefix_idx ... Index Cond: ((name ~>=~ 'iPhone 1') AND (name ~<~ 'iPhone 2'))

Production scenario

A marketplace runs 1,200 search requests per second at peak, 70% of them autocomplete. The trie serves autocomplete in-process (p99 under 0.5 ms, no database traffic). Trigram queries against 4 million names run on a read replica with a 12 GB GIN index at p99 of 25 ms. Writes to products cost about 3x more with the GIN index than without; the catalog team batches imports and sets fastupdate = on with a scheduled VACUUM to flush the pending list, because a large pending list makes reads slow.

Failure scenario

At 15:50 search p99 climbs from 25 ms to 2 seconds after a marketing campaign; CPU on the replica is at 100%. The query shape was fine; the input was not. Users were pasting product descriptions of 500+ characters into the search box, and each produced hundreds of trigrams, each with a large posting list, and a recheck over tens of thousands of candidates. The fix: cap the query at 100 characters, require at least 3 characters, and add a statement timeout of 200 ms on the search connection pool so a bad query fails fast instead of holding a core.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Short or very long queries. Two-character queries have few trigrams and match everything; long queries have too many. Bound both ends.
  • Common trigrams. A query like "the" matches half the table; similarity ranking helps, but the recheck is expensive. Raise the threshold or require more characters.
  • Unicode and case. Trigram indexes are case-insensitive for ILIKE; accents are not folded unless you index unaccent(name) via an expression index and query the same way.
  • Write amplification. GIN indexes are expensive to maintain; bulk-load with the index dropped and rebuilt, or rely on fastupdate plus vacuum.
  • Stale in-process tries. Rebuild on a schedule; swap atomically.
  • Trie memory. Bound the vocabulary; a trie over a whole catalog will not fit.
  • Relevance expectations. Trigram similarity is not relevance; for merchandising rules and facets, a search engine earns its keep.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior matches the structure to the query shape and the data size: trie for hot, bounded autocomplete; B-tree for prefix over big tables; trigram for typos and substrings; tsvector for text; a dedicated engine only when relevance tuning and facets demand it and the team can operate a second system. They bound every input, put search on a replica, set statement timeouts, and measure Rows Removed by Index Recheck as the health metric of trigram queries.

To a product manager: "Typo-tolerant search over all product names costs about 10 milliseconds and works today with PostgreSQL. 'Show me red shoes under 50 sorted by popularity with brand filters' is a different system, and I want to be sure we need it before we run one."

Common mistakes

  • LIKE '%x%' with only a B-tree.
  • A trie over an unbounded vocabulary.
  • No length limits on search input.
  • Trigram GIN on a table with heavy writes without planning vacuum.
  • Jumping to a search engine for a problem pg_trgm solves in 10 ms.

Interview questions

  1. "Autocomplete over 100,000 terms at 1,000 RPS: design and complexity." Expected: in-process trie with precomputed top-k, O(L + k), periodic rebuild. Follow-up: what if the vocabulary is 10 million?
  2. "Why can't a normal B-tree serve ILIKE '%hon%', and what does pg_trgm do instead?" Expected: prefix order only; trigram posting lists with recheck.
  3. "What is Rows Removed by Index Recheck and when does it become a problem?" Expected: candidates the index could not exclude; large values mean common trigrams or short queries.
  4. "How would you add typo tolerance to product name search?" Expected: trigram similarity shortlist, Levenshtein re-rank on the top 100.
  5. "When is it time for a dedicated search engine?" Expected: relevance tuning, facets, multi-field boosting, very high volume; and only if the team can operate the sync.

Practical exercise

Load 1 million product names. Build the prefix B-tree, the trigram GIN and the trie of the top 50,000 names. Measure p50/p99 for 100 autocomplete prefixes (trie), 100 prefix queries (B-tree) and 100 typo queries (trigram). Then remove the input length cap and send a 600-character query.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Trie p99 under 1 ms; B-tree prefix p99 under 5 ms; trigram p99 under 30 ms.
  • The 600-character query is rejected by validation, and with validation bypassed it is cut off by the statement timeout.
  • EXPLAIN output for each query type is captured and annotated.

8.22 Worked example: dependency resolution with topological sort

Concept

Dependency resolution takes a set of things that declare what they need and produces an order (or a parallel schedule) in which every need is satisfied before it is used. It is topological sorting applied to packages (npm), modules (NestJS), database objects (tables with foreign keys), infrastructure (Terraform resources) and startup routines (connect to the config store before the database, before the cache, before accepting traffic). The section on topological sorting gave the algorithm; this example shows the three places a NestJS backend engineer meets it every week.

Why does it exist?

Because "just initialize things in the order they are written" is a global assumption built from local knowledge, and it fails silently: a service that reads config before the config module has loaded gets undefined; a test that truncates customers before orders hits a foreign-key error; a build that installs packages in the wrong order links against a missing dependency. Resolution makes the order a computed fact rather than a convention.

Mental model

Imagine setting up a new office. The internet must be connected before the computers can be configured, the computers before the software, the software before training. Some tasks are independent (paint the walls, order chairs). A good project manager lists every task's prerequisites and works out both the order and what can happen at the same time. That list of prerequisites is the dependency graph; the plan is its topological order.

How it works

npm. package.json files declare edges; the resolver builds a graph of packages with version constraints, deduplicates where semver allows, and writes package-lock.json as the resolved graph. Installation order respects dependencies (a package's postinstall runs after its dependencies are present). npm tolerates cycles between packages (it links them and hopes), which is why a circular dependency at the module level in your own code (a.ts imports b.ts imports a.ts) produces undefined exports at runtime rather than an error; tools like madge --circular src/ run the cycle detection you learned in the DFS section over your import graph, and belong in CI.

NestJS. The module graph is imports; the provider graph is constructor injection. Nest instantiates modules and providers in dependency order and calls lifecycle hooks (onModuleInit, onApplicationBootstrap) with modules ordered by their distance from the root, so dependencies are initialized before dependents. Cycles at the module level fail at startup with the "module at index [n] is undefined" error; cycles at the provider level need forwardRef, which delays resolution and is a smell that usually means a third provider should own the shared logic.

// A provider-level cycle and its honest fix.
// Smell: OrdersService needs PaymentsService, PaymentsService needs OrdersService.
@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(@Inject(forwardRef(() => PaymentsService)) private readonly payments: PaymentsService) {}
}

// Fix: extract what both need into a lower-level provider with no upward dependency.
@Injectable()
export class OrderLedgerService { /* record and read order financial state */ }

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService { constructor(private readonly ledger: OrderLedgerService) {} }

@Injectable()
export class PaymentsService { constructor(private readonly ledger: OrderLedgerService) {} }

Database objects. Foreign keys are dependency edges: orders.customer_id -> customers.id means customers must be created first and truncated or dropped last. TypeORM's schema synchronization and migration generator order CREATE TABLE statements by these edges; test fixtures that clean the database must truncate in reverse topological order or use TRUNCATE ... CASCADE. You can read the edges from the catalog:

-- Foreign-key edges: child table -> parent table
SELECT c.conrelid::regclass AS child_table, c.confrelid::regclass AS parent_table
FROM pg_constraint c
WHERE c.contype = 'f' AND c.connamespace = 'public'::regnamespace;
flowchart LR
    Customers["customers"] --> Orders["orders"]
    Products["products"] --> OrderItems["order_items"]
    Orders --> OrderItems
    Orders --> Payments["payments"]
    Warehouses["warehouses"] --> Inventory["inventory"]
    Products --> Inventory

Creation order is any topological order of this graph (customers, products, warehouses, orders, inventory, order_items, payments); deletion order is the reverse.

Practical example

A test suite resets the database between test files. The naive DELETE FROM in alphabetical order fails on foreign keys; TRUNCATE ... CASCADE works but wipes tables the test did not touch and is slow on large fixture sets. Computing the topological order once from pg_constraint and truncating in reverse order is exact, fast and does not need to be updated when someone adds a table.

NestJS example

A startup orchestrator for integrations that declare dependencies on each other (the search index needs the catalog client; the recommendation client needs both), using the topologicalOrder function from the topological sort section and running independent integrations in parallel level by level:

// bootstrap/integrations-bootstrap.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnApplicationBootstrap } from '@nestjs/common';
import { topologicalOrder, Task } from '../scheduling/topological-sort';

export interface Integration { id: string; dependsOn: string[]; init(): Promise<void>; }

@Injectable()
export class IntegrationsBootstrapService implements OnApplicationBootstrap {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(IntegrationsBootstrapService.name);
  constructor(private readonly integrations: Integration[]) {}   // provided via a multi-provider token

  async onApplicationBootstrap(): Promise<void> {
    const tasks: Task[] = this.integrations.map((i) => ({ id: i.id, dependsOn: i.dependsOn, priority: 0 }));
    const { order, cyclic } = topologicalOrder(tasks);
    if (cyclic.length > 0) throw new Error(`integration dependency cycle: ${cyclic.join(', ')}`);

    // Level-by-level: everything whose dependencies are done runs concurrently
    const done = new Set<string>();
    const byId = new Map(this.integrations.map((i) => [i.id, i]));
    while (done.size < order.length) {
      const level = order.filter((id) => !done.has(id) && byId.get(id)!.dependsOn.every((d) => done.has(d)));
      await Promise.all(level.map(async (id) => {
        const started = Date.now();
        await byId.get(id)!.init();
        this.logger.log(`integration ${id} ready in ${Date.now() - started} ms`);
      }));
      for (const id of level) done.add(id);
    }
  }
}

The level loop is O(V²) in the worst case because it re-scans order each round; for a few dozen integrations that is nothing, and the clarity is worth it. For thousands of nodes, keep the in-degree map from Kahn's algorithm live instead.

PostgreSQL example

Reverse-topological truncation computed from the catalog, as a function you can call from test setup:

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION truncate_all_in_fk_order(schema_name text DEFAULT 'public') RETURNS void
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  remaining text[];
  ready text[];
  t text;
BEGIN
  SELECT array_agg(tablename::text) INTO remaining
  FROM pg_tables WHERE schemaname = schema_name AND tablename <> 'migrations';

  WHILE cardinality(remaining) > 0 LOOP
    -- ready = tables no remaining table references (leaves of the reversed graph)
    SELECT array_agg(r) INTO ready FROM unnest(remaining) AS r
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM pg_constraint c
      WHERE c.contype = 'f' AND c.confrelid = (schema_name || '.' || r)::regclass
        AND c.conrelid::regclass::text = ANY(remaining) AND c.conrelid <> c.confrelid);
    IF ready IS NULL THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'foreign-key cycle among: %', remaining; END IF;   -- Kahn's leftover check
    FOREACH t IN ARRAY ready LOOP
      EXECUTE format('TRUNCATE TABLE %I.%I', schema_name, t);
    END LOOP;
    SELECT array_agg(r) INTO remaining FROM unnest(remaining) AS r WHERE NOT (r = ANY(ready));
  END LOOP;
END $$;

This is Kahn's algorithm in PL/pgSQL: each loop iteration truncates the current "ready" set (tables nothing else points to) and removes them from the graph. Self-referencing tables (categories.parent_id) are excluded from the cycle test by the conrelid <> confrelid clause, since TRUNCATE handles them fine.

Production scenario

A monorepo with 60 NestJS modules and 400 providers starts in 1.8 seconds; the module graph resolution itself is a few milliseconds. What costs time is onModuleInit hooks that connect to external systems serially. Grouping them as in the bootstrap service above, so that the 12 independent integrations connect concurrently, cuts startup to 0.6 seconds, which matters when Kubernetes rolls 40 pods and each one is not ready until bootstrap completes.

Failure scenario

At 11:00 a deploy fails to start: Nest can't resolve dependencies of the NotificationsService (?, TemplateService). Please make sure that the argument UsersService at index [0] is available in the NotificationsModule context. A developer added UsersService to a constructor without importing UsersModule (or without UsersModule exporting it). This is dependency resolution telling you an edge points to a node the graph cannot see. The fix is the import and export; the process fix is a smoke test that boots the application in CI, since the graph is only resolved at startup.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Provider cycles hidden behind forwardRef. They resolve, but initialization order between the two is undefined; refactor.
  • Import cycles at the TypeScript level. undefined at runtime, no startup error; detect with madge in CI.
  • Foreign-key cycles. Two tables referencing each other need deferred constraints and careful truncation.
  • Dynamic modules with async factories. forRootAsync adds edges through inject; missing imports in the async options is a common resolution failure.
  • Global modules. @Global() hides edges; use sparingly so the graph stays readable.
  • Lockfile drift. npm install without committing the lockfile changes the resolved graph between machines; use npm ci.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior keeps dependency graphs explicit and acyclic, at every layer: packages, modules, providers, tables, startup steps. They put cycle detection in CI (madge, a boot smoke test, a fresh-database migration run) so the graph is validated before deployment. They treat forwardRef and @Global() as debts with a comment explaining why. They make startup order computed, and use it to parallelize what is independent.

Common mistakes

  • Reaching for forwardRef instead of extracting a shared provider.
  • Truncating tables in alphabetical order.
  • Serial onModuleInit chains for independent integrations.
  • No CI check for import cycles.
  • Assuming npm's tolerance of package cycles means your code's cycles are harmless.

Interview questions

  1. "How does NestJS decide provider instantiation and onModuleInit order?" Expected: dependency graph from imports and injection; modules by distance from root; hooks respect it.
  2. "What does forwardRef do and why is it a smell?" Expected: lazy resolution to tolerate a cycle; the cycle usually means a missing lower-level provider.
  3. "Truncate every table in a schema safely. Approach?" Expected: read FK edges from pg_constraint, Kahn's algorithm, truncate in reverse order.
  4. "Why do TypeScript import cycles fail silently?" Expected: partially initialized module objects; detect with static analysis.
  5. "How do you cut startup time in a large NestJS app with many external connections?" Expected: compute the dependency levels and initialize each level concurrently.

Practical exercise

Run madge --circular src/ on a real project and fix one cycle by extracting a shared provider. Write the truncate_all_in_fk_order function and use it in a Jest global setup. Build the integrations bootstrap with three fake integrations (two independent, one dependent) and measure startup with serial versus level-parallel initialization.

Acceptance criteria:

  • madge reports zero cycles and CI fails if one is reintroduced.
  • Test database resets succeed with foreign keys enabled and complete in under 200 ms for the fixture set.
  • Level-parallel bootstrap is faster than serial by roughly the duration of the shorter independent integration, and a planted cycle fails startup with the offending ids.

8.23 Algorithmic thinking in code review

Concept

Most complexity bugs are not found by a profiler. They are found by a reviewer who reads a pull request, sees a loop, asks "what is inside it?", and does the multiplication in their head. A profiler tells you where time went after the incident; a reviewer stops the incident from shipping. This section is the reading technique: the eight shapes that turn a linear function into a quadratic or exponential one, the realistic input size where each starts to hurt, and the rewrite.

Why does it exist?

Because quadratic code passes every test. Tests run with 10 rows, staging has 200, and the largest customer in production has 40,000. O(n²) at n=10 is 100 operations: invisible. At n=40,000 it is 1.6 billion: a 30-second request, a blocked event loop, a fleet-wide timeout. The defect was present on day one and only the input grew. Reviewers who read for complexity catch it in the two minutes it takes to read the diff; nobody catches it later without an outage.

Mental model

Imagine reading a recipe. "For each guest, walk to the shop and buy one egg." With 4 guests it is a strange recipe. With 400 guests it is a week of walking. The reviewer's job is not to time the cook: it is to notice the shop trip inside the guest loop and ask how many guests we will ever have. Every complexity smell in this section is a shop trip inside a loop; the only question is how expensive the trip is and how many guests turn up.

How it works

Read every loop with three questions, in this order:

  1. What does n actually become in production? Not in the test. The biggest tenant, the biggest order, the biggest CSV, in twelve months.
  2. What is inside the loop body, and what is its cost? A property read is O(1). A find, includes, indexOf, filter, sort, JSON.parse, a query, an HTTP call or a regex is not.
  3. Multiply. n times the body cost is the complexity. If the answer contains n², n² log n, or 2ⁿ, ask for the rewrite before approving.
flowchart TB
    Start["Diff contains a loop, map, forEach or reduce"] --> N["What is n at the largest tenant?"]
    N --> Body["What is inside the body?"]
    Body --> O1["Property access, arithmetic, Map or Set lookup"]
    Body --> ON["find, includes, indexOf, filter, sort"]
    Body --> IO["await query, await http, JSON.parse, regex"]
    O1 --> OK["O of n: approve"]
    ON --> Quad["O of n squared: ask for a Map or Set"]
    IO --> Batch["N plus 1 or blocking: ask for batching or streaming"]

The eight shapes, each with the smell, the complexity, the size where it stops being free, and the rewrite.

1. Nested loops over database results. Two result sets joined in JavaScript.

// Smell: an in-memory nested-loop join
for (const order of orders) {                         // 5,000 orders
  for (const item of items) {                         // 20,000 items
    if (item.orderId === order.id) order.items.push(item);
  }
}

O(n × m) = 100 million comparisons, about 400–900 ms of blocked event loop. It is invisible at 50 orders and 200 items (10,000 comparisons, under a millisecond). Rewrite: group the child rows into a Map once, then one lookup per parent: O(n + m), about 6 ms. Or push the join into PostgreSQL, which has hash joins and does this for a living.

2. find / includes / indexOf inside a map. The most common O(n²) in a TypeScript codebase, because it reads like a one-liner.

// Smell: linear scan inside a linear loop
const enriched = orders.map((o) => ({
  ...o,
  customer: customers.find((c) => c.id === o.customerId),   // O(n) inside O(n)
  isVip: vipIds.includes(o.customerId),                      // another O(n)
}));

At n = 500 this is 250,000 comparisons: under a millisecond, ships happily. At n = 5,000 it is 25 million comparisons across the two scans and measures about 70–90 ms of blocked event loop on a modern container: every other request in that process waits. At n = 50,000 it is roughly 7 seconds, which is not a slow endpoint, it is an outage. Rewrite:

const byId = new Map(customers.map((c) => [c.id, c]));   // O(m), built once
const vip = new Set(vipIds);                             // O(k), built once
const enriched = orders.map((o) => ({ ...o, customer: byId.get(o.customerId), isVip: vip.has(o.customerId) }));

O(n + m + k), about 2 ms at n = 5,000. The rule for review: any linear search inside a linear loop is a Map or a Set that has not been built yet.

3. N+1 queries. This is an algorithmic problem that happens to be expressed in an ORM. The loop is O(n); the body is a network round trip.

for (const order of orders) {                                   // 500 orders
  order.customer = await this.customers.findOneBy({ id: order.customerId });   // 1.2 ms each
}

O(n) queries × 1.2 ms = 600 ms, of which almost none is database work; it is 500 round trips. Rewrite as two queries and a Map: WHERE id = ANY($1) with the distinct ids, then join in memory: about 8 ms. In TypeORM that is relations: { customer: true } or a DataLoader; in Sequelize, include. The reviewer's tell is await inside for. Not every await in a loop is wrong (bounded, deliberately serialized work is fine), but every one must be justified in the PR.

4. Sorting inside a loop. sort is O(k log k) and mutates.

for (const group of groups) {                     // 2,000 groups
  const recent = allEvents.sort((a, b) => b.at - a.at).filter((e) => e.groupId === group.id).slice(0, 5);
}

O(n × m log m) = 2,000 × 10,000 × 13 ≈ 260 million comparisons, several seconds. It also mutates allEvents under everyone else. Rewrite: sort once outside the loop, group into a Map<groupId, Event[]> in one pass, then take the first five per group: O(m log m + m + n). Better still, let PostgreSQL do it with row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY group_id ORDER BY at DESC).

5. Building a giant array before responding instead of streaming. The complexity is linear; the memory is not.

const all = await this.repo.find({ where: { tenantId } });   // 800,000 rows
return all.map(toCsvLine).join('\n');                        // one 400 MB string

Node's default old-space is around 1.5–2 GB in a typical container; a 400 MB string plus the 800,000 hydrated entities behind it (each entity is several hundred bytes of object headers and hidden classes, so 600 MB or more) is an OOMKilled pod, and join on a huge array is a single allocation that can fail on its own. Rewrite: a server-side cursor (QueryRunner.stream() in TypeORM, pg-query-stream) piped through a transform into the response, so peak memory is one batch. Memory is a complexity dimension; O(n) space with a large n and a hard heap limit is a crash, not a slowdown.

6. JSON.parse on multi-megabyte payloads. JSON.parse is linear and native, so it looks free. It is also synchronous: it blocks the event loop for its entire duration and allocates several times the input size.

A 10 MB JSON body parses in roughly 80–120 ms and produces 40–60 MB of heap. At 20 requests per second of 10 MB uploads, the event loop is blocked more than it is free, p99 across every unrelated endpoint on that pod collapses, and the liveness probe starts failing (see Part 9 — Operating Systems and Runtime for the event loop, and Part 30 — Resilience Patterns for what that does to probes). Rewrite: cap body-parser limit to what the API actually needs ('256kb' for JSON APIs), take large payloads as an upload to object storage plus a job, and stream-parse when you must parse in-process.

7. Regex with catastrophic backtracking. The only shape in this list that is exponential.

const RE = /^(\w+\s?)+$/;            // nested quantifier: the classic ReDoS shape
if (RE.test(input)) { /* ... */ }

On a 22-character string that fails to match at the end, the engine explores on the order of 2²² paths: a few hundred milliseconds. At 30 characters it is minutes, on the single thread that serves every other request. One crafted 40-character string in a name field takes a pod down, and the attacker needs no volume. Rewrite: remove the nested quantifier (/^\w+(\s\w+)*$/), cap input length before matching, prefer explicit parsing or class-validator decorators over hand-written regexes, and run eslint-plugin-security or a ReDoS linter in CI.

8. Recomputing the same aggregate per row. A constant hoisted into a loop by accident.

for (const item of cart.items) {                                     // 40 items
  const total = await this.orders.sum('totalCents', { customerId }); // same answer 40 times
  applyDiscountTier(item, total);
}

O(n) identical queries, or O(n × m) if the aggregate is computed in memory over another collection. The value does not depend on item. Rewrite: compute once above the loop. The reviewer's tell is that no loop variable appears in the expression.

Before and after, with realistic numbers measured on one 2 vCPU container:

Smell Complexity Realistic n Cost before Rewrite Cost after
In-memory nested-loop join O(n × m) 5,000 × 20,000 400–900 ms blocked Group children into a Map, or join in SQL 6 ms
find/includes inside map O(n²) 5,000 70–90 ms blocked Build Map/Set once 2 ms
N+1 queries O(n) round trips 500 600 ms, mostly latency WHERE id = ANY($1) plus Map 8 ms
sort inside a loop O(n × m log m) 2,000 × 10,000 3–6 s, plus mutation bug Sort once and group, or window function 40 ms
Materialize then respond O(n) space 800,000 rows 600 MB+, OOMKilled Cursor plus streaming response 30 MB steady
JSON.parse of a large body O(n), synchronous 10 MB 80–120 ms loop block Body size limit plus upload-and-job Rejected at 256 KB
Nested-quantifier regex O(2ⁿ) 30 chars Minutes, one core Rewrite pattern, cap length Microseconds
Aggregate recomputed per row O(n) queries 40 50 ms Hoist above the loop 1.2 ms

Practical example

A GET /admin/orders/report endpoint was written against a seeded database of 300 orders and reviewed by three people. In production the largest merchant had 48,000 orders in the reporting window. The handler did an in-memory join (shape 1), a find per row for the customer (shape 2), and a sort inside the grouping loop (shape 4). Each is defensible in isolation; multiplied, the endpoint took 41 seconds and blocked the event loop for most of it, so every other request served by that pod timed out. Three Map builds and one hoisted sort brought it to 380 ms.

NestJS example

The rewrite pattern, as it appears in a real service, with the batching helper that removes the N+1 and the Map that removes the quadratic:

// orders/orders-report.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Between, In, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';
import { Customer } from '../customers/customer.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersReportService {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Order) private readonly orders: Repository<Order>,
    @InjectRepository(Customer) private readonly customers: Repository<Customer>,
  ) {}

  async build(tenantId: string, from: Date, to: Date) {
    const orders = await this.orders.find({ where: { tenantId, createdAt: Between(from, to) } });

    // One query for every customer referenced, not one per order: O(1) round trips
    const customerIds = [...new Set(orders.map((o) => o.customerId))];
    const customers = await this.customers.find({ where: { id: In(customerIds) } });
    const byId = new Map(customers.map((c) => [c.id, c]));            // O(m) once

    // O(n) with O(1) lookups inside; nothing linear lives in this loop
    return orders.map((o) => ({
      id: o.id,
      total: o.totalCents,
      customerName: byId.get(o.customerId)?.name ?? 'unknown',
    }));
  }
}

In(customerIds) becomes WHERE id IN (...), which has a parameter-count ceiling; above a few thousand ids, chunk the array or use = ANY($1::uuid[]) with a single array parameter. That ceiling is itself a review item.

PostgreSQL example

The reviewer's question "is this loop really a join?" usually has a SQL answer. The three-shape endpoint above collapses into one query whose plan you can read:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT o.id, o.total_cents, c.name,
       row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.created_at DESC) AS rn
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 AND o.created_at >= $2 AND o.created_at < $3;
WindowAgg  (actual time=182.4..268.9 rows=48012 loops=1)
  ->  Sort  (actual time=182.3..196.1 rows=48012 loops=1)
        Sort Key: o.customer_id, o.created_at DESC
        Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 9114kB
        ->  Hash Join  (actual time=12.8..108.2 rows=48012 loops=1)
              Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)
              ->  Index Scan using orders_tenant_created_idx on orders o (actual time=0.04..61.2 rows=48012 loops=1)
              ->  Hash  (actual time=12.6..12.6 rows=9200 loops=1)
Execution Time: 274.1 ms

The Hash Join is exactly the Map you would have built in JavaScript, built by code that has been optimized for thirty years. When you see loops=48012 on an inner node in a plan, that is the database doing shape 2 for you: usually a missing index, occasionally a genuinely correct nested loop.

Production scenario

A team added an algorithmic pass to their review template: for every PR touching a request path, the description must state the largest realistic n and the complexity of any new loop. In six months it caught eleven quadratic paths before release, two ReDoS patterns and four N+1s. Cost: about ninety seconds per review. Compare with one Sev-2 incident, which costs a day of engineering time plus the customer conversation.

Failure scenario

At 09:40 a Monday the checkout API's p99 went from 120 ms to 9 s, only for one merchant. No deploy that morning; the deploy had been eleven days earlier. The find inside map in the promotions engine had been fine at 900 active promotions; over the weekend a bulk import took that merchant to 6,400. Nothing changed in the code; n changed. The graph that identified it was event-loop lag per pod, not CPU (CPU looked normal because one core at 100% on a 4-core pod is 25%). The fix was a two-line Map. The prevention was an assertion in the promotions loader that logs a warning above 2,000 promotions, and a load test seeded with the largest tenant's data instead of the seed fixture.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • n is small today. The reviewer must ask what it is at the largest tenant in a year, not what the fixture has.
  • Quadratic hidden behind a helper. enrich(orders, customers) looks O(n) at the call site; the reviewer must open it.
  • Array.prototype.sort mutates. A sort inside a loop is both slow and a correctness bug for anyone holding the same array.
  • Set/Map keys are compared by reference for objects. A Set of objects does not deduplicate by value; use a primitive key.
  • Spread inside a loop. acc = [...acc, x] inside a reduce copies the accumulator every iteration: a hidden O(n²) that looks functional and elegant.
  • Object.keys inside a loop over the same object. Rebuilds the key array each time.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They read diffs for shape before they read them for style. They know that the three questions (what is n, what is in the body, multiply) take fifteen seconds and catch most performance incidents. They ask authors to state n in the PR description, because the author knows the domain and the reviewer often does not. They do not accept "we can optimize later" for a quadratic in a request path, because "later" is an incident. They also refuse the opposite mistake: rewriting a clear O(n²) over ten elements into an unreadable O(n), because a loop over a fixed, small, bounded collection is not a bug.

To a product manager: "This page works fine for our average customer and will take forty seconds for our biggest one. The change is small and I want it in this release, not the next."

Common mistakes

  • Approving a PR because the tests pass and the fixture is small.
  • Treating N+1 as an ORM configuration issue rather than an algorithm.
  • Optimizing the loop body's constant factor instead of removing the linear scan inside it.
  • Assuming native methods (find, includes, JSON.parse) are free because they are implemented in C++.
  • Measuring CPU percentage on a multi-core pod instead of event-loop lag.

Interview questions

  1. You see items.find(...) inside orders.map(...) in a pull request. What do you say, and what numbers do you use to justify it? Expected: O(n²); state n at the largest tenant; ~25 million comparisons and ~80 ms of blocked loop at n = 5,000; rewrite with a Map built once.
  2. Why is an N+1 query an algorithmic problem and not just an ORM problem? Expected: the loop makes n round trips; the cost is latency × n regardless of ORM; the fix is batching, which changes the complexity of round trips from O(n) to O(1).
  3. Which of these is worst at n = 30 and why: O(n²), O(n log n), O(2ⁿ)? Expected: 2³⁰ is a billion; constants and small n matter, but exponential shapes are a different category and are usually a regex or a naive recursion.
  4. How do you spot a memory complexity problem in review? Expected: anything that materializes a whole result set; look for find() without pagination, join on a large array, buffering before responding; ask for cursors and streaming.
  5. A page got slow with no deploy. Where do you look first? Expected: input size growth; a quadratic that crossed its threshold; per-tenant metrics; event-loop lag.

Practical exercise

Take a real endpoint in your codebase that fans out over a collection. Seed a database with the largest realistic tenant (not the fixture). Measure p99 and event-loop p99 with perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay, at 1x, 10x and 100x the seed size. Then apply the rewrites in this section.

Acceptance criteria:

  • You can plot latency against n and state whether the curve is linear or quadratic from the shape.
  • Event-loop p99 during the 100x run is under 50 ms after the rewrite and you can name the specific line that caused it before.
  • The PR template in your repo now asks for n and the complexity of new loops.

8.24 Choosing the right algorithm for a backend problem

The hard part of applied algorithms is rarely implementing them. It is deciding where the algorithm should live: in your Node process, inside PostgreSQL, inside Redis, or in a background job. The wrong location is the more expensive mistake, because it is the one you cannot fix with a Map.

Three rules decide the location:

  1. Move the algorithm to the data when the data is large. Filtering, joining, sorting and aggregating a million rows belongs in PostgreSQL, which has indexes, hash joins, and a query planner. Pulling a million rows into Node to filter them is transferring megabytes to do work the database already did better.
  2. Move the algorithm to memory when the data is small, hot and shared. Rate-limit counters, top-k autocompletion, session state and leaderboards belong in Redis or in-process, because a round trip to PostgreSQL costs more than the whole computation.
  3. Move the algorithm off the request path when it is O(n log n) or worse over a large n. Reports, exports, recomputed recommendations and graph traversals over the whole dataset belong in a job with a queue, a progress record and a result the user polls for or receives by email.
Problem Approach Complexity Where it lives
Find one entity by id B-tree index lookup O(log n) PostgreSQL
Membership test on a hot, bounded set Hash set O(1) In-process Set, or Redis SISMEMBER
Membership test on a huge set, false positives acceptable Bloom filter O(k) Redis (BF.EXISTS) or in-process
Deduplicate ids from a request Hash set O(n) Application code
Join two result sets Hash join O(n + m) PostgreSQL; Map in the app only for small, already-fetched sets
Top N by score Partial sort / heap, or sorted set O(n log k) PostgreSQL ORDER BY ... LIMIT; Redis ZREVRANGE for hot leaderboards
Paginate a large list Keyset pagination over an index O(log n + k) PostgreSQL
Autocomplete over a bounded vocabulary Trie with precomputed top-k O(L + k) In-process, rebuilt on a schedule
Typo-tolerant search Trigram index Proportional to posting lists PostgreSQL pg_trgm
Fixed-window or sliding-window rate limit Counter / sorted set with atomic script O(1) or O(log n) Redis, one round trip via Lua
Token bucket per user Counter plus timestamp, atomic O(1) Redis
Schedule the next job to run Min-heap or indexed ORDER BY run_at LIMIT O(log n) PostgreSQL with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, or a queue
Evict the least recently used entry Hash map plus doubly linked list O(1) In-process cache, or Redis maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
Shortest or cheapest path Dijkstra with a binary heap O((V + E) log V) Background job; cache the result
Order tasks by dependency Kahn's topological sort O(V + E) Application code at startup, or a job
Detect a cycle DFS with colours, or Kahn's leftover check O(V + E) CI check, or application code
Reachability, "who can see this" BFS with a visited set and a depth cap O(V + E) Application code with bounds; materialize for hot reads
Fewest coins / interval scheduling Greedy, when the exchange argument holds O(n log n) Application code, with the proof written down
Optimal split with dependencies between choices Dynamic programming O(n × W) or O(n × m) Background job if the table is large
Fuzzy string distance for re-ranking Levenshtein DP over the top 100 candidates O(a × b) per pair Application code, over a bounded shortlist
Count distinct over billions of events HyperLogLog O(1) space per key Redis PFCOUNT, or PostgreSQL extension
Recompute an expensive aggregate Incremental update, or materialized view Amortized O(1) per write PostgreSQL materialized view refreshed by a job

The column that matters most in a design review is the last one. "We will do the graph traversal in the service" and "we will do the graph traversal in a nightly job and cache the result" are the same algorithm with completely different operational consequences.

8.25 The complexity cheat sheet

Everything from Part 7 — Data Structures and Part 8, consolidated. Time complexities are for the standard implementation; n is the number of elements.

Data structures

Structure Access Search Insert Delete Space Use it when
Array (fixed) O(1) O(n) n/a n/a O(n) You index by position and the size is known
Dynamic array (JS Array) O(1) O(n) O(1) amortized at the end, O(n) at the front O(n) O(n) Default list; never shift() in a hot loop
String (immutable) O(1) char O(n + m) substring O(n) concat n/a O(n) Build with an array plus join, not += in a loop
Singly linked list O(n) O(n) O(1) at a known node O(1) at a known node O(n) You splice constantly and never index; rare in application code
Doubly linked list O(n) O(n) O(1) at a node O(1) at a node O(n) The recency list inside an LRU cache
Stack O(1) top O(n) O(1) O(1) O(n) Undo, DFS, parser, call-stack simulation
Queue O(1) front O(n) O(1) O(1) O(n) BFS, job buffering; use a ring buffer or two stacks, not shift()
Deque O(1) ends O(n) O(1) ends O(1) ends O(n) Sliding-window maximum, work stealing
Hash map (Map) n/a O(1) average, O(n) worst O(1) average O(1) average O(n) Lookup by key; the answer to most O(n²) review findings
Hash set (Set) n/a O(1) average O(1) average O(1) average O(n) Membership and deduplication
Binary search tree (unbalanced) O(h) O(h) O(h) O(h) O(n) Only as a teaching device; degenerates to a list
Balanced BST / B-tree O(log n) O(log n) O(log n) O(log n) O(n) Ordered data, range scans; this is a database index
Binary heap O(1) min/max O(n) O(log n) O(log n) O(n) Priority queue, scheduler, top-k, Dijkstra frontier
Trie n/a O(L) O(L) O(L) O(total chars) Prefix search over a bounded vocabulary
Graph (adjacency list) n/a O(V + E) traverse O(1) edge O(deg) O(V + E) Any "depends on", "follows", "connects to" relation
Bloom filter n/a O(k), false positives O(k) not supported ~10 bits per item at 1% FP "Definitely not present" checks in front of an expensive lookup
LRU cache (map + list) O(1) O(1) O(1) O(1) O(capacity) Bounded in-process cache with eviction

Algorithms

Algorithm Best Average Worst Space Use it when
Linear search O(1) O(n) O(n) O(1) Small or unsorted collections only
Binary search O(1) O(log n) O(log n) O(1) Sorted array, or searching an answer space (capacity, threshold)
Insertion sort O(n) O(n²) O(n²) O(1) Tiny or nearly-sorted arrays; what sort uses under ~10 elements
Merge sort O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n) Stable sort needed; external sorting of data larger than memory
Quicksort O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n²) O(log n) General in-memory sorting; V8's sort is a hybrid (TimSort)
Heapsort O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n log n) O(1) Worst-case guarantee with no extra memory
Counting / radix sort O(n + k) O(n + k) O(n + k) O(n + k) Small integer key range (status codes, ages, buckets)
Two pointers O(n) O(n) O(n) O(1) Sorted input, pair sums, merging, deduplicating in place
Sliding window O(n) O(n) O(n) O(k) Contiguous subarray or time-window aggregates
BFS O(V + E) O(V + E) O(V + E) O(V) Shortest path in hops, level-by-level expansion
DFS O(V + E) O(V + E) O(V + E) O(V) recursion depth Cycle detection, connected components, topological order
Topological sort (Kahn) O(V + E) O(V + E) O(V + E) O(V) Dependency order; leftover nodes prove a cycle
Dijkstra (binary heap) O((V + E) log V) same same O(V) Cheapest path with non-negative weights
Bellman-Ford O(V × E) O(V × E) O(V × E) O(V) Negative weights, or detecting negative cycles
Union-Find (path compression) ~O(1) ~O(α(n)) ~O(α(n)) O(n) Connected components, grouping, deduplication by equivalence
Greedy O(n log n) typically same same O(1)–O(n) The exchange argument holds and you can state it
DP (1-D, e.g. coin change) O(n × W) same same O(W) Overlapping subproblems, optimal substructure
DP (2-D, e.g. edit distance) O(a × b) same same O(min(a, b)) rolling Sequence comparison over bounded inputs
Memoized recursion O(states) same same O(states) The recurrence is clear and the state space is bounded
Trigram / inverted index search proportional to posting lists same same 2–3x text Substring, typo and full-text search at database scale

8.26 Edge cases and failure modes

An algorithm can be correct, well-chosen and still wrong in production. These are the ways.

flowchart LR
    A["Correct algorithm"] --> B["Correct at the tested input size"]
    B --> C["Correct at production input size"]
    C --> D["Correct under the real memory limit"]
    D --> E["Correct under concurrency and mutation"]
    E --> F["Correct for the business rule"]
    F --> G["Actually shipped"]
    C -.->|"constant factor dominates"| X1["Slower than the naive version"]
    D -.->|"heap or work_mem exceeded"| X2["OOMKilled or spill to disk"]
    E -.->|"graph changed mid-traversal"| X3["Wrong or non-terminating result"]
    F -.->|"greedy assumption false"| X4["Confidently wrong answer"]

  • Unbounded recursion hitting the call stack. Node's default stack holds roughly 10,000–12,000 frames. A recursive DFS over a category tree is fine at depth 12 and throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded on a 20,000-node linked chain built by a bad import, or on a cycle nobody detected. Fix: convert hot traversals to an explicit stack with a visited set and a depth cap, and treat "depth exceeded" as a data-quality alert, not a 500.

  • An O(n log n) sort that spills to disk in PostgreSQL. The plan is optimal; work_mem is 4 MB and the sort needs 300 MB. Sort Method: external merge Disk: 312400kB turns a 1.4 s in-memory sort into 9 s of I/O, and log_temp_files = 0 is how you see it. Fix: SET LOCAL work_mem inside the specific transaction, an index that provides the order, or fewer rows to sort. Raising work_mem globally trades this incident for an out-of-memory one (see Part 18 — PostgreSQL Internals).

  • A hash map degrading when keys collide. O(1) is average, not worst. Adversarial or pathological keys (all hashing to the same bucket) make a Map behave like a list, and JavaScript objects used as maps with hundreds of thousands of dynamic keys also fall out of V8's fast paths and grow a megamorphic shape. Fix: use Map, not {}, for dynamic keys; never build a map keyed directly by unbounded user input without a size cap; and remember that a Set of 10 million strings is real memory, not free.

  • Dijkstra on a graph that changes while you traverse it. The algorithm assumes a static graph. If your edges are database rows and another transaction updates a weight mid-traversal, the "shortest path" you return satisfies no consistent snapshot of the data. Fix: read the graph inside one repeatable-read transaction or one snapshot, or accept the staleness explicitly and say so in the response. The same applies to BFS over a follower graph that is being written to.

  • A greedy algorithm that is provably wrong for the business rule. Greedy coin change works for {1, 5, 10, 25} and fails for {1, 3, 4} (greedy gives 6 = 4+1+1, optimal is 3+3). Greedy shipment packing works until the finance rule "always fill the cheapest carrier first" is added, at which point locally optimal is globally expensive. Fix: write the exchange argument down next to the code. If you cannot write it, you do not have a greedy problem, you have a DP problem or an approximation you must label as one.

  • A DP table that does not fit in the heap. Edit distance over two 200,000-character documents is a 40-billion-cell table. Even the rolling one-row optimization is fine; the naive 2-D table is not. Knapsack with W in cents rather than rupees is 100x the table. Fix: rolling arrays, coarser units, a bounded shortlist (Levenshtein over the top 100 trigram candidates, never over the catalog), or a different algorithm entirely.

  • Constant factors dominating at real input sizes. A "better" O(n log n) implementation with allocations per element loses to an O(n²) scan of 50 elements every time. Binary search over an array of 8 items is slower than a linear scan because of branch prediction and cache locality. Fix: benchmark at the actual n before optimizing; keep the simple version when n is bounded and small, and comment the bound so the next reader knows why.

  • Amortized guarantees that fail at the worst moment. A dynamic array's O(1) append is amortized: one append in n copies the whole array. At 5 million elements that single append is a 40 MB copy and a garbage-collection pause, and it happens under peak load. Fix: pre-size when you know the size, or stream instead of accumulating.

  • Cache-friendly versus cache-hostile. Two O(n) loops are not equal: iterating a flat array of numbers is an order of magnitude faster than chasing pointers through a linked list of objects, because of memory locality. This is why Array beats a linked list in practice for almost everything an application does.

  • Complexity measured in the wrong unit. O(n) HTTP calls is not the same as O(n) array reads even though both are linear; the constant is 200,000x. Always ask what the unit of work is: a CPU cycle, a heap allocation, a page read, or a network round trip.

  • Correct algorithm, wrong data structure feeding it. A perfect Dijkstra implementation fed by orders.find(...) per neighbour is O(V × E). The algorithm's complexity assumes O(1) adjacency lookups.

  • Non-determinism from an unstable sort. V8's sort is stable, but a comparator that returns inconsistent results (comparing floats with tolerance, or comparing objects by a mutable field) produces different orders on different runs, which shows up as flaky pagination and duplicated or missing rows across pages. Fix: total order with a unique tiebreaker, always.

Senior Checklist — Part 8

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can state the time and space complexity of any function I write, and I know the difference between best, average, worst and amortized
  • I can analyse nested loops, recursive calls and library methods, and I know the real cost of find, includes, sort, spread and JSON.parse
  • I know when a sort is worth it, which sort PostgreSQL is using, and when ORDER BY ... LIMIT beats sorting in the application
  • I can write binary search without an off-by-one error, and I can apply it to an answer space, not just an array
  • I can recognise a two-pointer or sliding-window problem and write the O(n) version instead of the O(n²) one
  • I convert deep recursion to an explicit stack, and I bound depth and detect cycles in every traversal
  • I choose BFS or DFS on purpose, with a visited set and a depth cap, and I can explain the memory profile of each
  • I can model a real backend problem as a graph and implement topological sort with cycle reporting
  • I can implement Dijkstra with a heap and say when Bellman-Ford or a precomputed cache is the right answer instead
  • I only use a greedy algorithm when I can write down the exchange argument, and I recognise when the business rule breaks it
  • I can identify overlapping subproblems, write the recurrence, memoize it, and convert to a bottom-up table with rolling state
  • I can design a rate limiter, a job scheduler and a cache eviction policy from first principles and state the complexity of each operation
  • I can explain why a B-tree lookup is O(log n) in page reads and what Buffers: shared hit/read means
  • I know which search problem needs a trie, a prefix B-tree, a trigram index or a full-text index, and the cost of each
  • I read pull requests for complexity: I ask what n is at the largest tenant and multiply it by the loop body
  • I can spot an N+1, a quadratic scan, a sort in a loop and a catastrophic regex in a diff without running anything
  • I know where each algorithm should live: application code, PostgreSQL, Redis, or a background job

Part 8 — Key Takeaways

  • Complexity is about growth, not speed. O(n²) at n=10 is invisible and at n=40,000 is an outage; the code never changed, n did.
  • Every linear search inside a linear loop is a Map or a Set that has not been built yet. That single rewrite fixes most quadratic code in a TypeScript backend.
  • N+1 is an algorithm, not an ORM setting: n round trips at 1.2 ms each is 600 ms of pure latency. Batch to O(1) queries and join with a Map.
  • Space is a complexity dimension with a hard limit. Materializing 800,000 rows is not slow, it is OOMKilled; use cursors and streams.
  • Native and synchronous is not free. JSON.parse of 10 MB blocks the event loop for 100 ms, and a nested-quantifier regex is exponential on one crafted 30-character string.
  • Move the algorithm to the data when the data is large, to memory when it is small and hot, and off the request path when it is O(n log n) or worse over a big n.
  • O(1) average is not O(1) worst. Hash maps degrade on collisions, dynamic arrays copy on growth, and amortized guarantees fail at peak.
  • Constant factors and memory locality decide real performance at small n. Benchmark at the actual input size before replacing a simple loop.
  • Recursion has a hard ceiling around 10,000 frames in Node. Every traversal needs an explicit stack option, a visited set and a depth cap.
  • A greedy algorithm you cannot prove is a wrong answer waiting for a business rule change. Write the exchange argument or use DP.
  • Algorithms assume a static, consistent input. A graph that changes under a traversal, or a comparator without a unique tiebreaker, produces confidently wrong output.
  • The plan is the algorithm. Hash Join, Sort Method: external merge, loops=48012 and Rows Removed by Index Recheck are complexity facts printed by PostgreSQL for free.
  • Reading a diff for complexity takes fifteen seconds: what is n, what is in the loop body, multiply. It is the cheapest performance work you will ever do.

Part 9 — Operating Systems and the Node.js Runtime

A NestJS application is a single operating-system process running one JavaScript thread on top of V8 and libuv. Every production incident you will ever debug in that application eventually bottoms out in one of a handful of operating-system ideas: a process ran out of memory, a file descriptor leaked, a signal was ignored, a thread blocked, a scheduler throttled you, a lock was taken in the wrong order. Senior engineers are not faster typists than mid-level engineers. They are the people in the room who can say "this is an FD leak, not a database problem" at 02:14 and be right.

This part builds that instinct in two layers. Section A covers the operating-system concepts every backend engineer must own. Section B goes deep into the Node.js runtime: V8, the event loop, libuv, workers, streams, memory and garbage collection. Section C ties it together by tracing one NestJS request from the kernel's TCP accept queue to the keep-alive socket write, showing exactly where CPU is spent, where I/O waits, and where p99 latency hides.

9.1 Processes and threads

Concept

A process is a running program. When you type node dist/main.js, the kernel creates a process: it gets a process id (PID), its own private virtual address space (memory that no other process can see), its own table of open file descriptors (files, sockets, pipes), its own environment variables, its own signal handlers, and at least one thread of execution.

A thread is a path of execution inside a process. Every thread has its own call stack, its own CPU registers and its own program counter (the "where am I in the code" pointer), but all threads in a process share the same heap, the same file descriptors and the same address space. A Node.js process is not single-threaded. It runs one JavaScript thread (the main thread, where your NestJS code executes), plus a libuv thread pool (4 threads by default), plus V8 helper threads for garbage collection and compilation. What is single-threaded is your JavaScript.

Why does it exist?

Without processes, every program on a machine would share one memory space, and a bug in a PDF library would corrupt the memory of your database.
