Processes give isolation: one crashes, the others survive. They also give accounting: the kernel can limit CPU, memory and file descriptors per process, which is exactly what a Kubernetes container limit is under the hood (a cgroup wrapped around a process tree).

Threads exist because processes are expensive to create and cannot share memory without ceremony. If you want two things to happen at once inside one program and share data cheaply, you use threads. The price is that shared memory needs coordination (mutexes, atomics), and coordination is where race conditions and deadlocks live.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant. The building is the process: it has its own pantry (memory), its own set of keys to doors and delivery bays (file descriptors), and its own address. Each cook inside is a thread: cooks have their own notepad (stack) but share the pantry (heap). Two cooks reaching for the last onion at the same time is a race condition. A second restaurant across the street is another process: it cannot reach into your pantry. If it wants an onion, it has to send a delivery (inter-process communication through a pipe or a socket).

Node.js is a restaurant with one head chef (the JavaScript thread) who never does the slow chores. Chopping and washing (file reads, DNS lookups, password hashing) are handed to four kitchen helpers (the libuv thread pool) or to the building's own dumbwaiter system (the kernel's asynchronous network I/O), and the chef keeps taking orders.

How it works

  1. The shell calls fork() to clone itself and then execve("/usr/bin/node", ...) to replace the clone with the Node binary. The kernel builds a fresh address space: code pages mapped from the binary, a stack for the main thread, an empty heap, and file descriptors 0, 1 and 2 (stdin, stdout, stderr) inherited from the parent.
  2. Node's C++ bootstrap creates a V8 isolate (one JavaScript heap) and a libuv event loop on the main thread. It also starts a small V8 platform thread pool (default 4 threads, controlled by --v8-pool-size) that V8 uses for concurrent garbage-collection marking and background compilation.
  3. The libuv thread pool is created lazily the first time something needs it (the first fs.readFile, dns.lookup, crypto.pbkdf2 or zlib call). Its size is UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE, default 4, maximum 1024.
  4. Threads are created with the clone() system call sharing the address space. Each thread gets its own stack (8 MB of virtual space by default on Linux, ulimit -s; only the pages actually touched are backed by physical memory).
  5. The kernel scheduler sees threads, not processes, as the unit of scheduling. Your 11-thread Node process is 11 schedulable entities, but only one of them runs JavaScript.
  6. When the process exits, the kernel reclaims everything: memory, descriptors, threads. This is why "restart the pod" fixes leaks: the kernel is the ultimate garbage collector.
flowchart TB
    subgraph P["Node.js process, PID 4021"]
        M["Main thread: V8 isolate + event loop + your NestJS code"]
        subgraph L["libuv thread pool, UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=4"]

You can count them on a running pod:

# threads of the node process inside the container
cat /proc/1/status | grep Threads
# Threads: 11

# list them with names (Linux)
ls /proc/1/task | wc -l

Processes vs threads

Aspect Process Thread
Memory Own private address space Shares the process's heap and globals
Creation cost Hundreds of microseconds to milliseconds; a new Node process is 30–70 ms because V8 must bootstrap Tens of microseconds for an OS thread; a Node worker_thread is 10–30 ms because it needs its own V8 isolate
Memory cost A fresh Node process is roughly 30–50 MB RSS An OS thread is a few hundred KB touched; a Node worker is 5–10 MB because it has its own heap
Failure isolation A crash (segfault, OOM kill) affects only that process An uncaught native crash kills the whole process; in Node, an uncaught JS exception in a worker only terminates that worker
Communication Pipes, sockets, shared memory segments, message queues; data must be serialized Direct memory access; in Node, postMessage (structured clone) or SharedArrayBuffer
Context switch More expensive: page tables change, TLB flushes Cheaper: same address space
Node.js mapping child_process, cluster, one container per replica worker_threads, the libuv pool, V8 helpers
PostgreSQL mapping One backend process per client connection Not used for connections; used internally for parallel workers via processes, not threads

Practical example

An e-commerce order service runs as one container: one Node process, ~11 threads, ~180 MB RSS under load. It keeps a TypeORM pool of 10 connections to PostgreSQL. On the database side, each of those 10 connections is a separate PostgreSQL backend process, forked by the postmaster, each costing roughly 5–10 MB of RSS plus whatever work_mem its queries use. Twenty replicas of the order service therefore create 200 backend processes on the database. That relationship, "one pooled connection here equals one process there", is the single most useful fact about PostgreSQL's process model, and it explains why connection poolers like PgBouncer exist.

# on the database host
ps -o pid,rss,cmd -C postgres | head
#   PID   RSS CMD
#  1188 24512 postgres: checkpointer
#  1189  9876 postgres: background writer
#  1190 11240 postgres: walwriter
#  1191  8420 postgres: autovacuum launcher
#  2310 18904 postgres: orders orders_db 10.0.3.14(51234) idle
#  2311 21112 postgres: orders orders_db 10.0.3.14(51236) SELECT

NestJS example

A small runtime-info endpoint is worth having in every service. It answers "which process am I talking to, how long has it been alive, how many threads does it have" in one HTTP call, which is invaluable when a rolling deploy leaves you unsure which pod version is serving traffic.

// runtime/runtime.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { threadId } from 'node:worker_threads';
import * as os from 'node:os';

@Controller('internal/runtime')
export class RuntimeController {
  @Get()
  info() {
    // /proc/self/status is Linux-only; guard it so local macOS dev does not crash
    let threads: number | null = null;
    try {
      const status = readFileSync('/proc/self/status', 'utf8');
      threads = Number(/Threads:\s+(\d+)/.exec(status)?.[1] ?? null);
    } catch {
      threads = null;
    }

    return {
      pid: process.pid,                 // process id inside the container namespace
      ppid: process.ppid,               // 0 or 1 if node is PID 1 without an init process
      threadId,                         // 0 on the main thread, >0 inside a worker_thread
      threads,                          // main + libuv pool + V8 helpers
      uptimeSeconds: Math.round(process.uptime()),
      nodeVersion: process.version,
      uvThreadPoolSize: process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE ?? '4 (default)',
      cpus: os.availableParallelism(),  // what the kernel exposes, not the cgroup quota
      hostname: os.hostname(),          // equals the pod name in Kubernetes
    };
  }
}

Protect this route behind an internal-only guard or network policy; it leaks nothing secret, but you do not want it indexed.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL is a multi-process system. The postmaster listens on port 5432 and forks a new backend process for every accepted connection. That process lives for the whole session, which is why connecting to PostgreSQL costs 20–50 ms (fork, authentication, TLS handshake) and why you always pool.

-- every row is a process; backend_type tells you which kind
SELECT pid, backend_type, usename, application_name, state, wait_event_type, wait_event
FROM pg_stat_activity
ORDER BY backend_type, pid;

-- how close are we to the ceiling?
SELECT count(*) AS connections,
       current_setting('max_connections')::int AS max_connections
FROM pg_stat_activity;

-- parallel query = real parallelism using extra *processes* (not threads)
SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 4;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT status, count(*) FROM orders WHERE created_at > now() - interval '30 days' GROUP BY status;
--  Finalize GroupAggregate  (cost=... rows=5) (actual time=812.4..815.1 rows=5 loops=1)
--    ->  Gather Merge  (workers planned: 4, workers launched: 4)
--          ->  Partial HashAggregate ... (actual time=790.2..790.3 rows=5 loops=5)
--                ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (actual rows=1240000 loops=5)
--                      Buffers: shared hit=98432 read=41220

loops=5 in the parallel scan means the leader plus four worker processes each scanned about 1.24 million of the 6.2 million rows. Each worker is a full OS process with its own work_mem allowance, so parallel queries multiply memory usage.

TypeORM example

Pool size is the knob that maps your process to PostgreSQL's processes. In TypeORM the pg pool options go under extra.

// database.module.ts
import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';

export const databaseModule = TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync({
  inject: [ConfigService],
  useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
    type: 'postgres',
    url: config.getOrThrow<string>('DATABASE_URL'),
    autoLoadEntities: true,
    extra: {
      max: config.get<number>('DB_POOL_MAX', 10),    // 10 pooled connections = 10 PG backend processes
      idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,                     // close idle connections, freeing PG processes
      connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000,                // fail fast instead of hanging when PG is saturated
      statement_timeout: 15_000,                     // server-side kill for runaway queries
      application_name: `orders-api-${process.env.HOSTNAME ?? 'local'}`, // visible in pg_stat_activity
    },
  }),
});

application_name is a small habit with a big payoff: when the DBA sees 200 idle backends, they can tell which service and which pod owns each one.

Sequelize example

import { SequelizeModule } from '@nestjs/sequelize';

export const sequelizeModule = SequelizeModule.forRoot({
  dialect: 'postgres',
  host: process.env.DB_HOST,
  port: 5432,
  username: process.env.DB_USER,
  password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD,
  database: 'orders_db',
  autoLoadModels: true,
  pool: {
    max: 10,          // upper bound on PG backend processes from this replica
    min: 2,           // keep two warm to avoid the 20-50 ms connect cost on the first request
    acquire: 5_000,   // wait at most 5 s for a free connection, then throw
    idle: 30_000,
  },
  dialectOptions: { application_name: `orders-api-${process.env.HOSTNAME ?? 'local'}` },
});

Production scenario

A payments platform runs 24 replicas of a NestJS service, pool size 20 each. That is up to 480 backend processes on a PostgreSQL primary configured with max_connections = 500. Under normal load only about 120 of them are active at any moment; the other 360 are idle backends each holding 8–10 MB, about 3.5 GB of RAM doing nothing. When a marketing campaign doubles traffic, the autoscaler adds 12 replicas, the 25th replica's pool tries to open its 20 connections, and PostgreSQL answers FATAL: sorry, too many clients already. The service handled 2,000 requests per second fine; the process model, not the query plan, was the limit.

The standard fix is PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode between the services and the database. The services keep pools of 20, PgBouncer multiplexes those 720 client connections onto 60 real backend processes, and the database's memory is spent on shared_buffers instead of idle processes.

Failure scenario

At 09:40 on a Monday, a deploy scaled the catalog service from 10 to 40 pods to absorb an expected traffic peak. Each pod opened its TypeORM pool eagerly on startup. PostgreSQL hit max_connections at pod 31. Pods 31 through 40 failed their startup connection, NestJS threw during TypeOrmModule initialisation, the process exited with code 1, and Kubernetes put them into CrashLoopBackOff. Worse, every restart attempt grabbed a few connections during its brief life, so the healthy pods started seeing connectionTimeoutMillis errors as well. The on-call fixed it by scaling back to 25 pods and raising max_connections temporarily; the permanent fix was PgBouncer plus min: 0 in the pool so pods do not hold connections they are not using.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Node running as PID 1 in a container without an init process does not reap zombie child processes and does not get default signal behaviour. Use docker run --init, tini, or make sure your Dockerfile uses the exec form CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"] rather than the shell form.
  • A Node process that forks children (child_process) and then dies leaves the children orphaned; in Kubernetes the whole container is torn down, but with PM2 on a VM they can linger and keep ports open.
  • os.cpus().length reports the host's CPUs, not the container's CPU quota. A 64-core node with a 500m CPU limit still reports 64.
  • PostgreSQL backend processes are per connection, not per query: an idle-in-transaction connection is a live process holding locks and a snapshot, which blocks VACUUM from cleaning rows.
  • Each PostgreSQL backend can allocate work_mem per sort or hash operation, so a query with three hash joins in 200 concurrent backends can consume 200 × 3 × work_mem, which is how database servers get OOM-killed.
  • Thread-per-connection servers (classic Java servlet containers) allocate a stack per connection; 10,000 idle WebSocket connections cost 10,000 stacks. Node's model costs one small object per connection.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The first question a senior asks about any component is "what is the unit of isolation and what is the unit of cost?" For Node it is the process (isolation) and the event loop (cost: one blocked loop blocks every request in that process). For PostgreSQL it is the backend process, so the true capacity of a database is measured in active connections against cores, not in max_connections.

They refuse to scale pods without checking the pool math: replicas × pool.max must stay below max_connections minus a reserve for migrations, admins and replication. They prefer more small processes over a few huge ones because the blast radius of an OOM kill or an event-loop stall is smaller. And they explain it to a product manager like this: "Every copy of our service reserves ten seats at the database. If we add copies without adding seats, new copies cannot sit down, and they crash on the doorstep."

Common mistakes

  • Believing Node is single-threaded and therefore that bcrypt.hash "cannot block anything". It occupies one of only four libuv threads; four concurrent logins with cost 12 stall every file read and DNS lookup for 250 ms.
  • Sizing pools by feel (max: 100 "to be safe"), which multiplies across replicas into a database process storm.
  • Running cluster inside a container that already has a CPU limit of one core, creating four workers that time-slice one CPU and add context-switch overhead for no throughput.
  • Ignoring application_name, then spending an hour on the database trying to figure out which of 14 services owns the 300 idle connections.

Interview questions

  1. Is Node.js single-threaded? Expected: the JavaScript execution is single-threaded; the process has a libuv pool (default 4) and V8 helper threads. Follow-up: name three operations that use the pool. (fs, dns.lookup, crypto.pbkdf2/scrypt/randomBytes, zlib.)
  2. Why does PostgreSQL need a connection pooler, but Redis usually does not? Expected: PostgreSQL forks a process per connection (5–10 MB, 20–50 ms setup); Redis serves all clients from one thread with a small per-client struct, so thousands of connections are cheap.
  3. You have 30 replicas with pool size 20 and max_connections = 400. What happens on the next scale-up, and what are two fixes? Expected: too many clients already; fixes are PgBouncer/RDS Proxy or reducing pool size and using min: 0.
  4. What does a process own that a thread does not? Expected: address space, FD table, PID, signal dispositions, environment, cgroup accounting.
  5. When would you choose child_process.fork over worker_threads? Expected: when you need failure isolation, a different binary, or separate memory limits; workers are for CPU-bound JS that shares memory cheaply.
  6. What does Threads: 11 in /proc/self/status mean for a Node process? Expected: main thread + libuv pool + V8 platform threads (+ inspector when enabled); it does not mean 11 JavaScript threads.

Practical exercise

Build a GET /internal/runtime endpoint as above and run the service under Docker with --cpus=0.5 --memory=256m. Then:

  • Open 50 concurrent connections to PostgreSQL through the pool (set max: 50) and observe them in pg_stat_activity with application_name.
  • Lower max_connections on a local PostgreSQL to 20 and reproduce the startup crash. Fix it with min: 0 and a pool size the database can afford.

Acceptance criteria: you can state, from the endpoint and from pg_stat_activity, exactly how many threads your process has and how many backend processes it owns on the database, and the service starts cleanly when the database has only 20 free connection slots.

9.2 CPU scheduling and context switching

Concept

CPU scheduling is how the kernel decides which runnable thread gets which CPU core, and for how long. A core can run exactly one thread at a time. If there are more runnable threads than cores, the scheduler gives each a time slice (typically a few milliseconds), then switches. On Linux the scheduler is CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler), replaced by EEVDF in kernel 6.6, both aiming to give every thread a fair share weighted by its priority (nice value).

A context switch is the act of stopping one thread on a core and starting another: saving the registers and program counter of the outgoing thread, loading those of the incoming one, and, if it belongs to a different process, switching page tables. The direct cost is 1–5 microseconds. The indirect cost is larger: the new thread finds the CPU caches and the TLB (the cache of virtual-to-physical address translations) full of the previous thread's data, so its first few thousand memory accesses are slow. Realistic all-in cost is 10–30 microseconds of lost work per switch.

Why does it exist?

Scheduling exists because there are always more things to do than cores: 400 concurrent HTTP requests on an 8-core box. Context switching is the mechanism that lets one core serve them all. But it is not free, and a design that creates one thread per request pays for it on every I/O wait. Node's design avoids most of it: one thread waits for all sockets at once using the kernel's readiness notification (epoll), so there is no switch when a request blocks on the database; the JavaScript thread just moves on to another ready callback.

Mental model

Imagine one bank teller and a queue of customers, each of whom needs to leave the counter for five minutes to fetch a document. A thread-per-request bank hires 1,000 tellers, most of whom are standing around waiting, and the manager (scheduler) spends the day walking between counters deciding who gets to work. Node's bank has one teller and a pager system: when a customer leaves to fetch a document, the teller serves the next person; when the document is ready, the customer's pager buzzes and they rejoin the front of the line. One teller, no walking, as long as no single customer takes 30 minutes at the counter (a blocked event loop).

How it works

  1. Every thread is in one of three states: running (on a core), runnable (ready, waiting in a per-core run queue) or blocked (waiting for I/O, a lock, a timer, or a futex). Blocked threads cost no CPU.
  2. The scheduler assigns a virtual runtime to each runnable thread. The one with the smallest virtual runtime (the one that has had the least fair share) runs next. Slices are 1–6 ms depending on the number of runnable threads (sched_min_granularity_ns and friends).
  3. A switch happens when the slice expires (preemption), when the running thread blocks (voluntary switch), or when a higher-priority thread wakes up.
  4. On a switch, the kernel saves the outgoing thread's registers into its kernel stack, picks the next thread, restores its registers, and if the process differs, loads a new page-table root (CR3 on x86), which invalidates most of the TLB.
  5. In a container with a CPU limit, the kernel's CFS bandwidth controller adds a quota: with limits.cpu: 500m, the container's threads may run for a combined 50 ms in every 100 ms period. Once the quota is used, all its threads are throttled until the next period, even if the cores are idle. A Node process that does 60 ms of JSON work in one period is frozen for 40 ms, and every in-flight request sees that as latency.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Runnable: thread created
    Runnable --> Running: scheduler picks it
    Running --> Runnable: time slice expired or preempted
    Running --> Blocked: waits on socket, disk, lock, timer
    Blocked --> Runnable: I/O ready, lock free, timer fired
    Running --> Throttled: cgroup CPU quota exhausted
    Throttled --> Runnable: next 100 ms period
    Running --> [*]: exit

Why 1,000 threads is not free, in numbers: 1,000 threads on 8 cores means 992 are always waiting. If each does 1 ms of work between I/O waits, the machine performs roughly 8,000 switches per second per core just to keep them rotating, spending 10–20% of its CPU on switching and cache misses. Each thread also carries a kernel stack (16 KB) and a user stack (8 MB virtual, 50–100 KB touched), so the thread stacks alone are 50–100 MB, plus the scheduler's bookkeeping for 1,000 entries per run queue.

How Node avoids it: one JavaScript thread runs callbacks back-to-back with no kernel involvement between them; a "switch" between two requests is just a function return followed by a function call, roughly 100 nanoseconds. Blocking on I/O never blocks the thread, because the I/O is asynchronous at the kernel level. The libuv pool threads do context-switch, but there are only four of them and they sleep on a condition variable when idle.

Practical example

A food-delivery API processes 1,200 requests per second on a 2-vCPU pod. Each request costs about 0.8 ms of JavaScript CPU (routing, validation, serialisation) and waits 12 ms for PostgreSQL. In a thread-per-request design that is ~15 threads live at any moment, fine. At 12,000 requests per second it becomes 150 live threads and the switch overhead starts to bite. In Node the 12 ms wait costs nothing; the loop is busy 0.8 ms × 1,200 = 960 ms per second of wall time, so one process is at ~96% loop utilisation, and the honest fix is a second replica, not more threads.

NestJS example

The most common scheduling surprise in Kubernetes is CFS throttling. You cannot see it from process.cpuUsage(). Read it from the cgroup and expose it as a metric. This service polls cpu.stat every 15 seconds and logs when the throttle counter grows.

// runtime/cpu-throttle.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Interval } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

@Injectable()
export class CpuThrottleService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(CpuThrottleService.name);
  private lastThrottled = 0;

  @Interval(15_000)
  async sample() {
    let stat: string;
    try {
      stat = await readFile('/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat', 'utf8'); // cgroup v2 path
    } catch {
      return; // not in a cgroup v2 container (local dev)
    }
    // cpu.stat lines look like "nr_throttled 1234"
    const get = (key: string) =>
      Number(new RegExp(`(?:^|\\n)${key} (\\d+)`).exec(stat)?.[1] ?? 0);
    const periods = get('nr_periods');
    const throttled = get('nr_throttled');
    const throttledUsec = get('throttled_usec');

    if (throttled > this.lastThrottled) {
      const delta = throttled - this.lastThrottled;
      this.logger.warn(
        `CPU throttled in ${delta} of the last periods (${((throttled / Math.max(periods, 1)) * 100).toFixed(1)}% lifetime), ` +
          `total throttled time ${(throttledUsec / 1000).toFixed(0)} ms`,
      );
    }
    this.lastThrottled = throttled;
  }
}

If you run Prometheus, prefer the kubelet's container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total and alert when throttled periods exceed 25% of total periods for a latency-sensitive service. The remedy is almost always to raise or remove the CPU limit while keeping the CPU request for scheduling.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL suffers from the same physics. Every active backend is a runnable process; 400 of them on a 16-core server spend more time switching than executing.

-- active backends versus cores; if this is routinely > 2-3x your cores, you are thrashing
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'active') AS active,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'idle')   AS idle,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'idle in transaction') AS idle_in_tx
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend';

-- a common sizing rule: pool_size ~= (2 * cores) + effective_spindle_count
-- for a 16-core, NVMe box: 32-40 active connections; put PgBouncer in front for the rest
SHOW max_parallel_workers;                 -- caps how many extra processes parallel queries may spawn
SHOW max_parallel_workers_per_gather;      -- per query

That rule is why a busy PostgreSQL box behaves better with PgBouncer limiting it to 40 active backends than with 400 connections all hammering it: fewer runnable processes, fewer switches, better cache locality.

Production scenario

A ride-booking pricing service was given limits.cpu: 1 and requests.cpu: 1. Its p50 was 6 ms but p99 was 180 ms, with a suspicious cluster around 40–100 ms. container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total showed 38% of periods throttled. The cause: V8's garbage collector uses helper threads, and a scavenge on the helper threads plus the main thread's work exceeded the 100 ms quota in busy periods, so the whole container was frozen for the rest of the period. Raising the limit to 2 (keeping the request at 1) dropped throttled periods below 2% and p99 to 24 ms. No code changed.

Failure scenario

At 18:05 a batch job in the same process (a @Cron that re-priced 50,000 products in a tight loop) started. The loop took 900 ms of CPU. With a 500m limit, the container was throttled for 50 ms of every 100 ms, stretching the 900 ms of work to about 1.8 s, and during that entire window the event loop was busy, so every HTTP request queued behind it. Readiness probes timed out (they were served by the same loop), Kubernetes pulled the pod from the Service endpoints, the remaining pods took the load and hit the same cron a few seconds later. A cascading brownout from one loop and one CPU limit. The fix was to move the job to a worker thread and chunk it with setImmediate yields, and to run crons on a dedicated worker deployment rather than on API pods.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • CPU limits throttle by quota, not by core: a multithreaded GC can use your whole quota in 30 ms and freeze the main thread for 70 ms.
  • nice and priorities are process-wide inside a container; you cannot make the event loop thread higher priority than the libuv pool without native code.
  • Hyper-threads are not cores: 2 vCPUs on most clouds is one physical core with SMT. CPU-bound throughput does not double.
  • Noisy neighbours on a shared node steal cache and memory bandwidth; identical pods can show 30% different latency depending on placement.
  • Timers are scheduled by the loop, not the kernel: a setTimeout(fn, 10) fires at least 10 ms later, and if the loop is busy or throttled, much later.
  • Clock time keeps moving while you are throttled; a 5 s HTTP timeout can expire on a request that did 20 ms of real work.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They separate latency from throughput. Throughput problems are solved with more replicas; latency problems are usually solved by taking CPU work off the event loop and by removing CPU throttling. They set CPU requests honestly (for the scheduler) and are sceptical of CPU limits for latency-sensitive services, because a limit converts a brief burst into a guaranteed stall. They never run heavy crons on API pods. And they explain throttling to a product manager as a prepaid phone plan: you get 50 minutes every 100, and when they are gone the phone goes dead even if the tower is idle.

Common mistakes

  • Reading os.cpus().length and spawning that many cluster workers inside a 1-CPU container.
  • Diagnosing throttling as "the database is slow" because the timing wrapper around the query includes the time the process was frozen.
  • Setting limits.cpu equal to requests.cpu on a service with bursty CPU (JSON-heavy endpoints, GC) and then chasing p99 in application code.
  • Believing that adding threads to a CPU-bound workload beyond the core count increases throughput; it only increases switching.

Interview questions

  1. What is the cost of a context switch and why does it matter for a thread-per-request server? Expected: 1–5 µs direct, 10–30 µs with cache effects; at thousands of switches per second per core, 10–20% of CPU disappears.
  2. How does Node serve 10,000 concurrent connections with one thread? Expected: the kernel's readiness notification (epoll) lets one thread wait on all sockets; the loop runs ready callbacks back-to-back; no thread blocks on I/O.
  3. What does a Kubernetes CPU limit of 500m actually do? Expected: a CFS quota of 50 ms per 100 ms period across all threads of the container; exceeding it freezes the container until the next period. Follow-up: why can a GC cause throttling? (Helper threads consume quota.)
  4. Why is a pool of 40 active connections often faster than 400 on a 16-core PostgreSQL? Expected: fewer runnable processes, fewer switches, better cache use, less lock contention.
  5. A setTimeout(fn, 100) fires after 900 ms. List three possible reasons. Expected: busy event loop, CPU throttling, GC pause; the timer is a lower bound.

Practical exercise

Run a NestJS service with docker run --cpus=0.5. Add an endpoint that does 30 ms of synchronous CPU work (a loop computing hashes). Load it at 20 requests per second with autocannon and record p50/p99. Then read /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat before and after. Repeat with --cpus=2.

Acceptance criteria: you can show the nr_throttled delta, correlate it with the p99 difference between the two runs, and explain in two sentences why the latency did not simply double at half the CPU.

9.3 Memory: RSS, heap, stack and process.memoryUsage()

Concept

A process's memory is not one blob. It is a set of regions with different rules:

  • Text: the machine code of the binary and shared libraries, read-only, shared between processes running the same binary.
  • Stack: one per thread. A last-in-first-out region that holds each function call's local variables and return address. Grows when a function is called, shrinks when it returns. Fixed maximum size.
  • Heap: the region for data whose lifetime is not tied to a single function call: objects, arrays, strings, closures, Buffers. Managed in Node by V8's garbage collector (for JavaScript objects) and by the C allocator (for native memory such as Buffer backing stores and OpenSSL structures).
  • Mapped regions: shared libraries, memory-mapped files, and large allocations the allocator got directly from the kernel with mmap.

RSS (resident set size) is the number of physical RAM pages currently mapped into the process, across all these regions, including the shared-library pages that are also counted in every other process using them. It is what top, ps, docker stats and the Kubernetes memory limit look at. VSZ (virtual size) is the total address space reserved, most of which may never be touched; it is almost never useful.

In Node, process.memoryUsage() returns five numbers:

{
  "rss": 187563008,
  "heapTotal": 98304000,
  "heapUsed": 71219200,
  "external": 21930000,
  "arrayBuffers": 18900000
}
  • heapUsed: bytes of live-or-not-yet-collected JavaScript objects in V8's heap.
  • heapTotal: bytes V8 has reserved for the heap (used plus free space it keeps for upcoming allocations).
  • external: memory allocated by C++ objects bound to JavaScript objects, mostly Buffer backing stores and strings created from native code.
  • arrayBuffers: the subset of external that belongs to ArrayBuffer and Buffer instances.
  • rss: everything, including the V8 heap, external memory, native code, thread stacks, and libuv/OpenSSL/ICU allocations.

A useful mental equation: rss ≈ heapTotal + external + native code and libraries (~40–60 MB) + thread stacks + allocator overhead.

Why does it exist?

Two regions exist because two allocation patterns exist. Function-local data has a perfectly predictable lifetime (dies when the function returns), so a stack can allocate it by moving a pointer, a handful of nanoseconds, and free it for free. Everything else has an unpredictable lifetime, so it goes to the heap and someone must find space for it and later reclaim it. That someone, in Node, is V8's garbage collector, and it is the reason heapUsed looks like a sawtooth on your Grafana dashboard.

You need to understand RSS because that is the number the kernel enforces. V8 knows nothing about your container's 512 MiB limit; it will happily grow its heap past it, and the kernel will kill the process without a JavaScript error.

Mental model

Imagine a cafeteria. The stack is the pile of trays at the entrance: you take one from the top, you return it to the top, and nobody ever has to search for a free tray. The heap is the warehouse behind the kitchen: shelves everywhere, a warehouse manager (the allocator) who must find a free spot for each new delivery, and a cleaner (the garbage collector) who periodically walks the shelves throwing away food nobody has a ticket for. RSS is the floor space the building currently occupies in the mall; the mall owner (the kernel) does not care how you use it, only that you do not exceed your lease (the cgroup limit).

How it works

  1. On startup, V8 reserves a large virtual range for the heap but commits physical pages lazily. heapTotal starts around 5–10 MB and grows as objects are allocated.
  2. New objects are allocated in the new space (young generation) by bumping a pointer. When it fills (16 MB semi-space by default on 64-bit; varies by version), a scavenge copies the live objects out and resets the pointer. Objects that survive two scavenges are promoted to the old space.
  3. Objects larger than about 128 KB skip the new space and go directly into the large object space, which is part of the old generation. A 5 MB JSON.parse result or a 1 million element array lives there from birth.
  4. Buffer data does not live in the V8 heap. Buffer.alloc(10 * 1024 * 1024) allocates 10 MB with the C allocator and records it as external / arrayBuffers. The small JavaScript Buffer object on the V8 heap holds a pointer to it. When the Buffer object is collected, V8 frees the backing store.
  5. RSS grows when V8 or the C allocator touches new pages. It does not necessarily shrink after a garbage collection: V8 releases freed pages back to the kernel only gradually, and glibc's malloc may keep freed memory in its arenas. A process that once peaked at 900 MB can sit at 700 MB RSS with 200 MB of live heap.
  6. Each thread's stack is 8 MB of virtual space on Linux, but only the pages actually written count towards RSS, typically 50–200 KB per thread. V8 additionally enforces its own JavaScript stack limit of about 984 KB (--stack-size), which is why deep recursion throws a RangeError long before the OS stack is exhausted.
flowchart LR
    subgraph RSS["RSS as the kernel sees it"]
        subgraph V8["V8 heap, heapTotal"]
            NS["New space, young objects"]
            OS["Old space, promoted objects"]
            LOS["Large object space, > 128 KB"]
            CS["Code space, JIT output"]
        end
        EXT["External: Buffer backing stores, native strings"]
        NAT["Native: node binary, OpenSSL, ICU, libuv"]
        STK["Thread stacks: main + libuv pool + V8 helpers"]
    end

For finer detail than process.memoryUsage(), the v8 module exposes the limit and the per-space breakdown:

import * as v8 from 'node:v8';

const stats = v8.getHeapStatistics();
// heap_size_limit is the ceiling set by --max-old-space-size (plus young generation)
console.log((stats.heap_size_limit / 1024 / 1024).toFixed(0), 'MB limit');
console.log((stats.used_heap_size / 1024 / 1024).toFixed(0), 'MB used');

for (const space of v8.getHeapSpaceStatistics()) {
  // new_space, old_space, code_space, large_object_space, ...
  console.log(space.space_name, (space.space_used_size / 1024 / 1024).toFixed(1), 'MB');
}

Practical example

A file-upload service in an e-commerce backend accepts product images, resizes them, and pushes them to S3. The dashboard shows RSS at 900 MB while heapUsed is a calm 120 MB. Engineers look for a "JavaScript memory leak" and find nothing. The memory is in arrayBuffers: each upload is held in a Buffer while sharp resizes it, ten concurrent 30 MB uploads plus their resized variants are 600 MB of external memory, invisible to heap snapshots. The fix is not GC tuning; it is streaming uploads to disk or S3 with pipeline and bounding concurrency.

NestJS example

Every service should expose memory in two places: a Prometheus metric for trends, and a health check for self-defence. The health check below uses @nestjs/terminus. Wiring it into the liveness probe makes Kubernetes restart a pod that has leaked past a threshold, which is a deliberate choice: an automatic restart at 03:00 beats a page at 03:00. Keep the threshold well below the container limit so the restart is graceful rather than an OOM kill.

// health/health.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import {
  HealthCheck,
  HealthCheckService,
  MemoryHealthIndicator,
  TypeOrmHealthIndicator,
} from '@nestjs/terminus';

const MB = 1024 * 1024;

@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  constructor(
    private readonly health: HealthCheckService,
    private readonly memory: MemoryHealthIndicator,
    private readonly db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator,
  ) {}

  // liveness: "is this process still sane?" - restart it if not
  @Get('live')
  @HealthCheck()
  live() {
    return this.health.check([
      () => this.memory.checkHeap('heap', 700 * MB),   // container limit 1 GiB, heap limit 768 MB
      () => this.memory.checkRSS('rss', 900 * MB),     // leaves ~120 MB before the kernel kills us
    ]);
  }

  // readiness: "can this process serve traffic right now?" - pull it from the Service if not
  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    return this.health.check([() => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 1500 })]);
  }
}

For metrics, prom-client's collectDefaultMetrics() already exports process_resident_memory_bytes, nodejs_heap_size_used_bytes, nodejs_heap_size_total_bytes, nodejs_external_memory_bytes and per-space gauges. Graph RSS against the container limit, not against the heap.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL has the same split, and its EXPLAIN ANALYZE output tells you when a query has fallen off the "stack" into disk. work_mem is the per-operation, per-backend budget for sorts and hashes; exceed it and PostgreSQL spills to temporary files.

SHOW work_mem;                 -- 4MB by default; per sort/hash node, per backend
SHOW shared_buffers;           -- shared memory for the buffer cache, typically 25% of RAM

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT customer_id, sum(total_cents)
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY 2 DESC;
--  Sort  (cost=... rows=412000) (actual time=2410.3..2498.7 rows=412000 loops=1)
--    Sort Key: (sum(total_cents)) DESC
--    Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 18456kB          <- spilled: work_mem too small
--    ->  HashAggregate  (actual time=1980.1..2105.2 rows=412000 loops=1)
--          Batches: 5  Memory Usage: 4121kB  Disk Usage: 32768kB   <- hash spilled too
--          Buffers: shared hit=120433 read=88210, temp read=6400 written=6400

SET work_mem = '64MB';         -- for this session only, e.g. a reporting connection
-- rerun: Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 41210kB ; Batches: 1 Memory Usage: 49153kB

The senior caution: work_mem is multiplied by every concurrent sort or hash across every backend. 64MB × 200 connections × 3 operations is 38 GB of potential memory. Raise it per session for reporting connections, not globally.

TypeORM example

The most common way a NestJS process blows its heap is hydrating too many entities. A TypeORM entity instance costs roughly 0.5–2 KB on the heap (object, hidden-class link, column values, relation placeholders). find() over 1 million orders is 1–2 GB before the response is even serialised.

// orders/orders-report.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersReportService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Order) private readonly orders: Repository<Order>) {}

  // BAD: loads every row as an entity; heap grows with the table
  async totalsNaive(): Promise<number> {
    const all = await this.orders.find({ where: { status: 'PAID' } });
    return all.reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.totalCents, 0);
  }

  // GOOD 1: push the work to PostgreSQL; the heap holds one row
  async totalsAggregated(): Promise<number> {
    const row = await this.orders
      .createQueryBuilder('o')
      .select('coalesce(sum(o.total_cents), 0)', 'total')
      .where('o.status = :status', { status: 'PAID' })
      .getRawOne<{ total: string }>();
    return Number(row?.total ?? 0);
  }

  // GOOD 2: when you must touch every row, page with a keyset so memory is bounded
  async *iteratePaid(batch = 1000): AsyncGenerator<Order[]> {
    let lastId = 0;
    while (true) {
      const rows = await this.orders
        .createQueryBuilder('o')
        .where('o.status = :status AND o.id > :lastId', { status: 'PAID', lastId })
        .orderBy('o.id', 'ASC')
        .take(batch)
        .getMany();
      if (rows.length === 0) return;
      lastId = rows[rows.length - 1].id;
      yield rows;                 // caller processes 1000 entities, then they become garbage
    }
  }
}

Sequelize example

Sequelize model instances are heavier than TypeORM entities (each carries dataValues, _previousDataValues, _changed, options). For read-only bulk work, always pass raw: true.

const rows = await this.orderModel.findAll({
  where: { status: 'PAID', id: { [Op.gt]: lastId } },
  order: [['id', 'ASC']],
  limit: 1000,
  raw: true,          // plain objects, ~5x smaller than model instances
  attributes: ['id', 'totalCents', 'customerId'],   // do not hydrate 40 columns you will not read
});

Production scenario

A typical NestJS API with TypeORM and ~150 entities idles at 90–130 MB RSS: 45 MB of that is the Node binary and libraries, 30–50 MB is the heap after startup (decorator metadata, TypeORM entity metadata, route maps), the rest is external and stacks. Under 800 requests per second it allocates around 100–300 MB per second of short-lived objects (request objects, DTOs, query results, JSON strings), so heapUsed sawtooths between 80 and 160 MB with a scavenge every 50–100 ms, and RSS settles around 250–320 MB. Sensible container settings for that profile: limits.memory: 512Mi with --max-old-space-size=384.

Failure scenario

At 11:20 a product manager exported "all orders for 2025" from an admin screen. The endpoint did repository.find() with no limit: 2.1 million rows. heapUsed climbed from 140 MB to 1.4 GB in 25 seconds. Two things could have happened next, and which one tells you the cause:

  • If the container had --max-old-space-size=384, V8 would have run increasingly desperate full GCs (each pausing the loop for 200–600 ms), then aborted with FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory, exit code 134. Every in-flight request on that pod died, but the log said exactly why.
  • Without the flag, V8's default limit was 4 GB (computed from the host's 16 GB of RAM, not the container's 512 MiB), so RSS crossed 512 MiB with no warning and the kernel sent SIGKILL. Exit code 137, Reason: OOMKilled, no JavaScript log line at all.

This team had the second case, and it took them an hour to connect a silent 137 to a single admin click. The fixes were a mandatory take limit on list endpoints, a streamed CSV export (see 9.23), and --max-old-space-size so that heap exhaustion produces a diagnosable error.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • RSS counts shared-library pages in every process that maps them; summing RSS across 40 pods on a node overstates real usage.
  • RSS rarely returns to baseline after a spike; a "leak" that plateaus is often just allocator retention. Confirm with heapUsed trend and heap snapshots.
  • Buffer.allocUnsafe and Buffer.from for small sizes carve slices from an 8 KB shared pool; keeping one 20-byte slice alive keeps the whole 8 KB slab alive.
  • Objects over ~128 KB go straight to the large object space; creating many of them makes full GCs frequent without the young generation ever helping.
  • V8 has a maximum string length (about 512 MB to 1 GB of characters depending on version). JSON.stringify of a huge response throws RangeError: Invalid string length rather than OOM.
  • glibc malloc creates a memory arena per thread; with libuv's pool and V8's helpers, RSS can bloat from fragmentation. MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 is a well-known mitigation for native-heavy workloads.
  • heapTotal can exceed --max-old-space-size briefly because the flag bounds the old generation only; the young generation and code space are separate.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They graph three lines together: RSS, heapUsed, and the container limit. The gap between RSS and heap tells them whether the problem is JavaScript objects (heap growth) or Buffers and native memory (external growth). They set --max-old-space-size on every container, both to force a diagnosable failure and to make V8 collect earlier. They bound every collection in memory: pagination on list endpoints, streaming on exports, batch sizes on consumers. And they explain memory to a product manager by saying: "The process has a room with a fixed floor plan. If the export tries to bring every order into the room at once, the building's manager evicts us without a conversation."

Common mistakes

  • Reading heapUsed and ignoring external, then hunting for a leak that is actually Buffers.
  • Running containers without --max-old-space-size, so failures are silent 137s instead of logged 134s.
  • Loading entire tables with find() for aggregation that PostgreSQL could do in one SUM.
  • Treating the RSS plateau after a spike as a leak and restarting pods on a schedule instead of fixing the spike.
  • Sizing work_mem globally to make one report fast, then discovering the database can allocate 30 GB under load.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between RSS and heapUsed in a Node process, and which one does Kubernetes enforce? Expected: heapUsed is live JS objects in V8; RSS is all resident memory including Buffers, native code, and stacks; Kubernetes enforces RSS via the cgroup.
  2. A pod exits with code 137 and no error log. Another exits with 134 and a "heap out of memory" message. What is the difference? Expected: 137 is SIGKILL from the cgroup OOM killer (RSS over the limit); 134 is V8 aborting when its own heap limit was reached. Follow-up: how do you make the first look like the second? (--max-old-space-size below the container limit.)
  3. Why does a Buffer of 100 MB not show up in heapUsed? Expected: backing stores are allocated outside V8's heap and reported as external/arrayBuffers.
  4. Where does a 5 MB parsed JSON object live in the V8 heap and why does it matter? Expected: large object space, old generation; it bypasses the cheap scavenger and increases full-GC pressure.
  5. How would you compute the memory cost of work_mem = 128MB on a database with 300 connections? Expected: it is per operation, per backend: worst case is 128 MB × operations per query × active backends.
  6. Why might RSS stay high after the heap has been collected? Expected: V8 and the C allocator retain freed pages; fragmentation; arenas.

Practical exercise

Write a script that allocates 200 MB of Buffers, then 200 MB of JavaScript objects, calling process.memoryUsage() and v8.getHeapSpaceStatistics() after each step and after global.gc() (run with --expose-gc). Then run a NestJS list endpoint with and without take: 100 against a table of 1 million rows.

Acceptance criteria: you can explain each of the five memoryUsage() numbers from your own output, show which V8 space the objects landed in, and demonstrate the endpoint's heap stays under 200 MB with pagination and exceeds 1 GB without it.

9.4 Virtual memory, paging, swap and the OOM killer

Concept

Virtual memory means every process sees its own private, contiguous address space (128 TB on 64-bit Linux) that the kernel maps onto physical RAM one 4 KB page at a time through page tables. Addresses in your program are virtual; the CPU's memory management unit translates them, with a small cache called the TLB remembering recent translations.

Paging is the kernel's ability to have a virtual page not currently backed by RAM. Touching such a page raises a page fault: a minor fault if the kernel just needs to allocate a zeroed page (cheap, ~1 µs), a major fault if it must read the contents from disk (expensive, 100 µs on NVMe, 10 ms on spinning disk).

Swap is disk space where the kernel can park pages of anonymous memory (heap, stack) when RAM is short. The page cache is the opposite direction: RAM used to cache file contents, which is where most of PostgreSQL's data lives when it is not in shared_buffers.

The OOM killer is what runs when there is no page left to give: the kernel picks a process (the one with the highest oom_score, roughly the largest memory consumer adjusted by oom_score_adj) and sends it SIGKILL. Inside a cgroup (a container), the same logic runs against the cgroup's memory.max limit: exceed it and the kernel kills a process inside that container. That is OOMKilled, exit code 137.

Why does it exist?

Virtual memory gives isolation (your pointer cannot reach another process's page), lazy allocation (malloc(1 GB) costs nothing until pages are touched), overcommit (the kernel can promise more than physical RAM because most promises are never fully used), and the ability to run programs larger than RAM. Swap extends that last ability. The OOM killer exists because overcommit means promises can be broken, and the kernel would rather kill one process than freeze the machine.

Mental model

Imagine a library with a small reading room (RAM) and a vast basement archive (disk). Books you are actively reading are on your desk (resident pages). When the desk is full and you need another book, the librarian moves the one you have not touched in longest down to the basement (swap out). If your work keeps needing books from the basement, every page turn becomes a trip downstairs (thrashing), and a task that took a minute takes an hour. When even the basement is full, the librarian asks the person with the most books to leave immediately (OOM kill).

How it works

  1. The CPU executes a load from a virtual address. The TLB is checked; on a hit, the physical address is known in a nanosecond. On a miss, the CPU walks the page tables (a few memory reads).
  2. If the page table says "not present", the CPU raises a page fault and the kernel takes over. For a never-touched heap page, it allocates a zeroed frame and returns: a minor fault. For a page that was swapped out, it reads from swap: a major fault, and the thread is blocked while the disk works.
  3. Under memory pressure, the kernel scans its LRU lists. It prefers to drop clean page-cache pages (they can be re-read from the file) over swapping anonymous pages; vm.swappiness (0–100, default 60) tilts that preference.
  4. In a cgroup, memory accounting includes anonymous memory and the page cache the container created (logs it wrote, files it read). When usage approaches memory.max, the kernel first reclaims the container's page cache, then, if swap is enabled for the cgroup, swaps, then invokes the OOM killer restricted to that cgroup.
  5. Kubernetes disables swap on nodes by default (kubelet historically refuses to start with swap enabled; swap support for burstable pods arrived as a beta feature much later). So in a typical cluster there is no gentle slowdown before death: a pod that exceeds its limit goes straight to SIGKILL. kubectl describe pod shows Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137.
  6. The kubelet sets oom_score_adj by QoS class: Guaranteed pods (requests equal limits) get -997 and are killed last during node-level pressure; BestEffort pods get 1000 and die first; Burstable pods are in between, scaled by how much of the node they request.
flowchart LR
    A["JS reads obj.field at virtual address"] --> B{"TLB hit?"}
    B -->|"yes, ~1 ns"| C["Physical RAM access, ~100 ns"]
    B -->|"no"| D["Page table walk"]
    D --> E{"Page present?"}
    E -->|"yes"| C
    E -->|"no, never touched"| F["Minor fault: allocate zeroed page, ~1 us"]
    E -->|"no, swapped out"| G["Major fault: read from disk, 100 us to 10 ms"]
    F --> C
    G --> C
    C --> H{"cgroup over memory.max?"}
    H -->|"yes"| I["Reclaim page cache, then OOM kill: SIGKILL, exit 137"]

Why swapping kills a database server: PostgreSQL's whole performance model assumes that shared_buffers and the OS page cache are in RAM. A buffer hit is ~100 nanoseconds of memory access. If the kernel swaps out part of shared_buffers or a backend's work_mem, that hit becomes a 100 µs to 10 ms disk read, a 1,000× to 100,000× slowdown. Queries that took 2 ms take seconds; connections pile up waiting; more backends use more memory; more memory swaps; the spiral ends with the OOM killer shooting a backend. When that happens, the postmaster treats it as a crash of a child, terminates every other backend (terminating connection because of crash of another server process), and restarts in crash recovery. Every application pool reconnects at once. One report query can do this.

That is why the PostgreSQL documentation recommends vm.overcommit_memory = 2 (strict accounting, so malloc fails and PostgreSQL returns a clean out of memory error for that query instead of the whole cluster restarting) and a low vm.swappiness.

Practical example

Reading an OOM kill from the node:

kubectl describe pod orders-api-7d9f8c5b6-x2k4p
#    Last State:     Terminated
#      Reason:       OOMKilled
#      Exit Code:    137
#      Started:      Sat, 06 Sep 2026 10:12:41 +0000
#      Finished:     Sat, 06 Sep 2026 11:04:07 +0000
#    Restart Count:  3

# on the node (or via a node-problem-detector), dmesg shows who and why
dmesg -T | grep -i "killed process"
# [Sat Sep  6 11:04:07 2026] Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 4021 (node)
#   total-vm:1187204kB, anon-rss:519844kB, file-rss:14320kB, shmem-rss:0kB

anon-rss of 519 MB against a 512 MiB limit. The heap flag was missing, and the default V8 limit was computed from the node's 32 GB of RAM.

NestJS example

A memory-aware guard for expensive endpoints implements load shedding: when the heap is close to its limit, refuse new export jobs with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of letting the next request be the one that kills the pod. This protects the cheap endpoints (which are most of your traffic) from the expensive ones.

// common/guards/memory-pressure.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, Injectable, ServiceUnavailableException } from '@nestjs/common';
import * as v8 from 'node:v8';

@Injectable()
export class MemoryPressureGuard implements CanActivate {
  private readonly limit = v8.getHeapStatistics().heap_size_limit; // from --max-old-space-size
  private readonly threshold = 0.85;                                // shed above 85% of the heap limit

  canActivate(_context: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const used = process.memoryUsage().heapUsed;
    if (used / this.limit > this.threshold) {
      // 503 is correct: the failure is ours and temporary; clients and load balancers may retry elsewhere
      throw new ServiceUnavailableException({
        message: 'Server under memory pressure, retry shortly',
        retryAfterSeconds: 5,
      });
    }
    return true;
  }
}

// orders/orders-export.controller.ts
@UseGuards(MemoryPressureGuard)
@Get('export')
exportOrders() { /* streaming export, see 3.23 */ }

Pair it with a horizontal pod autoscaler on memory or on request rate, so shedding is a brief safety valve rather than a steady state.

PostgreSQL example

The memory-related settings a senior checks on every PostgreSQL host, with the reasoning:

SHOW shared_buffers;          -- 25% of RAM on a dedicated host, e.g. 8GB on 32GB
SHOW effective_cache_size;    -- 50-75% of RAM; a planner *hint* about page cache size, allocates nothing
SHOW work_mem;                -- per operation per backend; keep the global value small
SHOW maintenance_work_mem;    -- VACUUM, CREATE INDEX; can be large, few run at once
SHOW huge_pages;              -- 'try' or 'on': 2 MB pages for shared_buffers = far fewer TLB misses

-- PG 14+: see which memory contexts a backend is using right now
SELECT name, used_bytes, total_bytes FROM pg_backend_memory_contexts ORDER BY total_bytes DESC LIMIT 5;

And the kernel side, which is not SQL but is part of the same decision:

sysctl vm.overcommit_memory     # 2 for PostgreSQL: fail malloc rather than invoke the OOM killer
sysctl vm.overcommit_ratio      # 80-90 with mode 2, so the DB can still use most of RAM
sysctl vm.swappiness            # 1-10: keep shared_buffers in RAM at all costs
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled   # 'madvise' or 'never' for databases and Redis

Note the last line: transparent huge pages cause latency spikes for Redis (fork for BGSAVE must copy 2 MB pages instead of 4 KB pages on write) and for PostgreSQL. huge_pages = on in PostgreSQL uses explicit huge pages, which is the good kind.

Production scenario

A Redis instance serving session data uses 6 GB on an 8 GB VM. BGSAVE forks the process for the snapshot; the child shares pages copy-on-write with the parent, but every write during the snapshot copies a page. On a busy afternoon, 1.5 GB of pages are copied during a snapshot, the VM starts swapping, Redis latency goes from 0.3 ms to 40 ms, and every NestJS request that touches a session inherits that 40 ms. The fix was vm.overcommit_memory = 1 (so the fork does not fail), maxmemory at 4 GB with an eviction policy, and moving the snapshot to a replica. Redis logs this warning on startup for exactly this reason.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged: database p99 went from 4 ms to 9 seconds in ninety seconds. pg_stat_activity showed 180 active backends, most waiting on IO:DataFileRead. free -m on the host showed 3.8 GB of swap in use on a machine with 64 GB of RAM. Cause: a new analytics job ran twelve concurrent report queries, each with SET work_mem = '512MB' and four hash joins, on top of the normal load. 12 × 4 × 512 MB was 24 GB of hash tables on top of 16 GB of shared_buffers. The kernel swapped out part of the buffer cache to make room, and every ordinary query then paid disk latency for what used to be a memory hit. Ten minutes later the OOM killer shot one backend, the postmaster restarted, and every service reconnected at once. Resolution: vm.overcommit_memory = 2 so the reports fail cleanly next time, a work_mem cap on the reporting role (ALTER ROLE reports SET work_mem = '64MB'), and a concurrency limit of three on the job.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Buffers: shared read=... in EXPLAIN means "not in shared_buffers"; the page may still have come from the OS page cache, which is why track_io_timing and the I/O timing lines matter for the real answer.
  • Container memory usage includes the page cache created by the container. The kubelet's eviction decision uses container_memory_working_set_bytes, which includes active file cache; a pod writing large log files locally can look far heavier than its RSS.
  • Swap on Kubernetes nodes is usually off; a workload tuned on a swapping laptop will behave differently in production.
  • A Guaranteed QoS pod is killed last during node pressure, but its own limit is enforced just as strictly.
  • Node's V8 default heap limit is derived from host RAM, not the cgroup. Always set --max-old-space-size in containers.
  • Memory-mapped files (mmap) count towards RSS only for the pages touched; a 2 GB SQLite or index file may show as 50 MB.
  • Fork-based snapshots (Redis BGSAVE, PostgreSQL basebackups are not fork-based, but pg_dump from a big backend is fine) can transiently double memory through copy-on-write.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They never let a database host swap: they would rather a query fail with out of memory than the whole cluster crawl. They configure the kernel and the database and the container as one system, because a limit in any layer that the other layers do not know about produces silent kills. In Kubernetes they assume no swap, set memory limits equal to requests for stateful things, and give Node an explicit heap limit at about 75% of the container limit. When asked by a product manager why a bigger box does not fix an OOM, they explain that the failure was a pattern (loading everything at once), and patterns scale with data, not with hardware.

Common mistakes

  • Enabling swap on a database server "as a safety net" and getting a ten-minute brownout instead of a one-second error.
  • Setting work_mem globally to a large value because one report was slow.
  • Leaving vm.overcommit_memory = 0 on a PostgreSQL host, so the OOM killer, not PostgreSQL, decides which query dies.
  • Diagnosing a 137 exit as "the app crashed" and adding a try/catch.
  • Ignoring oom_score_adj and running a critical API as BestEffort (no requests or limits), which makes it the first victim during node pressure.

Interview questions

  1. What happens, step by step, when a container exceeds its memory limit in Kubernetes? Expected: cgroup reclaims page cache, swap is usually disabled, the kernel's OOM killer picks a process in the cgroup, SIGKILL, exit 137, kubelet restarts with backoff.
  2. Why is swapping so much worse for a database than for a web server? Expected: databases rely on cached pages for nanosecond hits; swapped pages turn those into disk reads, and the resulting slowdown compounds through connection pileup.
  3. What does vm.overcommit_memory = 2 change for PostgreSQL? Expected: malloc fails instead of the OOM killer firing; PostgreSQL returns an error for one query instead of restarting all backends.
  4. What is the difference between a minor and a major page fault, and which one shows up as latency? Expected: minor is allocating a zeroed page (~1 µs); major reads from disk (100 µs to 10 ms) and blocks the thread.
  5. Why should Redis have vm.overcommit_memory = 1? Expected: BGSAVE forks; the fork would fail under strict accounting even though copy-on-write means the child rarely needs the full copy.
  6. Why do you set --max-old-space-size to about 75% of the container limit? Expected: RSS includes external memory, native code, and stacks; the heap must leave room for them, and the flag makes V8 fail loudly before the kernel fails silently.

Practical exercise

Run a NestJS service in Docker with --memory=256m and an endpoint that allocates 300 MB of objects, first without any heap flag and then with --max-old-space-size=192. Capture the exit code and logs in both cases, read docker inspect for OOMKilled: true, and add MemoryPressureGuard to the endpoint.

Acceptance criteria: you can show one run ending in 137 with no application log, one ending in 134 with the V8 heap-limit message, and a third where the guard returns 503 before either happens.

9.5 File descriptors

Concept

A file descriptor (FD) is a small non-negative integer that a process uses to refer to an open kernel resource. "File" is a historical word; on Linux, almost everything you can read from or write to is an FD: regular files, the listening TCP socket, every accepted client connection, every outbound connection to PostgreSQL, Redis, or a payment gateway, pipes, the epoll instance libuv uses to wait on sockets, timer and event objects, and /dev/null. Descriptors 0, 1 and 2 are stdin, stdout and stderr.

Each process has a limit on how many FDs it may hold open at once: the soft limit shown by ulimit -n (commonly 1024 on a bare VM, often 1,048,576 in containers), which can be raised up to the hard limit (ulimit -Hn). There is also a system-wide ceiling, fs.file-max. When a process hits its limit, system calls that would create a new FD fail with EMFILE ("too many open files"); when the whole system is out, they fail with ENFILE.

In a Node service this matters because sockets are FDs. A leaked database client, a leaked outbound HTTP connection or a leaked file handle is an FD that never comes back. When the pool of numbers runs dry, the server cannot even accept() new connections.

Why does it exist?

The FD is the kernel's uniform handle: one small integer, one set of system calls (read, write, close, poll), whether the thing behind it is a disk file or a TCP stream. Uniformity is what lets libuv treat a socket and a pipe the same way in the event loop. The per-process limit exists because every open descriptor consumes kernel memory (a socket with buffers can be hundreds of KB) and because a runaway process must not be able to exhaust the whole machine.

Mental model

Imagine a coat check at a theatre. Each coat you hand over gets a numbered ticket; the ticket is the file descriptor, the coat room is the kernel's open-file table. You can only hold a limited number of tickets. If you keep checking coats and never collect them, eventually the attendant refuses: "no more tickets". In our world, the coat you forgot is a pg.Client you created and never called end() on, and the refusal is EMFILE.

How it works

  1. open(), socket(), accept(), pipe(), epoll_create() each ask the kernel for a new descriptor. The kernel picks the lowest unused number and points it at an open-file description (offset, flags) which points at the underlying inode or socket.
  2. close(fd) releases the number. Because numbers are reused immediately, a stale reference to a closed FD can silently point at a different resource later; Node's handle abstraction (net.Socket, fs.FileHandle) exists partly to prevent that class of bug.
  3. libuv wraps each socket in a handle (uv_tcp_t) and registers the FD with epoll. The handle keeps the event loop alive until it is closed. A net.Socket you stop referencing is not closed by garbage collection; the FD stays open until destroy() or end() is called or the peer closes.
  4. When accept() fails with EMFILE, libuv uses a trick: it keeps one spare FD open at startup; on EMFILE it closes the spare, accepts the pending connection, immediately closes it (the client sees a reset instead of hanging in the backlog), and reopens the spare. Your server still cannot serve anyone, but at least the listen queue does not fill up with connections that will time out.
  5. Inspecting a live process:
ulimit -n                          # soft limit for the current shell
cat /proc/1/limits | grep "open files"   # inside the container, for PID 1
ls -l /proc/1/fd | wc -l           # how many are open right now
ls -l /proc/1/fd | awk '{print $NF}' | sed 's/:.*//' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
#    212 socket
#      5 anon_inode
#      3 /dev/null
#      2 pipe
// Node 17+: what is keeping the event loop alive, by type
console.log(process.getActiveResourcesInfo());
// [ 'TCPServerWrap', 'TCPSocketWrap', 'TCPSocketWrap', 'Timeout', 'FSReqCallback' ]
flowchart LR
    subgraph P["Process FD table"]
        F0["0 stdin"]
        F1["1 stdout, pipe to container runtime"]
        F3["3 epoll instance"]
        F7["7 listening socket :3000"]
        F12["12 accepted client socket"]
        F13["13 socket to PostgreSQL"]
        F14["14 socket to Redis"]
        F15["15 socket to payment gateway"]
    end
    F7 --> K["kernel socket, accept queue"]
    F12 --> S1["kernel socket buffers, ~200 KB when busy"]
    F13 --> PG["PostgreSQL backend process"]

Practical example

Count the FDs an order service holds at 500 requests per second behind an AWS ALB:

Category Typical count Why
stdin/stdout/stderr, epoll, eventfd, signal pipe 6–8 runtime plumbing
listening socket 1 server.listen(3000)
accepted client sockets 50–300 ALB keeps several keep-alive connections per ALB node
PostgreSQL pool 10 one FD per pooled connection
Redis (ioredis default + subscriber) 2–4
outbound HTTP keep-alive (payment, geocoding) 0–50 bounded by maxSockets or the undici pool size
log file (if writing to disk) 1

About 100–400 in steady state. A ulimit -n 1024 on a VM leaves little headroom for a burst; a leak of even five FDs per minute ends the process in a few hours.

NestJS example

Two things belong in every service: an FD gauge, and pool usage that cannot leak. prom-client's default metrics already export process_open_fds and process_max_fds on Linux; alert when the ratio passes 70%. For the pool, the rule is try/finally, no exceptions:

// database/pg-raw.service.ts
import { Injectable, OnApplicationShutdown } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Pool, PoolClient } from 'pg';

@Injectable()
export class PgRawService implements OnApplicationShutdown {
  private readonly pool = new Pool({
    connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
    max: 10,
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000,   // do not wait forever for a leaked-out pool
    idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,
  });

  // The pool itself is bounded: at most 10 sockets, however busy we get.
  // What leaks is a checked-out client that is never released.
  async withClient<T>(work: (client: PoolClient) => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    const client = await this.pool.connect();
    try {
      return await work(client);
    } finally {
      client.release();               // ALWAYS, even when work() throws
    }
  }

  async onApplicationShutdown() {
    await this.pool.end();            // close the 10 sockets on SIGTERM
  }
}

The dangerous alternative, which caused the incident in 9.30, is new Client() per request without client.end(). Each Client is its own socket, unbounded by any pool.

For outbound HTTP, never use the default agent with unlimited sockets in a service that talks to a slow dependency:

// payments/payment-http.provider.ts
import { Agent } from 'undici';

export const paymentAgent = new Agent({
  connections: 32,            // hard cap on sockets to the gateway: a slowdown cannot become an FD storm
  keepAliveTimeout: 30_000,
  connect: { timeout: 3_000 },
  headersTimeout: 5_000,
  bodyTimeout: 10_000,
});

PostgreSQL example

Each leaked application socket is a live backend process on the database. PostgreSQL can defend itself from clients that hold sessions open and forget them:

-- kill sessions that have been idle inside a transaction for more than 60 s (holding locks, blocking VACUUM)
ALTER SYSTEM SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';
-- PG 14+: kill sessions that are idle (outside a transaction) for an hour; leaked clients die server-side
ALTER SYSTEM SET idle_session_timeout = '1h';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

-- who is holding what right now
SELECT pid, application_name, state, now() - state_change AS in_state_for
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
ORDER BY in_state_for DESC;

-- PostgreSQL has its own per-backend FD budget for table and index files
SHOW max_files_per_process;   -- default 1000; heavily partitioned schemas can hit it

TypeORM example

The classic TypeORM leak is a QueryRunner that is created for a transaction and not released on the error path. The connection stays checked out; after max such errors the pool is empty and every request waits connectionTimeoutMillis and fails.

// orders/orders.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';
import { InventoryItem } from '../inventory/inventory-item.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  // Explicit QueryRunner: full control, full responsibility
  async placeOrderExplicit(input: { sku: string; qty: number; customerId: number }): Promise<Order> {
    const qr = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner();
    await qr.connect();
    await qr.startTransaction();
    try {
      const affected = await qr.manager
        .createQueryBuilder()
        .update(InventoryItem)
        .set({ stock: () => 'stock - :qty' })
        .where('sku = :sku AND stock >= :qty', { sku: input.sku, qty: input.qty })
        .execute();
      if (affected.affected !== 1) throw new Error('OUT_OF_STOCK');

      const order = await qr.manager.save(Order, { ...input, status: 'PLACED' });
      await qr.commitTransaction();
      return order;
    } catch (err) {
      await qr.rollbackTransaction();
      throw err;
    } finally {
      await qr.release();            // the line whose absence empties the pool
    }
  }

  // Managed transaction: TypeORM releases the runner for you on both paths
  placeOrderManaged(input: { sku: string; qty: number; customerId: number }): Promise<Order> {
    return this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
      const affected = await manager
        .createQueryBuilder()
        .update(InventoryItem)
        .set({ stock: () => 'stock - :qty' })
        .where('sku = :sku AND stock >= :qty', { sku: input.sku, qty: input.qty })
        .execute();
      if (affected.affected !== 1) throw new Error('OUT_OF_STOCK');
      return manager.save(Order, { ...input, status: 'PLACED' });
    });
  }
}

Prefer the managed form. Use the explicit form only when you need SAVEPOINTs or a runner that outlives one callback.

Sequelize example

Sequelize has the same split: an unmanaged transaction (await sequelize.transaction()) must be committed or rolled back by you on every path, or the connection leaks; a managed transaction (callback form) is released automatically.

// managed: connection is returned on commit and on rollback
await this.sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  const [affected] = await this.inventoryModel.update(
    { stock: this.sequelize.literal('stock - 1') },
    { where: { sku, stock: { [Op.gte]: 1 } }, transaction: t },
  );
  if (affected !== 1) throw new Error('OUT_OF_STOCK');
  await this.orderModel.create({ sku, customerId, status: 'PLACED' }, { transaction: t });
});

Production scenario

A notification service calls a third-party email API with the default Node http.Agent (maxSockets: Infinity, no keep-alive). Normally it opens and closes 50 connections per second, ~30 FDs live at any moment. One afternoon the email provider slows to 8 seconds per request. At 50 requests per second with 8 seconds in flight, 400 sockets are open, then 800 as retries kick in. Each socket is an FD and an ephemeral port; RSS climbs with the buffered request bodies; EMFILE appears in the logs at 1,024; the readiness probe (also an HTTP request into the same process) fails and the pod is restarted, every few minutes, for an hour. A bounded Agent (connections: 32) plus a 5-second timeout and a circuit breaker turns that into a clean stream of fast failures.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged for 5xx on checkout. Logs on three pods were full of Error: connect EMFILE 10.0.5.12:5432 - Local (undefined:undefined) and Error: accept EMFILE: too many open files. ls /proc/1/fd | wc -l on a surviving pod returned 1019 and climbing at about 4 per minute. ss -tnp showed 900 established sockets to PostgreSQL from one pod whose pool was configured for 10. A recent change had introduced a "quick" analytics helper that did const client = new Client(config); await client.connect(); await client.query(...) and returned without client.end(). Every analytics call leaked one socket and one PostgreSQL backend. Rollback took two minutes; the postmortem added process_open_fds to the standard dashboard, an alert at 70% of the limit, and idle_session_timeout on the database so a future leak dies server-side within an hour instead of living until the process is killed. The full story with the timeline is in 9.30.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • EMFILE on accept means clients see connection timeouts or resets, not HTTP errors; your error dashboard may look clean while availability is zero.
  • The shell's ulimit -n does not apply to systemd services; set LimitNOFILE=65536 in the unit file. In Docker use --ulimit nofile=65536:65536; in Kubernetes the container runtime's default applies (usually large), and you cannot set it per pod without privileged tricks.
  • Node cannot raise its own soft limit without a native module; the limit must be right before the process starts.
  • Outbound sockets closed by you enter TIME_WAIT for 60 s. That is not an FD, but each holds an ephemeral port; ~28,000 ports means at most ~470 new connections per second to one destination without keep-alive. The symptom is EADDRNOTAVAIL, the cousin of EMFILE.
  • fs.watch uses inotify watches (fs.inotify.max_user_watches), a separate limit that bites in development with large node_modules.
  • A streaming response abandoned by the client (user closes the tab during a CSV export) can leave the source stream paused and its database connection checked out forever unless you destroy the source on res.on('close') (see 9.23).
  • graceful-fs retries EMFILE for file operations only; it does nothing for sockets.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat every resource that is acquired as something that must be released on every path, and they structure code so the release is impossible to forget: a withClient helper, managed transactions, pipeline for streams, using-style wrappers. They bound every pool: database, Redis, outbound HTTP, worker threads. They know that a leak's symptom is time-delayed and appears somewhere else (on the database, on the load balancer), so they watch process_open_fds as a first-class SLI. They explain it to a product manager as coat-check tickets: "we forgot to collect one coat per analytics click; at the thousandth click the theatre stopped letting anyone in."

Common mistakes

  • Creating new Client() or new Pool() inside a request handler or a service method instead of once per process.
  • Forgetting release() on the error path of an explicit transaction.
  • Using the default unlimited HTTP agent to call a dependency that can slow down.
  • Assuming garbage collection closes sockets and file handles.
  • Alerting only on HTTP 5xx, so an accept EMFILE outage (connections never reach the app) is invisible until customers call.

Interview questions

  1. Why is a TCP connection a file descriptor, and what does that imply for a Node server? Expected: the kernel exposes sockets through the same handle table as files; every connection, inbound or outbound, consumes one of a limited set of descriptors.
