  2. A pod logs EMFILE but the pool size is 10. What are the likely causes? Expected: clients created outside the pool, leaked outbound HTTP sockets, abandoned streams holding connections, file handles not closed.
  3. What is the difference between EMFILE and ENFILE? Expected: per-process versus system-wide limit.
  4. How does libuv behave when accept() fails with EMFILE? Expected: it uses a reserved spare FD to accept and immediately close the connection so the backlog does not fill with clients that will hang.
  5. How would you make a leaked database session die even if the application never fixes the bug? Expected: idle_session_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout on PostgreSQL.
  6. Explain ephemeral port exhaustion and how it differs from FD exhaustion. Expected: closed outbound sockets sit in TIME_WAIT for 60 s and hold a local port, not an FD; keep-alive fixes it.

Practical exercise

Write a NestJS endpoint that deliberately leaks one pg.Client per call. Run the container with --ulimit nofile=256:256, hit the endpoint 250 times, and observe: the FD count via /proc/1/fd, the backend count in pg_stat_activity, the exact error the next request gets, and what happens to the health endpoint. Then fix it with withClient and add an FD gauge.

Acceptance criteria: you can show the error message for EMFILE on accept, prove from pg_stat_activity that each leaked client is a database process, and demonstrate that after the fix the FD count is flat under load.

9.6 Signals and graceful shutdown

Concept

A signal is a one-word asynchronous message the kernel (or another process) delivers to a process: "terminate", "interrupt", "hang up", "you touched invalid memory". Each signal has a default action, and most can be caught by installing a handler. The ones a backend engineer meets daily:

Signal Number Sent by Default Catchable Meaning in practice
SIGINT 2 Ctrl+C in a terminal terminate yes local dev stop
SIGTERM 15 kill, Docker, Kubernetes, PM2, systemd terminate yes "please shut down cleanly"
SIGKILL 9 kill -9, OOM killer, Kubernetes after the grace period terminate no immediate death, no cleanup
SIGHUP 1 terminal closed, config reload conventions terminate yes often "reload config"
SIGUSR1 10 you terminate yes Node uses it to start the inspector
SIGUSR2 12 you, nodemon terminate yes free for the application; good for --heapsnapshot-signal
SIGPIPE 13 kernel, writing to a closed pipe terminate yes Node ignores it by default

When a process dies from a signal, its exit code is 128 plus the signal number: 130 for SIGINT, 143 for SIGTERM, 137 for SIGKILL. That is why OOMKilled pods show exit code 137.

Graceful shutdown is what a process does between receiving SIGTERM and exiting: stop taking new work, finish or hand off the work in progress, release resources (database pools, brokers, files), flush logs and telemetry, and then exit. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30), then sends SIGKILL.

Why does it exist?

Signals are the operating system's only way to talk to a process that is not listening on anything. Without SIGTERM, the only way to stop a service would be SIGKILL, which drops every in-flight request mid-response, leaves transactions to be rolled back by the database, abandons half-processed queue jobs, and loses buffered logs. Graceful shutdown exists because deploys happen many times a day, and each one must be invisible to users.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant at closing time. A good manager (SIGTERM handler) locks the front door so no new guests come in, lets seated guests finish their meal, settles the bills, turns off the stove, and locks up. SIGKILL is the power company cutting the electricity: everyone leaves in the dark, the food burns, and tomorrow morning you find out which bills were never paid. Kubernetes is a landlord who says "you have 30 minutes to close, then I cut the power."

How it works

The Kubernetes side, which you must understand to understand why the naive handler still produces 502s:

  1. Something deletes the pod (a rolling update, a scale-down, a node drain). The API server marks the pod Terminating.
  2. Two things start in parallel. The endpoints controller removes the pod's IP from the Service; kube-proxy on every node and every ingress controller must then observe that change and update their rules, which takes from hundreds of milliseconds to several seconds. Meanwhile the kubelet on the pod's node runs the container's preStop hook (if any) and then sends SIGTERM to PID 1 of each container.
  3. Because those are parallel, a pod can receive SIGTERM while load balancers are still routing new connections to it. If the app stops accepting immediately, those connections are refused: the user sees a 502 from the ingress.
  4. After terminationGracePeriodSeconds counting from the start of step 2 (the preStop duration is included), the kubelet sends SIGKILL to anything still alive.

The application side, in NestJS:

  1. app.enableShutdownHooks() in main.ts makes Nest listen for termination signals (all of them by default; you can restrict it with enableShutdownHooks([ShutdownSignal.SIGTERM, ShutdownSignal.SIGINT])).
  2. On a signal, Nest runs the lifecycle in this order across all modules: onModuleDestroy(), then beforeApplicationShutdown(signal), then it closes the HTTP server and the underlying connections, then onApplicationShutdown(signal). Providers from @nestjs/typeorm and @nestjs/sequelize close their connections in these hooks, and @nestjs/bullmq closes its workers.
  3. After the hooks complete, Nest re-raises the signal on itself with default handling, so the process exits with the conventional code (143 for SIGTERM).
  4. Node detail: installing a process.on('SIGTERM') handler replaces the default terminate action. If your handler never calls process.exit() and never lets Nest finish, the process lives until SIGKILL.
sequenceDiagram
    participant API as KubeAPI
    participant EP as Endpoints
    participant LB as Ingress
    participant KL as Kubelet
    participant APP as NestJS
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    API->>EP: pod Terminating
    API->>KL: pod Terminating
    par endpoint removal propagates
        EP-->>LB: remove pod IP, takes 0.5 to 5 s
    and kubelet stops the container
        KL->>APP: preStop hook, sleep 8
        KL->>APP: SIGTERM
    end
    APP->>APP: readiness returns 503
    APP->>APP: server.close, stop accepting
    APP->>APP: finish in-flight requests
    APP->>DB: close pool connections
    APP-->>KL: exit 143
    Note over KL,APP: SIGKILL if still alive after terminationGracePeriodSeconds

Practical example

The checklist for a service that survives deploys with zero errors:

  1. Dockerfile uses the exec form CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"], not CMD node dist/main.js (the shell form makes /bin/sh PID 1, and sh does not forward SIGTERM to node). Do not use npm start as the entrypoint for the same reason.
  2. preStop: exec: command: ["sleep", "8"] gives the endpoint removal time to propagate while the app keeps serving.
  3. terminationGracePeriodSeconds is larger than preStop plus the longest in-flight work you are willing to wait for: 30 s for an API, 120–300 s for a queue worker with long jobs.
  4. The readiness probe returns 503 as soon as shutdown starts, so any load balancer that checks health stops sending traffic early.
  5. server.keepAliveTimeout is set higher than the load balancer's idle timeout (for an ALB with 60 s idle: keepAliveTimeout = 65_000, headersTimeout = 66_000), so the app never closes an idle keep-alive connection the ALB is about to reuse, which is a separate source of 502s.

NestJS example

// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  app.enableShutdownHooks();                       // SIGTERM/SIGINT -> lifecycle hooks -> app.close()

  const server = app.getHttpServer();
  server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000;                // > ALB idle timeout (60 s)
  server.headersTimeout = 66_000;                  // must exceed keepAliveTimeout

  await app.listen(3000);
  Logger.log(`pid ${process.pid} listening`, 'Bootstrap');
}
bootstrap();
// health/shutdown-state.service.ts
import { BeforeApplicationShutdown, Injectable, Logger, OnApplicationShutdown } from '@nestjs/common';
import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises';

@Injectable()
export class ShutdownStateService implements BeforeApplicationShutdown, OnApplicationShutdown {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(ShutdownStateService.name);
  private shuttingDown = false;
  private inFlight = 0;

  get isShuttingDown() { return this.shuttingDown; }
  requestStarted() { this.inFlight++; }
  requestFinished() { this.inFlight--; }

  // Runs BEFORE Nest closes the HTTP server: flip readiness, then give the LB a moment.
  async beforeApplicationShutdown(signal?: string) {
    this.logger.warn(`received ${signal}; entering drain mode with ${this.inFlight} requests in flight`);
    this.shuttingDown = true;               // readiness now returns 503
    await sleep(5_000);                     // in addition to preStop; cheap insurance
    const deadline = Date.now() + 15_000;
    while (this.inFlight > 0 && Date.now() < deadline) await sleep(100);
    if (this.inFlight > 0) this.logger.error(`${this.inFlight} requests still in flight at deadline`);
  }

  // Runs AFTER the server and DB connections are closed.
  onApplicationShutdown(signal?: string) {
    this.logger.warn(`shutdown complete after ${signal}`);
  }
}
// health/readiness.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, ServiceUnavailableException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ShutdownStateService } from './shutdown-state.service';

@Controller('health')
export class ReadinessController {
  constructor(private readonly state: ShutdownStateService) {}

  @Get('ready')
  ready() {
    if (this.state.isShuttingDown) throw new ServiceUnavailableException('draining');
    return { status: 'ok' };
  }
}

A tiny middleware calling requestStarted()/requestFinished() (on res.on('finish') and res.on('close')) completes the picture. For queue consumers, @nestjs/bullmq closes workers during shutdown; a job that is mid-run when the worker closes is finished if it completes within the grace period, and otherwise becomes stalled and is retried by another worker, which is why every job must be idempotent.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL is itself a signal-driven system, and it reacts to your process dying:

  • When your socket closes, the backend notices on its next read or write, rolls back any open transaction, and releases locks. A backend in the middle of a 10-minute query will not notice until it tries to send a row; client_connection_check_interval (PG 14+) makes it poll the socket so a dead client's query is cancelled promptly.
  • pg_cancel_backend(pid) sends SIGINT to a backend: cancel the current query, keep the session. pg_terminate_backend(pid) sends SIGTERM: end the session.
  • pg_ctl stop -m smart | fast | immediate sends SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGQUIT to the postmaster: wait for clients, abort transactions and shut down cleanly, or crash-stop and recover on restart.
ALTER SYSTEM SET client_connection_check_interval = '10s';   -- notice dead clients during long queries
ALTER SYSTEM SET statement_timeout = '30s';                  -- belt and braces
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

-- during a deploy, see sessions still open from pods that should be gone
SELECT pid, application_name, state, backend_start
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE application_name LIKE 'orders-api-%'
ORDER BY backend_start;

TypeORM example

@nestjs/typeorm destroys the DataSource during shutdown automatically when shutdown hooks are enabled. If you construct a DataSource yourself (a second database, a read replica), own its lifecycle explicitly:

// database/analytics-datasource.provider.ts
import { OnApplicationShutdown, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class AnalyticsDataSource implements OnApplicationShutdown {
  readonly ds = new DataSource({
    type: 'postgres',
    url: process.env.ANALYTICS_DATABASE_URL,
    extra: { max: 4, application_name: 'orders-api-analytics' },
  });

  async onApplicationShutdown() {
    if (this.ds.isInitialized) await this.ds.destroy();   // returns the 4 backends to PostgreSQL
  }
}

Sequelize example

@nestjs/sequelize likewise calls sequelize.close() on shutdown. For a manually created instance, close it in onApplicationShutdown; close() waits for checked-out connections to be returned, so a leaked unmanaged transaction can hold the shutdown until SIGKILL. That is one more reason to use managed transactions.

Production scenario

A payments API deploys 20 times a day with 12 replicas and maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0. Each deploy replaces pods one by one; each replacement drains for about 13 seconds (8 s preStop plus a few seconds of in-flight work). Before the preStop and readiness changes, each deploy produced 30–60 HTTP 502s at the ingress, roughly 0.02% of daily traffic, which is small until you remember they were payments: some clients retried, and a few payments were captured twice because the first attempt had reached the gateway before the socket was reset. After the changes, deploys produce zero 502s, and every payment call carries an idempotency key so a retry cannot double-charge (see Part 20 for transactions and Part 29 for idempotency).

Failure scenario

At 16:40 a deploy of the orders worker took exactly 30 seconds per pod and every deploy caused a burst of duplicate "order shipped" emails. The Dockerfile had CMD npm run start:prod. npm was PID 1, node was its child, and the SIGTERM from the kubelet reached npm, which exited without forwarding it. The Node process was left running with no signal at all until SIGKILL 30 seconds later. BullMQ jobs in progress were killed mid-run, marked stalled, and retried by the new pod; the email step in the job was not idempotent. Fix: exec-form CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"], enableShutdownHooks(), terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120 for the worker deployment, and an idempotency check on the email step keyed by orderId:shipped.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Node as PID 1 with no signal handler: the kernel does not apply default signal actions to PID 1, so SIGTERM is silently ignored and the process lives until SIGKILL. Either install handlers (Nest does) or run under tini / --init.
  • Streaming and long-lived connections (SSE, WebSockets, a 5-minute CSV export) prevent server.close() from completing. Use server.closeIdleConnections() (Node 18.2+) immediately and server.closeAllConnections() at a deadline.
  • Two shutdown handlers (Nest's plus a hand-written process.on('SIGTERM')) can race: one calls process.exit(0) before the other finishes closing the pool.
  • Kafka consumers must commit offsets and leave the group on shutdown; a SIGKILL leaves the partition assigned until the session timeout expires, stalling consumption for up to session.timeout.ms.
  • @Cron jobs mid-run at shutdown are simply cut off; long jobs belong in queues with checkpoints.
  • Worker threads do not receive the signal; the main thread must terminate() or message them.
  • Windows has no POSIX signals; SIGTERM handlers never fire there, and SIGINT is emulated for Ctrl+C. Do not test shutdown behaviour on Windows and assume it matches Linux.
  • A preStop sleep counts against the grace period; sleep 25 with a 30 s grace period leaves 5 s for draining.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They assume every process will be killed at the worst possible moment, and they design so that this is boring: idempotent jobs, transactions that the database rolls back on disconnect, offsets committed after processing, no in-memory queues holding unacknowledged work. Graceful shutdown then becomes an optimisation for the common case, not a correctness requirement. They test it: kubectl delete pod under load with an error-rate graph open is a standard pre-production check. To a product manager: "Every deploy is like closing a restaurant for a few seconds; we make sure the door locks before the kitchen stops, and we never leave a bill half-paid."

Common mistakes

  • Shell-form CMD or npm start as the container entrypoint, swallowing SIGTERM.
  • Closing the listener the instant SIGTERM arrives, before load balancers have stopped routing.
  • Forgetting to flip readiness, so a load balancer that checks health keeps sending traffic during the drain.
  • terminationGracePeriodSeconds shorter than the longest job, then blaming the queue for duplicates.
  • keepAliveTimeout lower than the load balancer's idle timeout, producing rare 502s that get blamed on "network flakiness".

Interview questions

  1. What exactly does Kubernetes do when it terminates a pod, and where is the race? Expected: endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel; a preStop sleep and an early readiness flip close the gap. Follow-up: what is the exit code after SIGKILL? (137.)
  2. Why does CMD npm start break graceful shutdown? Expected: npm or sh becomes PID 1 and does not forward SIGTERM; node never sees it and is SIGKILLed at the deadline.
  3. What order do NestJS lifecycle hooks run in on SIGTERM? Expected: onModuleDestroy, beforeApplicationShutdown(signal), server and connections close, onApplicationShutdown(signal); Nest then re-raises the signal.
  4. A Node process ignores SIGTERM even though no handler is installed. Why? Expected: it is PID 1 in the container; the kernel skips default actions for PID 1.
  5. How should a BullMQ worker behave on SIGTERM, and what happens to a job that is mid-run at SIGKILL? Expected: stop taking jobs, finish the current one within the grace period; a killed job becomes stalled and is retried, so jobs must be idempotent.
  6. Why must server.keepAliveTimeout exceed the load balancer's idle timeout? Expected: otherwise Node closes an idle connection at the same moment the LB reuses it, which the LB reports as a 502.

Practical exercise

Deploy a NestJS service locally with kind or minikube, add preStop, enableShutdownHooks, the ShutdownStateService, and a readiness endpoint. Run autocannon at 200 requests per second, then kubectl rollout restart. Compare the error count with and without the preStop sleep and the readiness flip. Then replace the exec-form CMD with the shell form and observe the 30-second SIGKILL.

Acceptance criteria: zero non-2xx responses during a rollout with the full setup; a measurable count of failures without it; and logs showing the lifecycle hooks in order, with exit code 143.

9.7 Concurrency vs parallelism

Concept

Concurrency is dealing with many things at once: several tasks are in progress during the same period, taking turns. Parallelism is doing many things at the same instant: several tasks execute simultaneously on different cores.

Node.js is concurrent by design and parallel only by choice. One JavaScript thread interleaves thousands of in-flight requests, switching between them at every await. It becomes parallel only when work leaves that thread: the kernel performing socket I/O, the libuv pool hashing a password, a worker thread rendering a PDF, or a second process on another core. A single NestJS process handling 2,000 concurrent requests is running one of them at a time; it just never waits.

Why does it exist?

The distinction exists because most backend time is spent waiting, not computing. A typical request does 0.5–2 ms of JavaScript and waits 5–50 ms for PostgreSQL, Redis and other services. Concurrency turns that waiting into throughput without adding cores. Parallelism is needed only when the computing itself is the bottleneck, and it comes with a cost: shared memory needs coordination, and coordination is where the bugs in 9.8 and 9.9 live.

Mental model

Imagine one barista with a row of espresso machines. She starts a shot on machine 1, and while it pours she steams milk for order 2, then takes payment for order 3, then returns to machine 1 when the shot is done. That is concurrency: one worker, many orders in progress, zero idle time as long as no single step requires her full attention for a minute. Parallelism is hiring a second barista. If the coffee shop's bottleneck is the pouring time (I/O), a second barista barely helps; if the bottleneck is grinding beans by hand (CPU), she doubles output.

How it works

  1. A request handler runs synchronously until its first await on something not yet resolved (a database query, an HTTP call).
  2. The async function returns a pending promise; its remaining code is stored as a continuation. The call stack unwinds to the event loop.
  3. The loop picks up the next ready callback: another request's continuation, a timer, an incoming connection. Thousands of requests can be suspended this way; each costs a few hundred bytes of closure, not a thread.
  4. The kernel and libuv do the actual I/O in parallel with your JavaScript. When a response arrives, the promise resolves, and its continuation is queued as a microtask and runs at the next opportunity.
  5. Two requests' code never runs at the same instant on the main thread, so a plain variable can never be corrupted mid-write. But their sequences of steps interleave, so check-then-act logic across an await is exactly as racy as it would be with threads.
time ->
Request A: [validate]--await pg--------------[serialize]--
Request B:            [validate]--await redis--[serialize]------------
Request C:                        [validate]---await pg----------------[serialize]
Main thread: A  B  C   (idle: kernel + PG working)   B  A  C

The wall time for A, B and C together is roughly the longest individual wait, not the sum. The main thread was busy for six small slices and free the rest of the time.

Practical example

An order-detail endpoint needs the order, the customer, and current inventory for each line. Sequential awaits cost 8 + 6 + 9 = 23 ms of waiting. Concurrent awaits with Promise.all cost about 9 ms. The catch a senior notices: each concurrent query takes its own pooled connection. Three concurrent queries per request at 400 requests per second is 1,200 connection-acquisitions per second; with a pool of 10 and 9 ms per query, the pool is at ~108% utilisation and requests start queueing for a connection. Concurrency inside a request is a lever, and pool size is the counterweight.

NestJS example

// orders/order-detail.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { In, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';
import { Customer } from '../customers/customer.entity';
import { InventoryItem } from '../inventory/inventory-item.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrderDetailService {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Order) private readonly orders: Repository<Order>,
    @InjectRepository(Customer) private readonly customers: Repository<Customer>,
    @InjectRepository(InventoryItem) private readonly inventory: Repository<InventoryItem>,
  ) {}

  async get(orderId: number) {
    const order = await this.orders.findOneOrFail({ where: { id: orderId }, relations: { lines: true } });

    // Independent I/O: run concurrently. Each takes its own pooled connection for ~5-10 ms.
    const [customer, stock] = await Promise.all([
      this.customers.findOneByOrFail({ id: order.customerId }),
      this.inventory.findBy({ sku: In(order.lines.map((l) => l.sku)) }),
    ]);

    return { order, customer, stock };
  }
}

Two rules: use Promise.all only for independent work, and never fan out over an unbounded list (see the failure scenario). For partial tolerance (the recommendation widget may fail without failing the order), use Promise.allSettled and degrade explicitly.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL is parallel in two senses. Across connections it is truly parallel: each backend is a process on its own core, and MVCC lets readers proceed without blocking writers. Within one connection it is strictly sequential: the wire protocol processes one statement at a time, so "concurrent" queries on a single connection are queued by the driver. That is why Promise.all inside a transaction gains nothing: a transaction is one connection.

-- two sessions: parallel across backends, no blocking between reader and writer (MVCC)
-- session 1
BEGIN; UPDATE inventory_items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE sku = 'SKU-1';   -- holds a row lock
-- session 2
SELECT stock FROM inventory_items WHERE sku = 'SKU-1';                     -- returns the old committed value, does not wait
-- session 1
COMMIT;

-- within a single query, parallelism is explicit and uses extra processes
SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 4;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT count(*) FROM order_events WHERE created_at > now() - interval '7 days';
--  Gather  (workers planned: 4, workers launched: 4)

TypeORM example

Inside dataSource.transaction, everything must go through the transaction's manager and must be awaited in sequence. Queries fired in parallel on the transactional manager are serialised on the one connection anyway; they just make the code misleading.

await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  // sequential on purpose: one connection, one statement at a time
  await manager.decrement(InventoryItem, { sku: 'SKU-1' }, 'stock', 1);
  await manager.save(Order, { sku: 'SKU-1', status: 'PLACED' });
});

// outside a transaction, independent reads may run concurrently on separate pooled connections
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([this.orders.count(), this.customers.count()]);

Never use an injected Repository (which acquires its own connection) for a write that must be part of the transaction; that write commits independently.

Sequelize example

await this.sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  await this.inventoryModel.decrement('stock', { by: 1, where: { sku: 'SKU-1' }, transaction: t });
  await this.orderModel.create({ sku: 'SKU-1', status: 'PLACED' }, { transaction: t });
});

Sequelize supports CLS (Sequelize.useCLS(namespace)) to pass the transaction implicitly; with concurrent code that is easy to get wrong, so prefer passing transaction: t explicitly.

Production scenario

A checkout endpoint fans out to five internal services: pricing, tax, shipping, fraud, loyalty. Sequentially that is 5 × 40 ms = 200 ms; concurrently it is the slowest of the five, ~50 ms. But fraud is occasionally slow (2 s at p99). With Promise.all and no timeout, checkout's p99 became fraud's p99. The fix was a per-call timeout (AbortSignal.timeout(300)) and Promise.allSettled, with fraud falling back to a rule-based check when it times out. Concurrency multiplies exposure to the slowest dependency; every fan-out needs a timeout and a fallback decision.

Failure scenario

At 07:30 a nightly job started: "recalculate loyalty tiers for all customers". The implementation was await Promise.all(customers.map((c) => this.recalc(c))) over 180,000 customers. Every recalc opened a query. Within a second, 180,000 promises were pending, the pool of 10 had 179,990 waiters, connectionTimeoutMillis fired for most of them, and the process's heap climbed to 1.2 GB holding the closures and the error objects. The pod was OOM-killed, restarted, and the cron ran again. Unbounded concurrency is not concurrency; it is a self-inflicted denial of service. The fix was a concurrency limiter (p-limit(20)) and batching by keyset, which finished the job in nine minutes at a flat 90 MB of heap.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Promise.all rejects on the first failure but does not cancel the others; they keep running and holding connections.
  • Concurrency inside one transaction is an illusion (one connection); across transactions it is real and raises lock contention.
  • Concurrent writes to the same row serialise on the row lock; concurrency can reduce throughput on hot rows (see Part 20 on lock contention).
  • A for...of with await is sequential; forEach with an async callback is fire-and-forget with unhandled rejections. Both are common bugs in opposite directions.
  • Interleaving at await means any invariant that spans two awaits can be violated by another request in between.
  • Worker threads and processes give real parallelism but pay serialisation costs on every message; a 10 MB payload copied to a worker can cost more than the computation.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask two questions about any slow path: "Is it waiting or is it computing?" Waiting is solved by concurrency and by removing round trips; computing is solved by moving work off the loop or to more processes. They bound every fan-out with a concurrency limit and a timeout, and they size pools against the concurrency they intend to allow. They explain it to a product manager as the barista: one person can serve many customers as long as no single order needs ten minutes of grinding.

Common mistakes

  • Sequential awaits for independent work ("it works, it is just slow").
  • Promise.all over thousands of items.
  • Believing "Node is single-threaded, so I cannot have race conditions".
  • Using a repository inside a transaction callback and wondering why the write survived a rollback.
  • Adding worker threads to an I/O-bound service.

Interview questions

  1. Explain concurrency versus parallelism with Node as the example. Expected: interleaving at await on one thread versus simultaneous execution on multiple cores; Node is concurrent by default and parallel via libuv, workers, processes, and the kernel.
  2. Why does Promise.all inside a TypeORM transaction not speed anything up? Expected: one transaction is one connection and the protocol is sequential per connection.
  3. A fan-out to five services makes your p99 equal the worst service's p99. What do you change? Expected: per-call timeouts, allSettled with explicit degradation, circuit breakers.
  4. You have 400 requests per second, each running three concurrent 9 ms queries. How big must the pool be? Expected: Little's law: 1,200 × 0.009 ≈ 11 connections busy on average; size for peaks, ~20.
  5. When does adding a worker thread help, and when does it hurt? Expected: helps for CPU-bound work over ~5–10 ms; hurts for I/O-bound work and for tiny tasks where message copying dominates.

Practical exercise

Take an endpoint that makes three independent queries sequentially. Measure p50/p99 with autocannon at 300 requests per second. Convert to Promise.all, measure again, then reduce the pool to 5 and measure a third time. Add a waitingCount gauge on the pool.

Acceptance criteria: you can show the latency improvement, the point at which pool waiting appears, and explain from the numbers why "more concurrency" stopped helping.

9.8 Race conditions

Concept

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the timing of operations that were assumed to be ordered. The two classic shapes are check-then-act ("if stock > 0 then decrement") and read-modify-write ("read balance, add 10, write balance"). Between the check and the act, or between the read and the write, someone else changes the state, and your action is based on stale information.

In Node, races do not come from threads preempting each other mid-statement. They come from two places: interleaving at await inside one process, and multiple processes (20 replicas of the same service) acting on shared state in PostgreSQL or Redis. The second is by far the more common in production, and it is why the atomic primitives in 9.12 matter more than any in-process lock.

Why does it exist?

Races exist because state is shared and operations are not instantaneous. Every "read it, think about it, write it back" sequence that spans a network round trip is a window of a few milliseconds during which the world can change. Under low traffic the window is rarely hit and the bug looks like a ghost; under a flash sale it is hit hundreds of times a second.

Mental model

Imagine two ticket agents at two windows, both looking at the same board that says "1 seat left". Both tell their customer "yes, you got it", both walk over to the board, and both cross out the last seat. Two people hold a ticket for one seat. The board was correct; the sequence "look, promise, update" was not atomic. The fix is not a faster agent; it is a rule that the promise and the update are one motion (an atomic decrement) or that only one agent may touch the board at a time (a lock).

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as RequestA
    participant B as RequestB
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    A->>PG: SELECT stock WHERE sku=X
    PG-->>A: stock = 1
    B->>PG: SELECT stock WHERE sku=X
    PG-->>B: stock = 1
    A->>PG: UPDATE SET stock = 0 WHERE sku=X
    B->>PG: UPDATE SET stock = 0 WHERE sku=X
    Note over A,B: both succeed, two orders for one unit
  1. Request A reads stock = 1 and awaits the result (the main thread moves on).
  2. Request B, on the same pod or on another pod, reads stock = 1.
  3. A computes 1 - 1 = 0 and writes 0. B computes 1 - 1 = 0 and writes 0.
  4. Both proceed to create an order. Inventory shows 0; two customers are promised the same unit.

The same pattern with an in-process cache: request A misses the cache and starts loading; request B misses too and starts loading; both write the cache (harmless) but both hit the database (a stampede). Or worse: a value is invalidated, and a slow request that read the old value before the invalidation writes it back into the cache after the invalidation, poisoning the cache with stale data until the next TTL.

Practical example

The four races every e-commerce backend has met:

Race Symptom Correct primitive
Oversell: two orders for the last unit negative stock, cancellations atomic conditional UPDATE, or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
Double coupon redemption coupon used 3 times unique constraint on (coupon_id, order_id) plus atomic UPDATE ... WHERE uses < max_uses
Duplicate signup with the same email two users, login chaos unique index; catch 23505, never "check then insert"
Get-or-create (customer profile) duplicate profiles INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING, then select

Every one of these was originally written as findOne followed by save, and every one passed its unit tests.

NestJS example

The buggy version and the fixed version of stock reservation. The fix delegates atomicity to PostgreSQL: one statement that checks and decrements under the row lock.

// inventory/inventory.service.ts
import { Injectable, ConflictException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { InventoryItem } from './inventory-item.entity';

@Injectable()
export class InventoryService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(InventoryItem) private readonly items: Repository<InventoryItem>) {}

  // RACY: two requests can both pass the check
  async reserveRacy(sku: string, qty: number): Promise<void> {
    const item = await this.items.findOneByOrFail({ sku });
    if (item.stock < qty) throw new ConflictException('OUT_OF_STOCK');
    item.stock -= qty;                       // computed from a stale read
    await this.items.save(item);             // UPDATE ... SET stock = <stale - qty>
  }

  // CORRECT: the check and the decrement are one statement, serialised by the row lock
  async reserve(sku: string, qty: number): Promise<void> {
    const result = await this.items
      .createQueryBuilder()
      .update(InventoryItem)
      .set({ stock: () => 'stock - :qty' })
      .where('sku = :sku AND stock >= :qty', { sku, qty })
      .execute();
    if (result.affected !== 1) throw new ConflictException('OUT_OF_STOCK');
  }
}

The in-process race, single-flight loading, is solved with a map of in-flight promises so concurrent callers share one load:

// common/single-flight.ts
export class SingleFlight<T> {
  private readonly inFlight = new Map<string, Promise<T>>();

  run(key: string, loader: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    const existing = this.inFlight.get(key);
    if (existing) return existing;                         // second caller joins the first load
    const p = loader().finally(() => this.inFlight.delete(key));
    this.inFlight.set(key, p);
    return p;
  }
}

This only de-duplicates within one process. Across 20 pods you still get up to 20 loads, which is usually acceptable; if not, a Redis lock (9.10) is the next step.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL gives you three tools, in increasing order of cost:

-- 1. Atomic conditional update (cheapest; no explicit transaction needed)
UPDATE inventory_items
SET stock = stock - 2
WHERE sku = 'SKU-1' AND stock >= 2
RETURNING stock;
-- Under READ COMMITTED, if another transaction holds the row lock, this waits, then RE-EVALUATES
-- the WHERE clause against the newly committed row. If stock is now 1, zero rows are updated.

-- 2. Pessimistic lock when you need to read, decide in application code, then write
BEGIN;
SELECT stock FROM inventory_items WHERE sku = 'SKU-1' FOR UPDATE;   -- other writers wait here
-- application decides...
UPDATE inventory_items SET stock = stock - 2 WHERE sku = 'SKU-1';
COMMIT;

-- 3. Constraints as the last line of defence: a race cannot produce an impossible row
ALTER TABLE inventory_items ADD CONSTRAINT stock_non_negative CHECK (stock >= 0);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX coupon_once_per_order ON coupon_redemptions (coupon_id, order_id);

The CHECK constraint means that even a racy code path fails loudly (23514) instead of producing negative stock. Constraints are the cheapest race-condition insurance you will ever buy.

TypeORM example

Optimistic locking: keep a version column, and make the update conditional on the version you read. @VersionColumn makes TypeORM increment the column on save(), but do not rely on save() to detect a conflict; write the conditional update explicitly and check affected.

@Entity('orders')
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id: number;
  @Column() status: string;
  @VersionColumn() version: number;
}

async transition(orderId: number, from: string, to: string, expectedVersion: number): Promise<void> {
  const res = await this.orders
    .createQueryBuilder()
    .update(Order)
    .set({ status: to, version: () => 'version + 1' })
    .where('id = :id AND status = :from AND version = :v', { id: orderId, from, v: expectedVersion })
    .execute();
  if (res.affected !== 1) throw new ConflictException('ORDER_MODIFIED_CONCURRENTLY');
}

// pessimistic alternative inside a transaction
await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  const order = await manager.findOne(Order, { where: { id: orderId }, lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' } });
  // ... decide, then manager.save(order)
});

Sequelize example

Sequelize has built-in optimistic locking: set version: true on the model and save() adds WHERE version = <read value>, throwing OptimisticLockError when the row changed underneath you.

@Table({ tableName: 'orders', version: true })
export class Order extends Model { /* columns */ }

const order = await this.orderModel.findByPk(orderId);
order.status = 'SHIPPED';
try {
  await order.save();                     // UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof OptimisticLockError) throw new ConflictException('ORDER_MODIFIED_CONCURRENTLY');
  throw err;
}

// pessimistic
const locked = await this.orderModel.findByPk(orderId, { lock: t.LOCK.UPDATE, transaction: t });

Production scenario

A flash sale offers 1,000 units at 09:00. In the first ten seconds, 52,000 reserve requests arrive across 16 pods. With the atomic UPDATE, exactly 1,000 succeed; the other 51,000 get a fast 409 because their UPDATE affects zero rows. The hot row is the bottleneck: each update holds the row lock for ~0.3 ms, so the row can absorb ~3,000 updates per second, and the queue at the lock adds up to 15 ms of latency at the peak. Acceptable. With the racy version, the team once sold 1,340 units. The postmortem's line "it passed all tests" is the sentence every senior remembers.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged: stock_non_negative constraint violations spiking. Good news: the constraint had caught a race. Bad news: the code path was a new "reserve for cart" feature written as findOne, compare, save. Under a bot-driven burst, dozens of requests interleaved. Because of the constraint, the damage was errors rather than oversell; the fix was a one-line change to the atomic update. Without the constraint, the page would have come from the warehouse three days later.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Retries create races: a client that times out and retries a non-idempotent decrement double-decrements. Idempotency keys are part of race-condition hygiene.
  • Replication lag: reading from a replica, deciding, and writing to the primary is check-then-act with an extra few hundred milliseconds of staleness.
  • Cache invalidation races: a slow reader can repopulate a cache with stale data after a write invalidated it. Use short TTLs or versioned keys.
  • "First request wins" by timestamp fails under clock skew between pods; use a database sequence or a Redis INCR for ordering.
  • Under SERIALIZABLE isolation, PostgreSQL detects many races and aborts with 40001; you must retry. It is the heavyweight answer for complex invariants.
  • Node races often hide behind Promise.all: two branches of the same request touching the same row.
  • Unique-constraint checks in TypeORM's save() for "upsert" logic are not atomic; use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (repository.upsert or createQueryBuilder().insert().orIgnore()).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They assume every await is a point where the world changes, and they push every invariant into a place that can enforce it atomically: a single conditional UPDATE, a unique index, a CHECK, a Redis command. They never trust a read to still be true a millisecond later. They prefer optimistic techniques for low-contention rows (order status transitions) and pessimistic locks for high-contention rows updated in complex ways (wallet balances). To a product manager: "Two customers can click within the same millisecond; the database is the only referee fast enough to say who was first, so we let it decide, not the application."

Common mistakes

  • findOne then save for anything that another request could also change.
  • Checking uniqueness in code and inserting without a unique index.
  • Assuming single-threaded means race-free.
  • "Fixing" a race with an in-process mutex while running 20 replicas.
  • Retrying without an idempotency key, converting a timeout into a duplicate.

Interview questions

  1. Node is single-threaded. Can it have race conditions? Expected: yes; interleaving at await within a process and across replicas; show the oversell example.
  2. How does UPDATE ... WHERE stock >= n prevent oversell under READ COMMITTED? Expected: the row lock serialises updaters and PostgreSQL re-evaluates the WHERE on the latest committed version after waiting.
  3. Optimistic versus pessimistic locking: when do you choose which? Expected: optimistic for low contention and long user think-time; pessimistic for hot rows with short critical sections. Follow-up: what happens to a FOR UPDATE when the client disconnects? (Rolled back on socket close.)
  4. What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it in one process and across many? Expected: single-flight map in-process; a lock or probabilistic early refresh across processes.
  5. Why are unique constraints and check constraints part of race-condition design? Expected: they make racy code fail loudly instead of corrupting data.

Practical exercise

Write the racy reserveRacy and the atomic reserve. Seed stock = 50 and fire 500 concurrent requests with autocannon -c 100. Count successful orders and final stock for each version. Then add the CHECK constraint and repeat the racy version.

Acceptance criteria: the racy version oversells; the atomic version ends at exactly zero stock with exactly 50 successes; the constrained racy version produces 23514 errors and never negative stock.

9.9 Deadlocks

Concept

A deadlock is a standstill: two or more parties each hold a resource and wait for a resource another party holds, in a cycle, so none can ever proceed. Four conditions must all be true (Coffman's conditions): resources are exclusively held (mutual exclusion), holders wait for more while holding (hold and wait), resources cannot be taken away (no preemption), and the waits form a cycle (circular wait). Break any one condition and deadlock is impossible; in practice you break circular wait by always acquiring resources in the same order.

Backend engineers meet deadlocks in two places: in PostgreSQL, where two transactions lock rows in opposite orders and the database detects and kills one; and in application code, where an await waits for something that cannot happen until the current code releases what it holds, such as a connection pool.

Why does it exist?

Deadlock is not a feature; it is a consequence of having locks at all. It exists because locks are the only way to protect multi-step updates, and multi-step updates in different orders create cycles. Understanding the four conditions matters because the fixes are direct: ordered acquisition, shorter transactions, lock timeouts, and retries.

Mental model

Imagine a one-lane bridge with a car entering from each end at the same time. Each is now on the bridge, holding its half, waiting for the other to back up. Neither will. PostgreSQL is a traffic warden who, after one second, orders one car to reverse (aborts one transaction with deadlock detected) so the other can cross. Your application code has no such warden: a deadlocked pool hangs until a timeout, and if there is no timeout, forever.

How it works

flowchart LR
    T1["Transaction 1: holds lock on wallet A, wants wallet B"]
    T2["Transaction 2: holds lock on wallet B, wants wallet A"]
    T1 -->|"waits for"| T2
    T2 -->|"waits for"| T1
    D["deadlock_timeout 1 s: PostgreSQL finds the cycle, aborts one, error 40P01"]
  1. Transaction 1 updates wallet A (row lock on A). Transaction 2 updates wallet B (row lock on B).
  2. Transaction 1 tries to update B and waits for T2's lock. Transaction 2 tries to update A and waits for T1's lock. Cycle.
  3. After deadlock_timeout (default 1 s) of waiting, the waiting backend runs the deadlock detector: it builds the wait-for graph among all backends and looks for a cycle.
  4. If it finds one, it aborts its own transaction with ERROR: deadlock detected (SQLSTATE 40P01) and a DETAIL naming the processes and the rows. The other transaction proceeds as if nothing happened.
  5. The client of the aborted transaction gets an exception. The correct response is to retry the whole transaction, because the other transaction has now committed and the world is different.

The application-level deadlock, which PostgreSQL cannot see:

  1. A request starts a transaction with a QueryRunner, taking one of 5 pooled connections.
  2. Inside the transaction, it calls a service method that uses an injected repository, which needs another connection from the same pool.
  3. Under load, 5 requests are each inside step 1, holding all 5 connections, each waiting for a 6th. Nobody releases. The pool's acquire timeout (or nothing) ends it.

Practical example

The textbook case is a wallet transfer. Two users pay each other at the same time: transfer A -> B locks A then B; transfer B -> A locks B then A. Under 100 transfers per second on a payments platform this happens several times a minute. Two more that surprise people: updating a parent row and inserting child rows (an INSERT into order_items takes a FOR KEY SHARE lock on the referenced orders row, and an UPDATE on that order in another transaction conflicts) and bulk updates that touch overlapping row sets in different physical orders.

NestJS example

Ordered locking plus a retry on 40P01:

// wallets/wallet-transfer.service.ts
import { Injectable, ConflictException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource, QueryFailedError } from 'typeorm';
import { Wallet } from './wallet.entity';

const DEADLOCK = '40P01';
const SERIALIZATION_FAILURE = '40001';

@Injectable()
export class WalletTransferService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async transfer(fromId: number, toId: number, cents: number, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.withDeadlockRetry(async () => {
      await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
        // Break circular wait: always lock the lower id first, whatever the transfer direction
        const [firstId, secondId] = fromId < toId ? [fromId, toId] : [toId, fromId];
        const rows = await manager
          .createQueryBuilder(Wallet, 'w')
          .setLock('pessimistic_write')
          .where('w.id IN (:...ids)', { ids: [firstId, secondId] })
          .orderBy('w.id', 'ASC')            // deterministic lock order
          .getMany();

        const from = rows.find((w) => w.id === fromId)!;
        const to = rows.find((w) => w.id === toId)!;
        if (from.balanceCents < cents) throw new ConflictException('INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS');

        await manager.decrement(Wallet, { id: fromId }, 'balanceCents', cents);
        await manager.increment(Wallet, { id: toId }, 'balanceCents', cents);
        await manager.insert('wallet_transfers', { idempotencyKey, fromId, toId, cents }); // unique key
      });
    });
  }

  private async withDeadlockRetry<T>(work: () => Promise<T>, attempts = 3): Promise<T> {
    for (let i = 1; ; i++) {
      try {
        return await work();
      } catch (err) {
        const code = err instanceof QueryFailedError ? (err.driverError as { code?: string }).code : undefined;
        if ((code !== DEADLOCK && code !== SERIALIZATION_FAILURE) || i >= attempts) throw err;
        await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 20 * i + Math.random() * 50));   // jittered backoff
      }
    }
  }
}

The idempotencyKey insert with a unique constraint makes the retry safe even if the client also retries.

PostgreSQL example

Reproduce, observe and defend:

-- session 1                                   -- session 2
BEGIN;                                         BEGIN;
UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 100 WHERE id = 1;
                                               UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 50 WHERE id = 2;
UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents + 100 WHERE id = 2;   -- waits
                                               UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents + 50 WHERE id = 1;  -- waits... 1 s later:
-- ERROR:  deadlock detected
-- DETAIL:  Process 2311 waits for ShareLock on transaction 71822; blocked by process 2310.
--          Process 2310 waits for ShareLock on transaction 71823; blocked by process 2311.
-- HINT:  See server log for query details.

-- who is blocking whom, right now
SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, state, left(query, 60) AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

-- defences
SET lock_timeout = '2s';                       -- give up waiting for a lock (error 55P03) instead of piling up
SELECT * FROM wallets WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;      -- fail immediately if locked
SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 10;   -- queue workers never deadlock
SHOW deadlock_timeout;                         -- 1s; do not lower it much, detection is expensive

log_lock_waits = on writes a line for every wait longer than deadlock_timeout, which is the best early warning for contention that has not yet become a deadlock.

TypeORM example

The pool deadlock and its fix: everything inside the transaction must use manager, never an injected repository.

// WRONG: this.customers is a Repository bound to the DataSource, it acquires a second connection
await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  const customer = await this.customers.findOneBy({ id });      // 2nd connection from the same pool
  await manager.save(Order, { customerId: customer!.id });
});

// RIGHT: derive the repository from the transactional manager
await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  const customer = await manager.getRepository(Customer).findOneBy({ id });
  await manager.save(Order, { customerId: customer!.id });
});

Set extra.connectionTimeoutMillis so that if this mistake ships, it produces errors within seconds rather than a silent hang.

Sequelize example

Sequelize can retry deadlocks for you at the connection level, and the same pool-deadlock rule applies: pass transaction: t to every query inside the callback.

SequelizeModule.forRoot({
  dialect: 'postgres',
  retry: { match: [/deadlock detected/i, /could not serialize access/i], max: 3 },  // retry whole queries
  pool: { max: 10, acquire: 5_000 },       // acquire timeout turns a pool deadlock into an error
});

await this.sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  const wallets = await this.walletModel.findAll({
    where: { id: [fromId, toId] },
    order: [['id', 'ASC']],                // deterministic lock order
    lock: t.LOCK.UPDATE,
    transaction: t,
  });
  // ... decrement/increment with { transaction: t }
});

Note that retry re-runs a query, not your whole transaction; for multi-statement transactions you still need application-level retry.

Production scenario

A wallet service processes 300 transfers per second. Before ordered locking, it logged 40–80 40P01 errors per hour, each retried transparently, each costing one second of deadlock_timeout wait plus the retry. After ordering by id, deadlocks dropped to zero, and the p99 of transfers fell from 1.2 s (dominated by the 1 s detection wait) to 18 ms. Deadlocks are rarely an availability problem in PostgreSQL; they are a latency problem, because detection costs a full second.

Failure scenario

At 14:20 the orders API stopped responding. CPU was near zero, PostgreSQL showed 12 idle-in-transaction backends and nothing else, and every request timed out after 30 s. A new "create order" flow opened a transaction with a QueryRunner, then called customersService.ensureProfile(), which used its own injected repository and therefore needed a second pooled connection. Pool size was 12. The moment 12 orders were in flight, all 12 connections were held by transactions waiting for a 13th connection that could never come. There was no connectionTimeoutMillis, so nothing ever errored; the pod just stopped. Kubernetes did not restart it because the liveness probe was a static 200. The fix was the manager.getRepository rule, a 5-second connection timeout, and a liveness check that runs a real query.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Foreign keys take FOR KEY SHARE locks on parent rows; parent updates plus child inserts across transactions can deadlock without any explicit FOR UPDATE.
  • Index page locks and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on ranges can deadlock even with consistent row ordering if two scans traverse in different directions; ordering by the primary key on an index scan is the safe pattern.
  • Lowering deadlock_timeout speeds detection but makes the detector run more often; keep it at 1 s and fix the ordering instead.
  • lock_timeout aborts the statement; the transaction is then in an aborted state and must be rolled back.
  • Async application deadlocks include: awaiting a mutex you already hold (non-reentrant), two services awaiting each other's onModuleInit, and Atomics.wait on the main thread waiting for a worker that is waiting for the main thread.
  • A retry without idempotency turns a deadlock into a duplicate.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design lock order into the code, not into comments: sort ids, lock parent before child, always the same order in every code path. They keep transactions short (no HTTP calls inside a transaction, ever) so that locks are held for milliseconds. They set lock_timeout, statement_timeout, and pool acquire timeouts so that a mistake produces an error, not a hang. They treat every 40P01 as a retryable event with a metric on it, and they alert when the rate changes. To a product manager: "Two payments occasionally try to cross the same bridge from opposite ends; the database makes one of them back up and try again a moment later. We make sure that retry is invisible."

Common mistakes

  • Locking rows in the order the request happened to list them.
  • Calling another service (which opens its own connection) inside a transaction.
  • No acquire timeout on the pool, so a pool deadlock is a silent hang.
  • Retrying only the failed statement instead of the whole transaction.
  • Treating deadlock detected as a bug to be swallowed rather than a signal to fix ordering.

Interview questions

  1. Explain how PostgreSQL detects a deadlock and what the client should do. Expected: wait-for graph after deadlock_timeout; one transaction aborted with 40P01; client retries the whole transaction with backoff.
  2. How do you make wallet transfers deadlock-free? Expected: acquire row locks in a global order (by id), keep the transaction short, retry 40P01.
  3. Describe a deadlock that involves no explicit locks. Expected: FK FOR KEY SHARE on parent rows versus parent updates; or a pool deadlock in application code.
  4. Why is a connection pool deadlock invisible to PostgreSQL? Expected: the waiting happens in the application before a connection exists; PG sees only idle-in-transaction sessions.
  5. What does SKIP LOCKED change for queue workers? Expected: workers never wait on each other's rows, so no contention or deadlock; each takes the next unlocked job.

Practical exercise

Implement transfer without ordering and run 200 concurrent random transfers among 10 wallets; count 40P01 errors and measure p99. Add ordered locking and the retry helper; repeat. Then reproduce the pool deadlock with max: 2 and an injected repository inside a transaction, and watch it hang; add connectionTimeoutMillis and fix the code.

Acceptance criteria: measurable deadlock count before and zero after; a demonstrable hang that becomes a fast error with the timeout; total wallet balance unchanged across all runs.

9.10 Mutex

Concept

A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) is a lock with one holder. Whoever holds it may run the protected code (the critical section); everyone else waits until it is released. It is the simplest tool for turning a multi-step sequence into something that behaves as if it were one step.

A backend engineer meets mutexes at three scopes:

  • In-process: protecting a sequence that spans awaits inside one Node process, for example refreshing an OAuth token exactly once when it expires. Libraries such as async-mutex provide this.
  • In the database: row locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) and advisory locks (pg_advisory_xact_lock), which make PostgreSQL act as a mutex service for any key you choose.
  • Distributed: a lock held in Redis (SET key token NX PX ttl) so that only one of 20 replicas performs an action, such as running a scheduled job or processing a given order.

Why does it exist?

Because some sequences cannot be made atomic by a single statement. "Fetch a new token from the identity provider, store it, then use it" involves an HTTP call in the middle. "Regenerate the daily report" takes minutes. When you cannot make the operation atomic, you make it exclusive. The cost is serialisation: whatever is behind the mutex runs one at a time, so it must be short, and it must always be released.

Mental model

Imagine a single-occupancy bathroom with a key hanging on a hook. You take the key (acquire), go in, come out, hang the key back (release). If you walk off with the key in your pocket (an exception path that never releases), everyone waits forever. If the key has a rule "auto-returns to the hook after 30 seconds" (a TTL), then a slow occupant might still be inside when the next person walks in (two holders). Every mutex design is a trade between "never stuck" and "never two inside".

How it works

  1. Acquire must itself be atomic: a test-and-set or compare-and-swap that checks "is it free?" and marks it "taken" in one indivisible step. In-process, JavaScript's single thread makes a plain if (!locked) locked = true atomic as long as there is no await between the check and the set. In Redis, SET key value NX is atomic because Redis executes one command at a time. In PostgreSQL, the lock manager does it.
  2. Waiters queue. A fair mutex hands the lock to waiters in order; an unfair one lets whoever tries first take it.
  3. The holder runs the critical section, which must be as short as possible and must not itself wait for anything that could need the same lock (non-reentrant deadlock).
  4. Release must happen on every path, hence try/finally. Distributed locks also need ownership: release only if the lock value is your token, otherwise a slow holder whose lock expired could release the next holder's lock.
  5. Liveness protection: a TTL (Redis PX), a transaction scope (PostgreSQL xact advisory locks are released on commit or rollback, including on disconnect), or a watchdog. A lock that cannot expire is a lock that will one day be held by a dead process.
flowchart LR
    A["Request wants critical section"] --> B{"SET lock token NX PX 30000"}
    B -->|"OK"| C["Run critical section"]
    B -->|"nil, someone holds it"| W["Wait with backoff or fail fast"]
    W --> B
    C --> R["Lua: if GET lock == token then DEL"]
    R --> E["Released"]
    C -->|"process dies"| T["TTL expires after 30 s"]
    T --> E

Practical example

Three real uses in an e-commerce backend:

  • Single-flight token refresh: 200 concurrent requests notice the payment gateway token expired. Without a mutex, 200 refresh calls hit the identity provider (and it rate-limits you). With one, the first refreshes, the other 199 wait ~100 ms and reuse the result.
  • One scheduled job across replicas: the @Cron('0 * * * *') "expire abandoned carts" job must run once per hour, not once per pod. A PostgreSQL advisory lock is the simplest leader election you will ever deploy.
  • Per-order processing lock: a webhook from the payment provider and a user's "cancel" click arrive for the same order in the same 50 ms. A Redis lock keyed by order:{id} serialises them.

NestJS example

In-process single flight with async-mutex:

// payments/gateway-token.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Mutex } from 'async-mutex';

@Injectable()
export class GatewayTokenService {
  private token: { value: string; expiresAt: number } | null = null;
  private readonly refreshMutex = new Mutex();

  async get(): Promise<string> {
    if (this.token && this.token.expiresAt > Date.now() + 30_000) return this.token.value;

    // Only one refresh at a time; concurrent callers wait here, then re-check
    return this.refreshMutex.runExclusive(async () => {
      if (this.token && this.token.expiresAt > Date.now() + 30_000) return this.token.value; // double-check
      const fresh = await this.fetchToken();       // one HTTP call for the whole burst
      this.token = fresh;
      return fresh.value;
    });
  }

  private async fetchToken(): Promise<{ value: string; expiresAt: number }> {
    const res = await fetch(process.env.GATEWAY_TOKEN_URL!, { method: 'POST', signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3_000) });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`token refresh failed: ${res.status}`);
    const body = (await res.json()) as { access_token: string; expires_in: number };
    return { value: body.access_token, expiresAt: Date.now() + body.expires_in * 1000 };
  }
}

A distributed lock in Redis with ownership-checked release:

// common/redis-lock.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

const RELEASE_IF_OWNER = `
  if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) end
  return 0
`;

@Injectable()
export class RedisLockService {
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  // Returns a release function, or null if the lock is held by someone else.
  async tryAcquire(key: string, ttlMs: number): Promise<(() => Promise<void>) | null> {
    const token = randomUUID();
    const ok = await this.redis.set(`lock:${key}`, token, 'PX', ttlMs, 'NX');   // atomic in Redis
    if (ok !== 'OK') return null;
    return async () => {
      await this.redis.eval(RELEASE_IF_OWNER, 1, `lock:${key}`, token);         // never delete someone else's lock
    };
  }

  async withLock<T>(key: string, ttlMs: number, work: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T | null> {
    const release = await this.tryAcquire(key, ttlMs);
    if (!release) return null;                                                  // caller decides: skip, retry, 409
    try {
      return await work();
    } finally {
      await release();
    }
  }
}

And the once-per-cluster cron, using PostgreSQL:

// carts/cart-expiry.job.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class CartExpiryJob {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(CartExpiryJob.name);
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  @Cron('0 * * * *')
  async run() {
    // Transaction-scoped advisory lock: released on commit, rollback, or disconnect (pod death)
    await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
      const [{ locked }] = await manager.query('SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock($1) AS locked', [42_001]);
      if (!locked) { this.logger.log('another replica holds the cart-expiry lock, skipping'); return; }
      const res = await manager.query(
        `UPDATE carts SET status = 'EXPIRED' WHERE status = 'OPEN' AND updated_at < now() - interval '7 days'`,
      );
      this.logger.log(`expired ${res[1]} carts`);
    });
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

-- transaction-scoped advisory lock keyed by a string: serialise all work on one order
BEGIN;
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('order:8812'));     -- waits until free; auto-released at COMMIT/ROLLBACK
-- ... multi-statement work on order 8812 ...
COMMIT;

-- non-blocking variant for "skip if busy"
SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('report:daily'));  -- true or false immediately

-- bound the wait so a stuck holder produces an error, not a pile-up
SET lock_timeout = '3s';

-- see who holds advisory locks
SELECT l.pid, l.objid, a.application_name, a.state
FROM pg_locks l JOIN pg_stat_activity a USING (pid)
WHERE l.locktype = 'advisory';

Advisory locks cost one row in the lock table and nothing on disk; they are the right tool for "one at a time per key" whenever the work is database-centric.

TypeORM example

Inside dataSource.transaction, the advisory lock is one manager.query away, as in the cron above. For row-level exclusivity, setLock('pessimistic_write') inside a transaction is the mutex; TypeORM throws PessimisticLockTransactionRequiredError if you forget the transaction, which is a helpful guard.

Sequelize example

await this.sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  await this.sequelize.query('SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(:key))', { replacements: { key: `order:${id}` }, transaction: t });
  // ... exclusive work on the order using { transaction: t } ...
});

Production scenario

A subscription-billing service runs a renewal job hourly on 6 replicas. Before locking, each replica charged every due subscription, and the deduplication relied on the payment provider's idempotency keys, which worked until a key-generation bug made them per-attempt. Twelve customers were charged six times. After adding pg_try_advisory_xact_lock, exactly one replica runs each hour; the others log "skipping" in under a millisecond. Cost: one query per replica per hour. This is the entire "leader election" implementation, and for database-centric jobs it beats a Kubernetes lease or ZooKeeper by a mile of simplicity.

Failure scenario

At 03:10 the nightly "rebuild search index" job did not run, and neither did the next three nights. The job held a Redis lock with no TTL (SET NX without PX), and the pod that held it had been OOM-killed mid-run three days earlier. Every subsequent attempt saw the lock and skipped. The fix was a TTL slightly longer than the job's worst-case runtime (2 h), plus a heartbeat that extends the TTL while the job is alive, plus a metric "job last succeeded at" with an alert at 26 h. The deeper lesson: a lock with no expiry is a promise that the holder will never crash, and nobody can keep that promise.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • TTL too short: the holder is still working when the lock expires; a second holder enters. Use a fencing token (a monotonically increasing number the protected resource checks) when correctness depends on it, or keep the critical section far shorter than the TTL.
  • Redis failover: a lock written to the primary may not have replicated to the replica that gets promoted; two holders. Redlock exists for this; for most jobs, a PostgreSQL advisory lock is simpler and strictly consistent.
  • Non-reentrant mutexes deadlock if the critical section calls a function that acquires the same mutex.
  • Holding an in-process mutex across an HTTP call with no timeout blocks every waiter until the call returns.
  • Session-level advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock) live until unlocked or the session ends; with a pooler in transaction mode, "the session" is not yours, and the lock may be released or leak unexpectedly. Prefer xact locks.
  • hashtext() collisions between different strings are possible (32-bit); use a namespace integer plus id, or pg_advisory_xact_lock(int, int) with two keys.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They reach for a mutex only after asking whether the operation can be made atomic instead (9.12). When they do, they choose the smallest scope that works: in-process for per-process state, PostgreSQL advisory for database work, Redis for cross-service coordination that must be fast. Every lock they write has a TTL or a transaction scope, ownership-checked release, and a metric. They keep critical sections tiny and never put a network call inside one unless it is the whole point. To a product manager: "Only one person can hold the key to the report room; if they faint inside, the key returns to the hook automatically after ten minutes."

Common mistakes

  • SET NX without PX.
  • DEL on release without checking the token.
  • Using an in-process mutex to protect state that lives in the database, while running many replicas.
  • Long critical sections (a mutex around an entire request).
  • Forgetting the double-check after acquiring: the reason you waited may already be resolved.

Interview questions

  1. How do you implement a safe distributed lock in Redis? Expected: SET key token NX PX ttl, release with a Lua compare-and-delete, TTL longer than the critical section, optional heartbeat. Follow-up: what breaks during failover?
  2. When would you use a PostgreSQL advisory lock instead of Redis? Expected: database-centric work, need for strict consistency, automatic release on disconnect, no extra infrastructure.
  3. What is a fencing token and when is a TTL alone insufficient? Expected: a monotonically increasing token the resource validates; needed when a paused holder resuming after expiry could corrupt state.
  4. How do you run a cron once across N replicas? Expected: pg_try_advisory_xact_lock inside the job's transaction, or a Redis lock with TTL and a heartbeat.
  5. Why is a mutex around await fetch() risky? Expected: it serialises all callers behind the slowest network call; needs a timeout and should be single-flight only.

Practical exercise

Implement GatewayTokenService with and without the mutex, then fire 200 concurrent requests that need a token while the token endpoint is stubbed to take 200 ms. Count calls to the stub. Then implement CartExpiryJob with the advisory lock and run three instances of the service against one database.

Acceptance criteria: 1 stub call with the mutex versus ~200 without; exactly one instance performs the expiry each run and the others log "skipping"; killing the running instance mid-job releases the lock immediately.

9.11 Semaphore

Concept

A semaphore is a counter with a wait queue: it holds N permits, acquire takes one (waiting if none are free) and release returns one. A mutex is a semaphore with N = 1. Semaphores exist to say "at most N of these at once".

The most important semaphore in your stack is one you never call by that name: the database connection pool. max: 10 is ten permits; pool.connect() is acquire; client.release() is release; connectionTimeoutMillis is the acquire timeout. Every other bounded resource is the same shape: worker-thread pools, outbound HTTP connection caps, BullMQ concurrency, p-limit.

Why does it exist?

Every real resource has a capacity: PostgreSQL has cores, a payment gateway allows 20 concurrent calls per merchant, a worker pool has 4 threads, your own process has a memory limit that 10,000 in-flight PDF renders would blow. Unbounded concurrency does not make things faster; it turns capacity limits into cascading failures. A semaphore makes the limit explicit and turns "overload" into a queue with a timeout, which is something you can measure and alert on.

Mental model

Imagine a car park with 10 spaces and a counter at the barrier. The counter is the semaphore. Cars enter while the counter says spaces are free; when it reaches zero, cars queue at the barrier. When a car leaves, the barrier lets one in. If cars queue for more than five minutes, they give up and go elsewhere (acquire timeout) instead of blocking the road behind them (a full event loop of waiters).

How it works

  1. State: a permit count and a FIFO queue of waiters.
  2. acquire: if permits > 0, decrement and return immediately. Otherwise append the caller to the queue and return a promise; start a timer that removes the caller and rejects the promise if it fires first.
  3. release: if there is a waiter, hand the permit straight to it (wake it); otherwise increment the count.
  4. Observability: the current in-use count, the queue length (waitingCount in pg), and the time spent waiting are the three metrics. Queue length rising is the earliest sign that a dependency is slowing down.
  5. Sizing follows Little's law: permits needed = arrival rate × average hold time. 800 queries per second × 12 ms average = 9.6 connections busy on average; size for peaks and variance, so 15–20.
pool.max = 10
in use  [##########]  10/10
waiting [ 7 requests ]  <- each has connectionTimeoutMillis = 5000 ticking

Practical example

An orders API calls a shipping-rate provider that allows 8 concurrent connections per API key and returns HTTP 429 beyond that. Without a semaphore, a burst of 50 checkouts produces 42 rate-limit errors and 42 retries, which produce more 429s. With a semaphore of 8 permits and a 2-second acquire timeout, 8 calls run, the rest wait up to 2 seconds, and anything beyond that gets a fast, honest 503 with Retry-After. This pattern is also called a bulkhead: the slow dependency cannot consume all of the process's capacity.

NestJS example

A small semaphore (about 30 lines) is often better than a dependency, because you control the timeout and the metrics:

// common/semaphore.ts
export class Semaphore {
  private permits: number;
  private readonly queue: Array<() => void> = [];

  constructor(readonly max: number) { this.permits = max; }

  get inUse() { return this.max - this.permits; }
  get waiting() { return this.queue.length; }

  async acquire(timeoutMs: number): Promise<() => void> {
    if (this.permits > 0) { this.permits--; return this.releaser(); }
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const timer = setTimeout(() => {
        const i = this.queue.indexOf(waiter);
        if (i >= 0) this.queue.splice(i, 1);
        reject(new Error('SEMAPHORE_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT'));
      }, timeoutMs);
      const waiter = () => { clearTimeout(timer); this.permits--; resolve(this.releaser()); };
      this.queue.push(waiter);
    });
  }

  private releaser(): () => void {
    let released = false;
    return () => {
      if (released) return;                 // idempotent release
      released = true;
      this.permits++;
      const next = this.queue.shift();
      if (next) next();                     // hand the permit to the oldest waiter
    };
  }
}
// shipping/shipping-rates.service.ts
import { Injectable, ServiceUnavailableException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Semaphore } from '../common/semaphore';

@Injectable()
export class ShippingRatesService {
  private readonly gate = new Semaphore(8);                    // provider allows 8 concurrent calls

  async quote(address: string, weightGrams: number) {
    let release: () => void;
    try {
      release = await this.gate.acquire(2_000);                // bounded wait
    } catch {
      throw new ServiceUnavailableException({ message: 'shipping provider busy', retryAfterSeconds: 2 });
    }
    try {
      const res = await fetch(process.env.SHIPPING_URL!, {
        method: 'POST',
        body: JSON.stringify({ address, weightGrams }),
        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3_000),                    // hold time is bounded too
      });
      return await res.json();
    } finally {
      release();
    }
  }
}

For queue consumers, the semaphore is a config line: @Processor('pdf', { concurrency: 4 }) in @nestjs/bullmq limits each worker process to 4 jobs at once.

PostgreSQL example

The connection pool is a client-side semaphore; the database has its own hard limit and no queue: beyond max_connections, it refuses. PgBouncer adds a server-side semaphore with a queue.

SHOW max_connections;                 -- hard limit, no queueing: excess gets "too many clients"
SHOW superuser_reserved_connections;  -- keep 3 for admins so you can still log in during an incident

-- PgBouncer (pgbouncer.ini, not SQL): a real semaphore in front of PostgreSQL
-- pool_mode = transaction
-- default_pool_size = 40           ; permits per database/user pair
-- max_client_conn = 2000           ; clients allowed to wait
-- query_wait_timeout = 5           ; acquire timeout in seconds

Pool waiting is invisible from inside PostgreSQL: a request waiting for a permit has not sent a byte to the server. If your database dashboard is calm and your API is slow, check waitingCount.

TypeORM example

Expose the pg pool's counters. TypeORM's PostgreSQL driver keeps the pg.Pool in driver.master; it is internal but stable, and widely used for metrics.

// database/pool-metrics.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Interval } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Gauge } from 'prom-client';
import type { Pool } from 'pg';

@Injectable()
export class PoolMetricsService {
  private readonly total = new Gauge({ name: 'pg_pool_total', help: 'connections open' });
  private readonly idle = new Gauge({ name: 'pg_pool_idle', help: 'connections idle' });
  private readonly waiting = new Gauge({ name: 'pg_pool_waiting', help: 'requests waiting for a connection' });

  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  @Interval(5_000)
  sample() {
    const pool = (this.dataSource.driver as unknown as { master: Pool }).master;
    this.total.set(pool.totalCount);
    this.idle.set(pool.idleCount);
    this.waiting.set(pool.waitingCount);     // the number to alert on
  }
}

Sequelize example
