Sequelize's pool (sequelize-pool) exposes size, available, using, waiting via sequelize.connectionManager.pool. The acquire option is the acquire timeout; when it fires you get TimeoutError: ResourceRequest timed out, which is the Sequelize spelling of "semaphore acquire timeout".

SequelizeModule.forRoot({
  dialect: 'postgres',
  pool: { max: 15, min: 0, acquire: 5_000, idle: 10_000 },  // 15 permits, 5 s acquire timeout
});

Production scenario

An order service at 800 requests per second with a 12 ms average query and 1.3 queries per request needs 800 × 1.3 × 0.012 ≈ 12.5 connections busy on average. With max: 10, the pool is over capacity, waitingCount sits at 30–60, and p99 climbs to 200 ms with a healthy database. With max: 20, waiting is zero and p99 is 28 ms. With max: 100, nothing improves on the API, and the database now has 12 × 100 = 1,200 potential backends across 12 replicas. The right number was 20, found from Little's law and confirmed by the waiting gauge.

Failure scenario

At 12:50 a report endpoint began running a 9-second query. Fourteen users clicked it. With max: 10, ten connections were held for 9 seconds each while every checkout request waited in the pool queue; connectionTimeoutMillis was 30 s, so nothing failed, everything just took 9 seconds. The API looked "down" for two minutes while the database was at 8% CPU. Fixes: a separate small pool for reporting (a bulkhead: max: 3 on its own DataSource), statement_timeout on that pool, and a 5-second acquire timeout on the main pool so overload surfaces as a fast 503, not a slow success.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A permit held across an unbounded operation (no timeout) is a permit lost for the duration; hold time must be bounded as strictly as acquire time.
  • FIFO queues can starve latency-sensitive callers behind bulk work; give bulk work its own semaphore.
  • Releasing twice corrupts the count (the idempotent releaser above prevents it).
  • Per-process semaphores multiply by replica count; a provider limit of 8 with 12 replicas needs 8 total, not 8 each. Use Redis for a global counting semaphore or set per-replica permits to floor(8 / replicas).
  • min connections in a pool are permits pre-paid at startup; with 40 replicas and min: 5, that is 200 idle backends.
  • In pg, a client that throws inside pool.connect() callback style without release is a permanently lost permit; the pool shrinks silently to zero.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They see every dependency as a car park with a fixed number of spaces and insist on knowing the number. They give each dependency its own bulkhead so that one slow provider cannot consume the capacity meant for another. They size with arithmetic, verify with the waiting gauge, and set acquire and hold timeouts so overload becomes a fast, visible error. To a product manager: "The shipping provider lets eight of our requests in at a time. We queue politely behind that door for two seconds; after that we tell the customer to try again rather than making everyone else wait."

Common mistakes

  • No acquire timeout, converting overload into a silent hang.
  • One pool for both interactive requests and heavy reports.
  • Semaphore per replica when the limit is global.
  • Raising max instead of finding why hold time grew.
  • Not measuring waitingCount, so pool saturation is misdiagnosed as database slowness.

Interview questions

  1. Why is a connection pool a semaphore, and what are its acquire and release? Expected: N permits; connect()/release(); timeouts and queue length as the key metrics.
  2. Compute the pool size for 800 rps at 12 ms per query. Expected: Little's law, ~10 average, size ~15–20 for variance.
  3. What is a bulkhead and how would you implement one in NestJS? Expected: separate semaphores/pools per dependency so one cannot exhaust the others; a Semaphore or separate DataSource.
  4. Your API is slow but the database is idle. Name the first metric you check. Expected: pool waitingCount / acquire wait time.
  5. How do you enforce a global concurrency limit across 12 replicas? Expected: a Redis-backed counting semaphore (with TTL per permit), or divide permits per replica.

Practical exercise

Wrap a stubbed slow dependency (300 ms, max 5 concurrent before it returns 429) with the Semaphore above. Load with 50 concurrent clients. Measure 429s, 503s and latency with permits at 5, 10 and unlimited; graph inUse and waiting.

Acceptance criteria: zero 429s at 5 permits, a bounded waiting queue with 2-second timeouts producing 503s under overload, and a written sentence explaining why unlimited permits produced the worst overall latency.

9.12 Atomic operations

Concept

An atomic operation is one that cannot be observed half-done and cannot interleave with another operation on the same target. Either it happened entirely or not at all, and no one saw the middle. Atomicity is what turns "read, compute, write" into a single safe step, which is why it is the best answer to race conditions: no locks to forget, no TTLs to tune.

Backend engineers have three atomic primitives at hand:

  • In the CPU / across worker threads: Atomics.add, Atomics.compareExchange, Atomics.wait / Atomics.notify on a SharedArrayBuffer, implemented with hardware instructions such as lock xadd and compare-and-swap.
  • In Redis: every single command is atomic because Redis executes commands one at a time on one thread: INCR, INCRBY, SET NX, HINCRBY, LPUSH; MULTI/EXEC and Lua scripts make multi-command sequences atomic.
  • In PostgreSQL: a single statement executes atomically with respect to other transactions on the rows it touches: UPDATE inventory_items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE sku = $1 AND stock > 0. This is the atomic primitive of relational databases and the one you will use most.

Why does it exist?

Because "check then act" across a network is a race, and locks are expensive and fragile. An atomic decrement is faster than a lock (no round trip to acquire, no round trip to release), cannot be left held by a crashed process, and cannot deadlock. When the invariant can be expressed as one statement or one command, atomicity is strictly better than locking.

Mental model

Imagine a turnstile at a stadium. Counting people by having a clerk look at the counter, add one on a notepad, and write it back is a race: two clerks can both read 500. A turnstile increments the count as part of the same physical motion that lets one person through. Nobody can pass without incrementing; the count can never be off by one. INCR and stock = stock - 1 are turnstiles.

How it works

For the PostgreSQL primitive, step by step:

  1. The UPDATE finds the row via the index and tries to take the row lock. If another transaction holds it (it is mid-update), this statement waits.
  2. When the lock is granted, under READ COMMITTED PostgreSQL re-evaluates the WHERE clause against the newest committed version of the row (the mechanism is called EvalPlanQual). If stock > 0 no longer holds, the row is skipped: zero rows updated.
  3. If the condition still holds, the new row version is written with stock - 1 computed from the current value, not from anything the application read earlier.
  4. RETURNING sends back the new value, so the application learns the result without a second query.
  5. Concurrent updaters serialise on the row lock, one after another, each seeing the previous one's result. No lost updates, no oversell, no lock code in your application.
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as RequestA
    participant B as RequestB
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    A->>PG: UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE sku=X AND stock > 0
    B->>PG: UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE sku=X AND stock > 0
    Note over PG: A holds the row lock, B waits
    PG-->>A: 1 row, RETURNING stock = 0
    Note over PG: B re-checks WHERE on the committed row, stock > 0 is false
    PG-->>B: 0 rows

For Redis: INCR key reads the value, adds one and writes it back inside the single command thread; no other command can run between the read and the write. For Atomics: the CPU performs the read-modify-write as one bus-locked instruction, so two worker threads incrementing the same Int32Array slot never lose an update.

Practical example

The three everyday uses:

  • Inventory: the conditional decrement above.
  • Rate limiting: INCR the key rl:{userId}:{minute}; set an expiry when the result is 1; reject when the result exceeds the limit. Round trip ~0.3 ms.
  • Idempotency claim: SET idem:{key} processing NX EX 86400; only the first of N duplicate requests gets OK and proceeds.

NestJS example

A rate limiter with an atomic INCR and expiry in one Lua script (two commands, one atomic step):

// ratelimit/rate-limit.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

// INCR and PEXPIRE must be atomic together; otherwise a crash between them leaves a key with no TTL
const INCR_WITH_TTL = `
  local c = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
  if c == 1 then redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end
  return c
`;

type RedisWithCommands = Redis & { incrWithTtl(key: string, ttlMs: number): Promise<number> };

@Injectable()
export class RateLimitService {
  private readonly redis: RedisWithCommands;

  constructor(redis: Redis) {
    redis.defineCommand('incrWithTtl', { numberOfKeys: 1, lua: INCR_WITH_TTL });   // loads once, EVALSHA after
    this.redis = redis as RedisWithCommands;
  }

  // Fixed window: at most `limit` hits per `windowMs` per subject
  async hit(subject: string, limit: number, windowMs: number): Promise<{ allowed: boolean; remaining: number }> {
    const window = Math.floor(Date.now() / windowMs);
    const count = await this.redis.incrWithTtl(`rl:${subject}:${window}`, windowMs);
    return { allowed: count <= limit, remaining: Math.max(0, limit - count) };
  }
}

(@nestjs/throttler with a Redis storage does the same thing for you; the point here is to see the atomicity.)

Counting across worker threads without a lock:

// workers/progress.ts (main thread)
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads';

const shared = new SharedArrayBuffer(2 * Int32Array.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT);
const counters = new Int32Array(shared);            // [0] = processed, [1] = failed
for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) new Worker(__dirname + '/resize.worker.js', { workerData: { counters } });
setInterval(() => console.log('processed', Atomics.load(counters, 0), 'failed', Atomics.load(counters, 1)), 1000);

// workers/resize.worker.ts
import { workerData } from 'node:worker_threads';
const counters = workerData.counters as Int32Array;   // same memory, not a copy
// after each image:
Atomics.add(counters, 0, 1);                           // safe from 4 threads at once; counters[0]++ is not

PostgreSQL example

-- THE atomic primitive: check and change in one statement
UPDATE inventory_items
SET stock = stock - 1, updated_at = now()
WHERE sku = 'SKU-1' AND stock > 0
RETURNING stock;
-- 1 row: success and the new stock. 0 rows: out of stock. Nothing else is possible.

-- atomic upsert counter (page views per product per day)
INSERT INTO product_views (product_id, day, views)
VALUES (881, current_date, 1)
ON CONFLICT (product_id, day) DO UPDATE SET views = product_views.views + 1
RETURNING views;

-- atomic claim of the next job for exactly one worker
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'RUNNING', worker = 'pod-7', started_at = now()
WHERE id = (
  SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'QUEUED' ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1
)
RETURNING *;

-- what is NOT atomic: two statements, even in a transaction, are two steps others can interleave with
-- unless you lock: SELECT stock ... FOR UPDATE; UPDATE ...

TypeORM example

// query builder form: full control of the SET expression and WHERE
const res = await this.items
  .createQueryBuilder()
  .update(InventoryItem)
  .set({ stock: () => 'stock - 1' })
  .where('sku = :sku AND stock > 0', { sku })
  .returning(['stock'])
  .execute();
if (res.affected !== 1) throw new ConflictException('OUT_OF_STOCK');
const newStock = res.raw[0].stock as number;

// repository sugar for the unconditional case, still atomic in SQL
await this.items.increment({ sku }, 'reservedCount', 1);
await this.items.decrement({ sku, stock: MoreThan(0) }, 'stock', 1);   // criteria can carry the condition

Sequelize example

const [affected] = await this.inventoryModel.update(
  { stock: this.sequelize.literal('stock - 1') },
  { where: { sku, stock: { [Op.gt]: 0 } } },
);
if (affected !== 1) throw new ConflictException('OUT_OF_STOCK');

// sugar
await this.inventoryModel.increment('reservedCount', { by: 1, where: { sku } });

Production scenario

A ticketing platform sells 20,000 seats for a concert; 300,000 requests arrive in the first minute. Each seat row gets its own conditional UPDATE, so contention is spread across 20,000 rows and the database processes ~9,000 updates per second at 40% CPU. Before the seats, a Redis DECR on a per-event counter (available:{eventId}) sheds the hopeless requests in 0.3 ms without touching PostgreSQL: when the counter is below zero, respond "sold out" immediately. Two atomic primitives, in two systems, one for speed and one for truth.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged for a Redis memory alert. Keys: 41 million. A rate limiter had been written as INCR followed by a separate EXPIRE call, and a deploy had introduced a bug that threw between the two calls for one class of users. Every one of their windows created a key that never expired. Redis hit maxmemory, and with the noeviction policy every write in the platform (sessions, carts, locks) began failing. The Lua version above cannot leave a key without a TTL, because the two commands are one atomic step. The postmortem also added maxmemory-policy volatile-lru so that a future leak evicts expiring keys before failing writes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Atomic is not durable: a Redis INCR acknowledged before fsync can be lost on a crash; use PostgreSQL for money.
  • Atomic per key is not atomic across keys; use MULTI/Lua (same-slot keys in Cluster, via hash tags {order:123}) or a database transaction.
  • Atomics work only on integer typed arrays over SharedArrayBuffer; objects still need message passing.
  • A single PostgreSQL statement is atomic, but it waits for the row lock; a hot row is a serialisation point at ~3,000 updates per second.
  • Under REPEATABLE READ, an UPDATE that finds the row changed since the snapshot fails with 40001 instead of re-evaluating; retry the transaction.
  • Replicas: reading the counter from a replica after an atomic update on the primary can show the old value for hundreds of milliseconds.
  • RETURNING on zero rows returns nothing; do not confuse "no row" with "stock was zero" if the sku might not exist. Distinguish with a second check or a CASE expression.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Their first instinct for any invariant is "can I write it as one statement?" If yes, they do, and they let the database or Redis be the referee. They reserve locks for multi-step sequences that cannot be collapsed, and transactions with FOR UPDATE for complex decisions that need application code. They choose Redis atomics for speed on data they can afford to lose and PostgreSQL atomics for truth. To a product manager: "We never count seats by looking and then writing; we use a turnstile, so the count cannot be wrong even if a hundred people push through at the same instant."

Common mistakes

  • findOne then save (read-modify-write in the application).
  • INCR and EXPIRE as separate calls.
  • MULTI/EXEC for keys in different Redis Cluster slots (it fails with CROSSSLOT).
  • Trusting a replica read immediately after an atomic write on the primary.
  • Using counters[0]++ on a SharedArrayBuffer and getting "mostly right" counts.

Interview questions

  1. Why is UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0 safe under concurrency? Expected: row lock serialises updaters; the WHERE is re-evaluated on the current committed row; the arithmetic uses the current value. Follow-up: what changes under REPEATABLE READ? (40001 and retry.)
  2. How would you implement a rate limiter with Redis, and what is the classic mistake? Expected: atomic INCR with TTL in one Lua script; the mistake is a separate EXPIRE that can be skipped.
  3. What makes a Redis command atomic? Expected: single-threaded command execution; multi-command atomicity via MULTI/EXEC or Lua.
  4. When are Atomics the right tool in Node? Expected: shared counters and flags across worker threads over SharedArrayBuffer; not for objects, not across processes.
  5. Atomicity versus durability: give a Redis example. Expected: INCR is atomic but may be lost before fsync; money belongs in PostgreSQL.

Practical exercise

Implement the rate limiter twice: GET/SET in application code, and the Lua INCR version. Fire 2,000 requests in one second with autocannon -c 200 at a limit of 1,000 per minute and count how many were allowed. Then implement the inventory decrement with RETURNING and race it as in 9.8.

Acceptance criteria: the naive limiter allows noticeably more than 1,000; the atomic one allows exactly 1,000; every key it creates has a TTL (TTL key is never -1); inventory ends at exactly zero.

9.13 Garbage collection

Concept

Garbage collection (GC) is automatic reclamation of memory that a program can no longer reach. You allocate objects freely; a collector periodically finds which objects are still reachable from the program's roots (the call stack, global variables, closures currently in scope, native handles such as open sockets and timers) and frees everything else.

Three ideas carry most of the weight:

  • Reachability, not "unused": an object is garbage only when nothing can reach it. An object you never read again but that sits in a Map is reachable, and therefore not garbage. That single sentence explains most memory leaks in Node (see 9.25).
  • Generational collection: empirically, most objects die young (a request's DTO, a query result, a JSON string), and objects that survive a while tend to survive a long time (entity metadata, caches, connection objects). So the heap is split into a small young generation collected very often and cheaply, and a large old generation collected rarely and expensively.
  • Stop-the-world pauses: while the collector moves or marks objects, JavaScript cannot run. A pause on the main thread stops every request in flight in that process, which is why GC shows up in your latency percentiles rather than in your CPU graph.

Why does it exist?

Manual memory management (malloc/free) produces the two worst bug classes in systems programming: use-after-free (reading memory that has been recycled, a security hole) and leaks from forgotten frees. GC trades a little CPU and some unpredictable pauses for the guarantee that memory safety is never the application programmer's problem. For a backend team shipping features daily, that trade is almost always right. The job is to understand the pauses well enough to keep them out of the p99.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel. Guests check in constantly (allocations). Housekeeping cannot clean a corridor while guests walk through it, so the corridor is closed for a few seconds (stop-the-world). The ground-floor rooms turn over every night (young generation): cleaning them is fast because most are empty by morning, and the staff simply carry the few remaining guests' bags to a long-stay floor (promotion). The long-stay floors (old generation) are cleaned once a week; that takes hours because every room must be checked (marking) and furniture rearranged to close gaps (compaction). A hotel that keeps every guest's luggage forever in the lobby (a cache with no eviction) makes every weekly clean longer, until the corridors are closed more than they are open.

How it works

  1. Allocation in the young generation is a pointer bump: "the next free byte is here; you get 64 bytes; the pointer is now 64 bytes further." Nanoseconds.
  2. When the young generation fills, a minor GC (a scavenge, in V8's vocabulary) runs: it walks from the roots (and from a small record of old-to-young pointers called the remembered set) and copies the live young objects to a fresh area. Everything not copied is garbage by construction. Cost is proportional to live objects, not to garbage, so a young generation full of dead request objects is collected in 1–5 ms.
  3. Objects that survive two minor collections are promoted to the old generation.
  4. When the old generation grows past a threshold, a major GC runs: mark (walk every reachable object from the roots and flag it), sweep (put unmarked space on free lists), and sometimes compact (move objects together so free space is contiguous). Cost is proportional to the size of the old generation, which is why big caches make every major GC slower.
  5. Modern collectors reduce the pause: marking is done incrementally (in small steps between your callbacks) and concurrently (on helper threads while JavaScript runs). The remaining stop-the-world part in V8 is typically tens of milliseconds on a 500 MB old generation, but hundreds of milliseconds to seconds on multi-gigabyte heaps or under CPU throttling.
  6. Write barriers keep the incremental/concurrent marking correct: every time JavaScript writes a pointer into an object, a tiny check records it so the collector does not miss an object that became reachable mid-mark. That is part of the "GC tax" on every property write.
flowchart LR
    A["new Object in request handler"] --> Y["Young generation, semi-space"]
    Y -->|"minor GC every 20-100 ms, 1-5 ms pause, copies live objects"| S{"survived twice?"}
    S -->|"no: dead, reclaimed for free"| F["Free"]
    S -->|"yes: promoted"| O["Old generation"]
    O -->|"major GC when old space grows, mark-sweep-compact, 10-500 ms pause"| M{"still reachable?"}
    M -->|"no"| F
    M -->|"yes: caches, metadata, leaks"| O

Why long GC pauses appear as p99 latency, in numbers. A service handles 800 requests per second with a median of 12 ms. Once every 30 seconds a major GC pauses the main thread for 150 ms. During those 150 ms about 120 requests are either in flight or arriving; every one of them gains up to 150 ms. That is 120 out of 24,000 requests per 30 seconds, exactly 0.5%, so the p99 is untouched but the p99.5 and p99.9 jump to ~160 ms. Halve the interval (a bigger allocation rate, or a heap twice as full) and the p99 itself moves. GC never appears in the average; it lives entirely in the tail.

Practical example

An order service's allocation profile per request: the parsed body (2 KB), DTO instances (1 KB), a TypeORM query result hydrated into entities (1 KB per row, 20 rows), the response object and its JSON string (30 KB). Roughly 60 KB of garbage per request; at 800 requests per second that is ~48 MB per second, so a 16 MB young generation fills three times per second and scavenges run every ~330 ms, each taking 1–3 ms. That is healthy. The service also holds a 300 MB in-memory product cache in the old generation. Every major GC must mark all 300 MB of it, so major pauses are 80–120 ms instead of the 15 ms they would be with the cache in Redis. The cache is "free" in CPU terms until you look at the tail.

NestJS example

Measure GC pauses in production rather than guessing. Node's perf_hooks emits an entry for every collection; prom-client's default metrics already export nodejs_gc_duration_seconds by kind, but a small observer lets you log the outliers with context.

// runtime/gc-monitor.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PerformanceObserver, constants } from 'node:perf_hooks';

const KIND: Record<number, string> = {
  [constants.NODE_PERFORMANCE_GC_MINOR]: 'minor',            // scavenge
  [constants.NODE_PERFORMANCE_GC_MAJOR]: 'major',            // mark-sweep-compact
  [constants.NODE_PERFORMANCE_GC_INCREMENTAL]: 'incremental', // marking steps
  [constants.NODE_PERFORMANCE_GC_WEAKCB]: 'weakcb',
};

@Injectable()
export class GcMonitorService implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(GcMonitorService.name);
  private observer?: PerformanceObserver;

  onModuleInit() {
    this.observer = new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
      for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
        const kind = KIND[(entry.detail as { kind: number } | undefined)?.kind ?? 0] ?? 'unknown';
        if (entry.duration > 50) {                                // log only pauses that matter to latency
          const { heapUsed, heapTotal } = process.memoryUsage();
          this.logger.warn(
            `GC ${kind} paused ${entry.duration.toFixed(1)} ms; heapUsed=${(heapUsed / 1048576).toFixed(0)}MB heapTotal=${(heapTotal / 1048576).toFixed(0)}MB`,
          );
        }
      }
    });
    this.observer.observe({ entryTypes: ['gc'] });
  }

  onModuleDestroy() {
    this.observer?.disconnect();
  }
}

Correlate the warnings with your latency histogram: if every p99.9 spike lines up with a major line, you have your answer before opening a profiler.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL has a garbage collector too, and it has the same failure modes. Under MVCC, an UPDATE does not overwrite a row; it writes a new version and leaves the old one as a dead tuple. VACUUM is the collector that reclaims dead tuples, and autovacuum is the generational heuristic: it triggers per table when dead tuples exceed autovacuum_vacuum_threshold + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor × rows (50 + 20% by default). A table with 10 million rows can accumulate 2 million dead tuples before autovacuum runs, and those dead tuples make every index scan read pages full of garbage: bloat.

-- the PostgreSQL equivalent of watching heapUsed grow
SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,
       round(100.0 * n_dead_tup / greatest(n_live_tup + n_dead_tup, 1), 1) AS dead_pct,
       last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC
LIMIT 5;
--  relname        | n_live_tup | n_dead_tup | dead_pct | last_autovacuum
--  order_events   |  48210033  |   9120455  |     15.9 | 2026-09-06 02:11:07
--  inventory_items|    812000  |    640120  |     44.1 | 2026-09-05 23:40:12   <- hot rows, updated constantly

-- more aggressive collection for a hot table, the equivalent of a smaller young generation
ALTER TABLE inventory_items SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02, autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 2);

-- what blocks the collector: long transactions hold a snapshot, so dead tuples cannot be removed
SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS age, state, left(query, 50)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 3;

The parallel is exact: a leaked reference in Node (a Map entry) and a long-open transaction in PostgreSQL (an idle-in-transaction session) both keep the collector from reclaiming what is otherwise dead. And PostgreSQL's ultimate stop-the-world is transaction ID wraparound protection: if autovacuum cannot keep up, the database eventually refuses writes until a VACUUM completes.

Production scenario

A catalog API runs 12 pods, each with a 1 GiB limit and --max-old-space-size=768. Steady state: heapUsed oscillates between 220 and 380 MB; scavenges every 200 ms at 1–2 ms; major GCs every 45 seconds at 25–40 ms. The p99 is 35 ms and the p99.9 is 70 ms; the second number is the GC. A feature adds a 400 MB in-process cache. Major GC pauses rise to 140–180 ms and, because the old generation is now near the limit, they run every 8 seconds instead of every 45. The p99 becomes 160 ms with no change to any query. Moving the cache to Redis (0.3 ms per lookup) restores the p99 to 36 ms; the "free" cache had cost 125 ms of tail latency.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged for p99 latency on the notifications API, which had been climbing for six hours. CPU was at 90% but throughput was flat. --trace-gc on one pod (attached via kill -USR1 and the inspector) showed a major GC every 1.5 seconds, each pausing 400–600 ms, each recovering almost nothing: heap 740 MB before, 735 MB after. The old generation was full of live objects, so V8 was collecting frantically and finding no garbage: the death spiral just before heap out of memory. The cause was a Map<string, Promise<Notification>> used as a "recent notifications" cache with no eviction; six hours of traffic had put 3.2 million entries in it. The full story is in 9.30. The tell-tale signature is worth memorising: frequent major GCs that reclaim little means the heap is full of reachable objects, which means a leak, not a tuning problem.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • GC pause duration scales with live old-generation size; a 2 GB heap of legitimate cache means 500 ms+ pauses whatever you tune. Big state belongs outside the process.
  • CPU throttling in Kubernetes stretches pauses: a 30 ms concurrent mark that needs three threads can be frozen by the CFS quota into a 100 ms stall (see 9.2).
  • Promotion of short-lived objects: if the young generation is too small for your allocation rate, objects that would have died young get promoted, and the old generation fills with garbage that only a major GC can reclaim. --max-semi-space-size is the knob (see 9.26).
  • Large objects (over ~128 KB) skip the young generation entirely; an endpoint that builds many big arrays pressures the major collector directly.
  • Finalizers and WeakRef cleanup run at unpredictable times; never depend on them for resource release (sockets, file handles).
  • A global.gc() call in production code (with --expose-gc) is a stop-the-world full collection; it is a debugging tool, not a fix.
  • Heap snapshots themselves pause the process for seconds on large heaps; take them on one pod pulled from the load balancer.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat the heap as a working set, not a storage tier: what lives in the old generation should be small, stable, and worth marking on every major GC. Caches with growth potential go to Redis; big result sets are streamed; per-request data is allowed to die young. They watch three signals: major GC frequency, major GC pause duration, and heap reclaimed per major GC. A change in the first two is a capacity or allocation issue; a fall in the third is a leak. They explain GC to a product manager as housekeeping: "The corridors close for a moment while the rooms are cleaned; the more luggage we keep in the lobby, the longer the corridors stay closed, so we keep the lobby empty."

Common mistakes

  • Blaming the database for p99 spikes that align perfectly with major GC events.
  • Adding an unbounded in-memory cache "because memory is cheap", then paying for it in latency.
  • Raising --max-old-space-size to "fix" a leak, which only makes the eventual pauses longer.
  • Alerting on average latency, where GC is invisible.
  • Ignoring n_dead_tup in PostgreSQL and then discovering a 10x bloated table during an incident.

Interview questions

  1. Why is GC visible in p99 but not in average latency? Expected: pauses are rare and short relative to the interval, so they affect a small fraction of requests severely; the mean barely moves while the tail jumps. Follow-up: show the arithmetic for 800 rps and a 150 ms pause every 30 s.
  2. Explain the generational hypothesis and what it buys. Expected: most objects die young; a small young generation collected by copying live objects is cheap because cost is proportional to survivors, not garbage.
  3. What is the signature of a memory leak in GC logs? Expected: increasingly frequent major GCs that reclaim little; heap-after-GC trends upward.
  4. How does a long-running transaction in PostgreSQL resemble a leaked reference in Node? Expected: both prevent the collector from reclaiming dead data (dead tuples versus unreachable-but-referenced objects).
  5. Your major GC pauses are 300 ms. Name three possible causes and the fix for each. Expected: large live heap (move state out of process), CPU throttling (raise limit), promotion of short-lived objects (larger semi-space).

Practical exercise

Run a NestJS endpoint under autocannon at 500 requests per second with --trace-gc enabled, and record the interval and pause of major collections. Then add a Map that stores each request's body forever, run for five minutes, and watch the trace change. Finally add the GcMonitorService and correlate its warnings with autocannon's p99.9.

Acceptance criteria: you can read a --trace-gc line and state heap before, heap after, and pause; you can show the "frequent major GC, little reclaimed" pattern from your own leak; and you can point to the exact latency percentile at which the GC first becomes visible.

9.14 V8: JIT, hidden classes, inline caches and deoptimisation

Concept

V8 is the JavaScript engine inside Node.js. It takes your TypeScript-compiled JavaScript and executes it through a pipeline of increasingly aggressive compilers:

  1. The parser turns source into an abstract syntax tree.
  2. Ignition, a bytecode interpreter, runs the code immediately and, while doing so, records type feedback: which kinds of values each operation actually saw.
  3. Sparkplug, a baseline compiler, turns bytecode into machine code with no optimisation, for a quick speed-up on warm code.
  4. Maglev (newer versions) and TurboFan are the JIT (just-in-time) optimising compilers. When a function is hot (called often, or looping long), they compile it into fast machine code specialised for the types the feedback has seen, guarded by checks. If a guard fails, the code deoptimises: it bails out to the interpreter and the function may be recompiled later with broader assumptions.

Two mechanisms make the specialised code fast:

  • Hidden classes (V8 calls them maps): JavaScript objects have no declared layout, so V8 invents one. Every object created the same way (same properties, added in the same order) shares a hidden class that says "property sku is at offset 8, qty at offset 16". A property read becomes "check the hidden class, load from offset 16", which is what a C struct access costs.
  • Inline caches (ICs): each property-access site (line.qty at line 42) remembers which hidden classes it has seen. One class: monomorphic, a single compare and a load, about a nanosecond. Two to four: polymorphic, a short chain of compares. More: megamorphic, a hash-table lookup on every access, 10–30× slower and impossible to inline.

"Monomorphic code is faster" therefore means: functions that always see objects of the same shape get straight-line machine code; functions that see many shapes get generic slow paths.

Why does it exist?

JavaScript is dynamically typed, and dynamic languages are slow if executed naively: every a + b must ask "what are a and b?" every time. V8's answer is to guess from what it has seen, compile for the guess, and verify with a cheap guard. This is why JavaScript is fast enough to run a 20,000-request-per-second API on one core, and also why the same code can suddenly become 10× slower when a single call site starts seeing a new kind of object.

Mental model

Imagine a waiter at a restaurant with regulars. Table 4 is always the same couple ordering the same dish; the waiter stops asking, brings the dish, and glances to confirm it is them (monomorphic call site with a guard). If four different regulars rotate through table 4, the waiter keeps a short list and checks which one it is (polymorphic). If a different stranger sits there every night, the waiter must ask from scratch every time (megamorphic). And if one night the couple orders something completely different, the waiter's shortcut was wrong; he apologises, goes back to asking (deoptimisation), and only rebuilds the shortcut once the new pattern is stable.

How it works

flowchart LR
    SRC["JavaScript source"] --> IG["Ignition bytecode interpreter, collects type feedback"]
    IG -->|"warm"| SP["Sparkplug baseline machine code"]
    SP -->|"hot, stable feedback"| TF["TurboFan or Maglev optimised code with guards"]
    TF -->|"guard fails: new shape, new type"| DE["Deoptimise back to interpreter"]
    DE --> IG
    TF -->|"guards hold"| FAST["1 ns property loads, inlined calls"]

Hidden class transitions in a pricing loop, step by step:

  1. const line = { sku: 'A1', qty: 2 } creates an object with hidden class C0 (empty), transitions to C1 (sku), then C2 (sku, qty). Every object literal written the same way ends in C2.
  2. line.discount = 0.1 on some lines transitions those to C3 (sku, qty, discount). The call site line.discount inside the loop now sees C2 and C3: polymorphic. If some lines get discount before qty, that is another class C3'. Four or more and the site goes megamorphic.
  3. delete line.discount is worse: V8 gives up on a fixed layout and switches the object to dictionary mode (a hash map). Every access on it is a hash lookup forever.
  4. Arrays have elements kinds: [1, 2, 3] is PACKED_SMI_ELEMENTS (small integers); push 1.5 and it becomes PACKED_DOUBLE_ELEMENTS; push a string or null and it becomes PACKED_ELEMENTS (generic). Leaving a hole (arr[10] = x on a length-3 array) makes it HOLEY_*. Transitions only go towards the more generic kind, and generic kinds mean slower loops.
  5. Numbers: integers that fit in 31 bits are Smis stored inline; anything else is a HeapNumber, a boxed allocation. A field that is sometimes 0 and sometimes 0.5 makes its accesses polymorphic across representations.
  6. When optimised code deoptimises, --trace-deopt prints why. After a few deopts of the same function, V8 marks it "never optimise", and it runs in the interpreter for the life of the process.
node --trace-deopt dist/main.js 2>&1 | grep -A2 priceLine | head
# [bailout (kind: deopt-eager, reason: wrong map): begin. deoptimizing priceLine, opt id 12, bytecode offset 45
#   ;;; deoptimize at <pricing.service.js:57:23>, wrong map
# (abbreviated; the real output includes addresses and frame details)

wrong map is "I compiled for hidden class C2 and saw C3". not a Smi and not a heap number are the numeric equivalents.

Practical example

A 5-million-line CSV export runs a priceLine(line) function on every row: read six properties, do arithmetic, write three. Monomorphic: ~30 ns per line, 150 ms total for the pricing step. Megamorphic (because rows come from three code paths that build the object in different orders, and one path deletes a temporary field): ~400 ns per line, 2 s. In a request handler this is invisible; in the export job it is the difference between "done" and "hit the 30-minute job timeout" once the row count grows.

For everyday NestJS CRUD, none of this matters: a request does a few thousand property accesses and waits milliseconds for I/O. V8's rules matter in hot loops over many objects: exports, batch pricing, feed ranking, in-memory joins, CSV parsing, big JSON transforms. Learn the rules, apply them there, and profile before applying them anywhere else.

NestJS example

Shape-stable objects for a hot path: a class whose constructor assigns every field, in the same order, always, with null rather than "absent" for optional values.

// pricing/priced-line.ts
export class PricedLine {
  // Every instance gets every field, in this order: one hidden class for the whole loop
  constructor(
    public readonly sku: string,
    public readonly qty: number,
    public readonly unitCents: number,
    public readonly discountBps: number,      // 0 when no discount, never undefined
    public totalCents = 0,
    public taxCents = 0,
  ) {}
}

// pricing/pricing.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PricedLine } from './priced-line';

export interface RawLine { sku: string; qty: number; unit_cents: number; discount_bps: number | null }

@Injectable()
export class PricingService {
  toPriced(raw: RawLine): PricedLine {
    // normalise at the boundary: DB nulls become 0 here, so the hot loop never sees null
    return new PricedLine(raw.sku, raw.qty, raw.unit_cents, raw.discount_bps ?? 0);
  }

  priceAll(lines: PricedLine[], taxBps: number): number {
    let grand = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < lines.length; i++) {             // plain loop: fastest, easiest for V8 to optimise
      const l = lines[i];
      const gross = l.qty * l.unitCents;
      const discount = Math.floor((gross * l.discountBps) / 10_000);
      l.totalCents = gross - discount;                    // Smi arithmetic throughout
      l.taxCents = Math.floor((l.totalCents * taxBps) / 10_000);
      grand += l.totalCents + l.taxCents;
    }
    return grand;
  }
}

Three habits are visible: normalise at the boundary, assign all fields in the constructor, never delete. And when a hot loop crosses ~50 ms of CPU, the right answer is a worker thread (9.20) regardless of how monomorphic it is.

Profile before believing any of this applies to you:

node --cpu-prof --cpu-prof-dir=./profiles dist/jobs/export.js
# open the .cpuprofile in Chrome DevTools > Performance, or use `npx speedscope profiles/*.cpuprofile`

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL has a JIT too, with the same trade-off: compilation costs time up front and only pays off on long-running work. It compiles expression evaluation and tuple deforming with LLVM when the estimated cost exceeds jit_above_cost (100,000 by default).

SHOW jit;                      -- on by default since PG 12
SHOW jit_above_cost;           -- 100000

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT customer_id, sum(total_cents * (1 - discount_bps / 10000.0))
FROM order_lines WHERE created_at > now() - interval '90 days'
GROUP BY customer_id;
--  ...
--  JIT:
--    Functions: 9
--    Options: Inlining true, Optimization true, Expressions true, Deforming true
--    Timing: Generation 1.8 ms, Inlining 12.4 ms, Optimization 61.2 ms, Emission 38.7 ms, Total 114.1 ms
--  Execution Time: 1840.2 ms

-- OLTP queries that run in 2 ms lose badly if a bad estimate triggers a 100 ms JIT compile:
ALTER ROLE orders_api SET jit = off;          -- common on OLTP roles; keep it on for the reporting role

The lesson transfers exactly: a JIT is a bet that the work is long enough to pay for the compile. For a 5-second analytical query, 114 ms of JIT is a win; for a 2 ms lookup that got a wrong cost estimate, it is a 50× regression that shows up as a mysterious p99 spike.

TypeORM example

Result objects from TypeORM are shape-stable per query: getRawMany() builds every row with the same keys in the same order, and entities come from the same class constructor. Shapes diverge when the same processing function receives rows from different queries with different select lists. Keep one query per hot path, or map to a class at the boundary as above.

// one select list for the export, always the same columns in the same order
const stream = await this.dataSource
  .createQueryBuilder()
  .select(['ol.sku AS sku', 'ol.qty AS qty', 'ol.unit_cents AS unit_cents', 'ol.discount_bps AS discount_bps'])
  .from('order_lines', 'ol')
  .where('ol.order_id >= :from AND ol.order_id < :to', { from, to })
  .stream();
// map each raw row with pricing.toPriced() before the hot loop

Production scenario

A marketplace's "seller settlement" job prices 40 million order lines nightly. Written as rows.map(r => ({ ...r, total: ... })) over rows from four different repositories, the job ran 38 minutes, with --cpu-prof showing 70% of the time in a megamorphic total computation and in spread-copying objects. Rewritten with a single PricedLine class and a for loop, it ran in 9 minutes; moved into four worker threads, in 3 minutes. The order of those two changes matters: parallelising megamorphic code four ways still costs four cores for 10 minutes.

Failure scenario

At 05:40 the on-call was paged: the nightly settlement job had exceeded its 30-minute deadline for the first time. Nothing in the query plans had changed. A refactor two days earlier had added, in the per-line function, delete line.internalFlag to avoid leaking an internal field into the output. That one line switched 40 million objects to dictionary mode and made every subsequent property access a hash lookup. Runtime went from 9 to 41 minutes. The fix was to never put internalFlag on the hot object in the first place (map to PricedLine at the boundary), and the postmortem added a runtime budget alert at 15 minutes so a 4× regression pages someone at a sensible hour.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Generic utility functions (get(obj, path), generic serialisers, class-transformer) are megamorphic by nature; that is fine, just do not put them inside a hot loop.
  • Passing objects with optional fields (discount?: number) creates shape families; prefer null defaults set in one place.
  • Object.assign/spread in a loop creates new objects per iteration; allocation, not shape, becomes the cost.
  • Functions too large to inline or with try/catch around hot code used to be deopt hazards; modern V8 handles both, so profile rather than folklore.
  • Mixed int/double in the same field or array forces HeapNumber boxing.
  • arguments, eval, with still block optimisation.
  • Cold-start cost: right after deploy, every hot function runs in the interpreter for a while; the first seconds of a pod's life are 2–5× slower. Warm up before adding a pod to the load balancer if p99 during rollouts matters.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know that 95% of backend code is I/O-bound and that V8 optimisation folklore is a distraction there. They keep the rules for the 5%: stable shapes, boundary normalisation, plain loops, typed arrays for numeric crunching, workers for anything over ~50 ms. They profile with --cpu-prof before and after every "optimisation", and they explain to a product manager that the engine learns patterns and rewards consistency, so "the export got slow because we started building each row a little differently".

Common mistakes

  • Micro-optimising request handlers where 98% of the time is a database wait.
  • delete on hot objects.
  • Different construction paths producing the "same" object type with different property orders.
  • Using undefined and null and "absent" interchangeably for the same field.
  • Treating --trace-deopt noise from startup (hundreds of harmless deopts while feedback stabilises) as a problem.

Interview questions

  1. What is a hidden class and why does property order matter? Expected: V8's inferred layout for objects; different addition orders create different classes; call sites seeing many classes become megamorphic and slow.
  2. Explain monomorphic, polymorphic and megamorphic inline caches with a backend example. Expected: one shape, up to four, many; pricing loop over rows built by different code paths.
  3. What causes a deoptimisation and what happens afterwards? Expected: a guard fails (new shape or type); V8 returns to bytecode and may reoptimise; repeated deopts disable optimisation for that function.
  4. When does V8 performance actually matter in a NestJS service? Expected: hot loops over many objects (exports, batch jobs); not in ordinary I/O-bound handlers. Follow-up: how do you prove it? (--cpu-prof.)
  5. What does PostgreSQL's JIT have in common with V8's, and when do you turn it off? Expected: compile-cost versus runtime trade; turn off for OLTP roles where misestimated costs cause compile spikes.

Practical exercise

Write priceAll twice: once with PricedLine, once with objects built in three different property orders and a delete. Run each over 5 million generated lines with performance.now() timing and --trace-deopt. Then profile the slow one with --cpu-prof.

Acceptance criteria: a measured speed difference of at least 3×, a wrong map line from the trace, and a profile screenshot or summary identifying the megamorphic access.

9.15 The call stack

Concept

The call stack is the per-thread stack region from 9.3 as seen from JavaScript: a last-in-first-out list of frames, one per function call in progress. Calling a function pushes a frame holding its arguments, local variables and the return address; returning pops it. The stack trace you see on an error is a walk down this list.

V8 limits the JavaScript stack to about 984 KB on 64-bit systems (--stack-size, in KB), independent of the operating system's 8 MB thread stack. Depending on frame size that is roughly 10,000–15,000 nested calls. Exceeding it throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, which in a NestJS app becomes an HTTP 500 for that request, or, if it happens outside a request context, a crash.

An important property of async code: every await continuation starts on an empty stack. The event loop calls it fresh. So recursion through await does not deepen the stack (but it can loop forever), and a stack trace after an await shows at async OrdersService.place reconstructed by V8's async stack traces rather than real frames.

Why does it exist?

Function calls need somewhere to keep their state, and a stack is the cheapest possible structure for it: allocation is a pointer move, deallocation is free, and locality is perfect. The size limit exists so that runaway recursion produces an error in milliseconds rather than consuming all memory over minutes.

Mental model

Imagine a clerk answering a question that requires asking a colleague, who must ask another colleague. Each unanswered question is a sticky note on a spike; the answer comes back only when the top note is resolved. If a question leads to itself ("to know the parent's price, ask the child; to know the child's price, ask the parent"), notes pile up until the spike is full and the clerk gives up: stack overflow. await is the clerk putting the note in a tray, going home, and picking up the tray in the morning with an empty spike.

How it works

Stack during a NestJS request (top = most recent):

  PostgresQueryRunner.query          <- about to await the socket
  SelectQueryBuilder.getMany
  Repository.find
  OrdersService.list                 <- your code
  OrdersController.list              <- your code
  RouterProxy.handler                 (NestJS)
  Layer.handle / next                 (Express router)
  Server.emit 'request'               (Node http)
  parserOnIncoming                    (llhttp callback)
  <event loop: poll phase>            (libuv, C++)
  1. Each frame holds arguments, locals, and the return address. Frame size depends on the number of locals; big functions mean fewer frames fit.
  2. Error captures the stack at construction: walking frames costs time, so V8 limits it to Error.stackTraceLimit (10) frames by default. Throwing thousands of errors per second in a hot path costs measurable CPU; raise the limit only in development.
  3. When the handler awaits, the whole stack above the event loop unwinds. The continuation is a closure holding the locals; the frames are gone. Memory for 10,000 suspended requests is 10,000 small closures, not 10,000 stacks.
  4. Calling a function with a huge argument list (Math.max(...ids)) pushes every argument onto the stack; with ~100,000+ elements this alone overflows it.
  5. Overflow throws RangeError. V8 leaves a small reserve so that catch blocks can run; you can catch it, but you cannot do much in the catch block without overflowing again.

Practical example

The four ways backend code actually hits the limit:

Pattern Where it appears Fix
Recursive walk of a tree with a cycle in the data category trees, org charts, comment threads, where a bad row points at itself iterative walk with a visited set and a depth cap; a database CHECK and cycle-safe recursive CTE
Spreading a huge array into arguments Math.max(...orderIds), arr.push(...millionRows) a loop, reduce, or Array.prototype.concat
Serialising a circular object graph ClassSerializerInterceptor on entities with bidirectional relations loaded (order.lines[0].order) @Exclude() on back-references, DTOs instead of entities, or relations only one way
Synchronous re-entrant emit an EventEmitter listener that emits the same event setImmediate/queue instead of recursion

NestJS example

A category tree that cannot overflow, no matter what the data looks like:

// catalog/category-tree.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Category } from './category.entity';

export interface CategoryNode { id: number; name: string; children: CategoryNode[] }

@Injectable()
export class CategoryTreeService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(CategoryTreeService.name);
  private static readonly MAX_DEPTH = 32;

  constructor(@InjectRepository(Category) private readonly categories: Repository<Category>) {}

  async build(): Promise<CategoryNode[]> {
    const rows = await this.categories.find({ select: { id: true, name: true, parentId: true } }); // one query, no recursion in SQL
    const byId = new Map<number, CategoryNode>(rows.map((r) => [r.id, { id: r.id, name: r.name, children: [] }]));
    const roots: CategoryNode[] = [];

    // Link parents iteratively: no recursion, one pass
    for (const r of rows) {
      const node = byId.get(r.id)!;
      const parent = r.parentId === null ? undefined : byId.get(r.parentId);
      if (!parent || r.parentId === r.id) roots.push(node);      // self-parent or missing parent becomes a root
      else parent.children.push(node);
    }

    // Detect cycles with an explicit stack instead of the call stack
    const seen = new Set<number>();
    const stack: Array<{ node: CategoryNode; depth: number }> = roots.map((node) => ({ node, depth: 0 }));
    while (stack.length > 0) {
      const { node, depth } = stack.pop()!;
      if (seen.has(node.id)) { this.logger.error(`cycle detected at category ${node.id}`); node.children = []; continue; }
      if (depth > CategoryTreeService.MAX_DEPTH) { this.logger.error(`depth cap hit at category ${node.id}`); node.children = []; continue; }
      seen.add(node.id);
      for (const child of node.children) stack.push({ node: child, depth: depth + 1 });
    }
    return roots;
  }
}

And the serialisation trap, which produces RangeError inside ClassSerializerInterceptor when both sides of a relation are loaded:

// orders/order-line.entity.ts
import { Entity, ManyToOne, PrimaryGeneratedColumn } from 'typeorm';
import { Exclude } from 'class-transformer';
import { Order } from './order.entity';

@Entity('order_lines')
export class OrderLine {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id: number;

  @Exclude()                                 // never serialise the back-reference: it points at the parent, which points here
  @ManyToOne(() => Order, (o) => o.lines)
  order: Order;
}

Returning DTOs mapped from entities avoids the problem entirely and is the senior default.

PostgreSQL example

Push tree walks into the database with a recursive CTE, and make the database refuse cycles:

-- the data-level guard: a category cannot be its own parent
ALTER TABLE categories ADD CONSTRAINT category_not_self_parent CHECK (parent_id IS NULL OR parent_id <> id);

-- PG 14+: CYCLE clause stops the recursion when a path repeats, instead of running forever
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT id, name, parent_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM categories WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.name, c.parent_id, t.depth + 1
  FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id
  WHERE t.depth < 32                                    -- depth cap, belt and braces
)
CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT id, name, depth, is_cycle FROM tree ORDER BY path;

-- PostgreSQL has its own stack limit for deeply nested expressions and recursive functions
SHOW max_stack_depth;    -- 2MB; "stack depth limit exceeded" is the SQL cousin of RangeError

TypeORM example

For real hierarchies, TypeORM's tree entities (@Tree('closure-table') or 'materialized-path') with TreeRepository avoid recursion in both SQL and JavaScript:

@Entity()
@Tree('materialized-path')
export class Category {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id: number;
  @Column() name: string;
  @TreeChildren() children: Category[];
  @TreeParent() parent: Category;
}

// service
const tree = await this.dataSource.getTreeRepository(Category).findTrees({ depth: 8 });   // depth-bounded

Production scenario

A comment-thread endpoint on a social feature renders nested replies recursively. Threads rarely exceed depth 20, but a bot created a 12,000-deep reply chain in one night. Each request for that thread threw RangeError after 400 ms of recursion, and because the exception filter logged the full stack of 10 frames plus the error, the logs were harmless. The real cost was the 400 ms of wasted CPU on every hit as crawlers found the URL: 15% of the event loop on one pod for a page that always 500ed. Depth-capped iterative rendering, plus a maximum reply depth enforced at write time, ended it.

Failure scenario

At 09:02 every request to GET /categories returned 500 with RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. A data-fix script the night before had set parent_id = id on one category to "detach" it. The recursive tree builder followed the self-loop until the stack overflowed. The home page depends on the category tree, so the site's most-visited page was down for 25 minutes. Three fixes shipped: the CHECK constraint above (so the bad row is impossible), the iterative builder with cycle detection (so bad data degrades to a log line), and a cached tree in Redis with a 5-minute TTL (so the home page does not rebuild the tree per request anyway).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Raising --stack-size above what the OS thread actually provides causes a segmentation fault instead of a RangeError; on worker threads the limit is resourceLimits.stackSizeMb (default 4).
  • JSON.stringify on a circular object throws TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON, not RangeError; class-transformer recurses and does hit RangeError.
  • Deeply nested JSON input (a malicious 100,000-level array) can overflow parsers or serialisers; limit body size and nesting depth at the edge.
  • Error.stackTraceLimit = Infinity in production makes every thrown error expensive.
  • Async recursion (async function retry() { ... return retry(); }) does not overflow the stack; it can loop forever with no error at all, which is worse.
  • Catching RangeError and retrying "later" rarely helps; the same data overflows again.
  • Source maps (--enable-source-maps) make stack traces point at TypeScript lines at a startup and per-error cost; keep them for readability, but know they exist when profiling error-heavy paths.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat recursion over data as a smell: data comes from users and databases, and it will one day contain a cycle or a depth nobody expected. They write iterative walks with explicit stacks, cap depth, validate structure at write time with constraints, and let the database do hierarchies with CTEs or tree tables. They never return entities with bidirectional relations straight from a controller. To a product manager: "The system follows a chain of links one step at a time; if the chain loops back on itself, it must notice and stop, rather than following the loop until it falls over."

Common mistakes

  • Recursive tree builders with no depth cap.
  • Math.max(...bigArray) and push(...bigArray).
  • Loading both sides of a relation and serialising the entity.
  • Assuming async recursion is "safe" because it does not overflow.
  • Reading a truncated 10-frame stack trace and missing the real origin; log the error's cause chain.

Interview questions

  1. Why does Math.max(...ids) throw RangeError for 200,000 ids? Expected: spread pushes every element as an argument onto the stack; the stack overflows before the function runs.
  2. Why is a stack trace after an await short, and how does V8 show the async caller? Expected: continuations run from an empty stack; async stack traces reconstruct at async frames from promise chains.
  3. How would you render an arbitrarily deep comment thread safely? Expected: iterative traversal with an explicit stack, depth cap, and a write-time maximum depth; or a recursive CTE with CYCLE.
  4. Why can a NestJS controller returning an entity throw RangeError? Expected: ClassSerializerInterceptor recurses through circular relations; fix with @Exclude() or DTOs.
  5. What is the difference between RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded and PostgreSQL's stack depth limit exceeded? Expected: both are recursion limits; V8's --stack-size versus max_stack_depth; both should be fixed by removing the recursion rather than raising the limit.

Practical exercise

Insert a self-referencing category and hit a naive recursive tree endpoint; capture the error and its CPU cost. Replace it with the iterative builder and the CHECK constraint; confirm the constraint rejects the bad row. Then reproduce RangeError through ClassSerializerInterceptor with a bidirectional relation and fix it with @Exclude().

Acceptance criteria: the naive endpoint 500s with RangeError; the constraint makes the bad data impossible; the iterative endpoint returns a tree with the cycle logged; the serialisation case is reproduced and fixed with the @Exclude() diff shown.

9.16 The event loop

Concept

The event loop is the program that runs your program. It is a loop inside libuv, on the main thread, that repeatedly asks the kernel "what is ready?" and runs the JavaScript callbacks for whatever is: an incoming HTTP request, a PostgreSQL response, a timer that has expired, a file read that finished. Your NestJS controllers, services, guards and interceptors all run inside callbacks invoked by this loop. When no callback is running, the loop is blocked in the kernel waiting for events, costing nothing.

Each turn of the loop visits a fixed sequence of phases, each with its own queue of callbacks:

  1. timers: callbacks of setTimeout and setInterval whose time has come.
  2. pending callbacks: I/O callbacks deferred from the previous turn (for example certain TCP error reports).
  3. idle, prepare: internal bookkeeping.
  4. poll: wait for I/O events and run their callbacks: socket data, connection accepted, file read completed, DNS lookup returned. This is where the loop sleeps when there is nothing to do, and where almost all of a web server's work happens.
  5. check: setImmediate callbacks.
  6. close callbacks: socket.on('close') and similar.

And one rule that matters more than the phases: after every single callback, Node drains the process.nextTick queue completely, then the promise microtask queue completely, before running the next callback. await continuations, .then handlers and queueMicrotask all run there.

Why does it exist?

A thread-per-request server spends its life switching threads (9.2). The event loop replaces that with one thread and a list of things to do, fed by the kernel's readiness notification. The result is that a single process serves thousands of concurrent connections with no locks and no context switches between requests. The price is a hard rule: no callback may run for long, because while one runs, every other request in the process waits.

Mental model

Imagine an air-traffic controller with one radio. She works from a rotating clipboard of lists: scheduled departures (timers), planes reporting in (poll), things to do right after the current call (nextTick and promises), and things to do after the current sweep of the lists (setImmediate). She handles each radio call quickly and moves on. If one pilot keeps her on the radio for five minutes (a synchronous 5-second computation), every other plane circles. Nothing about the clipboard is slow; it only breaks when one call is long.

How it works

flowchart TB
    T["timers: expired setTimeout and setInterval"] --> P["pending callbacks: deferred I/O errors"]
    P --> I["idle, prepare: internal"]
    I --> L["poll: epoll_wait, then run I/O callbacks: HTTP requests, pg responses, fs results"]
    L --> C["check: setImmediate callbacks"]
    C --> X["close callbacks: socket close"]
    X -->|"loop alive: handles or pending requests"| T
    X -->|"nothing left"| E["process exits"]
    M["after EVERY callback: drain nextTick queue, then promise microtasks, repeat until both empty"]
  1. libuv updates its notion of "now" once per turn (so all timers in one turn agree on the time).
  2. timers: for each timer whose deadline is at or before now, run its callback (then drain microtasks). setTimeout(fn, 0) is really 1 ms; timers are a lower bound, never a schedule.
  3. poll: libuv computes how long it may block: zero if setImmediate callbacks are queued or handles are closing; otherwise the time until the nearest timer; or forever if there are no timers. It calls epoll_wait with that timeout. When it returns, each ready descriptor's callback runs (then microtasks). An HTTP request arrives here; a pg response is parsed here.
  4. check: all setImmediate callbacks queued so far run (then microtasks after each).
  5. close callbacks, then the loop asks "am I alive?": are there active handles (a listening server, open sockets, referenced timers) or pending requests (an in-flight file read)? If not, the process exits. A setInterval for metrics keeps a process alive forever unless you unref() it.

The ordering rules, with exact output. Inside an I/O callback the order is fully deterministic:

// ordering.ts - run with: node ordering.js
import { readFile } from 'node:fs';

readFile(__filename, () => {
  console.log('A: inside readFile callback (poll phase)');
  setTimeout(() => console.log('F: setTimeout 0 (timers phase, next turn)'), 0);
  setImmediate(() => {
    console.log('D: setImmediate (check phase, this turn)');
    process.nextTick(() => console.log('E: nextTick queued inside setImmediate'));
  });
  process.nextTick(() => console.log('B: nextTick (drained right after this callback)'));
  Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C: promise then (after the nextTick queue)'));
  console.log('A2: end of the callback');
});
A: inside readFile callback (poll phase)
A2: end of the callback
B: nextTick (drained right after this callback)
C: promise then (after the nextTick queue)
D: setImmediate (check phase, this turn)
E: nextTick queued inside setImmediate
F: setTimeout 0 (timers phase, next turn)

Why: the callback runs to completion (A, A2). Node drains nextTicks (B) then promises (C). The poll phase is over and immediates are pending, so the loop goes to check (D), and after that callback drains its nextTick (E). The next turn begins with timers (F). This is the rule to remember: from inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always runs before setTimeout(0).

From the main module, the same two lines are non-deterministic:

setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0);
setImmediate(() => console.log('immediate'));
// Sometimes "timeout, immediate", sometimes "immediate, timeout":
// if the loop starts less than 1 ms after these lines ran, the timer is not yet due when the timers
// phase runs, so the poll phase is entered, then check (immediate), then timers on the next turn.

And the microtask drain happens between every callback, not between phases (Node 11 and later):

setTimeout(() => { console.log('T1'); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('T1 micro')); }, 0);
setTimeout(() => { console.log('T2'); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('T2 micro')); }, 0);
// T1, T1 micro, T2, T2 micro

One more rule that surprises people: awaiting an already-resolved promise does not yield to I/O. It only yields to other microtasks.

for (let i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) {
  await Promise.resolve();      // one microtask hop per iteration; the poll phase never runs during this loop
}
// HTTP requests, pg responses and timers all wait until the loop finishes.
// To yield to I/O, await a macrotask:
import { setImmediate as yieldToLoop } from 'node:timers/promises';
await yieldToLoop();

Practical example

A request's life across the phases: the connection is accepted in poll; the request bytes are parsed in poll; your controller runs inside that poll callback; await repository.find() sends the query and returns to the loop; the loop serves other requests; the response bytes arrive in a later poll phase; the pg driver resolves the promise; your continuation runs in the microtask drain right after that poll callback; the response is written; socket.on('close') fires in close callbacks when the client disconnects. A setTimeout for a retry runs in timers; a chunked batch job that await setImmediate()s between chunks runs one chunk per turn in check, with every other phase served in between.

Which primitive to use:

Need Use Runs
Run after the current operation, before any I/O (emit an event after the constructor returns) process.nextTick before promises, before the loop continues
Same, but respect promise ordering, or you are in a library that must be platform-neutral queueMicrotask / Promise.resolve().then after nextTicks, before the loop continues
Yield to I/O between chunks of CPU work await setImmediate() from timers/promises check phase, after poll
Delay by at least N ms (retry backoff, debounce) setTimeout timers phase, N ms is a lower bound
Recurring background work setInterval with .unref() if it must not keep the process alive timers phase

NestJS example

Cooperative chunking: a reindex job that would otherwise hold the loop for 2 seconds, rewritten to run in 5 ms slices so that HTTP requests are served between slices.

// search/reindex.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { setImmediate as yieldToLoop } from 'node:timers/promises';
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks';

@Injectable()
export class ReindexService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(ReindexService.name);

  async reindex(products: Array<{ id: number; name: string; tags: string[] }>) {
    const CHUNK = 200;                                 // ~5 ms of CPU per chunk on this workload
    const started = performance.now();
    let cpuMs = 0;

    for (let i = 0; i < products.length; i += CHUNK) {
      const t0 = performance.now();
      this.indexChunk(products.slice(i, i + CHUNK));   // synchronous CPU work
      cpuMs += performance.now() - t0;
      await yieldToLoop();                             // check phase: every pending I/O callback runs before we continue
    }

    this.logger.log(
      `reindexed ${products.length} products: ${cpuMs.toFixed(0)} ms CPU over ${(performance.now() - started).toFixed(0)} ms wall`,
    );
  }

  private indexChunk(chunk: Array<{ id: number; name: string; tags: string[] }>) {
    for (const p of chunk) this.tokenise(p.name, p.tags);
  }

  private tokenise(name: string, tags: string[]) { /* build inverted index entries */ }
}

Total CPU is unchanged; the maximum delay any other request sees drops from 2,000 ms to about 5 ms. For work beyond a few hundred milliseconds total, or work that must not compete with requests at all, use a worker thread (9.20).

PostgreSQL example

Timeouts live in two places, and the event loop decides which one you can trust. pg's query_timeout is a JavaScript timer: it can only fire when the loop reaches the timers phase. PostgreSQL's statement_timeout runs in the backend process and does not care whether your loop is blocked.

// database.module.ts (TypeORM extra options are passed to pg)
extra: {
  statement_timeout: 10_000,   // server-side: the backend cancels the query at 10 s, always
  query_timeout: 12_000,       // client-side: a JS timer; fires late if the loop is busy, never early
  idle_in_transaction_session_timeout: 30_000,
},

If the loop is blocked for 4 seconds by a big JSON.parse, a query that started just before will show as 14 seconds of "database latency" from the application's point of view, while pg_stat_statements shows 2 ms. Measuring latency in JavaScript measures the event loop as much as the database.

TypeORM example

TypeORM's maxQueryExecutionTime logs queries whose wall time, measured in JavaScript, exceeds a threshold. That wall time includes loop delays, pool waits and GC pauses.

TypeOrmModule.forRoot({ /* ... */ maxQueryExecutionTime: 1000, logging: ['warn'] });
// "query is slow: SELECT ... execution time: 1432" may mean the loop was busy, not the query.
// Cross-check with pg_stat_statements.mean_exec_time before blaming the database.

Sequelize example

Sequelize's benchmark: true passes the same JavaScript-measured duration to the logging function; the same caveat applies.

SequelizeModule.forRoot({ /* ... */ benchmark: true, logging: (sql, ms) => { if (ms && ms > 1000) logger.warn(`${ms} ms: ${sql}`); } });

Production scenario

A rides API runs one process per pod. Its event loop utilisation (performance.eventLoopUtilization()), which is the fraction of time the loop spends running callbacks rather than waiting, sits at 0.35 at 600 requests per second. At 1,400 requests per second it reaches 0.8, and p99 climbs from 30 ms to 140 ms with the database untouched: requests are queueing for the loop. The autoscaler was keyed to CPU, which read 55% because the libuv and GC threads made the process look less busy than its loop was. Switching the scaling signal to loop utilisation (target 0.6) fixed the p99 and, as a bonus, cut the pod count at night.

// runtime/loop-utilization.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Interval } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { performance, EventLoopUtilization } from 'node:perf_hooks';
import { Gauge } from 'prom-client';

@Injectable()
export class LoopUtilizationService {
  private last: EventLoopUtilization = performance.eventLoopUtilization();
  private readonly gauge = new Gauge({ name: 'nodejs_eventloop_utilization', help: '0..1 busy fraction' });

  @Interval(5_000)
  sample() {
    const now = performance.eventLoopUtilization();
    this.gauge.set(performance.eventLoopUtilization(now, this.last).utilization);   // delta over the last 5 s
    this.last = now;
  }
}

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged: one pod of the payments API was failing its liveness probe every 40 seconds and restarting, over and over. CPU on the pod was 100% on one core. A metrics client library had been configured to "retry immediately" on send failure, implemented as process.nextTick(() => this.flush()). The metrics sink was down. Every flush failed and queued another nextTick, and because the nextTick queue is drained completely before the loop continues, the loop never reached the poll phase again: no HTTP, no health check, no database responses, forever. Kubernetes killed the pod, the new pod connected to the same dead sink, and the cycle repeated. The fix was a setTimeout backoff (a timer yields to every phase) and a bounded retry count. Recursive nextTick is the one way to hang an idle Node process with zero I/O.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • setTimeout(fn, 0) is clamped to 1 ms; timers with the same deadline run in insertion order; a timer can fire late by however long the loop was busy, never early.
  • setInterval drifts: if a callback takes longer than the interval, invocations are not queued up, but the schedule slides. For precise schedules use @nestjs/schedule cron with idempotent jobs, not accumulated intervals.
  • Unhandled promise rejections are processed at the end of the microtask drain; since Node 15 the default is to throw, which crashes the process. Every fire-and-forget promise needs a .catch.
  • A long synchronous callback delays every phase, including timers that were due, statement_timeout-style client timers, health checks, and graceful-shutdown signal handlers (signals are delivered to the loop as events).
  • unref()'d timers do not keep the process alive; a cron-only worker with nothing else referenced exits immediately.
  • Callbacks scheduled from a worker thread run on the worker's loop; each worker has its own event loop.
  • await in a for loop over an array of already-resolved values is a microtask storm that starves I/O; batch and yield.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They see the loop as the one shared resource in the process and budget it like money: no callback over a few milliseconds, CPU work chunked or moved to workers, timers treated as lower bounds, and loop utilisation and lag on the dashboard next to latency. They scale on loop utilisation, not on CPU percent. They know the ordering rules cold, because they explain "the timeout fired late", "the health check failed while the pod was fine" and "the event was emitted before anyone listened". To a product manager: "One controller handles every plane; we keep every radio call under a few milliseconds so nobody circles."

Common mistakes

  • Blocking the loop with synchronous work and then blaming the database for the resulting timeouts.
  • Using setTimeout as a scheduling guarantee.
  • Recursive process.nextTick or a tight await Promise.resolve() loop.
  • Scaling on CPU percent when the loop is the bottleneck.
  • Forgetting .catch on background promises and discovering the process exits on the first rejection.

Interview questions

  1. List the phases of the event loop and say where an HTTP request is handled. Expected: timers, pending, idle/prepare, poll, check, close; requests and most I/O in poll; microtasks drained after every callback.
  2. Inside an I/O callback, in what order do setTimeout(0), setImmediate, process.nextTick and Promise.then run? Expected: nextTick, promise, setImmediate, setTimeout; explain why each. Follow-up: and from the main module? (setTimeout versus setImmediate is non-deterministic.)
  3. Why does await Promise.resolve() in a loop not let HTTP requests through? Expected: microtasks drain fully before the loop advances; only a macrotask (setImmediate) yields to the poll phase.
  4. A setTimeout(fn, 5000) fires after 9 seconds. Name the causes. Expected: loop blocked by synchronous work, CPU throttling, GC pauses, a microtask or nextTick flood.
  5. How would you decide whether a service needs more pods? Expected: event loop utilisation or lag, not CPU percent, because helper threads inflate CPU while the loop is the bottleneck.
  6. What keeps a Node process alive, and how do you let it exit? Expected: active handles and requests; unref() timers and close servers and sockets.

Practical exercise

Reproduce the three ordering examples and confirm the output. Then write a request handler that runs 500 ms of synchronous CPU, load it at 20 requests per second, and measure the latency of a separate trivial endpoint on the same process. Rewrite with await setImmediate() chunking and measure again. Finally implement the nextTick starvation and watch the health check fail.

Acceptance criteria: exact printed output for each example with a one-line explanation per line; a before/after latency table for the trivial endpoint showing the chunking effect; and a demonstration that setTimeout backoff instead of nextTick lets the health check respond.

9.17 Microtasks and macrotasks

Concept

A macrotask (or just "task") is one callback from one of the loop's phases: a timer firing, an I/O completion, a setImmediate, a close event. A microtask is a piece of work that must run before the loop moves on to the next macrotask: a promise reaction (.then, .catch, .finally, the continuation after an await), a queueMicrotask callback, and, in Node, a process.nextTick callback.

Node keeps two microtask queues and drains them in a fixed order after every macrotask: first the whole nextTick queue, then the whole promise queue, and it repeats until both are empty. Microtasks queued by microtasks run in the same drain. The loop does not advance until the drain is finished, which is why microtasks are both a precise ordering tool and a starvation hazard.

Why does it exist?
