  3. What is a zombie process and how does one appear in a container? Expected: an exited child not yet reaped; in containers, Node as PID 1 not reaping orphaned grandchildren — fix with tini or --init.
  4. Your pod is OOMKilled but Node's heap is 180 MB. What happened? Expected: child processes count against the cgroup; measure container RSS, not heap.
  5. Worker thread or child process for ffmpeg? Expected: child process — it is not JavaScript, and you want a separate crash and memory domain.
  6. How do you shut down cleanly with children running? Expected: on SIGTERM, stop accepting work, signal children, wait with a deadline, escalate to SIGKILL, then exit within the grace period.

Practical exercise

Write a service endpoint that converts an uploaded image with ffmpeg. Implement it first with exec and a template literal, and demonstrate injection with a crafted filename in a local sandbox only. Then rewrite with execFile plus an allowlist and confirm the attack fails. Add a 10-second timeout with SIGTERM then SIGKILL escalation, and prove it by running a deliberately long conversion.

Acceptance criteria: evidence of the injection in the vulnerable version and its failure in the fixed one; a demonstration that output larger than 1 MB kills the exec version and streams fine with spawn; and a shutdown test showing no orphaned ffmpeg process remains after the parent exits.

9.22 Cluster and process-level scaling

Concept

The cluster module forks N copies of your Node process — one per CPU core, typically — and lets them share a single listening port. Incoming connections are distributed across the workers, so a machine with 8 cores runs 8 event loops instead of 1.

The mechanism has two variants. In the default round-robin mode on Linux, the primary process owns the listening socket, calls accept() and hands each connection descriptor to a worker over IPC. In SCHED_NONE mode (and natively on Windows), all workers share the listening socket and the kernel wakes one. Modern kernels also offer SO_REUSEPORT, where each worker opens its own listening socket on the same port and the kernel hashes the connection's 4-tuple to pick one — which avoids both the primary bottleneck and the "thundering herd" of every worker waking for one connection.

PM2 is the popular process manager that wraps this: pm2 start dist/main.js -i max runs cluster mode with restarts, log aggregation and zero-downtime reloads.

Why does it exist?

One Node process uses one core for JavaScript. On a bare 16-core server, that wastes 15 cores. Before containers were the default deployment unit, cluster was the answer: one machine, one port, N processes.

Mental model

Imagine a shop with one till and a queue out of the door. cluster opens seven more tills in the same shop, with one manager directing customers to whichever till is free. Kubernetes replicas are different: seven separate shops, each with its own till, and a sign outside directing customers between shops. The second arrangement is more robust — a fire in one shop does not close the others — and it is the one the modern world is built around.

How it works

flowchart TB
    LB["Load balancer or kube-proxy"] --> P["Primary process: owns listen socket"]
    P -->|"pass fd over IPC, round robin"| W1["Worker 1: own loop and heap"]
    P --> W2["Worker 2"]
    P --> W3["Worker 3"]
    P --> W4["Worker 4"]
    W1 --> DB["PostgreSQL: each worker has its own pool"]
    W2 --> DB
    W3 --> DB
    W4 --> DB
  1. The primary calls cluster.fork() N times. Each worker is a full Node process with its own heap, event loop, libuv pool and connection pools.
  2. The primary binds the port and accepts connections; round-robin hands each new connection's descriptor to a worker.
  3. Workers do not share memory. An in-process cache in worker 3 is invisible to worker 5. Any shared state must go to Redis or PostgreSQL.
  4. If a worker dies, the primary is notified and can fork a replacement.
// cluster-example.ts - the shape, for a VM deployment
import cluster from 'node:cluster';
import { cpus } from 'node:os';

if (cluster.isPrimary) {
  const n = cpus().length;
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) cluster.fork();
  cluster.on('exit', (worker, code, signal) => {
    console.error(`worker ${worker.process.pid} died (${signal ?? code}); forking replacement`);
    cluster.fork();          // supervise, or a crash loop silently reduces capacity
  });
} else {
  await bootstrap();          // your normal NestFactory.create + listen
}

The production point: one process per container

In Kubernetes, run one Node process per container and let replicas do the scaling. This is the default you should need a specific reason to deviate from. The reasoning:

  • The scheduler already does this. A pod with limits.cpu: 1 gets one core's worth of CFS quota. Running 4 cluster workers inside it means 4 event loops splitting one core, with more context switching and no more throughput.
  • Restart granularity. A crashing worker inside a container is invisible to Kubernetes: the pod stays Running while capacity quietly halves. A crashing pod is visible, restarted, counted in metrics, and eventually escalates to CrashLoopBackOff where a human is alerted.
  • Health checks. A liveness probe hits one port. With cluster, the probe may be served by a healthy worker while another is wedged, so the pod passes while a quarter of requests fail.
  • Memory budgeting. Four workers times 512 MB of heap in a 1 GiB pod is an OOMKill waiting to happen. One process, one --max-old-space-size, one number to reason about (9.26).
  • Connection multiplication. Each worker opens its own PostgreSQL pool. 4 workers times 20 connections times 10 pods is 800 connections; PostgreSQL's default max_connections is 100.
  • Observability. Metrics, profiles, heap snapshots and --inspect are per-process. Cluster mode means aggregating four sets of everything, and prom-client needs the extra AggregatorRegistry plumbing to report correctly.
  • Rolling updates and graceful shutdown already work per pod. Doing it per worker as well is a second, buggier implementation of the same thing.

The exceptions, where cluster or PM2 still earns its place:

  • Bare VMs or on-premises servers with no orchestrator: one 16-core box, one port. Cluster is exactly right.
  • A pod deliberately given several cores (limits.cpu: 4) for a workload where per-pod overhead is high — a large in-process cache, an expensive warm-up, a big model loaded into memory — so that duplicating the pod would waste far more memory than duplicating the process. Here 4 workers sharing one warm cache in one pod can be the cheaper shape.
  • Legacy platforms (Elastic Beanstalk, a single EC2 instance behind an ALB) where the deployment unit is a machine.
  • Local development on a many-core laptop for load testing.

If you do run multiple processes per container, set limits.cpu to at least the worker count, size each worker's heap so the total fits the memory limit with room to spare, use PM2 or a supervisor that exits the container when a worker cannot be restarted, and make the health check aggregate across workers.

NestJS example

A clean cluster bootstrap that respects graceful shutdown and does not fight Kubernetes:

// main-cluster.ts - only used on VM deployments
import cluster from 'node:cluster';
import { cpus } from 'node:os';
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

const WORKERS = Number(process.env.WEB_CONCURRENCY ?? cpus().length);

async function bootstrapWorker() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  app.enableShutdownHooks();                 // onModuleDestroy runs on SIGTERM
  const server = await app.listen(3000);
  server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000;

  process.on('SIGTERM', async () => {
    await app.close();                       // stop accepting, drain in-flight, close pools
    process.exit(0);
  });
}

if (cluster.isPrimary && WORKERS > 1) {
  let shuttingDown = false;
  for (let i = 0; i < WORKERS; i++) cluster.fork();

  cluster.on('exit', (worker, code, signal) => {
    if (shuttingDown) return;
    if (code === 0) return;                                  // deliberate exit
    setTimeout(() => cluster.fork(), 1_000).unref();          // delay: avoid a hot restart loop
  });

  process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
    shuttingDown = true;
    for (const w of Object.values(cluster.workers ?? {})) w?.process.kill('SIGTERM');
  });
} else {
  void bootstrapWorker();
}

Two things this gets right that most examples get wrong: a delay before re-forking (an immediate re-fork on a startup crash spins the CPU at 100% forever), and propagating SIGTERM to workers so in-flight requests drain.

PostgreSQL example

The connection arithmetic that kills clustered deployments:

-- What the database sees
SELECT count(*) AS conns, state FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;
--  conns | state
--    780 | idle
--     14 | active
SHOW max_connections;   -- 500
-- FATAL: sorry, too many clients already

Each PostgreSQL connection costs roughly 5 to 10 MB of backend memory and a process. The formula you must be able to do in your head:

total connections = pods x processes-per-pod x pool size (+ 1 per process for migrations/health)
10 pods x 4 workers x 20 = 800   -- refused
10 pods x 1 process x 15 = 150   -- fine, and PgBouncer makes it 25 server-side

One process per pod turns a four-way multiplication into a three-way one. Put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of the database and the number stops mattering at all (see Part 18 — PostgreSQL Internals).

Production scenario

A team moved a NestJS API from EC2 (PM2 cluster mode, 8 workers on a 8-vCPU instance) to Kubernetes and kept pm2-runtime start -i max in the Dockerfile. Pods had limits.cpu: 1. PM2 read the node's CPU count — 64, on a large instance type — and forked 64 workers into a 1-core, 2 GiB pod.

Symptoms: startup took 4 minutes, RSS sat at 1.9 GiB, every request was slow, PostgreSQL hit max_connections, and CPU throttling was at 90%. The metrics showed low CPU usage (the pod was throttled, not busy), which sent the investigation in the wrong direction for two hours.

The fix was deleting PM2 from the image: CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"], replicas: 8, limits.cpu: 1, --max-old-space-size=1536, pool size 15. Latency p99 fell from 2.1 s to 60 ms and the monthly bill dropped, because the cluster version had been paying for throttled, oversubscribed pods.

The trap generalises: os.cpus().length inside a container returns the host's core count, not your CPU limit. Anything that auto-sizes from it — PM2, thread pools, piscina defaults — will over-provision wildly. Read the cgroup quota instead, or set an explicit environment variable.

// util/cpu-budget.ts - honest CPU count inside a container
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { cpus } from 'node:os';

export function cpuBudget(): number {
  if (process.env.CPU_LIMIT) return Number(process.env.CPU_LIMIT);
  try {
    // cgroup v2: "max 100000" (unlimited) or "100000 100000" (1 core)
    const [quota, period] = readFileSync('/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max', 'utf8').trim().split(' ');
    if (quota !== 'max') return Math.max(1, Math.floor(Number(quota) / Number(period)));
  } catch { /* not in a cgroup v2 container */ }
  return cpus().length;
}

Failure scenario

At 21:00 a checkout service on PM2 cluster mode started returning 500s for about 12% of requests while all health checks were green and the dashboard showed the process "online".

One of the 8 workers had an unhandled exception in a startup path and was crashing on its first request. PM2's restart counter incremented, PM2 restarted it, it crashed again, and the loop continued at hundreds of restarts per minute — but the container stayed up and the load balancer kept the pod in service. One eighth of connections was routed to a worker that was always in the process of dying. The alert that eventually fired was a customer complaint.

With one process per pod, the same bug produces a CrashLoopBackOff pod that fails its readiness probe, is removed from the Service endpoints within seconds, and pages someone. The difference is not the bug; it is the visibility of the failure, and that is the strongest argument for one process per container.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • os.cpus().length reports host cores, not the container's CPU limit. Everything that auto-sizes from it over-provisions.
  • Cluster workers share no memory: in-process caches, rate-limit counters and WebSocket connection maps become inconsistent per worker. Move them to Redis.
  • Sticky sessions do not exist across workers by default; a WebSocket upgrade may land on a different worker from the one holding state.
  • Round-robin distributes connections, not requests. With HTTP keep-alive, one long-lived connection sends thousands of requests to the same worker, so load can be badly skewed.
  • A worker blocked by a synchronous 5-second operation is still routed connections; nothing detects it.
  • prom-client needs AggregatorRegistry for cluster mode, or /metrics reports whichever worker answered.
  • Graceful shutdown must be implemented in both the primary and every worker, or SIGTERM kills in-flight requests.
  • An immediate re-fork on a startup crash burns 100% CPU forever; always back off.
  • SO_REUSEPORT avoids the primary bottleneck but distributes by 4-tuple hash, so distribution can be uneven with few clients.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask what the deployment unit is. On Kubernetes: one process per container, scale with replicas, and treat any suggestion of cluster mode as needing a written justification. On a VM: cluster, sized to cores, with supervision and back-off. They know the connection arithmetic before proposing a topology, and they never let a library auto-size from os.cpus() inside a container.

Above all, they optimise for visible failure. A design where a broken worker is invisible to the orchestrator is a design that turns a five-minute incident into a two-hour one.

To a product manager: "We run one copy of the app per box, and add boxes when we need capacity. That way, when one breaks, the system notices and replaces it automatically."

Common mistakes

  • Keeping PM2 cluster mode after moving to Kubernetes.
  • Sizing workers from os.cpus() inside a container.
  • In-memory caches and rate limiters in a clustered app, giving N inconsistent copies.
  • No back-off on re-fork.
  • Forgetting that each worker multiplies database connections.
  • Health checks that pass while a sibling worker is crash-looping.

Interview questions

  1. How does cluster share a port across processes? Expected: the primary owns the listening socket and passes accepted connection descriptors over IPC (round-robin), or workers share the socket / use SO_REUSEPORT.
  2. Why is one process per container the norm in Kubernetes? Expected: the orchestrator already schedules by core; restart granularity, health-check accuracy, memory budgeting, connection counts and per-process observability all improve.
  3. When would you still use cluster or PM2? Expected: bare VMs, multi-core pods where per-process warm-up or cache memory is expensive to duplicate, legacy platforms.
  4. A pod with limits.cpu: 1 runs PM2 with -i max and is slow. Explain. Expected: os.cpus() reports host cores; dozens of workers oversubscribe one core's quota, causing throttling and memory pressure.
  5. How many database connections does 10 pods x 4 workers x pool 20 make, and what breaks? Expected: 800; PostgreSQL refuses past max_connections, each backend costs memory; fix with fewer processes or PgBouncer.
  6. Your clustered app returns errors for 1/8 of requests but health checks are green. What is happening? Expected: one worker crash-looping invisibly behind a healthy pod; argue for per-pod processes.

Practical exercise

Deploy the same NestJS app two ways: (a) one pod with limits.cpu: 4 running cluster with 4 workers, and (b) 4 pods with limits.cpu: 1 each running one process. Load both with the same profile and compare p50/p99, total PostgreSQL connections, and behaviour when you inject a crash into one worker or pod. Then set limits.cpu: 1 on the clustered pod without changing the worker count and measure the CPU throttling metric.

Acceptance criteria: a comparison table of latency, connection count and recovery time; documented evidence of how long each setup takes to remove a broken instance from service; and a demonstration that os.cpus().length inside the container does not match the CPU limit, with cpuBudget() returning the correct number.

9.23 Streams

Concept

A stream is an interface for moving data a piece at a time instead of all at once. Instead of "read the whole 4 GB file into a Buffer, then write it", you read 64 KB, write 64 KB, and repeat — so peak memory is one chunk, not one file.

Node has four stream types:

Type Direction Examples
Readable produces data fs.createReadStream, http.IncomingMessage (a request body), a pg query stream, child.stdout
Writable consumes data fs.createWriteStream, http.ServerResponse, child.stdin, an S3 upload
Duplex both, independently net.Socket, a WebSocket
Transform a Duplex where output is a function of input zlib.createGzip, crypto.createCipheriv, your CSV formatter

By default streams carry binary chunks (Buffer or string). In object mode (objectMode: true) each chunk is any JavaScript value — a database row, a parsed CSV record, a domain event. Object mode is what makes streams useful for data pipelines, not just files. The unit of the internal buffer changes too: in binary mode highWaterMark counts bytes (default 64 KB for Readable, 16 KB for Writable); in object mode it counts objects (default 16).

Why does it exist?

Memory is the scarcest resource in a container. A NestJS pod with a 1 GiB limit can afford maybe 700 MB of heap. Any operation whose memory cost scales with input size rather than with concurrency is a time bomb: it works on 10,000 rows in staging and OOMKills on 5,000,000 rows in production.

Streams convert a memory problem into a time problem. A 2 GB export takes 40 seconds either way; the difference is whether it takes 2 GB of RAM or 30 MB.

Streams also change time to first byte. A buffered export sends nothing for 40 seconds and then 2 GB. A streamed export sends the header row in 80 ms, so the browser starts downloading immediately and no proxy times out waiting for headers.

Mental model

Imagine emptying a swimming pool. The buffered approach is to find a container big enough for the whole pool, fill it, carry it, and empty it. You need a pool-sized container.

The streamed approach is a hose. Water flows continuously; at any moment only a few litres are inside the hose. You never need a pool-sized container — but you do need the drain at the other end to keep up. If the drain is slower than the tap, either the hose bursts or something must tell the tap to slow down. That "something" is backpressure (9.24), and it is not an optional extra: a stream without backpressure is just a slower way to run out of memory.

How it works

flowchart LR
    S["Readable: pg-query-stream"] -->|"chunk"| RB["read buffer, highWaterMark 100 rows"]
    RB --> T["Transform: row to CSV line"]
    T --> WB["write buffer, highWaterMark 16 KB"]
    WB --> W["Writable: HTTP response socket"]
    W -->|"write returns false when the kernel buffer is full"| WB
    WB -->|"pause upstream"| T
    T -->|"pause upstream"| S
    W -->|"drain event"| WB

The mechanics of a Readable in flowing mode:

  1. The stream calls its internal _read(size) to fetch data from the source.
  2. Data is pushed into the readable buffer with push(chunk).
  3. If the buffer holds at least highWaterMark, push() returns false, meaning stop producing. A well-implemented source honours this.
  4. Consumers receive chunks via 'data' events or for await...of.
  5. push(null) signals end-of-stream, which emits 'end'.

And a Writable:

  1. write(chunk) either passes the chunk straight to _write() or queues it.
  2. If the queued bytes reach highWaterMark, write() returns false.
  3. When the queue drains below the mark, the stream emits 'drain'.
  4. end() finishes the stream, which emits 'finish' once everything is flushed.

pipeline() versus .pipe()

.pipe() is the old API and it is broken in one specific, dangerous way: it does not forward errors and it does not clean up. If the destination errors, the source is left open. If the source errors, the destination is never closed. Over hours, a service that does this leaks file descriptors, database cursors and sockets.

// BROKEN: if res errors (client disconnects mid-download), the file stream stays open forever.
// Every aborted download leaks one file descriptor. At ~1,000 fds you get EMFILE.
createReadStream(path).pipe(res);

pipeline() (and its promise form in node:stream/promises) fixes all of it: it wires errors from every stage to a single place, destroys every stream in the chain on failure, and resolves or rejects once. Since Node 15 you should treat it as mandatory.

import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';

// CORRECT: any error anywhere destroys every stream and rejects here.
try {
  await pipeline(createReadStream(path), createGzip(), res);
} catch (err) {
  // Includes ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE when the client aborts mid-download.
  logger.warn({ err }, 'download failed or was aborted');
}

The rule to memorise: .pipe() is acceptable only inside a pipeline() call or in a throwaway script. In application code, always pipeline.

Practical example: exporting 5 million orders as CSV

This is the canonical case, and it is worth doing in full. Requirement: an admin downloads a CSV of all orders in a date range. In production that range can contain 5,000,000 rows, roughly 250 bytes each — about 1.2 GB of CSV.

The version that OOMKills:

// orders/export.service.ts - the naive version. Works in staging with 8,000 rows.
async exportCsv(from: Date, to: Date): Promise<string> {
  const orders = await this.repo.find({ where: { createdAt: Between(from, to) } });   // 5,000,000 entities
  return ['id,customer,total,status', ...orders.map(o => `${o.id},${o.customerId},${o.totalCents},${o.status}`)].join('\n');
}

Memory profile: the pg driver builds a result set of 5M row objects (roughly 1.5 GB), TypeORM hydrates 5M entity instances on top (another 2 to 3 GB, because each entity is a class instance with metadata), map allocates 5M strings, and join allocates one 1.2 GB string. Peak heap over 5 GB in a 1 GiB pod. In practice the pod is OOMKilled about 40 seconds in, with no error logged, no partial result and a 137 exit code. The client sees a connection reset.

The streaming version:

// orders/export.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Transform, Readable } from 'node:stream';
import QueryStream from 'pg-query-stream';
import type { PoolClient } from 'pg';

interface OrderRow { id: string; customer_id: string; total_cents: string; status: string; created_at: Date }

@Injectable()
export class OrderExportService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(OrderExportService.name);
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  /**
   * Returns a Readable of CSV bytes. Memory is bounded by batchSize x row size,
   * not by the number of rows in the result.
   */
  async streamCsv(from: Date, to: Date): Promise<Readable> {
    // Take a raw pg client from TypeORM's pool. We MUST release it ourselves.
    const client = (await this.dataSource.driver.obtainMasterConnection()) as PoolClient;

    const query = new QueryStream(
      `SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.total_cents, o.status, o.created_at
         FROM orders o
        WHERE o.created_at >= $1 AND o.created_at < $2
        ORDER BY o.created_at`,
      [from, to],
      { batchSize: 1_000, highWaterMark: 1_000 },   // rows fetched per round trip from the server cursor
    );

    const rows = client.query(query) as unknown as Readable;   // object-mode Readable of row objects

    const toCsv = new Transform({
      writableObjectMode: true,       // input: row objects
      readableObjectMode: false,      // output: Buffers
      highWaterMark: 64 * 1024,
      construct(cb) { this.push('id,customer_id,total_cents,status,created_at\n'); cb(); },
      transform(row: OrderRow, _enc, cb) {
        // Escape per RFC 4180: quote and double any embedded quotes.
        const esc = (v: unknown) => { const s = String(v ?? ''); return /[",\n]/.test(s) ? `"${s.replace(/"/g, '""')}"` : s; };
        cb(null, `${esc(row.id)},${esc(row.customer_id)},${esc(row.total_cents)},${esc(row.status)},${row.created_at.toISOString()}\n`);
      },
    });

    let released = false;
    const release = () => { if (!released) { released = true; client.release(); } };
    rows.on('end', release);
    rows.on('error', release);
    rows.on('close', release);        // client aborted the download: release the connection and cursor

    return rows.pipe(toCsv);          // safe here only because the controller wraps it in pipeline()
  }
}
// orders/export.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Query, Res, StreamableFile, Header, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Response } from 'express';
import { OrderExportService } from './export.service';
import { AdminGuard } from '../auth/admin.guard';

@Controller('admin/orders')
@UseGuards(AdminGuard)
export class OrderExportController {
  constructor(private readonly exports: OrderExportService) {}

  @Get('export.csv')
  @Header('Content-Type', 'text/csv; charset=utf-8')
  @Header('Content-Disposition', 'attachment; filename="orders.csv"')
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'no-store')
  async export(@Query('from') from: string, @Query('to') to: string, @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response) {
    const stream = await this.exports.streamCsv(new Date(from), new Date(to));
    // StreamableFile handles piping and destroys the source if the response is aborted.
    return new StreamableFile(stream, { type: 'text/csv' });
  }
}

Memory profile, measured:

Buffered version Streamed version
Peak heap, 8,000 rows 90 MB 42 MB
Peak heap, 500,000 rows 1.1 GB 46 MB
Peak heap, 5,000,000 rows OOMKilled at ~40 s 48 MB
Time to first byte 40 s (or never) 85 ms
Total time, 5M rows n/a 96 s
Event-loop lag p99 during export 2,400 ms 9 ms

The heap stays flat because at any moment the process holds at most 1,000 row objects from the cursor, a few CSV lines in the transform buffer, and 64 KB in the socket write buffer. The loop lag stays low because each chunk is a few hundred microseconds of work with an I/O yield between chunks.

Two details that matter more than the code:

  • batchSize: 1_000 controls the server-side cursor fetch size. Setting it to 1 makes 5 million round trips (a network-latency disaster); setting it to 100,000 puts 100,000 rows in memory at once (defeating the purpose). Between 500 and 5,000 is almost always right.
  • The connection is held for the whole export. A 96-second export occupies one pool slot for 96 seconds. Three concurrent exports on a pool of 15 is fine; forty is a pool exhaustion incident. Rate-limit exports, or move them to a background job that writes to S3 and emails a link.

NestJS example: StreamableFile and the pipeline rule

StreamableFile is the NestJS wrapper that tells the framework "this response is a stream". It handles the piping, sets headers from the options, and — importantly — destroys the underlying stream when the response closes early.

// files/files.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Param, StreamableFile, NotFoundException, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { createReadStream, promises as fsp } from 'node:fs';
import { join } from 'node:path';

@Controller('files')
export class FilesController {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(FilesController.name);

  @Get(':id/download')
  async download(@Param('id') id: string): Promise<StreamableFile> {
    if (!/^[a-f0-9-]{36}$/.test(id)) throw new NotFoundException();     // no path traversal
    const path = join('/var/data/files', `${id}.pdf`);
    const stat = await fsp.stat(path).catch(() => { throw new NotFoundException(); });

    const stream = createReadStream(path, { highWaterMark: 256 * 1024 });
    stream.on('error', (err) => this.logger.error({ err, path }, 'read stream failed'));

    return new StreamableFile(stream, {
      type: 'application/pdf',
      disposition: `attachment; filename="${id}.pdf"`,
      length: stat.size,        // sets Content-Length so the browser shows a progress bar
    });
  }
}

And an interceptor that measures streamed responses, because a stream that never finishes is invisible to normal request-duration middleware:

// common/stream-metrics.interceptor.ts
import { Injectable, NestInterceptor, ExecutionContext, CallHandler } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, tap } from 'rxjs';
import { Counter, Histogram } from 'prom-client';

@Injectable()
export class StreamMetricsInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  private readonly aborted = new Counter({ name: 'stream_responses_aborted_total', help: 'client aborted a streamed response' });
  private readonly duration = new Histogram({ name: 'stream_response_seconds', help: 'full stream duration', buckets: [1, 5, 30, 120, 600] });

  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const res = ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse();
    const end = this.duration.startTimer();
    // 'close' fires whether the response finished or the socket was destroyed.
    res.on('close', () => { if (!res.writableFinished) this.aborted.inc(); end(); });
    return next.handle().pipe(tap());
  }
}

TypeORM example

TypeORM's own stream() on the query builder returns the driver's stream and is a legitimate alternative when you want the query builder's ergonomics:

const stream = await this.dataSource
  .createQueryBuilder(Order, 'o')
  .select(['o.id', 'o.totalCents', 'o.status'])       // never SELECT * in an export
  .where('o.createdAt BETWEEN :from AND :to', { from, to })
  .orderBy('o.createdAt')
  .stream();                                          // Readable of RAW rows: { o_id, o_totalCents, ... }

Two caveats. First, the rows are raw, with aliased column names, not hydrated entities — which is exactly what you want, because entity hydration is the expensive part. Second, TypeORM does not release the underlying connection for you in every version; verify with pg_stat_activity that connections return to the pool after an aborted export, and wrap with explicit release if not.

Sequelize example

Sequelize has no first-class streaming API. Use the raw pg client from its pool:

// Sequelize: reach through to pg for streaming.
const conn = await sequelize.connectionManager.getConnection({ type: 'READ' }) as import('pg').PoolClient;
try {
  const rows = conn.query(new QueryStream('SELECT id, total_cents FROM orders WHERE created_at >= $1', [from]));
  await pipeline(rows, toCsv, res);
} finally {
  sequelize.connectionManager.releaseConnection(conn);   // always release, even on abort
}

The alternative — findAll with limit/offset in a loop — works but degrades: OFFSET 4000000 makes PostgreSQL scan and discard four million rows on every page. If you must paginate, use keyset pagination (WHERE (created_at, id) > ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 1000), which stays O(page) forever.

Production scenario

A finance team's month-end reconciliation downloads a 900 MB CSV on the first of every month. Before streaming, that request took the pod down every month at 09:00 like clockwork, and the team had learned to "just retry it a few times". Nobody had filed a bug because it eventually worked when traffic was low.

After the streaming rewrite, the export runs in 71 seconds with 50 MB of heap, other endpoints keep a 45 ms p99 throughout, and the only remaining concern is the pool slot it holds. That was solved by moving exports over 100,000 rows to a BullMQ job that streams to S3 and emails a presigned URL, leaving the synchronous endpoint for small ranges. This is the mature shape: stream for correctness, and move long exports off the request path entirely.

Failure scenario

At 10:40 an internal reporting service started failing with EMFILE: too many open files after four days of uptime. Restarting fixed it for another four days.

The service streamed report files with createReadStream(path).pipe(res). When a user closed the browser tab mid-download — common, because reports were large — the response socket was destroyed. .pipe() propagates neither the error nor the close to the source, so the file read stream stayed open forever, holding a descriptor and a 256 KB buffer. About 300 aborted downloads per day, times four days, crossed the 1,024 descriptor limit. ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l showed 1,024 entries, most pointing at deleted report files.

The fix was one line: await pipeline(createReadStream(path), res). pipeline destroys the source when the destination closes, which is exactly the missing behaviour. The team also added an fd-count gauge to the dashboard, because a slowly climbing descriptor count is one of the most reliable early warnings a service can emit.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Client aborts mid-stream: with .pipe() you leak; with pipeline you get ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE, which is a normal event, not an error to alert on.
  • An error thrown inside a Transform after the first chunk is written means the client already received HTTP 200 and a partial body. You cannot retract a status code. Validate before streaming, and use a trailer or a sentinel line for integrity if the consumer can check it.
  • Mixing await inside a 'data' handler does not pause the stream: chunks keep arriving and queue in memory. Use for await...of or a Transform with an async transform.
  • Object-mode highWaterMark counts objects, not bytes. highWaterMark: 16 with 5 MB objects is 80 MB of buffer.
  • Content-Length is unknown for a generated stream, so the response uses Transfer-Encoding: chunked; some legacy clients and proxies dislike it.
  • Reverse proxies buffer. nginx with proxy_buffering on will accumulate your carefully streamed response in its memory or on disk; set proxy_buffering off and X-Accel-Buffering: no for genuine streaming.
  • Compression interacts with flushing: zlib holds bytes until it has enough to compress. For server-sent events, call flush() or disable compression.
  • A database cursor holds a transaction snapshot open. A 20-minute export blocks VACUUM from cleaning newer dead tuples and inflates table bloat (see Part 18).
  • Long streamed responses can exceed load balancer idle timeouts if there are gaps between chunks; keep data flowing or send heartbeat bytes.
  • stream.destroy() does not always emit 'error'; listen for 'close' too if you need guaranteed cleanup.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask one question of every endpoint: does memory scale with input size? If yes, it must stream, no matter how small today's data is, because the row count only goes up. They use pipeline reflexively and treat a bare .pipe() in a review as a defect. They think about the connection cost of a long stream, not just the memory, and push exports over a threshold onto a queue.

They also know the limits of streaming: it does not make anything faster, it makes it bounded. And it moves the failure from "we ran out of memory" to "we held a connection for 90 seconds", which is a better failure but still a failure to design around.

To a product manager: "The export no longer loads the whole report into memory before sending it. It sends it as it reads it, so it starts immediately and cannot crash the server — but it still takes a minute and a half, and while it runs it uses one of our database slots."

Common mistakes

  • .pipe() in application code, leaking descriptors on every aborted download.
  • find() returning millions of hydrated entities.
  • Buffering a whole response to compute Content-Length.
  • await inside a 'data' handler, believing it pauses the stream.
  • Object-mode highWaterMark set as if it counted bytes.
  • Never releasing the database client on abort.
  • Forgetting proxy_buffering off, so the whole streaming design is undone at the proxy.

Interview questions

  1. Name the four stream types and give a real example of each. Expected: Readable/Writable/Duplex/Transform with pg-query-stream, HTTP response, socket, gzip.
  2. Why is pipeline() mandatory rather than .pipe()? Expected: error forwarding and cleanup; without it an aborted client leaks the source stream and its descriptor. Follow-up: what error do you see when a client aborts? ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE.
  3. Design a CSV export of 5 million rows in a 1 GiB pod. Expected: server-side cursor with a batch size, object-mode Transform, streamed response, bounded memory, plus a note on holding a pool connection and moving big exports to a job.
  4. What is object mode and what changes about highWaterMark? Expected: chunks are arbitrary values; the mark counts objects (default 16), not bytes.
  5. You stream a response and an error occurs after 200 bytes. What does the client see? Expected: HTTP 200 with a truncated body; the status is already sent. Discuss validating first and integrity markers.
  6. Why might a streamed response still arrive all at once in production? Expected: proxy buffering (nginx proxy_buffering), compression buffering, or a CDN.

Practical exercise

Seed an orders table with 2,000,000 rows. Implement the export twice: once with repository.find() plus join, once with pg-query-stream plus a Transform and StreamableFile. Run both in a container limited to 512 MiB and record peak RSS, time to first byte, total time and event-loop lag p99. Then abort the download at 30% with curl --max-time 3 in both .pipe() and pipeline() variants and count open descriptors afterwards with ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l.

Acceptance criteria: the buffered version OOMKills and the streamed version stays under 100 MB; a measured table of the four metrics; and descriptor counts proving pipeline cleans up while .pipe() leaks exactly one descriptor per aborted download.

9.24 Backpressure

Concept

Backpressure is the feedback signal that tells a fast producer to slow down because a slow consumer cannot keep up. Without it, the difference between production rate and consumption rate accumulates somewhere — and in Node, "somewhere" is always the heap.

In Node's stream API, backpressure has three concrete parts:

  • highWaterMark: how much a stream will buffer before it says stop. Default 64 KB for a Readable, 16 KB for a Writable, 16 objects in object mode.
  • write() returning false: the Writable's buffer is at or above the mark. This is not an error and the write was still accepted; it is a request to stop writing.
  • The 'drain' event: the buffer has fallen below the mark; it is safe to resume.

pipeline() and .pipe() implement this handshake for you. Every hand-written producer must implement it explicitly, and that is where the bugs live.

Why does it exist?

Because production rate and consumption rate are never equal, and the mismatch compounds. Reading from a local SSD at 800 MB/s and writing to a client on a hotel Wi-Fi at 2 Mb/s is a ratio of 3,200 to 1. In one second of that mismatch you buffer 800 MB. There is no amount of RAM that makes this safe; only flow control does.

The failure without it is characteristic and easy to recognise: memory grows linearly with time while CPU stays low, then the process is OOMKilled with no error, no stack trace and exit code 137.

Mental model

Imagine a conveyor belt from a factory to a packing station. The factory can make 100 boxes a minute; the packer can pack 20. Without a signal, boxes pile up on the floor until the room is full and the roof caves in.

Backpressure is the packer's red button. When the belt has 16 boxes waiting, the button lights up and the factory stops. When the pile drops to 8, the light goes off and the factory restarts. Total throughput is still 20 boxes a minute — backpressure does not make the packer faster — but the room never fills up. That is the whole point: backpressure trades latency for survival.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Producer
    participant W as WritableBuffer
    participant K as KernelSocketBuffer
    participant C as SlowClient
    P->>W: write chunk, returns true, buffer under the mark
    P->>W: write chunk, returns true
    P->>W: write chunk, returns FALSE, buffer at highWaterMark
    Note over P: producer MUST stop and wait
    W->>K: flush as the socket accepts bytes
    K->>C: TCP segments, limited by the receive window
    C-->>K: ACK, window opens
    K-->>W: socket writable again
    W-->>P: drain event
    P->>W: write(chunk) resumes

Note that there are two buffers in series, and TCP's own flow control is the outermost one. The client's advertised receive window shrinks as its buffer fills, the kernel stops sending, the kernel's send buffer fills, write() starts returning EAGAIN, libuv queues in userspace, and socket.write() returns false. The signal propagates all the way from a slow phone on a train back to your for loop — but only if every layer honours it.

The correct hand-written producer:

// The canonical write-with-backpressure loop.
import { once } from 'node:events';
import type { Writable } from 'node:stream';

async function writeAll(dest: Writable, rows: AsyncIterable<string>): Promise<void> {
  for await (const row of rows) {
    if (!dest.write(row)) {
      // Buffer is full. Stop producing until it drains. This await is the entire mechanism.
      await once(dest, 'drain');
    }
  }
  dest.end();
}

And the version people actually write, which is the bug:

// BROKEN: ignores the return value. Every unwritten chunk queues in the process heap.
for await (const row of rows) {
  dest.write(row);        // returns false thousands of times; nobody looks
}

The heap graph of an unbounded producer

Run both versions writing 5 million CSV rows to a client throttled to 1 Mb/s and sample process.memoryUsage() every second:

Ignoring backpressure                  Honouring backpressure
t=0s    heapUsed  38 MB                t=0s    heapUsed  38 MB
t=5s    heapUsed 210 MB                t=5s    heapUsed  44 MB
t=10s   heapUsed 402 MB                t=10s   heapUsed  43 MB
t=15s   heapUsed 611 MB                t=15s   heapUsed  45 MB
t=20s   heapUsed 812 MB                t=20s   heapUsed  44 MB
t=23s   <OOMKilled, exit 137>          t=600s  heapUsed  46 MB, transfer complete

The left column is a straight line with a slope equal to (production rate minus consumption rate). That linear-growth-with-flat-CPU shape is the fingerprint of missing backpressure, and it is different from a memory leak, which usually grows in steps and correlates with request count rather than with a single long operation.

Backpressure in HTTP responses

res is a Writable, so the same rules apply. In practice you get this for free by using pipeline, and you break it by writing in a loop.

// BROKEN: 100,000 synchronous writes. The socket accepts maybe 64 KB; the rest queues in the heap,
// and the loop is blocked for the whole duration so nothing else is served.
for (const order of orders) res.write(JSON.stringify(order) + '\n');

// CORRECT: an async generator plus pipeline. Backpressure and cleanup are both handled.
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';
import { Readable } from 'node:stream';

await pipeline(
  Readable.from(async function* () {
    for await (const order of orderCursor) yield JSON.stringify(order) + '\n';
  }()),
  res,
);

Readable.from(asyncGenerator) is the single most useful backpressure tool in modern Node: the generator is only advanced when the consumer wants more, so await inside it naturally throttles production.

Backpressure in Kafka consumers

A Kafka consumer's backpressure is pause/resume on partitions, and getting it wrong causes rebalancing storms rather than OOM — though it can cause both.

// kafka/order-events.consumer.ts
import { Injectable, OnModuleInit, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Kafka, Consumer } from 'kafkajs';

@Injectable()
export class OrderEventsConsumer implements OnModuleInit {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(OrderEventsConsumer.name);
  private consumer!: Consumer;
  private inFlight = 0;
  private readonly MAX_IN_FLIGHT = 50;

  async onModuleInit() {
    const kafka = new Kafka({ clientId: 'orders', brokers: (process.env.KAFKA_BROKERS ?? '').split(',') });
    this.consumer = kafka.consumer({
      groupId: 'order-projections',
      // The single most important backpressure setting: how long we may take per batch
      // before the broker considers us dead and rebalances the group.
      sessionTimeout: 30_000,
      heartbeatInterval: 3_000,
      maxBytesPerPartition: 1 * 1024 * 1024,     // bound how much arrives at once
    });
    await this.consumer.connect();
    await this.consumer.subscribe({ topic: 'order.events', fromBeginning: false });

    await this.consumer.run({
      eachBatchAutoResolve: false,
      eachBatch: async ({ batch, resolveOffset, heartbeat, commitOffsetsIfNecessary, isRunning, isStale, pause }) => {
        for (const message of batch.messages) {
          if (!isRunning() || isStale()) break;

          if (this.inFlight >= this.MAX_IN_FLIGHT) {
            // Explicit backpressure: stop fetching this partition, resume in 5 s.
            const resume = pause();
            setTimeout(resume, 5_000);
            break;
          }

          this.inFlight++;
          try {
            await this.handle(message);            // downstream work: PostgreSQL write
            resolveOffset(message.offset);         // only commit what actually succeeded
          } finally {
            this.inFlight--;
          }
          await heartbeat();                       // keep the session alive during slow batches
        }
        await commitOffsetsIfNecessary();
      },
    });
  }

  private async handle(message: unknown): Promise<void> { /* project into a read model */ }
}

The failure mode without this is worth stating precisely: if eachBatch takes longer than sessionTimeout without a heartbeat, the broker evicts the consumer, the group rebalances, another consumer picks up the same partition from the last committed offset, reprocesses the same messages, is also too slow, and the group rebalances forever while processing nothing. Consumer lag climbs, throughput reaches zero, and every message is processed multiple times. Backpressure here means fetching less and heartbeating, not buffering more.

Backpressure in for await loops

for await...of over an async iterable is naturally backpressured: the loop body must finish before the next value is requested. That is the good case.

It stops being backpressured the moment you fan out:

// BROKEN: fire-and-forget inside a for await. 5,000,000 promises created as fast as rows arrive.
for await (const row of cursor) {
  void this.enrich(row);                 // no await: unbounded concurrency and unbounded memory
}

// ALSO BROKEN in a different way: unbounded parallelism via Promise.all over a huge array.
await Promise.all(rows.map(r => this.enrich(r)));    // 5M concurrent HTTP calls

// CORRECT: bounded concurrency. Backpressure is the semaphore (3.11).
const CONCURRENCY = 20;
const running = new Set<Promise<void>>();
for await (const row of cursor) {
  const p = this.enrich(row).finally(() => running.delete(p));
  running.add(p);
  if (running.size >= CONCURRENCY) await Promise.race(running);   // wait for a slot
}
await Promise.all(running);

This bounded-concurrency loop is one of the half-dozen patterns worth memorising. It gives you throughput without unbounded memory, and the concurrency number becomes a tunable you can reason about against your database pool size and your downstream rate limits.

NestJS example: a bounded background processor

// reconciliation/reconcile.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron, CronExpression } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Gauge } from 'prom-client';

@Injectable()
export class ReconcileService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(ReconcileService.name);
  private readonly backlog = new Gauge({ name: 'reconcile_backlog_rows', help: 'rows still to reconcile' });
  private running = false;

  @Cron(CronExpression.EVERY_HOUR)
  async run(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.running) { this.logger.warn('previous run still going; skipping'); return; }   // no overlap
    this.running = true;
    try {
      // Keyset pagination: bounded memory, bounded query cost, resumable after a restart.
      let lastId = '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000';
      for (;;) {
        const rows = await this.dataSource.query(
          `SELECT id, order_id, amount_cents FROM payments
            WHERE id > $1 AND reconciled_at IS NULL
            ORDER BY id LIMIT 500`, [lastId]);
        if (rows.length === 0) break;
        for (const row of rows) await this.reconcileOne(row);     // sequential: bounded pressure on the PSP API
        lastId = rows[rows.length - 1].id;
        this.backlog.dec(rows.length);
      }
    } finally { this.running = false; }
  }

  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}
  private async reconcileOne(row: unknown): Promise<void> { /* call PSP, update row */ }
}

The running flag is backpressure at the job level: if an hourly job takes 70 minutes, overlapping runs would double the load on the payment provider and race on the same rows. Skipping is almost always better than overlapping.

Production scenario

A logistics platform streams GPS pings from 12,000 vehicles into Kafka and a consumer writes them to PostgreSQL. Ping rate is 12,000 every 10 seconds, or 1,200 per second. Each insert takes 1.5 ms, so one consumer can handle roughly 650 per second, and there are 4 partitions with 4 consumers: 2,600 per second of capacity against 1,200 of demand. Comfortable.

During a network incident, vehicles buffer locally and then all replay at once: 400,000 pings arrive in 30 seconds. Without backpressure the consumer fetches everything it can, holds 400,000 objects in memory, blows past sessionTimeout and rebalances forever. With maxBytesPerPartition bounding the fetch, batched inserts of 500 rows in one statement, and heartbeats inside the batch loop, the consumer drains the backlog in 4 minutes at a steady 60 MB of heap. Consumer lag spikes to 400,000 and decays smoothly to zero — which is exactly what a healthy system under a burst looks like.

Failure scenario

At 19:05, a pod serving an internal analytics endpoint was OOMKilled. It restarted, served traffic for 11 minutes, and was OOMKilled again. The pattern repeated all evening. Heap grew linearly at about 40 MB/s while CPU sat at 12%.

The endpoint streamed a large JSON array to an internal BI tool. The code was for (const row of rows) res.write(JSON.stringify(row) + ','); — no backpressure check. The BI tool ran in an office over a VPN at roughly 3 Mb/s. Node produced serialized rows at hundreds of megabytes per second and the socket accepted 3 Mb/s. The difference queued in res's internal buffer, which is process heap.

The tell was that it only happened when that one client was connected; fast local clients never triggered it, so it never appeared in staging. The fix was await pipeline(Readable.from(generator), res) plus a Prometheus gauge on res.writableLength for the p99 of streamed responses, so that a slow consumer becomes a visible metric rather than a crash.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Ignoring write()'s return value is the single most common cause of linear memory growth in Node services.
  • highWaterMark is a soft limit: a single write() larger than the mark is always accepted in full. Writing a 50 MB buffer queues 50 MB regardless of the setting.
  • In object mode the mark counts objects. Sixteen 10 MB objects is 160 MB of "bounded" buffer.
  • 'drain' only fires if write() previously returned false. Waiting for drain unconditionally hangs forever.
  • A slow client on a mobile network is the worst case, and it never appears in local testing.
  • Backpressure does not propagate through an EventEmitter. A custom emitter-based producer has no flow control at all.
  • Kafka: too much in-flight work without heartbeats causes rebalance storms; the cure is fetching less, not buffering more.
  • Redis pipelines and MULTI blocks buffer commands in the client. An unbounded pipeline is the same bug in a different library.
  • HTTP/2 has its own per-stream flow-control windows, so a single stalled stream does not block the connection, but the userspace buffering issue is unchanged.
  • res.writableLength and res.writableHighWaterMark are readable at any time and make excellent metrics; almost nobody exports them.
  • Backpressure raises latency by design. A saturated system with correct backpressure gets slow, which is the point; add load shedding (see Part 30 — Reliability Patterns) if slow is not acceptable.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat every producer/consumer boundary as a place where rates differ and ask what happens to the difference. The answer must always be one of: the producer blocks, we drop data deliberately, or we persist to a bounded durable buffer. "It queues in memory" is never an acceptable answer, because memory is the one buffer with no limit until the OOM killer supplies one.

They know that backpressure is not a stream API detail; it is the same idea as a connection pool's queue limit, a semaphore's permit count, a Kafka consumer's fetch size, a thread pool's bounded queue and a rate limiter. Learning it once in streams means recognising it everywhere.

To a product manager: "If we send data faster than the customer's connection can take it, the extra has to sit somewhere. We make our side wait instead of piling it up, so a slow customer gets a slow download instead of taking down the service for everyone."

Common mistakes

  • Never checking write()'s return value.
  • Promise.all over an unbounded array as a "parallelism" strategy.
  • Fire-and-forget calls inside a for await loop.
  • Raising highWaterMark to "fix" slowness, which only delays the OOM.
  • Overlapping cron runs with no guard.
  • Diagnosing linear memory growth as a leak and hunting for retained objects that are not there.
  • Kafka consumers that increase sessionTimeout instead of reducing batch work.

Interview questions

  1. What does stream.write() returning false mean, and what must you do? Expected: the internal buffer reached highWaterMark; stop writing and wait for 'drain'. The chunk was still accepted.
  2. Draw the memory graph of a fast producer and a slow consumer with no backpressure. Expected: linear growth with flat CPU, ending in OOMKilled/exit 137; contrast with a leak's stepwise, request-correlated growth.
  3. How does TCP flow control relate to write() returning false? Expected: receiver window closes, kernel send buffer fills, EAGAIN, libuv queues in userspace, write() returns false; the signal chains from the client's network to your loop.
  4. How do you bound concurrency over a 5-million-row cursor? Expected: for await with a running set and Promise.race, or a semaphore; never Promise.all over the whole set.
  5. What is backpressure in a Kafka consumer? Expected: pause partitions, limit maxBytesPerPartition and batch size, heartbeat during processing; failing to do so causes rebalance storms and reprocessing.
  6. Is raising highWaterMark ever the right fix? Expected: only to reduce syscall overhead for a consumer that is fast on average and bursty; it never fixes a sustained rate mismatch.

Practical exercise

Build an endpoint that streams 2,000,000 JSON lines. Write version A ignoring write()'s return value and version B using pipeline with an async generator. Consume both with a client throttled to 1 Mb/s (curl --limit-rate 128k) and sample process.memoryUsage().heapUsed every second into a CSV; plot both. Then add a res.writableLength gauge and confirm it stays near highWaterMark in version B and grows without bound in version A.

Acceptance criteria: two plotted memory curves, one linear to OOM and one flat; the exact second at which version A is killed and the derived production-minus-consumption rate; and a bounded-concurrency version of a per-row enrichment step that holds at most 20 in-flight operations, proven with a concurrency gauge.

9.25 Memory leaks in Node

Concept

A memory leak in a garbage-collected runtime is not memory the collector forgot. V8's collector is correct: it frees everything unreachable. A leak is memory that is still reachable from a root — a global, a module-level variable, an active closure, a live event listener, a running timer — but that your program will never use again.

The distinction matters because it tells you how to hunt: you are not looking for a bug in V8, you are looking for a reference you did not intend to keep.

Leaks in a long-lived server process are especially punishing. A CLI that leaks 2 MB per run does not matter; it exits. A NestJS pod that leaks 2 MB per hour hits a 1 GiB limit in about two weeks, gets OOMKilled at 03:00 on a Sunday, and looks like a mystery because the deploy that introduced it was fourteen days earlier.

Why does it matter?

Because in Kubernetes, memory is a hard limit enforced by the kernel, not a soft target. When the container's RSS exceeds limits.memory, the OOM killer terminates the process with SIGKILL. There is no exception, no stack trace, no chance to log anything, no graceful shutdown. You see exit code 137, OOMKilled in the pod status, and in-flight requests are dropped mid-response.

Before that, the process usually spends minutes near the heap limit, where V8 runs increasingly aggressive garbage collection, adding hundreds of milliseconds of pause to p99 latency. A leaking service is a slow service long before it is a dead one.

Mental model

Imagine a warehouse where a robot removes any box that nobody holds a rope to. It never makes a mistake. But you have a habit of tying a rope to every box that arrives and hanging the rope on a hook by the door "just in case". The robot sees a rope, so it leaves the box. After a year the warehouse is full of boxes nobody has looked at, all held by ropes on that one hook.

The hook is your module-level Map. The leak is not the robot's fault.

The four classic leaks, with real NestJS code

1. The unbounded module-level cache in a singleton provider.

NestJS providers are singletons by default and live for the entire process lifetime. Any collection on one grows forever unless you bound it.

// LEAKING: pricing/pricing.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class PricingService {
  // Singleton provider, so this Map lives as long as the pod.
  // One entry per (productId, customerId, currency) combination. Never evicted.
  private readonly cache = new Map<string, { price: number; computedAt: number }>();

  async priceFor(productId: string, customerId: string, currency: string): Promise<number> {
    const key = `${productId}:${customerId}:${currency}`;
    const hit = this.cache.get(key);
    if (hit) return hit.price;
    const price = await this.computePrice(productId, customerId, currency);
    this.cache.set(key, { price, computedAt: Date.now() });   // grows without bound
    return price;
  }

  private async computePrice(p: string, c: string, cur: string): Promise<number> { return 0; }
}

The arithmetic: 40,000 products times 200,000 active customers times 3 currencies is 24 billion possible keys. In practice the working set is smaller, but with 500,000 unique keys per day at roughly 180 bytes each (key string plus object plus Map overhead), that is 90 MB per day. Day 8 is an OOMKill.

The fix is either a bounded LRU with a TTL, or Redis. Redis is usually right, because a cache in process memory is per-pod, inconsistent across replicas, and lost on every deploy.

// FIXED: bounded LRU with a TTL, plus a metric so the cache is observable.
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { LRUCache } from 'lru-cache';
import { Gauge } from 'prom-client';

@Injectable()
export class PricingService {
  private readonly cache = new LRUCache<string, number>({
    max: 50_000,                       // hard entry cap
    maxSize: 32 * 1024 * 1024,         // and a byte cap
    sizeCalculation: (_v, k) => k.length * 2 + 64,
    ttl: 5 * 60_000,                   // stale prices are a correctness bug, not just memory
  });
  private readonly size = new Gauge({
    name: 'pricing_cache_entries', help: 'entries in the in-process price cache',
    collect() { /* set from the cache on scrape */ },
  });

  async priceFor(productId: string, customerId: string, currency: string): Promise<number> {
    const key = `${productId}:${customerId}:${currency}`;
    const hit = this.cache.get(key);
    if (hit !== undefined) return hit;
    const price = await this.computePrice(productId, customerId, currency);
    this.cache.set(key, price);
    this.size.set(this.cache.size);
    return price;
  }

  private async computePrice(p: string, c: string, cur: string): Promise<number> { return 0; }
}

Rule: every in-process collection that grows with traffic needs a bound and a gauge. If you cannot state its maximum size in megabytes, it is a leak.

2. Event listener accumulation on a long-lived emitter.

// LEAKING: orders/order-notifier.service.ts
import { Injectable, Scope } from '@nestjs/common';
import { EventEmitter2 } from '@nestjs/event-emitter';

@Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST })     // a NEW instance per request
export class OrderNotifierService {
  constructor(private readonly events: EventEmitter2) {   // but a SINGLETON emitter
    // One listener added per request, never removed. The closure retains `this`,
    // which retains the request-scoped injection subtree.
    this.events.on('order.created', (payload) => this.notify(payload));
  }
  private notify(p: unknown) { /* ... */ }
}

At 200 requests per second this adds 200 listeners per second to a singleton emitter. Node warns at 11 listeners (MaxListenersExceededWarning) and then goes quiet, so the warning scrolls past in the logs once and is never seen again. Two hours later there are 1.4 million listeners, each retaining a request-scoped object graph, and every emit('order.created') calls all of them.

Fixes, in order of preference:

// Best: use the declarative decorator on a SINGLETON provider. Nest registers the handler once.
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { OnEvent } from '@nestjs/event-emitter';

@Injectable()                                   // default singleton scope
export class OrderNotifierService {
  @OnEvent('order.created', { async: true })
  async handleOrderCreated(payload: { orderId: string }): Promise<void> { /* ... */ }
}

// If you genuinely must subscribe imperatively, remove the listener in the lifecycle hook.
@Injectable()
export class TemporarySubscriber implements OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly handler = (p: unknown) => this.notify(p);
  constructor(private readonly events: EventEmitter2) { this.events.on('order.created', this.handler); }
  onModuleDestroy() { this.events.off('order.created', this.handler); }   // same function reference
  private notify(p: unknown) {}
}

The same shape appears with process.on('SIGTERM', ...) inside a factory, socket.on('close', ...) inside a per-message handler, and redisClient.on('error', ...) registered per query. emitter.listenerCount(event) as a gauge catches all of them.

3. Closures capturing large buffers.

This one is subtle because the retained object is not the one you are thinking about.

// LEAKING: uploads/upload.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class UploadService {
  private readonly pending = new Map<string, () => Promise<void>>();

  async register(uploadId: string, fileBuffer: Buffer): Promise<void> {   // fileBuffer is 40 MB
    const checksum = createHash('sha256').update(fileBuffer).digest('hex');
    // This closure only USES `checksum` and `uploadId` - but V8's context object for this
    // scope also holds `fileBuffer`, so all 40 MB stays alive as long as the callback does.
    this.pending.set(uploadId, async () => {
      await this.markVerified(uploadId, checksum);
    });
  }
  private async markVerified(id: string, c: string) {}
}

V8 allocates one context object per closure-creating scope, and every closure created in that scope shares it. If any closure in the scope survives, the whole context survives, including variables the surviving closure never mentions. (V8 does optimise away variables no closure in the scope references, but as soon as one closure touches fileBuffer — or the function is not optimised — everything is retained.)

The fix is to narrow the scope so the big value is not in it:

// FIXED: extract the small values, and build the closure in a scope that never sees the buffer.
async register(uploadId: string, fileBuffer: Buffer): Promise<void> {
  const checksum = createHash('sha256').update(fileBuffer).digest('hex');
  this.pending.set(uploadId, this.makeVerifier(uploadId, checksum));   // fileBuffer not in this scope
}
private makeVerifier(uploadId: string, checksum: string): () => Promise<void> {
  return async () => { await this.markVerified(uploadId, checksum); };
}

The same trap appears with setTimeout(() => log(id), 60_000) written inside a handler that also holds a large parsed request body, and with promise chains where a rejected-but-retained promise holds its whole creation context.

4. Timers never cleared.

// LEAKING: sessions/session.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class SessionService {
  private readonly sessions = new Map<string, { user: User; timer: NodeJS.Timeout }>();

  touch(sessionId: string, user: User): void {
    // A new interval per touch. The old one is never cleared, so it keeps running
    // AND keeps `user` alive through its closure. Both the timer and the user leak.
    const timer = setInterval(() => this.refresh(sessionId), 30_000);
    this.sessions.set(sessionId, { user, timer });
  }
  private refresh(id: string) {}
}

Every active timer is a libuv handle and a GC root. A setInterval never cleared keeps its closure, and therefore everything the closure captures, alive forever — and keeps the process alive on shutdown, which is why SIGTERM sometimes hangs until Kubernetes escalates to SIGKILL.

// FIXED: clear before replacing, clear on removal, and use lifecycle hooks.
touch(sessionId: string, user: User): void {
  const existing = this.sessions.get(sessionId);
  if (existing) clearInterval(existing.timer);          // never stack timers
  const timer = setInterval(() => this.refresh(sessionId), 30_000);
  timer.unref();                                        // do not keep the process alive
  this.sessions.set(sessionId, { user, timer });
}
onModuleDestroy() { for (const s of this.sessions.values()) clearInterval(s.timer); this.sessions.clear(); }

For anything recurring in NestJS, prefer @Interval / @Cron from @nestjs/schedule: the framework registers and tears down the handles for you.

A leaking NestJS interceptor

Interceptors are singletons instantiated once and invoked on every request, which makes them a perfect leak vector. This one looks reasonable and leaks three ways at once:

// LEAKING: common/audit.interceptor.ts
import { Injectable, NestInterceptor, ExecutionContext, CallHandler } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, tap } from 'rxjs';

@Injectable()
export class AuditInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  // (1) Unbounded array of every request ever seen.
  private readonly trail: Array<{ at: number; user: string; body: unknown; res: unknown }> = [];

  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const res = ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse();

    // (2) A listener added per request to a socket that may be kept alive for thousands of requests.
    req.socket.on('close', () => this.flush());

    return next.handle().pipe(
      tap((data) => {
        // (3) Retains the full request body and full response body, including 8 MB uploads.
        this.trail.push({ at: Date.now(), user: req.user?.id, body: req.body, res: data });
      }),
    );
  }
  private flush() {}
}

Three independent leaks: an unbounded array, listeners accumulating on keep-alive sockets (a socket serving 5,000 requests collects 5,000 close listeners), and retention of large request and response payloads. At 300 requests per second with an average 6 KB body, the array alone grows at 1.8 MB/s — the pod dies in under ten minutes.

// FIXED: emit, do not accumulate. Never retain payloads. Never add per-request socket listeners.
import { Injectable, NestInterceptor, ExecutionContext, CallHandler, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, tap, catchError, throwError } from 'rxjs';
import { Counter, Histogram } from 'prom-client';

@Injectable()
export class AuditInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(AuditInterceptor.name);
  private readonly requests = new Counter({ name: 'http_requests_total', help: 'requests', labelNames: ['route', 'status'] });
  private readonly duration = new Histogram({ name: 'http_request_seconds', help: 'duration', labelNames: ['route'] });

  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const route = req.route?.path ?? 'unknown';       // low cardinality: the ROUTE, never the URL with ids
    const end = this.duration.startTimer({ route });

    return next.handle().pipe(
      tap(() => { end(); this.requests.inc({ route, status: '2xx' }); }),
      catchError((err) => {
        end();
        this.requests.inc({ route, status: 'error' });
        // Log identifiers, never bodies. The log ships out of the process; the array never did.
        this.logger.warn({ route, userId: req.user?.id, err: err?.message }, 'request failed');
        return throwError(() => err);
      }),
    );
  }
}

Note the label cardinality warning too: labelNames: ['route'] with the route pattern is bounded; using req.url would create one time series per order id and leak memory inside prom-client itself. Unbounded metric labels are a leak that looks like a monitoring feature.

How to find a leak

flowchart TB
    A["RSS climbing over hours or days"] --> B{"Does heapUsed climb too?"}
    B -->|"yes"| C["JavaScript leak: take heap snapshots"]
    B -->|"no"| D{"Is it external or arrayBuffers?"}
    D -->|"yes"| E["Buffers, sockets, native addon"]
    D -->|"no"| F["Native memory: child processes, fragmentation, glibc arenas"]
    C --> G["Snapshot at t0, t1, t2 under steady load"]
    G --> H["Comparison view: sort by delta size"]
    H --> I["Retainers path: find the root holding the objects"]
    I --> J["Fix, redeploy, confirm heapUsed is flat over 24 h"]

Step 1: confirm it is a JavaScript heap leak. process.memoryUsage() splits the picture:

// runtime/memory.service.ts - trend every metric, not just heapUsed
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Interval } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { Gauge } from 'prom-client';
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

@Injectable()
export class MemoryMetricsService {
  private readonly g = {
    rss: new Gauge({ name: 'node_memory_rss_bytes', help: 'resident set size' }),
    heapTotal: new Gauge({ name: 'node_memory_heap_total_bytes', help: 'heap reserved by V8' }),
    heapUsed: new Gauge({ name: 'node_memory_heap_used_bytes', help: 'live JS objects' }),
    external: new Gauge({ name: 'node_memory_external_bytes', help: 'C++ objects bound to JS' }),
    arrayBuffers: new Gauge({ name: 'node_memory_array_buffers_bytes', help: 'Buffers and ArrayBuffers' }),
    containerRss: new Gauge({ name: 'container_memory_current_bytes', help: 'cgroup memory.current' }),
  };

  @Interval(15_000)
  sample(): void {
    const m = process.memoryUsage();
    this.g.rss.set(m.rss);
    this.g.heapTotal.set(m.heapTotal);
    this.g.heapUsed.set(m.heapUsed);
    this.g.external.set(m.external);
    this.g.arrayBuffers.set(m.arrayBuffers);
    try {
      // The number the OOM killer actually looks at, including child processes and page cache.
      this.g.containerRss.set(Number(readFileSync('/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current', 'utf8').trim()));
    } catch { /* not cgroup v2 */ }
  }
}

Read it like this:

Pattern Diagnosis
heapUsed climbs steadily, rss follows JavaScript leak: retained objects. Take snapshots.
heapUsed flat and sawtoothing, rss climbs external/arrayBuffers (Buffers, sockets), native addon, or heap fragmentation
arrayBuffers climbs Buffers retained: streams without backpressure, a Buffer cache, an unreleased socket
Container RSS >> Node RSS Child processes, or page cache from heavy file I/O
heapUsed grows linearly during one long request Not a leak: missing backpressure (9.24)
Sawtooth with a rising floor Real leak underneath normal GC activity — look at the minima after major GCs, not the peaks

That last row is the most useful diagnostic habit in this section. Heap graphs always look like a sawtooth. Only the troughs matter; if the trough after each major GC is higher than the previous trough, you have a leak.

Step 2: heap snapshots. Start the pod with the inspector bound to localhost and port-forward:

# In the pod (never expose 9229 publicly - the inspector is full code execution)
node --inspect=127.0.0.1:9229 dist/main.js
# From your machine
kubectl port-forward pod/api-7c9f 9229:9229
# Then open chrome://inspect, click "inspect", go to the Memory tab.

The workflow that actually finds leaks is comparison snapshots:

  1. Let the pod warm up under steady load for 10 minutes.
  2. Take snapshot 1. Note the total size.
  3. Apply a known workload — for example exactly 10,000 requests to the suspect endpoint.
  4. Force a GC (the Memory tab's bin icon, or start with --expose-gc and call global.gc()), then take snapshot 2.
  5. Repeat for snapshot 3.
  6. Select snapshot 3, switch the view to Comparison against snapshot 1, and sort by Delta size.

Objects with a large positive delta and a count that grew by roughly your request count are your leak. Click one, open Retainers at the bottom, and follow the chain up to a root. That chain literally reads as the answer: Object -> closure context -> Array -> AuditInterceptor -> ... -> (GC roots).

Three shortcuts worth knowing:

  • Filter by "Objects allocated between snapshot 1 and 2" in the class filter to hide everything pre-existing.
  • (string) and (array) at the top of the delta list usually point at an accumulating array of log lines or keys.
  • (closure) growth with a large Retained Size is the closure-capture leak (leak 3 above).

Step 3: snapshots without a debugger. In production you often cannot attach an inspector, and taking a snapshot of a 1.5 GB heap pauses the process for several seconds and needs heap-sized free memory. --heapsnapshot-signal is the safest mechanism:

# deployment.yaml
env:
  - name: NODE_OPTIONS
    value: "--heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2"
volumeMounts:
  - name: diagnostics
    mountPath: /diagnostics
kubectl exec api-7c9f -- kill -USR2 1              # writes Heap.<date>.<pid>.<seq>.heapsnapshot to cwd
kubectl cp api-7c9f:/app/Heap.20260909.1.0.001.heapsnapshot ./snap1.heapsnapshot
# Load it in Chrome DevTools -> Memory -> Load

Do this on a pod you have first removed from the load balancer (kubectl label pod api-7c9f app- if your Service selects on that label), because the pause will fail health checks. v8.writeHeapSnapshot(path) from inside an admin-only endpoint is the programmatic equivalent, and --heap-prof gives you allocation sampling with far less impact when you want to know where memory is allocated rather than what is retained.

Step 4: clinic doctor for the first-pass diagnosis, which tells you which of the four resources is the problem before you commit to a deep investigation:

npx clinic doctor --on-port 'autocannon -c 50 -d 120 http://localhost:3000/orders' -- node dist/main.js
# Produces an HTML report with event loop delay, heap, CPU and active handles over time,
# plus a plain-English verdict such as "possible memory leak" or "event loop blocked".
npx clinic flame -- node dist/main.js       # where CPU time goes
npx clinic bubbleprof -- node dist/main.js  # where async time goes

clinic doctor's active-handles graph is underrated: a handle count that only rises is a socket, timer or stream leak, and you learn that in two minutes without any snapshots.

Production scenario

A notifications service on 8 pods, 1 GiB each, had a Map<userId, WebSocket[]> for delivering push messages. Sockets were added on connect and removed on 'close' — except when the process itself initiated the close during a shard rebalance, where the removal path was missed. About 0.4% of disconnects leaked one entry.

At 40,000 connections per hour, that is 160 leaked entries per hour, each retaining a socket object and its buffers: roughly 4 MB/hour. Nine days later the first pod was OOMKilled, and because pods had staggered start times, they died one by one over the following week — which made it look like an infrastructure problem rather than a code problem.

The catch was a gauge: websocket_map_entries next to websocket_active_connections. The two lines diverged immediately and unmistakably. Total time to diagnose after adding the gauge: eight minutes.

The lesson generalises: for every collection whose size should track a real-world quantity, export both numbers and alert on the divergence. It turns a nine-day mystery into a graph.

Failure scenario

At 03:12 on a Sunday, four of six payment API pods were OOMKilled within ten minutes of each other. The remaining two absorbed the traffic, hit their own limits, and by 03:26 the service was fully down. The night before, a deploy had added a "recently viewed products" feature.

The implementation stored recently viewed items in a Map on a singleton service, keyed by session id, with no eviction. Weekday traffic had disguised it: pods were redeployed every few hours during the week, resetting the leak. Over a quiet weekend with no deploys, the pods ran for 40 hours uninterrupted and all crossed the limit at roughly the same time — because they had all started at the same time on Friday evening.

Timeline of the response: 03:12 first page; 03:19 exit code 137 identified as OOMKilled, not a crash; 03:24 the deploy diff reviewed and the unbounded Map spotted; 03:31 rollback started; 03:38 service restored. The permanent fix was an LRU with max: 10_000 and ttl: 30 minutes, moved to Redis a week later so the data survived deploys.

Two lessons the team wrote down: frequent deploys hide leaks (a service that only survives because you restart it is already broken), and an alert on container_memory_working_set_bytes / limit > 0.85 sustained for 15 minutes would have paged someone on Saturday afternoon with a warning instead of on Sunday morning with an outage.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • heapUsed never returning to its previous floor after load subsides is the definitive leak signal; peaks are noise.
  • Closures retain their entire scope's context object, including variables they do not reference.
