And dns.lookup is a pool task, so outbound HTTP calls consume the same four threads as your file logging.

The settings that actually matter

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (default 4, max 1024). Raise it only when profiling shows pool queueing while CPU is idle — which means the pool work is I/O-bound (slow network filesystem, slow DNS), not CPU-bound. For CPU-bound pool work (bcrypt, zlib), raising it past the core count converts thread queueing into CPU queueing and adds context switches. Practical ceiling: 2 x vCPU. Set it in the container environment, never in code, because libuv reads it once at first use.

--max-old-space-size=<MB> (default derived from host memory, which is wrong in every container). Set it to about 75% of the container memory limit. This is the single highest-value setting in this list: get it wrong upward and you get OOMKilled with no stack trace; get it wrong downward and you get avoidable GC pressure. See 9.26 for the full arithmetic.

--max-semi-space-size=<MB> (default 16 on 64-bit). Controls the young generation. Raising to 32 or 64 for allocation-heavy services means fewer scavenges and fewer premature promotions to old space, often halving major GC frequency for about 150 MB more RSS. The one flag beyond heap size that reliably pays for itself — but measure before and after.

NODE_OPTIONS is how you pass all of the above without editing the entrypoint. It is read at startup and applies to child Node processes too, which is a trap: NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=768 is inherited by every worker you fork, so four forked children each think they may use 768 MB.

Keep-alive timeouts. server.keepAliveTimeout must exceed your load balancer's idle timeout, or you get intermittent, unexplainable 502s (9.19). server.headersTimeout must exceed keepAliveTimeout. server.requestTimeout bounds slowloris-style stalled bodies.

Connection pool size. Not a Node flag, but the number that most often shapes p99 (9.28). The arithmetic: pods x processes-per-pod x pool size must stay comfortably under PostgreSQL's max_connections, and the pool must be large enough that its queue is usually empty. Start at 10 to 20 per process and watch the pool wait metric.

ulimit -n. Every socket, file and pipe is a descriptor. The container default is often 1024, which a busy service exceeds. Raise it to 65,536 and monitor the count.

A recommended baseline: NestJS pod, 1 vCPU / 1 GiB

# deployment.yaml - a defensible starting point, not a universal truth
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-api
spec:
  replicas: 4
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45      # must exceed your longest request + drain time
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/orders-api:1.42.0
          command: ["node", "dist/main.js"]   # one process. No PM2, no cluster (3.22)
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi" }
            limits:   { cpu: "1",    memory: "1Gi" }   # memory request == limit: Guaranteed QoS
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: "production"
            - name: NODE_OPTIONS
              value: "--max-old-space-size=768 --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=1"
            - name: UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE
              value: "4"                      # 1 vCPU: more threads would only add switching
            - name: DB_POOL_SIZE
              value: "12"
            - name: DB_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS
              value: "10000"
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 3000 }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 3               # 15 s to leave the load balancer
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 3000 }
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 6               # 60 s: slower than readiness, on purpose
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]   # let endpoints propagate before SIGTERM
// main.ts - the runtime settings that live in code
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import { json } from 'express';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule, { bufferLogs: true });

  app.use(json({ limit: '1mb' }));                      // bound step 6 of the request trace (3.28)
  app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true, transform: true }));
  app.enableShutdownHooks();                            // onModuleDestroy runs on SIGTERM

  const server = await app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0');
  server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000;                     // > ALB idle timeout of 60 s
  server.headersTimeout = 66_000;                       // > keepAliveTimeout
  server.requestTimeout = 30_000;
  server.maxConnections = 10_000;

  process.on('SIGTERM', async () => {
    // 1. readiness starts failing (probe sees the flag), 2. drain, 3. close pools, 4. exit
    await app.close();
    process.exit(0);
  });
}
bootstrap();
// database.module.ts - the pool and timeout settings
TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync({
  useFactory: () => ({
    type: 'postgres',
    url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
    poolSize: Number(process.env.DB_POOL_SIZE ?? 12),
    extra: {
      statement_timeout: Number(process.env.DB_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS ?? 10_000),  // server-side, always fires
      idle_in_transaction_session_timeout: 30_000,                               // kills stuck transactions
      connectionTimeoutMillis: 3_000,                                            // fail fast on pool exhaustion
      keepAlive: true,
    },
    maxQueryExecutionTime: 1_000,                       // log slow queries (measured in JS - see 3.16)
    entities: [Order, OrderItem, Customer],             // explicit, not globs (3.18)
    synchronize: false,                                 // never true in production
  }),
});

The reasoning behind each number for this specific shape:

  • One process, 4 replicas rather than 4 workers in one pod: visible failures, simple memory budget, one-quarter the database connections (9.22).
  • 768 MB heap in a 1 GiB pod: leaves roughly 256 MiB for the binary, native stacks, socket buffers, external Buffers and fragmentation (9.26).
  • UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=4 unchanged: with 1 vCPU, four threads already exceed the available parallelism. Raise it only if profiling shows pool queueing with idle CPU.
  • Pool size 12: 4 pods x 12 = 48 connections plus health checks, comfortable against a max_connections of 200, and large enough that the pool queue is normally empty at a few hundred requests per second.
  • statement_timeout 10 s and connectionTimeoutMillis 3 s: the database enforces its own limit regardless of loop state, and pool exhaustion fails fast instead of piling up.
  • preStop: sleep 10 plus a 45-second grace period: Kubernetes removes the pod from the Service asynchronously, so a pod can receive traffic for a few seconds after SIGTERM. The sleep covers the gap; app.close() drains the rest.

Scaling signals

Autoscale on event loop utilisation (target ~0.6) rather than CPU percent. CPU is misleading because GC threads and libuv pool threads inflate it while the loop, the real bottleneck, may be idle — or the reverse, where a throttled pod shows low CPU while being unable to run. Where the platform only supports CPU, use a custom metric adapter to expose nodejs_eventloop_utilization.

The five dashboard panels every Node service should have, in order of diagnostic value:

  1. nodejs_eventloop_lag_p99_seconds and nodejs_eventloop_utilization
  2. nodejs_gc_pause_seconds p99 by kind, and major GC frequency
  3. Database pool: in use, waiting, wait duration p99
  4. node_memory_heap_used_bytes versus container_memory_working_set_bytes versus the limit
  5. Open file descriptors and active handles

Those five explain the overwhelming majority of "the app is slow and everything looks fine" incidents.

9.30 Three incidents from the runtime

Incident A: the event loop blocked by synchronous bcrypt

Symptom. 19:02 on a Friday. A marketing campaign went live at 19:00 with a push notification to 400,000 users. Login traffic rose from 8 to 140 requests per second across 6 pods. Within two minutes, every endpoint on the service — product search, cart, order history — was timing out at the API gateway's 10-second limit. Error rate 78%. Pods were not restarting; they were answering, just far too slowly.

Timeline.

19:00  campaign push sent
19:02  gateway 5xx rate crosses 5%, first page
19:04  on-call joins. CPU per pod: 99% on one core. Memory: normal. GC: normal.
19:06  PostgreSQL checked: 4 active connections, mean_exec_time 1.4 ms. Database exonerated.
19:09  scaled 6 -> 18 pods. No improvement. Each new pod also pinned at 99% of one core.
19:14  event loop lag dashboard: p99 = 8,400 ms. Not a database problem. A CPU problem on the loop.
19:17  CPU profile from one pod (kubectl exec, node --prof for 20 s, --prof-process):
       71% of ticks in bcrypt_lib, called synchronously.
19:19  git blame on auth.service.ts: a refactor 9 days earlier changed
       `await bcrypt.compare(...)` to `bcrypt.compareSync(...)` "to simplify the code".
       Cost factor had also been raised from 10 to 14 in the same PR for "security".
19:24  hotfix deployed: revert to the async form.
19:31  loop lag back to 4 ms; error rate 0.2%. Scaled back to 6 pods at 20:15.

Investigation. The two changes compounded. bcrypt.compareSync runs on the main thread rather than the libuv pool, so each call blocked the entire event loop. Cost factor 14 is 16 times more work than cost factor 10: roughly 1.1 seconds of CPU per verification instead of 70 ms.

At 140 logins per second across 6 pods, each pod handled about 23 logins per second at 1.1 seconds each — demanding 25 seconds of CPU per second on a resource that provides one. The loop was permanently saturated and the backlog grew without bound. Scaling to 18 pods reduced it to about 8 logins per second per pod, still 8.8 seconds of demand per second. Scaling could never have fixed this; it needed about 150 pods.

Why the dashboards lied. CPU at 99% looked like "we need more pods". The database looked healthy because it was healthy. Loop lag was the only metric that pointed at the truth, and it was on a secondary dashboard nobody opened for twelve minutes.

Fix and prevention.

// The permanent fix: async form, a justified cost factor, offloaded to a bounded worker pool,
// and hash time as a first-class metric with an alert.
@Injectable()
export class AuthService {
  constructor(private readonly hashPool: HashPoolService) {}      // piscina, maxThreads = cpus - 1

  async verify(plain: string, hash: string): Promise<boolean> {
    return this.hashPool.compare(plain, hash);                     // never *Sync on the main thread
  }
}
  • Cost factor set to 12 (about 250 ms) with a documented capacity number: a 1 vCPU pod can verify at most 4 passwords per second. That number now appears in the capacity plan.
  • Per-IP and per-account rate limiting on /auth/login with @nestjs/throttler.
  • An ESLint rule banning *Sync crypto and fs outside src/bootstrap/.
  • Loop lag promoted to the primary dashboard, with a page at p99 > 500 ms for 3 minutes.

The one-sentence lesson. A Sync suffix in a request path is a decision to serialize your entire service behind that call.

Incident B: file-descriptor exhaustion from a leaked pg client (EMFILE)

Symptom. 06:40 on a Tuesday, four days after a release. One pod started returning Error: connect EMFILE 10.4.2.11:5432 on every request. Over the next three hours the other five pods failed the same way, one at a time, in the order they had been started. Restarting a pod fixed it for exactly four days.

Timeline.

Fri  release deployed. All 6 pods restarted.
Tue 06:40  pod-3 starts throwing EMFILE. Removed from service by readiness probe.
Tue 06:45  on-call restarts pod-3. Recovers instantly. Assumed transient.
Tue 07:55  pod-1 throws EMFILE. Pattern noticed.
Tue 08:10  ls -l /proc/1/fd | wc -l inside pod-5 (still healthy): 812 and rising ~8/minute.
           Container ulimit -n: 1024.
Tue 08:14  ls -l /proc/1/fd | grep socket | wc -l  ->  766 sockets.
           ss -tanp | grep 5432 | wc -l  ->  741 ESTABLISHED connections to PostgreSQL.
           But the TypeORM pool size is 15.
Tue 08:22  pg_stat_activity on the primary: 4,300 connections from the API's pod CIDR,
           almost all state='idle', backend_start spread over four days.
Tue 08:35  code review of the release finds an admin export endpoint using
           dataSource.driver.obtainMasterConnection() with no release on the error path.
Tue 09:05  hotfix with try/finally deployed. FD count flat at 61 thereafter.

Investigation. The release added the CSV export from 9.23 — but an earlier draft of it. It took a raw client from the pool and released it on 'end', but not on 'error' or 'close'. Every aborted download (a user closing the tab, a gateway timeout at 60 seconds on large exports) leaked one client: one file descriptor in the pod, one backend process in PostgreSQL, and one open cursor holding a transaction snapshot.

Roughly 8 leaked clients per hour, times 96 hours, is about 770 descriptors — plus the pod's legitimate sockets, HTTP connections and open files, crossing 1,024. EMFILE then affects everything: new PostgreSQL connections fail, incoming HTTP connections cannot be accepted, and even opening a log file fails. The error message names whichever operation happened to be next, which is why it looked like a database problem.

There was a second, quieter casualty. Each leaked connection held an idle transaction with an old snapshot, so VACUUM could not remove dead tuples newer than the oldest snapshot. The orders table had grown 40% in dead space over those four days, and query plans were degrading in parallel.

Fix and prevention.

// Always release in a finally. Always.
const client = await this.dataSource.driver.obtainMasterConnection() as PoolClient;
try {
  await pipeline(client.query(new QueryStream(sql, params)), toCsv, res);
} finally {
  client.release();          // runs on success, error, and client abort
}
  • idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 30000 on the database, so a leaked connection is reaped server-side within 30 seconds even when the client forgets. This alone would have prevented the outage.
  • ulimit -n raised to 65,536, which buys time but is not a fix.
  • A process_open_fds gauge with an alert at 60% of the limit. A linearly rising descriptor count is the most reliable early warning a service can emit, and it would have paged someone on Saturday morning.
  • A pg_stat_activity alert on connections older than one hour in idle in transaction.

The one-sentence lesson. Every resource you acquire manually needs a finally, and every resource count needs a gauge — a leak is a straight line on a graph and a mystery without one.

Incident C: OOMKilled pods from an in-memory Map plus a heap limit above the container limit

Symptom. 03:12 Sunday. Four of six payment API pods OOMKilled within ten minutes; the remaining two absorbed the traffic and died by 03:26. Complete outage for 12 minutes. No application error logs — the logs simply stopped mid-line.

Timeline.

Fri 18:40  release: "recently viewed products" feature.
Sat 00:00  pods running 5 h. RSS 480 MiB. Nobody looking.
Sun 03:12  pod-2 and pod-4 OOMKilled (exit 137). Pods restart.
Sun 03:16  pod-1, pod-5 OOMKilled.
Sun 03:19  on-call paged. kubectl describe pod: "Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137".
Sun 03:22  no stack trace, no FATAL ERROR from V8. So V8 never hit ITS limit -> the kernel killed it.
           NODE_OPTIONS: --max-old-space-size=2048. Container limit: 1Gi. The bug is visible in one line.
Sun 03:24  release diff reviewed: a Map<sessionId, Product[]> on a singleton, no eviction.
Sun 03:26  remaining pods die. Full outage.
Sun 03:31  rollback started.
Sun 03:38  service restored.

Investigation. Two independent mistakes that were individually survivable and together fatal.

Mistake one: the unbounded Map. A singleton provider stored up to 20 recently viewed products per session id, with no TTL and no eviction. At roughly 30,000 unique sessions per hour and about 2 KB per entry, that is 60 MB per hour of pure leak.

Mistake two: --max-old-space-size=2048 in a 1 GiB pod. Someone had raised it months earlier "to give the app more room" after an unrelated incident. It meant V8 believed it could grow to 2 GB and therefore applied no memory pressure at all: no aggressive collection, no heap-limit error, no warning. It sailed straight past the 1 GiB cgroup limit and the kernel killed it with SIGKILL — which is why there was no stack trace, no snapshot, no log line and no graceful shutdown.

Why all four pods at once. All six had started within minutes of each other on Friday evening and leaked at the same rate, so they crossed the limit together. And the leak had been invisible all week because weekday deploys restarted the pods every few hours. The service had been broken since Friday; the weekend simply stopped hiding it.

Fix and prevention.

// Bounded, TTL'd, and observable. Moved to Redis a week later so it survives deploys
// and is shared across replicas.
private readonly recentlyViewed = new LRUCache<string, Product[]>({
  max: 20_000,
  ttl: 30 * 60_000,
  updateAgeOnGet: true,
});
env:
  - name: NODE_OPTIONS
    # 75% of the 1 GiB limit. Now V8 hits ITS limit first and dies with a stack trace and a snapshot.
    value: "--max-old-space-size=768 --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=1"
  • Alert: container_memory_working_set_bytes / container_spec_memory_limit_bytes > 0.85 for 15 minutes. This would have paged someone on Saturday afternoon, with hours to spare and no customer impact.
  • A CI check asserting --max-old-space-size is between 60% and 80% of the manifest's memory limit. A ten-line script that makes this class of incident structurally impossible.
  • A code review rule: every module-level or provider-level collection must state its bound.
  • Pod start times deliberately staggered, so correlated failures become sequential ones and the first pod's death is a warning rather than part of the outage.

The one-sentence lesson. A heap limit above the container limit converts every memory bug into an unexplained kill; and a service that only stays up because you deploy often is already broken.

9.31 Edge cases and failure modes

A consolidated list for Part 9. Each of these has caused a real outage somewhere.

Processes, threads and scheduling

  • os.cpus().length returns the host's core count inside a container, so anything auto-sizing from it (PM2, worker pools, GC heuristics in libraries) over-provisions wildly. Read the cgroup quota.
  • CFS throttling produces latency spikes that look identical to GC pauses and to network latency. Check container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total before theorising.
  • A CPU limit below 1 core means the process is descheduled mid-period; a 100 ms period with 200 ms of demand gives you 100 ms of pure stall.
  • Setting requests far below limits puts the pod in Burstable QoS and makes it an eviction candidate under node pressure.

Memory and GC

  • Node's default heap limit derives from host memory: always set --max-old-space-size explicitly in a container.
  • A heap limit at or above the container limit guarantees OOMKilled (exit 137, SIGKILL, no stack trace) instead of a diagnosable V8 error.
  • --max-old-space-size bounds only the main isolate. Worker threads need resourceLimits; child processes need their own budget; Buffers live outside the heap in external.
  • Heap sawtooth peaks are noise; only the troughs after major GCs reveal a leak.
  • A large live set makes every major GC expensive forever. Scaling out duplicates the problem rather than solving it.
  • Taking a heap snapshot pauses the process for seconds and needs heap-sized headroom, so it can trigger the OOM you are diagnosing. Remove the pod from service first.
  • Prometheus label cardinality (per-user, per-URL labels) is a memory leak wearing a monitoring costume.

Event loop and microtasks

  • A recursive process.nextTick or a tight await Promise.resolve() loop starves I/O completely: the process is 100% busy and answers nothing, including health checks.
  • setTimeout is a lower bound, never a schedule; a blocked loop makes client-side query timeouts fire late and the database look slow.
  • Unhandled promise rejections terminate the process by default since Node 15. Every fire-and-forget promise needs a .catch.
  • Synchronous work is uninterruptible: no timeout, no cancellation, no signal delivery until it returns.
  • monitorEventLoopDelay sees only the main loop; work on the libuv pool or in workers is invisible to it.

libuv pool and async I/O

  • The pool has 4 threads shared process-wide with no priorities, no cancellation and no timeout. One stuck native call permanently removes a slot.
  • UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE is read once, at first use; setting it in code after any fs call silently does nothing.
  • Raising the pool above the core count converts thread queueing into CPU queueing plus context switches, and each thread costs stack memory.
  • dns.lookup is a pool task and is not cached by Node; a DNS outage pins threads for the resolver timeout.
  • keepAliveTimeout shorter than the load balancer's idle timeout causes intermittent, unreproducible 502s.
  • EMFILE from descriptor exhaustion breaks everything at once — new sockets, new files, new connections — and the error names whichever operation was next.
  • Ephemeral port exhaustion on outbound-heavy services gives EADDRNOTAVAIL; fix with keep-alive agents.
  • Half-open connections (laptop lid closed, NAT timeout) are never reported by epoll; only TCP keep-alive or an application heartbeat reclaims them.

Workers, children and processes

  • Each worker is a full V8 isolate with its own heap; unbounded worker creation is an OOM in a fixed-size container.
  • Structured clone serialises on the sending thread: sending 10 MB to a worker blocks your main thread for ~80 ms and offloads nothing.
  • worker.terminate() is the only way to stop a synchronous loop, and it skips all cleanup.
  • process.exit() inside a worker kills the whole process.
  • exec with any interpolated user input is remote code execution; maxBuffer overflow silently kills the child.
  • Child process memory and CPU count against the container's cgroup limits, so a pod can be OOMKilled with a small Node heap.
  • Node as PID 1 does not reap orphaned grandchildren: use tini or docker run --init.
  • SIGKILL on the parent orphans children, which keep running inside the pod's cgroup.
  • Cluster workers share no memory, so in-process caches, rate limiters and WebSocket maps become N inconsistent copies.
  • A crash-looping cluster worker is invisible to Kubernetes: the pod stays Running while a fraction of requests fail.

Streams and backpressure

  • .pipe() forwards neither errors nor cleanup: every aborted download leaks a descriptor. Use pipeline().
  • Ignoring write()'s return value produces linear memory growth with flat CPU, ending in OOMKilled.
  • Object-mode highWaterMark counts objects, not bytes: sixteen 10 MB objects is 160 MB of "bounded" buffer.
  • A single write() larger than highWaterMark is always accepted in full, whatever the setting.
  • An error thrown after the first chunk means the client already has HTTP 200 and a truncated body; you cannot retract a status code.
  • await inside a 'data' handler does not pause the stream; chunks keep arriving and queue in memory.
  • nginx proxy_buffering on silently undoes your entire streaming design at the proxy.
  • A long-running cursor holds a transaction snapshot open, blocking VACUUM and inflating table bloat.
  • Promise.all over an unbounded array is unbounded concurrency and unbounded memory.
  • Kafka: too much work per batch without heartbeats causes rebalance storms and endless reprocessing. Fetch less; do not buffer more.

Request pipeline

  • No body-size limit means JSON.parse cost is attacker-controlled.
  • A regex with nested quantifiers over overlapping classes plus no length bound is a one-request denial of service.
  • pg parses result rows on the main thread: a 100,000-row query blocks the loop even though the query was async.
  • An HTTP call inside a database transaction holds a pool connection and locks for the external service's latency.
  • A client that disconnects mid-request does not cancel your handler; you pay for the query, the transaction and the serialization anyway.
  • A JavaScript request timeout bounds the response, not the work. Only statement_timeout stops the query.
  • Liveness probes that check dependencies restart every pod simultaneously during a database blip. Liveness must be cheap and local; readiness may check dependencies.
  • Kubernetes removes a pod from Service endpoints asynchronously, so traffic can arrive after SIGTERM. A preStop sleep covers the gap.
  • terminationGracePeriodSeconds shorter than your longest request means in-flight requests are SIGKILLed during every deploy.

Senior Checklist — Part 9

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can name, for any Node API, whether it runs on the main thread, the libuv pool, kernel async I/O or a worker thread
  • I can explain the event loop phases and predict the exact output of a nextTick / promise / setImmediate / setTimeout ordering puzzle
  • I can trace a POST /orders request from TCP accept to socket write and mark every step CPU-bound or I/O-bound
  • I can compute the correct --max-old-space-size for a given container memory limit and explain each term in the budget
  • I can read --trace-gc output line by line, including mutator utilisation, and say whether the process is healthy
  • I can find a memory leak with comparison heap snapshots and a retainers path, and take a snapshot safely from a production pod
  • I can explain backpressure, spot code that ignores write()'s return value, and write a bounded-concurrency loop
  • I can write a streaming export of millions of rows with bounded memory using pipeline()
  • I can decide between a worker thread, a child process, a background job and another replica, and justify the choice
  • I can measure event loop lag and utilisation, expose them as metrics, and use utilisation as the autoscaling signal
  • I can recognise a ReDoS-vulnerable regex and bound input length before it is matched
  • I can explain why one process per container is the default in Kubernetes and name the exceptions
  • I can diagnose EMFILE, OOMKilled (exit 137) and CFS throttling from their distinct signatures
  • I can configure keep-alive, header, request and shutdown timeouts so they are consistent with the load balancer and the orchestrator

Part 9 — Key Takeaways

  • Node runs your JavaScript on one thread but the process has many: 4 libuv pool threads, V8 helper threads, and any workers you create. "Single-threaded" is about your code, not the process.
  • Know the resource for every operation. Sockets are free and kernel-async; fs, dns.lookup, async crypto and zlib share four pool threads; everything else you write is on the loop.
  • The event loop's only rule is that no callback may run long. Every synchronous millisecond is a millisecond charged to every concurrent request, which is why *Sync in a handler is a decision to serialize your service.
  • Measure event loop lag and utilisation, not CPU percent. Lag is the symptom, utilisation is the saturation, and utilisation is the right autoscaling signal.
  • Set --max-old-space-size to about 75% of the container memory limit. Above the limit you get OOMKilled with no stack trace; the default is derived from host memory and is always wrong in a container.
  • A memory leak is a reference you did not mean to keep. Every long-lived collection, listener and timer needs a bound, an owner and a gauge — and only the heap troughs after major GCs tell you the truth.
  • GC cost scales with what you keep, not what you allocate. A big in-process cache is a permanent tax on every major GC, and adding pods duplicates the tax.
  • If memory scales with input size, it must stream. pipeline() is mandatory: .pipe() leaks a descriptor on every aborted response.
  • Backpressure is not optional. Ignoring write()'s return value gives linear memory growth with flat CPU, and the same idea — bounded queues — applies to Kafka consumers, connection pools, worker pools and for await loops.
  • Use a worker thread only for CPU-bound work over ~50 ms with a transferable payload; use a child process for non-JavaScript binaries; use a queue for anything durable; and use another replica for everything else.
  • One process per container in Kubernetes. Cluster mode hides failures from the orchestrator, multiplies database connections and complicates every memory and metrics decision.
  • In the request trace, most latency is waiting and almost none is your code — but your code is the shared resource. p99 hides in connection pool waits, loop lag, GC pauses, large serialization and slow clients, in roughly that order.
  • Hold shared resources for as little time as possible: the connection, the transaction, the loop. Almost every incident in this part is a version of holding one of them too long.

Part 10 — Networking and HTTP

Every request your NestJS application serves has already survived a long journey before your controller sees it. It was a DNS lookup, then a TCP handshake, then a TLS negotiation, then a stream of bytes parsed into an HTTP request, then a load balancer decision, and only then a JavaScript object called req. When something goes wrong in production, it is very often in one of those earlier layers, and the error you see in your logs is only a symptom.

This part teaches the network from the bottom up, always with one question in mind: how would I meet this in a real backend system? You will learn the layers, IP addresses and ports, DNS, TCP and UDP, the handshake and its cost, latency versus bandwidth, VPC design, and then HTTP in real depth: versions, methods, headers, status codes, cookies, keep-alive, pooling, compression, streaming, caching, TLS and CORS. We finish with a full end-to-end trace of a browser calling a NestJS API, and a catalogue of the failure modes that senior engineers have all been paged for at least once.

10.1 The layered model: OSI and the practical TCP/IP view

Concept

Networking is organised in layers. Each layer does one job and hands its result to the layer above. The classic teaching model is the seven-layer OSI model. The model that real systems are actually built on is the four-layer TCP/IP model. You need both: OSI for vocabulary ("a Layer 4 load balancer", "a Layer 7 firewall"), TCP/IP for understanding what actually happens.

OSI layer Name What it carries TCP/IP layer Where you meet it as a backend engineer
7 Application HTTP, DNS, gRPC, SMTP Application NestJS, Express, Postgres wire protocol, Redis RESP
6 Presentation TLS, encoding, compression Application TLS termination, gzip, JSON serialization
5 Session Session setup, TLS session resumption Application Mostly folded into TLS and app code
4 Transport TCP segments, UDP datagrams, ports Transport Network Load Balancer, net.Socket, connection pools
3 Network IP packets, routing, addresses Internet VPC, subnets, NAT gateway, security groups
2 Data link Ethernet frames, MAC addresses, Wi-Fi Link Cloud handles it; you see it as MTU issues
1 Physical Electrical signals, fibre, radio Link Never, unless a cable gets cut in a data centre

Why does it exist?

Without layering, every application would need to know how to route packets across the internet, detect lost data, and negotiate encryption. Layering means your NestJS handler only knows about HTTP, TCP only knows about reliable byte delivery between two ports, and IP only knows how to get a packet one hop closer to its destination. Each layer can be replaced independently: HTTP/3 swapped TCP for QUIC without changing your controllers.

The practical value for you is diagnosis. When a request fails, the layer tells you who to blame:

  • "Connection refused" is Layer 4: nothing is listening on that port.
  • "No route to host" or a timeout with no response at all is Layer 3: a security group, a route table, or a dead subnet.
  • "502 Bad Gateway" is Layer 7: the load balancer spoke HTTP to your app and got a broken answer.
  • "Certificate has expired" is Layer 6: TLS, before a single HTTP byte was exchanged.

Mental model

Imagine sending a gift to a friend abroad. You write a letter (application data). You put it in an envelope with the friend's name (application header). You place that in a box with a room number (port), then in a courier package with the street address (IP address), then the courier loads it on a truck with a licence plate (MAC address). Every step wraps the previous one. At the destination, each layer unwraps its own envelope and hands the inside up. This wrapping is called encapsulation, and the layers never open each other's envelopes.

How it works

flowchart TB
    subgraph App["Application layer"]
        H["HTTP request: POST /orders"]
    end
    subgraph Tls["Presentation: TLS"]
        T["Encrypted TLS record"]
    end
    subgraph Transport["Transport layer"]
        S["TCP segment: src port 51234, dst port 443, seq, ack"]
    end
    subgraph Internet["Internet layer"]
        P["IP packet: src 10.0.1.15, dst 52.14.9.2, TTL"]
    end
    subgraph Link["Link layer"]
        F["Ethernet frame: MAC addresses, up to 1500 bytes MTU"]
    end
    H --> T --> S --> P --> F

Step by step, for one HTTP request leaving your laptop:

  1. Your HTTP client builds the text POST /orders HTTP/1.1 plus headers and a JSON body.
  2. TLS encrypts that into one or more records so no router on the path can read it.
  3. TCP splits the encrypted bytes into segments, numbers them, and adds source and destination ports.
  4. IP wraps each segment in a packet with source and destination addresses and hands it to the network card.
  5. Ethernet or Wi-Fi puts each packet in a frame of at most 1,500 bytes (the MTU, maximum transmission unit) and sends it.
  6. Every router along the way looks only at the IP header, decrements the TTL (time to live) hop counter, and forwards.
  7. At the server, the process reverses: frame, packet, segment, TLS record, HTTP request, and finally req.body in NestJS.

Where the pieces of the standard stack live:

Component Layer What it looks at
AWS Network Load Balancer (NLB) 4 IP and TCP/UDP headers only; forwards bytes, never parses HTTP
AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB), NGINX, Envoy 7 Full HTTP: paths, headers, host names; can route /api/* to one target group
Web Application Firewall (WAF) 7 HTTP content: SQL injection patterns, bad user agents, rate limits per IP
Security groups, network ACLs 3 and 4 Source IP, destination port, protocol
TLS termination 6 Certificates, cipher negotiation, decryption
NestJS 7 Only the decrypted HTTP request; it has no idea a TLS handshake happened
PostgreSQL wire protocol 7 over TCP Its own binary message protocol on port 5432

Practical example

A food-delivery API on AWS: the browser hits api.fooddash.com. That name resolves to an ALB (Layer 7) that terminates TLS (Layer 6), checks the Host header, matches the listener rule path is /v1/*, and forwards plain HTTP/1.1 to a target group of NestJS pods. Between the ALB and the pods sits a security group (Layer 3/4) that only allows TCP 3000 from the ALB's security group. The pods talk to RDS PostgreSQL on TCP 5432 inside a private subnet (Layer 3 design). The WAF in front of the ALB blocks requests whose body matches ' OR 1=1 at Layer 7 before they cost you a database round trip.

NestJS example

NestJS lives entirely at Layer 7, but it can be told about the lower layers. A trust-proxy setting, for example, is how you tell Express that Layer 3 source addresses have been rewritten by the load balancer and the real client IP now lives in a Layer 7 header.

// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { NestExpressApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule);

  // The ALB rewrites the Layer 3 source IP. Trust exactly one proxy hop so
  // req.ip reads the last value of X-Forwarded-For instead of the ALB's IP.
  app.set('trust proxy', 1);

  const server = app.getHttpServer();
  // Layer 4 knobs that matter for the "502 behind an ALB" bug (see 4.9).
  server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000; // must exceed the ALB idle timeout (60 s)
  server.headersTimeout = 66_000;   // must exceed keepAliveTimeout

  await app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0'); // bind on all interfaces inside the container
}
bootstrap();

The '0.0.0.0' matters: binding to 127.0.0.1 inside a container means the app listens only on the loopback interface, and the load balancer's health checks (arriving on the container's network interface) get "connection refused" at Layer 4. That is one of the most common "my pod is healthy locally but the target group says unhealthy" tickets.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL sits at Layer 7 with its own protocol, but you configure it at Layers 3 and 4. listen_addresses is a Layer 3 binding decision; pg_hba.conf is a Layer 3 allow-list; port is Layer 4.

-- Which interfaces PostgreSQL is bound to (Layer 3)
SHOW listen_addresses;   -- '*' inside RDS; '0.0.0.0' or a private IP self-hosted

-- Which port (Layer 4)
SHOW port;               -- 5432

-- Who is connected, from which Layer 3 address and Layer 4 port
SELECT pid, usename, client_addr, client_port, state, wait_event_type
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = 'orders';

client_addr tells you which application pod holds the connection. During a connection-exhaustion incident this is the first query you run, because it tells you whether one runaway pod or every pod is hogging connections.

Production scenario

A typical production request path with numbers: a browser in Mumbai calls an API in ap-south-1. DNS 5 ms (cached), TCP handshake 12 ms, TLS 1.3 handshake 12 ms, ALB routing 1 ms, NestJS handling 20 ms including a 4 ms Postgres query, response 6 ms on the wire. About 56 ms total. Move the same user to a us-east-1 deployment and every round trip becomes 220 ms, so the handshake phases alone cost 440 ms before HTTP begins. Layer 3 geography dominates Layer 7 optimisation; this is why we place regions near users and why keep-alive (reusing the connection) is worth more than shaving 2 ms off a query.

Failure scenario

At 09:40 on a Monday, a new deployment moved the checkout service from one Kubernetes node group to another. Every request began failing with ECONNREFUSED from the ALB health checker, the target group went to zero healthy targets, and the ALB started returning 503 to customers. The app logs showed nothing; the app never received any traffic. The cause was Layer 3: the new node group's security group did not allow inbound TCP 3000 from the ALB's security group. No Layer 7 debugging (logs, tracing, code) could have found it. The on-call engineer ran nc -zv <pod-ip> 3000 from a pod in the old node group (success) and from the ALB's subnet (timeout), and fixed the rule in two minutes. Total outage: 14 minutes, mostly spent looking at the wrong layer.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A Layer 4 NLB cannot inject X-Forwarded-For; if you need the client IP behind an NLB you must enable proxy protocol v2 and parse it, or use an ALB.
  • A Layer 7 balancer parses HTTP, so a malformed request (bad chunked encoding, oversized headers) is rejected by the ALB with 400 and never reaches your logs.
  • WebSocket upgrades are a Layer 7 feature that must be supported by every Layer 7 hop; an ALB supports them, some corporate proxies do not.
  • Security groups are stateful: an allowed inbound connection automatically allows its return traffic. Network ACLs are stateless: you must open the ephemeral return port range (1024 to 65535) or replies are dropped silently.
  • MTU mismatch across a VPN or overlay network (Layer 2) causes large packets to vanish while small ones work; health checks pass and real responses hang. See 10.15.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior engineer names the layer before touching the keyboard. "Is this a routing problem, a connection problem, a TLS problem, or an HTTP problem?" Each has a different tool: traceroute or VPC reachability analyzer for Layer 3, nc -zv or ss -tan for Layer 4, openssl s_client for Layer 6, curl -v for Layer 7. They also decide where to put logic deliberately: TLS terminates at the ALB (cheap, central certificate management), rate limiting at the WAF or API gateway (before it costs CPU), business validation in NestJS (where it belongs). Explaining it to a product manager: "The building has a front gate, a receptionist, and your team's office. The gate was locked. Nobody in the office could have fixed it."

Common mistakes

  • Debugging a 503 by adding console.log to the controller when the app never received the request. Check the target group health first.
  • Binding to localhost inside a container.
  • Believing an NLB can route on URL path. It cannot; it only sees ports.
  • Opening 0.0.0.0/0 inbound on the database security group "temporarily" during an incident and forgetting it.
  • Assuming that because curl from your laptop works, the load balancer in another subnet can also reach the pod.

Interview questions

  1. At which layer does an ALB operate, and what can it do that an NLB cannot? Layer 7; it can route by path, host and header, terminate TLS, inject X-Forwarded-For, and return its own 4xx/5xx. Follow-up: when would you still choose an NLB? For raw TCP protocols, extremely high throughput, static IPs, or preserving the client IP without headers.
  2. Your service returns "connection refused" to the load balancer but works with curl localhost inside the pod. Name three causes. Bound to 127.0.0.1; wrong container port mapping; security group blocks the LB's source.
  3. Where does TLS live, and why does that mean your NestJS code cannot see the client certificate when TLS is terminated at the ALB? Layer 6 at the ALB; after termination the request is plain HTTP. The ALB can forward certificate details only in headers if configured for mTLS passthrough or verify mode.
  4. Why are security groups stateful but network ACLs stateless, and what bug does that cause? Security groups track connections and allow replies automatically; NACLs evaluate every packet, so forgetting the ephemeral port range drops replies.
  5. What does encapsulation mean for the size of a packet, and why does a 1,500-byte MTU matter for a 1,460-byte TLS record? Each layer adds headers (IP 20 bytes, TCP 20 to 60 bytes), so the payload that fits in one frame is about 1,460 bytes; anything larger fragments or, with a "don't fragment" flag, is dropped.

Practical exercise

Deploy a small NestJS app in Docker on a cloud VM. Break it deliberately at three different layers and diagnose each only with command-line tools, writing down which command proved which layer: (a) bind it to 127.0.0.1, (b) block the port in the firewall, (c) put an expired self-signed certificate in front with NGINX. Acceptance criteria: for each break you can state the failing layer, the single command that proved it, and the fix, without reading application logs.

10.2 IP addresses, ports, NAT, subnets and CIDR

Concept

An IP address identifies a network interface. A port identifies a process on that interface. Together, (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol) is the 5-tuple that uniquely identifies one TCP connection. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits (10.0.1.15), giving about 4.3 billion addresses; we ran out, so NAT (network address translation) lets many private devices share one public address, and IPv6 (128 bits, 2600:1f18:22a:1b00::5) gives effectively unlimited addresses. A subnet is a contiguous block of addresses described in CIDR notation such as 10.0.1.0/24, where /24 means the first 24 bits are the network and the remaining 8 bits (256 addresses) identify hosts.

Why does it exist?

Ports exist because one machine runs many services: NestJS on 3000, Postgres on 5432, Redis on 6379, and thousands of outbound client connections. Without ports, an IP address could only host one conversation. Subnets exist to group machines and apply rules to groups: "the database subnet accepts traffic only from the application subnet". NAT exists because the world has far more devices than IPv4 addresses, and as a bonus it hides internal topology. CIDR exists because the original class A/B/C address scheme wasted enormous ranges; CIDR lets you carve any power-of-two-sized block.

Mental model

Imagine an office tower. The street address is the IP address. The floor and room number is the port. A subnet is one floor; the building's security policy says "floor 3 (databases) only admits people coming from floor 2 (applications)". NAT is the building's single public phone number: everyone inside can call out, and the receptionist remembers which extension made which call so replies come back to the right desk, but nobody outside can call an extension directly.

How it works

Ports. Ports are 16-bit numbers, 0 to 65535. Ports below 1024 are privileged (a process must run as root to bind them, which is why containers usually bind 3000 or 8080 and let the load balancer own 443). When your NestJS app opens an outbound connection to Postgres, the OS picks a free ephemeral port as the source port. On Linux the default range is 32768 to 60999, so about 28,000 ports.

The 5-tuple and ephemeral port exhaustion. Each outbound connection to the same destination (IP, port) needs a unique source port. If a NestJS pod opens a new TCP connection per request to a payment gateway without keep-alive, and each closed connection sits in TIME_WAIT for 60 seconds (Linux default, see 10.4), then at 500 requests per second you accumulate 30,000 sockets in TIME_WAIT and run out of ephemeral ports. New connections fail with EADDRNOTAVAIL. This is one of the most misdiagnosed production failures: the app is healthy, the gateway is healthy, but every call fails.

CIDR arithmetic. /n means n network bits; hosts = 2^(32-n). AWS reserves 5 addresses per subnet (network, router, DNS, future use, broadcast).

CIDR Addresses Usable in AWS Typical use
/16 65,536 65,531 Whole VPC (10.0.0.0/16)
/20 4,096 4,091 Large Kubernetes pod subnet
/24 256 251 Application subnet per AZ
/27 32 27 Database subnet per AZ
/32 1 1 One host; used in security group rules

NAT. A NAT gateway rewrites the source IP of outbound packets from a private address (10.0.2.40) to its own public elastic IP, records the mapping in a translation table keyed by the 5-tuple, and rewrites replies back. This is source NAT. It is stateful, it has a per-gateway connection limit (an AWS NAT gateway supports about 55,000 simultaneous connections to a single destination, limited by its own ephemeral ports), and it costs money per gigabyte, which is why sending terabytes to S3 through a NAT gateway instead of a VPC gateway endpoint is a classic bill surprise.

A typical VPC design.

flowchart LR
    Internet["Internet"] --> IGW["Internet Gateway"]
    IGW --> ALB["ALB in public subnets 10.0.0.0/24 and 10.0.1.0/24"]
    ALB --> App["NestJS pods in private subnets 10.0.10.0/24 and 10.0.11.0/24"]
    App --> DB["RDS PostgreSQL in isolated subnets 10.0.20.0/27 and 10.0.21.0/27"]
    App --> Redis["ElastiCache Redis in isolated subnets"]
    App --> NAT["NAT Gateway in public subnet"]
    NAT --> IGW
    App --> S3EP["S3 Gateway Endpoint, no NAT cost"]
  • Public subnet: has a route to the internet gateway. Only the load balancer and the NAT gateway live here. Nothing in it should hold data.
  • Private subnet: no direct inbound route from the internet; outbound goes through the NAT gateway. Application pods live here so they can call Stripe or Twilio but cannot be reached directly.
  • Isolated subnet: no route to the internet at all. The database and cache live here. Even if an attacker gets a shell in a pod, exfiltrating a dump requires pivoting through the NAT, which you monitor.

IPv6. IPv6 addresses are written as eight groups of four hex digits with :: compressing consecutive zeros. There is no NAT in IPv6 by design; every device gets a globally routable address, and privacy comes from firewalls, not address hiding. Mobile networks in India, the US and much of Asia are increasingly IPv6-only with a translation layer (NAT64/DNS64) to reach IPv4 services. If your API has only an A record and no AAAA record, those clients reach you through carrier translation that adds latency and occasionally breaks. Publish both, and make sure your logging and rate limiting handle 128-bit addresses (a VARCHAR(15) column for IPs is an IPv6 bug waiting to happen; use INET).

Practical example

A ride-booking backend calls a maps provider for every fare estimate. At launch it used fetch() with a fresh connection per call. Traffic hit 400 estimates per second at the evening peak. Within three minutes, ss -s on the pods showed 28,000 sockets in TIME_WAIT, and calls started failing with connect EADDRNOTAVAIL 10.0.10.14:0. The fix was an HTTP agent with keep-alive and a pool of 50 connections per pod, dropping the connection rate from 400 per second to near zero. The number of ports needed went from 28,000 to 50.

NestJS example

// maps-client.service.ts
import { Injectable, OnModuleDestroy } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Agent, request } from 'undici';

@Injectable()
export class MapsClientService implements OnModuleDestroy {
  // One pooled agent per process. Each pooled socket is one ephemeral port.
  private readonly agent = new Agent({
    connections: 50,          // hard cap on sockets to this origin
    keepAliveTimeout: 30_000, // keep idle sockets 30 s, below the provider's idle limit
    keepAliveMaxTimeout: 60_000,
    connect: { timeout: 3_000 },
  });

  async estimate(originId: string, destId: string): Promise<number> {
    const res = await request('https://maps.example.com/v1/route', {
      method: 'POST',
      dispatcher: this.agent,
      headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ originId, destId }),
      headersTimeout: 2_000,
      bodyTimeout: 2_000,
    });
    if (res.statusCode !== 200) {
      await res.body.dump(); // release the socket back to the pool
      throw new Error(`maps provider returned ${res.statusCode}`);
    }
    const data = (await res.body.json()) as { seconds: number };
    return data.seconds;
  }

  async onModuleDestroy() {
    await this.agent.close(); // drain the pool on shutdown, avoid dangling sockets
  }
}

The important lines are the connections cap (bounded port usage), the keep-alive timeouts (sockets reused instead of churned), and dump() on error paths, because a response body that is never consumed keeps its socket out of the pool.

PostgreSQL example

The database side of the same story: each pod's connection pool is a set of TCP connections from the app subnet to the database subnet. You can see exactly which IP and ephemeral port each one uses, and you can enforce network-level rules with pg_hba.conf in CIDR notation.

-- Count connections per source address (which pod is holding what)
SELECT client_addr, count(*) AS conns,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'idle') AS idle,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'active') AS active
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
GROUP BY client_addr
ORDER BY conns DESC;

-- Store client IPs correctly: INET handles both IPv4 and IPv6, and supports CIDR ops
CREATE TABLE login_audit (
  id         bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id    uuid NOT NULL,
  client_ip  inet NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Find logins from a whole office subnet in one query
SELECT user_id, client_ip, created_at
FROM login_audit
WHERE client_ip <<= '203.0.113.0/24'::cidr
  AND created_at > now() - interval '1 day';

The pg_hba.conf line that enforces "only the application subnets may connect" reads hostssl orders app_user 10.0.10.0/23 scram-sha-256. The /23 covers both 10.0.10.0/24 and 10.0.11.0/24, which is a tidy example of CIDR arithmetic in daily use.

TypeORM example

The TypeORM DataSource options are where the pool size is set, and pool size multiplied by pod count is the number of database-side sockets you consume.

// data-source.ts
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export const AppDataSource = new DataSource({
  type: 'postgres',
  host: process.env.PG_HOST,          // a private DNS name, never a public IP
  port: Number(process.env.PG_PORT ?? 5432),
  username: process.env.PG_USER,
  password: process.env.PG_PASSWORD,
  database: 'orders',
  ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: true },
  extra: {
    max: 10,                          // 10 pods x 10 = 100 sockets at the database
    idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,        // release idle sockets so ports and PG backends free up
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000,   // fail fast when the pool is exhausted
    keepAlive: true,                  // TCP keepalive probes (see 4.4) through NAT and LBs
  },
  entities: [__dirname + '/**/*.entity.js'],
});

Sequelize example

// sequelize.config.ts
import { Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export const sequelize = new Sequelize(process.env.PG_DATABASE!, process.env.PG_USER!, process.env.PG_PASSWORD!, {
  host: process.env.PG_HOST,
  port: 5432,
  dialect: 'postgres',
  dialectOptions: {
    ssl: { require: true, rejectUnauthorized: true },
    keepAlive: true,
  },
  pool: {
    max: 10,       // same maths: pods x max must stay under PG max_connections
    min: 2,
    idle: 30_000,  // ms before an idle socket is closed
    acquire: 5_000 // ms to wait for a free socket before throwing
  },
  logging: false,
});

Production scenario

A payments service with 20 pods, each pooling 10 connections, holds 200 sockets to a Postgres instance whose max_connections is 200. That leaves zero connections for migrations, PgBouncer, or the on-call engineer's psql. Real numbers from a mid-sized e-commerce system: max_connections = 500, a PgBouncer layer in front doing transaction pooling, and application pools sized at 5 per pod. The NAT gateway in the same account moved 40 TB per month to S3 before someone added a gateway endpoint; the NAT data processing charge alone was about 1,800 USD a month, reduced to zero by a single route table entry.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 on a Saturday the on-call was paged: "checkout error rate 38%". Pods were healthy, CPU was 20%, the database was idle. Logs showed connect EADDRNOTAVAIL on calls to the fraud-scoring service. ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l on a pod returned 27,900. A colleague had "simplified" the fraud client the previous afternoon by replacing a pooled agent with bare axios calls and no agent, so every call opened and closed a TCP connection. At 450 calls per second, ports ran out in under a minute of peak traffic. The rollback restored the pooled agent; the follow-up added a Prometheus alert on node_sockstat_TCP_tw (sockets in TIME_WAIT) above 15,000.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Ephemeral port exhaustion is per (source IP, destination IP, destination port); one destination that receives all your traffic hits the limit first.
  • net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1 lets Linux reuse TIME_WAIT sockets for new outbound connections safely; tcp_tw_recycle was removed in Linux 4.12 because it broke clients behind NAT.
  • A NAT gateway's own ephemeral port pool is shared by every pod behind it; 20 pods each churning connections to the same SaaS endpoint can exhaust the gateway even when each pod is fine. Symptom: ErrorPortAllocation metric on the NAT gateway.
  • Overlapping CIDR ranges between two VPCs make peering impossible; plan 10.0.0.0/16 versus 10.1.0.0/16 from day one.
  • Kubernetes pods each get an IP from a pod CIDR; a /24 node subnet with 30 pods per node needs a separate, larger pod range or nodes stop scheduling with "insufficient IP addresses".
  • Storing IPs in VARCHAR(15) truncates IPv6 addresses (up to 45 characters); use INET.
  • Rate limiting per IP behind carrier-grade NAT throttles thousands of legitimate mobile users who share one public IPv4 address.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They budget ports and connections like memory: pods multiplied by pool size, plus per-request outbound fan-out, compared against max_connections, NAT capacity and the ephemeral range. They design the VPC so that the blast radius of a compromised pod is small: three subnet tiers, no public IPs on anything that holds data, and egress through a NAT they can monitor and, in an emergency, cut. They refuse to whitelist 0.0.0.0/0 on a data tier. To a product manager: "The database is in a room with no windows and one door, and only the application floor has a key. That is why the fix for the compromised laptop last month was a one-line firewall change rather than a data breach notification."

Common mistakes

  • Creating a new HTTP client or Pool per request. Every one of those is a port and a handshake.
  • Sizing every pod's pool at 50 "to be safe" and then wondering why Postgres refuses connections at 10 pods.
  • Putting the database in a public subnet with a security group "so it is easy to connect from home".
  • Ignoring IPv6 until a mobile carrier's users report timeouts.
  • Routing S3 and DynamoDB traffic through the NAT gateway.

Interview questions

  1. What is the 5-tuple, and why does it explain ephemeral port exhaustion? Source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol; each new connection to the same destination needs a fresh source port, and TIME_WAIT holds ports for 60 s, so high connection churn to one destination exhausts about 28,000 ports.
  2. How many usable addresses are in a /27 AWS subnet, and would you use it for a Kubernetes node subnet? 27 usable; no, pods need many IPs per node, use /20 or larger pod ranges.
  3. Why do we put the database in a private or isolated subnet even though it has a password? Defence in depth: credentials leak, zero-days happen, and a subnet without an internet route makes exfiltration and brute force far harder. Follow-up: how do you run migrations then? From a pod or a bastion inside the VPC, through CI runners with VPC access.
  4. Explain source NAT and one operational limit of a cloud NAT gateway. Rewrites private source addresses to a public one and tracks the mapping; limited to about 55,000 concurrent connections per destination, with a ErrorPortAllocation metric when exceeded.
  5. A mobile carrier's users report timeouts to your API but desktop users are fine. What do you check? Whether you publish an AAAA record and whether your stack (ALB dualstack, WAF rules, IP parsing, rate-limit keys) handles IPv6.

Practical exercise

On a Linux VM, write a small Node script that makes 50,000 sequential HTTP requests to a local server with Connection: close, watching ss -s in another terminal. Record when EADDRNOTAVAIL appears. Then repeat with a keep-alive agent and record the socket count. Acceptance criteria: you can explain the two socket counts, you can calculate the maximum connection rate your ephemeral range supports at a 60-second TIME_WAIT, and you can name the sysctl that would let you reuse TIME_WAIT sockets safely.

10.3 DNS: turning names into addresses

Concept

DNS (Domain Name System) is the distributed database that maps names such as api.fooddash.com to IP addresses such as 52.14.9.2. Every request from a browser, every call from your NestJS app to Postgres by hostname, every Kubernetes service call to orders-service.default.svc.cluster.local, starts with a DNS lookup. DNS is the first network operation in every request path, and because of that it is also the first thing that can be slow, wrong or stale.

The record types you will meet as a backend engineer:

Record Maps Backend use
A name to IPv4 address api.fooddash.com -> 52.14.9.2
AAAA name to IPv6 address dual-stack endpoints
CNAME name to another name api.fooddash.com -> my-alb-123.ap-south-1.elb.amazonaws.com
ALIAS / Route 53 alias apex name to an AWS resource fooddash.com -> ALB (CNAMEs are not allowed at the zone apex)
SRV service to host and port Kubernetes headless services, Consul
TXT arbitrary text domain verification, SPF, ACME challenges for TLS certificates
NS delegation to name servers which servers are authoritative for a zone

Why does it exist?

IP addresses change. Load balancers get replaced, databases fail over to a replica with a different address, and Kubernetes pods are born and die by the minute. Humans and configuration files need a stable name. DNS provides the indirection: your code holds PG_HOST=orders-db.internal, and an operator can swap the machine behind it without a deployment. Without DNS you would hard-code addresses, and every failover would need a code change.

Mental model

Imagine asking for a shop's address. You first check your own memory (browser cache). Then your phone's contacts (OS resolver cache). Then you call a friend who knows everyone (the recursive resolver, such as your ISP's or 8.8.8.8). If the friend does not know, they call the city directory (root servers) to find who handles .com, then the .com registry to find who handles fooddash.com, then finally the company's own switchboard (the authoritative name server) that gives the address. Everyone along the way writes the answer down with an expiry date (the TTL, time to live) so the next person asking gets it faster.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant OS as OS resolver
    participant R as Recursive resolver
    participant Root as Root servers
    participant TLD as com TLD servers
    participant Auth as Route53 authoritative
    B->>B: check browser cache for api.fooddash.com
    B->>OS: getaddrinfo api.fooddash.com
    OS->>OS: check hosts file and OS cache
    OS->>R: query A api.fooddash.com
    R->>R: check resolver cache
    R->>Root: who serves com
    Root-->>R: NS for com
    R->>TLD: who serves fooddash.com
    TLD-->>R: NS for fooddash.com at Route53
    R->>Auth: A api.fooddash.com
    Auth-->>R: 52.14.9.2 TTL 60
    R-->>OS: 52.14.9.2
    OS-->>B: 52.14.9.2
  1. Browser cache. Chrome keeps resolved names for about 60 seconds regardless of TTL. First hit: 0 ms.
  2. OS resolver. The operating system checks /etc/hosts, then its own cache (systemd-resolved on Linux, the DNS Client service on Windows). Typically under 1 ms.
  3. Recursive resolver. Configured in /etc/resolv.conf (in Kubernetes this is CoreDNS at the cluster IP; in a VPC it is the Amazon-provided resolver at the VPC base address plus two, for example 10.0.0.2). If it has a cached answer, 1 to 5 ms. If not, it performs the full recursion.
  4. Recursion. Root servers (13 logical addresses, hundreds of anycast instances) point to the .com servers, which point to the authoritative servers for fooddash.com. A cold recursion costs 30 to 120 ms.
  5. Authoritative answer. Route 53 returns the record with its TTL. Every cache on the path stores it for at most TTL seconds.
  6. TTL expiry. After TTL seconds, the next query repeats step 3 onwards. A TTL of 60 seconds means a change propagates within about a minute to well-behaved resolvers; a TTL of 86,400 (one day) means yesterday's address may be served for a day.

DNS normally travels over UDP port 53 in a single packet each way (limited to 512 bytes classically, larger with EDNS0). Answers that do not fit fall back to TCP. DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) encrypt the query for privacy but change nothing about resolution logic.

DNS in Node.js. Node has two ways to resolve a name and they behave very differently:

  • dns.lookup() calls the OS function getaddrinfo(). That call is synchronous and blocking, so libuv runs it on the threadpool (default size 4). It respects /etc/hosts, the OS cache and resolv.conf search domains. It is what http.request, net.connect, pg and ioredis use by default.
  • dns.resolve() and the dns.Resolver class talk to DNS servers directly using c-ares, fully asynchronously, on the event loop. They ignore /etc/hosts and the OS cache.

The threadpool detail matters. If your NestJS app makes 200 concurrent outbound HTTP calls and each triggers a dns.lookup, only 4 can resolve at a time; the rest queue. Under a slow resolver (say 100 ms), 200 lookups take 200 divided by 4 times 100 ms, which is 5 seconds. Worse, the same threadpool serves fs operations, crypto.pbkdf2, zlib compression, and every other blocking libuv task, so slow DNS starves file reads and password hashing. Symptoms: high event-loop lag with idle CPU.

Node does not cache DNS results by itself. Every http.request without a keep-alive agent performs a fresh dns.lookup. With keep-alive, the socket is reused and no lookup happens. Since Node 20, autoSelectFamily (Happy Eyeballs) tries IPv6 and IPv4 in parallel with a 250 ms gap so one broken family does not stall connections.

Service discovery in Kubernetes. Every Service gets a DNS name <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local served by CoreDNS, resolving to the service's stable ClusterIP. kube-proxy then load balances that virtual IP to pod IPs with iptables or IPVS rules, so the DNS answer stays stable while pods churn. Headless services (clusterIP: None) return the pod IPs directly as multiple A records, which is how StatefulSets (Postgres operators, Kafka) address individual members. A common trap: resolv.conf inside a pod has ndots:5, meaning any name with fewer than five dots is first tried with each search domain appended. Calling api.stripe.com from a pod generates lookups for api.stripe.com.default.svc.cluster.local, api.stripe.com.svc.cluster.local, api.stripe.com.cluster.local, and only then api.stripe.com; four wasted queries per call. Use a trailing dot (api.stripe.com.) or set dnsConfig.options ndots: 2.

Route 53 basics. Route 53 is AWS's authoritative DNS. Hosted zones hold records; routing policies decide which answer to give: simple, weighted (canary 5% of traffic to a new region), latency-based (answer with the region closest to the resolver), failover (primary with a health check, secondary when it fails), and geolocation. Alias records point at ALBs, CloudFront and S3 with no TTL cost because Route 53 resolves them internally. Health checks poll an endpoint every 10 or 30 seconds from multiple locations and flip failover records when the majority fail. Private hosted zones give internal names such as orders-db.internal to resources in a VPC.

Practical example

An e-commerce platform runs api.shop.com as a Route 53 alias to an ALB in ap-south-1 and a failover record pointing to eu-west-1. Inside the VPC, orders-db.internal is a private zone CNAME to the RDS endpoint orders-prod.cluster-abc.ap-south-1.rds.amazonaws.com, which RDS itself updates on failover. The NestJS pods resolve orders-db.internal once per pool connection; because the pool holds connections for many minutes, DNS is barely visible in traces. The outbound Stripe client uses a keep-alive agent, so api.stripe.com is resolved a handful of times per hour per pod rather than on every payment.

NestJS example

Two production-grade practices in one service: a resolver-backed cache for outbound hostnames so the libuv threadpool is never a DNS bottleneck, and a health indicator that verifies the database hostname still resolves (an early signal after a failover with stale caches).

// dns-cache.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { LookupFunction } from 'net';
import { Resolver } from 'dns/promises';

interface CacheEntry { addresses: string[]; expiresAt: number; }

@Injectable()
export class DnsCacheService {
  private readonly resolver = new Resolver(); // async c-ares, not the threadpool
  private readonly cache = new Map<string, CacheEntry>();

  // A lookup function compatible with http.Agent and undici's connect option.
  readonly lookup: LookupFunction = (hostname, _options, callback) => {
    const hit = this.cache.get(hostname);
    if (hit && hit.expiresAt > Date.now()) {
      return callback(null, hit.addresses[0], 4);
    }
    this.resolver.resolve4(hostname, { ttl: true })
      .then((records) => {
        const minTtl = Math.max(5, Math.min(...records.map((r) => r.ttl)));
        const addresses = records.map((r) => r.address);
        // Never cache longer than the authoritative TTL, and never below 5 s.
        this.cache.set(hostname, { addresses, expiresAt: Date.now() + minTtl * 1000 });
        callback(null, addresses[0], 4);
      })
      .catch((err) => {
        // Serve stale on resolver failure rather than failing the request outright.
        if (hit) return callback(null, hit.addresses[0], 4);
        callback(err as NodeJS.ErrnoException, '', 4);
      });
  };
}
// health.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HealthCheck, HealthCheckService, TypeOrmHealthIndicator } from '@nestjs/terminus';
import { lookup } from 'dns/promises';

@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  constructor(private health: HealthCheckService, private db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator) {}

  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    return this.health.check([
      () => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 1500 }),
      async () => {
        // Fails readiness if the DB name stops resolving (private zone deleted, resolver down).
        const { address } = await lookup(process.env.PG_HOST!);
        return { dns: { status: 'up', address } };
      },
    ]);
  }
}

Wire the cached lookup into an agent with new http.Agent({ keepAlive: true, lookup: dnsCache.lookup }) or into undici with new Agent({ connect: { lookup: dnsCache.lookup } }). Respecting the TTL is the whole point: a cache that ignores TTL is exactly the failover bug described below.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL itself is a DNS client (for replication and dblink) and a DNS subject (its hostname is what your pool resolves). The most useful DNS-related SQL is checking where your connections actually landed after a failover, which tells you whether stale DNS is still pointing writers at the old primary.

-- Am I connected to the primary or a replica? After a failover, a pool that
-- resolved the old address may still be talking to what is now a read replica.
SELECT inet_server_addr() AS server_ip,
       inet_server_port() AS server_port,
       pg_is_in_recovery() AS is_replica;

-- Writes on a replica fail with this error, which is the classic stale-DNS symptom:
-- ERROR: cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction

RDS Multi-AZ failover works by updating the DNS record of the cluster endpoint to the new primary with a 5-second TTL. Any client that cached the old address for longer, or that holds open connections to the old host, keeps writing to a machine that is now read-only until the connection is dropped. Well-behaved drivers see the connection reset, discard the pooled socket, and resolve again.

TypeORM example

TypeORM does not resolve DNS itself; the pg driver does through dns.lookup. What you control is how quickly a stale connection is discarded after a failover. Set connection and query timeouts so a dead primary does not hang the pool for minutes.

// data-source.ts (excerpt)
export const AppDataSource = new DataSource({
  type: 'postgres',
  host: 'orders-db.internal', // private hosted zone CNAME to the RDS cluster endpoint
  extra: {
    max: 10,
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 3_000,   // stale IP + SYN timeout would otherwise take 2 minutes
    idleTimeoutMillis: 20_000,        // idle sockets die soon, forcing a fresh DNS lookup
    statement_timeout: 10_000,        // a query stuck on a dead node fails in 10 s
    keepAlive: true,
    keepAliveInitialDelayMillis: 10_000,
  },
});

The idleTimeoutMillis choice is a DNS decision in disguise: the shorter it is, the sooner every connection is rebuilt with a fresh lookup after a failover. Ten to thirty seconds is a sensible balance.

Sequelize example

Sequelize supports read replication with separate hostnames, which means two DNS names and two failover behaviours to think about. Point the replica entry at the RDS reader endpoint, whose DNS answer rotates across replicas.

import { Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export const sequelize = new Sequelize('orders', process.env.PG_USER!, process.env.PG_PASSWORD!, {
  dialect: 'postgres',
  replication: {
    write: { host: 'orders-db.internal' },            // cluster writer endpoint via private zone
    read: [{ host: 'orders-db-ro.internal' }],        // reader endpoint; DNS round-robins replicas
  },
  pool: { max: 10, min: 1, idle: 20_000, acquire: 3_000 },
  dialectOptions: { keepAlive: true, statement_timeout: 10_000 },
});

Production scenario

Numbers from a real mid-sized deployment: 40 pods, each with a pool of 8 connections, reconnecting on a 20-second idle timeout, generate about 100 DNS queries per minute to CoreDNS for the database name. CoreDNS in a small cluster comfortably answers 10,000 queries per second, so the load is trivial. The place DNS did hurt was the ndots:5 problem: a notification service calling api.sendgrid.com 300 times per second was generating 1,500 DNS queries per second, and CoreDNS latency climbed to 40 ms under the load, which added 160 ms per outbound call. A trailing dot on the hostname cut CoreDNS traffic by 80% and the p95 of the notification path fell from 420 ms to 190 ms.

Failure scenario

At 03:52 the primary RDS instance in ap-south-1a failed. RDS promoted the standby in 1b and updated the cluster endpoint DNS within 40 seconds. Half the fleet recovered. The other half kept logging cannot execute UPDATE in a read-only transaction for 31 minutes. Those pods ran an older base image whose resolv.conf pointed at a sidecar DNS cache configured with a minimum TTL of 30 minutes "to reduce DNS load". It served the old primary's address long after Route 53 said otherwise. Because the old instance came back as a replica, connections succeeded and reads worked, so health checks passed and nothing was restarted. The fix during the incident was a rolling restart of the affected deployment; the permanent fix removed the minimum-TTL override and added a synthetic check that performs a tiny write every 30 seconds and alerts on read-only transaction.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Stale TTL after failover: any cache that enforces a floor on TTL (Java's old default of caching forever, custom sidecars, some corporate resolvers) sends traffic to dead or demoted addresses.
  • Negative caching: a resolver that saw NXDOMAIN for a freshly created name caches the "does not exist" answer for the zone's negative TTL (often 300 to 900 seconds). A new subdomain "not working" for 10 minutes after creation is usually this.
  • Threadpool starvation: hundreds of concurrent dns.lookup calls with a slow resolver block file reads and bcrypt hashing. Increase UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (up to 1024) or use a resolver-backed cache.
  • ndots:5 amplification in Kubernetes: four wasted queries per external call.
  • Search domain hijack: with ndots, a typo'd hostname can resolve to an unexpected internal service.
  • UDP truncation: answers with many records exceed 512 bytes, fall back to TCP, and a firewall that only allows UDP 53 causes intermittent failures.
  • Round-robin surprise: multiple A records are returned in rotating order; dns.lookup returns the first, so one pod may hammer one backend.
  • Resolver outage: if CoreDNS pods are evicted or the VPC resolver is throttled (1,024 packets per second per network interface in AWS), every new connection in the cluster fails at once. Monitor CoreDNS latency and error rate as a tier-0 service.
  • Split-horizon confusion: the same name resolves to a public IP from a laptop and a private IP from inside the VPC; debugging from the wrong side gives wrong conclusions.
  • Clock and TTL: a TTL is relative to when the cache stored the answer; it does not depend on wall-clock synchronisation, but health-check based failover does depend on the checker's view of time.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat DNS as a tier-0 dependency with its own SLO and dashboards, because when it fails everything fails at once. They choose TTLs deliberately: 60 seconds for records that participate in failover, longer (300 to 3,600) for stable records to reduce resolver load. They never cache DNS longer than the TTL, and they never cache "forever". They know that a failover plan that relies on DNS is only as fast as the slowest cache between the client and the authority, so for the database they also rely on connection-level detection: short connect timeouts, statement_timeout, and drivers that discard sockets on read-only transaction errors. They ask: "If this name changes at 03:00, which components will notice, and how long will it take?" To a product manager: "Changing an address in the phone book does not help if half the office keeps using the number written on a sticky note."

Common mistakes

  • Hard-coding IP addresses in environment variables "because DNS is slow".
  • Caching DNS results in application memory with no expiry.
  • Not knowing that dns.lookup is threadpool-bound, then blaming the event loop for a resolver outage.
  • Forgetting the trailing dot or ndots setting in Kubernetes, quadrupling CoreDNS load.
  • Using a CNAME at the zone apex (shop.com), which is not allowed; use a Route 53 alias record.
  • Setting a 24-hour TTL on the API record and then needing to move the load balancer in an emergency.
  • Exposing the RDS endpoint name publicly and relying on a security group alone; use a private zone and no public accessibility.

Interview questions

  1. Walk through what happens when a browser resolves api.shop.com for the first time. Browser cache, OS cache and hosts file, recursive resolver cache, root then TLD then authoritative servers, answer cached with TTL at every hop. Why it matters: it explains both the 100 ms cold-start penalty and why changes take TTL seconds to propagate. Follow-up: where do you put a CDN in this path?
  2. Why does dns.lookup in Node use the libuv threadpool, and what production problem does that cause? It wraps the blocking getaddrinfo OS call; with a slow resolver, the four default threads become a queue, starving fs, zlib and crypto tasks. Follow-up: how do you fix it? Keep-alive agents so lookups are rare, a TTL-respecting resolver cache, or a larger UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE.
  3. Your RDS instance failed over but a subset of pods still fail writes 20 minutes later. What happened? A DNS cache with a TTL floor, or long-lived pooled connections to the old host now serving as a replica. Follow-up: name two defences. Idle timeouts to force reconnection, and driver-level handling of read-only errors.
