  4. What is ndots:5 and why does it matter for a service making many external calls? Kubernetes appends search domains to names with fewer than five dots, causing up to four failed lookups before the correct one.
  5. How would you canary a new region using DNS alone, and what is the catch? Route 53 weighted records at 5%; the catch is that resolvers cache, so the split is approximate and rollbacks take TTL seconds.
  6. What does a Kubernetes Service DNS name resolve to, and how does a headless service differ? A stable ClusterIP that kube-proxy load balances; headless returns pod IPs directly, used for stateful members.

Practical exercise

Build a small NestJS service that calls an external API 200 times concurrently. Measure the p95 latency with dns.lookup defaults and UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=4, then with a keep-alive agent, then with a TTL-respecting resolver cache. Point the service at a hostname you control, lower its TTL to 30 seconds, change the record, and time how long the service takes to follow the change under each configuration. Acceptance criteria: a table of p95 latencies and propagation times for the three setups, and a one-paragraph explanation of why the keep-alive agent changes both numbers.

10.4 TCP and UDP: the transport layer

10.4.1 TCP: a reliable, ordered byte stream

Concept

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) gives two processes a reliable, ordered byte stream over an unreliable network. You write bytes in one end; they come out the other end in the same order, with nothing missing and nothing duplicated, or the connection reports an error. TCP has no idea what a "message" or an "HTTP request" is. It only knows bytes. Framing (where one request ends and the next begins) is the application protocol's job, which is why HTTP has Content-Length and chunked encoding.

UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is the opposite: fire-and-forget datagrams with no ordering, no retransmission, no connection. It is used where speed matters more than completeness (video, games, DNS, and now HTTP/3 via QUIC).

Why does it exist?

IP delivers packets one hop at a time and makes no promises: packets can be lost, duplicated, reordered or corrupted. A database protocol or an HTTP request cannot tolerate that. TCP adds sequence numbers, acknowledgements, retransmission, checksums, flow control (do not overwhelm the receiver) and congestion control (do not overwhelm the network). Every backend protocol you use daily (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, Postgres, Redis, Kafka, gRPC, SMTP) rides on TCP because they all need "every byte, in order".

Mental model

Imagine dictating a long contract over a bad phone line. You number every sentence. The listener repeats back "got up to sentence 42". If you do not hear that within a few seconds, you repeat sentence 43 onwards. You also ask "how many sentences can you write down before you need a break?" (the receive window) and you speak slower when you notice you are being asked to repeat too often (congestion control). That is TCP.

How it works

  1. Segments and sequence numbers. The byte stream is cut into segments, each stamped with the sequence number of its first byte. The receiver acknowledges the next byte it expects (ACK 4381 means "I have everything up to byte 4380").
  2. Retransmission. If an ACK does not arrive before the retransmission timeout (RTO, initially about 1 second, then adapted to the measured round trip), the sender resends. Three duplicate ACKs trigger a faster "fast retransmit".
  3. Flow control: the receive window. The receiver advertises how many bytes it can still buffer (rwnd). The sender never has more than that many unacknowledged bytes in flight. Linux auto-tunes buffers up to several megabytes; with window scaling, the window can exceed the original 64 KB limit.
  4. Congestion control. The sender maintains a congestion window (cwnd), starting small (10 segments, about 14 KB, in modern Linux) and growing each round trip (slow start) until loss is detected, then backing off. Throughput on a fresh connection is limited by cwnd, not by bandwidth: a 1 MB response over a 100 ms RTT link needs about 7 round trips just for slow start to ramp up, roughly 700 ms before bandwidth even matters. This is the second reason keep-alive matters: a warm connection has an already-grown cwnd.
  5. Nagle's algorithm. To avoid sending many tiny packets, TCP by default holds small writes until either a full segment accumulates or the previous segment is acknowledged. Combined with delayed ACKs on the receiver (waits up to 40 ms to piggyback an ACK), this can add 40 ms to every small write-then-wait exchange. Node sets socket.setNoDelay(true) by default on HTTP sockets since v12; for raw net.Socket and some drivers you must set it explicitly. A Redis client doing thousands of small commands per second with Nagle enabled is measurably slower.
  6. Bandwidth-delay product. The maximum throughput of one connection is window / RTT. A 64 KB window over a 100 ms RTT gives at most 640 KB per second regardless of the link speed. Cross-region replication and large S3 uploads need big windows or parallel streams.

UDP and QUIC. UDP adds only ports and a checksum to IP. It is the foundation for DNS (one packet each way, no handshake), NTP, video and voice, and QUIC, the transport under HTTP/3. QUIC re-implements TCP's reliability in user space on top of UDP, adding per-stream ordering (no head-of-line blocking across streams), built-in TLS 1.3, and connection IDs that survive a change of client IP address. You will meet UDP in a NestJS system through DNS, through StatsD metrics (hot-shots sends UDP datagrams that are dropped rather than queued when the collector is slow, which is exactly what you want from a metrics path), and through CloudFront or an HTTP/3-capable edge in front of your API.

Practical example

An inventory service streams a 40 MB CSV export to a client in another region. With a cold connection: DNS, handshake, TLS, then slow start ramps cwnd from 14 KB up over about 10 round trips at 150 ms each, and only then does the transfer approach link speed. Total: about 4 seconds, of which 1.5 seconds was TCP warming up. With a warm keep-alive connection from a previous request, the same export finishes in about 2.5 seconds. Nothing in the application changed.

NestJS example

Where you touch TCP from NestJS: the HTTP server's socket options, a raw TCP microservice transport, and driver keep-alive settings. Here is a NestJS TCP microservice consumer with explicit socket tuning, plus the server-side socket handling for the HTTP app.

// main.ts (excerpt): tune the HTTP server's TCP behaviour
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { Server } from 'http';
import { Socket } from 'net';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  const server: Server = app.getHttpServer();

  server.on('connection', (socket: Socket) => {
    socket.setNoDelay(true);              // disable Nagle: small JSON responses go out immediately
    socket.setKeepAlive(true, 30_000);    // TCP keepalive probes after 30 s idle (see 4.4.3)
  });

  // Reject clients that never finish sending headers (slowloris; see 4.15)
  server.headersTimeout = 30_000;
  server.requestTimeout = 60_000;

  await app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0');
}
bootstrap();
// inventory.module.ts: a NestJS TCP transport client for an internal service
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ClientsModule, Transport } from '@nestjs/microservices';

@Module({
  imports: [
    ClientsModule.register([
      {
        name: 'PRICING_SERVICE',
        transport: Transport.TCP,
        options: { host: 'pricing.internal', port: 4010 },
      },
    ]),
  ],
})
export class InventoryModule {}

The NestJS TCP transport frames messages itself (length-prefixed JSON) precisely because TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries. If you ever write a raw net.Server, you must do that framing yourself; assuming one data event equals one message is the classic bug that works on localhost and breaks in production when segments coalesce or split.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL's wire protocol is a byte stream of typed messages over TCP. The server exposes its TCP keepalive settings so idle connections through a NAT or load balancer stay alive, and it enforces its own idle timeouts.

-- Server-side TCP keepalive (seconds); 0 means "use the OS default"
SHOW tcp_keepalives_idle;      -- e.g. 60: probe after 60 s of silence
SHOW tcp_keepalives_interval;  -- e.g. 10: retry every 10 s
SHOW tcp_keepalives_count;     -- e.g. 6: give up after 6 failed probes

-- Kill sessions that sit idle inside a transaction holding locks (a client that
-- died mid-transaction behind a NAT can hold row locks for hours otherwise)
ALTER SYSTEM SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

-- Find such sessions right now
SELECT pid, client_addr, state, now() - state_change AS idle_for, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
ORDER BY idle_for DESC;

Production scenario

A pricing service handles 3,000 requests per second, each doing five Redis GETs. With Nagle enabled on the Redis client socket, p50 latency was 43 ms; with setNoDelay(true) (ioredis sets it by default, but a custom wrapper had disabled it) p50 dropped to 2.1 ms. The 40 ms was the delayed-ACK timer interacting with Nagle: a textbook case that still appears in production every year.

Failure scenario

A reporting service opened a raw TCP socket to a legacy fixed-width-record server and parsed each data event as one record. It passed every test. In production, records were sometimes truncated or merged, roughly once per few thousand. TCP had split a 512-byte record across two segments at an MTU boundary, and at other times coalesced two records into one read. The fix was a proper framing buffer: accumulate bytes, emit complete 512-byte records, keep the remainder.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Message boundaries do not exist in TCP; framing bugs surface only under real network conditions.
  • A large receive window with a slow consumer means megabytes buffered in kernel memory per connection; 10,000 slow clients can exhaust socket memory.
  • Slow start after idle: Linux resets cwnd after an idle period (tcp_slow_start_after_idle = 1), so even a keep-alive connection ramps again after a few hundred milliseconds of silence.
  • Nagle plus delayed ACK adds 40 ms on write-write-read patterns.
  • UDP has no backpressure; a metrics library sending 100,000 datagrams per second silently drops what the receiver cannot take.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know that a "fast network" does not make a fresh connection fast; round trips and slow start do. They reuse connections, keep them warm, and think in RTTs rather than megabits. They insist on framing when writing raw TCP, and they choose UDP only when losing data is acceptable (metrics, telemetry, media). To a product manager: "Opening a new phone call for every sentence is slower than keeping the line open, no matter how fast people talk."

Common mistakes

  • Treating socket.on('data') chunks as messages.
  • Disabling setNoDelay "to batch packets" and then measuring 40 ms floors.
  • Expecting one TCP connection to saturate a 10 Gbps cross-region link.
  • Using UDP for anything that must not be lost.

Interview questions

  1. What guarantees does TCP give, and what does it not give? Reliable, ordered, duplicate-free byte delivery with flow and congestion control; no message boundaries, no latency bound, no guarantee the peer is alive right now.
  2. Explain the bandwidth-delay product and why cross-region transfers are slow on one connection. Throughput is at most window divided by RTT; 64 KB over 100 ms is 640 KB per second.
  3. Why can setNoDelay(true) reduce latency by 40 ms? Nagle waits for an ACK before sending another small segment; delayed ACK waits up to 40 ms; together they stall request-response protocols.
  4. When would you pick UDP for a backend feature? Metrics, logs where loss is acceptable, real-time media, and via QUIC for HTTP/3 at the edge.
  5. What does slow start mean for a keep-alive connection that has been idle 5 seconds? Linux resets the congestion window after idle, so the first response ramps again; tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0 disables that on servers you control.

Practical exercise

Write a raw net server that receives length-prefixed JSON messages, and a client that sends 10,000 messages of random sizes between 10 bytes and 100 KB as fast as possible. Verify every message arrives intact, then break your framing on purpose and observe the failure. Acceptance criteria: a framing buffer that handles split and merged segments, a test that sends a message one byte at a time, and a measurement of throughput with and without setNoDelay.

10.4.2 The three-way handshake and why connection pooling exists

Concept

Before any data flows, TCP performs a three-way handshake: the client sends SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK, the client sends ACK. It costs one full round trip before the first byte of application data can be sent. With TLS on top, another round trip (TLS 1.3) or two (TLS 1.2) follow. Every new connection pays this tax, which is why keep-alive, connection pooling and HTTP/2 multiplexing exist: they pay once and reuse.

Why does it exist?

Both sides need to agree on starting sequence numbers, window sizes, and options (window scaling, selective ACK, MSS) before either can trust an acknowledgement. The random initial sequence number also protects against stale packets from an earlier connection being accepted by mistake and against blind spoofing.

Mental model

Imagine a phone call. You dial (SYN). The other side picks up and says "hello?" (SYN-ACK). You say "hi, it's me" (ACK). Only now can you start talking. On a local call that takes a fraction of a second. On a satellite line with a two-second delay, it takes several seconds before either of you says anything useful. Now imagine hanging up and redialling for every single sentence.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as NestJS server
    Note over C,S: RTT is 100 ms cross region
    C->>S: SYN seq=1000 options MSS window scale SACK
    Note right of S: server queues in SYN backlog
    S->>C: SYN-ACK seq=5000 ack=1001
    C->>S: ACK ack=5001
    Note over C,S: 1 RTT elapsed, connection ESTABLISHED
    C->>S: TLS ClientHello or first HTTP bytes can ride on this ACK
    Note over C,S: TLS 1.3 adds 1 more RTT, HTTP request adds 1 RTT
    S->>C: HTTP response after about 3 RTT total = 300 ms plus server time
  1. The client picks an ephemeral port and a random initial sequence number, and sends SYN.
  2. The server's kernel, not Node, receives it. If the listen socket's SYN backlog is full, the SYN is dropped (or answered with a SYN cookie). Node never knows.
  3. The server replies SYN-ACK. The half-open connection now sits in the SYN queue.
  4. The client replies ACK. The connection moves to the accept queue (backlog argument of server.listen, default 511 in Node). The client can send data immediately with the ACK.
  5. Node's event loop calls accept(), pops the connection, and emits connection. If Node is busy (event-loop lag), connections wait in the accept queue; if the queue fills, the kernel drops further ACKs and clients see timeouts, not errors.

Cost per new connection, typical numbers:

Scenario RTT Handshake TLS 1.3 Total before first HTTP byte
Pod to pod, same AZ 0.3 ms 0.3 ms 0.6 ms about 1 ms plus CPU for crypto
Client to ALB, same region 10 ms 10 ms 10 ms 20 ms
Mobile 4G to same region 50 ms 50 ms 50 ms 100 ms
Cross continent 150 ms 150 ms 150 ms 300 ms

TLS adds CPU too: an RSA-2048 handshake costs about 1 to 2 ms of CPU on the server, ECDSA about a quarter of that. At 1,000 new connections per second that is a full CPU core doing nothing but handshakes. With keep-alive, 1,000 requests per second might need 20 handshakes per second.

TCP Fast Open and TLS session resumption / 0-RTT exist to skip parts of this on repeat connections, but they are edge optimisations; the real win is reuse.

Practical example

A checkout page issues 30 API calls on load. Without keep-alive, over a 50 ms mobile RTT, that is 30 handshakes at 100 ms each; because browsers cap at 6 connections per host on HTTP/1.1, the handshake cost alone spreads across 5 waves, about 500 ms. With HTTP/2 on the ALB, one handshake serves all 30 calls: 100 ms once.

NestJS example

The server side of the handshake you control is the accept backlog and how fast you drain it. On the client side, pooling is what avoids the handshake entirely.

// main.ts (excerpt)
const server = app.getHttpServer();
// Accept queue size: bursts of new connections beyond this are dropped by the kernel.
await app.listen({ port: 3000, host: '0.0.0.0', backlog: 1024 } as never);

app.listen in NestJS accepts the same arguments as server.listen, so the object form with backlog works; the as never cast only silences the TypeScript overload for the object form. Combine it with net.core.somaxconn = 1024 on the node, or the kernel silently caps the backlog.

// payments-http.module.ts: pooled HttpModule so the gateway handshake is paid rarely
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HttpModule } from '@nestjs/axios';
import { Agent as HttpsAgent } from 'https';

@Module({
  imports: [
    HttpModule.register({
      baseURL: 'https://api.payments.example.com',
      timeout: 3_000,
      httpsAgent: new HttpsAgent({
        keepAlive: true,          // reuse sockets; skip the TCP and TLS handshakes
        maxSockets: 64,           // upper bound on concurrent connections
        maxFreeSockets: 16,       // idle sockets kept warm
        timeout: 30_000,          // idle socket timeout, below the gateway's idle limit
      }),
    }),
  ],
})
export class PaymentsHttpModule {}

PostgreSQL example

Postgres connection establishment is worse than a plain handshake: TCP handshake, TLS handshake, then Postgres startup messages, SCRAM authentication (four messages), and a fresh backend process fork on the server, typically 5 to 20 ms and a few megabytes of memory. This is why every serious deployment pools.

-- How many backends exist right now, and how many are just idle pool members
SELECT count(*) AS total,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'idle') AS idle_pooled,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'active') AS active
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_type = 'client backend';

-- Connection churn: rising numbackends with a flat active count means pools are
-- rebuilding sockets; check idle timeouts and connection_timeout settings
SELECT datname, numbackends, xact_commit, xact_rollback
FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = 'orders';

With PgBouncer in transaction mode in front, the application's 200 sockets map to perhaps 40 real backends, and the expensive fork-plus-auth handshake happens only when PgBouncer grows its pool.

Production scenario

An API at 2,000 RPS with keep-alive disabled by a misconfigured client library performed 2,000 TLS handshakes per second. CPU on 8 pods sat at 85% with only 20% attributable to application code; the rest was OpenSSL. Enabling keep-alive dropped handshakes to about 30 per second and CPU to 25%.

Failure scenario

At 18:00 a marketing push sent 40,000 users to a flash sale within a minute. New connections arrived at 3,000 per second. The Node accept backlog was the default 511 and the event loop was busy rendering JSON, so the accept queue filled and the kernel dropped ACKs. Clients hung for their SYN retry timeouts (1 s, 3 s, 7 s) and then retried, tripling the SYN rate. netstat -s | grep -i listen showed "SYNs to LISTEN sockets dropped" climbing by thousands per second. Raising somaxconn and backlog to 4,096, scaling pods, and putting HTTP/2 on the ALB so browsers reused connections resolved it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • SYN floods: attackers send SYNs and never ACK; SYN cookies protect the backlog at the cost of losing TCP options.
  • Accept queue overflow drops the final ACK silently; clients see timeouts, not refusals.
  • Half-open connections after a client crashes mid-handshake linger until the SYN-ACK retries expire.
  • EADDRNOTAVAIL on the client side is port exhaustion, not a server problem.
  • TLS handshake CPU is a real capacity limit; terminate at the ALB with ECDSA certificates.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They count round trips. Every new connection is at least 2 RTT before useful work; on mobile that is 100 to 300 ms. They design for reuse: keep-alive everywhere, HTTP/2 at the edge, pooled database and cache connections, and warm pools before traffic spikes. They size accept backlogs for bursts. To a product manager: "Each new customer connection is a handshake and an ID check before we can even hear their order. We keep the door open for repeat customers so they skip the queue."

Common mistakes

  • Creating a Pool or Agent per request.
  • Leaving backlog at defaults on a high-connection-rate service.
  • Measuring latency from a warm local client and being surprised by mobile numbers.

Interview questions

  1. Describe the three-way handshake and why it costs one RTT before data. SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK; the client's first data can ride on the ACK, but nothing before it.
  2. What is the accept backlog and what happens when it overflows? The queue of completed handshakes waiting for accept(); overflow drops ACKs and clients time out.
  3. Why does a fresh HTTPS connection cost two or three RTTs, and how do pooling and HTTP/2 change the equation? TCP 1 RTT, TLS 1.3 1 RTT (7.2 needs 2); pooling and multiplexing pay it once for many requests.
  4. Where does TLS handshake CPU go, and how do you reduce it? Asymmetric crypto per handshake; use ECDSA certs, session resumption, terminate at the LB, and reuse connections.

Practical exercise

Use curl -w with time_connect, time_appconnect and time_starttransfer against your API from a laptop and from a pod in the cluster. Then run 200 sequential requests with and without --keepalive. Acceptance criteria: a table showing the handshake share of total latency in each case, and a written recommendation for the mobile app team on connection reuse.

10.4.3 Connection termination, TIME_WAIT and keepalive probes

Concept

Closing a TCP connection is a four-step exchange: each side sends FIN and receives an ACK. The side that closes first enters TIME_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime (60 seconds on Linux) to be sure late packets do not corrupt a new connection using the same 5-tuple. A half-open connection is one where one side believes it is open and the other has forgotten it, which happens when a process crashes, a NAT table entry expires, or a load balancer silently drops an idle flow. TCP keepalive probes are tiny packets sent after an idle period to detect exactly that.

Why does it exist?

Without an orderly close, neither side knows whether the last bytes arrived. Without TIME_WAIT, a delayed segment from an old connection could be accepted by a new one with the same ports. Without keepalive probes, a server behind a NAT would hold a dead connection (and a Postgres backend, and a row lock) forever.

Mental model

Imagine ending a phone call politely: "I'm done" (FIN), "okay" (ACK), "me too" (FIN), "okay" (ACK). Then you keep the line reserved for a minute in case a delayed "wait, one more thing" arrives. A half-open connection is when one person quietly walked away and the other is still holding the receiver, waiting. A keepalive probe is saying "you still there?" every so often.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Active closer
    participant P as Passive closer
    A->>P: FIN
    Note left of A: FIN_WAIT_1
    P->>A: ACK
    Note right of P: CLOSE_WAIT until app calls close
    Note left of A: FIN_WAIT_2
    P->>A: FIN
    Note right of P: LAST_ACK
    A->>P: ACK
    Note left of A: TIME_WAIT for 60 s then CLOSED
    Note right of P: CLOSED
  1. The application that calls close() first sends FIN; it can no longer send but can still receive.
  2. The peer's kernel ACKs immediately and moves to CLOSE_WAIT. The peer application must call close() too; if it never does (a leaked socket in Node), the connection sits in CLOSE_WAIT forever. Thousands of CLOSE_WAIT sockets always mean an application bug.
  3. The peer sends its own FIN, the first side ACKs, and the first side enters TIME_WAIT for 60 seconds. This is why the side that closes first pays the TIME_WAIT cost. Servers that close connections (Connection: close) accumulate TIME_WAIT and that is fine for a listening port; clients that close first burn ephemeral ports.
  4. A RST (reset) is the impolite close: sent when data arrives for a socket that does not exist, when a process dies, or when a load balancer aborts. The peer sees ECONNRESET.

Half-open connections and idle timeouts. NAT gateways, ALBs, firewalls and Kubernetes conntrack all keep a table of flows and drop entries after an idle period (AWS NAT gateway: 350 seconds; ALB idle timeout: 60 seconds default; many corporate firewalls: 300 seconds). After that, packets on the old connection are dropped or reset. A NestJS pod that opened a Postgres connection, sat idle for 10 minutes, and then sends a query will wait for the full retransmission cycle (up to 15 minutes with default tcp_retries2) before failing. Meanwhile the request hangs.

TCP keepalive probes fix this. After tcp_keepalive_time seconds of silence (Linux default 7,200, far too long), the kernel sends an empty probe every tcp_keepalive_intvl seconds (75), up to tcp_keepalive_probes times (9). If nothing answers, the socket errors. Set from Node with socket.setKeepAlive(true, 30_000), which sets the idle time; the interval and count come from sysctls (net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_intvl=10, net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_probes=3 are sensible pod values). A keepalive probe also refreshes NAT and conntrack entries so the flow is never forgotten in the first place.

HTTP keep-alive is not TCP keepalive. HTTP keep-alive means "reuse this connection for the next request". TCP keepalive means "send probes to check the peer is alive". Both matter; see 10.9 for the HTTP side.

Practical example

A NestJS worker holds a Postgres pool of 5 connections and processes a queue that goes quiet for 20 minutes at night. The next job's first query hangs for 15 minutes. The NAT between the worker's subnet and the database (in a peered VPC) dropped the idle flow after 350 seconds. Enabling keepAlive: true in the pg pool with a 30-second initial delay solved it: probes every 30 seconds keep the NAT entry alive, and if the database really dies the pool learns within about a minute.

NestJS example

// database.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm';

@Module({
  imports: [
    TypeOrmModule.forRoot({
      type: 'postgres',
      host: process.env.PG_HOST,
      port: 5432,
      username: process.env.PG_USER,
      password: process.env.PG_PASSWORD,
      database: 'orders',
      autoLoadEntities: true,
      extra: {
        max: 10,
        keepAlive: true,                       // enable TCP keepalive on each pooled socket
        keepAliveInitialDelayMillis: 30_000,   // first probe after 30 s idle
        idleTimeoutMillis: 60_000,             // close idle sockets after 60 s
        connectionTimeoutMillis: 3_000,
        statement_timeout: 15_000,             // never wait 15 minutes on a half-open socket
      },
    }),
  ],
})
export class DatabaseModule {}
// graceful-shutdown.ts: close connections politely so clients see FIN, not RST
import { INestApplication } from '@nestjs/common';

export function enableGracefulShutdown(app: INestApplication) {
  app.enableShutdownHooks(); // SIGTERM triggers onModuleDestroy and app.close()
  const server = app.getHttpServer();
  process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
    // Stop accepting new connections; in-flight requests finish, idle keep-alive sockets close.
    server.close();
    // Node 18.2+ closes idle keep-alive connections immediately; older versions need
    // a manual sweep so the pod terminates before the Kubernetes grace period ends.
    server.closeIdleConnections?.();
  });
}

PostgreSQL example

The database is the place where half-open connections do the most damage: a client that vanished mid-transaction leaves a backend holding locks.

-- Backends whose client may be gone: idle in transaction for a long time
SELECT pid, client_addr, client_port, backend_start, state_change,
       now() - state_change AS stuck_for
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
  AND now() - state_change > interval '2 minutes';

-- Terminate them (the locks are released and the transaction rolled back)
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
  AND now() - state_change > interval '5 minutes';

-- Make the server detect dead clients itself (PostgreSQL 14+): check the socket every 10 s
ALTER SYSTEM SET client_connection_check_interval = '10s';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

Production scenario

Fleet-wide numbers from a Kubernetes cluster of 60 NestJS pods: after enabling TCP keepalive with a 30-second idle time on every outbound socket, the count of requests that timed out at exactly the 30-second gateway timeout dropped from about 40 per day to zero. Those 40 had been half-open connections to a partner API behind a firewall with a 5-minute idle cutoff.

Failure scenario

At 05:10 a database maintenance window rebooted the RDS instance. It came back in 90 seconds. The application pods, whose pool sockets had been open to the old process, did not notice: the reboot happened on the same IP, the NAT tables were intact, and no RST reached them because the network stack restarted. Every pooled connection was half-open. The first query on each waited for tcp_retries2 (about 15 minutes) before erroring, and the pool's connectionTimeoutMillis only applied to acquiring new sockets, not to existing dead ones. The API was effectively down for 15 minutes after a 90-second reboot. The remediation: keepAlive with a 20-second delay, statement_timeout of 10 seconds, and a readiness probe that runs SELECT 1 through the pool so a pod with a dead pool is pulled from the load balancer.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • CLOSE_WAIT accumulation means your process never called close(): leaked sockets, unconsumed response bodies, or an HTTP agent that never releases.
  • TIME_WAIT accumulation on a client means connection churn; on a server it is normal.
  • RST from a load balancer during deploy: pods removed from the target group while requests are in flight get ECONNRESET unless the deregistration delay (draining) is set and the app handles SIGTERM gracefully.
  • Kubernetes conntrack table full (nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet) silently drops new flows; it shows as random connection timeouts across the node.
  • Keepalive probes are only as good as the sysctls that control interval and count; a 30-second delay with 9 probes at 75 seconds still takes 11 minutes to detect death.
  • Half-close: a peer that sends FIN may still be reading; HTTP clients that half-close after sending a request are rare but legal.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They assume every idle connection will be silently killed by something in the path and design so that the application finds out quickly: keepalive probes, statement timeouts, request timeouts, and readiness checks that exercise the pool. They handle SIGTERM so that shutdown produces FINs, not RSTs, and they set load balancer draining to match. They monitor CLOSE_WAIT, TIME_WAIT and conntrack usage as first-class metrics. To a product manager: "If the line goes dead, we want to notice in thirty seconds, not fifteen minutes. That is a setting, and we had it wrong."

Common mistakes

  • Relying on the OS default keepalive of two hours.
  • Not consuming HTTP response bodies, leaking sockets into CLOSE_WAIT.
  • Killing pods without draining, causing ECONNRESET storms on every deploy.
  • Confusing HTTP keep-alive with TCP keepalive.
  • Assuming a database reboot will reset client sockets.

Interview questions

  1. Why does TIME_WAIT exist and which side pays for it? To absorb delayed segments before the 5-tuple is reused; the side that closes first.
  2. What causes thousands of sockets in CLOSE_WAIT and how do you find the bug? The app never called close(); look for unconsumed bodies and leaked clients, use ss -tanp state close-wait.
  3. A query hangs for 15 minutes after a database reboot. Why, and what are the three settings that fix it? Half-open socket, no keepalive; keepAlive with a short delay, statement_timeout, and pool health checks.
  4. How does a NAT gateway break idle connections, and how do keepalive probes help? It drops flow entries after an idle period; probes refresh the entry and detect death.
  5. What is the difference between FIN and RST, and when does a load balancer send each? FIN is orderly close; RST is abort. An ALB sends RST when a target is deregistered without draining or when the target resets first.

Practical exercise

Run a NestJS app with a Postgres pool in Docker Compose. Use docker pause on the database container (simulating a silent network drop), issue a query, and time how long it takes to fail with default settings. Then enable keepalive with a 10-second delay, sysctl interval 5 and count 3, and repeat. Finally kill the app with SIGTERM during a load test with and without graceful shutdown and count ECONNRESET errors. Acceptance criteria: three measured timings, and a runbook entry describing what CLOSE_WAIT, TIME_WAIT and conntrack alerts mean for this service.

10.5 Latency, bandwidth, packet loss and retransmission

Concept

Four words describe how a network behaves, and they are often confused:

  • Latency is how long one bit takes to get from A to B. Measured as RTT (round-trip time) in milliseconds. It is bounded by physics: light in fibre travels about 200 km per millisecond, so Mumbai to Frankfurt (about 6,500 km of cable) is at least 33 ms one way, 65 ms round trip, and in practice 110 to 140 ms.
  • Bandwidth is how many bits per second the pipe can carry. Measured in Mbps or Gbps. Adding bandwidth does not reduce latency, in the same way that adding lanes to a motorway does not make one car go faster.
  • Packet loss is the fraction of packets that never arrive. Even 1% loss devastates TCP throughput because every loss triggers retransmission and a congestion back-off.
  • Retransmission is TCP resending a lost segment after a timeout or duplicate ACKs. It costs at least one extra RTT, and often much more because the retransmission timeout (RTO) has a floor of 200 ms on Linux.

And one more that senior engineers obsess over: tail latency. Your p50 might be 20 ms while your p99 is 900 ms. Users notice the p99. A page that fans out to 20 backend calls will hit the p99 of at least one of them on almost every load.

Why does it exist?

These are not design choices; they are facts about physical networks that your architecture must respect. The reason to name them is that each one calls for a different fix. Latency is fixed by fewer round trips, closer regions, and caching. Bandwidth is fixed by smaller payloads, compression and CDNs. Loss is fixed by retries, better paths and protocols like QUIC. Tail latency is fixed by timeouts, hedging, and removing variance (GC pauses, lock waits, cold caches). Applying the wrong fix is common: teams "add bandwidth" (a bigger instance) to fix a latency problem and see no change.

Mental model

Imagine a water pipe from a reservoir to your house. Latency is how long a drop takes to travel the pipe. Bandwidth is the pipe's diameter. A wider pipe delivers more water per second but the first drop still takes just as long to arrive. Packet loss is a leak: some water never arrives and the reservoir has to send it again. Tail latency is that one shower every morning when the pressure inexplicably drops for ten seconds.

How it works

Where latency comes from. RTT is propagation (distance), transmission (bytes divided by bandwidth), queueing (waiting in router buffers, which balloons under congestion; this is bufferbloat), and processing at each hop. On a good path, propagation dominates. On a congested mobile network, queueing dominates and RTT swings from 40 ms to 800 ms within seconds.

Why a 5 MB JSON response is slow on mobile. Take a product catalogue endpoint returning 5 MB of uncompressed JSON to a phone on 4G with 20 Mbps downlink and 60 ms RTT, and 0.5% packet loss.

  1. Transmission alone: 5 MB is 40 Mbit; at 20 Mbps, that is 2 seconds minimum.
  2. Slow start: TCP begins at about 14 KB per RTT and doubles; reaching a window that fills 20 Mbps at 60 ms (about 150 KB in flight) takes roughly 4 round trips, 240 ms, during which only about 200 KB moved.
  3. Loss: 5 MB is about 3,500 packets; at 0.5% loss, about 17 packets are lost. Each loss halves the congestion window (or worse, triggers a 200 ms+ RTO if it is the last packet in flight). Realistic throughput drops to perhaps 8 Mbps. Now the transfer is 5 seconds.
  4. Parsing: JSON.parse on 5 MB takes 30 to 80 ms on a mid-range phone and holds the main thread; the memory spike can crash a WebView.
  5. The user saw a spinner for 5 to 6 seconds. With gzip (JSON compresses 5 to 10x) the same payload is about 600 KB, transferred in under a second; with pagination (50 products at a time, 40 KB) it is 150 ms.

The lesson: bytes on the wire are the lever. Latency and loss multiply the cost of every byte.

Retransmission mechanics. The sender keeps a timer per connection. RTO starts at 1 second for the first segment (SYN), then is computed from smoothed RTT plus four times the RTT variance, with a 200 ms floor on Linux. If three duplicate ACKs arrive first, fast retransmit resends without waiting for the timer. Selective ACK (SACK) lets the receiver say exactly which segments arrived so only the gaps are resent. On a lossy path, the effective throughput follows the Mathis formula: roughly MSS / (RTT * sqrt(loss)). With 1,460-byte segments, 100 ms RTT and 1% loss, that is about 1.2 Mbps regardless of link speed. Loss, not bandwidth, becomes the ceiling.

Tail latency. In a system where each backend call has a 1% chance of taking more than 500 ms, a request that makes 20 such calls has a 1 - 0.99^20 = 18% chance of being slow. Fan-out amplifies tail latency; this is why senior engineers ask "how many downstream calls does this endpoint make?" before asking "how fast is each call?". Sources of tail latency in a NestJS system: garbage collection pauses (10 to 200 ms on a large heap), event-loop lag from a synchronous JSON.stringify of a large object, pool exhaustion waits, Postgres lock waits, a cold Redis key, a DNS threadpool queue, a TLS handshake on a new connection, and slow start after idle.

flowchart LR
    R["Request"] --> A["Call A p99 500 ms"]
    R --> B["Call B p99 500 ms"]
    R --> C["Call C p99 500 ms"]
    A --> J["Join"]
    B --> J
    C --> J
    J --> O["Response p99 is far worse than any single call"]

Practical example

A ride-booking app's "nearby drivers" endpoint called location, pricing, ETA and driver-profile services in sequence: 4 calls at 15 ms p50 each, 60 ms total at p50. At p99 each call was 300 ms, and sequential fan-out meant the endpoint's p99 was over 700 ms. Two changes: run the four calls in parallel with Promise.all (p50 dropped to 18 ms), and set a 150 ms timeout on the driver-profile call with a fallback to a cached profile (p99 dropped to 320 ms). Neither change touched bandwidth; both attacked round trips and tail variance.

NestJS example

Three tools against latency and tails in one interceptor: a per-request deadline, parallel fan-out, and a size guard that refuses to send a response the client will choke on.

// timeout.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor, RequestTimeoutException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, throwError, TimeoutError } from 'rxjs';
import { catchError, timeout } from 'rxjs/operators';

@Injectable()
export class TimeoutInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  // A hard deadline below the ALB idle timeout so the client gets a clean 504
  // from us rather than a mystery timeout from the load balancer.
  constructor(private readonly ms = 10_000) {}

  intercept(_ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    return next.handle().pipe(
      timeout(this.ms),
      catchError((err) =>
        err instanceof TimeoutError ? throwError(() => new RequestTimeoutException()) : throwError(() => err),
      ),
    );
  }
}
// nearby.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class NearbyService {
  constructor(
    private readonly location: LocationClient,
    private readonly pricing: PricingClient,
    private readonly eta: EtaClient,
    private readonly profiles: ProfileClient,
  ) {}

  async nearby(riderId: string, lat: number, lng: number) {
    // Parallel fan-out: total latency is the max of the four, not the sum.
    const [drivers, surge, etas] = await Promise.all([
      this.location.nearbyDrivers(lat, lng, { timeoutMs: 400 }),
      this.pricing.surgeFor(lat, lng, { timeoutMs: 300 }),
      this.eta.estimate(lat, lng, { timeoutMs: 400 }),
    ]);

    // A soft dependency: use a short timeout and degrade instead of failing the request.
    const profiles = await this.profiles
      .batchGet(drivers.map((d) => d.id), { timeoutMs: 150 })
      .catch(() => this.profiles.cachedBatch(drivers.map((d) => d.id)));

    // Respond with only what the map needs; the full driver object is 4 KB each.
    return drivers.slice(0, 20).map((d) => ({
      id: d.id, lat: d.lat, lng: d.lng,
      etaSeconds: etas[d.id], surge, name: profiles[d.id]?.firstName,
    }));
  }
}

The slice(0, 20) and the trimmed shape are the bandwidth fix; Promise.all and the timeouts are the latency and tail fix.

PostgreSQL example

Latency between the application and the database is paid per round trip, so the number of queries per request matters more than the speed of any one query. The N+1 pattern turns a 2 ms page into a 400 ms page across 200 round trips, even inside one AZ at 0.3 ms RTT, once you add pool checkout and parse time per query.

-- N+1: one query per order to fetch its items (200 round trips)
-- SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = $1;  -- executed 200 times

-- One round trip: aggregate the items into JSON per order
SELECT o.id, o.status, o.total_cents,
       COALESCE(json_agg(json_build_object('sku', i.sku, 'qty', i.qty)) FILTER (WHERE i.id IS NOT NULL), '[]') AS items
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.user_id = $1 AND o.created_at > now() - interval '30 days'
GROUP BY o.id
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

-- Verify it is one indexed pass, not a sequential scan of items
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT ... ;
-- GroupAggregate  (cost=1.15..212.40 rows=50 width=96) (actual time=0.09..1.84 rows=50 loops=1)
--   ->  Nested Loop Left Join  (actual time=0.05..1.31 rows=214 loops=1)
--         ->  Index Scan using orders_user_created_idx on orders o (actual time=0.03..0.21 rows=50 loops=1)
--         ->  Index Scan using order_items_order_id_idx on order_items i (actual time=0.01..0.02 rows=4 loops=50)
--   Buffers: shared hit=312
-- Execution Time: 1.97 ms

Also watch the bandwidth side: SELECT * on a table with a 2 MB jsonb column ships 2 MB per row across the network. Select the columns you need.

TypeORM example

The same idea in TypeORM: batch loads and column selection, with a statement timeout so a slow query cannot become a tail-latency event for every caller.

// orders.repository.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersRepository {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Order) private readonly repo: Repository<Order>) {}

  async recentForUser(userId: string): Promise<Order[]> {
    return this.repo
      .createQueryBuilder('o')
      .leftJoinAndSelect('o.items', 'i')        // one round trip, not N+1
      .select(['o.id', 'o.status', 'o.totalCents', 'o.createdAt', 'i.sku', 'i.qty']) // trim bytes
      .where('o.userId = :userId', { userId })
      .andWhere("o.createdAt > now() - interval '30 days'")
      .orderBy('o.createdAt', 'DESC')
      .take(50)
      .setQueryRunner(undefined as never)         // default runner; shown to note statement_timeout lives in pool extra
      .getMany();
  }
}

The setQueryRunner line is only there to point out that TypeORM has no per-query timeout API; the pool-level statement_timeout in extra (see 10.4.3) is the real guard.

Sequelize example

// orders.service.ts (Sequelize)
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectModel } from '@nestjs/sequelize';
import { Op } from 'sequelize';
import { Order } from './order.model';
import { OrderItem } from './order-item.model';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(@InjectModel(Order) private readonly orders: typeof Order) {}

  recentForUser(userId: string) {
    return this.orders.findAll({
      attributes: ['id', 'status', 'totalCents', 'createdAt'],      // trim bytes on the wire
      include: [{ model: OrderItem, attributes: ['sku', 'qty'], separate: false }], // single JOIN query
      where: { userId, createdAt: { [Op.gt]: new Date(Date.now() - 30 * 86_400_000) } },
      order: [['createdAt', 'DESC']],
      limit: 50,
    });
  }
}

Production scenario

Real numbers from an e-commerce API: p50 42 ms, p99 610 ms, p99.9 2.4 s. Breaking down the p99 with tracing showed 35% was Postgres lock waits on a hot inventory row, 25% was GC pauses on pods with a 1.5 GB heap, 20% was outbound calls to a tax service with no timeout, and the remainder was slow start on fresh connections from an ALB with a 60-second idle timeout during low traffic. Fixes over one quarter: an advisory lock with a 200 ms wait limit and a queue for the hot row, smaller pods (512 MB heap, more replicas) to shorten GC, a 300 ms timeout with cached fallback on tax, and HTTP/2 between the ALB and the pods. p99 went to 180 ms; p50 barely moved. Tail latency is where the work is.

Failure scenario

At 21:30 on a cricket final night, a mobile carrier's backbone degraded and packet loss on that carrier rose to 3%. The API's p50 was unchanged from the data centre's point of view, but users on that carrier saw the home feed (a 900 KB JSON response) take 20 seconds. Alerts did not fire because server-side latency was fine; the bytes were leaving the ALB quickly and dying in the carrier's network. Real-user monitoring from the app showed the problem. The team shipped a change that night: gzip on the feed endpoint (900 KB to 140 KB) and a page size of 20 instead of 100. Under the same loss, 140 KB transferred in about 2 seconds. Long term they added Brotli and a CDN edge that serves HTTP/3, which handles loss far better than TCP.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Bufferbloat: RTT to a mobile client swings from 40 ms to 1 s; timeouts tuned for the data centre fire spuriously.
  • Loss on the last packet of a response triggers a full RTO (200 ms minimum) rather than fast retransmit, because there are no following packets to generate duplicate ACKs. Small responses suffer disproportionately.
  • Asymmetric paths: the request takes 50 ms, the response 200 ms; ping shows the average and hides it.
  • Coordinated omission: load testers that wait for a response before sending the next request under-report tail latency. Use open-loop load tools (k6 with arrival rate, wrk2).
  • Large responses and JSON.stringify: serialising 5 MB blocks the event loop for tens of milliseconds, adding tail latency to every other request on the pod.
  • Retry amplification: a client that retries on timeout doubles the load on a system that is slow because it is overloaded (see 10.15).
  • The p99 of a dependency becomes your p50 if you call it 70 times per request.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They separate the levers: distance and round trips for latency, bytes for bandwidth, protocols and paths for loss, variance for tails. They measure at the client (real-user monitoring), not only at the server, because the server cannot see the carrier's loss. They put a budget on every endpoint: at most N downstream calls, at most M KB of response, a deadline that is propagated to every call. They refuse to add fields to a response "in case the client needs them". To a product manager: "Halving the response size did more for the app than doubling the server count would have. The users' network is the slowest part of our system and we do not own it."

Common mistakes

  • Optimising a 3 ms query while the endpoint sends 2 MB.
  • Reporting averages; the average hides the tail that users feel.
  • Sequential await chains where calls are independent.
  • No timeouts on outbound calls, so one slow dependency becomes everyone's tail.
  • Load testing from inside the same AZ and calling the result "user latency".
  • Assuming a bigger instance fixes latency.

Interview questions

  1. Explain the difference between latency and bandwidth with a backend example. Latency is per-round-trip delay (why an N+1 query pattern is slow); bandwidth is bytes per second (why a 5 MB response is slow). More bandwidth does not fix N+1.
  2. Why is a 5 MB JSON response slow on mobile even on a fast 4G link? Slow start, loss-triggered back-off, the Mathis limit, and client parse time; compression and pagination fix it, more server capacity does not.
  3. What is tail latency and why does fan-out make it worse? The slow tail of the distribution; the probability that at least one of N calls is slow grows as 1 - (1-p)^N.
  4. Give three sources of tail latency inside a Node service and how to reduce each. GC pauses (smaller heaps, more pods), event-loop blocking (avoid sync serialisation of large objects, offload), pool waits (size pools, add timeouts).
  5. Why does loss on the last packet of a small response hurt more than loss in the middle? No duplicate ACKs follow, so fast retransmit cannot fire and the sender waits for the full RTO.
  6. What is coordinated omission? Load tools that wait for slow responses send fewer requests during slow periods, under-sampling exactly the moments that matter.

Practical exercise

Use tc netem on a Linux VM (or Docker with --cap-add NET_ADMIN) to add 80 ms delay and 1% loss to the interface, then measure the transfer time of a 5 MB JSON response from a NestJS endpoint with and without gzip, and with a paginated 50 KB version. Then instrument the endpoint with OpenTelemetry and produce a p50, p95, p99 table under a k6 open-loop test at 200 RPS. Acceptance criteria: a table of transfer times across the three variants and two network conditions, and one paragraph identifying which of latency, bandwidth or loss dominated each cell.

10.6 HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3

Concept

HTTP is the application protocol your NestJS app speaks. It has three versions in production use, and they differ not in what a request means but in how requests are put on the wire:

  • HTTP/1.1 (1997): plain text. One request at a time per connection. Persistent connections (keep-alive) by default. Chunked transfer encoding for streaming. Still the version most servers, including Node's http module and therefore NestJS by default, speak behind the load balancer.
  • HTTP/2 (2015): binary framing. Many requests multiplexed on one connection. Header compression (HPACK). Server push (deprecated in practice). Required by gRPC. Almost always run over TLS. What browsers speak to your ALB or CDN.
  • HTTP/3 (2022): the same semantics over QUIC, a UDP-based transport with TLS 1.3 built in, 0-RTT resumption, per-stream loss recovery, and connection migration across IP changes. Served by CDNs and some load balancers at the edge; your NestJS app does not speak it and does not need to.

Why does it exist?

HTTP/1.1's limitation is head-of-line (HOL) blocking: on one connection, the second response cannot start until the first is fully sent. Browsers worked around it by opening up to 6 connections per host, which multiplied handshake cost and starved TCP's congestion control. HTTP/2 solved application-level HOL blocking with multiplexing, but TCP-level HOL blocking remained: one lost packet stalls every stream on that connection because TCP delivers bytes in order. HTTP/3 moved to QUIC so that a lost packet stalls only the stream it belonged to, and so that a phone moving from Wi-Fi to 4G keeps its connection.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant with one waiter per table (HTTP/1.1): the waiter takes one order, walks to the kitchen, brings it back, and only then takes the next order. Six waiters per table (browser connections) help, but the kitchen door gets crowded. HTTP/2 is one waiter carrying a tray with many numbered orders in both directions at once. HTTP/3 is that same waiter, but if one plate is dropped, only that dish is remade while the others are still served; and the waiter follows you if you move tables.

How it works

HTTP/1.1 on the wire. A request is text lines terminated by \r\n, a blank line, then the body. The server parses until the blank line, reads Content-Length bytes (or chunked frames), and only then can parse the next request on the same socket. Node's http parser (llhttp) does this parsing and hands NestJS a req object.

POST /v1/orders HTTP/1.1\r\n
Host: api.fooddash.com\r\n
Content-Type: application/json\r\n
Content-Length: 58\r\n
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...\r\n
\r\n
{"restaurantId":"r_91","items":[{"sku":"BRG-1","qty":2}]}

Pipelining (sending several requests without waiting) exists in the spec but responses must still return in order, and proxies handled it so badly that every browser disabled it. In practice HTTP/1.1 means one request in flight per connection.

HTTP/2 framing. After the TLS handshake negotiates h2 via ALPN (application-layer protocol negotiation), the connection carries binary frames: HEADERS, DATA, SETTINGS, WINDOW_UPDATE, RST_STREAM, PING, GOAWAY. Each frame belongs to a stream identified by an integer. A request is a HEADERS frame (possibly with DATA frames) on a new stream; the response comes back on the same stream id. Streams are interleaved, so 30 API calls share one TCP connection and one TLS session. Header names and values are compressed with HPACK, which keeps a dynamic table on both sides so a repeated Authorization: Bearer ... header costs a couple of bytes after the first time. Flow control is per stream and per connection. Server push let a server send resources the client had not asked for; Chrome removed support in 2022 and 103 Early Hints replaced the use case. Do not design around push.

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant S1 as HTTP1 server
    participant S2 as HTTP2 server
    Note over B,S1: HTTP/1.1, one connection, sequential
    B->>S1: GET /orders
    S1-->>B: 200 orders body
    B->>S1: GET /cart
    S1-->>B: 200 cart body
    B->>S1: GET /profile
    S1-->>B: 200 profile body
    Note over B,S2: HTTP/2, one connection, three streams interleaved
    B->>S2: HEADERS stream 1 GET /orders
    B->>S2: HEADERS stream 3 GET /cart
    B->>S2: HEADERS stream 5 GET /profile
    S2-->>B: DATA stream 3 cart
    S2-->>B: DATA stream 5 profile
    S2-->>B: DATA stream 1 orders part 7
    S2-->>B: DATA stream 1 orders part 8

HTTP/2 in the AWS path. An ALB accepts HTTP/2 from clients by default and, for each incoming stream, opens or reuses an HTTP/1.1 connection to the target. Your NestJS app sees ordinary HTTP/1.1 requests; the multiplexing benefit exists between the browser and the ALB, where the slow, lossy, high-RTT network is. Since 2020 the ALB can also speak HTTP/2 to targets (protocol version HTTP2 on the target group), which mostly matters for gRPC. Node has a built-in http2 module and NestJS can run on it with the Fastify adapter's http2: true option, but because the ALB terminates HTTP/2 anyway, almost no one does this in production.

gRPC uses HTTP/2 as its transport: each RPC is a stream, messages are length-prefixed protobuf in DATA frames, and trailers carry the status. This is why gRPC needs end-to-end HTTP/2 (an ALB with an HTTP/2 target group or an NLB) and why it cannot pass through an HTTP/1.1 proxy. NestJS supports gRPC through @nestjs/microservices with Transport.GRPC.

HTTP/3 and QUIC. QUIC runs over UDP. Each connection has a connection ID independent of IP and port, so a phone that switches from Wi-Fi to cellular continues the same connection (connection migration). TLS 1.3 is integrated: a first connection costs one round trip (versus two for TCP plus TLS 1.3), and a resumed connection can send application data in the first packet (0-RTT), which is safe only for idempotent requests because a replayed 0-RTT packet would be executed twice. Loss recovery is per stream, so one lost packet does not stall unrelated streams. HTTP/3 is what CloudFront, Cloudflare and Google Front Ends offer to browsers; the edge translates to HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 towards your origin.

Comparison:

Property HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 HTTP/3
Transport TCP TCP QUIC over UDP
Framing text binary frames binary frames
Requests per connection in flight 1 many (default 100 to 250 streams) many
HOL blocking per connection, at HTTP level at TCP level only none across streams
Header compression none HPACK QPACK
TLS optional practically required built in (7.3)
New connection cost 1 RTT TCP plus TLS same 1 RTT total, 0-RTT on resume
Browser connections per host 6 1 1
Where you meet it NestJS, Node http, LB to target browser to ALB/CDN, gRPC CDN edge, mobile
Node support http http2 none in core

Practical example

A checkout page on a social-commerce site made 42 XHR calls on load. On HTTP/1.1 through a classic ELB with a 60 ms mobile RTT, the browser used 6 connections, each with a 120 ms handshake, and the calls queued in 7 waves: 1.3 seconds until the last response. Moving to an ALB with HTTP/2 made it one connection, one handshake, and all 42 requests in flight at once: 380 ms until the last response, dominated by the slowest single API. Nothing in the NestJS code changed. Later, fronting the ALB with CloudFront (HTTP/3 to mobile clients) cut another 80 to 100 ms for users on lossy networks and eliminated reconnects when users walked out of Wi-Fi range.

NestJS example

The default NestJS server is HTTP/1.1 and that is correct behind an ALB. Two things you should still do: make the app tolerate HTTP/2-origin traffic (lowercase header names, no reliance on Connection headers, since HTTP/2 forbids them and the ALB strips them) and, when you actually need HTTP/2 to the app for gRPC, use the microservices transport.

// main.ts: HTTP/1.1 app behind an ALB that terminates HTTP/2 and TLS
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, transform: true }));

  // Headers arrive lowercase whether the client spoke HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2; Node
  // normalises them, so always read req.headers['x-request-id'], never 'X-Request-Id'.
  await app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0');
}
bootstrap();
// grpc-main.ts: an internal gRPC service that needs HTTP/2 end to end
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { MicroserviceOptions, Transport } from '@nestjs/microservices';
import { join } from 'path';
import { PricingModule } from './pricing.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.createMicroservice<MicroserviceOptions>(PricingModule, {
    transport: Transport.GRPC,
    options: {
      package: 'pricing',
      protoPath: join(__dirname, 'proto/pricing.proto'),
      url: '0.0.0.0:50051',
      // Keep the HTTP/2 connection alive through NATs and LBs between calls.
      keepalive: { keepaliveTimeMs: 30_000, keepaliveTimeoutMs: 5_000, keepalivePermitWithoutCalls: 1 },
    },
  });
  await app.listen();
}
bootstrap();

If you expose this gRPC service through an ALB, the target group must use protocol version GRPC (HTTP/2 to targets) and health checks must be gRPC health checks; an HTTP/1.1 target group will return 502 for every call.

PostgreSQL example

There is no HTTP inside Postgres, but the HTTP version at the edge changes the shape of database load: HTTP/2 lets a browser fire 40 API calls at once, and each one may checkout a pool connection. A page that was naturally rate-limited by 6 browser connections can now open 40 concurrent queries per user. Watch for it in pg_stat_activity bursts and size pools and per-user concurrency accordingly.

-- Concurrent active queries per application user right now; a burst that tracks
-- page loads is the HTTP/2 fan-out effect
SELECT application_name, usename, count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'active') AS active_now
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
GROUP BY application_name, usename
ORDER BY active_now DESC;

Production scenario

Numbers from a marketplace API: enabling HTTP/2 on the ALB lowered the count of new TCP connections at the ALB from about 9,000 per minute to 1,100 per minute at the same request rate, and the browser-measured time-to-interactive on the product page fell from 2.9 s to 1.7 s on 4G. Behind the ALB, the NestJS pods saw no protocol change but did see burstier concurrency: p99 pool wait time rose from 2 ms to 11 ms until pool size was raised from 8 to 12 per pod and one endpoint was changed to batch three queries into one.

Failure scenario

A team migrated an internal service to gRPC and put it behind the existing ALB with an HTTP/1.1 target group. Every call returned 502 Bad Gateway. The ALB accepted the client's HTTP/2 stream, translated it to HTTP/1.1, and the gRPC server replied with an HTTP/2 preface that the ALB's HTTP/1.1 client could not parse. The fix was a new target group with protocol version GRPC, plus a gRPC health check. The lesson: gRPC is not "just HTTP"; it needs HTTP/2 on every hop, including trailers, which many HTTP/1.1 proxies drop.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • HTTP/2 forbids Connection, Keep-Alive, Transfer-Encoding and Upgrade headers; an app that sets Connection: close on responses will have it stripped by the ALB, and one that checks for Connection: upgrade will never see it from HTTP/2 clients.
  • One HTTP/2 connection multiplexes everything, so a single slow stream with a large body can consume the connection-level flow-control window and delay others; per-stream windows matter.
  • HTTP/2 rapid reset attacks (CVE-2023-44487): clients open and immediately reset thousands of streams, exhausting server CPU. ALBs and CDNs mitigate this; Node's http2 server has maxSessionMemory and stream limits you must set if you expose HTTP/2 directly.
  • An ALB coalesces many HTTP/2 client streams onto a small number of HTTP/1.1 target connections; your per-connection assumptions (client IP from the socket, one client per connection) are false. Use X-Forwarded-For.
  • HTTP/3 0-RTT replays: a non-idempotent request accepted in 0-RTT could be executed twice; edges only allow 0-RTT for safe methods, and origins receive an Early-Data: 1 header they can reject with 425 Too Early.
  • UDP blocked by corporate firewalls means HTTP/3 fails; browsers fall back to HTTP/2 using the Alt-Svc header, which adds a race on the first visit.
  • Mixed protocols in tests: a load tool speaking HTTP/1.1 to the ALB will not reproduce HTTP/2 fan-out concurrency on the database.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They put HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 where the bad network is (the edge) and keep HTTP/1.1 where the network is good and the tooling is mature (between the ALB and the pods), unless gRPC forces HTTP/2 end to end. They know the ALB is a protocol translator, which shapes how they read headers, how they count connections, and how they plan database concurrency. They treat server push and pipelining as dead. To a product manager: "Upgrading the front door to HTTP/2 made the app feel twice as fast on mobile, with zero code changes and a config switch on the load balancer. The kitchen still works the same way."

Common mistakes

  • Setting Connection: keep-alive or Connection: close headers in application code.
  • Relying on the socket's remote address for the client IP behind any Layer 7 balancer.
  • Believing HTTP/2 between the ALB and the pods will speed up an API; the ALB-to-pod hop is 0.5 ms RTT and gains nothing.
  • Putting gRPC behind an HTTP/1.1 target group.
  • Assuming the browser's 6-connection limit still throttles fan-out after moving to HTTP/2.

Interview questions

  1. What is head-of-line blocking in HTTP/1.1, and how do HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 each address it? One response blocks the next on a connection; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection (removing HTTP-level HOL but keeping TCP-level HOL), HTTP/3 runs streams over QUIC with independent loss recovery.
  2. Your NestJS app is behind an ALB with HTTP/2 enabled. What protocol does the app see, and what changes for you? HTTP/1.1; headers are lowercase, Connection headers vanish, many clients share each target connection, and concurrency per user rises.
  3. Why does gRPC need HTTP/2, and what happens if you put it behind an HTTP/1.1 proxy? Streams, trailers and binary framing; the proxy returns 502 or drops trailers, breaking status codes.
  4. What is 0-RTT and why is it dangerous for a POST /payments? Application data in the first packet of a resumed connection; it can be replayed, so only idempotent requests may use it.
  5. Explain what the Alt-Svc header does. Advertises that the same origin is reachable over HTTP/3 on UDP 443, so the next connection tries QUIC.
  6. Is server push worth using? No; browsers removed it. Use 103 Early Hints and preload headers.

Practical exercise

Deploy a NestJS API behind an NGINX or ALB that supports HTTP/2. Build a page that fires 40 concurrent XHR calls. Measure the load time in Chrome DevTools with HTTP/2 enabled and disabled (--disable-http2 flag). Then observe pg_stat_activity during a page load under each mode. Acceptance criteria: two waterfall screenshots or timings, a count of peak concurrent database queries under each mode, and a written pool-size recommendation that accounts for the difference.

10.7 HTTP methods, headers and status codes

10.7.1 Methods: safe, idempotent, and why retries depend on it

Concept

An HTTP method states the intent of a request. Two properties of a method matter far more than its name:

  • Safe: the request does not change server state. Caches may store the response, crawlers may issue it freely, and a proxy may replay it.
  • Idempotent: sending the request once or ten times leaves the server in the same state. The response may differ (the second DELETE returns 404), but the state does not.
Method Safe Idempotent Typical NestJS use Retry on timeout?
GET yes yes read a resource or list yes, freely
HEAD yes yes check existence, size, ETag without a body yes
OPTIONS yes yes CORS preflight, capability discovery yes
PUT no yes full replace: PUT /carts/:id yes
DELETE no yes remove: DELETE /sessions/:id yes
POST no no create, or any action: POST /orders, POST /payments/:id/capture only with an idempotency key
PATCH no no (in general) partial update: PATCH /orders/:id with {"status":"packed"} only if the patch is absolute, not relative

PATCH is not idempotent in general because a patch like {"op":"increment","qty":1} applied twice adds two. A patch that sets absolute values ({"status":"packed"}) happens to be idempotent, but the client cannot know that from the method, so treat PATCH as unsafe to retry unless you add an idempotency key or an If-Match precondition.

Why does it exist?

The network fails after the request is sent and before the response arrives. The client then faces a question it cannot answer: did the server do the work? For an idempotent method, it does not matter; retry. For a non-idempotent method, a blind retry creates a duplicate order, a double charge, or two emails. Method semantics are the contract that lets load balancers, SDKs, retry libraries and browsers decide when a retry is safe. Browsers will re-issue a GET when the connection drops; they show a "resubmit form?" dialog for POST. Cloud SDKs retry idempotent calls automatically.

Mental model

Imagine sending a text message to a friend: "What time is dinner?" (GET) can be sent twice harmlessly. "Set dinner to 8pm" (PUT) sent twice is still 8pm. "Add one guest" (POST) sent twice adds two guests unless you also say "this is request #42", so your friend can ignore the duplicate.

How it works

  1. A client sends POST /orders. The request reaches NestJS, the order is created, and the response is lost because a NAT dropped the flow.
  2. The client's HTTP library sees a timeout. If it is configured to retry unsafe methods, it sends POST /orders again.
  3. Without protection, a second order is created.
  4. With an Idempotency-Key header (a client-generated UUID per logical operation), the server looks up the key before doing work. If the key exists, it returns the stored response. If not, it records the key (with a lock or unique constraint) and proceeds. The key's lifetime is typically 24 hours.
  5. For PUT, the same retry is harmless by definition, which is why senior engineers prefer client-generated IDs and PUT /orders/:clientGeneratedId over POST /orders where possible.

Practical example

A food-delivery app's checkout POST /orders succeeded on the server but the phone lost signal before the response. The app retried three times. Three orders, three charges, one furious customer. The fix combined an Idempotency-Key per checkout attempt with a unique index on (user_id, idempotency_key) so even two concurrent retries could not both insert.

NestJS example

// idempotency.interceptor.ts
import {
  BadRequestException, CallHandler, ConflictException, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, from, of } from 'rxjs';
import { switchMap, tap } from 'rxjs/operators';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { Request, Response } from 'express';

@Injectable()
export class IdempotencyInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>();
    const res = ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    if (req.method !== 'POST' && req.method !== 'PATCH') return next.handle();

    const key = req.header('idempotency-key');
    if (!key) throw new BadRequestException('Idempotency-Key header is required');
    const userId = (req as Request & { user?: { id: string } }).user?.id ?? 'anon';
    const redisKey = `idem:${userId}:${req.method}:${req.path}:${key}`;

    return from(this.redis.set(redisKey, 'IN_PROGRESS', 'EX', 86_400, 'NX')).pipe(
      switchMap(async (acquired) => {
        if (acquired) return null;                       // first time: run the handler
        const stored = await this.redis.get(redisKey);
        if (stored === 'IN_PROGRESS') throw new ConflictException('Request already in progress'); // 409
        return JSON.parse(stored!) as { status: number; body: unknown };
      }),
      switchMap((replay) =>
        replay
          ? of(replay.body).pipe(tap(() => res.status(replay.status)))
          : next.handle().pipe(
              tap((body) => this.redis.set(redisKey, JSON.stringify({ status: res.statusCode, body }), 'EX', 86_400)),
            ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

The NX set is the lock: two concurrent retries cannot both proceed. A handler failure should delete the key so the client can retry; add that in an error path with catchError. Store the response so a replay returns the same 201 and body rather than a new one.

PostgreSQL example

Redis is fast but the database is the source of truth; a unique constraint is the last line of defence when Redis is flushed or a second data centre shares the table.

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id               uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id          uuid NOT NULL,
  idempotency_key  text NOT NULL,
  status           text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'created',
  total_cents      integer NOT NULL CHECK (total_cents >= 0),
  created_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Two retries with the same key cannot both insert; the loser gets a unique violation (23505)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX orders_user_idem_uidx ON orders (user_id, idempotency_key);

-- Insert-or-return pattern: the retry gets the original row back instead of an error
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, idempotency_key, total_cents)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (user_id, idempotency_key) DO UPDATE SET user_id = EXCLUDED.user_id
RETURNING id, status, total_cents, (xmax = 0) AS inserted;

The xmax = 0 trick tells you whether the row was freshly inserted (true) or already existed (false), so the handler can return 201 on first creation and 200 on replay.

TypeORM example

// orders.service.ts
import { ConflictException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  async create(userId: string, idempotencyKey: string, totalCents: number): Promise<Order> {
    return this.ds.transaction(async (em) => {
      const existing = await em.findOne(Order, { where: { userId, idempotencyKey } });
      if (existing) return existing; // replay: same result, no new side effects
      try {
        return await em.save(em.create(Order, { userId, idempotencyKey, totalCents }));
      } catch (e: unknown) {
        // Unique violation from a concurrent retry that won the race
        if ((e as { code?: string }).code === '23505') {
          const winner = await em.findOneOrFail(Order, { where: { userId, idempotencyKey } });
          return winner;
        }
        throw new ConflictException('could not create order');
      }
    });
  }
}

Sequelize example

// orders.service.ts (Sequelize)
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectModel } from '@nestjs/sequelize';
import { UniqueConstraintError } from 'sequelize';
import { Order } from './order.model';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(@InjectModel(Order) private readonly orders: typeof Order) {}

  async create(userId: string, idempotencyKey: string, totalCents: number) {
    const [order, created] = await this.orders
      .findOrCreate({ where: { userId, idempotencyKey }, defaults: { totalCents } })
      .catch(async (e) => {
        if (e instanceof UniqueConstraintError) {
          const row = await this.orders.findOne({ where: { userId, idempotencyKey }, rejectOnEmpty: true });
          return [row, false] as const;
        }
        throw e;
      });
    return { order, statusCode: created ? 201 : 200 };
  }
}

Production scenario

A payments API processes 800 captures per minute. About 0.4% of client requests are retries after a timeout, 3 per minute. Without idempotency that is 3 double charges per minute, 4,300 per day. With Idempotency-Key stored in Redis (24-hour TTL, about 1.2 million keys, 200 MB) and the unique index as backstop, the duplicate rate is zero and the replay path is served in under 2 ms.

Failure scenario

An SDK team enabled "retry all 5xx and timeouts" in a shared HTTP client. Every service that used it started retrying POSTs. A downstream notification service that had a 30-second timeout during a slow period received three copies of each request. Customers got three "your order shipped" emails. The client library was changed to retry only idempotent methods by default, and to retry POST only when the caller supplied an idempotency key.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A retry that arrives while the original is still executing: the NX lock returns 409; the client should back off and retry, then get the stored response.
  • Idempotency keys reused across different payloads: return 422 if the key exists with a different request hash.
  • Key scope: scope to the user and the route, or one client's key could collide with another's.
  • DELETE returning 404 on the second try is correct; clients must treat 404 after a DELETE retry as success.
  • PUT with server-generated fields (updated_at) is still idempotent in state terms; do not confuse changing timestamps with non-idempotence.
  • Browsers may automatically retry a GET whose connection dropped before any response bytes arrived; a GET that has side effects (GET /orders/:id/cancel) will be executed twice.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design every mutating endpoint to answer "what happens if this arrives twice?" before writing it. They prefer client-generated IDs and PUT, use Idempotency-Key for POST, and forbid side effects in GET. They configure retries per method. To a product manager: "Retries are what make the app feel reliable on bad networks, and idempotency is what makes retries safe. Without both, we choose between a flaky app and double charges."

Common mistakes

  • GET /reports/generate that creates a file.
  • Retrying POST on timeout without a key.
  • Treating PATCH as idempotent because "it usually is".
  • Generating the idempotency key on the server, which defeats its purpose.

Interview questions

  1. Define safe and idempotent, and give a method that is one but not the other. Safe means no state change; idempotent means repeated calls leave the same state. DELETE is idempotent but not safe.
  2. Why is POST dangerous to retry, and how do you make it safe? Not idempotent; use a client-generated Idempotency-Key with a stored response and a unique constraint.
  3. A client times out on DELETE /items/42 and retries, getting 404. Is that a bug? No; the state is the same, and the client should treat it as success.
  4. When is PATCH idempotent? When it sets absolute values; relative operations like increments are not.
  5. How do you prevent two concurrent retries from both creating an order? A SET NX lock in Redis and a unique index in the database as backstop.

Practical exercise

Implement POST /orders with an Idempotency-Key. Write a Jest test that fires the same request 20 times in parallel and asserts exactly one row exists, one 201, and nineteen 200 or 409 responses with identical bodies. Acceptance criteria: the test passes against a real Postgres and Redis in Docker, and killing Redis mid-test still results in exactly one row.

10.7.2 Headers that matter

Concept

Headers are the metadata of a request or response: key-value pairs that tell the other side how to interpret the body, who is asking, what is acceptable, and how the response may be cached or retried. Names are case-insensitive; Node lowercases them all. A production NestJS API should treat the following as part of its contract.

Why does it exist?

Without headers, a body is just bytes. Headers let one URL serve JSON and CSV, let intermediaries cache safely, carry identity, propagate tracing context, and let a server tell a client precisely how to retry.
