Many outages are header bugs: a missing Cache-Control that let a CDN cache a personalised response, a Content-Type of text/html on a JSON error page, or an X-Forwarded-For that was trusted from an untrusted source.

Mental model

Imagine a parcel. The address label (Host), the "fragile, this way up" sticker (Content-Type), the customs declaration (Content-Length), the sender's ID badge (Authorization), the "do not store in warehouse" note (Cache-Control: no-store), and the tracking number (X-Request-Id). The parcel's contents are the body; everything on the outside is a header.

How it works

Header Direction What it does NestJS practice
Content-Type both media type of the body, e.g. application/json; charset=utf-8 set automatically for objects; set explicitly for CSV, PDF, application/problem+json
Content-Length both body size in bytes set by Node when the body is known; absent with chunked streaming
Accept request what the client can consume: application/json, text/csv content negotiation in a controller; reject unsupported with 406
Authorization request credentials: Bearer <jwt>, Basic <base64> read in a Passport guard; never log it
Cache-Control both caching rules (see 10.11) interceptor that sets private, no-store for user data, public, max-age for catalog
ETag / If-None-Match response / request resource version; conditional GET returns 304 see 10.11
If-Match request precondition: only apply if the version matches optimistic concurrency on PATCH, 412 on mismatch
Idempotency-Key request client-generated key to dedupe retries required on POST that charges or creates
X-Request-Id both correlation id across services and logs generate in middleware if absent; echo in the response; put in every log line
traceparent both W3C trace context for OpenTelemetry propagated automatically by the OTel SDK
X-Forwarded-For request client IP chain added by proxies trust only the hop added by your ALB; trust proxy setting
X-Forwarded-Proto request original scheme (https) at the LB needed to build absolute URLs and set Secure cookies correctly
Retry-After response seconds (or date) to wait before retrying; with 429 and 503 set from the rate limiter and during maintenance
Location response URL of a created resource (201) or redirect target (3xx) @Header or res.setHeader after creation
Vary response which request headers affect the response; caches key on them Vary: Accept-Encoding, Authorization when responses differ by those
Content-Encoding response gzip, br set by compression middleware
Strict-Transport-Security response force HTTPS for a period set by helmet
WWW-Authenticate response how to authenticate, sent with 401 Bearer realm="api"

Two headers deserve extra attention:

X-Forwarded-For is a comma-separated chain: client, proxy1, proxy2. Each proxy appends the address it saw. An attacker can send X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4 and, if you take the first value, you rate limit the wrong address. Express's trust proxy setting resolves this: with trust proxy = 1, req.ip is the value immediately before your one trusted hop, which is what the ALB appended. Never trust more hops than you own.

X-Request-Id is the single most useful header for operations. Generate a UUID at the edge (ALBs add X-Amzn-Trace-Id; API gateways add their own), or in your first middleware if none arrived, attach it to the async context, include it in every log line and every outbound call, and return it in the response so a support ticket can quote it.

NestJS example

// request-id.middleware.ts
import { Injectable, NestMiddleware } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'async_hooks';
import { randomUUID } from 'crypto';
import { NextFunction, Request, Response } from 'express';

export const requestContext = new AsyncLocalStorage<{ requestId: string }>();

@Injectable()
export class RequestIdMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  use(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
    // Accept an upstream id (ALB, gateway) but never trust arbitrary length or characters.
    const incoming = req.header('x-request-id');
    const requestId = incoming && /^[A-Za-z0-9-]{8,64}$/.test(incoming) ? incoming : randomUUID();
    res.setHeader('X-Request-Id', requestId);           // echo so the client can quote it
    requestContext.run({ requestId }, () => next());    // available to every log and outbound call
  }
}
// exports.controller.ts: content negotiation with Accept
import { Controller, Get, Header, Headers, NotAcceptableException, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Response } from 'express';

@Controller('exports')
export class ExportsController {
  @Get('orders')
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'private, no-store')
  async orders(@Headers('accept') accept: string | undefined, @Res() res: Response) {
    const wantsCsv = accept?.includes('text/csv');
    const wantsJson = !accept || accept.includes('application/json') || accept.includes('*/*');
    if (!wantsCsv && !wantsJson) throw new NotAcceptableException('Supported: application/json, text/csv'); // 406

    res.setHeader('Vary', 'Accept');                    // caches must key on Accept
    if (wantsCsv) {
      res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/csv; charset=utf-8');
      res.setHeader('Content-Disposition', 'attachment; filename="orders.csv"');
      return res.send('id,status,total_cents\n');
    }
    return res.json({ orders: [] });
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Headers rarely touch SQL directly, but the request id should: log it with slow queries so a trace in Grafana links to a row in pg_stat_statements or the Postgres log.

-- Tag the session so the request id appears in pg_stat_activity and in log_line_prefix (%a)
SET LOCAL application_name = 'orders-api:req-7f3a9c1e';

-- Then the slow-query log line reads:
-- 2026-09-06 10:22:01 UTC [orders-api:req-7f3a9c1e] LOG: duration: 1432.118 ms  statement: SELECT ...

In pg, run SET LOCAL application_name = $1 at the start of each transaction, or pass application_name in the connection string and rely on tracing for the request id.

Production scenario

A support ticket says "my order failed at 14:05". With X-Request-Id echoed in the app's error toast and present in every log line across the gateway, the API, the payment worker and the Postgres slow log, the engineer finds the full path in 30 seconds. Without it, they grep 4 million log lines for a user id and guess.

Failure scenario

A rate limiter keyed on the first X-Forwarded-For value was bypassed by a scraper that set the header to random IPs. 40 million product pages were scraped in a night. The fix was trust proxy: 1 and keying on req.ip, plus a WAF rule.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Header size limits: Node rejects headers over 16 KB (--max-http-header-size) with 431; an ALB's limit is 64 KB for all headers. A JWT with 200 roles can hit this.
  • Duplicate headers: most are joined with commas; Set-Cookie is an array; Content-Length twice is a request smuggling vector and is rejected.
  • Content-Type without charset on text responses leads to mojibake for non-ASCII names.
  • Missing Vary: Accept-Encoding lets a cache serve gzip to a client that did not ask for it.
  • Retry-After ignored by clients that retry immediately; combine with server-side rate limiting.
  • Case: Node lowercases; an app that reads req.headers['X-Request-Id'] gets undefined.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They define a small set of mandatory headers for every service (request id, trace context, content type, cache control) and enforce them with middleware and tests, not with code review. They never trust a client-supplied header for security decisions unless it was added by a hop they control. To a product manager: "The tracking number on every request is why we can tell you exactly what happened to a customer's order in under a minute."

Common mistakes

  • Logging the Authorization header.
  • Reading the first X-Forwarded-For value.
  • Forgetting Vary.
  • Serving JSON with text/html (a browser may execute it).
  • Sending Retry-After with a 500.

Interview questions

  1. How do you get the real client IP behind an ALB, and what is the trap? X-Forwarded-For with trust proxy set to the number of hops you own; the trap is trusting client-supplied values.
  2. What does Vary do and when does omitting it cause a bug? Tells caches which request headers change the response; omitting Vary: Accept-Encoding mixes compressed and uncompressed bodies.
  3. Design the request id flow across three services. Generate at the edge, propagate on every outbound call, log everywhere, echo in responses.
  4. Why is Content-Type: application/json on error responses important? Clients and browsers parse based on it; HTML error pages break JSON clients and can be an XSS vector.

Practical exercise

Add a middleware that enforces X-Request-Id, an interceptor that sets Cache-Control defaults, and a Jest e2e test that asserts every response carries X-Request-Id, a correct Content-Type, and Vary: Accept-Encoding when compressed. Acceptance criteria: tests green, and a log line that includes the request id for a deliberately slow query.

10.7.3 Status codes: what a NestJS API should return, and what the load balancer returns on its own

Concept

A status code tells the client, and every proxy between you and the client, what happened. Clients branch on it: retry, refresh a token, show a validation error, or give up. Load balancers and CDNs also generate their own codes when they cannot reach you, and distinguishing "the app said 503" from "the ALB said 503" is a daily task in operations.

Why does it exist?

Without a shared vocabulary, every client would need to parse error bodies. Status codes let generic infrastructure (browsers, SDK retry logic, CDNs, monitoring) act correctly without understanding your domain. A 503 with Retry-After triggers back-off; a 401 triggers a token refresh; a 304 saves bandwidth; a 422 shows a form error. Getting them wrong makes clients retry when they should not and give up when they should retry.

How it works

Classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx the client did something wrong, 5xx the server failed. The practical guide:

Code Meaning When a NestJS API returns it Should the client retry?
200 OK success with body GET, PATCH, PUT that returns the resource, idempotent replay of a POST n/a
201 Created resource created POST /orders first time; include Location n/a
202 Accepted accepted for async processing POST /exports that enqueues a job; body has a status URL n/a
204 No Content success, no body DELETE, PUT that returns nothing n/a
301 Moved Permanently permanent redirect; caches remember API version retirement; use rarely for APIs follow
302 Found / 307 temporary redirect OAuth flows; 307 preserves the method follow
304 Not Modified cached copy is still valid conditional GET with matching ETag n/a
400 Bad Request malformed request invalid JSON, missing required header, bad query type no
401 Unauthorized not authenticated missing or expired token; send WWW-Authenticate after refreshing credentials
403 Forbidden authenticated but not allowed user is not the order's owner; role lacks permission no
404 Not Found no such resource unknown id; also used to hide existence from unauthorised users no
405 Method Not Allowed route exists, method does not DELETE /orders on a collection; include Allow no
409 Conflict state conflict duplicate email; idempotent request in progress; version conflict on @VersionColumn after re-reading state
410 Gone existed, deliberately removed deleted account endpoints, retired API version no
412 Precondition Failed If-Match did not match optimistic concurrency on PATCH after refetching and reapplying
413 Payload Too Large body over the limit upload over bodyParser limit or ALB limit no, shrink the body
415 Unsupported Media Type wrong Content-Type text/plain sent to a JSON endpoint no
422 Unprocessable Entity well-formed but semantically invalid class-validator DTO failures (NestJS uses 400 by default; many teams switch to 422) no, fix input
429 Too Many Requests rate limited @nestjs/throttler; include Retry-After after Retry-After
500 Internal Server Error unhandled exception a bug; the default from NestJS's exception filter for unknown errors maybe once, with a key
502 Bad Gateway upstream gave an invalid response almost always the LB, not you: target closed the connection, sent garbage, or reset yes, with back-off
503 Service Unavailable temporarily unable your app during shutdown or when a dependency is down (with Retry-After); the ALB when no healthy targets yes, with back-off
504 Gateway Timeout upstream did not respond in time the ALB after its idle timeout (60 s); your own timeout interceptor if you choose it maybe, idempotent only

Who returns what. The distinction matters during incidents:

Code Returned by the ALB itself when Returned by NestJS when
400 malformed HTTP, header too large, bad Host validation failure
413 body exceeds the ALB limit (1 MB for Lambda targets, larger for instances) bodyParser limit exceeded
460 client closed the connection before the ALB finished (ALB-specific code, appears in access logs only) never
502 target reset the connection, closed it while a request was in flight (the keep-alive race, 10.9), sent malformed headers, or TLS to target failed never; if you see 502 the app did not answer
503 zero healthy targets in the target group, or target group not attached health check failing on purpose during shutdown, or circuit open
504 target did not send response headers within the idle timeout only if you emit it deliberately

The ALB access log has fields elb_status_code and target_status_code; when they differ, the ALB generated the response. Alert on elb_status_code = 5xx AND target_status_code = "-" as "infrastructure 5xx" separately from application 5xx.

NestJS example

A global exception filter that maps domain errors to codes consistently, uses application/problem+json, includes the request id, and never leaks stack traces. Plus the two lines that turn validation failures into 422.

// http-exception.filter.ts
import { ArgumentsHost, Catch, ExceptionFilter, HttpException, HttpStatus, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request, Response } from 'express';
import { QueryFailedError } from 'typeorm';

@Catch()
export class AllExceptionsFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(AllExceptionsFilter.name);

  catch(exception: unknown, host: ArgumentsHost) {
    const res = host.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    const req = host.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>();
    const requestId = res.getHeader('X-Request-Id');

    let status = HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR;
    let title = 'Internal Server Error';
    let detail: unknown = undefined;

    if (exception instanceof HttpException) {
      status = exception.getStatus();
      const body = exception.getResponse();
      title = typeof body === 'string' ? body : (body as { message?: string }).message ?? exception.message;
      detail = typeof body === 'object' ? body : undefined;
    } else if (exception instanceof QueryFailedError) {
      const code = (exception as QueryFailedError & { code?: string }).code;
      if (code === '23505') { status = HttpStatus.CONFLICT; title = 'Duplicate resource'; }         // 409
      else if (code === '23503') { status = HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY; title = 'Invalid reference'; } // 422
      else if (code === '57014') { status = HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE; title = 'Query timed out'; res.setHeader('Retry-After', '2'); } // statement_timeout
    }

    if (status >= 500) this.logger.error({ requestId, path: req.path, err: exception }); // log 5xx with stack, never send it
    res.status(status).setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/problem+json').json({
      type: 'about:blank', title, status, detail, instance: req.originalUrl, requestId,
    });
  }
}
// main.ts (excerpt): make DTO validation failures 422 instead of the default 400
app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({
  whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true, transform: true,
  errorHttpStatusCode: HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY,
}));
app.useGlobalFilters(new AllExceptionsFilter());
// orders.controller.ts (excerpt): 201 with Location, 202 for async, 204 for delete
@Post()
@HttpCode(201)
async create(@Body() dto: CreateOrderDto, @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response) {
  const order = await this.orders.create(dto);
  res.setHeader('Location', `/v1/orders/${order.id}`);
  return order;
}

@Post(':id/export')
@HttpCode(202)
async export(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string) {
  const job = await this.exports.enqueue(id);
  return { jobId: job.id, statusUrl: `/v1/exports/${job.id}` };
}

@Delete(':id')
@HttpCode(204)
async remove(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string) {
  await this.orders.remove(id); // idempotent: removing a missing order is a no-op
}

PostgreSQL example

Postgres error codes (SQLSTATE) map cleanly to HTTP codes, and the mapping should live in one place (the filter above).

SQLSTATE Meaning HTTP
23505 unique violation 409
23503 foreign key violation 422
23514 check constraint violation 422
40001 serialization failure retry internally, then 409
40P01 deadlock detected retry internally, then 409
57014 query cancelled (statement_timeout) 503 with Retry-After
53300 too many connections 503
08006 connection failure 503 
-- Reproduce 57014 to test the mapping
SET statement_timeout = '100ms';
SELECT pg_sleep(1);
-- ERROR:  canceling statement due to statement timeout  (SQLSTATE 57014)

Production scenario

A healthy API at 1,500 RPS shows roughly: 92% 200, 4% 201/204, 2.5% 304, 1% 4xx (mostly 401 from expired tokens and 404), and under 0.05% 5xx. Alerting: application 5xx rate over 0.5% for 5 minutes; ALB-generated 5xx over 0.1% for 2 minutes (a lower threshold because it indicates infrastructure problems); 429 rate as a capacity signal, not an error.

Failure scenario

At 11:20 the error dashboard showed 503 at 30% of requests. Application logs showed nothing wrong. The ALB access log showed elb_status_code=503, target_status_code=-: the ALB itself, meaning no healthy targets. The readiness probe had begun failing because a new version of the health check pinged a Redis instance that was being resized; the app was otherwise fine. Lesson: the readiness check should fail only for dependencies without which the service cannot serve anything, and the dashboard should split ALB-generated codes from app codes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Returning 200 with {"error": ...} breaks every client's retry logic and every dashboard.
  • 401 versus 403: 401 triggers token refresh loops; returning 401 for authorisation failures makes clients refresh tokens forever.
  • 404 for authorisation hiding is fine but must be consistent, or an attacker learns which ids exist.
  • 500 from validation bugs (throwing plain Error) instead of 4xx makes clients retry things that can never succeed.
  • 502 storms on deploy indicate the keep-alive race (10.9) or missing draining.
  • 504 from the ALB means the client waited 60 seconds; your own timeout at 10 to 30 seconds gives a faster, more honest answer.
  • Redirecting POST with 301/302 changes it to GET in browsers; use 307/308.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They pick codes for what the client should do next, not for how the error feels. They own a single mapping from domain and database errors to codes. They separate infrastructure-generated codes from application-generated ones in every dashboard. They never return 500 for something the client can fix. To a product manager: "A 4xx is the customer's form to fix; a 5xx is our pager to answer. Mixing them up hides our bugs and blames the customer."

Common mistakes

  • 200 for everything with an error flag in the body.
  • 500 for validation failures.
  • 401 when the user is authenticated but not allowed.
  • 503 without Retry-After.
  • Not reading ALB access logs to see who generated a 5xx.

Interview questions

  1. When do you return 409 versus 412 versus 422? 409 for a state conflict (duplicate, in progress), 412 for a failed precondition header (If-Match), 422 for semantically invalid input.
  2. The ALB returns 502 but your app logs show nothing. What are the three likeliest causes? Keep-alive timeout race, target closed connection mid-request during a deploy without draining, malformed response headers.
  3. 401 or 403 for "you cannot view another user's order"? 403 (or 404 to hide existence); 401 means "who are you".
  4. How should a client treat 429 and 503? Back off using Retry-After with jitter; never tight-loop.
  5. Which status should a failed statement_timeout map to? 503 with Retry-After; the request may succeed later.
  6. Why is 202 useful and what must the response contain? For long-running work; a job id and a status URL.

Practical exercise

Write the global exception filter and a test suite that asserts the code for each of: invalid DTO, duplicate email, foreign-key failure, statement timeout, missing token, wrong owner, unknown id, rate limit. Then deploy behind an ALB, kill a pod during a load test, and produce a table from the ALB access log splitting elb_status_code from target_status_code. Acceptance criteria: all tests green, and a dashboard panel that separates app 5xx from ALB 5xx.

10.8 Cookies and sessions

Concept

HTTP is stateless: the server does not remember the previous request. A cookie is a small piece of data the server asks the browser to store (Set-Cookie response header) and the browser sends back on every later request to that site (Cookie request header). A session is server-side state associated with a client, usually looked up by an opaque session id carried in a cookie. The alternative, a JWT (JSON Web Token), puts signed claims into the token itself so the server needs no lookup; it can travel in a cookie or in an Authorization: Bearer header.

Cookie attributes control where and when the browser sends the cookie:

Attribute Effect Production setting for a session cookie
HttpOnly JavaScript cannot read it (document.cookie) always on; blocks token theft via XSS
Secure sent only over HTTPS always on
SameSite=Strict / Lax / None whether the cookie is sent on cross-site requests Lax for most apps; Strict for admin; None (with Secure) only for cross-site embeds
Domain which hosts receive it; omitting it means only the exact host omit, or .shop.com only if subdomains genuinely need it
Path URL prefix that receives it / or /api
Max-Age / Expires lifetime; absent means "session cookie", deleted when the browser closes Max-Age=86400 and a server-side idle timeout
__Host- prefix requires Secure, no Domain, Path=/ __Host-sid for the strongest binding

Why does it exist?

Without cookies, a user would log in on every request. Without HttpOnly, a single XSS bug hands every session to an attacker. Without SameSite, any website could make the user's browser submit a POST /transfer to your bank with the user's cookie attached (CSRF). Server-side sessions exist so that logout, revocation and "sign out of all devices" are instant; JWTs exist so that a fleet of services can verify identity without a shared lookup on every call.

Mental model

Imagine a gym. A session is the front desk's register: you show a numbered wristband (the cookie holding a session id) and the receptionist looks you up. Losing the wristband or the gym cutting it off ends access immediately. A JWT is a laminated pass with your name, membership level and expiry date, signed by the manager. Any door can check it without calling the desk, but if you are expelled the pass keeps working until it expires, unless every door also keeps a blocklist.

How it works

Cookie flow.

  1. POST /auth/login validates credentials.
  2. The server creates a session record in Redis: sess:9f2c... with { userId, roles, createdAt, ip, userAgent } and a TTL.
  3. The server responds with Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=9f2c...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=86400.
  4. The browser stores it and attaches Cookie: __Host-sid=9f2c... to every request to that host, including images and API calls made by page scripts.
  5. A NestJS guard reads the cookie, fetches the session from Redis (about 0.3 ms), attaches the user to the request, and refreshes the TTL (sliding expiration).
  6. Logout deletes the Redis key and sends Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=; Max-Age=0.

SameSite mechanics. Strict never sends the cookie on a request initiated from another site, so clicking a link from an email into your app arrives logged out. Lax sends it on top-level navigations with safe methods (GET from a link) but not on cross-site POST, iframes, or fetch; this blocks classic CSRF while keeping links working. None sends it everywhere and requires Secure; needed only when your API is embedded cross-site (a widget on a partner's page). Chrome defaults to Lax when the attribute is missing.

Session store choices.

Store Lookup latency Revocation Horizontal scaling Notes
Redis 0.2 to 1 ms instant yes, shared the standard; TTLs built in
PostgreSQL 1 to 5 ms instant yes, shared fine at low scale; needs cleanup job
In-memory microseconds instant on that pod only no; needs sticky sessions never in production
Stateless JWT 0 lookup, about 0.05 ms to verify not without a blocklist trivially short TTL plus refresh token

JWT in a cookie versus session cookie. A JWT in an HttpOnly cookie gets the XSS protection of cookies and the stateless verification of JWTs, but keeps the revocation weakness. The common senior pattern: a short-lived access JWT (5 to 15 minutes) in memory or a cookie, plus a long-lived opaque refresh token stored server-side (Redis or Postgres) and sent in an HttpOnly cookie scoped to Path=/auth/refresh. Revocation kills the refresh token; the access token dies within minutes. See Part on Authentication and Security for the full treatment; here we focus on the transport.

Size and count limits. Browsers allow about 4 KB per cookie and around 180 cookies per domain, and every cookie rides on every request to that host. A 3 KB JWT cookie on a page that loads 60 images adds 180 KB of upload per page load on a mobile uplink. Keep cookies small, and serve static assets from a cookieless domain or CDN.

Practical example

A food-delivery web app uses __Host-sid sessions in Redis with a 24-hour idle timeout and a 30-day absolute limit. The mobile apps use the same login endpoint but receive a JSON body with an access JWT and refresh token instead of a cookie, because native HTTP clients do not have a browser's cookie jar semantics or CSRF exposure. Both flows hit the same Redis-backed session table, so "log out everywhere" works across web and mobile.

NestJS example

Sessions in Redis with express-session and connect-redis, wired in main.ts, plus a guard that loads the user and a controller that sets and clears the cookie correctly.

// main.ts (excerpt)
import session from 'express-session';
import { RedisStore } from 'connect-redis';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { NestExpressApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-express';

const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule);
app.set('trust proxy', 1); // required so `secure: true` cookies work behind the ALB (X-Forwarded-Proto)

const redis = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL!, { enableOfflineQueue: false, connectTimeout: 2_000 });
app.use(
  session({
    name: '__Host-sid',
    secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET!,          // signs the cookie so a forged id is rejected before Redis
    store: new RedisStore({ client: redis, prefix: 'sess:', ttl: 86_400 }), // 24 h idle timeout
    resave: false,
    saveUninitialized: false,                      // do not create sessions for anonymous traffic
    rolling: true,                                 // sliding expiration on activity
    cookie: {
      httpOnly: true,
      secure: true,
      sameSite: 'lax',
      path: '/',
      maxAge: 86_400_000,                          // ms; keep in step with the store TTL
    },
  }),
);
// session-auth.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request } from 'express';

interface SessionData { userId?: string; roles?: string[]; }

@Injectable()
export class SessionAuthGuard implements CanActivate {
  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request & { session: SessionData; user?: unknown }>();
    if (!req.session?.userId) throw new UnauthorizedException(); // 401: not logged in
    req.user = { id: req.session.userId, roles: req.session.roles ?? [] };
    return true;
  }
}
// auth.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, HttpCode, Post, Req, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request } from 'express';
import { LoginDto } from './dto/login.dto';
import { AuthService } from './auth.service';

@Controller('auth')
export class AuthController {
  constructor(private readonly auth: AuthService) {}

  @Post('login')
  @HttpCode(200)
  async login(@Body() dto: LoginDto, @Req() req: Request & { session: Record<string, unknown> }) {
    const user = await this.auth.validate(dto.email, dto.password);
    if (!user) throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid credentials');
    // Regenerate the session id on privilege change to defeat session fixation
    await new Promise<void>((resolve, reject) => req.session.regenerate((err) => (err ? reject(err) : resolve())));
    req.session.userId = user.id;
    req.session.roles = user.roles;
    return { id: user.id, email: user.email };
  }

  @Post('logout')
  @HttpCode(204)
  async logout(@Req() req: Request & { session: { destroy: (cb: (err?: unknown) => void) => void } }) {
    // destroy() deletes the Redis key and express-session clears the cookie
    await new Promise<void>((resolve, reject) => req.session.destroy((err) => (err ? reject(err) : resolve())));
  }
}

The regenerate() on login is the detail juniors skip: without it, an attacker who plants a known session id in the victim's browser before login (session fixation) shares the authenticated session afterwards.

PostgreSQL example

Even with sessions in Redis, keep a durable record of refresh tokens or long-lived sessions in Postgres so that "sign out all devices" and audit work after a Redis flush.

CREATE TABLE user_sessions (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id       uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  token_hash    bytea NOT NULL,                         -- sha256 of the refresh token; never store the token
  user_agent    text,
  client_ip     inet,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_seen_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at    timestamptz NOT NULL,
  revoked_at    timestamptz
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX user_sessions_token_hash_uidx ON user_sessions (token_hash);
CREATE INDEX user_sessions_user_active_idx ON user_sessions (user_id) WHERE revoked_at IS NULL;

-- Sign out everywhere
UPDATE user_sessions SET revoked_at = now() WHERE user_id = $1 AND revoked_at IS NULL;

-- Nightly cleanup (or pg_cron) so the table does not grow forever
DELETE FROM user_sessions WHERE expires_at < now() - interval '7 days';

TypeORM example

// user-session.entity.ts
import { Column, CreateDateColumn, Entity, Index, ManyToOne, PrimaryGeneratedColumn } from 'typeorm';
import { User } from '../users/user.entity';

@Entity('user_sessions')
export class UserSession {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id!: string;

  @ManyToOne(() => User, { onDelete: 'CASCADE' }) user!: User;

  @Index({ unique: true })
  @Column({ type: 'bytea' }) tokenHash!: Buffer;

  @Column({ type: 'inet', nullable: true }) clientIp!: string | null;

  @Column({ type: 'timestamptz' }) expiresAt!: Date;

  @Column({ type: 'timestamptz', nullable: true }) revokedAt!: Date | null;

  @CreateDateColumn({ type: 'timestamptz' }) createdAt!: Date;
}

Sequelize example

// user-session.model.ts
import { Column, DataType, ForeignKey, Model, Table } from 'sequelize-typescript';
import { User } from '../users/user.model';

@Table({ tableName: 'user_sessions', timestamps: false })
export class UserSession extends Model {
  @Column({ type: DataType.UUID, primaryKey: true, defaultValue: DataType.UUIDV4 }) id!: string;
  @ForeignKey(() => User) @Column(DataType.UUID) userId!: string;
  @Column({ type: DataType.BLOB, unique: true }) tokenHash!: Buffer;
  @Column(DataType.INET) clientIp!: string | null;
  @Column(DataType.DATE) expiresAt!: Date;
  @Column(DataType.DATE) revokedAt!: Date | null;
  @Column({ type: DataType.DATE, defaultValue: DataType.NOW }) createdAt!: Date;
}

Production scenario

A marketplace with 2 million monthly users keeps about 400,000 active sessions in Redis at roughly 300 bytes each, 120 MB. Session lookups run at 4,000 per second with a p99 of 1.1 ms. When Redis was migrated to a cluster with a 30-second failover, enableOfflineQueue: false meant login-required requests failed fast with 503 for 30 seconds rather than piling up 120,000 blocked requests; the rest of the site (anonymous browsing) was unaffected because saveUninitialized: false meant anonymous traffic never touched Redis.

Failure scenario

At 16:45, after a deploy that "just changed the cookie domain to .shop.com so the blog could show the username", every user was logged out, and then some users saw other users' names. The old cookie (Domain omitted, host-only for www.shop.com) and the new one (Domain=.shop.com) coexisted with the same name; browsers sent both, in an order that varies by path length and creation time, and the session middleware read whichever came first. A rollback plus an explicit cookie name change (sid to sid2) fixed it. Lesson: changing Domain, Path or Name creates a second cookie, not an updated one; plan the migration.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Secure cookies are never set over plain HTTP; behind an ALB without trust proxy, Express thinks the request is HTTP and silently skips Set-Cookie. Login "works" but no cookie appears.
  • SameSite=None without Secure is rejected by browsers.
  • Cookies are sent to every path by default; a cookie meant for /api also rides along with image requests.
  • Session TTL sliding on every request means a bot that polls keeps a session alive forever; add an absolute lifetime.
  • Redis down: sessions become unavailable; decide fast-fail versus degraded anonymous mode.
  • Session data bloat: storing the cart in the session pushes Redis memory and serialisation cost; store ids, not objects.
  • CSRF with SameSite=Lax still allows top-level GET navigations; never mutate state on GET.
  • Subdomain takeover: a cookie with Domain=.shop.com is readable by any subdomain, including a forgotten old.shop.com pointing at an expired S3 bucket.
  • Clock skew on JWT exp claims: a server 2 minutes behind accepts expired tokens; one ahead rejects fresh ones. Use NTP and a small leeway.
  • Cookie jar limits: a 4 KB JWT with many claims can exceed the per-cookie limit and be dropped silently.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They pick sessions for browser apps by default (instant revocation, small cookies, mature tooling) and JWTs for service-to-service and mobile where a lookup per call is impractical, always with a short expiry and a refresh token. They set every cookie attribute deliberately and use the __Host- prefix. They plan cookie changes as migrations. To a product manager: "Log out everywhere works in one second because we kept the register at the front desk. If we had used only stamped passes, a stolen pass would work until it expired."

Common mistakes

  • Storing the JWT in localStorage (readable by any XSS).
  • Omitting HttpOnly "so the frontend can read the user id"; send the id in the body instead.
  • Not regenerating the session id at login.
  • Using in-memory sessions in a multi-pod deployment and wondering why users get logged out on every request.
  • Sliding expiry with no absolute limit.

Interview questions

  1. Compare server-side sessions and JWTs on revocation, scaling and payload size. Sessions: instant revocation, need a shared store, tiny cookie. JWT: no lookup, no revocation without a blocklist, larger cookie.
  2. What does SameSite=Lax block and what does it still allow? Blocks cross-site POST, iframes and fetch with cookies; allows top-level GET navigations.
  3. Why does Secure break behind a load balancer without trust proxy? Express sees HTTP, refuses to set the Secure cookie.
  4. Explain session fixation and its fix. Attacker pre-sets a session id; regenerate on login.
  5. Where should a refresh token live in a browser app? HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie scoped to the refresh path, hashed in the database.
  6. What happens if you rename a cookie or change its Domain? A second cookie coexists; plan a migration.

Practical exercise

Implement login, logout and "sign out all devices" with Redis sessions and a Postgres session table. Write e2e tests that assert the Set-Cookie attributes, that a fixed session id does not survive login, that a cross-site POST is rejected, and that revoking in Postgres invalidates the session on the next request. Acceptance criteria: tests pass behind an NGINX that sets X-Forwarded-Proto, and the cookie is under 200 bytes.

10.9 Keep-alive and connection pooling

10.9.1 HTTP keep-alive and the classic 502 bug

Concept

HTTP keep-alive means reusing one TCP connection for many HTTP requests, one after another. It is the default in HTTP/1.1 and mandatory in HTTP/2. It is a different thing from TCP keepalive (10.4.3), which sends probes to detect dead peers; HTTP keep-alive is about reuse, TCP keepalive is about liveness.

Every hop has its own idea of how long an idle connection may live: the browser, the CDN, the load balancer, the Node server, and the outbound agents your app uses. When two adjacent hops disagree about who closes an idle connection first, you get intermittent 502 Bad Gateway. This is the single most common networking bug in Node deployments behind an ALB, NGINX or any reverse proxy.

Why does it exist?

A new connection costs a TCP handshake and a TLS handshake (10.4.2): 2 to 3 round trips and a millisecond or two of CPU. At 1,000 requests per second that would be 1,000 handshakes per second. Keep-alive amortises the cost across hundreds of requests. Idle timeouts exist because a connection that is kept open forever holds a file descriptor, kernel buffers and, behind a proxy, a slot in the proxy's connection table; someone must reap idle ones.

Mental model

Imagine a taxi rank with a rule: a taxi waits five minutes for a passenger, then leaves. A dispatcher, standing at the rank, believes taxis wait for an hour and confidently sends a customer to a taxi at minute six. The customer walks to an empty spot. That is a 502: the proxy sent a request into a connection the server had just closed. The fix is trivial once stated: the taxi must wait longer than the dispatcher expects, never shorter.

How it works

The relevant timers in a standard AWS deployment:

Hop Timer Default Meaning
Browser idle connection reuse about 60 s to 5 min reuses HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 connections
ALB (client side) idle timeout 60 s closes client connections idle longer than this
ALB (target side) idle timeout same 60 s setting reuses target connections; sends the next request on any idle connection under 60 s old
Node http.Server keepAliveTimeout 5 s closes an idle keep-alive socket after 5 s of no requests
Node http.Server headersTimeout 60 s max time to receive full headers; must be greater than keepAliveTimeout
Node http.Server requestTimeout 300 s max time for a whole request
NGINX upstream keepalive_timeout 60 s idle upstream connection lifetime
Node outbound http.Agent timeout on free sockets none by default how long the pool keeps an idle socket
undici Agent keepAliveTimeout 4 s idle socket lifetime in the pool

The race, step by step:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant LB as ALB idle 60s
    participant N as Node keepAliveTimeout 5s
    C->>LB: GET /orders
    LB->>N: GET /orders on socket S1
    N-->>LB: 200 OK
    LB-->>C: 200 OK
    Note over N: S1 idle 5.000 s, Node sends FIN
    Note over LB: S1 has been idle 5.001 s, still considered reusable
    C->>LB: GET /cart
    LB->>N: GET /cart on socket S1 in flight while FIN arrives
    N-->>LB: RST or FIN, request bytes discarded
    LB-->>C: 502 Bad Gateway
  1. The ALB forwards a request to a Node pod over socket S1 and gets a response. S1 is now idle on both sides.
  2. Node's keepAliveTimeout (5 s) expires first. Node closes S1 by sending FIN.
  3. In the few milliseconds it takes the FIN to reach the ALB, or simply because the ALB checks idleness only when it needs a connection, the ALB picks S1 for the next request and writes the request bytes.
  4. The bytes arrive at a closed socket. The kernel replies RST. Node never sees the request, so nothing is logged.
  5. The ALB, having sent a request and received a reset with no response, returns 502 to the client. The access log shows elb_status_code=502 target_status_code=-.

The probability per request is small (the window is a few milliseconds around every 5-second idle boundary), so it shows up as a 0.01% to 0.5% background 502 rate that no one can reproduce and that rises during low traffic, when connections go idle more often.

The rule. At every hop, the upstream (server-side) idle timeout must be longer than the downstream (client-side) idle timeout, so the client always closes first, and a client that closes first never sends a request into a dead socket. For an ALB with a 60-second idle timeout, set Node's keepAliveTimeout to 65 seconds and headersTimeout to 66 seconds (Node requires headersTimeout to exceed keepAliveTimeout, or the headers timer closes keep-alive sockets early). The same rule applies to NGINX upstreams (keepalive_timeout on Node above the NGINX keepalive_timeout) and to your own outbound agents (your agent's idle timeout below the third-party server's idle timeout).

Some proxies retry idempotent requests on connection reset, which hides the bug for GET and reveals it only for POST. The ALB does not retry; it returns 502.

Practical example

A checkout API behind an ALB saw a stable 0.08% 502 rate for months, dismissed as "network noise". During a quiet night it rose to 1.2% because most target connections were idle. One config change (keepAliveTimeout = 65000, headersTimeout = 66000) brought the rate to zero the next day.

NestJS example

// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { Server } from 'http';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  const server: Server = app.getHttpServer();

  // The ALB idle timeout is 60 s. The server must outlive it so the ALB always closes first.
  const lbIdleTimeoutMs = Number(process.env.LB_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS ?? 60_000);
  server.keepAliveTimeout = lbIdleTimeoutMs + 5_000; // 65 s
  server.headersTimeout = lbIdleTimeoutMs + 6_000;   // 66 s, must be greater than keepAliveTimeout
  server.requestTimeout = 120_000;                   // whole-request cap; below this, our own 504 interceptor fires

  await app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0');
}
bootstrap();

For Fastify (@nestjs/platform-fastify), pass the same values as adapter options: new FastifyAdapter({ keepAliveTimeout: 65_000, connectionTimeout: 0 }); headersTimeout is not exposed by Fastify's constructor options, so set it on app.getHttpServer() after creation, exactly as above.

PostgreSQL example

The identical race exists between your pool and PgBouncer or the database. If the pool keeps an idle client for 30 seconds but PgBouncer's server_idle_timeout or the database's idle session timeout closes it at 20 seconds, the next checkout hands you a dead socket and the first query fails with Connection terminated unexpectedly.

-- PostgreSQL 14+: server-side idle session cutoff. Keep it LONGER than the app pool's
-- idleTimeoutMillis so the pool closes first and never hands out a dead socket.
ALTER SYSTEM SET idle_session_timeout = '10min';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

-- With PgBouncer in the path: pgbouncer.ini
-- server_idle_timeout = 600   ; seconds, must exceed the app pool idle timeout
-- client_idle_timeout = 0     ; do not cut clients that are pooled on the app side

Rule of thumb: pg pool idleTimeoutMillis (e.g. 30 s) is shorter than PgBouncer server_idle_timeout (600 s), which is shorter than PostgreSQL idle_session_timeout (10 min or disabled). Client closes first at every hop.

Production scenario

An API cluster of 24 pods behind an ALB serves 1,800 RPS with about 40 target connections per pod, most of them reused thousands of times before being closed by the ALB at the 60-second idle mark. New target connections: about 5 per second cluster-wide. After the timeout fix, ALB HTTPCode_ELB_502_Count went from 1,400 per day to about 3 per day, all of which coincided with deployments (pods terminating mid-request, fixed separately with deregistration delay).

Failure scenario

At 03:20 the 502 alert fired for a payments webhook receiver. Traffic at that hour was 2 requests per minute, which meant every ALB-to-target connection sat idle past Node's 5-second cutoff between requests, and nearly every request hit a socket the pod had just closed. The webhook sender (a payment provider) retried each 502 with exponential back-off, then gave up after 6 attempts, and 11 payment confirmations were lost. Recovery required a reconciliation job against the provider's API. The permanent fix was the timeout rule plus making the webhook handler idempotent so replays from the provider's dashboard were safe.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • headersTimeout less than or equal to keepAliveTimeout reintroduces the bug in Node 18+, because the headers timer fires on idle keep-alive sockets.
  • Pods behind both an ALB and a service mesh sidecar (Envoy) have two hops to align; Envoy's default upstream idle timeout is 1 hour, which is fine, but its cluster-level idle_timeout can be lowered by platform teams.
  • During a deploy, Kubernetes sends SIGTERM; if the app keeps serving on existing sockets but the ALB is not told to drain (deregistration delay, readiness flipping to false first), in-flight requests get RST when the container dies.
  • Serverless targets (Lambda behind an ALB) have no keep-alive between ALB and function; the rule applies only to container and instance targets.
  • Outbound: your http.Agent keeps a free socket for 60 seconds by default only if you set timeout; a third-party API that closes idle connections after 10 seconds will reset your next request. Set the agent's free-socket timeout below the remote's idle timeout, and retry ECONNRESET on idempotent requests.
  • Half-open sockets from NAT expiry (10.4.3) look identical in the logs to the keep-alive race; TCP keepalive probes distinguish them.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They draw every hop in the request path and write down its idle timeout before deploying a service, and they check the rule "server outlives client" at each hop. They alert on load balancer generated 5xx separately, with a low threshold. They treat a nonzero background 502 rate as a bug, never as noise. To a product manager: "Two machines disagreed by one second about when to hang up. That was the entire cause of the lost payment confirmations."

Common mistakes

  • Leaving Node's 5-second default behind a 60-second ALB.
  • Setting keepAliveTimeout but not headersTimeout.
  • Setting the same value on both sides (still a race).
  • Fixing it with retries at the client instead of fixing the timers.
  • Copying an NGINX config with keepalive_timeout 75s in front of a Node server with 65 seconds (wrong direction).

Interview questions

  1. Explain the ALB-to-Node 502 bug and its fix. Node closes idle sockets at 5 s, the ALB reuses them for 60 s; requests hit dead sockets. Set Node's keepAliveTimeout above the ALB idle timeout and headersTimeout above that.
  2. What is the general rule for idle timeouts along a chain of proxies? Each server-side timeout must exceed the client-side timeout of the hop before it, so clients close first.
  3. How would you prove the bug from logs? ALB access log with elb_status_code=502 and target_status_code=-, no matching app log, correlation with low-traffic periods.
  4. Does the same problem exist with database pools? Yes: pool idle timeout must be shorter than PgBouncer's and the server's idle cutoffs.
  5. Why does HTTP/2 not eliminate this class of bug? HTTP/2 connections also go idle and get closed; GOAWAY handling is cleaner but the server-outlives-client rule still applies.

Practical exercise

Run NestJS behind NGINX with proxy_http_version 1.1, keepalive 32 in the upstream block, and a Node keepAliveTimeout of 2 seconds. Send one request every 2.0 to 2.1 seconds for ten minutes and count 502s in the NGINX log. Then apply the rule and repeat. Acceptance criteria: a nonzero 502 count before, zero after, and a short written explanation referencing the exact timers involved.

10.9.2 Outbound connection pooling: http.Agent, undici and pool sizing

Concept

A connection pool is a set of pre-opened, reusable connections to one destination. Inbound, the load balancer pools connections to your pods. Outbound, your NestJS service should pool connections to every HTTP dependency (payment gateway, maps, internal services), to Postgres, and to Redis. Node's http.Agent (used by axios, node-fetch and @nestjs/axios) and undici (the client behind Node's global fetch) are the two HTTP pool implementations you will meet.

Why does it exist?

Without a pool, every outbound call pays a DNS lookup, a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake, and a slow-start ramp (10.4 and 10.5), and churns an ephemeral port into TIME_WAIT (10.2). A pool turns that into a reused warm socket: a 40 ms overhead becomes 0 ms. A pool also gives you a cap: a bounded number of concurrent connections per destination, which protects the dependency and your own port range from a traffic spike.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel switchboard with a fixed number of outside lines. Guests pick up a free line, talk, and hang up, and the line is instantly ready for the next guest. If all lines are busy, guests queue. That queue, and how long a guest is willing to wait, is the part that matters during an incident.

How it works

  1. A request needs a connection to api.payments.example.com:443.
  2. The agent checks its free list for that origin. If a warm socket exists and is not past its idle timeout, it is used immediately.
  3. Otherwise, if the number of open sockets to that origin is below maxSockets (http.Agent) or connections (undici), a new one is opened: DNS, TCP, TLS.
  4. Otherwise the request waits in the agent's queue until a socket frees. Unbounded queues are how one slow dependency turns into memory growth and a latency cliff.
  5. When the response body is fully consumed, the socket returns to the free list. If the body is not consumed, the socket is stuck: this is the most common pool leak.
  6. Free sockets past their idle timeout are closed; the remote's idle timeout must be longer (10.9.1).

Sizing. For a dependency with average latency L seconds at a call rate of R per second, you need about R * L connections in use (Little's law), plus headroom for tails. For 200 calls per second at 50 ms, that is 10 connections; set the cap at 3 to 5 times that (30 to 50) to absorb p99 spikes, and set a queue timeout so callers fail fast rather than pile up. Per pod, not per process cluster: with 20 pods, the dependency sees 20 times your cap.

http.Agent versus undici.

Feature http.Agent undici Agent / Pool
Used by http.request, axios, node-fetch, @nestjs/axios global fetch in Node 18+, undici.request
Keep-alive default off before Node 19; on since Node 19 on
Concurrency cap maxSockets per origin (default Infinity) connections per origin (default unlimited), pipelining
Idle socket timeout timeout option, applies to free sockets keepAliveTimeout (4 s default), keepAliveMaxTimeout
Per-request timeouts you must implement (axios timeout is total) headersTimeout, bodyTimeout separately
Performance fine 2 to 3 times higher throughput in benchmarks; less allocation
HTTP/2 no experimental allowH2

NestJS example

A single, injectable pooled client per dependency, with explicit caps, timeouts, and a queue-wait guard, plus a health signal from pool stats.

// payments-client.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy, ServiceUnavailableException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Pool, errors } from 'undici';

@Injectable()
export class PaymentsClientService implements OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(PaymentsClientService.name);
  private readonly pool = new Pool('https://api.payments.example.com', {
    connections: 40,             // hard cap per pod; 20 pods x 40 = 800 at the provider
    pipelining: 1,               // HTTP/1.1, one request per socket at a time
    keepAliveTimeout: 20_000,    // below the provider's 30 s idle cutoff: we close first
    keepAliveMaxTimeout: 60_000,
    connect: { timeout: 2_000 },
  });

  async capture(paymentId: string, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<{ status: string }> {
    // Refuse to queue when the pool is saturated: fail fast instead of piling up.
    const stats = this.pool.stats;
    if (stats.pending > 100) throw new ServiceUnavailableException('payments pool saturated');

    try {
      const res = await this.pool.request({
        method: 'POST',
        path: `/v1/payments/${paymentId}/capture`,
        headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', 'idempotency-key': idempotencyKey },
        body: '{}',
        headersTimeout: 3_000,   // time to first byte of headers
        bodyTimeout: 3_000,      // time between body chunks
      });
      if (res.statusCode >= 500) {
        await res.body.dump();   // always consume so the socket returns to the pool
        throw new ServiceUnavailableException(`payments returned ${res.statusCode}`);
      }
      return (await res.body.json()) as { status: string };
    } catch (e) {
      if (e instanceof errors.HeadersTimeoutError || e instanceof errors.BodyTimeoutError) {
        this.logger.warn({ paymentId, msg: 'payments timeout' });
        throw new ServiceUnavailableException('payments timeout');
      }
      throw e;
    }
  }

  onModuleDestroy() {
    return this.pool.close();
  }
}

For code that must stay on axios (@nestjs/axios), the equivalent is an https.Agent({ keepAlive: true, maxSockets: 40, maxFreeSockets: 10, timeout: 20_000 }) passed in HttpModule.register, plus timeout: 3_000 on the request.

PostgreSQL example

The database pool follows the same rules, with one extra concern: each pooled connection is a server process. Size for pods * max under max_connections minus a reserve, and measure wait time.

-- Global budget
SHOW max_connections;               -- e.g. 200
SHOW superuser_reserved_connections; -- e.g. 3; keep a few for the on-call

-- Are pools waiting? In pg you measure this on the client (pool.waitingCount);
-- on the server you see it as near-max backends with mostly 'idle' state:
SELECT count(*) AS backends,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'active') AS active
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_type = 'client backend';
-- If backends is near max_connections but active is small, the pools are oversized
-- and the fix is smaller pools (or PgBouncer), not a bigger database.

TypeORM example

// Expose pool stats for a readiness probe and metrics
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { PostgresDriver } from 'typeorm/driver/postgres/PostgresDriver';
import { Pool } from 'pg';

@Injectable()
export class DbPoolMetrics {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  snapshot() {
    const pool = (this.ds.driver as PostgresDriver).master as Pool; // the underlying pg Pool
    return { total: pool.totalCount, idle: pool.idleCount, waiting: pool.waitingCount };
  }
}

Export waiting as a Prometheus gauge; a rising waiting with a flat total at the cap is the exact signature of pool saturation, and it should page before latency does.

Sequelize example

// Sequelize pool with acquire timeout so saturation fails fast
export const sequelize = new Sequelize(process.env.DATABASE_URL!, {
  dialect: 'postgres',
  pool: { max: 8, min: 1, idle: 20_000, acquire: 2_000, evict: 10_000 },
});
// sequelize.connectionManager.pool exposes size, available, using, waiting for metrics

Production scenario

A notifications service fans out to 4 providers. Per pod: 30 connections to the SMS provider (50 ms latency, 300 calls per second cluster-wide across 10 pods), 10 to email, 10 to push, 10 to an internal template service. Pool wait p99 stays under 1 ms in normal operation. During an SMS provider slowdown to 2 seconds, the 30-connection cap held the concurrent calls at 30 per pod, the pending queue guard rejected the overflow with 503, and the service kept email and push flowing. Without the cap, the service would have opened thousands of sockets and stalled everything.

Failure scenario

At 12:05 an internal service's memory grew from 300 MB to 2 GB in ten minutes and pods were OOM-killed. The cause was a pooled axios client whose responses were only read on the success path; every non-2xx response left its body unconsumed, so the socket never returned to the pool. maxSockets was Infinity, so new sockets were opened instead, each holding a response buffer. The fix: consume or dump every response body, set maxSockets, and add a pool-stat gauge.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Unconsumed response bodies leak sockets.
  • Unbounded queues turn a slow dependency into an OOM.
  • A pool per request (creating the agent inside the handler) is not a pool.
  • DNS changes are not seen by warm sockets; bound the socket lifetime (keepAliveMaxTimeout) so a failover is followed within a minute.
  • Behind a NAT gateway, all pods share the gateway's port budget to a single destination.
  • HTTP/1.1 pipelining above 1 is unsafe with most servers; leave it at 1.
  • Retrying on ECONNRESET is safe for idempotent requests and only for the first attempt on a reused socket; a fresh socket that resets indicates a real problem.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

One pooled client per dependency, injected, with caps, timeouts and metrics; never a bare fetch() in a service. They size pools with Little's law and validate under load. They put a queue limit or a circuit breaker in front of every pool so saturation is a fast, visible 503, not a slow collapse. To a product manager: "We keep forty phone lines open to the payment provider. When the provider slowed down, the lines filled and we told the extra callers to try again in a second instead of leaving everyone on hold."

Common mistakes

  • new Agent() per request.
  • maxSockets: Infinity (the http.Agent default).
  • Consuming the body only on success.
  • Total timeouts only, with no connect or headers timeout.
  • Ignoring the pool's pending count until the OOM.

Interview questions

  1. Size an outbound pool for 400 calls per second at 80 ms p50 and 400 ms p99. About 32 in use on average, 160 at p99; cap around 100 to 160 with a queue limit and fail-fast.
  2. Why does an unconsumed response body leak a connection? The socket stays reserved until the body is read or dumped.
  3. Compare http.Agent and undici. undici: faster, separate headers and body timeouts, keep-alive by default, sensible caps; http.Agent: ubiquitous, unlimited sockets by default.
  4. What signal tells you a pool is saturated before latency alarms? Pending or waiting count rising while open connections sit at the cap.
  5. How do warm sockets interact with DNS failover? They keep talking to the old IP; bound socket lifetime.

Practical exercise

Build a NestJS service that calls a mock dependency you control. Make the dependency sleep 2 seconds for 10% of calls. Load test at 300 RPS with an unbounded http.Agent, then with an undici Pool capped at 40 with a pending guard. Acceptance criteria: memory and socket counts for both runs, the p99 latency of the unaffected 90% of calls in each run, and a written pool configuration for production with justification.

10.10 Compression, streaming and chunked transfer

10.10.1 Compression: gzip and Brotli

Concept

HTTP compression shrinks the response body before it goes on the wire. The client advertises what it can decode in Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd; the server picks one, compresses, and sets Content-Encoding: br and Vary: Accept-Encoding. JSON, HTML, CSV and JavaScript compress 5 to 10 times. Images, video, PDFs and already-compressed archives do not compress at all and only burn CPU.

  • gzip (DEFLATE): universal, fast, ratio about 5x on JSON at level 6. Compression costs roughly 30 to 60 MB per second per core at level 6 in Node's zlib.
  • Brotli (br): 15 to 25% smaller than gzip at comparable speed for levels 4 to 5; levels 9 to 11 are far slower and belong to build-time compression of static assets, not dynamic API responses.
  • zstd: newer, fast; browser support arrived in Chrome 123 and Firefox 126, Node has zlib.zstdCompress from v22.15.

Why does it exist?

Bytes on the wire are the lever that latency and loss multiply (10.5). A 900 KB feed becomes 140 KB with gzip; on a lossy 4G link that is the difference between 20 seconds and 2 seconds. Compression also cuts bandwidth cost: cloud egress at about 0.09 USD per GB means a 5x reduction on 50 TB per month saves 3,600 USD.

Mental model

Imagine shipping feathers. Vacuum-packing them (compression) makes the box a fifth the size; it takes a minute per box (CPU) but saves hours of transport (bandwidth). Vacuum-packing a brick (a JPEG) does nothing except waste the minute.

How it works

  1. The client sends Accept-Encoding.
  2. The server decides: is the body compressible (Content-Type text, JSON, JavaScript, SVG)? Is it large enough (below about 1 KB, headers dominate and compression can make it larger)? Does the client accept an encoding we support?
  3. The server streams the body through a compressor. With a known full body, Content-Length is set to the compressed size; with streaming, chunked encoding is used.
  4. Vary: Accept-Encoding tells caches to store compressed and uncompressed variants separately.
  5. The client decompresses transparently; fetch and browsers do this before your code sees the body.

Where to compress. Compression can happen at the CDN, the ALB (ALBs do not compress; CloudFront does), a reverse proxy (NGINX), or the Node process. Node compression costs event-loop-adjacent CPU: zlib runs on the libuv threadpool, so a heavy compression load competes with DNS lookups and fs (10.3). At 500 responses per second of 200 KB each, gzip level 6 uses about 2 full cores. Prefer compressing at the CDN or NGINX when you have one; compress in Node when the API is called directly by clients or when the ALB is the only thing in front.

When NOT to compress.

  • Already-compressed content: images, video, application/zip, application/pdf (mostly), protobuf.
  • Tiny responses (threshold of about 1 KB).
  • Responses carrying secrets alongside attacker-controlled input over TLS: the BREACH attack recovers secrets (CSRF tokens) from compressed sizes. Do not compress responses that reflect user input next to a secret; or rotate tokens per request.
  • Server-Sent Events and long-lived streams where the compressor's buffering delays delivery; either disable, or flush after each event.
  • When CPU is the bottleneck and the network is a fast internal link (service-to-service in one AZ).

Practical example

A catalogue endpoint returns 40 products at 320 KB uncompressed. Enabling Brotli level 4 in the CDN cut it to 41 KB. Time to first render on a 4G phone fell from 2.1 s to 0.9 s. CPU on the NestJS pods was unaffected because the CDN did the work; the origin still sent 320 KB per cache miss, about 3% of requests.

NestJS example

compression middleware for Express, configured with a threshold, a filter that skips streams and binary types, and Brotli preference when the client supports it.

// main.ts (excerpt)
import compression from 'compression';
import { constants } from 'zlib';
import { Request, Response } from 'express';

app.use(
  compression({
    threshold: 1024,                       // do not compress bodies under 1 KB
    level: 6,                              // gzip level; 6 is the speed/ratio sweet spot for dynamic JSON
    brotli: { params: { [constants.BROTLI_PARAM_QUALITY]: 4 } }, // br when accepted; quality 4 for dynamic content
    filter: (req: Request, res: Response) => {
      if (req.headers['x-no-compression']) return false;           // per-request opt-out for debugging
      const type = String(res.getHeader('Content-Type') ?? '');
      if (type.startsWith('text/event-stream')) return false;      // SSE must not be buffered by a compressor
      if (/image|video|zip|pdf|octet-stream/.test(type)) return false; // already compressed
      return compression.filter(req, res);                          // default: text, json, js, svg
    },
  }),
);

The compression package added Brotli support in version 1.8 via the brotli option; on older versions only gzip and deflate are negotiated. For Fastify use @fastify/compress with { encodings: ['br', 'gzip'], threshold: 1024 } registered through app.register.

PostgreSQL example

Compression can begin before HTTP: TOAST compresses large text and jsonb values on disk, and the wire protocol itself is not compressed, so a 2 MB jsonb document travels to the app as 2 MB. If a column is only ever sent to the client as-is, storing it pre-compressed (bytea of gzip) and forwarding with Content-Encoding: gzip saves the database round trip bytes, the app CPU and the response bytes at once.

-- PostgreSQL 14+: choose the TOAST compression per column (lz4 is faster, pglz is default)
ALTER TABLE product_documents ALTER COLUMN body SET COMPRESSION lz4;

-- Inspect what is being compressed on disk
SELECT pg_column_compression(body) AS algo, pg_column_size(body) AS stored_bytes,
       octet_length(body::text) AS raw_bytes
FROM product_documents
ORDER BY raw_bytes DESC
LIMIT 5;

Production scenario

An API at 1,200 RPS with 60 KB average JSON responses: uncompressed egress 72 MB per second, about 186 TB per month; with gzip at the pods, 14 MB per second and roughly 36 TB, saving about 13,000 USD per month at list egress prices, at the cost of about 1.5 cores of zlib CPU across the fleet. Moving compression to CloudFront saved the cores too, since 85% of responses were cache hits served compressed from the edge.

Failure scenario

A team enabled compression() globally, including on a Server-Sent Events endpoint that pushed order status updates. Updates stopped arriving in real time; they appeared in batches every few seconds or on disconnect. The gzip stream buffered output until its internal block filled. The fix was excluding text/event-stream in the filter (and, where compression of SSE is really wanted, calling res.flush() after each event).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Missing Vary: Accept-Encoding: a cache serves a Brotli body to a client that cannot decode it, which looks like corrupted JSON.
  • Double compression: NGINX compresses an already-gzipped Node response; clients get garbage. Compress at exactly one hop.
  • Content-Length mismatch when a middleware sets it before compression changes the body size; let the compressor manage headers.
  • BREACH on responses that mix secrets and reflected input.
  • zlib on the threadpool: heavy compression starves DNS and file reads; raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE or move compression out of Node.
  • Compressing error responses: fine, but ensure the exception filter runs before the compressor writes headers.
  • Range requests (Range: bytes=...) and compression do not mix; ranges refer to the encoded body.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Compress at the edge where possible, in Node when necessary, never twice. Set a threshold, exclude binaries and streams, and always emit Vary. They measure the CPU cost and the byte savings and choose levels accordingly: level 4 to 6, never 9, for dynamic content. To a product manager: "Shrinking every response to a fifth of its size made the app faster on bad networks and cut the bandwidth bill, at the price of some CPU that we moved to the CDN."

Common mistakes

  • Compressing images and PDFs.
  • Compressing SSE.
  • Forgetting Vary.
  • Brotli quality 11 on dynamic responses (10 times slower than gzip for a few percent gain).
  • Enabling compression in both NGINX and Node.

Interview questions

  1. When should you not compress a response? Already-compressed types, tiny bodies, SSE and streams without flushing, secret-plus-reflected-input responses (BREACH), CPU-bound internal calls.
  2. What does Vary: Accept-Encoding prevent? Caches mixing encoded variants.
  3. Where in the AWS path can compression happen, and where would you put it? CloudFront, NGINX, Node; the ALB does not compress. Put it at the CDN if present, else Node with a threshold.
  4. Why does compression in Node affect DNS lookups? Both use the libuv threadpool.
  5. gzip versus Brotli for dynamic JSON? Brotli 4 to 5 gives 15 to 20% smaller output at similar CPU; either is fine, both beat none by a mile.

Practical exercise

Add compression to a NestJS API and measure, for a 300 KB JSON endpoint, the response size and p99 latency at 200 RPS for: none, gzip 6, Brotli 4, Brotli 11. Record pod CPU for each. Then add an SSE endpoint and demonstrate the buffering bug and its fix. Acceptance criteria: a table with size, latency and CPU per configuration, and a filter that excludes SSE and binaries.

10.10.2 Streaming and chunked transfer encoding

Concept

A normal HTTP response has a known size, announced in Content-Length. Chunked transfer encoding (Transfer-Encoding: chunked) lets a server send a body of unknown length as a series of size-prefixed chunks terminated by a zero-length chunk. That is what makes streaming possible: sending the first rows of a 2 GB CSV export before the last rows have been read from the database, with constant memory. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 have no chunked encoding because their framing is inherently streamed; the same NestJS code works on all three because Node handles the framing.

In NestJS, streaming comes in three shapes: StreamableFile (return a Node Readable from a handler and let NestJS pipe it), direct res.write() with @Res(), and Server-Sent Events via @Sse().

Why does it exist?

Without streaming, an export of 5 million orders means loading 5 million rows into memory, serialising a 2 GB string, and only then sending byte one. The pod OOMs, or the client times out at the ALB's 60-second idle limit before seeing any bytes. Streaming keeps memory flat (a few megabytes of buffers), starts the response in milliseconds, and keeps the connection active so idle timeouts never fire.

Mental model

Imagine a factory shipping pallets as they are produced, rather than waiting until the whole order of 10,000 units is finished and renting a warehouse to hold it in the meantime. The truck starts moving after the first pallet; the customer starts receiving in minutes; the factory never needs the warehouse. Chunked encoding is the label on each pallet saying how many units it holds and a final empty pallet meaning "that was the last one".

How it works

  1. The handler sets headers (Content-Type, Content-Disposition) and does not set Content-Length.
  2. Node writes the headers with Transfer-Encoding: chunked (HTTP/1.1) and begins emitting chunks as res.write() is called or as a piped stream produces data.
  3. Backpressure: if the client (or the ALB) reads slower than the server produces, the socket's write buffer fills, res.write() returns false, and a properly piped stream pauses the source (the database cursor) until drain. Ignoring backpressure and calling res.write() in a tight loop buffers the whole body in memory anyway.
  4. The database side must also stream: a cursor (pg-cursor or pg-query-stream) fetches rows in batches of, say, 1,000 rather than the whole result set. A SELECT of 5 million rows without a cursor is loaded into the driver's memory in full.
  5. The final zero-length chunk marks the end. If the server crashes mid-stream, the client sees a truncated body with no terminator, which is detectable; a Content-Length response cut short is detectable too, but a chunked one is explicit.
  6. Trailers (headers after the body) exist in chunked encoding and HTTP/2 and are how gRPC reports status; browsers mostly ignore them.

Interaction with load balancers. An ALB forwards chunks as they arrive, and its 60-second idle timeout counts the gap between bytes, not the total; a stream that sends something at least every few seconds never times out. A stalled stream (waiting 90 seconds on a slow query with nothing written) does. Some proxies buffer responses by default (NGINX proxy_buffering on), which kills the streaming benefit; set proxy_buffering off for streaming routes or send X-Accel-Buffering: no.

Practical example

A finance team requests a CSV of all orders in the last year: 4.2 million rows, 1.1 GB. The naive endpoint OOM-killed the pod at 1.5 GB heap after 40 seconds. The streaming version: a pg-query-stream cursor with a batch size of 2,000, a transform stream that formats each row as a CSV line, gzip, and StreamableFile. First byte after 60 ms, 1.1 GB (140 MB compressed) delivered in about 3 minutes, pod memory flat at 180 MB, and the ALB never timed out because bytes flowed continuously.

NestJS example

// exports.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Header, Query, Res, StreamableFile } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Response } from 'express';
import { Transform } from 'stream';
import { createGzip } from 'zlib';
import { ExportsService } from './exports.service';

@Controller('exports')
export class ExportsController {
  constructor(private readonly exports: ExportsService) {}

  @Get('orders.csv')
  @Header('Content-Type', 'text/csv; charset=utf-8')
  @Header('Content-Disposition', 'attachment; filename="orders.csv"')
  @Header('Content-Encoding', 'gzip')
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'private, no-store')
  @Header('X-Accel-Buffering', 'no') // tell NGINX-style proxies not to buffer
  async orders(@Query('since') since: string, @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response): Promise<StreamableFile> {
    const rows = this.exports.orderRowsSince(new Date(since)); // Readable in objectMode, streamed from a PG cursor

    const toCsv = new Transform({
      objectMode: true,
      transform(row: { id: string; status: string; total_cents: number; created_at: Date }, _enc, cb) {
        cb(null, `${row.id},${row.status},${row.total_cents},${row.created_at.toISOString()}\n`);
      },
    });

    // If the client disconnects, stop the database cursor instead of reading 4 million rows into nothing.
    res.on('close', () => rows.destroy());

    const header = Buffer.from('id,status,total_cents,created_at\n');
    toCsv.push(header);
    return new StreamableFile(rows.pipe(toCsv).pipe(createGzip({ level: 4 })));
  }
}
// exports.service.ts: stream rows from PostgreSQL with a cursor
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Readable } from 'stream';
import { Pool } from 'pg';
import QueryStream from 'pg-query-stream';

@Injectable()
export class ExportsService {
  constructor(private readonly pool: Pool) {}

  orderRowsSince(since: Date): Readable {
    const out = new Readable({ objectMode: true, read() {} });
    this.pool.connect().then((client) => {
      const query = new QueryStream(
        'SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at FROM orders WHERE created_at >= $1 ORDER BY created_at',
        [since],
        { batchSize: 2_000, highWaterMark: 4_000 }, // rows per fetch and buffered rows before pausing
      );
      const stream = client.query(query);
      stream.on('data', (row) => { if (!out.push(row)) stream.pause(); });
      out._read = () => stream.resume();              // backpressure: resume the cursor when the consumer drains
      stream.on('end', () => { out.push(null); client.release(); });
      stream.on('error', (err) => { out.destroy(err); client.release(err); });
      out.on('close', () => { stream.destroy(); client.release(); }); // client went away
    }).catch((err) => out.destroy(err));
    return out;
  }
}

pipe propagates backpressure automatically between rows, toCsv, gzip and the response socket; the manual pause/resume bridges the pg-query-stream cursor into the object-mode Readable. With TypeORM you get the same cursor through queryBuilder.stream(), which returns a ReadStream backed by pg-query-stream.

For Server-Sent Events (order status updates to a browser), NestJS provides @Sse(): return an Observable<MessageEvent>, set no compression, and send a comment line every 15 to 30 seconds as a heartbeat so the ALB idle timeout never fires.

@Sse('orders/:id/events')
events(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string): Observable<MessageEvent> {
  return merge(
    this.orderEvents.forOrder(id).pipe(map((e) => ({ data: e, type: 'status' }) as MessageEvent)),
    interval(20_000).pipe(map(() => ({ data: 'ping', type: 'heartbeat' }) as MessageEvent)), // keeps the ALB idle timer reset
  );
}

PostgreSQL example

The database side of streaming is the cursor. A DECLARE CURSOR with FETCH in batches keeps server memory and client memory flat; pg-query-stream does exactly this using the extended protocol's portal with a row limit.

BEGIN;
DECLARE orders_cur NO SCROLL CURSOR FOR
  SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at >= '2025-09-01'
  ORDER BY created_at;

FETCH FORWARD 2000 FROM orders_cur;   -- first batch
FETCH FORWARD 2000 FROM orders_cur;   -- next batch, and so on
CLOSE orders_cur;
COMMIT;

-- The plan should be an index scan in created_at order, not a sort of 4 million rows,
-- or the first batch waits for the full sort:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at
FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2025-09-01' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 2000;
-- Limit  (cost=0.56..214.92 rows=2000 width=48) (actual time=0.041..3.812 rows=2000 loops=1)
--   ->  Index Scan using orders_created_at_idx on orders  (actual time=0.039..3.402 rows=2000 loops=1)
--         Index Cond: (created_at >= '2025-09-01 00:00:00+00'::timestamptz)
--   Buffers: shared hit=1873
-- Execution Time: 4.102 ms

A cursor holds a transaction (and therefore a snapshot) open for the whole export. On a busy table that blocks VACUUM from reclaiming rows for the duration; keep exports bounded and consider a read replica.

TypeORM example

// Streaming through TypeORM's query builder (returns a pg-query-stream backed ReadStream)
const stream = await this.ds
  .createQueryBuilder()
  .select(['o.id', 'o.status', 'o.total_cents', 'o.created_at'])
  .from(Order, 'o')
  .where('o.created_at >= :since', { since })
  .orderBy('o.created_at', 'ASC')
  .stream();
// stream is a Readable of raw rows; pipe it exactly as in the controller above

Production scenario

A reporting service streams about 900 exports per day, median 80 MB, largest 3 GB. Pod memory during exports stays under 250 MB. Two limits protect the database: a concurrency semaphore of 3 exports per pod and a statement_timeout of 30 minutes on the export role.
