The ALB's idle timeout was raised to 120 seconds for this target group only, because a few exports pause for up to 90 seconds on a slow filter, and the app sends a comment line (# still working) on CSV exports every 20 seconds as a keep-alive when no rows have been emitted.

Failure scenario

At 14:30 the exports pod memory chart went vertical and the pod restarted every three minutes. The streaming endpoint had been changed to add a "total rows" header, which required counting first; the developer implemented it by collecting all rows into an array, computing the length, then writing them. Streaming was gone, and a 2 GB export was back to loading in memory. The review lesson: any code that needs the size before the first byte is not streaming; either run a separate COUNT(*) or send the total in a trailer or a final line.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Client disconnect mid-stream: without res.on('close') cleanup, the cursor runs to completion and the pool connection is held for minutes.
  • Errors after headers are sent: you cannot change the status code to 500; the client sees a truncated body. Validate and pre-check before writing the first byte; use trailers or a final sentinel line for post-hoc errors.
  • Proxies that buffer (proxy_buffering on) defeat streaming and reintroduce timeouts.
  • Compression middleware buffering SSE.
  • HTTP/1.0 clients do not support chunked encoding; Node falls back to Connection: close and streams anyway.
  • ALB idle timeout counts silence between chunks; a slow first query with no output for 60 seconds is a 504.
  • Long-open cursors block VACUUM and hold snapshots; bound export duration.
  • res.write() without checking the return value buffers unbounded data for slow clients (slow-read attacks, 10.15).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Any response that can exceed a few megabytes is streamed, with a cursor on the database side, backpressure end to end, cleanup on client disconnect, and a heartbeat for long-running streams. They know where the proxies buffer and set headers to stop it. They push very large exports to a background job that writes to S3 and returns 202 with a signed URL, because a 3 GB streaming HTTP response is fragile on mobile networks and tie up a pod for minutes. To a product manager: "The report starts downloading immediately and never crashes the server, but for anything above a gigabyte we email a download link instead of holding the connection open for ten minutes."

Common mistakes

  • Collecting all rows before writing.
  • No cursor on the database side.
  • Ignoring backpressure.
  • No cleanup on client disconnect.
  • Streaming through a buffering proxy and wondering why nothing arrives until the end.
  • Streaming SSE through a compressor.

Interview questions

  1. How does chunked transfer encoding work and why does HTTP/2 not need it? Size-prefixed chunks with a zero terminator; HTTP/2 frames are inherently sized.
  2. What is backpressure and what happens if you ignore it when streaming from Postgres to a slow client? The write buffer fills, write() returns false; ignoring it buffers the whole result in memory.
  3. How do you keep an ALB from timing out a long-running streaming response? Emit bytes at least every few seconds (heartbeat), or raise the idle timeout for that target group.
  4. What happens if an error occurs after headers were sent? Status cannot change; the body is truncated; use pre-validation and a trailer or sentinel.
  5. When would you not stream a large export over HTTP at all? Multi-gigabyte or long-running exports: background job, S3, signed URL, 202.

Practical exercise

Implement a streaming CSV export of 2 million synthetic orders using a Postgres cursor, backpressure and gzip. Verify with curl --limit-rate 200k that pod memory stays flat while the client reads slowly, and that killing curl mid-download releases the pool connection within a second. Acceptance criteria: memory graph, pg_stat_activity showing the cursor's backend ending on disconnect, and first byte under 100 ms.

10.11 ETags, conditional requests and Cache-Control

10.11.1 ETags and conditional requests

Concept

An ETag (entity tag) is an opaque string in a response header that identifies the exact version of a resource: ETag: "a3f9c2". A client that has a copy can send it back in a conditional request:

  • If-None-Match: "a3f9c2" on a GET: "only send the body if it changed". If not, the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body.
  • If-Match: "a3f9c2" on a PATCH or PUT: "only apply this change if the resource is still this version". If not, the server answers 412 Precondition Failed. This is HTTP's built-in optimistic concurrency control.

A strong ETag ("a3f9c2") means byte-for-byte identical; a weak ETag (W/"a3f9c2") means semantically equivalent (same data, possibly different encoding). Last-Modified with If-Modified-Since does the same job with a timestamp, at one-second resolution and without the concurrency use.

Why does it exist?

Bandwidth and correctness. A mobile app polling GET /orders/123 every 5 seconds should not download 6 KB each time when the order has not changed; a 304 costs about 200 bytes. And two support agents editing the same order should not silently overwrite each other; If-Match makes the second writer fail with 412, refresh, and retry against the new version.

Mental model

Imagine a library book with an edition number stamped on the spine. Before mailing you a new copy, the library asks "which edition do you have?"; if it is the current one, they just say "you are up to date" (304). Before accepting your proofreading corrections, they ask "which edition did you mark up?"; if a newer edition exists, they refuse (412) and ask you to redo your notes on the new one.

How it works

  1. On GET, the server computes an ETag. Options: a hash of the response body (Express does this by default for non-streamed responses with etag enabled, using a weak ETag), or better, a version number from the database (orders.version or xmin), which costs nothing to compute and works before the body is serialised.
  2. The response carries ETag: "17" (version 17) and a Cache-Control that allows revalidation.
  3. The client stores the body and the ETag. On the next GET, it sends If-None-Match: "17".
  4. The server looks up the current version. If it is still 17, it returns 304 with empty body and the same ETag; if it is 18, it returns 200 with the new body and ETag: "18". The 304 path can skip serialisation and, if the version is in Redis, skip Postgres.
  5. For updates, the client sends PATCH /orders/123 with If-Match: "17". The service does UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND version = 17, incrementing the version. Zero rows affected means someone else got there first: 412.
  6. If-None-Match: * on PUT means "create only if it does not exist", a race-free create.
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Agent A
    participant S as NestJS
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    A->>S: GET /orders/123
    S->>DB: SELECT ... version
    DB-->>S: version 17
    S-->>A: 200 ETag "17"
    A->>S: PATCH /orders/123 If-Match "17"
    S->>DB: UPDATE ... WHERE id=123 AND version=17
    DB-->>S: 1 row, version 18
    S-->>A: 200 ETag "18"
    A->>S: PATCH /orders/123 If-Match "17" from a stale tab
    S->>DB: UPDATE ... WHERE id=123 AND version=17
    DB-->>S: 0 rows
    S-->>A: 412 Precondition Failed

Practical example

A delivery-rider app polls its assigned order every 3 seconds. 20,000 active riders make about 6,700 requests per second. With version-based ETags and the current version cached in Redis, 97% of those requests are 304s served in 0.4 ms without touching Postgres; the remaining 3% are real changes. Egress dropped from 40 MB per second to about 2 MB per second.

NestJS example

An interceptor that implements If-None-Match using a version the handler attaches, and a controller using If-Match for optimistic concurrency.

// etag.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request, Response } from 'express';
import { Observable, of } from 'rxjs';
import { map } from 'rxjs/operators';

export interface Versioned { version: number; }

@Injectable()
export class EtagInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler<Versioned>): Observable<unknown> {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>();
    const res = ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    if (req.method !== 'GET' && req.method !== 'HEAD') return next.handle();

    return next.handle().pipe(
      map((body) => {
        const etag = `"${body.version}"`;                // strong ETag from the DB version, no hashing
        res.setHeader('ETag', etag);
        res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'private, no-cache'); // may store, must revalidate every time
        const inm = req.header('if-none-match');
        if (inm && inm.split(',').map((s) => s.trim()).includes(etag)) {
          res.status(304);
          return undefined;                                // 304 has no body
        }
        return body;
      }),
    );
  }
}
// orders.controller.ts (excerpt)
import { Body, Controller, Get, Headers, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, Patch, PreconditionFailedException, UseInterceptors } from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller('orders')
@UseInterceptors(EtagInterceptor)
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Get(':id')
  get(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string) {
    return this.orders.findOne(id); // returns { ..., version: 17 }
  }

  @Patch(':id')
  async patch(
    @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string,
    @Headers('if-match') ifMatch: string | undefined,
    @Body() dto: UpdateOrderDto,
  ) {
    if (!ifMatch) throw new PreconditionFailedException('If-Match header required'); // or 428 Precondition Required
    const expected = Number(ifMatch.replace(/"/g, ''));
    const updated = await this.orders.updateIfVersion(id, expected, dto);
    if (!updated) throw new PreconditionFailedException('Order was modified by someone else'); // 412
    return updated;
  }
}

Disable Express's default body-hash ETag with app.set('etag', false) when you supply your own, or two ETag headers race.

PostgreSQL example

-- A version column: bump it on every update
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN version integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1;

-- Conditional update: succeeds only if the client saw the current version
UPDATE orders
SET status = $2, version = version + 1, updated_at = now()
WHERE id = $1 AND version = $3
RETURNING id, status, version, updated_at;
-- 0 rows returned means a concurrent update happened: return 412

-- Cheap version lookup for 304 decisions (index-only scan on the primary key plus version)
CREATE INDEX orders_id_version_idx ON orders (id) INCLUDE (version);
SELECT version FROM orders WHERE id = $1;

xmin (the transaction id that last wrote the row) can serve as a free version, but it wraps and changes on any update including background ones; an explicit column is clearer.

TypeORM example

// order.entity.ts
import { Column, Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, VersionColumn } from 'typeorm';

@Entity('orders')
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id!: string;
  @Column() status!: string;
  @VersionColumn() version!: number; // TypeORM increments and checks it on save()
}
// orders.service.ts
async updateIfVersion(id: string, expected: number, dto: UpdateOrderDto): Promise<Order | null> {
  // Explicit conditional UPDATE: portable and returns 0 rows on conflict
  const result = await this.repo
    .createQueryBuilder()
    .update(Order)
    .set({ ...dto, version: () => 'version + 1' })
    .where('id = :id AND version = :expected', { id, expected })
    .returning('*')
    .execute();
  return result.affected === 1 ? (result.raw[0] as Order) : null;
}

repo.save() with a @VersionColumn throws OptimisticLockVersionMismatchError when the loaded entity's version is stale; the query-builder form above lets the client's If-Match header drive the expected version directly.

Sequelize example

// order.model.ts: enable optimistic locking
@Table({ tableName: 'orders', version: true }) // adds a `version` column and checks it on save
export class Order extends Model { ... }

// service
const [affected, rows] = await this.orders.update(
  { ...dto, version: literal('version + 1') },
  { where: { id, version: expected }, returning: true },
);
if (affected !== 1) throw new PreconditionFailedException();

Production scenario

An order-management UI with 300 concurrent agents produced about 12 overwrite incidents per week before If-Match; afterwards it produced about 40 412s per day, each shown as "this order was updated by someone else, please review", and zero silent overwrites. The 304 path on the same API serves 70% of GETs at a p99 of 1.2 ms.

Failure scenario

A team enabled Express's default ETag and CloudFront caching for a personalised endpoint. Express computed the weak ETag from the body, which differed per user, so revalidation was correct, but the Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 they added meant CloudFront served user A's body to user B for a minute. ETags do not fix a wrong Cache-Control; see 10.11.2.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Body-hash ETags require serialising the body even for 304; version-based ETags avoid the work.
  • Compressed responses: the ETag must differ per encoding or be weak; NGINX strips strong ETags when it compresses.
  • If-Match on a resource that does not exist should return 412, not 404, only if the client asserted a specific version; use 404 when the id is unknown.
  • Clients that ignore 412 and retry blindly reintroduce lost updates; the UI must refetch.
  • Weak versus strong comparison: If-None-Match uses weak comparison, If-Match uses strong; a W/ tag can never satisfy If-Match.
  • Multiple ETags in If-None-Match (comma-separated) must all be checked.
  • Version numbers must change on every write, including background jobs, or a 304 lies.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They add a version column to every entity that clients edit, and they expose it as the ETag. They make If-Match mandatory on PATCH for contended resources (428 Precondition Required when missing). They cache the version in Redis so the 304 path is nearly free. To a product manager: "When two agents edit the same order, the second one now sees a warning instead of silently erasing the first one's work."

Common mistakes

  • Relying on the default body-hash ETag for large responses.
  • Sending If-Match with a weak ETag.
  • Treating 412 as a server error in the client.
  • Forgetting to bump the version in bulk updates.

Interview questions

  1. Explain If-None-Match and If-Match and the codes each produces. Revalidation to 304; precondition to 412.
  2. Why prefer a version column over a body hash for ETags? No serialisation for 304, works for concurrency control, cheap to cache.
  3. How do you implement optimistic concurrency in SQL? UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?, check affected rows.
  4. What is the difference between weak and strong ETags and where does it bite? Byte-identical versus semantically equivalent; compression and If-Match.

Practical exercise

Add version-based ETags and If-Match to an orders API. Write a test where two clients read version 17, both PATCH; assert one gets 200 with version 18 and the other 412, and that a GET with If-None-Match: "18" returns 304 without querying Postgres (assert with a query counter or pg_stat_statements). Acceptance criteria: tests green and the 304 path measured under 2 ms.

10.11.2 Cache-Control: browser caches, CDNs and a NestJS interceptor

Concept

Cache-Control tells every cache between your server and the user whether and how long a response may be reused without asking again. The caches are the browser's HTTP cache, corporate proxies, and your CDN (CloudFront, Cloudflare, Fastly). The directives:

Directive Meaning Typical use
public any cache may store it, even if the request had Authorization product catalogue, images
private only the browser may store it; shared caches (CDN) must not user-specific data
no-store do not store anywhere payments, PII, tokens
no-cache may store, but must revalidate (If-None-Match) before every use data that changes but benefits from 304
max-age=N fresh for N seconds in any cache max-age=300 for a category listing
s-maxage=N overrides max-age for shared caches only CDN caches 1 hour, browser 1 minute
stale-while-revalidate=N serve stale for up to N seconds while fetching fresh in the background hide origin latency on popular items
stale-if-error=N serve stale for N seconds if the origin errors resilience against origin outages
must-revalidate once stale, must not be served without revalidating correctness-sensitive data
immutable will never change; do not revalidate even on reload fingerprinted assets app.8f3a.js

Freshness is decided by max-age and the response Age header (how long a cache has held it); an expired cached copy may still be used for revalidation via ETag. Expires is the older absolute-date form; Cache-Control wins when both exist. Vary (10.7.2) determines the cache key alongside the URL.

Why does it exist?

Origin capacity and latency. A CDN with a 95% hit rate turns 20,000 RPS at the edge into 1,000 RPS at your NestJS pods, and serves users from a node 10 ms away instead of a region 150 ms away. Getting it wrong in the safe direction (no-store on everything) wastes that. Getting it wrong in the dangerous direction (public on personalised data) leaks one user's data to another; that is a breach, and it has happened at large companies.

Mental model

Imagine a newspaper stand (the CDN) near your house and the printing press (your API) across the country. max-age is how long the stand may sell yesterday's paper before ordering a new one. private means the paper has your name on it and the stand must not resell it. no-store means it is a bank statement: hand it over and keep nothing. stale-while-revalidate lets the stand sell you the slightly old edition while a new one is already on the truck.

How it works

flowchart LR
    B["Browser cache"] -->|"miss or stale"| E["CDN edge"]
    E -->|"hit and fresh"| B
    E -->|"miss or stale"| O["ALB and NestJS origin"]
    O -->|"200 with Cache-Control and ETag"| E
    E -->|"stores if public and cacheable"| E
    E -->|"revalidate with If-None-Match"| O
    O -->|"304 refresh TTL"| E
  1. Browser checks its cache: fresh (max-age not exceeded) means no request at all, 0 ms.
  2. Stale in browser: it sends If-None-Match; a 304 from the CDN or origin refreshes it for a few hundred bytes.
  3. CDN checks its cache by key (URL plus Vary headers, plus whatever the CDN's cache policy includes, such as query strings or selected headers). Fresh: served from the edge, typically 5 to 30 ms from the user. Stale with stale-while-revalidate: served immediately, refreshed in the background.
  4. Miss: the CDN forwards to the origin, stores the response if Cache-Control allows (public or no private/no-store, and a max-age or s-maxage), and returns it.
  5. Purge: invalidation by path or by surrogate key (Cache-Tag or Surrogate-Key headers on Fastly/Cloudflare; CloudFront invalidations by path pattern, which take about a minute and cost money in volume). Design for short TTLs plus revalidation rather than relying on purges.

Which responses are safe to cache where:

Response Header Reason
Product detail, public public, max-age=60, s-maxage=600, stale-while-revalidate=300 CDN holds 10 minutes, browsers 1 minute, background refresh
Category listing with pagination public, max-age=30, s-maxage=120 changes often, still worth caching at the edge
Fingerprinted JS/CSS public, max-age=31536000, immutable URL changes when content changes
GET /me, GET /orders (user data) private, no-cache plus ETag browser may keep it, must revalidate; CDN never stores
POST /payments, tokens, PII exports no-store never on disk anywhere
Search results with Authorization private, max-age=0 personalised ranking; do not let public leak it
Health checks, feature flags no-store or max-age=5 freshness matters

Two traps: a response to a request with an Authorization header is not stored by shared caches unless public or s-maxage is present, so adding public to "make it faster" on an authenticated endpoint is the leak. And CDNs default to caching by URL only; if your response varies by Accept-Language or a cookie and you do not include that in Vary and in the CDN cache policy, users get each other's variants.

Practical example

A grocery app's GET /products/:id is called 15,000 times per second during a sale. With public, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=60 and version-based ETags, CloudFront's hit rate is 97%; the NestJS pods see 450 RPS, of which half are 304 revalidations. Price changes are propagated by bumping the product version and purging by Cache-Tag: product-8812, so a price update is visible at the edge within 2 seconds while the default TTL stays 5 minutes.

NestJS example

A decorator-driven interceptor that applies safe defaults and explicit per-route policies, and refuses public on responses to authenticated requests unless the route opts in.

// cache-control.decorator.ts
import { SetMetadata } from '@nestjs/common';
export const CACHE_POLICY = 'cache_policy';
export interface CachePolicy {
  scope: 'public' | 'private' | 'no-store';
  maxAge?: number; sMaxAge?: number; swr?: number; immutable?: boolean; noCache?: boolean;
}
export const CacheControl = (policy: CachePolicy) => SetMetadata(CACHE_POLICY, policy);
// cache-control.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';
import { Request, Response } from 'express';
import { Observable } from 'rxjs';
import { tap } from 'rxjs/operators';
import { CACHE_POLICY, CachePolicy } from './cache-control.decorator';

@Injectable()
export class CacheControlInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(private readonly reflector: Reflector) {}

  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>();
    const res = ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    const policy = this.reflector.getAllAndOverride<CachePolicy | undefined>(CACHE_POLICY, [ctx.getHandler(), ctx.getClass()]);

    return next.handle().pipe(
      tap(() => {
        if (req.method !== 'GET' && req.method !== 'HEAD') { res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'no-store'); return; }
        const authenticated = Boolean(req.header('authorization') || req.header('cookie'));
        // Safe default: authenticated GETs are private and revalidated; anonymous GETs are not cached unless declared.
        const p: CachePolicy = policy ?? (authenticated ? { scope: 'private', noCache: true } : { scope: 'no-store' });
        if (p.scope === 'public' && authenticated && !policy) p.scope = 'private'; // never leak by accident

        const parts: string[] = [p.scope];
        if (p.scope !== 'no-store') {
          if (p.noCache) parts.push('no-cache');
          if (p.maxAge !== undefined) parts.push(`max-age=${p.maxAge}`);
          if (p.sMaxAge !== undefined && p.scope === 'public') parts.push(`s-maxage=${p.sMaxAge}`);
          if (p.swr !== undefined) parts.push(`stale-while-revalidate=${p.swr}`);
          if (p.immutable) parts.push('immutable');
        }
        res.setHeader('Cache-Control', parts.join(', '));
        res.setHeader('Vary', 'Accept-Encoding'); // add Accept-Language or others when the body depends on them
      }),
    );
  }
}
// products.controller.ts (excerpt)
@Get(':id')
@CacheControl({ scope: 'public', maxAge: 60, sMaxAge: 600, swr: 300 })
product(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string) { return this.products.findOne(id); }

@Get('me/recommendations')
@CacheControl({ scope: 'private', maxAge: 30 })
recommendations(@Req() req: Request) { return this.reco.forUser(req.user.id); }

Register the interceptor globally (APP_INTERCEPTOR) so no route ships without a policy. The @nestjs/cache-manager CacheInterceptor is a different thing: it caches responses inside the process or Redis; it does not set HTTP headers. Use both when appropriate: server-side caching for expensive computations, Cache-Control for edge and browser caching.

PostgreSQL example

Edge caching changes the database's load shape: writes that must be visible quickly need a signal to purge or bump. A version and an updated_at on cached entities, plus a trigger or application event that publishes purges, keep the CDN honest.

-- Track versions for ETags and purge tags
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN version integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1;

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION bump_product_version() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  NEW.version := OLD.version + 1;
  NEW.updated_at := now();
  PERFORM pg_notify('product_changed', NEW.id::text); -- a listener issues the CDN purge by Cache-Tag
  RETURN NEW;
END $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER products_version_trg BEFORE UPDATE ON products
FOR EACH ROW WHEN (OLD.* IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.*) EXECUTE FUNCTION bump_product_version();

Production scenario

A media-heavy marketplace: CloudFront serves 98% of image bytes and 91% of API GETs for catalogue endpoints. Origin egress fell from 60 TB to 6 TB per month. During a 40-minute origin outage (a bad deploy), stale-if-error=600 kept the catalogue browsable from the edge; only checkout, which is no-store, was down. The post-incident review called the caching policy the reason the outage was a revenue dip and not a blackout.

Failure scenario

At 10:15 support tickets said "I can see someone else's cart". A developer had added Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 to a new GET /cart endpoint, copying it from the products controller. The CDN cached the first user's cart under the URL /cart and served it to everyone for 60 seconds at a time. The fix took one line; the incident took a day of customer communication and a breach assessment. The follow-up was the global interceptor above with the "never public when authenticated unless explicitly declared" rule and an e2e test that asserts private or no-store on every route that uses an auth guard.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • public on authenticated responses: data leak.
  • Missing Vary: wrong-language or wrong-encoding responses served from cache.
  • Cache key includes query string order: ?a=1&b=2 and ?b=2&a=1 are two entries; normalise at the CDN.
  • Cache stampede: when a popular item expires, thousands of misses hit the origin simultaneously; stale-while-revalidate and request coalescing at the CDN (CloudFront does this per edge) mitigate.
  • Purge lag: CloudFront invalidations take 10 to 60 seconds; use short s-maxage plus revalidation for anything time-sensitive.
  • Browser no-cache versus no-store confusion: no-cache stores and revalidates; no-store stores nothing.
  • max-age=0 still lets caches keep a copy for revalidation; that is fine and intended.
  • Error responses cached: a 500 with a default max-age from the CDN can pin an outage; set no-store on errors and configure CDN error TTLs to a few seconds.
  • Cookies on cacheable responses: many CDNs refuse to cache any response with Set-Cookie; strip session cookies from public endpoints.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They classify every endpoint into public-cacheable, private-revalidate, or no-store before it ships, with a default that fails safe. They use short TTLs at the edge with stale-while-revalidate and versioned ETags rather than long TTLs and purges. They add stale-if-error so the CDN carries them through origin incidents. They test cache headers in CI. To a product manager: "Ninety-five percent of catalogue views never reach our servers, which is why a sale that triples traffic costs us almost nothing, and why a personalised page must never be marked as shareable."

Common mistakes

  • Copying public headers onto personalised endpoints.
  • no-store on everything, throwing away the CDN.
  • Forgetting Vary.
  • Relying on purges for correctness.
  • Caching error responses.

Interview questions

  1. no-cache versus no-store? no-cache may store but must revalidate; no-store never stores.
  2. When does a shared cache store a response to a request with Authorization? Only with explicit public or s-maxage; that is the leak vector.
  3. Explain stale-while-revalidate and where it helps. Serve stale while refreshing; hides origin latency and absorbs stampedes on expiry.
  4. How do you make a price change visible at the edge within seconds while keeping a 10-minute TTL? Purge by tag or path on write, or short s-maxage with ETag revalidation.
  5. Design cache headers for /products/:id, /me, and /payments. public, max-age=60, s-maxage=600, swr; private, no-cache with ETag; no-store.

Practical exercise

Put a NestJS API behind a local CDN emulator or NGINX proxy_cache. Implement the interceptor above, then write e2e tests that assert: a public product is served from cache on the second request (check X-Cache or Age), an authenticated /me is never cached by the proxy, a 500 is not cached, and a product update becomes visible within 2 seconds via version-based revalidation. Acceptance criteria: all four assertions green, and a table of hit rates from a 5-minute load test.

10.12 TLS: encryption, certificates and where to terminate

Concept

TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the protocol that turns http:// into https://. It gives three things: confidentiality (nobody on the path can read the bytes), integrity (nobody can alter them undetected), and authentication (the client knows it is talking to the real api.shop.com, proven by a certificate signed by a certificate authority the client trusts). TLS 1.2 (2008) and TLS 1.3 (2018) are the versions in use; 1.0 and 1.1 are disabled everywhere serious. "SSL" is the old name; the protocol has been TLS for over twenty years but the word survives in library names.

A certificate binds a public key to one or more names (CN and Subject Alternative Names), is signed by a CA, and expires (90 days for Let's Encrypt and, since 2026, the industry is moving all public certificates towards short lifetimes). SNI (Server Name Indication) is the client saying which hostname it wants in the first handshake message so one IP can serve many certificates. mTLS (mutual TLS) adds a client certificate so the server authenticates the client too.

Why does it exist?

Without TLS, every password, session cookie and order travels in plain text across ISPs, coffee-shop Wi-Fi and cloud backbones, and any hop can rewrite a response. Browsers now mark plain HTTP as insecure and refuse Secure cookies and many APIs without it. Inside a VPC the risk is lower, but compliance regimes (PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2) and the reality of shared cloud networks mean traffic to the database and between services is usually encrypted too.

Mental model

Imagine sending a locked box. First, you and the recipient agree on a lock only you two can open (key exchange), using a tamper-proof method even if someone watches you agree (Diffie-Hellman). The recipient shows an ID card signed by a passport office you trust (the certificate) so you know the box goes to the right person. From then on, every parcel is locked with the shared key. TLS 1.3 made the agreement faster: one exchange instead of two.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server ALB
    Note over C,S: TLS 1.3 full handshake, 1 RTT
    C->>S: ClientHello with SNI, supported ciphers, key share, ALPN h2 http/1.1
    S->>C: ServerHello, key share, certificate chain, CertificateVerify, Finished
    Note over C: verify chain to trusted root, check name and expiry, derive keys
    C->>S: Finished plus first encrypted HTTP request
    S->>C: Encrypted HTTP response
    Note over C,S: TLS 1.2 needs 2 RTT: ClientHello, ServerHello and cert, ClientKeyExchange, Finished
  1. ClientHello. The client lists the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports, includes the hostname (SNI, in plain text unless Encrypted Client Hello is used), the protocols it wants via ALPN (h2, http/1.1), and, in 7.3, its ephemeral key share.
  2. ServerHello. The server picks the version and cipher, sends its key share, its certificate chain (leaf plus intermediates; the root is already on the client), a signature proving it holds the private key, and Finished. In 1.3 everything after ServerHello is already encrypted.
  3. Verification. The client checks that the chain leads to a trusted root, that the leaf's names include the requested hostname, that the current time is inside the validity window (this is where clock skew bites, 10.15), and optionally revocation (OCSP stapling). A failed check is CERT_HAS_EXPIRED, UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE (missing intermediate), or ERR_TLS_CERT_ALTNAME_INVALID (wrong name).
  4. Key derivation. Both sides derive symmetric session keys from the exchanged shares. The heavy asymmetric work (ECDHE plus a signature) is roughly 0.3 ms of CPU with ECDSA P-256 or 1 to 2 ms with RSA-2048 per handshake.
  5. Application data. Encrypted with AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 at gigabytes per second per core with hardware acceleration; bulk encryption is not the expensive part.
  6. Resumption. A returning client presents a session ticket; TLS 1.3 resumes in 1 RTT and can send data in 0-RTT (replayable; only for idempotent requests). TLS 1.2 resumes in 1 RTT instead of 2.

Where to terminate. Terminating means decrypting. Options:

Model Where TLS ends Pros Cons
Edge termination CDN or ALB; plain HTTP to pods inside the VPC central certificates (ACM auto-renews), no CPU in Node, HTTP/2 at the edge plaintext inside the VPC; compliance may forbid
Re-encryption ALB terminates, then new TLS to pods encrypted everywhere; ALB still sees HTTP for routing two handshakes; certificates on pods too
Passthrough NLB forwards TCP; Node terminates end-to-end, client cert visible to the app no Layer 7 routing at the LB; Node does the crypto CPU; certificate rotation on every pod
Service mesh mTLS sidecars terminate and originate zero-trust inside the cluster, identity per service operational complexity; extra hop and latency

The common production choice: ACM certificate on the ALB (auto-renewed, ECDSA where supported), HTTP/1.1 in plain text between the ALB and pods inside private subnets, TLS to RDS (sslmode=verify-full) and to Redis (in-transit encryption), and mTLS only where a service mesh or a partner integration demands it.

Cost. ALB TLS handshakes are metered as part of LCU usage; on Node, each RSA handshake is about 1.5 ms of CPU, meaning a pod doing 500 handshakes per second spends most of a core on TLS. Keep-alive and edge termination make that disappear. Bulk encryption of a 100 KB response is under 0.1 ms.

Practical example

api.shop.com resolves to an ALB with an ACM certificate for api.shop.com and *.shop.com. The listener on 443 uses the ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 policy (TLS 1.3 preferred, 1.2 allowed). The HTTP listener on 80 redirects to 443 with 301. Pods listen on plain HTTP 3000, reachable only from the ALB's security group. The NestJS app connects to RDS with ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: true, ca: rdsCaBundle }, so a spoofed database endpoint would fail verification.

NestJS example

Three things to get right in the app: honour the ALB's X-Forwarded-Proto so redirects and Secure cookies behave, verify TLS to the database and to outbound APIs, and, when the app must terminate TLS itself, do it with modern settings and hot-reloaded certificates.

// main.ts: app behind an ALB that terminates TLS
import helmet from 'helmet';
app.set('trust proxy', 1);                       // req.secure and req.protocol come from X-Forwarded-Proto
app.use(helmet({ hsts: { maxAge: 31_536_000, includeSubDomains: true, preload: true } })); // Strict-Transport-Security
// database TLS: verify the RDS certificate chain, never rejectUnauthorized: false in production
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
TypeOrmModule.forRoot({
  type: 'postgres',
  host: process.env.PG_HOST,
  ssl: {
    rejectUnauthorized: true,
    ca: readFileSync('/etc/ssl/certs/rds-global-bundle.pem', 'utf8'),
  },
  // ... other options
});
// self-terminating TLS (NLB passthrough or no LB): NestJS with httpsOptions and cert reload
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import { Server } from 'https';
import { constants } from 'crypto';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const load = () => ({
    key: readFileSync('/certs/tls.key'),
    cert: readFileSync('/certs/tls.crt'),             // leaf plus intermediates, in that order
  });
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule, {
    httpsOptions: {
      ...load(),
      minVersion: 'TLSv1.2',
      secureOptions: constants.SSL_OP_NO_TLSv1 | constants.SSL_OP_NO_TLSv1_1,
      honorCipherOrder: true,
    },
  });
  const server = app.getHttpServer() as Server;
  // cert-manager or ACM rotates files on disk; pick them up without a restart
  setInterval(() => server.setSecureContext(load()), 60 * 60 * 1000).unref();
  await app.listen(443, '0.0.0.0');
}
bootstrap();

server.setSecureContext() is a real Node https.Server and tls.Server method; it swaps the certificate for new connections without dropping existing ones.

PostgreSQL example

-- Is my session encrypted, and with what? (requires the sslinfo extension or pg_stat_ssl)
SELECT s.pid, s.ssl, s.version, s.cipher, a.client_addr
FROM pg_stat_ssl s JOIN pg_stat_activity a USING (pid)
WHERE a.backend_type = 'client backend';

-- Enforce TLS for application users in pg_hba.conf:
-- hostssl  orders  app_user  10.0.10.0/23  scram-sha-256
-- hostnossl all     all       0.0.0.0/0     reject

-- Server-side settings
SHOW ssl;                  -- on
SHOW ssl_min_protocol_version; -- TLSv1.2

Connection strings should use sslmode=verify-full so the client checks both the chain and the hostname; sslmode=require encrypts but does not authenticate the server, which permits a man-in-the-middle inside the network.

Production scenario

An API cluster serving 3,000 RPS behind an ALB performs about 40 client TLS handshakes per second (keep-alive and HTTP/2 do the rest). The ALB handles it; the pods do none. When a partner required mTLS for a webhook endpoint, the team put that single path on a separate ALB listener with the ALB's mutual TLS verify mode and an S3 trust store, and the app read the validated client certificate fields from X-Amzn-Mtls-Clientcert-Subject, avoiding TLS passthrough for the whole service.

Failure scenario

At 00:00 UTC on a Tuesday, every request to internal-payments.shop.com began failing with CERT_HAS_EXPIRED. That internal service used a manually issued one-year certificate that nobody had put in a calendar; ACM was not involved because the service sat behind an NLB with passthrough. Pods restarted in a loop because the readiness check called the service. Recovery took 55 minutes: issue a new certificate, push a secret, roll the deployment. The permanent fix moved the service behind an ALB with an ACM certificate, and added a Prometheus alert from the blackbox exporter on probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry below 14 days for every endpoint, internal and external.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Expired certificates, missing intermediates (works in browsers that cache intermediates, fails in Node with UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE), wrong SAN after a hostname change.
  • Clock skew: a client 10 minutes ahead rejects a freshly issued certificate as not yet valid; a container with a broken NTP is enough (10.15).
  • Root CA rotation: RDS rotated its CA bundle in 2024; apps that pinned the old CA lost database connectivity on a schedule announced months earlier.
  • rejectUnauthorized: false left in production: silent loss of authentication, and an audit finding.
  • SNI missing from custom clients (older net-based tools) leads to the default certificate and a name mismatch.
  • TLS handshake CPU under a new-connection storm (mobile retry storms, 10.15) saturates pods that terminate TLS themselves.
  • OCSP responder outages: with hard-fail revocation checking, a CA outage takes your site down; stapling with soft-fail is the usual compromise.
  • Mixed content: a page over HTTPS calling an API over HTTP is blocked by the browser.
  • HSTS preload is effectively permanent; a subdomain that must stay HTTP will be unreachable.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Terminate at the edge with managed certificates, encrypt to data stores with verification, and add mTLS only where identity between services is a real requirement. Automate issuance and renewal (ACM, cert-manager with Let's Encrypt), and alert on expiry for every certificate including internal ones. Never disable verification to make an error go away. To a product manager: "Every certificate is a passport with an expiry date. We used to renew them by memory; now a robot renews them and a second robot checks the first one did."

Common mistakes

  • rejectUnauthorized: false.
  • Manual certificates without expiry monitoring.
  • sslmode=require instead of verify-full.
  • Terminating TLS in Node behind an ALB for no reason and paying the CPU.
  • Forgetting the intermediate certificate in the chain file.

Interview questions

  1. Compare TLS 1.2 and 1.3 handshakes. 1.3 is 1 RTT with forward-secret key exchange only and encrypted server certificate; 1.2 is 2 RTT with optional RSA key exchange. Follow-up: what is 0-RTT and its risk? Replay.
  2. Where would you terminate TLS in an ALB plus NestJS plus RDS setup, and why? ALB with ACM, plaintext in private subnets, TLS with verification to RDS; central rotation and no Node CPU.
  3. What does SNI solve? Multiple certificates behind one IP; the client names the host before the certificate is chosen.
  4. How does mTLS differ and when is it worth it? Client certificates authenticate the caller; worth it for service meshes and partner integrations, costly operationally.
  5. A Node service fails with UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE while browsers work. Why? Missing intermediate in the server's chain; browsers fetch or cache intermediates, Node does not.
  6. How do you monitor certificate expiry? Blackbox exporter probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry, ACM expiry events, cert-manager metrics, alert at 14 days.

Practical exercise

Generate a private CA with openssl, issue a server certificate for api.local, and run NestJS with httpsOptions and setSecureContext reloading. Connect with curl --cacert and with a Node client using a custom ca. Then issue a certificate that expired yesterday and observe the error at each client. Finally set the container clock 15 minutes ahead with faketime and observe. Acceptance criteria: a table of error messages per failure, a working hot-reload demonstrated by rotating the certificate without restarting, and a Prometheus alert rule for expiry.

10.13 CORS: why the browser blocks your API and how NestJS enables it

Concept

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser mechanism. An origin is the scheme plus host plus port (https://app.shop.com). By default, JavaScript running on one origin may not read responses from another origin; that is the same-origin policy. CORS is the set of response headers a server sends to relax that rule for specific origins, methods and headers. It is enforced by browsers only; Postman, curl, mobile apps and other servers ignore it completely. CORS is not an authentication or access-control mechanism for your API; it protects users' browsers from malicious sites reading data from your API using the user's cookies.

Why does it exist?

Without the same-origin policy, evil.com could load in your browser and use fetch('https://bank.com/accounts') with your bank cookies attached, reading your balance. The policy blocks reading the response. CORS exists because legitimate apps do need cross-origin calls: app.shop.com calling api.shop.com. The server declares which origins are allowed and the browser enforces it.

Mental model

Imagine a receptionist at your API's building who only talks to visitors carrying a badge from an approved company. A stranger without a badge can still shout a question through the door (the request is sent), but the receptionist will not hand over the answer to them (the browser hides the response). And for unusual requests, the visitor must first ask "are you willing to accept a DELETE with a custom header from my company?" (the preflight).

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant JS as Browser at app.shop.com
    participant API as api.shop.com NestJS
    Note over JS,API: simple request, no preflight
    JS->>API: GET /products Origin: https://app.shop.com
    API-->>JS: 200 Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.shop.com
    Note over JS,API: non simple request, preflight first
    JS->>API: OPTIONS /orders Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method PATCH, Access-Control-Request-Headers content-type authorization
    API-->>JS: 204 Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods PATCH, Allow-Headers, Allow-Credentials true, Max-Age 600
    JS->>API: PATCH /orders/1 with JSON body and cookie
    API-->>JS: 200 Allow-Origin, Allow-Credentials true, Expose-Headers ETag
  1. The browser adds an Origin header to every cross-origin request.
  2. Simple requests (GET, HEAD, POST with Content-Type of application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain, and only safe-listed headers) are sent immediately. The response is delivered to JavaScript only if Access-Control-Allow-Origin matches the origin (or is * and the request had no credentials).
  3. Non-simple requests (PUT, PATCH, DELETE, Content-Type: application/json, an Authorization header, custom headers like Idempotency-Key) trigger a preflight: the browser sends OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers, and only sends the real request if the response allows them. Access-Control-Max-Age caches the preflight for up to 2 hours in Chrome (600 seconds is common), so a chatty API does not pay an extra round trip per call.
  4. Credentials (cookies, Authorization set by the browser, TLS client certs) are sent cross-origin only when the request sets credentials: 'include' and the response has Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true with an explicit origin, never *.
  5. Exposed headers: JavaScript can read only a safe-listed set of response headers (Content-Type, Cache-Control, and a few more) unless Access-Control-Expose-Headers names others, such as ETag, X-Request-Id, Location.
  6. The server still executes non-preflighted requests; CORS only hides the response. That is why CSRF protection (SameSite cookies, tokens) is separate from CORS.

Key facts:

  • The Origin in a CORS response must be a single exact value; to allow several origins, echo the request's origin after checking it against an allow-list, and add Vary: Origin so caches do not serve one origin's headers to another.
  • A * origin cannot be combined with credentials.
  • Preflights are OPTIONS requests that reach your app unless the gateway or CDN answers them; they must not require authentication.
  • Mobile apps and server-to-server calls never send preflights and never see CORS errors; the same API works for them regardless.
  • A "CORS error" in the console with a 5xx behind it is usually not a CORS bug: the error response lacked the headers because the exception filter or the gateway did not add them.

Practical example

app.shop.com (a React SPA) calls api.shop.com with a session cookie. The API allows origins https://app.shop.com and https://admin.shop.com, methods GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE, headers Content-Type, Authorization, Idempotency-Key, If-Match, exposes ETag, X-Request-Id, Location, allows credentials, and caches preflights for 10 minutes. A preview deployment at pr-812.preview.shop.com is allowed by a regex in non-production only.

NestJS example

// main.ts (excerpt)
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);

  const allowList = (process.env.CORS_ORIGINS ?? 'https://app.shop.com,https://admin.shop.com').split(',');
  const previewPattern = process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' ? /^https:\/\/pr-\d+\.preview\.shop\.com$/ : null;

  app.enableCors({
    origin: (origin, callback) => {
      // No Origin header: same-origin, curl, mobile, server-to-server. Allow (CORS does not apply).
      if (!origin) return callback(null, true);
      if (allowList.includes(origin) || previewPattern?.test(origin)) return callback(null, true);
      // Not allowed: respond without CORS headers so the browser blocks it; do not throw 500.
      return callback(null, false);
    },
    methods: ['GET', 'HEAD', 'POST', 'PATCH', 'DELETE', 'OPTIONS'],
    allowedHeaders: ['Content-Type', 'Authorization', 'Idempotency-Key', 'If-Match', 'X-Request-Id'],
    exposedHeaders: ['ETag', 'X-Request-Id', 'Location', 'Retry-After'],
    credentials: true,            // required for cookie sessions; origin must then be explicit, never *
    maxAge: 600,                  // cache preflights for 10 minutes
    optionsSuccessStatus: 204,
  });

  await app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0');
}
bootstrap();

enableCors accepts the same options as the cors package; origin as a function is what lets you echo the exact origin (with Vary: Origin, which the package adds). Make sure the global exception filter still lets the CORS headers through on error responses; because cors runs as early middleware, headers are set before the handler and survive an exception, but a gateway in front that generates its own 502 will not have them, which is why users see "CORS error" during outages.

For Fastify use @fastify/cors via app.register(fastifyCors, { ... }) with the same option names.

PostgreSQL example

CORS has no database angle. The one operational touch: if the allow-list lives in a table so that tenants can register their own origins (a white-label storefront product), cache it in memory with a short TTL, because the origin check runs on every cross-origin request and every preflight.

CREATE TABLE tenant_origins (
  tenant_id  uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id),
  origin     text NOT NULL CHECK (origin ~ '^https://[a-z0-9.-]+(:[0-9]+)?$'),
  PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, origin)
);
-- Load all origins at startup and refresh every 60 s; never query per request
SELECT origin FROM tenant_origins;

Production scenario

A public API with 40,000 browser users sees about 6% of its requests as OPTIONS preflights with maxAge: 600; without maxAge it was 38%, and the extra round trip added 50 to 150 ms to every first call in a burst. Preflights are answered in under 1 ms because they short-circuit before guards and never hit the database.

Failure scenario

At 09:05 a frontend deploy switched the SPA from www.shop.com to app.shop.com. Every API call failed in the browser with "blocked by CORS policy", while Postman worked fine and the API dashboards showed no errors, because the API executed every simple GET and simply omitted the headers. The allow-list was a hard-coded array in main.ts. The fix was adding the origin via the CORS_ORIGINS environment variable and redeploying, 20 minutes of a broken site for a one-line config. The follow-up moved the allow-list to configuration with a CI check that every frontend origin in the infrastructure repo is present.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials: true is rejected by browsers; cookie-based APIs need explicit origins.
  • Reflecting any Origin back unconditionally (origin: true) with credentials means any site can read a logged-in user's data; that is a vulnerability, not a convenience.
  • Preflight requires authentication: a guard applied to OPTIONS returns 401 and the browser reports a CORS failure.
  • Missing Vary: Origin on cached responses leaks one origin's allow header to another.
  • Custom headers not in allowedHeaders (a new X-Client-Version) break every call from the browser with a preflight failure.
  • Redirects during preflight are not allowed; a 301 from HTTP to HTTPS on the API origin breaks CORS if the frontend uses the wrong scheme.
  • localhost and 127.0.0.1 are different origins; http://localhost:3000 and http://localhost:5173 are different origins.
  • Error responses from the gateway or CDN lack CORS headers, so a 503 looks like a CORS error to the user; configure the gateway to add them.
  • CORS does not stop CSRF: a cross-site POST form submission is not a CORS request at all. Use SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat CORS as a browser safety feature, configured tightly (explicit origins, explicit headers, credentials only when needed, preflight caching), sourced from configuration, tested in CI, and applied at one layer only. They know that "CORS error" is a symptom to trace, not a diagnosis. They pair it with real CSRF protection and never mistake it for authorisation. To a product manager: "The browser refused to hand our own frontend the answers because the API's guest list still had the old address. Nothing was broken on the server; it was a list."

Common mistakes

  • origin: '*' or origin: true on an API with cookies.
  • Hard-coding origins in code.
  • Applying auth guards to OPTIONS.
  • No maxAge, doubling request count.
  • Debugging CORS with Postman, which does not enforce it.
  • Believing CORS protects the API from non-browser clients.

Interview questions

  1. What triggers a preflight, and how do you reduce their cost? Non-simple methods, application/json, custom or Authorization headers; Access-Control-Max-Age.
  2. Why can you not use * with credentials? Browsers refuse it; it would let any site read authenticated data.
  3. Is CORS a security control for your API? No; it protects browser users. Non-browser clients ignore it; use authentication and CSRF defences.
  4. A user reports a CORS error during an outage. What is likely happening? The gateway's 5xx lacks CORS headers; the real problem is the outage.
  5. How do you support multiple origins with cookies? Allow-list check, echo the exact origin, Vary: Origin, credentials: true.
  6. What is the difference between CORS and CSRF protection? CORS hides responses from other origins; CSRF protection stops other origins from causing state changes with the user's cookies.

Practical exercise

Serve a small HTML page from http://localhost:5173 that calls a NestJS API on http://localhost:3000 with fetch(..., { credentials: 'include' }) using PATCH and a custom header. Configure enableCors step by step until it works, observing each browser error message in DevTools. Then add a second allowed origin from an environment variable and write an e2e test that asserts the preflight response headers for allowed and disallowed origins. Acceptance criteria: a list of the distinct browser error messages you triggered and their causes, and green tests for both the allowed and blocked cases.

10.14 What exactly happens when I call a NestJS API from a browser or Postman?

Concept

Everything in this part comes together in one request. A user on a phone in Pune taps "My orders". The app calls GET https://api.fooddash.com/v1/orders?limit=20. About 220 milliseconds later, a list appears. This section traces every step between those two moments, with realistic timings, the actual bytes on the wire, and a budget showing where the 220 ms went. Postman follows the same path with two differences: it has no browser DNS cache and no same-origin policy, so no CORS preflight.

DNS -> TCP -> TLS -> HTTP -> Load Balancer -> NestJS -> Database -> Response

Why does it exist?

You cannot optimise, debug or size what you cannot see. Engineers who think a request is "controller, service, query" will look for a 200 ms problem in code that takes 8 ms. The trace is the map: it tells you which layer to suspect, which tool to use, and which fix is worth doing. It is also the single most common senior interview question in backend engineering, in some form.

Mental model

Imagine ordering food by phone from a restaurant in another city. You look up the number (DNS), dial and wait for someone to pick up (TCP), agree on a private language so nobody listening can understand (TLS), state your order (HTTP request), the receptionist routes it to the right kitchen (load balancer), a cook checks your ID and reads the order (NestJS middleware, guards, pipes), walks to the storeroom for ingredients (database), plates it (serialisation), vacuum-packs it (gzip), and the delivery comes back the same road. Every step has a duration; most of them are travel time, not cooking.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant R as DNS resolver
    participant LB as ALB
    participant N as NestJS pod
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    B->>B: cache check for api.fooddash.com
    B->>R: A and AAAA query
    R-->>B: 13.234.10.7 TTL 60
    B->>LB: TCP SYN
    LB-->>B: SYN-ACK
    B->>LB: ACK plus TLS ClientHello with SNI and ALPN
    LB-->>B: ServerHello, certificate, Finished
    B->>LB: Finished plus HTTP/2 HEADERS GET /v1/orders
    LB->>LB: listener rule match, pick healthy target
    LB->>N: HTTP/1.1 GET /v1/orders with X-Forwarded-For
    N->>N: middleware, guard, pipe, handler
    N->>PG: checkout pooled connection, SELECT
    PG-->>N: 20 rows
    N->>N: serialize, gzip
    N-->>LB: 200 chunked gzip
    LB-->>B: HTTP/2 DATA frames
    B->>B: decompress, JSON.parse, render

The numbered narrative, with timings for a phone on 4G in Pune, an ALB and NestJS in ap-south-1 (Mumbai), and RDS in the same AZ. RTT phone to ALB: 45 ms. RTT pod to database: 0.4 ms.

  1. The app builds the request (0 ms). fetch('/v1/orders?limit=20', { credentials: 'include' }). The browser decides this is a cross-origin GET with no custom headers, so no CORS preflight. If the app had added an Authorization header, an OPTIONS preflight would go first and cost a full extra round trip unless cached by Access-Control-Max-Age.

  2. Browser DNS cache (0 ms). Chrome checks its internal host cache (about 60 seconds). The app resolved this name two minutes ago, so it is stale.

  3. OS resolver (0.2 ms). getaddrinfo checks /etc/hosts equivalent and the OS cache. Miss.

  4. Recursive resolver (12 ms). The phone asks the carrier's resolver (or 8.8.8.8 with private DNS). The resolver had the record cached from another user with 40 seconds of TTL left, so no recursion: 12 ms is the round trip to the resolver. A cold recursion (root, .com, Route 53) would be 60 to 120 ms. Route 53 answers A 13.234.10.7 and AAAA 2406:da1a:...; the phone is IPv6-capable and, with Happy Eyeballs, tries both and keeps the first to connect.

  5. TCP three-way handshake (45 ms, 1 RTT). SYN to the ALB's address on port 443, SYN-ACK, ACK. The ALB is an anycast-free regional endpoint; its nodes sit in two public subnets. The connection is now ESTABLISHED on both sides; the ALB node's kernel accepted it, no application yet.

  6. TLS 1.3 handshake (45 ms, 1 RTT, plus about 1 ms of CPU each side). ClientHello with SNI api.fooddash.com and ALPN h2, http/1.1; the ALB picks the ACM certificate for that name, replies ServerHello plus certificate plus Finished. The phone validates the chain to a trusted root, checks the name and expiry, sends Finished, and the first HTTP bytes ride in the same flight. ALPN selected h2, so this is HTTP/2. On a repeat visit within the ticket lifetime, resumption keeps it at 1 RTT; TLS 1.2 would have cost 2.

  7. HTTP request on the wire (0.5 ms to serialise, then travels with step 6's last flight). In HTTP/2 the request is a HEADERS frame with HPACK-compressed pseudo-headers. Logically it is this request; what the ALB forwards to the pod, translated to HTTP/1.1, is byte-for-byte close to:

GET /v1/orders?limit=20 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.fooddash.com
X-Forwarded-For: 2406:da1a:9c0:1b2::4f
X-Forwarded-Proto: https
X-Forwarded-Port: 443
X-Amzn-Trace-Id: Root=1-66db3f2a-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718293a4b5
Accept: application/json
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br
Accept-Language: en-IN,en;q=0.9
Cookie: __Host-sid=s%3A9f2c1a...; 
If-None-Match: "4127"
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Linux; Android 14) ... Chrome/128
Origin: https://app.fooddash.com

  1. ALB listener and rules (1 ms). The HTTPS:443 listener's rules run in priority order: rule 1 path is /v1/* forwards to target group orders-api-prod; rule 10 host is admin.fooddash.com forwards elsewhere; the default returns a fixed 404. The ALB then picks a target from the healthy set using round robin (or least outstanding requests, if configured). Health: the target group checks GET /health/ready on port 3000 every 10 seconds, needs 2 consecutive successes to mark healthy and 2 failures to mark unhealthy, and only healthy targets receive traffic. If zero targets are healthy, the ALB returns 503 itself, without touching a pod. The ALB reuses an existing keep-alive connection to the chosen pod; a new one costs a 0.3 ms handshake inside the VPC.

  2. ALB to pod (0.5 ms RTT inside the VPC). Plain HTTP/1.1 on port 3000 into a private subnet; the pod's security group allows TCP 3000 only from the ALB's security group. The pod's kernel accept queue hands the socket to Node's event loop.

  3. Node HTTP parser (0.1 ms). llhttp parses the request line and headers into IncomingMessage. Express (under NestJS) builds req and res, lowercases headers, and applies trust proxy: 1, so req.ip is the last X-Forwarded-For value, the phone's IPv6 address.

  4. NestJS request pipeline (0.4 ms before the handler). In order: global middleware (RequestIdMiddleware generates or accepts X-Request-Id; express-session reads the cookie, verifies the signature, and fetches sess:9f2c1a from Redis in 0.3 ms), then guards (SessionAuthGuard confirms session.userId), then interceptors' "before" phase (TimeoutInterceptor starts a 10-second timer, EtagInterceptor and CacheControlInterceptor wait for the response), then pipes (ValidationPipe turns limit=20 into a number and checks it is between 1 and 100), and finally the handler OrdersController.list.

  5. Service and pool checkout (0.05 ms when a connection is idle; up to the pool's connectionTimeoutMillis when it is not). OrdersService.recentForUser(userId, 20) calls the repository; TypeORM asks the pg pool for a client. With 10 connections per pod and a p99 concurrency of 6, checkout is immediate. If all 10 were busy, this request would queue here, invisible to the database and visible only as pool.waitingCount.

  6. Query (0.4 ms network RTT plus 1.6 ms in Postgres). The driver sends a Parse/Bind/Execute sequence over the pooled TLS connection. Postgres plans (or reuses a prepared plan), scans orders_user_created_idx, joins 20 orders to their items, and returns 20 rows of about 300 bytes each. pg_stat_statements shows a mean of 1.6 ms for this query shape.

  7. Serialisation (0.6 ms). TypeORM hydrates entities; the service maps them to a response DTO with class-transformer's @Expose fields; JSON.stringify produces 6.2 KB. The EtagInterceptor attaches ETag: "4131" from the newest order's version; the client's If-None-Match: "4127" does not match, so a full 200 goes out. CacheControlInterceptor sets private, no-cache because a cookie is present.

  8. Compression (0.3 ms). The compression middleware sees Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br, a JSON body over the 1 KB threshold, and compresses 6.2 KB to about 1.1 KB with gzip level 6. Content-Encoding: gzip, Vary: Accept-Encoding, and chunked encoding are set because the compressed length is not known up front.

  9. Response on the wire, pod to ALB (0.5 ms). What the pod sends:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Encoding: gzip
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
ETag: "4131"
Cache-Control: private, no-cache
Vary: Accept-Encoding, Origin
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.fooddash.com
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Access-Control-Expose-Headers: ETag,X-Request-Id
X-Request-Id: 7f3a9c1e-2b1d-4a5e-9c0f-1e2d3c4b5a69
Date: Mon, 07 Sep 2026 06:12:41 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=65

45c
<1116 bytes of gzip data>
0

  1. ALB to phone (45 ms, half an RTT for the first byte, plus transmission). The ALB re-frames the response as HTTP/2 HEADERS and DATA frames, drops Connection and Transfer-Encoding (illegal in HTTP/2), and sends. 1.1 KB fits in one packet; no slow-start ramp is needed. The phone's radio was already awake from the request.

  2. Browser processing (3 ms). Decompress, JSON.parse 6.2 KB, hand to the app's state store, React re-render, paint. The user sees the list.

Where did 220 ms go. The numbers above sum to about 205 ms of network and CPU; the remaining margin is jitter on the mobile link. The budget:

Step Time Share Who owns it Lever
DNS (resolver RTT, cached upstream) 12 ms 5% carrier, Route 53 TTL longer browser session, keep-alive so it happens rarely
TCP handshake 45 ms 20% physics, region choice keep-alive, HTTP/2, region near users
TLS 1.3 handshake 45 ms 20% physics, ALB session resumption, keep-alive, 0-RTT for idempotent GETs via HTTP/3
Request bytes to ALB included above 0% small headers, HPACK, no preflight
ALB rule match, target selection 1 ms 0.5% ALB few rules, healthy targets
ALB to pod hop 0.5 ms 0.2% VPC same AZ, keep-alive to targets
Node parse plus NestJS pipeline (session lookup in Redis 0.3 ms) 0.5 ms 0.2% app keep middleware lean
Pool checkout 0.05 ms 0% app sized pool; alert on waiting
Postgres query plus round trip 2.0 ms 1% app and DB index, one round trip, column selection
Serialisation and interceptors 0.6 ms 0.3% app small DTOs
gzip 0.3 ms 0.1% app threshold, level 6
Response first byte to phone 45 ms 20% physics same as handshake levers
Response transmission (1.1 KB) about 1 ms 0.5% link compression, pagination
Browser decompress, parse, render 3 ms 1.4% frontend small payloads
Jitter, queueing on radio link about 15 ms 7% carrier nothing; budget for it
Total about 220 ms

Read the shares: about 150 ms, 70% of the total, is three mobile round trips (TCP, TLS, request-response). The application, database and serialisation together are under 4 ms, under 2%. On a warm connection (keep-alive, HTTP/2 stream on an existing connection), steps 2 to 6 vanish and the same request completes in about 50 to 60 ms: one RTT plus 4 ms of work. That is why keep-alive, HTTP/2 at the edge, and putting the region near the user are worth more than any query optimisation for this endpoint, and why the same endpoint measured from a pod in the cluster reports 4 ms and misleads everyone.

A 304 path (the client's If-None-Match matches) skips steps 13 to 15 on a version cached in Redis and returns about 200 bytes; on a warm connection it is a 46 ms request that costs the server 0.5 ms.

Practical example

Postman on a laptop in the office (fibre, 18 ms RTT to Mumbai), same endpoint, cold: DNS 9 ms (office resolver), TCP 18 ms, TLS 18 ms, request-response 18 ms plus 4 ms of work, total about 70 ms. Postman shows this in its timing tab as "DNS lookup", "TCP handshake", "SSL handshake", "Transfer start" (time to first byte) and "Download". The same call from a Kubernetes pod in the cluster: 0.3 ms TCP, 0.6 ms TLS, 4 ms work, about 5 ms total. Three clients, three very different numbers, one server that did the same 4 ms of work each time.

NestJS example

The instrumentation that makes this trace visible in production: a middleware that records server-side timing per phase and returns it in a Server-Timing header so the browser DevTools and Postman show where server time went, and a readiness endpoint that reflects the health of the dependencies the ALB should care about.

// server-timing.middleware.ts
import { Injectable, NestMiddleware } from '@nestjs/common';
import { NextFunction, Request, Response } from 'express';
import { performance } from 'perf_hooks';

@Injectable()
export class ServerTimingMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  use(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
    const start = performance.now();
    const marks: Record<string, number> = {};
    // Services call req.mark('db', ms) to record phase timings
    (req as Request & { mark: (name: string, ms: number) => void }).mark = (name, ms) => {
      marks[name] = (marks[name] ?? 0) + ms;
    };
    res.on('finish', () => void 0);
    const original = res.writeHead.bind(res);
    res.writeHead = ((...args: Parameters<typeof res.writeHead>) => {
      const total = performance.now() - start;
      const parts = Object.entries(marks).map(([k, v]) => `${k};dur=${v.toFixed(1)}`);
      parts.push(`app;dur=${total.toFixed(1)}`);
      res.setHeader('Server-Timing', parts.join(', ')); // shown in DevTools Network > Timing
      return original(...args);
    }) as typeof res.writeHead;
    next();
  }
}
// orders.service.ts (excerpt): mark the database phase
async recentForUser(req: Request & { mark: (n: string, ms: number) => void }, userId: string, limit: number) {
  const t0 = performance.now();
  const rows = await this.repo.recentForUser(userId, limit);
  req.mark('db', performance.now() - t0);
  return rows.map(toOrderDto);
}
// health.controller.ts: what the ALB target group polls
@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  constructor(private health: HealthCheckService, private db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator, private mem: MemoryHealthIndicator) {}

  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    return this.health.check([
      () => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 1_000 }),   // SELECT 1 through the pool: catches dead pools
      () => this.mem.checkHeap('heap', 900 * 1024 * 1024),       // stop taking traffic before OOM
    ]);
  }

  @Get('live')
  live() { return { status: 'ok' }; } // Kubernetes liveness: process is alive, never checks dependencies
}

With OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation (@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node), the same phases appear as spans (http.server, express.middleware, pg.query) under one trace whose id arrived in the traceparent header, and the ALB's X-Amzn-Trace-Id links the access log line to it.

PostgreSQL example

The query from step 13, with the plan that makes it 1.6 ms rather than 160 ms, and the statistics view that tells you its real-world mean.

-- The endpoint's query (parameterised; $1 user, $2 limit)
SELECT o.id, o.status, o.total_cents, o.version, o.created_at,
       COALESCE(json_agg(json_build_object('sku', i.sku, 'qty', i.qty) ORDER BY i.id)
                FILTER (WHERE i.id IS NOT NULL), '[]') AS items
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.user_id = $1
GROUP BY o.id
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
LIMIT $2;

-- Supporting indexes
CREATE INDEX orders_user_created_idx ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX order_items_order_id_idx ON order_items (order_id);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)  -- with $1 = a real user id, $2 = 20
-- Limit  (actual time=0.612..1.418 rows=20 loops=1)
--   ->  GroupAggregate  (actual time=0.610..1.409 rows=20 loops=1)
--         Group Key: o.id
--         ->  Nested Loop Left Join  (actual time=0.048..0.981 rows=83 loops=1)
--               ->  Index Scan using orders_user_created_idx on orders o  (actual time=0.031..0.142 rows=21 loops=1)
--                     Index Cond: (user_id = '3b1c...'::uuid)
--               ->  Index Scan using order_items_order_id_idx on order_items i  (actual time=0.009..0.021 rows=4 loops=21)
--                     Index Cond: (order_id = o.id)
--   Buffers: shared hit=167
-- Planning Time: 0.210 ms
-- Execution Time: 1.472 ms

-- What this query costs across the fleet
SELECT calls, round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS mean_ms, round(max_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS max_ms, rows
FROM pg_stat_statements
WHERE query LIKE 'SELECT o.id, o.status, o.total_cents%'
ORDER BY calls DESC LIMIT 1;
-- calls    | mean_ms | max_ms | rows
-- 18442310 | 1.63    | 212.4  | 368846200

The max_ms of 212 ms is the tail: lock waits or a cold cache after a failover. It matters for the p99, not the p50, and it is the number to chase after the network levers are exhausted.

Production scenario

For this endpoint at 1,400 RPS across 12 pods: browser-measured p50 210 ms cold, 58 ms warm; server-side p50 3.9 ms, p99 24 ms; ALB TargetResponseTime p99 26 ms; Postgres mean 1.6 ms. 62% of requests arrive on warm HTTP/2 connections, 31% are 304s. Dashboards show all four latencies side by side; when the browser number moves and the server number does not, the problem is in the first 150 ms of the budget and the fix is not in the code.

Failure scenario

At 19:40 the client-side p50 for "My orders" jumped from 210 ms to 640 ms while server-side p50 stayed at 4 ms. Every layer of the app looked healthy. The trace showed the extra 430 ms in step 6: TLS handshakes were happening on every request. A CDN configuration change earlier that day had set Connection: close on responses passing through it, so every call opened a new connection: DNS, TCP and TLS on each. Reverting the CDN change restored warm connections. The team added the browser-measured "connection reuse rate" from the Navigation Timing API to their dashboards, because the server could not have seen this at all.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A preflight adds a fourth round trip on the first call; caching it with Access-Control-Max-Age matters on mobile.
  • A cold recursive DNS lookup adds 60 to 120 ms; a stale TTL after failover sends the request to a dead IP and the TCP SYN times out for seconds (10.15).
  • Zero healthy targets: the ALB returns 503 at step 8, in 1 ms, with no pod involved.
  • A full pool: step 12 waits up to connectionTimeoutMillis; the trace shows a gap between the handler start and the query start.
  • A dead pooled socket (half-open): step 13 hangs until statement_timeout or keepalive detects it.
  • Keep-alive race: step 9 hits a socket the pod just closed; the ALB returns 502 and the pod logs nothing.
  • Missing Vary or wrong Cache-Control: a CDN in the path serves another user's orders at step 17.
  • Slow start on a cold connection makes a 200 KB response take four extra round trips; the 1.1 KB gzip body here fits in one packet.
  • Event-loop lag on the pod adds to every step between 10 and 15 at once; tail latency rises fleet-wide when one endpoint serialises a large object synchronously.
  • Node's JSON.stringify of a 5 MB payload at step 14 blocks the loop for tens of milliseconds and stalls other requests on that pod.
  • A Postman "Cloud agent" runs from a different geography than your laptop, so its timings differ from local runs.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They can recite this trace and put a number next to every line for their own system. They measure at four points (browser, ALB, app, database) and compare. They spend their effort in proportion to the budget: connection reuse and region placement first, payload size second, query time third. They know which 5xx comes from which box. When asked "why is the API slow?", their first question is "slow from where, and on a warm or cold connection?". To a product manager: "Our servers answer in four milliseconds. The other two hundred are the distance to the phone and the three handshakes we need before we can talk. We are cutting those by keeping the line open and moving closer to the user."

Common mistakes

  • Benchmarking from inside the cluster and reporting 4 ms as user latency.
  • Optimising a 1.6 ms query while every call pays a 90 ms handshake pair.
  • Adding an Authorization header (and thus a preflight) to an endpoint that could use the session cookie, without caching the preflight.
  • Health checks that hit dependencies the pod does not need, causing the ALB to drop healthy pods.
  • Not exporting Server-Timing or trace ids, so the browser and server numbers cannot be joined.

Interview questions

  1. Walk through what happens when a browser calls an HTTPS API, with approximate timings on mobile. DNS (0 to 120 ms), TCP (1 RTT), TLS 1.3 (1 RTT), request and response (1 RTT), plus a few ms of server work; on a warm connection only the last RTT remains. Why it matters: it demonstrates layered thinking and where latency really lives. Follow-ups: what changes with HTTP/2, HTTP/3, a CDN, a preflight?
  2. Server p50 is 4 ms, users see 200 ms. Where is the time, and what do you do? Round trips and handshakes; reuse connections, HTTP/2 at the edge, region placement, compression, 304s.
  3. Describe the NestJS request pipeline order. Middleware, guards, interceptors (before), pipes, handler, interceptors (after), exception filters.
  4. Which component returns 503 when no pod is healthy, and how do you tell? The ALB; access log shows elb_status_code=503 with no target status.
  5. What does the ALB change in the request before your app sees it? Adds X-Forwarded-* and X-Amzn-Trace-Id, translates HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1, strips hop-by-hop headers, may reuse a connection shared by many clients.
  6. How would you instrument this path so browser and server timings can be correlated? Request id and W3C traceparent propagated end to end, Server-Timing on responses, ALB access logs joined by trace id, RUM in the app.

Practical exercise

Deploy a NestJS orders endpoint behind an ALB (or NGINX with TLS and HTTP/2). Capture the full trace three ways: curl -w with time_namelookup, time_connect, time_appconnect, time_starttransfer and time_total from a laptop and from a pod; Chrome DevTools timing for the same call cold and warm; and an OpenTelemetry trace with Server-Timing. Build the "where did the time go" table for your own system. Acceptance criteria: the table sums to within 10% of the measured total for both the cold and warm cases, and you can name the single change that would remove the largest slice.

10.15 Edge cases and failure modes across networking

Concept

This section is the incident catalogue for everything in Part 10. Each entry follows the same shape: what the on-call sees, what is actually happening in which layer, how to prove it in minutes, and the fix that stops it recurring. These are not hypothetical. Every one of them has paged a real team, usually at night, and usually with application dashboards that looked perfectly healthy.

The senior mantra applies to the network exactly as it applies to code: Can it timeout? Can it fail? Can it become slow? Can it duplicate? Can it return a wrong response? Can it partially succeed? The network answers "yes" to all six, every day.

Why does it exist?

Application code is deterministic and testable; the network between two processes is neither. Most backend engineers spend their training on the deterministic half and meet the other half for the first time during an outage. Having a catalogue turns a 90-minute investigation into a 10-minute one, because the shapes repeat: "healthy app, failing users" has about a dozen causes and they are all in this list.

Mental model

Imagine a hospital's differential diagnosis chart: a set of symptoms points to a short list of conditions, each with a test that confirms or rules it out. "Server healthy, users failing" is the fever; the tests are dig, ss, the ALB access log, openssl s_client, tcpdump, and the sysctl values on the node.

How it works

The quick diagnosis matrix:

Symptom First suspect Confirming test
Timeouts to a service that recently failed over stale DNS dig +short name from the client host versus authoritative; compare with the connection's remote IP
